절: A5.1 Decompositions and their hardware character

A5.1 Decompositions and their hardware character

[Table 1. Matrix decompositions as IP blocks]
Decomposition | Form | Cost | Streaming? | Numerical character
LU | A = LU | n 3 /3 | No (pivoting needs lookahead) | Needs pivoting for stability
Cholesky | A = LL * | n 3 /6 | Yes | No pivoting needed for SPD; half the work of LU
QR (Givens) | A = QR | 2 mn 2 | Yes | Backward stable; rotations are well conditioned
QR (Householder) | same | fewer ops | Less so | Best stability
SVD | A = UΣV * | iterative | No | Most robust ; reveals rank and conditioning
Eigen (symmetric) | A = QΛQ * | iterative | No | Jacobi parallelises well
Schur / Hessenberg | — | n 3 | No | Control applications

The streaming column is the commercial column.
 Cholesky and Givens QR touch each input element once and can therefore be built with
 an hls::stream-style interface and no external memory; SVD and LU must
 revisit the array and therefore need an AXI master and a buffer. That single
 architectural difference changes the IP's integration story, its area, and its price.
 When a customer asks for “a matrix inverse block”, the first engineering
 question is whether the matrix is symmetric positive definite — because if it
 is, Cholesky gives a streaming solution at half the arithmetic, and if it is not, you
 are quoting a much larger block.

장: A5. Linear Algebra and Numerical Methods for Hardware
절: A5.2 Conditioning
글:
A5.2 Conditioning

κ(A) = σmax/σmin
     relative error ≲ κ(A) · εmachine

The rule of thumb that follows is directly usable:
 you lose roughly log10κ decimal digits. In fixed point,
 substitute ε = 2−F for F fractional bits and the
 statement becomes a word-length requirement:
 F ≳ log2κ + (bits of accuracy required). This is how a
 modelling engineer converts a mathematical property of the customer's data into a
 hardware parameter. It also explains why iterative refinement works: solve in
 low precision, compute the residual in high precision, correct, repeat. Each
 iteration roughly squares the accuracy, so three refinements from a rough start can
 reach near-full precision — but only if the condition number is modest, because
 κ enters the convergence factor. Measured behaviour: for a well-conditioned
 (isotropic) system the scheme reached 24.2 bits of accuracy; at correlation 0.99 it
 reached only 12.4 bits. An IP that advertises mixed-precision refinement must
 therefore state a conditioning limit, or it will fail at a customer whose data is
 correlated.

절: A5.3 Iterative solvers and their hardware mapping
글:
A5.3 Iterative solvers and their hardware mapping

[Table 2. Iterative methods]
Method | Update | Parallelism | Convergence
Jacobi | uses only previous iterate | Fully parallel | Slow; needs diagonal dominance
Gauss–Seidel | uses updated values immediately | Sequential within a sweep | Roughly twice Jacobi's rate
SOR | over-relaxed GS | Sequential | Tunable ω
Conjugate gradient | Krylov subspace | Parallel (dot products) | n steps exactly; √κ in practice
Richardson | x ← x + α( b − Ax ) | Fully parallel | Simplest; α must be tuned

There is a physical realisation worth knowing because it
 is repeatedly rediscovered and mis-described. An RC network that solves
 C dv/dt = −(Av − b) settles to
 A−1b, and is often presented as an “analogue
 Gauss–Seidel solver”. It is not: because all nodes evolve
 simultaneously from the same previous state, the continuous-time limit corresponds to
 Jacobi / Richardson, not Gauss–Seidel, which is defined by sequential
 in-sweep updates. The settling time is governed by
 1/λmin, i.e. by the condition number again. Under a normalisation
 that fixes λmax = 1, the measured settling-time-to-condition
 ratio was constant at 13.2 — the analogue solver buys constant factors, not
 asymptotic ones. Being able to state this precisely prevents a design house from
 accepting a proposal whose speedup claim rests on a misidentification.

장: A1. Signals, Systems and Linearity
절: A1. Signals, Systems and Linearity — 들어가며
글:
A1. Signals, Systems and Linearity

Every digital IP block is a system: it maps input sequences to
 output sequences. Before discussing any particular block we fix the vocabulary that
 makes such maps analysable, and — more importantly for a hardware engineer
 — we identify exactly which property of a system makes it cheap to
 build and which makes it expensive.

장: A1. Signals, Systems and Linearity
절: A1.1 Definitions
글:
A1.1 Definitions

[Table 3. System properties and their hardware consequences]
Property | Definition | Hardware consequence
Memoryless | y [ n ] depends only on x [ n ] | Pure combinational logic; no registers, no state to reset or scan
Causal | y [ n ] depends only on x [ k ], k  ≤  n | Required for real-time streaming. Non-causal filters are realised by adding latency , not by seeing the future
Linear | Superposition holds | Enables decomposition into impulse responses; permits frequency-domain design
Time-invariant | Delay in → same delay out | Coefficients are constants → can be hard-wired or stored once
BIBO stable | Bounded input → bounded output | ∑| h [ n ]| 
[그림] Figure 1. An LTI system is completely characterised by its impulse response. This single fact underpins all filter design.

The practical importance of linearity is not elegance but
 separability of verification. If a block is LTI you can characterise it with a
 single impulse and predict its response to every input; a random-stimulus campaign is
 then a redundancy check rather than the primary evidence. If it is not LTI
 — a decision-feedback equaliser, a μ-law compander, a saturating accumulator,
 any adaptive loop — superposition fails and you must verify over the operating
 region, which is exponentially more work. The first architectural question about
 any new block is therefore "where exactly is the nonlinearity?" Isolating it into
 the smallest possible sub-block is a verification cost decision, not an aesthetic
 one.

[Table 4. Realisations of the same convolution]
Method | Operations per output | Latency | When preferred
Direct convolution | N MACs | 0 (plus pipeline) | N ≲ 64
Overlap-add FFT | ~(2 log 2 L + 1) per sample | One block ( L samples) | Long filters; latency tolerable
Overlap-save FFT | Same order | One block | Streaming; avoids add stage
Frequency-domain adaptive | FFT + per-bin update | One block | Long adaptive filters (echo cancellation)

The crossover between direct and FFT-based convolution is
 not a fixed number of taps; it depends on the cost ratio of a multiplier to a
 memory word in the target technology, and on whether block latency is acceptable.
 In an ASIC at an advanced node, multipliers are comparatively cheap and SRAM is
 comparatively expensive, which pushes the crossover up. On an FPGA with hard
 DSP slices and abundant block RAM it moves the other way. Quoting a fixed
 crossover (“use FFT above 128 taps”) without naming the technology is a
 common and costly error in architecture documents.

장: A1. Signals, Systems and Linearity
절: A1.3 Correlation, matched filtering and the origin of SNR gain
글:
A1.3 Correlation, matched filtering and the origin of SNR gain

Cross-correlation is convolution with a time-reversed conjugated
 kernel. When the kernel is the transmitted pulse itself, the operation is a
 matched filter, and it maximises output SNR for a signal in additive white
 Gaussian noise.

SNRout,max = 2Es / N0

The result is worth internalising because it recurs in
 radar, in spread spectrum, in synchronisation preambles and in every correlator IP.
 The gain comes from integrating signal coherently while noise adds
 incoherently: over M samples, signal amplitude grows as M while
 noise amplitude grows as √M, hence power SNR improves by M
 (10 log10M dB). Two engineering consequences follow.
 First, coherent integration requires phase stability over the integration
 window; if the oscillator drifts, gain saturates — this is the practical
 limit on radar integration time and on preamble length. Second, the correlator's
 dynamic range must accommodate the M-fold growth, which is a fixed-point
 word-growth problem, not a signal-processing one.

장: A1. Signals, Systems and Linearity
절: A1.4 Group delay, phase linearity and why FIR dominates
글:
A1.4 Group delay, phase linearity and why FIR dominates

τg(ω) = − dφ(ω)/dω

A filter has linear phase when τg is
 constant: all frequency components are delayed equally, so pulse shapes are preserved
 and only shifted. An FIR filter with symmetric (or antisymmetric) coefficients has
 exactly linear phase. An IIR filter cannot, except trivially.

This is the decisive argument for FIR in data
 transmission. Non-constant group delay spreads a pulse asymmetrically, which is
 indistinguishable from channel dispersion and therefore directly closes the eye. In
 audio the ear is comparatively insensitive to phase and IIR is preferred for its
 efficiency; in a wireline receiver an IIR equaliser would introduce the very
 distortion it is meant to remove. The same mathematics leads to opposite
 engineering choices in two domains, and knowing why is the difference between
 applying a rule and understanding it. Note also the hardware corollary: symmetric
 FIR coefficients permit the folded structure that halves the multiplier count,
 so linear phase is not only free, it is cheaper.

|p| 1 | Divergent | Unusable
|p| → 1 − | Very narrow band; long memory | Coefficient quantisation can push the pole outside — the classic failure mode of high-order direct-form IIR

Quantifying the last row: for a direct-form IIR of order
 N, the sensitivity of pole pi to a denominator coefficient
 ak is
 ∂pi/∂ak =
 −piN−k /
 ∏j≠i(pi−pj).
 The denominator is a product of pole separations: clustered poles make the
 sensitivity explode. Cascaded second-order sections avoid this because each
 section contains only one conjugate pair, so no small separations appear in its own
 denominator. This is the quantitative reason behind the universal practice of
 implementing high-order IIR filters as cascaded biquads, and it is worth being able
 to state it rather than merely follow it.

[Table 7. Noise sources in silicon]
Mechanism | Spectrum | Expression | Design lever

kT/C | Sampled | v 2 = kT / C | Independent of resistance ; only C helps

Why flicker noise sets the architecture of precision
 analogue. 1/f noise is not reducible by filtering, because it lives at the
 frequencies where the signal of interest often lives (DC to kHz). The standard
 responses — chopping and auto-zeroing — both work by moving the signal
 to a higher frequency where only white noise remains, and both require digital
 support: a chopping clock, demodulation, and residual-ripple filtering. In a modern
 mixed-signal IP the digital half of that scheme is a well-defined block with a clean
 interface, and it is again a piece that a digital design house can own.

[Table 8. Jitter taxonomy used in link specifications]
Type | Symbol | Statistics | Cause | How it is separated
Random jitter | RJ | Gaussian, unbounded | Thermal, flicker | Fit tails of the bathtub curve
Deterministic jitter | DJ | Bounded | — | Peak-to-peak; decomposed below
Periodic | PJ | Sinusoidal | Supply coupling, spurs | FFT of the jitter sequence
Data-dependent | DDJ / ISI | Pattern-correlated | Channel loss | Compare per-pattern edge times
Duty-cycle distortion | DCD | Two-valued | Rise/fall asymmetry, threshold offset | Even/odd UI comparison
Bounded uncorrelated | BUJ | Bounded, random | Crosstalk | Statistical separation
Total jitter at BER | TJ(BER) | RJ⊗DJ convolution | — | TJ = DJ + 2·Q(BER)·RJ rms

The last row is the one that appears in every SerDes
 specification, and the factor Q(BER) is why: at BER 10−12,
 Q = 7.03, so TJ = DJ + 14.07 RJrms.
 Random jitter is multiplied by fourteen. This is why a small improvement in
 oscillator phase noise is worth a large amount of design effort, and why jitter
 separation — distinguishing RJ from DJ in a measurement — is a required
 capability rather than a nicety. A modelling engineer asked to produce a link budget
 must implement this convolution correctly; adding RMS values in quadrature, which is
 the intuitive move, is wrong because DJ is bounded and does not add that way.

장: A4. Probability, Random Processes and Noise
절: A4.4 Random processes
글:
A4.4 Random processes

[Table 9. Concepts and their use]
Concept | Statement | Use in IP design
Stationarity (WSS) | Mean constant, autocorrelation depends on lag only | Precondition for spectral analysis
Ergodicity | Time average = ensemble average | Justifies measuring one long record instead of many devices
Wiener–Khinchin | PSD = FT of autocorrelation | Links time and spectrum
Markov chain | Memoryless state evolution | Bus arbitration analysis, FIFO occupancy, error models
Gauss–Markov | Correlated Gaussian | Coloured noise models
Cyclostationarity | Statistics periodic in time | All digitally modulated signals ; exploited for blind synchronisation
Point process | Random event times | Soft errors, packet arrivals

Cyclostationarity is the theoretical basis for
 blind timing and carrier recovery: a modulated signal has periodically varying
 statistics at the symbol rate, so a suitable nonlinearity produces a spectral line at
 that rate even though the signal itself has no such line. Gardner and Mueller–Müller
 timing detectors are practical exploitations of this. Knowing the principle rather
 than the recipe is what lets an engineer design a detector for a modulation format
 that has no textbook detector — a situation that occurs constantly in
 proprietary links.

[Table 10. Sampling regimes]
Regime | Condition | Where used | Hardware cost

Oversampling (OSR > 1) | f s ≫ 2 B | ΣΔ converters, relaxed AAF | Quantisation noise spread over wider band: +3 dB SNR per doubling

Time-interleaving is where the design house earns its
 fee. An M-way interleaved ADC has three mismatch mechanisms, each producing
 a distinct spur family: offset mismatch gives tones at kfs/M
 independent of input; gain mismatch gives sidebands at
 kfs/M ± fin; timing skew
 gives the same sideband locations but with amplitude proportional to
 fin. The frequency dependence is the diagnostic: sweep the
 input and see which spur grows. Digital background calibration of all three is a
 standard deliverable in a modern ADC-DSP receiver, and it is a digital block
 — which means a fabless digital IP vendor can sell it even though the converter
 itself is analogue. This is a concrete example of finding a sellable digital block
 adjacent to an analogue one you cannot build.

장: A3. Sampling, Reconstruction and Quantisation
절: A3.2 Quantisation noise
글:
A3.2 Quantisation noise

SQNRdB = 6.02 B + 1.76 +
 10 log10(OSR)

[Table 11. Where the ideal formula breaks]
Effect | Mechanism | Consequence | Design response
Aperture jitter | Sampling instant uncertainty σ t | SNR = −20 log 10 (2π f in σ t ) | Dominates above ~1 GHz input ; clock design becomes the ADC spec
Thermal noise | kT/C of sampling capacitor | Floors SNR regardless of bits | Increase C (costs power and bandwidth)
DNL / INL | Element mismatch | Harmonic distortion, missing codes | Calibration, dynamic element matching
Comparator metastability | Finite regeneration time | Rare large errors | More regeneration time or error detection
Correlated quantisation | Low-amplitude periodic input | Quantisation noise becomes tonal, not white | Dither — deliberately added noise to decorrelate

The dither entry deserves emphasis because it is
 counter-intuitive: adding noise improves the result. Quantisation error is
 only white and signal-independent when the signal moves over many LSBs; for a small
 or slowly varying signal the error becomes periodic and produces discrete tones,
 which are far more objectionable than an equivalent amount of broadband noise (in
 audio they are audible; in a radar they look like targets). Subtractive dither —
 add a known pseudo-random sequence before quantising and subtract it after —
 removes the tones without the SNR penalty. A dither generator is a small, precisely
 specifiable digital block and therefore exactly the kind of thing a one-person IP
 house can build and sell as part of a converter-adjacent package.

절: A2.1 The DFT is not the DTFT
글:
A2.1 The DFT is not the DTFT

The DFT computes samples of the DTFT of a windowed, periodically
 extended sequence. Three artefacts follow, and all three appear as bugs in
 practice.

[Table 14. DFT artefacts]
Artefact | Cause | Symptom | Mitigation
Spectral leakage | Implicit rectangular window | A pure tone smears across bins | Apply a window (Hann, Blackman–Harris)
Scalloping loss | Tone falls between bin centres | Up to 3.9 dB amplitude error (rectangular) | Window, or interpolate the peak
Picket fence | Only N samples of a continuum | Frequency resolution limited to f s / N | Zero-pad (interpolates, does not add resolution)
Circular convolution | Periodic extension | Wrap-around in fast convolution | Zero-pad to N ≥ L + M −1

Zero-padding is routinely misdescribed as improving
 resolution. It does not. Resolution is set by the observation time
 T = N/fs; two tones closer than
 ≈1/T cannot be separated no matter how many zeros are appended. Padding
 interpolates the displayed spectrum, which makes peaks easier to locate but
 not easier to resolve. In a specification, resolution and interpolation must
 be stated separately.

[Table 15. Common windows]

Hann | 4 | −31 dB | General purpose
Hamming | 4 | −41 dB | Slightly better near sidelobe
Blackman–Harris (4-term) | 8 | −92 dB | Spur hunting in converter test
Kaiser (β adjustable) | tunable | tunable | Design-to-spec
Flat-top | ~9 | −90 dB | Amplitude accuracy (calibration)

B5. Analogue Building Blocks

A digital IP house does not design these, but it must model them,
 specify them, and understand which digital block can compensate which analogue
 imperfection — because that compensation is often the sellable part.

절: B5.1 Amplifiers
글:
B5.1 Amplifiers

[Table 17. Amplifier topologies]
Topology | Gain | Bandwidth | Where used
Common source | − g m r o | Moderate | Basic gain stage
Cascode | − g m ( g m r o ) r o | High (reduced Miller) | High-gain stages
Differential pair | — | — | Rejects common-mode noise ; the basis of nearly everything

Why a CTLE amplifies noise and an FFE does not have
 to. A CTLE is a linear analogue filter placed before the point where noise
 is added by the rest of the receiver, but after the channel has already
 attenuated the signal and after thermal noise from the channel and the front end.
 Boosting high frequency therefore boosts the noise already present in that band by the
 same factor. A digital FFE placed after the ADC has exactly the same problem. A
 DFE escapes it because it subtracts a decided symbol — a noiseless
 quantity — rather than amplifying a received one. This is the whole reason
 receivers combine a modest CTLE with a DFE instead of using a large CTLE alone, and
 it is a piece of reasoning that a modelling engineer must be able to reproduce when
 asked to justify an architecture.

The opposing shapes create the optimal loop bandwidth:
 wide enough to suppress VCO phase noise, narrow enough to suppress reference and
 fractional-N quantisation noise. The optimum is where the two contributions
 cross. This is a genuinely quantitative design decision that a system modeller can and
 should compute, and it is directly connected to the link jitter budget of
 Chapter A4 — the integrated phase noise becomes the RJ term that is multiplied
 by 14 at 10−12 BER. Chapters A4, B4 and B5 are three views of the
 same budget, and one of the marks of a senior engineer is holding them together.

Logical effort is the one hand method worth
 memorising. With g the logical effort of a gate (1 for an inverter, 4/3 for
 NAND2, 5/3 for NOR2), h the electrical effort (fanout), and p parasitic
 delay, the path delay is minimised when every stage carries equal effort
 f = (GH)1/N, and the optimal per-stage effort is
 ≈ 3.6 (≈4 in practice, whence "fanout-of-4"). This yields the
 optimal number of stages N ≈ log4(GH) directly.
 In an IP context it answers questions such as "how many buffer stages should the
 clock tree have?" or "is this 12-input decoder better as one stage or three?" before
 a single tool is run — which matters because those questions arise during
 architecture, when no netlist exists.

FO4 as a unit. Quoting delay in FO4 units makes a
 design comparable across processes: a 30-FO4 pipeline stage is 30 FO4 whether the
 node is 130 nm or 5 nm. A measured data point for calibration: in the open
 SkyWater 130 nm PDK, an inverter chain with Wp=2.0 μm,
 Wn=1.0 μm, L=0.15 μm and
 CL=6 fF gives FO4 ≈ 48 ps (ngspice; stage delays
 47.5 and 44.5 ps, rise time 67.9 ps). That implies a practical ceiling near
 1 GHz for a ~20-FO4 pipeline stage in that process — which is the
 quantitative reason a 56 GBd analogue decision loop is impossible there, and why an
 open-PDK project must choose a digital, sub-rate architecture.

Glitch power is an IP-level design decision that
 rarely appears in textbooks. In an unbalanced arithmetic tree, a node can toggle
 several times before settling, and each toggle costs full switching energy. Ripple-carry
 adders and unbalanced multiplier trees are notorious. Balancing the tree — or
 inserting a pipeline register that stops glitch propagation — can reduce
 datapath power by tens of percent at no functional cost. Because glitching is
 invisible in RTL simulation (it appears only in gate-level simulation with timing),
 it is systematically underestimated during architecture. A design house that
 reports power measured from a back-annotated gate-level run, with the customer's own
 data pattern, differentiates itself from one that reports a synthesis estimate.

A synthesisable IP is static CMOS by definition —
 everything else requires custom timing verification that a customer cannot repeat in
 their own flow. This is a commercial constraint, not a technical preference.
 The exception is the SerDes front end, where CML is unavoidable above a few GHz;
 that is precisely the part that is sold as a hard macro rather than RTL, and it is
 why the PMA/PCS boundary in a PHY falls where it does.

장: B4. Interconnect, Transmission Lines and Signal Integrity

B4. Interconnect, Transmission Lines and Signal Integrity

Below roughly 250 nm, wires stopped being ideal connections and became
 circuit elements. Above a few GHz they stop being lumped elements and become
 transmission lines. Both transitions change what a designer must do.

장: B4. Interconnect, Transmission Lines and Signal Integrity
절: B4.1 On-chip interconnect as distributed RC
글:
B4.1 On-chip interconnect as distributed RC

tdelay ≈ 0.38 RwCwL2
   (distributed RC line of length L)

[Table 24. Interconnect scaling and its remedies]
Problem | Cause | Remedy | Cost
Delay grows as L 2 | Distributed RC | Repeater insertion → delay becomes linear in L | Power and area; repeaters can be 30% of a large SoC's dynamic power
Resistance rises with scaling | Smaller cross-section, surface scattering | Thicker upper metal layers for global routes | Fewer routing tracks
Coupling capacitance dominates | Tall narrow wires, close spacing | Increase spacing; shield with ground lines | Routing area
Electromigration | Current density in narrow wires | Width rules, current limits | Area; constrains power grid design
IR drop | Resistance of the power grid | Grid density, decoupling capacitance | Metal resources

Optimal repeater insertion follows from minimising
 the total delay of a line broken into k segments each driven by a repeater of
 size h. The classic result is that the optimum makes the repeater's intrinsic
 delay comparable to the wire segment delay, giving
 kopt = L√(RwCw/(2R0C0)).
 The practical consequence for an IP vendor is that a block's timing cannot be
 guaranteed independent of its physical size: a 2 mm-wide block has internal
 wire delays that a synthesis-only estimate will miss entirely. This is why serious IP
 deliverables include a floorplan hint or a hardened layout, and why "it met timing in
 synthesis" is not a claim a customer will accept for a large block.

장: B4. Interconnect, Transmission Lines and Signal Integrity
절: B4.2 When a wire becomes a transmission line
글:
B4.2 When a wire becomes a transmission line

A connection must be treated as a transmission line when
 its electrical length is a significant fraction of the signal's wavelength — in
 practice when the propagation delay exceeds roughly one tenth of the signal rise time.
 Since tr shrinks with every process generation, the threshold length
 keeps falling.

Z0 = √(L/C)    
 vp = 1/√(LC) = c/√εr    
 Γ = (ZL−Z0)/(ZL+Z0)

[Table 25. Transmission-line effects in a link]
Effect | Physical cause | Frequency behaviour | Consequence
Conductor (skin) loss | Current crowds into a skin depth δ∝1/√ f | ∝ √ f | Dominant loss below ~20 GHz on PCB
Dielectric loss | tanδ of the substrate | ∝ f | Dominant at high frequency; chooses the laminate
Reflections | Impedance discontinuities (vias, connectors) | Resonant dips | Return loss; creates ISI that FFE cannot fully fix
Crosstalk (NEXT/FEXT) | Mutual L and C between traces | Rises with f | Limits lane density
Fibre weave effect | Inhomogeneous ε r of woven glass | — | Skew between differential pair halves
Mode conversion | Asymmetry in a differential pair | — | Differential energy becomes common mode → EMI

Why skin effect makes channel loss go as √f
 and why that shapes the equaliser. Skin depth δ = √(2ρ/ωμ)
 shrinks as 1/√f, so the effective conductor cross-section shrinks and
 resistance rises as √f. The resulting channel magnitude response is
 approximately exp(−k√f), which in the time domain produces a
 long, slowly decaying pulse tail rather than a sharp one. That specific tail
 shape is why decision-feedback equalisation works so well on wireline channels: the
 post-cursor ISI is long but the symbols causing it have already been decided, so they
 can be subtracted exactly without noise enhancement. The physics of the conductor
 selects the equaliser architecture. An engineer who knows only that "DFE cancels
 post-cursor ISI" cannot explain why a different channel — say a multipath radio
 channel with pre-cursor energy — needs a different structure.

절: B4.3 S-parameters
글:
B4.3 S-parameters

[Table 26. Scattering parameters for a two-port]
Parameter | Meaning | Specification name
S 11 | Input reflection | Return loss (dB, negative is good)
S 21 | Forward transmission | Insertion loss
S 12 | Reverse transmission | Isolation
S 22 | Output reflection | Output return loss
S dd , S cc | Differential / common mode | Mixed-mode S-parameters
S cd , S dc | Mode conversion | Asymmetry metric — an EMI predictor

S-parameters are used because at high frequency you
 cannot measure voltage and current at a port without perturbing it, but you can
 measure incident and reflected power waves. For a modelling engineer the practical
 point is the conversion to a time-domain model: a channel is delivered as a
 Touchstone (.s4p) file, and a link simulation needs its pulse response.
 Doing that conversion correctly requires enforcing causality and passivity on
 measured data that generally violates both because of measurement noise and band
 limitation. Non-causal channel models produce link simulations that are optimistic in
 a way that is very hard to notice. A channel-model conditioning tool is a small,
 genuinely sellable piece of software, and it is squarely modelling-team work.

절: B4.4 Power delivery and simultaneous switching noise
글:
B4.4 Power delivery and simultaneous switching noise

Vnoise = Lpackage · dI/dt
  +  Rgrid · I

[Table 27. Power integrity mechanisms]
Mechanism | Where | Mitigation
Static IR drop | On-chip grid resistance | Grid density, more straps
d I /d t noise (SSN) | Package and board inductance | Decoupling capacitance at three levels: on-die, package, board
Resonance | L pkg with on-die C | Anti-resonance peak typically 50–200 MHz ; add damping
Ground bounce | Shared return inductance | More ground pins, differential IO
Supply-induced jitter | V DD modulates delay | Regulate locally; use supply-insensitive delay cells in clock paths

Supply-induced jitter is the mechanism by which a
 digital design decision damages an analogue specification. A large
 synchronous block that starts and stops — a clock-gated accelerator, a burst-mode
 FEC decoder — produces a current step at the burst rate, which modulates the
 supply, which modulates the delay of the PLL's delay cells, which appears as a
 spur in the phase noise, which appears as periodic jitter (PJ) in the link budget.
 The FEC block is the root cause of a jitter specification failure, and nothing
 in either block's own verification would reveal it. This class of cross-domain
 coupling is why chip-level power-aware simulation exists, and why an IP datasheet
 should state the block's current profile, not merely its average power.

장: B1. The MOSFET — What a Digital Designer Must Know
절: B1. The MOSFET — What a Digital Designer Must Know — 들어가며
글:
B1. The MOSFET — What a Digital Designer Must Know

A digital IP engineer does not size transistors, but every timing
 number, every power figure and several verification hazards trace back to device
 behaviour. This chapter keeps only what changes decisions.

장: B1. The MOSFET — What a Digital Designer Must Know
절: B1.1 Regions of operation
글:
B1.1 Regions of operation

[Table 28. MOSFET regions]
Region | Condition | Current | Where it matters
Cut-off | V GS V GS − V TH | ½μC ox (W/L)(V GS −V TH ) 2 (1+λV DS ) | Analogue gain stages; the beginning of a digital transition
Velocity saturation | Short channel, high field | ∝ (V GS −V TH ) 1 — linear, not square | Modern nodes live here. Textbook square-law intuition overestimates drive

The last row is the single most important correction for
 anyone who learned the square law. In a short-channel device carriers reach their
 saturation velocity, so drive current becomes roughly proportional to overdrive
 rather than its square. Two practical consequences: (i) increasing supply
 voltage buys less speed than square-law intuition suggests, while dynamic power still
 rises as V2, so voltage scaling is a poor speed lever; (ii)
 stacking devices (as in a NAND with many inputs) costs more than the naive series-resistance
 estimate, which is why wide fan-in gates are avoided and logic is restructured into
 trees. When a synthesis tool reports that a 4-input gate is slower than two 2-input
 gates in series, this is why.

절: B1.2 Threshold voltage and its enemies
글:
B1.2 Threshold voltage and its enemies

[Table 29. V TH modulation effects]
Effect | Mechanism | Design consequence
Body effect | Source–bulk bias raises V TH | Stacked devices are slower than expected
DIBL | Drain field lowers the barrier | V TH falls with V DS → more leakage
Random dopant fluctuation | Discrete dopant atoms | σ VTH ∝ 1/√( WL ) — small devices mismatch more
Temperature | −1 to −2 mV/K | Hot chip is faster at low V DD (temperature inversion)
NBTI / PBTI ageing | Trap generation under stress | | V TH | drifts over years — timing must include an ageing margin
Multi- V TH offering | Process option | LVT for critical paths, HVT elsewhere: the primary leakage-vs-speed lever

Temperature inversion is a verification trap. At
 high supply voltage a chip is slowest when hot, so signing off at the high-temperature
 corner is conservative. At low supply voltage — which is where modern low-power
 modes operate — the VTH reduction outweighs mobility
 degradation and the chip is slowest when cold. Teams that carried forward a
 "hot is worst case" habit have taped out parts that fail at −40 °C.
 The corner list is not a formality; it is a statement about which physics dominates
 in the operating region you are selling into.

장: B1. The MOSFET — What a Digital Designer Must Know
절: B1.3 Scaling and what it stopped giving
글:
B1.3 Scaling and what it stopped giving

[Table 30. Dennard scaling and its breakdown]
Quantity | Ideal scaling (factor s >1) | What actually happened
Dimensions | 1/ s | Continued (with FinFET, GAA)
Supply V DD | 1/ s | Stalled near 0.7–0.9 V — V TH cannot follow without leakage explosion
Delay | 1/ s | Slower than ideal; interconnect does not scale

The end of Dennard scaling is the reason the industry
 turned to specialised accelerators, and therefore the reason the IP business
 grew. When a single general-purpose core could no longer be made faster within a
 power budget, the way to get performance became putting the right fixed-function
 block next to the processor. Every FEC, crypto, codec and NPU IP sold today exists
 because of this graph. Understanding it lets a design house argue its value
 proposition in the customer's own terms: not "our block is fast", but "your
 general-purpose alternative costs x times the energy per operation".

장: B3. Timing, Clocking and Static Timing Analysis
절: B3.1 The two inequalities
글:
B3.1 The two inequalities

Tclk ≥ tcq + tlogic,max
 + tsetup + tskew + tjitter

tcq,min + tlogic,min ≥ thold
 + tskew

The asymmetry between the two is the single most
 important operational fact in digital timing. A setup violation is fixed by
 lowering the clock frequency, so a chip that fails setup still works, just slower. A
 hold violation has no frequency term: the chip is broken at every frequency
 and the only remedy is a mask change. Consequently hold is fixed exhaustively before
 tape-out, by buffer insertion, while setup is traded against performance targets.
 In IP delivery this means the constraint file (SDC) you ship must make the customer's
 hold analysis possible — omitting clock definitions or false-path declarations
 can cause a customer to close hold on a path that does not exist, or worse, to miss
 one that does.

장: B3. Timing, Clocking and Static Timing Analysis
절: B3.2 Clock distribution
글:
B3.2 Clock distribution

[Table 31. Clock network structures]
Structure | Skew | Power | Use
H-tree | Low by symmetry | High | Regular arrays, large blocks
Buffered tree (CTS) | Tool-balanced | Moderate | Standard ASIC flow
Mesh / grid | Very low | Very high | High-performance CPUs
Spine + local trees | Moderate | Moderate | Common compromise
Useful skew | Deliberately non-zero | — | Borrow time from a fast stage to a slow one

Useful skew (clock borrowing) is worth knowing
 because it turns a timing failure into a scheduling problem. If stage A has
 slack and stage B does not, delaying B's launch clock moves margin from A to B.
 The tool does this automatically, but the consequence for an IP vendor is subtle:
 a block whose internal paths are already borrowing has little tolerance for the
 customer's clock tree. Reporting timing with an assumed skew budget, and stating
 that budget explicitly in the datasheet, prevents the integration failure where the
 block meets timing in the vendor's flow and misses it in the customer's.

절: B3.3 What STA cannot see
글:

Issue | Why STA misses it | What catches it

Exception declarations are the most dangerous artefact
 in a timing constraint file. Each set_false_path removes a path from
 analysis; if the declaration is wrong, that path is simply never checked and the
 failure appears only in silicon. A mature IP deliverable therefore ships its SDC with
 a written justification for every exception, and ideally with an assertion or formal
 property that proves the path is genuinely unexercisable. This is a place where a
 modelling engineer contributes directly: the argument that a path cannot be
 sensitised is a functional argument, and the person who wrote the reference model is
 usually the one who can make it.

MTBF = etr/τ /

The exponential in tr (resolution time
 allowed) is why adding one synchroniser stage improves MTBF by orders of magnitude
 rather than by a factor of two. With typical 28 nm flip-flop parameters
 (τ ≈ 20 ps), one extra stage at 1 GHz multiplies MTBF
 by e1000/20 = e50 — an astronomically large
 factor. The corollary is that two stages is almost always enough and three is
 almost always superstition, except at very high clock rates where
 tr per stage is small. Being able to compute this rather than
 follow a rule is what lets an IP vendor justify a latency budget to a customer who
 wants the crossing to be faster.

장: C1. Arithmetic Units — The Core of Every Datapath
절: C1.1 Addition
글:
C1.1 Addition

[그림] Figure 5. Adder architectures span an area–delay curve of roughly an order of magnitude in each axis.

[Table 33. Adder architectures]
Architecture | Delay | Area | Notes
Ripple carry | O( n ) | O( n ) | Baseline; fine for n ≤8 at low frequency
Carry-skip | O(√ n ) | O( n ) | Cheap improvement
Carry-select | O(√ n ) | ~2× | Duplicate blocks, select on carry
Carry-lookahead | O(log n ) | O( n log n ) | Classic
Kogge–Stone | O(log n ) | Large, heavy wiring | Minimum depth; wire-limited in practice
Brent–Kung | O(log n ) | Fewer wires | Depth 2log n ; better area
Carry-save | O(1) per add | O( n ) | Does not propagate carry — the key to fast multipliers and accumulators

Carry-save is the single most useful idea in this
 table. A carry-save adder takes three operands and produces two (sum and carry
 vectors) in constant time, because no carry propagates. A chain of them accumulates
 many terms at constant delay per term, and only the final conversion to a
 normal binary number requires a carry-propagate adder. This is why multiplier trees,
 FIR accumulators, and MAC units are built as "compress many partial products with
 carry-save, then one fast adder at the end". In an accumulation loop — the
 feedback path that limits every recursive filter — keeping the state in
 carry-save form removes the carry-propagate delay from the loop entirely. That
 single transformation has rescued more timing-critical datapaths than any other.

절: C1.2 Multiplication

C1.2 Multiplication

[Table 34. Multiplier construction]
Stage | Technique | Effect

Constant multiplication is a different problem and
 is worth separating in any specification. When one operand is a compile-time constant
 — filter coefficients, twiddle factors, scaling constants — the multiplier
 collapses into shifts and adds. Canonical signed digit (CSD) representation minimises

 algorithms share sub-expressions across a whole coefficient set. For a 32-tap FIR with
 fixed coefficients this routinely gives a 3–5× area reduction over generic

 run-time coefficients cannot use this, so "programmable coefficients" is an
 expensive feature that should be priced and specified as such, not thrown in
 because it seems flexible.

절: C1.3 Division, square root, and reciprocal
글:
C1.3 Division, square root, and reciprocal

[Table 35. Division approaches]
Method | Convergence | Hardware | Use
Restoring / non-restoring | 1 bit per cycle | Adder + shifter | Small area, high latency
SRT (radix-4/8) | 2–3 bits per cycle | Lookup for quotient digit | Standard in FPUs
Newton–Raphson | Quadratic (doubles digits) | Multipliers | Reuses the multiplier; good when one exists
Goldschmidt | Quadratic | Multipliers | Better pipelining than Newton

The most important division fact for an IP designer
 is architectural, not numerical: never put a divider in a feedback loop. Its
 latency enters the loop directly and sets the initiation interval. The standard
 transformation is to compute a reciprocal once outside the loop and multiply
 inside it. The Cholesky decomposition is a textbook example — the diagonal
 reciprocal is formed once per column and the column is then scaled by multiplication,
 which is why the inner loop can be pipelined at II = 1. This is also a
 place where the reference model and the RTL can legitimately differ: the model may
 divide, the RTL multiplies by a reciprocal, and the two agree only to within the
 reciprocal's rounding. The specification must state which one is normative.

Block floating point deserves more attention than it
 gets. In an FFT the signal magnitude grows by up to a factor of two per stage. Full
 floating point is overkill; fixed point requires either wide words or per-stage
 scaling that loses SNR. Block floating point keeps one exponent per stage (or per
 block) and normalises once, recovering most of floating point's dynamic range at a
 small fraction of the cost. For a modelling engineer this format is a trap,

 block-normalised behaviour bit for bit — the reference must model the
 normalisation decisions too. Specifying "bit-accurate reference model" without
 specifying the scaling policy produces months of false mismatches.

장: C3. Clock Domain Crossing, Reset and Low Power
절: C3.1 The CDC problem stated precisely
글:
C3.1 The CDC problem stated precisely

A signal crossing between unrelated clock domains
 violates setup or hold at the receiving flip-flop with non-zero probability. The
 flip-flop may enter a metastable state whose resolution time is unbounded (though
 exponentially unlikely to be long). This cannot be simulated: a logic
 simulator has no metastable value and will always resolve to 0 or 1.

[Table 37. CDC techniques by payload type]
Payload | Technique | Why | Failure if misapplied
1-bit level | Two-flop synchroniser | Allows a full cycle to resolve | —
1-bit pulse | Toggle synchroniser (level convert, then edge detect) | A pulse shorter than the destination period would be lost | Lost events
Multi-bit, unrelated | Synchronise a request; use a data hold register | Bits arriving in different cycles corrupt the value | Corrupted data words
Multi-bit counter | Gray code | Only one bit changes per increment | Wrong pointer → FIFO corruption
Stream | Asynchronous FIFO (Gray pointers, dual-port RAM) | Decouples rate and phase | —
Bus transaction | Handshake (req/ack) or credit | Explicit acknowledgement | —
Reset | Asynchronous assert, synchronous de-assert | De-assertion must not violate recovery/removal | Part of the design leaves reset a cycle late

Why Gray coding a FIFO pointer is safe even though
 the pointer is multi-bit. The synchroniser may sample a Gray pointer mid-transition,
 but since only one bit changes per increment, the sampled value is either the old or
 the new pointer — never a third value. An off-by-one pointer makes the FIFO
 report itself slightly fuller or emptier than it is, which is
 conservative: the FIFO may stall a cycle early but never overflows or underflows.
 The design is safe because its error mode is biased in the harmless
 direction. This principle — arrange for uncertainty to fail conservatively
 — generalises far beyond FIFOs and is one of the most transferable ideas in
 digital design.

장: C3. Clock Domain Crossing, Reset and Low Power
절: C3.2 Reset architecture
글:
C3.2 Reset architecture

[Table 38. Reset strategies]
Strategy | Advantage | Problem
Synchronous | No recovery/removal issue; clean STA | Needs a running clock — fails at power-up
Asynchronous | Works without a clock | De-assertion can violate recovery
Async assert, sync de-assert | Both advantages | Requires a reset synchroniser per domain — the standard solution
Reset-less registers | Area and routing saving | Must be provably initialised by data flow; a verification obligation

Reset de-assertion order is a specification item that
 is almost always omitted. If two blocks leave reset in different cycles and one
 samples the other's outputs, the receiving block may latch garbage. Within a block the
 designer controls this; across an IP boundary the customer controls it, and
 they cannot get it right unless the datasheet states the requirement. A good IP
 datasheet specifies: the reset polarity, whether it is synchronous or asynchronous,
 the minimum assertion width in cycles of each clock, and any required ordering between
 multiple resets. Omitting this produces intermittent bring-up failures that are
 blamed on the IP.

절: C3.3 Low power design
글:
C3.3 Low power design

[Table 39. Power reduction techniques by level]
Level | Technique | Saving | Verification burden
RTL | Clock gating | Large (clock tree is 20–40% of dynamic power) | Low — tools insert it automatically

Parallelism as a power technique is the least
 intuitive entry and the most powerful. Two copies of a block running at half the clock
 frequency deliver the same throughput; because they now have twice the time budget,
 the supply voltage can be lowered until the slower path just meets timing. Dynamic
 power scales as V2f, so halving f and reducing
 V by, say, 30% gives roughly 0.5 × 0.49 = 0.25 of the original
 power, at the cost of about twice the area. This trade — area for energy
 — is the fundamental reason accelerators are more efficient than processors,
 and it is the argument an IP vendor uses when selling a block against a software
 implementation. State it with the exponents and it is persuasive; state it as "our
 block is more efficient" and it is not.

[Table 40. DFT structures]
Structure | Tests what | Cost | IP implication
Scan chains | All flip-flops and combinational logic | Mux in every FF (~5–10% area, some delay) | IP must be scan-insertable : no gated clocks without test bypass, no latches, no async loops
MBIST | Embedded memories | Controller per memory group | Memory interfaces must be accessible
BSD (JTAG 1149.1) | Board-level interconnect | Boundary cells | —
LBIST | Logic, in-field | PRPG + MISR | Automotive/safety
ATPG coverage | — | — | Stuck-at >99%, transition >90% typical targets
Test compression | — | Decompressor/compactor | Reduces tester time and cost

Scan is a security hole. A scan chain can read
 and write every flip-flop in the design, including key registers. Production chips
 must therefore disable scan after manufacturing test, typically by blowing a fuse or
 advancing a life-cycle state. A security IP that does not document its scan-isolation
 requirement will be integrated insecurely. Conversely, an IP that cannot be scanned
 at all is unsellable, because the customer cannot achieve their test coverage
 target. The resolution — scannable, but with key registers excluded from the
 chain or cleared on scan entry — must be designed in, and it is a requirement
 that comes from neither function nor timing.

장: C2. Control: State Machines, Pipelines and Flow Control
절: C2.1 FSM encoding
글:
C2.1 FSM encoding

[Table 41. State encodings]
Encoding | Registers | Next-state logic | When
Binary | log 2 N | Complex | Many states, area critical
Gray | log 2 N | Complex | Adjacent states differ by one bit — low power, safer across CDC
One-hot | N | Simple (one AND per transition) | FPGA default ; fast; easy to check
Johnson | N /2 | Simple | Counters, ring sequencers
Hamming-protected | >log 2 N | — | Safety/security : illegal states detectable

Security-grade FSM encoding is a concrete example
 of a requirement that comes from a threat model rather than from function. If an
 attacker can flip a state bit with a laser or a voltage glitch, a binary-encoded FSM
 may land in a valid but wrong state — for instance skipping rounds of a cipher.
 Countermeasures are: sparse encodings with large Hamming distance so that a single
 flip lands in an illegal state; a default branch that raises an alarm rather than
 doing nothing; and duplicated FSMs with complementary encodings whose outputs
 must remain complementary. The last technique requires a synthesis barrier so the
 tool does not optimise the inverters away and merge the two copies — if it
 does, the redundancy disappears while functional verification still passes.
 That silent failure mode is the reason such designs contain explicit buffer
 primitives whose only purpose is to stop the optimiser.

장: C2. Control: State Machines, Pipelines and Flow Control
절: C2.2 Pipelining and its hazards
글:
C2.2 Pipelining and its hazards

[Table 42. Pipeline transformations]
Transformation | What it does | Cost | Limit
Pipelining | Insert registers between logic stages | Latency, area | Cannot cut a feedback loop
Retiming | Move existing registers across logic | None (if legal) | Total registers on each loop is invariant
Loop unrolling | Process k iterations per cycle | k × area | The loop's critical path is divided by k only in the feedforward part
Speculation | Compute all outcomes, select afterwards | Exponential in the number of speculated bits | Removes the decision from the loop
C-slow | Interleave k independent streams | Registers × k | Needs k independent problems
Algebraic transform | Restructure the recurrence itself | Design effort | The only way past a fundamental loop bound

The iteration bound is the hard limit that these
 transformations negotiate with. For a recursive system, the minimum achievable
 iteration period is
 T∞ = maxloops (tloop/wloop),
 where tloop is the total computation delay around a loop and
 wloop the number of registers in it. Retiming and pipelining cannot
 beat it; only changing the recurrence can. Recognising this quantity turns a vague
 "we need more speed" into a specific question: which loop, and can its algebra be
 rewritten? Look-ahead transformation (computing two steps of a recurrence in one)
 doubles w and thereby halves T∞, at the cost of more
 arithmetic. This is the abstract form of the unrolled DFE, radix-4 Viterbi ACS,
 and reformulated Berlekamp–Massey — three blocks that look unrelated and
 are the same transformation.

장: C2. Control: State Machines, Pipelines and Flow Control
절: C2.3 Flow control and backpressure
글:
C2.3 Flow control and backpressure

[Table 43. Handshake styles]
Style | Signals | Property | Hazard
Valid only | valid | Producer never stalls | Consumer must always accept — needs guaranteed rate
Valid/Ready | valid , ready | Full backpressure | Combinational loop if ready depends on valid
Credit-based | credits returned | Decouples latency from throughput | Credit accounting bugs
Req/Ack (4-phase) | handshake pairs | Async-safe | Slow (two round trips)

The valid/ready combinational loop is one of the
 most common integration failures in modular RTL. If module A's ready
 depends combinationally on its input valid, and module B's
 valid depends combinationally on its input ready, connecting
 them creates a zero-delay cycle. Each module is individually correct and passes its
 own tests. The standard remedies are a skid buffer (also called a spill
 register), which breaks the path at the cost of one register stage and one entry of
 buffering, or a rule that ready is registered. An IP that documents
 which of its interfaces are combinationally coupled — and ships a skid buffer
 — saves its customers a week each. This is exactly the kind of detail that
 distinguishes a product from a piece of code.

장: C2. Control: State Machines, Pipelines and Flow Control
절: C2.4 Arbitration
글:
C2.4 Arbitration

[Table 44. Arbiter types]
Type | Fairness | Latency | Use
Fixed priority | None (starvation possible) | Lowest | Strict QoS classes
Round robin | Fair | Low | General purpose
Weighted round robin | Proportional | Low | Mixed traffic classes
Matrix / LRU | Fair, true least-recently-used | Higher | Caches
Lottery | Statistical | Low | Rare
Age-based | Strict FIFO fairness | Higher | Avoids starvation strictly

Arbitration is where fairness and forward progress
 become formal properties rather than intentions. A round-robin arbiter is fair by
 construction; a fixed-priority arbiter is not, and a low-priority requester can starve
 forever. Whether starvation matters is a system question — it is acceptable for
 a debug port, fatal for a DMA that feeds a real-time codec. Because starvation is a
 liveness property ("eventually granted") rather than a safety property, it is
 natural to express and prove with formal tools, and arbiters are one of the few places
 where formal verification is both easy and genuinely valuable. Shipping a formally
 proven arbiter with its properties is a differentiator that costs a design house
 little.

장: D1. Instruction Set Architecture
절: D1. Instruction Set Architecture — 들어가며
글:
D1. Instruction Set Architecture

An ISA is a contract between hardware and software. For a modelling
 engineer it is the specification document in the most literal sense: the
 reference model is the ISA, written executably.

[Table 45. ISA design axes]
Axis | Options | Consequence for hardware
Operand model | Stack / accumulator / register–memory / load–store | Load–store simplifies pipelining; every RISC uses it
Instruction length | Fixed / variable / compressed | Fixed simplifies fetch; compressed (RVC, Thumb) saves 25–30% code size at the cost of alignment logic
Addressing modes | Few / many | Many modes need an address generation unit; few modes need more instructions
Condition handling | Flags / compare-and-branch | Flags create a serialising dependency ; RISC-V deliberately has none
Delay slots | Present (classic MIPS) / absent | Delay slots expose the pipeline in the ISA — a design mistake later reversed
Register count | 8 / 16 / 32 / more | More registers reduce spills but widen every instruction field
Exceptions | Precise / imprecise | Precise exceptions constrain the whole microarchitecture

Delay slots are the canonical example of leaking
 microarchitecture into architecture. MIPS exposed its single branch-delay slot so
 that the compiler could fill it, saving a stall in a five-stage pipeline. When later
 implementations had deeper pipelines and branch prediction, the delay slot became
 useless baggage that every implementation still had to honour. The lesson for IP
 design generalises: a specification that encodes today's implementation constrains
 tomorrow's. When writing a block's interface, ask which parts describe
 what and which describe how, and expose only the former.

Precise exceptions mean that when an exception is
 taken, all instructions before it have completed and none after it has had any
 effect. This is what makes an ISS a valid reference: the model can execute one
 instruction at a time and still describe a machine that executes many concurrently.
 Achieving it in an out-of-order machine requires a reorder buffer and speculative
 state, which is a large fraction of such a core's complexity. The entire
 step-and-compare verification methodology rests on precise exceptions; without
 them there would be no well-defined point at which model and RTL should agree.

장: D1. Instruction Set Architecture
절: D1.2 RISC-V as a case study
글:
D1.2 RISC-V as a case study

[Table 46. RISC-V structure]
Element | Content | Modelling note
Base integer | RV32I / RV64I — ~40 instructions | Small enough to model exhaustively
M | Multiply/divide | Division by zero is defined , not trapping
A | Atomics (LR/SC, AMO) | Requires a memory consistency model
F/D/Q | Floating point | IEEE 754; needs SoftFloat, not host arithmetic
C | Compressed 16-bit | Alignment: instructions may straddle a word
V | Vector | Vector-length agnostic — a model must track vl , vtype
B, Zk, Zc… | Bit manipulation, crypto, code size | —
Privileged | M/S/U modes, CSRs, PMP, virtual memory | Where most model bugs live : exception priority and CSR side effects

Exception priority is the most common source of
 reference-model defects in a CPU project. One instruction can simultaneously
 satisfy the conditions for several exceptions — misaligned address, page fault,
 access fault, breakpoint. The specification gives a strict priority order. A model
 that implements a different order is correct on almost every test and wrong on a
 narrow class of inputs that constrained-random stimulus may take weeks to find. The
 remedy is not more random testing but directed tests derived from the priority
 table itself: enumerate the table, construct one case per row, and check. This is
 a half-day of work that reliably finds bugs a month of random testing misses.

장: D3. Memory Hierarchy and Coherence
절: D3. Memory Hierarchy and Coherence — 들어가며
글:
D3. Memory Hierarchy and Coherence

[그림] Figure 6. The memory hierarchy. Each level trades capacity against latency by roughly an order of magnitude.

[Table 47. Cache design parameters]
Parameter | Effect | Trade
Block size | Exploits spatial locality | Too large wastes bandwidth and causes false sharing
Associativity | Reduces conflict misses | More comparators, longer hit time; 4–8 way is the usual optimum
Capacity | Reduces capacity misses | Area, leakage, hit latency
Write policy | Write-through vs write-back | Write-back reduces bandwidth; needs dirty bits and coherence
Allocation | Write-allocate vs not | Depends on write locality
Replacement | LRU / pseudo-LRU / random | True LRU is expensive beyond 4-way; pseudo-LRU is within 1%
Inclusion | Inclusive / exclusive / NINE | Affects snoop filtering

Misses classify as compulsory (first reference),
 capacity (working set exceeds the cache), conflict (limited
 associativity), and in multiprocessors coherence (invalidated by another
 core). The classification is useful because each class has a different remedy:
 prefetching for compulsory, larger cache for capacity, higher associativity or
 better indexing for conflict, and data layout changes for coherence.

[Table 48. Coherence protocols]
Protocol | States | Note
MSI | Modified, Shared, Invalid | Minimal
MESI | + Exclusive | Avoids a bus transaction on read–modify
MOESI | + Owned | Allows dirty sharing; saves writebacks
Directory-based | — | Scales beyond a bus ; required for many-core
Snoop filter | — | Reduces useless snoops in large systems

Memory consistency is not coherence. Coherence
 concerns a single address — all cores must see one order of writes to it.
 Consistency concerns the relative order of operations to different addresses.
 A machine can be perfectly coherent and still reorder a store to A before a store to
 B as observed by another core. The consistency model (sequential, TSO, release, RVWMO)
 specifies what reorderings are allowed and which fences prevent them. For a
 modelling engineer this is the hardest specification to capture, because the
 reference model is inherently sequential while the hardware is not: a simple
 step-and-compare against an ISS cannot verify a weak memory model. The correct
 approach is litmus tests — short multi-threaded programs with
 enumerated permitted outcomes — checked against the architecture's formal memory
 model. Knowing that a different verification technique is required, and why, is the
 point.

[Table 49. DRAM characteristics that leak into system design]
Property | Meaning | Design response
Row buffer | A row must be activated before access | Exploit row locality; schedule for open rows
t RCD , t RP , t RAS | Activate/precharge timings | Memory controller scheduling
Refresh | Every ~32–64 ms | Blocks access; matters for real-time guarantees
Bank/rank parallelism | Independent banks | Interleave addresses to exploit it
Burst length | Minimum transfer granularity | A 4-byte read still fetches 32–64 bytes
Rowhammer | Repeated activation disturbs neighbours | A security problem solved by refresh management — a DRAM controller feature

장: D2. Pipelining, Hazards and Speculation
절: D2. Pipelining, Hazards and Speculation — 들어가며
글:
D2. Pipelining, Hazards and Speculation

[그림] Figure 7. The classic five-stage pipeline and its three hazard classes.

[Table 50. Hazards and remedies]
Hazard | Cause | Remedy | Residual cost
Structural | Two instructions need the same resource | Duplicate the resource, or stall | Area
Data RAW | Read after write | Forwarding from EX/MEM | Load-use still costs one cycle
Data WAR / WAW | Anti- and output dependencies | Register renaming | Only in out-of-order designs
Control | Branch outcome unknown at fetch | Prediction + speculative execution | Misprediction penalty × rate
Memory ordering | Loads and stores to the same address | Store buffer with forwarding, memory disambiguation | Complexity

[Table 51. Branch prediction]
Predictor | Mechanism | Typical accuracy
Static (backward taken) | Loop heuristic | ~65%
Bimodal | 2-bit saturating counter per PC | ~85%
gshare | Global history XOR PC indexes the table | ~93%
Tournament | Choose between local and global predictors | ~95%
TAGE | Multiple history lengths with tags | >97%
Perceptron | Linear classifier over history | >97%
Return address stack | Dedicated stack for call/return | >99% for returns

Why a misprediction is expensive and getting more
 so. The penalty is the pipeline depth from fetch to resolve. In a 5-stage machine
 that is 2–3 cycles; in a 15-stage out-of-order machine it is 15–20, and
 the machine may have to discard dozens of in-flight instructions. With a 5% miss rate
 and a 15-cycle penalty, branches alone cost 0.75 cycles per branch — often more
 than every other stall combined. This is why predictor research continues to be
 worthwhile and why deep pipelines have diminishing returns. For an accelerator IP
 designer the lesson is the opposite and liberating: a fixed-function datapath has no
 branches, so none of this cost exists. Quantifying that difference — "your
 software loop spends 0.75 cycles per iteration on branch misprediction alone" —
 is one of the strongest arguments an accelerator vendor has.

장: D2. Pipelining, Hazards and Speculation
절: D2.2 Out-of-order execution
글:
D2.2 Out-of-order execution

[Table 52. Out-of-order machinery]
Structure | Purpose | Scaling limit
Register renaming (RAT) | Removes WAR/WAW | Physical register file size
Reservation stations / issue queue | Hold instructions until operands ready | Wakeup–select loop is the critical path
Reorder buffer (ROB) | In-order commit → precise exceptions | Entries scale with memory latency
Load/store queue | Memory disambiguation | Associative search cost
Scoreboard | Simpler alternative (no renaming) | Stalls on WAR/WAW

The wakeup–select loop — broadcasting a
 result tag, waking dependent instructions, selecting which to issue — must
 complete in one cycle for back-to-back dependent execution. It is a broadcast across
 the whole issue queue, so its delay grows with queue size and with issue width. This
 single loop, not transistor speed, is why issue widths have plateaued around 4–8
 and why further performance has come from more cores rather than wider ones. It is
 the same phenomenon as the DFE feedback loop and the Viterbi ACS loop: a recurrence
 whose latency cannot be pipelined away. Recognising the pattern across domains is
 exactly the transferable skill this book aims to build.

장: E2. Transforms in Hardware: FFT and Friends
절: E2. Transforms in Hardware: FFT and Friends — 들어가며
글:
E2. Transforms in Hardware: FFT and Friends

[Table 53. FFT algorithm families]
Algorithm | Complex multiplies | Structure | Note
Radix-2 DIT/DIF | ( N /2)log 2 N | Regular butterflies | Simplest control
Radix-4 | fewer | 4-point butterflies | ~25% fewer multiplies
Split-radix | fewest for radix-2 k | Irregular | Control complexity
Winograd / PFA | Minimum multiplies | Length must factor into coprimes | Niche
Pipelined SDF | — | One butterfly per stage + delay line | Streaming; the standard for OFDM
MDC | — | Multiple data paths | Higher throughput
SSR / parallel | — | Several samples per clock | When the data rate exceeds the clock rate

The resource that actually limits an FFT is memory and
 the twiddle factors, not the butterflies. A pipelined N-point SDF FFT needs
 log2N butterflies but a total of N−1 words of delay
 line, and a twiddle ROM whose size grows with N. For N = 4096
 that is thousands of words of storage against a dozen arithmetic units. Two standard
 optimisations follow: exploit twiddle symmetry to store only one eighth of a period
 and derive the rest by sign and swap, or generate twiddles with a CORDIC instead of a
 ROM. Which one wins depends on whether the target has cheap memory (FPGA) or cheap
 logic (ASIC) — another instance of the rule that architecture choices are
 technology-dependent and must be re-derived, not memorised.

Bit-reversed output order is an interface decision,
 not an implementation detail. A DIF FFT naturally produces its output in
 bit-reversed order. Reordering costs a full N-word buffer and its bandwidth. In
 many systems the consumer — a channel equaliser, a magnitude detector —
 does not care about order, so the reordering is pure waste. Competent designs pass the
 bit-reversed order through and let the next block absorb it. This means the
 reference model and the RTL will disagree about output order unless the specification
 says which convention is normative, and a large fraction of "FFT mismatch" bug
 reports are exactly this.

[Table 54. Numerical behaviour of fixed-point FFT]
Issue | Cause | Handling
Magnitude growth | Each radix-2 stage can double magnitude | Scale by ½ per stage (lose SNR), grow the word, or block floating point
Twiddle quantisation | Finite coefficient precision | Adds a noise floor; usually 2–4 bits more than data width
Rounding vs truncation | Bias accumulates over log N stages | Convergent rounding avoids DC bias
Overflow detection | Input-dependent | Saturate and flag, or scale conservatively

[Table 55. Other transforms used in IP]
Transform | Property | Application
DCT-II | Energy compaction for correlated signals | JPEG, H.264/HEVC (integer approximations)
Integer DCT | Exactly invertible, multiplier-free | Video codecs — avoids encoder/decoder drift
Hadamard | ±1 only | Secondary transform, spreading
Number-theoretic (NTT) | Exact modular arithmetic | Post-quantum crypto (ML-KEM/ML-DSA) , homomorphic encryption
Wavelet (DWT) | Time–frequency localisation | JPEG2000, denoising

The integer DCT in video codecs is a beautiful example
 of specification-driven design. An exact DCT requires irrational coefficients; any
 two implementations would round differently, and since the decoder's output feeds back
 into the encoder's prediction loop, the tiny differences would accumulate into visible
 drift. H.264 solved this by defining the transform to be a specific integer
 matrix, so every conforming implementation produces bit-identical results. The
 lesson generalises directly to IP work: when an algorithm sits in a feedback loop
 that spans two independently implemented systems, the specification must be bit-exact,
 not mathematical. The same reasoning applies to a DFE's tap update, to an
 adaptive equaliser shared between link partners, and to any distributed control
 loop.

장: E1. Digital Filters as Hardware
절: E1. Digital Filters as Hardware — 들어가며
글:
E1. Digital Filters as Hardware

[그림] Figure 8. Direct-form FIR. The tap count sets the multiplier count; the form sets the critical path.

[Table 56. FIR structures and their costs]
Structure | Multipliers | Critical path | Choose when
Direct form | N | 1 mult + log N adds | N small
Transposed direct form | N | 1 mult + 1 add (constant) | Almost always, for speed . Cost: high fanout on x [ n ]
Symmetric (folded) | ⌈ N /2⌉ | 1 add + 1 mult + 1 add | Linear phase — free 2× saving
Polyphase | N / M effective | — | Combined with rate change
Distributed arithmetic | 0 (LUTs) | W cycles | Fixed coefficients, LUT fabric
CSD / multiplierless | 0 | adds only | Fixed coefficients, ASIC area
Frequency domain | — | — | N ≳ 100 and block latency acceptable

The fanout cost of the transposed form is real and is
 often overlooked in architecture documents. The input sample must reach all
 N multipliers in one cycle. For N = 128 at 500 MHz this
 is a significant buffer tree whose delay and power must be budgeted. The usual remedy
 is to partition the filter into segments with a pipelined input distribution
 network — effectively reintroducing a small amount of direct-form structure.
 Real designs are hybrids, and a specification that names only "transposed FIR" is
 incomplete.

장: E1. Digital Filters as Hardware
절: E1.2 Filter design methods
글:
E1.2 Filter design methods

[Table 57. FIR design methods]
Method | Optimality | Control | Use
Windowing | Suboptimal | Simple | Quick designs
Frequency sampling | Suboptimal | Direct in frequency | —
Parks–McClellan (Remez) | Minimax optimal | Ripple in each band | Standard for equiripple specs
Least squares | L2 optimal | Weighted error | When energy matters more than peak
Convex optimisation | Flexible | Arbitrary constraints | Handles quantised coefficients directly

Designing in floating point and rounding afterwards is
 a mistake that costs stopband attenuation. Rounding a Parks–McClellan design
 to B bits perturbs each coefficient by up to half an LSB, and the resulting
 stopband degradation can be 10–20 dB. The correct procedure is to include
 the quantisation in the design: either use an integer-programming or convex
 formulation that searches over representable coefficients, or re-optimise the
 remaining coefficients after fixing some. For an IP vendor this is a concrete
 deliverable: ship the coefficient generator, not just the coefficients, so the
 customer can retune for their own band plan without repeating the analysis.

장: E1. Digital Filters as Hardware
절: E1.3 Multirate structures
글:
E1.3 Multirate structures

[Table 58. Rate conversion building blocks]
Block | Function | Key property
Decimator (↓ M ) | Filter then discard M −1 of every M | Filter first , or aliasing is irreversible
Interpolator (↑ L ) | Insert L −1 zeros then filter | Zeros create images; the filter removes them
Polyphase decomposition | Split the filter into M sub-filters | Avoids computing samples that are discarded — M × saving
CIC | Integrator–comb cascade | No multipliers ; passband droop must be compensated
Half-band | Every other coefficient is zero | ~2× saving for 2:1 rates
Farrow | Polynomial interpolation with variable delay | Arbitrary, time-varying resampling ratio — used in timing recovery

The CIC word-growth question is a classic fixed-point
 trap. An N-stage CIC with rate change R and differential delay
 M has DC gain (RM)N, so the integrators need
 Wout = Win + Nlog2(RM)
 bits. The textbook trick is to use two's-complement wrap-around in the
 integrators: intermediate values overflow, but because the comb stages later subtract,
 the overflow cancels exactly, provided the final result fits. This works
 because wrap-around arithmetic is a ring homomorphism. Replace wrap with
 saturation — an apparently safer choice — and the cancellation is
 destroyed and the filter breaks. A specification that says only "use saturating
 arithmetic throughout" would silently kill a correct CIC. This is why Part A's
 number-system chapter insists that overflow behaviour is a per-block decision.

장: E1. Digital Filters as Hardware
절: E1.4 Adaptive filters
글:
E1.4 Adaptive filters

[Table 59. Adaptive algorithms in hardware terms]
Algorithm | Update | Multipliers per tap per update | Convergence
LMS | w ← w + μ e x * | 2 | Slow; sensitive to eigenvalue spread
NLMS | μ normalised by ‖ x ‖ 2 | 2 + norm | Robust to input level
Sign-error LMS | uses sgn( e ) | 1 | Slower
Sign-data LMS | uses sgn( x ) | 1 | Slower
Sign-sign LMS | both signs | 0 — adds only | Slowest; used in every high-speed SerDes
RLS | inverse correlation update | O( N ) per tap | Fast; expensive
Frequency-domain LMS | block FFT | — | Fast for long filters

Why sign-sign LMS dominates at 56 GBd. Two
 independent facts combine. First, the channel changes on a timescale of milliseconds
 while symbols arrive every 18 ps — adaptation can be nine orders of
 magnitude slower than the datapath. Second, multipliers cannot run at the symbol
 rate at all. Taking only signs reduces the update to increment/decrement, which can be
 accumulated over thousands of symbols and applied occasionally. The resulting
 architecture has a fast datapath and a slow adaptation loop in a
 different clock domain. For a modelling engineer this separation must be explicit
 in the model, because a model that updates taps every symbol will not match RTL
 that updates them every 4096 symbols, even though both "implement sign-sign LMS".
 The update schedule is part of the specification.

장: F2. Error Control Coding
절: F2.1 The coding landscape
글:
F2.1 The coding landscape

[Table 60. Codes by structure and application]
Family | Alphabet | Decoding | Strength | Typical use
Parity / SECDED | binary | syndrome | 1-bit correct, 2-bit detect | Memory ECC , register files
Hamming / extended | binary | syndrome | — | Inner code in concatenation
BCH | binary | BM + Chien | t bit errors | Flash, optical
Reed–Solomon | GF(2 m ) | syndrome→BM→Chien→Forney | t symbol errors — burst tolerant | Ethernet KP4 , storage, DVB
Convolutional | binary | Viterbi (ML) | Random errors | Legacy wireless, satellite
Turbo | binary | iterative BCJR | Near capacity | 3G/4G
LDPC | binary | belief propagation (min-sum) | Near capacity | 5G NR data , Wi-Fi, 802.3ca, NAND
Polar | binary | SC / SC-List | Provably capacity-achieving | 5G control
Fountain (LT, Raptor) | binary | BP | Rateless | Broadcast, storage
Concatenated | mixed | inner then outer | Burst + random | 802.3dj 224G , deep space

Choosing a code is choosing an error model. A
 binary code assumes errors are independent bit flips; a symbol code assumes they
 cluster. Getting this wrong is expensive in both directions — a strong binary
 code performs poorly on bursts, and an RS code wastes redundancy on isolated bit
 errors. The correct procedure is to measure the error statistics of the actual
 slicer output, including DFE error propagation and any burst noise, and choose
 accordingly. In concatenated schemes the division of labour is explicit: the inner
 code cleans up random errors and the outer code mops up the bursts that the inner
 decoder's own failures produce. The inner decoder's failure mode is the outer
 decoder's input distribution — a subtlety that must be in the system
 model.

장: F2. Error Control Coding
절: F2.2 Reed–Solomon in detail
글:
F2.2 Reed–Solomon in detail

[Table 61. RS decoder pipeline]
Stage | Computation | Parallelism | Hardware character
Syndrome | S i = r (α fcr+ i ), i =0…2 t −1 | Fully parallel (2 t independent evaluations) | 2 t constant-multiplier accumulators
Key equation (BM) | Find σ( x ) | Sequential — 2 t dependent iterations | This is the critical path
Chien search | Roots of σ( x ) | Parallel over positions | n / P cycles
Forney | e j = ω/σ′ evaluated at roots | Parallel | Needs GF inversion (ROM or Itoh–Tsujii)
Correction | XOR into the buffer | Parallel | Requires the codeword buffered

The Berlekamp–Massey iteration is the same kind
 of obstacle as the DFE loop and the OOO wakeup loop. Each iteration depends on the
 previous discrepancy, so it cannot be pipelined away. The standard remedies mirror
 those in the other two cases: inversionless BM removes the GF inversion from
 the loop (replacing it with an extra multiplication), and reformulated BM
 restructures the recurrence so that fewer operations sit inside it. A design house
 that recognises this pattern can move an engineer from a SerDes project to an FEC
 project and expect them to be productive quickly, because the underlying problem is
 identical.

[Table 62. RS decoder behaviour that must appear in the datasheet]
Condition | Behaviour | Why it must be documented
≤ t symbol errors | Always corrected | The guarantee being sold
> t errors | Detected or mis-corrected | Not all are detected. Claiming otherwise is false
Mis-correction probability | Roughly n t /( t ! 2 m ( n − k − t ) ) | Customers at 10 −15 FLR need this number
Erasure decoding | Corrects up to n − k erasures | If the receiver can flag unreliable symbols, capacity doubles
Latency | Fixed, = pipeline depth | Real-time systems need the number

“All errors beyond t are detected”
 is a false statement that appears in datasheets. A received word with more than
 t errors may land within distance t of a different valid
 codeword, in which case the decoder confidently produces the wrong answer. A measured
 illustration on a small code, RS(15,9) with t = 3: injecting exactly
 four symbol errors 120 times gave 117 detected failures and 3 mis-corrections
 — never a correct recovery, but not always a detection either. An honest
 specification states the mis-correction probability; a verification plan must
 distinguish the three outcomes (corrected / detected / mis-corrected) rather than
 counting pass and fail.

장: F2. Error Control Coding
절: F2.3 LDPC
글:
F2.3 LDPC

[Table 63. LDPC decoding choices]
Choice | Options | Effect
Message form | Probability vs log-likelihood ratio | LLR turns products into sums — essential in hardware
Check-node update | Sum-product (tanh) vs min-sum | Min-sum loses ~0.5 dB, removes transcendental functions
Correction | Normalised or offset min-sum | Recovers most of the loss for one constant
Schedule | Flooding vs layered | Layered halves the iteration count; creates pipeline hazards
Parallelism | Fully parallel / row / block | Quasi-cyclic structure enables block parallelism
Early termination | Syndrome check per iteration | Large average power saving ; worst-case latency unchanged

LDPC's fixed-point rule is the opposite of the
 CIC's. An LLR's sign carries the hard decision. If an LLR wraps in two's
 complement, a strong belief in “0” becomes a strong belief in
 “1”, and the decoder does not merely lose precision — it is actively
 misled, and iteration amplifies the damage. Measured on a 5G NR base-graph decoder,
 reducing the message width by three bits gave BLER 0.250 with saturation and
 1.000 — complete failure — with wrap-around. Meanwhile the CIC
 filter of Chapter E1 requires wrap-around to function. There is no global
 "correct" overflow policy; it is a per-block property that must be stated in the
 specification and enforced by tests.

Layered scheduling and pipeline hazards. In a
 layered decoder, layer j may need a variable node that layer i is still
 updating, forcing a stall whose length depends on the pipeline depth D and on
 the layer ordering. It is tempting to optimise the ordering against a closed-form
 stall count, but that formula is only an upper bound: it assumes every
 potential conflict costs a full stall. A measured comparison on 5G NR base graph 1 at
 D = 4 gave the formula 108 stall cycles while a cycle-accurate model
 and the RTL both gave 80 — the difference between a 70.1% and a 62.0%
 efficiency loss. Optimising a schedule against the wrong objective function finds
 the wrong schedule. Build the cycle-accurate model first; it is a day of work and
 it changes the answer.

F1.1 Why the architecture looks like this

The structure above is not arbitrary; each block exists because a
