[Table 64. The forcing chain]
Limit encountered | Response | New problem created
Channel loss rises as √ f (skin effect) | Equalise | Analogue boost amplifies noise as well as signal
CTLE alone cannot open the eye at 30 dB loss | Add DFE (subtracts decided symbols, no noise gain) | DFE feedback must close within 1 UI
1 UI = 17.86 ps at 56 GBd; latch + summer + wire + setup > 23 ps | Speculate (unroll) and parallelise (sub-rate) | Area grows; still not enough alone
Baud rate cannot be raised further — the channel will not pass it | PAM4 : two bits per symbol at the same baud rate | 9.54 dB SNR penalty
PAM4 raw BER is ~10 −4 , far from 10 −15 | Forward error correction (RS-FEC KP4) | Latency, and FEC becomes mandatory in the standard
Analogue equalisation cannot be adapted precisely enough | Sample first with a fast ADC, equalise digitally | Time-interleaved ADC mismatch; huge digital block
200 Gb/s per lane: even KP4 is not enough | Concatenated FEC (outer RS-KP4 + inner Hamming) | More latency; more complex decoder

This table is the single most useful thing to
 memorise about high-speed links, because it lets you derive the architecture
 rather than recall it, and it identifies where a newcomer can contribute. Notice that
 the last four rows are all digital responses to analogue limits. That
 migration — from analogue equalisation to digital — is why a digital IP
 house can participate in SerDes at all, and it is still in progress.

장: F1. The Wireline Link, End to End
절: F1.2 Timing budget arithmetic
글:
F1.2 Timing budget arithmetic

[Table 65. DFE first-tap loop budget at 56 GBd (1 UI = 17.86 ps)]
Element | Delay | Comment
Slicer (latch) clock-to-Q | 12 ps | Regeneration plus output drive
Summer | 8 ps | Analogue summing node settling
Wiring | 6 ps | Layout-dependent; often underestimated
Setup at next slicer | 5 ps | —
Total loop | 31.0 ps | —
Available | 17.86 ps | 1 UI
Margin | −13.14 ps | Infeasible
Latch + wire + setup alone | 23 ps | Still exceeds 1 UI

The last row is decisive and is often missed.
 Unrolling removes the summer from the loop by pre-computing both hypotheses,
 but the latch, the wiring and the setup time remain — and they already exceed
 one UI. Therefore no amount of speculation alone reaches 56 GBd; sub-rate
 parallelism is mandatory. Stating this as a measured budget rather than an
 opinion is what turns an architecture argument into an engineering conclusion, and it
 is exactly the kind of analysis a modelling engineer is expected to produce before any
 RTL exists.

장: F1. The Wireline Link, End to End
절: F1.3 Equaliser taxonomy
글:
F1.3 Equaliser taxonomy

[Table 66. Equalisers compared]
Type | Location | Removes | Noise effect | Constraint
TX FFE (de-emphasis) | Transmitter | Pre- and post-cursor | None (pre-distortion) | Reduces transmitted amplitude
CTLE | RX analogue | Broad high-frequency loss | Amplifies noise | Limited number of poles/zeros
RX FFE | RX digital | Pre- and post-cursor | Amplifies noise | Needs ADC; tap count × rate
DFE | RX digital | Post-cursor only | None (uses decisions) | 1 UI loop; error propagation
MLSE / Viterbi | RX digital | Optimal sequence detection | None | Complexity grows as M L
Nonlinear (Volterra, NN) | RX digital | Nonlinear channel effects | — | Training, complexity; an active research area

Error propagation is the price of the DFE's
 noise-free subtraction. A wrong decision is fed back and corrupts the next few
 symbols, so errors arrive in bursts rather than independently. Two consequences
 follow, and both are design decisions rather than analysis details. First, the raw
 BER is worse than an independent-error model predicts, so a link budget built on
 Q-function arithmetic alone is optimistic. Second — and more usefully —
 bursty errors are exactly what a symbol-oriented code like Reed–Solomon
 handles well, because several wrong bits inside one symbol still count as one
 symbol error. The choice of RS over a binary code at the FEC layer is therefore
 partly a consequence of the DFE at the equaliser layer. Layers that look
 independent in a block diagram are coupled through their error statistics.

장: F1. The Wireline Link, End to End
절: F1.4 Clock and data recovery
글:
F1.4 Clock and data recovery

[Table 67. CDR phase detectors]
Detector | Samples needed | Characteristic | Used with
Alexander (bang-bang) | Data + edge (2×) | Binary output; nonlinear | Classic NRZ links
Hogge | Data + edge | Linear output | Lower jitter, more complex
Gardner | 2× oversampling | Modulation-independent | Wireless, some wireline
Mueller–Müller | Baud-rate only | Uses ISI structure; needs equalised signal | ADC-DSP receivers — no 2× sampling needed
Oversampling / majority | 3–8× | Simple, robust, low rate | Low-speed links, FPGA

Why Mueller–Müller won in ADC-based receivers.
 At 56 GBd, sampling at 2× the baud rate means 112 GS/s — roughly doubling
 the ADC's power and area, which are already the dominant cost. MM extracts a timing
 error from baud-rate samples alone by exploiting the asymmetry of the equalised pulse
 response: it drives the sampling phase to the point where the first pre-cursor and
 first post-cursor are equal. The subtlety is that MM's lock point depends on the
 equaliser, so CDR and equaliser adaptation interact; a modelling engineer who
 simulates them independently will not see the interaction, and joint convergence
 failures are a classic late-stage surprise. Model the loops together or state
 explicitly that you have not.

G2. Radar: Signal Processing as an IP Block Family

Automotive and industrial radar is one of the largest current markets
 for signal-processing IP, and its chain is a clean illustration of how physical
 parameters become hardware parameters.

Pr = PtG2λ2σ
 / ((4π)3R4)   (radar equation)

The fourth-power range dependence is the defining fact of
 radar: doubling the detection range requires sixteen times the received power. Since
 transmit power and antenna gain are bounded, the remaining lever is
 processing gain — coherent integration — which is entirely a
 digital matter and therefore entirely IP.

[그림] Figure 10. FMCW radar. Range appears as a beat frequency; velocity appears as phase progression across successive chirps.

장: G2. Radar: Signal Processing as an IP Block Family
절: G2.1 FMCW parameter derivation
글:
G2.1 FMCW parameter derivation

[Table 68. From requirement to hardware parameter]
Requirement | Relation | Hardware consequence
Range resolution Δ R | Δ R = c /2 B | Sweep bandwidth — 4 GHz gives 3.75 cm
Maximum range R max | f b,max = 2 R max S / c | ADC sample rate and IF bandwidth
Velocity resolution Δ v | Δ v = λ/(2 N c T c ) | Number of chirps per frame → frame memory
Maximum velocity | v max = λ/(4 T c ) | Chirp repetition period
Angular resolution | ≈ λ/( N a d cosθ) | Number of antennas → number of RX chains
Processing gain | 10log( N s N c ) | FFT sizes → compute and memory

The range–Doppler map is a two-dimensional FFT
 and its dimensions come straight from the table: a fast-time FFT across samples within
 one chirp yields range bins; a slow-time FFT across chirps at each range bin yields
 Doppler bins. A typical automotive frame — 256 samples × 128 chirps
 × 8 virtual antennas — requires a corner-turn between the two FFTs, and
 that transpose, not the FFTs, dominates the memory bandwidth. Designing the
 memory organisation (ping-pong banks, tiled transpose, or on-the-fly second-stage
 accumulation) is the real architectural work. This is a recurring theme: in
 data-intensive blocks the arithmetic is rarely the bottleneck.

장: G2. Radar: Signal Processing as an IP Block Family
절: G2.2 Detection
글:
G2.2 Detection

[Table 69. CFAR detectors]
Type | Noise estimate | Strength | Weakness
CA-CFAR | Mean of surrounding cells | Simple, efficient in homogeneous noise | Masks targets near clutter edges
GO-CFAR | Greater of the two halves | Handles clutter edges | Loses closely spaced targets
SO-CFAR | Smaller of the two halves | Resolves close targets | High false alarm at edges
OS-CFAR | k -th order statistic | Robust to interfering targets | Needs a sorter — more hardware
Adaptive / ML | learned | Best in complex scenes | Verification difficulty

CFAR sets a threshold, not a decision. The
 multiplier α is chosen so that the probability of false alarm is fixed regardless
 of the noise level — that is what "constant false alarm rate" means. For
 CA-CFAR with N reference cells,
 α = N(PFA−1/N − 1). Two
 hardware consequences: the block needs a divider or a reciprocal table, and it needs
 the N reference cells buffered, which for a 2-D CFAR means a sliding window over
 a two-dimensional array. OS-CFAR's sorter is the most hardware-hungry element in a
 typical radar back end, and choosing between a full sorting network and an
 approximate selection is a genuine PPA decision that a design house can differentiate
 on.

장: G2. Radar: Signal Processing as an IP Block Family
절: G2.3 Angle estimation and MIMO
글:
G2.3 Angle estimation and MIMO

[Table 70. Angle-of-arrival methods]
Method | Resolution | Computation | Robustness
FFT beamforming | Rayleigh limit | One FFT | Very robust
Capon / MVDR | Super-resolution | Matrix inverse per snapshot | Needs good covariance estimate
MUSIC | Super-resolution | Eigendecomposition | Needs the source count
ESPRIT | Super-resolution | SVD + rotation | Needs array structure
Compressive sensing | High | Iterative solver | Sensitive to model mismatch

This is where Part A's matrix decompositions become
 products. MUSIC needs the eigendecomposition of an N×N
 covariance matrix per snapshot; Capon needs its inverse. For an 8–16 element
 array that is a small, dense, Hermitian, positive-definite problem —
 exactly the case where Cholesky applies and streams. A design house that owns a
 parameterised streaming Cholesky or Jacobi eigenvalue block can sell it into radar,
 into MIMO communications, and into adaptive beamforming, because all three reduce to
 the same kernel. Recognising that one kernel serves three markets is how a small IP
 portfolio becomes viable.

MIMO radar's virtual array deserves a precise
 statement because it is the main reason automotive radar improved so quickly. With
 Nt transmitters and Nr receivers, transmitting
 orthogonal waveforms (time-, frequency-, or code-division) and separating them at the
 receiver yields Nt×Nr distinct
 transmit–receive paths, which behave like a physical array of that many
 elements. Three transmitters and four receivers give a twelve-element virtual array
 — a threefold improvement in angular resolution at the cost of digital
 separation logic rather than antennas and RF chains. Once again the solution to a
 physical limit is a digital block.

장: G1. Electromagnetics for the Digital Engineer

G1. Electromagnetics for the Digital Engineer

A digital IP engineer meets electromagnetics at three boundaries: the
 package and board that carry the block's signals, the channel a SerDes must equalise,
 and the antenna of a radio or radar system whose baseband processing is the block
 itself. This chapter covers what is needed at those boundaries.

장: G1. Electromagnetics for the Digital Engineer
절: G1.1 From Maxwell to circuits
글:
G1.1 From Maxwell to circuits

[Table 71. Regimes and the model that applies]
Regime | Condition | Model | Consequence
Lumped | size ≪ λ | KCL/KVL, R L C | Voltage is well defined everywhere
Quasi-static | size ≲ λ/10 | Lumped + parasitics | Inductance begins to matter
Distributed | size ≳ λ/10 | Transmission line | Position matters; reflections occur
Full wave | structure comparable to λ | Maxwell solvers | Radiation, resonance, modes

The threshold keeps moving toward the designer.
 The criterion is not clock frequency but edge rate: significant spectral content
 extends to roughly 0.35/tr. A 50 ps edge has content to
 7 GHz regardless of whether the clock is 100 MHz, and at 7 GHz a
 2 cm trace is a transmission line. Slow clocks do not protect you from fast
 edges. This is why deliberately slowing output slew rates is a legitimate design
 technique — and why an IP's output driver strength is a specification item with
 EMI consequences, not just a timing one.

G1.2 Transmission lines

Z0 = √((R + jωL)/(G + jωC))
  →  √(L/C)  (lossless)

[Table 72. Line types]
Type | Z 0 range | Where
Microstrip | 50–100 Ω | Outer PCB layer; radiates more
Stripline | 50–100 Ω | Inner layer; better shielded, slower (higher ε eff )
Coplanar waveguide | tunable | On-chip RF; ground on the same layer
Differential pair | 85–100 Ω differential | The standard for high-speed serial
On-chip global wire | — | Usually RC-dominated, not a true TL

[Table 73. Termination strategies]
Scheme | Placement | Power | Note
Series (source) | At driver | Low | Doubles the driver's output swing requirement
Parallel | At receiver | High (static) | Best match
Thevenin | At receiver | High | Sets a DC bias
AC-coupled | In line | Low | Requires DC-balanced coding (8b/10b, 64b/66b)
On-die termination (ODT) | Inside the chip | Moderate | Calibrated against an external precision resistor

AC coupling and line coding are linked requirements.
 A series capacitor blocks DC, so a long run of identical symbols causes the signal to
 droop toward the decision threshold — baseline wander. The line code must
 therefore bound the run length and keep the running disparity small. 8b/10b does this
 with an explicit disparity rule at 25% overhead; 64b/66b uses a scrambler and accepts a
 small probability of a long run, at 3% overhead. The coding choice is thus
 determined by an analogue component. An engineer who knows only the coding layer
 cannot explain why 64b/66b needs a scrambler with a particular polynomial, nor why
 certain data patterns are used as stress tests.

G1.3 Antennas and propagation

Pr = PtGtGr

[Table 74. Antenna and propagation quantities]
Quantity | Definition | Design relevance
Gain G | Directivity × efficiency | Trades coverage for range
Effective aperture | A e = G λ 2 /4π | Higher frequency → smaller aperture for the same gain
Beamwidth | ≈ 70°λ/ D | Array size sets angular resolution
Path loss exponent | 2 (free space) to 4+ (urban) | Link budget
Multipath / delay spread | — | Sets the equaliser or OFDM CP length
Doppler shift | f d = 2 v /λ | Coherence time; tracking loop bandwidth

Delay spread converts directly into a hardware
 parameter. If the channel's impulse response lasts τmax, a
 single-carrier receiver needs an equaliser spanning τmax/Ts
 symbols, and an OFDM receiver needs a cyclic prefix at least that long. The first
 costs taps (area, adaptation time); the second costs throughput (the CP is overhead).
 This is the quantitative form of the choice between single-carrier and OFDM,
 and it explains why wireline links — where delay spread is long but the channel
 is static — use equalisers, while wireless links with time-varying multipath use
 OFDM. The same physics, opposite conclusions, because the rate of change
 differs.

장: G1. Electromagnetics for the Digital Engineer
절: G1.4 Noise figure and receiver chains
글:
G1.4 Noise figure and receiver chains

Ftotal = F1 +
 (F2−1)/G1 + (F3−1)/(G1G2)
 + …

Friis's formula justifies the entire architecture of a
 receiver front end. Because later stages are divided by the cumulative gain ahead
 of them, the first amplifier dominates the noise figure — hence the low-noise
 amplifier, placed as close to the antenna as possible, often before any filter whose
 insertion loss would add directly to F1. The counterweight is
 linearity: gain early in the chain means large signals later, so the cascaded
 third-order intercept point degrades as
 1/IIP3total = 1/IIP31 + G1/IIP32 + …
 Noise pushes gain forward; linearity pushes it backward. Every receiver's gain
 distribution is a solution to that tension, and the digital back end inherits the
 result as its required dynamic range — which is to say, as its ADC bit count.

[Table 75. From RTL to GDSII]

Logic synthesis | generic → standard cells | Constraints, effort, V TH mix | Over-constrained clock → area and power explosion
DFT insertion | + scan chains | Chain count and length | Scan shift timing

Floorplanning is where an IP block's shape becomes a
 commercial issue. A block delivered as RTL will be placed by the customer, whose
 aspect ratio, pin locations and macro placement may be nothing like the vendor's. If
 the block's internal timing depends on a particular arrangement — a wide
 datapath that must stay compact, a memory that must sit next to its controller —
 then the RTL alone is not a sufficient deliverable. Serious IP therefore ships a
 floorplan guideline, sometimes a hardened macro, and always a statement of the
 assumed aspect ratio and utilisation. A block that met timing in the vendor's flow
 and misses in the customer's is the single most damaging support event a small IP
 house can have, because it is expensive to debug remotely and it destroys
 confidence.

[Table 76. Sign-off corners]
Axis | Values | Why
Process | SS, TT, FF, SF, FS | Global and local variation
Voltage | min, nominal, max | IR drop and regulation tolerance
Temperature | −40, 25, 125 °C | Both extremes — temperature inversion makes cold the worst case at low V
RC extraction | Cmin, Cmax, RCmin, RCmax | Metal thickness variation
Mode | functional, scan, BIST, low power | Different constraints apply
Ageing | fresh, end-of-life | NBTI/PBTI drift

The corner count multiplies. Five process points
 × three voltages × three temperatures × four RC × four modes is

 is statistical or parametric OCV (POCV), which models variation as a
 distribution rather than enumerating corners, plus careful selection of dominant

[Table 77. High-level synthesis in the flow]
Aspect | Reality

Strength | Design-space exploration: one source, many area/throughput points
Weakness | Generated RTL is hard to read and debug; timing closure less predictable

Where it loses | Control-dominated logic, precise cycle-level interfaces

[Table 78. Threat model, mechanism, countermeasure]
Threat | Mechanism | Countermeasure | Verifiable by simulation?

Power / EM (SPA, DPA, CPA) | Switching activity correlates with data | Masking (Boolean or arithmetic), threshold implementations, DOM | No — requires TVLA on silicon or power simulation

The fourth column is the key organisational insight for
 a modelling engineer. A functional regression, no matter how complete, is blind to
 four of the seven rows. Saying “the AES block is verified” is therefore
 ambiguous, and in a security review the ambiguity will be challenged. The mature
 formulation is: functional equivalence to FIPS-197 is verified by NIST vectors and
 constrained-random comparison against an independent model; side-channel resistance is
 assessed separately by TVLA on the test chip; fault resistance is assessed by
 gate-level fault injection. Three claims, three methods, three owners.

[Table 79. Masking: the principle and its cost]
Concept | Statement | Consequence

Nonlinear operations | Shares must interact | The expensive part — this is why the AES S-box is rebuilt in arithmetic

DOM | Domain separation + fresh randomness + registers | Provably glitch-resistant; needs a continuous randomness supply

Randomness becomes a system-level resource. A
 DOM-protected S-box consumes fresh random bits on every evaluation. An AES core

절: H1. Verification: Theory and Organisation — 들어가며

H1. Verification: Theory and Organisation

[그림] Figure 11. The three-team structure. It exists to make “correct” an operational, testable notion.

Verification consumes more effort than design in every serious IP
 project — commonly cited at 60–70% of the schedule. Understanding why it
 is organised as it is prevents a great deal of wasted work.

장: H1. Verification: Theory and Organisation
절: H1.1 Why two independent implementations
글:
H1.1 Why two independent implementations

A specification written in prose is ambiguous; a single
 implementation is self-consistent by construction and therefore cannot reveal its own
 misreadings. Two implementations built independently from the same specification will
 agree only where both read it the same way. Disagreement localises ambiguity.
 This is the same principle as dissimilar redundancy in avionics, applied to
 development rather than to operation.

The argument fails if the two implementations are not
 independent. If the modeller and the designer sit together, share an
 interpretation, and one consults the other's code when unsure, the common-mode error
 rate rises and the regression turns green on a shared misunderstanding. Organisations
 counter this in three ways: physical or organisational separation; deriving one
 implementation from a formal, executable specification (the RISC-V Sail model
 is the canonical example, generating both prose and a C emulator from one source); and
 an external oracle — standard test vectors from NIST, IEEE or a
 conformance suite. The third is the strongest and the cheapest, and it is the
 reason standards-based blocks are the best first product for a small IP house.

장: H1. Verification: Theory and Organisation
절: H1.2 The verification stack
글:
H1.2 The verification stack

[Table 81. Verification levels]
Level | Checks | Catches | Cannot catch
Lint | Coding rules | Latches, width mismatches, incomplete sensitivity | Anything functional
CDC / RDC static | Crossing structure | Missing synchronisers, reconvergence | Functional protocol errors
Unit simulation | Block behaviour vs model | Most functional bugs | Integration, timing
Formal property | Exhaustive over state space | Deadlock, unreachable states, protocol violations | Deep datapath equivalence (state explosion)
Formal equivalence (LEC) | RTL vs netlist | Synthesis and ECO errors | Specification errors
Integration / SoC sim | Blocks together | Interface mismatches, arbitration | Long-running system behaviour
Gate-level with timing | Netlist + SDF | X-propagation, timing-dependent bugs | Slow; limited coverage
Emulation / FPGA prototype | Real software on real RTL | Software-visible bugs, long sequences | Analogue, timing corners
Post-silicon | Actual device | Everything else | — but fixes are expensive

X-propagation deserves a specific warning because it
 is asymmetric between RTL and gates. In RTL simulation, an if (x)
 with an unknown condition may take a branch and produce a definite value, hiding the
 uncertainty — this is X-optimism. In gate-level simulation the same
 unknown spreads — X-pessimism. A design that relies on registers being
 initialised by data flow rather than by reset can therefore pass RTL simulation and
 fail in gates, or vice versa. The remedies are X-propagation-aware simulation modes
 and, better, explicit initialisation of any register whose value is read before it
 is written. For an IP vendor this is also a deliverable question: if your block
 requires n cycles of reset before its outputs are valid, say so.

장: H1. Verification: Theory and Organisation
절: H1.3 Coverage and closure
글:
H1.3 Coverage and closure

[Table 82. Coverage metrics]
Metric | Measures | Automatic? | Weakness
Line / block | Statements executed | Yes | Says nothing about values
Branch / condition | Decisions taken | Yes | —
Expression (MC/DC) | Each condition independently affects the outcome | Yes | Required for DO-254 / ISO 26262
Toggle | Every bit changed both ways | Yes | Weak functional signal
FSM state / transition | States and arcs visited | Yes | —
Functional (covergroups) | Scenarios the engineer defined | No | Blind to scenarios nobody thought of
Assertion | Properties actually exercised | Partly | Vacuous passes must be excluded
Mutation / fault injection | Whether the testbench would notice a bug | Yes | The only metric that tests the testbench

Mutation coverage is the metric that answers the
 question the others avoid: would this testbench detect a bug if there were one?
 The procedure is to inject a small, semantically meaningful change — invert a
 comparison, drop a term, stick a bit — and confirm the regression turns red. A
 mutant that survives identifies a check that does not exist or a stimulus that never
 reaches the code. This is cheap to automate and routinely reveals that a large
 fraction of a mature suite is inert. The same technique applies to the reference
 model itself, which is otherwise unverified: break the model deliberately and
 confirm the model's own self-checks fail. A verified reference model is a
 differentiator that very few IP vendors can claim.

장: H1. Verification: Theory and Organisation
절: H1.4 The scoreboard problem
글:
H1.4 The scoreboard problem

[Table 83. Comparison strategies]
Situation | Strategy | Pitfall
In-order, fixed latency | FIFO compare | —
In-order, variable latency | FIFO + timeout | Timeout too tight → false failures
Out-of-order, tagged | Per-tag queues | A single queue produces both false failures and false passes
Multiple legal orders | Compare against a set of allowed outcomes | Requires the model to enumerate them
Don't-care fields | Mask before comparing | Masking too much hides real bugs
Weak memory model | Litmus tests , not trace comparison | Trace comparison is simply invalid here

The AXI case is worth stating concretely because it is so
 common. AXI guarantees ordering only within an ID; transactions with different
 IDs may complete in any order. A scoreboard with one queue will report a failure when
 the DUT legitimately reorders across IDs, and — more dangerously — may
 accept a genuine intra-ID reordering as long as the totals match. The correct
 structure is one queue per ID, and knowing this is a direct consequence of having
 read the protocol specification rather than inferring behaviour from waveforms. It is
 a frequent and productive point of contact between the modelling and verification
 teams.

장: H1. Verification: Theory and Organisation
절: H1.5 Regression engineering
글:
H1.5 Regression engineering

[Table 84. Regression discipline]
Practice | Reason
Record the seed with every run | Without it a failure is not reproducible
Classify failures automatically | Triage time dominates otherwise
Track failure signatures , not counts | Distinguishes new from known
Never close an intermittent failure as ‘flaky’ | Intermittent failures are usually real races
Keep a golden log of the last known-good | Enables bisection
Measure regression runtime | A suite nobody can run nightly is not a suite
Separate infrastructure failures | Licence and disk errors must not be counted as bugs

The prohibition on dismissing intermittent failures is
 the most frequently violated rule in this book. An intermittent failure means the
 outcome depends on something the test does not control — a race, an
 uninitialised value, a timing-dependent path. All three exist in the silicon too.
 Closing such a ticket does not remove the bug; it removes the evidence. The
 correct disposition is to keep it open with the failing seed recorded, even if it
 cannot be root-caused immediately.

장: I2. Algebraic Structures for Hardware
절: I2.1 Groups, rings, fields
글:
I2.1 Groups, rings, fields

[Table 85. Structures and the hardware they license]
Structure | Operations | Guarantee | Hardware consequence
Group | one associative op with inverses | Cancellation | Reversible transforms
Ring | + and ×, no division | Closure under both | Two's-complement W -bit arithmetic is a ring — wrap-around is exact, so operation order does not matter
Field | + × and division | Every non-zero element invertible | GF(2 m ) arithmetic for codes and crypto
Vector space over a field | — | Linearity | Linear codes: encoding and syndrome are matrix products
Polynomial ring F [ x ]/( f ) | — | — | Cyclic codes, NTT, lattice cryptography

The ring property of two's-complement arithmetic is the
 formal reason behind a practical rule. Because W-bit two's complement is
 the ring ℤ/2Wℤ, addition and multiplication are exact
 modulo 2W, associative and commutative. Intermediate overflow
 therefore cancels exactly, provided the final result is in range, and the order of
 accumulation cannot change the answer. Saturation destroys the ring structure:
 once a value is clamped, information is lost and order matters. This is why a CIC
 filter requires wrap-around and why an LDPC decoder requires saturation
 — the two blocks rely on opposite algebraic properties. Stating this as
 algebra rather than as folklore makes it possible to decide the question for a new
 block instead of guessing.

장: I2. Algebraic Structures for Hardware
절: I2.2 Finite fields in detail
글:
I2.2 Finite fields in detail

[Table 86. GF(2 m ) implementation choices]
Representation | Multiplication | Inversion | Best for
Polynomial basis | Shift-and-XOR, reduce | Extended Euclid or Itoh–Tsujii | General purpose; most codes
Normal basis | More complex | Squaring is a free cyclic shift | Inversion-heavy workloads (ECC)
Log/antilog tables | Add logs | Negate the log | Small fields (m ≤ 12); the usual RS choice
Tower field | GF(2 8 )→GF(2 4 )→GF(2 2 ) | Recursive | Maskable — the AES DOM S-box
Composite field | — | — | Area reduction

The choice of irreducible polynomial is a
 specification item, not an implementation detail. Two implementations of
 GF(210) using different primitive polynomials produce entirely different
 — though isomorphic — arithmetic, and codewords from one will not decode in
 the other. Standards therefore fix the polynomial: AES uses
 x8+x4+x3+x+1, and
 IEEE 802.3 Clause 91 fixes the field for RS(544,514). A reference model
 that hard-codes a plausible polynomial without checking the standard will interoperate
 with nothing. The defensive practice is to make the polynomial a parameter, assert
 that it is primitive (verify that α generates all 2m−1
 non-zero elements), and record in the code whether the value has been confirmed
 against the specification text.

[Table 87. Where finite fields appear]
Application | Field | Operation that dominates
Reed–Solomon | GF(2 8 ), GF(2 10 ) | Multiply, invert
BCH | GF(2 m ) | Multiply
AES | GF(2 8 ) | Inverse (S-box), ×2 and ×3 (MixColumns)
AES-GCM | GF(2 128 ) | Carry-less multiply
Elliptic curves | GF( p ) or GF(2 m ) | Modular multiply (Montgomery)
ML-KEM / ML-DSA | ℤ q [ x ]/( x n +1) | Number-theoretic transform
CRC | GF(2)[ x ] | Polynomial remainder (LFSR)
Erasure coding (RAID) | GF(2 8 ) | Matrix multiply

Post-quantum cryptography brings a new arithmetic
 requirement into mainstream silicon. ML-KEM and ML-DSA operate in a polynomial
 ring modulo a small prime (3329 and 8380417 respectively), and their bottleneck is the
 number-theoretic transform — an FFT over that ring. The hardware looks like an
 FFT but with modular multipliers instead of complex ones, and modular reduction by a
 fixed small prime admits efficient tricks (Montgomery, Barrett, or prime-specific
 shift–add chains). For a design house, an NTT block parameterised over
 modulus and length is a single kernel serving several standards, in the same way
 that a Cholesky block serves radar, MIMO and beamforming. Finding these shared kernels
 is how a small portfolio covers a large market.

장: I4. Discrete Mathematics and Graphs in Hardware
절: I4. Discrete Mathematics and Graphs in Hardware — 들어가며
글:
I4. Discrete Mathematics and Graphs in Hardware

[Table 88. Graph problems in the design flow]
Problem | Where it appears | Complexity | Practical method
Topological sort | Netlist evaluation, scheduling | Linear | Exact
Longest path | Static timing analysis | Linear on a DAG | Exact — this is what STA computes
Cycle detection | Combinational loop check | Linear | Exact
Min-cut / max-flow | Partitioning, retiming | Polynomial | Exact
Graph colouring | Register allocation, channel assignment | NP-hard | Heuristic
Clique / independent set | Binding in HLS | NP-hard | Heuristic
Shortest path | Routing | Polynomial | A*, maze routing
Steiner tree | Multi-pin net routing | NP-hard | Heuristic
Isomorphism | LVS (layout vs schematic) | Unknown class | Practical algorithms

Recognising that a design task is a known graph problem
 is worth more than knowing an algorithm for it. Static timing analysis is longest
 path on a DAG — which is why combinational loops must be forbidden: they make the
 problem ill-posed, not merely difficult. Retiming is a min-cost flow problem, which is
 why it is exactly solvable while placement (a quadratic assignment problem) is not.
 The tractability boundary explains the tool landscape: tasks on the polynomial
 side have exact tools that engineers trust, and tasks on the NP-hard side have
 heuristics whose results engineers must inspect. A designer who knows which side a
 problem lies on knows whether to argue with the tool.

[Table 89. Boolean algebra and representations]
Representation | Property | Use
Truth table | Exponential size | Small functions, LUT mapping
SOP / POS | Two-level | PLA, simple synthesis
BDD | Canonical for a fixed variable order | Equivalence checking ; order-sensitive size
AIG (And-Inverter Graph) | Compact, not canonical | Modern synthesis and formal engines
CNF + SAT | — | Bounded model checking, equivalence
SMT | Theories beyond Boolean | Word-level formal verification

The shift from BDDs to SAT reshaped formal
 verification. BDDs are canonical, which makes equivalence a pointer comparison,
 but their size explodes for arithmetic functions such as multipliers and is acutely
 sensitive to variable ordering. Modern SAT solvers, with conflict-driven clause
 learning, handle far larger instances without canonicity. The practical consequence
 for an IP engineer is that formal property checking is now feasible on real control
 logic — arbiters, FIFOs, protocol adapters, FSM reachability — where a
 decade ago it was a specialist activity. It remains infeasible on deep datapaths, so
 the division of labour is: formal for control, simulation with a golden model for
 datapath. Knowing which side of that line a block falls on is how a verification
 plan is written.

장: I1. Information Theory
절: I1.1 Entropy and its operational meanings
글:
I1.1 Entropy and its operational meanings

H(X) = −∑x p(x) log2 p(x)
     I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y)

[Table 90. Information-theoretic quantities and where they bind hardware]
Quantity | Meaning | Operational limit it sets
Entropy H ( X ) | Average information per symbol | Lossless compression cannot go below it — bounds a codec's ratio
Min-entropy H ∞ | −log 2 max x p ( x ) | The measure NIST SP 800-90B requires for an entropy source; always ≤ H
Conditional entropy | Remaining uncertainty given side information | Leakage analysis in side-channel evaluation
Mutual information | Information one variable carries about another | Side-channel leakage metric ; also the quantity maximised by capacity
Channel capacity C | max I ( X ; Y ) | No code can exceed it; tells you how far your FEC is from optimal
Rate–distortion R ( D ) | Minimum rate for distortion D | Lossy codec bound — the theoretical floor of a video encoder
Kolmogorov complexity | Shortest program producing the string | Uncomputable; conceptual only

Min-entropy is the one an IP engineer must get right,
 and it is not Shannon entropy. A biased source that outputs 0 with probability
 0.9 has Shannon entropy 0.47 bits but min-entropy only
 −log2(0.9) = 0.152 bits. Certification uses min-entropy because
 security must hold against the most likely guess, not the average case. A TRNG
 that claims "0.5 bits of entropy per sample" on Shannon grounds and is conditioned on
 that basis will fail validation and, worse, will produce keys with less
 unpredictability than advertised. The conditioning ratio — how many raw bits
 are compressed into one output bit — is derived from min-entropy, and it is a
 hardware parameter.

장: I1. Information Theory
절: I1.2 Capacity results that matter in practice
글:
I1.2 Capacity results that matter in practice

[Table 91. Capacity expressions]
Channel | Capacity | Design meaning
AWGN | B log 2 (1+SNR) | The reference against which every modem is measured
Binary symmetric (BSC) | 1 − H b ( p ) | Hard-decision decoding loses ~2 dB versus soft
Binary erasure (BEC) | 1 − ε | Erasure decoding doubles RS correction capability
MIMO ( N t × N r ) | ≈ min( N t , N r ) log(1+SNR) | Capacity scales with antennas, not power
Fading with CSI | E[log(1+| h | 2 SNR)] | Motivates adaptive modulation and coding
Band-limited with ISI | water-filling over the channel response | The theoretical justification for OFDM bit loading

The soft-versus-hard decision gap is the most
 actionable number here. Passing hard decisions to a decoder discards the
 reliability information the slicer had, and costs roughly 2 dB on an AWGN
 channel. In a link budget 2 dB is enormous — it is the difference between
 needing an extra equaliser tap and not. This is why modern FEC interfaces carry LLRs
 rather than bits, why the slicer in an ADC-based receiver reports a multi-bit
 soft value, and why the fixed-point width of that LLR is a system-level parameter
 rather than a local choice. An interface that carries one bit where it could carry
 four has thrown away 2 dB before the decoder starts.

장: I1. Information Theory
절: I1.3 Source coding
글:
I1.3 Source coding

[Table 92. Compression methods in hardware]
Method | Principle | Hardware character
Huffman | Prefix code by symbol probability | Table lookup; variable-length decode is serial
Canonical Huffman | Ordered code lengths | Compact tables, faster decode
Arithmetic / range | Interval subdivision | Better ratio; strictly serial — a throughput bottleneck
CABAC | Context-adaptive binary arithmetic | The critical path of an H.264/HEVC decoder
ANS / rANS | Asymmetric numeral systems | Arithmetic-coding ratio with table-driven speed; used in AV1, Zstd
LZ family | Dictionary matching | Match search is the expensive part
RLE | Run lengths | Trivial; still used for coefficient maps

Entropy coding is where video decoders stop
 parallelising. Transform, prediction and filtering all parallelise over blocks,
 but arithmetic decoding is inherently sequential: the next symbol's interval depends
 on the current state. This is why real decoders introduce architectural workarounds
 — slices and tiles that reset the context so they can be decoded independently,
 wavefront parallel processing, or the bypass modes that skip context modelling for
 near-uniform symbols. The bitstream syntax was designed around a hardware
 constraint, which is the clearest possible illustration that standards and
 architectures co-evolve.

장: I3. Optimisation and Numerical Methods
절: I3. Optimisation and Numerical Methods — 들어가며
글:
I3. Optimisation and Numerical Methods

[Table 93. Optimisation problems that appear in IP design]
Problem | Class | Method | Where
Filter coefficient design | Convex (minimax) | Remez, convex solvers | FIR design with quantised coefficients
Equaliser tap solution | Least squares | Normal equations, QR | MMSE equaliser initialisation
Bit allocation | Integer, convex relaxation | Water-filling then rounding | OFDM loading, quantisation budgeting
Scheduling / binding | NP-hard | ILP, list scheduling, force-directed | HLS internals
Retiming | Polynomial | Leiserson–Saxe | Timing optimisation
Placement | NP-hard | Analytic + partitioning | Physical design
Layer/schedule ordering | Combinatorial | Local search, simulated annealing | LDPC layered decoding order
Word-length assignment | Mixed integer | Heuristic + simulation | Fixed-point conversion

The objective function must be the true cost, not a
 convenient proxy. A measured example: optimising an LDPC layer ordering against a
 closed-form stall estimate produced a schedule that a cycle-accurate model scored
 differently — the formula predicted 108 stall cycles where the true figure was
 80. Because the formula is an upper bound that assumes every potential conflict
 materialises, it ranks schedules incorrectly, and the search converges on the wrong
 one. Build the accurate evaluator before the optimiser; a search is only as good
 as the function it is minimising, and a fast wrong objective is worse than a slow
 right one.

[Table 94. Numerical methods and their hardware suitability]
Method | Convergence | Hardware note
Newton–Raphson | Quadratic | Needs a multiplier and a good seed; used for reciprocal and rsqrt
Goldschmidt | Quadratic | Better pipelining than Newton (no dependency chain)
CORDIC | Linear (one bit per iteration) | Shifts and adds only
Polynomial (minimax) | Fixed degree | Remez-fitted polynomials beat Taylor for equal degree
Piecewise polynomial + LUT | — | The usual production answer
Iterative refinement | Doubles accuracy per step | Limited by conditioning — see A5.2

Taylor series should almost never appear in shipped
 hardware. A Taylor expansion minimises error at a single point and degrades away
 from it; a minimax (Remez) polynomial of the same degree distributes error evenly and
 typically achieves the same worst-case accuracy with one or two fewer terms. Since
 each term is a multiply–add, that is a direct area and latency saving. The
 standard production recipe is: reduce the argument to a small interval using the
 number's exponent, evaluate a low-degree minimax polynomial on that interval, then
 reconstruct. Knowing that the textbook series is the wrong tool is a small piece of
 knowledge with a consistently measurable payoff.

장: J2. Accelerators: Systolic Arrays and the Roofline
절: J2. Accelerators: Systolic Arrays and the Roofline — 들어가며
글:
J2. Accelerators: Systolic Arrays and the Roofline

[그림] Figure 12. The roofline model. A kernel's arithmetic intensity determines whether more compute or more bandwidth helps.

Attainable performance =
 min(Peak compute, Bandwidth × Arithmetic intensity)

The roofline is the first slide of any accelerator
 proposal, and it decides the architecture. Arithmetic intensity — useful
 operations per byte moved from memory — is a property of the algorithm and its
 dataflow, not of the hardware. A naive matrix multiply that re-reads operands has low
 intensity and is memory-bound: adding multipliers achieves nothing. Tiling the
 computation so that each loaded element is reused n times multiplies the
 intensity by n and moves the kernel rightward past the ridge, at which point
 additional compute finally pays. Every accelerator architecture is, at bottom, a
 scheme for raising arithmetic intensity.

[그림] Figure 13. A systolic array. Operands flow through the array and are reused by every processing element they pass.

[Table 95. Accelerator dataflow taxonomy]
Dataflow | What stays resident | Best when
Weight stationary | Weights in the PE | Weights are reused across many activations (CNN inference)
Output stationary | Partial sums in the PE | Long reduction chains; minimises partial-sum movement
Row stationary | A row of the convolution | Balances all three reuse types
No local reuse | Nothing | Simple, memory-bound

[Table 96. Precision in inference accelerators]
Format | Bits | Effect | Hardware cost
FP32 | 32 | Baseline | Reference
BF16 | 16 | Same exponent range as FP32, fewer mantissa bits | ~1/2 multiplier area; drop-in for training
FP16 | 16 | Smaller range — needs loss scaling | ~1/2
INT8 | 8 | Requires calibration or QAT | ~1/4 area, ~1/4 energy of FP32
INT4 / INT2 | 4/2 | Significant accuracy loss without care | Smaller still
Binary / ternary | 1–2 | XNOR–popcount replaces multiply | No multipliers at all
Mixed / per-channel scale | — | Recovers most INT8 accuracy | Per-channel scaling logic

Binary networks replace arithmetic with logic, which
 changes the whole cost structure. When weights and activations are ±1, a
 multiply becomes an XNOR and the accumulation becomes a population count. A 256-input
 dot product is then 256 XNOR gates and a popcount tree — a few hundred gates
 instead of 256 multipliers. The trade is accuracy, recovered partially by keeping the
 first and last layers at higher precision and by batch normalisation folded into a
 threshold comparison. For an IP house this is attractive because the resulting
 block is small, fully synthesisable, and has no dependence on DSP hard macros,
 which makes it portable across FPGA and ASIC targets.

[Table 97. Accelerator interface decisions]
Decision | Options | Consequence
Weight delivery | Resident in the bitstream vs streamed at run time | Dominates the system architecture : bandwidth vs flexibility
Granularity | Layer-at-a-time vs fused layers | Fusion removes intermediate memory traffic
Control | Fixed sequence vs programmable | Flexibility vs area
Memory | Scratchpad vs cache | Scratchpad is deterministic ; cache is easier to program
Sparsity | Dense vs structured vs unstructured | Unstructured sparsity rarely pays in hardware

장: J4. Image and Video Coding
절: J4. Image and Video Coding — 들어가며
글:
J4. Image and Video Coding

[Table 98. Codec pipeline stages]
Stage | Purpose | Hardware character
Prediction (intra) | Exploit spatial correlation | Many modes → mode decision is a search
Prediction (inter / motion) | Exploit temporal correlation | Motion estimation dominates encoder cost
Transform | Energy compaction (integer DCT) | Multiplier-free integer approximations
Quantisation | Lossy step — rate control lives here | Divide by a table value
Entropy coding | Remove remaining redundancy (CABAC) | Serial bottleneck
Loop filter (deblocking, SAO, ALF) | Remove artefacts | In the reconstruction loop — must be bit-exact
Reference frame store | — | DRAM bandwidth dominates

Encoder and decoder are asymmetric by design. The
 standard specifies only the decoder; the encoder may choose modes however it likes,
 provided the bitstream is conformant. This means encoder quality is a product
 differentiator while decoder correctness is a conformance requirement, and the two
 have completely different verification strategies: a decoder is verified against
 conformance bitstreams with bit-exact expected output, whereas an encoder is evaluated
 on rate–distortion curves and must only produce decodable output. A design house
 entering video should know which side it is selling into, because the effort profiles
 differ by an order of magnitude.

[Table 99. Standards and their distinguishing features]
Codec | Year | Key additions | Hardware impact
JPEG | 1992 | 8×8 DCT, Huffman | Simple, still ubiquitous
H.264/AVC | 2003 | Integer transform, CABAC, variable block size | Integer transform removes encoder/decoder drift
HEVC/H.265 | 2013 | CTU up to 64×64, 35 intra modes, SAO | Much larger mode search
VP9 / AV1 | 2013/2018 | Royalty-free, ANS coding, many partitions | Very large encoder search space
VVC/H.266 | 2020 | More partitions, ALF, affine motion | Further complexity
JPEG XS / lightweight | — | Low latency, visually lossless | Line-based, small buffers — a good niche for a small IP house

Bit-exactness inside the reconstruction loop is
 non-negotiable. The decoder's output feeds the encoder's prediction, so any
 arithmetic difference accumulates frame after frame — drift. This is why every
 in-loop operation (transform, quantisation, interpolation filters, deblocking) is
 specified as exact integer arithmetic with defined rounding, and why a reference model
 for a codec must reproduce those operations bit for bit rather than
 mathematically. A floating-point reference model of a video codec is not a
 reference model.

장: J1. On-Chip Memory
절: J1. On-Chip Memory — 들어가며
글:
J1. On-Chip Memory

[Table 100. Memory types available to an IP block]
Type | Bit cell | Density | Notes
6T SRAM | 6 transistors | High | Standard; compiled by the foundry
8T / 10T SRAM | 8–10 T | Lower | Better read stability, low-voltage operation
Register file | Latch or flop array | Low | Multi-port, fast, expensive
Flip-flop array | — | Lowest | Synthesisable — the only portable option for small storage
Dual-port SRAM | 8T | Lower | True dual port costs ~30–40% more area
Pseudo dual port | 6T, time-multiplexed | High | Half the bandwidth
ROM | — | Very high | Constants, microcode, S-boxes
eDRAM / MRAM / RRAM | — | Very high | Process-specific; limited availability

For an IP vendor the portability question dominates the
 density question. A compiled SRAM is smaller and faster than a flip-flop array,
 but it is a foundry-specific macro: shipping RTL that instantiates one ties the
 customer to a particular process and library. The standard resolution is a
 memory wrapper — the IP instantiates a thin module with a defined
 interface, and the customer maps it to their compiler's output or to a behavioural
 model. A well-built IP ships the wrapper, a synthesisable fallback, and a document
 specifying the required timing (read latency, write behaviour on a read–write
 collision). Omitting the collision behaviour is a frequent and expensive
 omission, because different compilers do different things and the block's
 correctness may depend on which.

[Table 101. Memory design considerations]
Issue | Consequence | Handling
Read/write collision | Behaviour is compiler-dependent | Specify it ; forbid it in the design if possible
Banking | Enables parallel access | Address mapping becomes a design choice
Wide words vs many banks | Power and area trade | Follow the access pattern
ECC | Soft-error protection | Adds a cycle of latency and ~12–25% bits
Scrubbing | Corrects accumulated errors | Background read–correct–write
Redundancy and repair | Yield | Foundry feature; needs BIST/BIRA
Retention voltage | Low-power state | Below it, data is lost

ECC on memory is a reliability calculation, not a
 preference. Soft-error rate is quoted in FIT per megabit (failures in
 109 device-hours), typically a few hundred FIT/Mb at sea level for SRAM.
 A 10 Mb on-chip memory at 300 FIT/Mb gives 3000 FIT, or roughly one upset
 per 38 years per device — negligible for a phone, unacceptable for a fleet of
 a million servers, where it means an upset every twenty minutes somewhere in the
 fleet. The same silicon needs ECC in one market and not in another, which is
 why it must be a parameter rather than a fixed design choice, and why the datasheet
 must state the FIT contribution with and without it.

장: J3. On-Chip Interconnect and Networks
절: J3. On-Chip Interconnect and Networks — 들어가며
글:
J3. On-Chip Interconnect and Networks

[Table 102. Interconnect topologies]
Topology | Scaling | Latency | Use
Shared bus | Poor beyond ~8 masters | Low | Small SoC
Crossbar | O ( N 2 ) area | Low | Moderate port counts
Mesh NoC | Good | O (√ N ) hops | Many-core
Torus | Good | Lower diameter | —
Ring | Simple | O ( N ) | Moderate core counts
Tree / fat tree | Good for hierarchical traffic | — | Cache hierarchies
Butterfly / Clos | Good | Uniform | Switches

[Table 103. NoC design issues]
Issue | Cause | Solution
Deadlock | Cyclic dependency among buffers | Virtual channels, turn-model routing (e.g. dimension-order)
Livelock | Packets circulate without progress | Bounded misrouting, ageing
Head-of-line blocking | One blocked packet stalls the queue | Virtual channels
Fairness | Some sources starve | Arbitration policy
QoS | Mixed traffic classes | Priority virtual channels, rate limiting
Flow control | Buffer overflow | Credit-based

Deadlock freedom is a structural property and should be
 established structurally, not tested. Dimension-order routing (traverse X fully,
 then Y) makes cyclic buffer dependencies impossible in a mesh, and the argument is a
 short proof rather than a simulation campaign. Adaptive routing performs better under
 load but reintroduces the possibility, which is then removed by reserving an escape
 virtual channel that uses dimension-order. This is an unusually clean example of
 the general principle that architecture should make undesirable states unreachable
 rather than merely unlikely — the same principle behind sparse FSM encodings
 and Gray-coded FIFO pointers.

[Table 104. Chip-to-chip and chiplet interfaces]
Standard | Scope | Note
PCIe | Board-level, packetised | Gen6 uses PAM4 and FLIT mode
CXL | Cache-coherent over PCIe PHY | Memory expansion and pooling
UCIe | Die-to-die in a package | Very short reach → very low energy per bit
BoW / AIB | Die-to-die | Open alternatives
HBM | Memory via silicon interposer | Very wide, moderate rate
Ethernet | Rack and beyond | —

Chiplets change the economics that an IP business
 operates in. When a system is partitioned across dies, the interface between them
 becomes a standardised product boundary, and a company can sell an entire die rather
 than an RTL block. Energy per bit is the defining metric: on-chip wires are
 ~0.1 pJ/bit, UCIe die-to-die ~0.5 pJ/bit, and long-reach SerDes
 ~5–10 pJ/bit. That two-order-of-magnitude spread is why partitioning
 decisions are made at the package level and why die-to-die PHY IP became valuable so
 quickly. A digital design house cannot build the PHY, but the link layer,
 the retry and CRC logic, and the protocol adapters above it are all synthesisable
 — the familiar pattern of a sellable digital block adjacent to an unreachable
 analogue one.

장: K4. Current Research Directions
절: K4. Current Research Directions — 들어가며
글:
K4. Current Research Directions

This chapter surveys the areas where current literature is active, so
 that a reader who has absorbed the preceding chapters can approach a recent paper
 knowing what problem it is addressing and which established constraint it is trying to
 relax.

[Table 105. Active areas and the constraint each attacks]
Area | Constraint attacked | Approach | Open problem
Post-quantum cryptography | Shor's algorithm breaks RSA/ECC | Lattice (ML-KEM/ML-DSA), hash-based (SLH-DSA) | Large keys; NTT throughput; side-channel protection of lattice arithmetic
In-memory computing | Von Neumann data movement energy | Analogue MAC in memory arrays (RRAM, SRAM) | ADC overhead often cancels the saving; device variability
Approximate computing | Exactness is expensive | Truncated multipliers, stochastic computing, voltage overscaling | Error bounds must be guaranteed, not measured
Chiplets / UCIe | Reticle limit and yield vs die area | Disaggregation with standard die-to-die links | Test, thermal, known-good-die
Nonlinear equalisation | Linear equalisers fail on nonlinear channels | Volterra series, neural equalisers | Power and latency; verification of a learned block
Concatenated FEC for 224G | KP4 alone insufficient at 200G/lane | Outer RS-KP4 + inner Hamming(128,120) | Latency budget; decoder complexity
Formal at scale | Simulation cannot cover state space | Word-level model checking, SMT | Datapath equivalence remains hard
ML for EDA | Heuristics in placement/routing | Learned cost models, RL for scheduling | Reproducibility and trust in sign-off
Open PDK / open EDA | Tool licence cost as a barrier | SkyWater/IHP PDKs, OpenROAD, Yosys | Analogue and advanced-node support
Cryogenic and superconducting | CMOS energy floor | SFQ logic, cryo-CMOS | Infrastructure; interface to room temperature

How to read a paper in any of these areas. Each row
 names a constraint from earlier chapters. In-memory computing attacks the roofline's
 memory-bound region (J2); approximate computing attacks the fixed-point
 accuracy–area trade (A3, C1); neural equalisation attacks the linear-model
 assumption behind every equaliser in F1; chiplets attack the yield-versus-area
 relation in K3. Identifying which constraint a paper is relaxing, and what it pays
 for the relaxation, is a faster route to understanding than reading the method
 first — and it immediately tells you whether the result transfers to your
 own problem, because you know which assumption it depends on.

A caution that applies to all of these areas.
 Reported gains are measured at an operating point the authors chose. Before accepting
 a claim, locate three things: the baseline (is it a strong implementation or a
 straw man?), the operating conditions (process, voltage, data set, channel), and the
 point at which the advantage disappears. A result quoted without the crossover point
 is a data point, not a design rule — and in an IP business, mistaking one for
 the other is how a year is lost.

The PCS/PMA boundary is the commercial boundary of the
 whole industry. Vendors describe their products in exactly these terms —
 "hardened PMA with a soft PCS layer" — because the PMA is tied to a process node
 and must be delivered as a hard macro, while the PCS is process-independent RTL. For
 a digital design house this boundary defines what is reachable: everything from the
 PCS upward. It is also where the open-source landscape is thinnest — 10G BASE-R
 PCS exists in open form, but 100G-and-above multi-lane PCS and RS-FEC do not —

The gearbox is the piece newcomers underestimate.
 A 66-bit block does not fit a 64-bit datapath, so the PCS must repack a 66-bit stream

 only after 32 blocks. The resulting barrel shifter and control state machine are a
 surprisingly large fraction of the PCS. Multi-lane 100G+ adds alignment markers,
 lane deskew and reordering on top. The "simple" coding layer is mostly plumbing,

Wear-out is a timing constraint, not an afterthought.
 NBTI shifts |VTH| over the device lifetime, so a path that just met
 timing on day one may fail after five years. Sign-off therefore uses an aged library
 or an explicit derate — commonly 5–10%. For an IP vendor this matters in a
 specific way: a frequency claim is implicitly a claim about a lifetime, and the
 two must be quoted together. "500 MHz" at fresh silicon and "500 MHz over ten years at

장: K1. Wireless Physical Layers
절: K1.1 OFDM
글:
K1.1 OFDM

[그림] Figure 14. OFDM transmitter. The cyclic prefix is the trick that makes frequency-domain equalisation valid.

Why the cyclic prefix works, stated precisely.
 A linear convolution with the channel is not diagonalised by the DFT; a circular
 convolution is. Prepending the last Ncp samples of the symbol makes
 the channel's linear convolution look circular to the receiver, provided
 Ncp exceeds the channel's delay spread. The channel matrix then
 becomes diagonal in the DFT basis, so equalisation reduces to dividing each subcarrier
 by one complex number. An N-tap time-domain equalisation problem has been
 exchanged for Ncp/N of lost throughput. That trade is the
 entire justification for OFDM, and it explains why the CP length in every standard is
 tied to the expected delay spread of its deployment environment.

[Table 113. OFDM impairments and their remedies]
Impairment | Effect | Remedy | Where implemented
PAPR | Sum of subcarriers has a high peak | Clipping, tone reservation, SLM; or use SC-FDMA uplink | Digital pre-distortion; amplifier back-off
Carrier frequency offset | Destroys subcarrier orthogonality (ICI) | Estimate from preamble/pilots, correct before FFT | Digital
Sampling clock offset | Progressive phase rotation | Track with pilots | Digital
Phase noise | Common phase error + ICI | Estimate CPE from pilots | Digital
I/Q imbalance | Mirror-image interference | Estimate and compensate | Digital
Doppler | Time-varying channel within a symbol | Shorter symbols, or per-symbol tracking | Design-level

Frequency offset is the impairment that must be fixed
 first and fixed well. A residual offset destroys orthogonality and produces
 inter-carrier interference that no subsequent equaliser can undo, because the
 subcarriers are no longer separable. The tolerance is roughly 1% of the subcarrier
 spacing for negligible loss; in 5G NR with 30 kHz spacing that is 300 Hz
 — at 3.5 GHz carrier, under 0.1 ppm. This single requirement sets
 the crystal specification for the whole device, which is a good illustration of a
 digital-layer requirement propagating down to a bill-of-materials cost.

K1.2 MIMO

[Table 114. MIMO techniques]
Technique | Objective | Requirement | Processing
Spatial multiplexing | Throughput | Rich scattering | Matrix inversion or successive cancellation per subcarrier
Space–time coding | Diversity | None | Simple combining (Alamouti)
Beamforming | SNR, interference | Channel knowledge at the TX | Weight computation
Massive MIMO | Both | Many antennas, reciprocity | Large matrix operations; Cholesky/QR territory
MU-MIMO | Multi-user capacity | Multi-user CSI | Precoding (ZF, MMSE, dirty paper)

[Table 115. MIMO detection algorithms]
Detector | Complexity | Performance | Hardware
Zero forcing | One matrix inverse | Noise enhancement | Cholesky on H H H
MMSE | One matrix inverse | Better at low SNR | Same, with a regularising term
V-BLAST / SIC | Iterative | Better | Ordering + repeated inversion
Sphere decoding | Variable | Near-ML | Data-dependent latency — awkward
K-best | Fixed | Near-ML | Fixed latency — preferred in hardware
Belief propagation | Iterative | Good | Fits with LDPC decoding

K-best beats sphere decoding in hardware for a reason
 that has nothing to do with performance. Sphere decoding prunes a search tree
 adaptively, so its runtime depends on the channel and the noise realisation; a
 pipelined receiver with a fixed symbol rate cannot accommodate variable latency without
 buffering for the worst case, which negates the saving. K-best keeps a fixed number of
 candidates at every level, giving constant throughput and latency at slightly worse
 error performance. Determinism is worth more than average-case efficiency in a
 streaming datapath, and this principle recurs in FEC (fixed iteration counts),
 in SVD (fixed sweep counts), and in CFAR (fixed window sizes).

장: L4. Feedback and Control
절: L4. Feedback and Control — 들어가며
글:
L4. Feedback and Control

Feedback loops appear throughout an IP portfolio: PLLs, CDRs, adaptive
 equalisers, AGC, DVFS controllers, thermal throttling, and the convergence of iterative
 decoders. The same small set of concepts governs all of them.

[Table 116. Control concepts and their hardware instances]
Concept | Meaning | Instance
Open-loop gain | Gain around the loop | PLL K PD K VCO
Loop bandwidth | Where gain crosses unity | The central design parameter of every loop
Phase margin | Phase at crossover, relative to −180° | Latency inside a digital loop is a stability problem,
 not merely a performance one. A digital adaptation loop that computes an error,
 pipelines it through several stages, and then applies a correction has inserted pure
 delay, which subtracts phase without reducing gain — exactly what destroys phase
 margin. The loop can oscillate even though every block in it is correct. The standard
 remedies are to reduce the loop gain (slower adaptation), to shorten the loop, or to
 compensate explicitly. A model that applies the correction instantaneously will not
 show the instability, so the pipeline delay must be in the model. This is one of
 the most common gaps between a working model and non-working hardware.

[Table 117. Adaptation loops in a receiver and their interactions]
Loop | Controls | Typical bandwidth | Interacts with
AGC | Input amplitude | Fast | Everything downstream
CDR | Sampling phase | Moderate | Equaliser — MM lock point depends on it
CTLE adaptation | Analogue peaking | Slow | FFE
FFE/DFE adaptation | Tap weights | Slow | CDR
Offset calibration | Comparator offsets | Very slow | Slicer thresholds
Interleaving calibration | ADC mismatch | Very slow | All of the above

Six loops sharing one signal is the hardest part of a
 modern receiver, and it is a systems problem rather than a circuit one. Each loop
 is stable alone; together they can hunt, lock to a wrong point, or fail to converge
 from certain initial conditions. The standard engineering response is bandwidth
 separation — giving each loop a rate an order of magnitude apart so that
 faster loops appear instantaneous to slower ones and slower loops appear constant to
 faster ones — plus a defined start-up sequence. Both the separation and the
 sequence belong in the specification, and verifying convergence from adverse
 initial conditions is a system-model task that no block-level testbench will
 perform.

장: L2. Power Delivery and Conversion
절: L2. Power Delivery and Conversion — 들어가며
글:
L2. Power Delivery and Conversion

[Table 118. Voltage regulator types]
Type | Efficiency | Ripple | Response | Where
LDO | V out / V in — poor if the drop is large | Very low | Fast | Sensitive analogue, small currents
Buck (switching) | 85–95% | Higher (switching ripple) | Slower | Digital cores, large currents
Boost | — | — | — | Raising a voltage
Charge pump | Moderate | — | — | Small currents, no inductor
Integrated voltage regulator | — | — | Very fast | Per-domain DVFS on die
Switched-capacitor | Good at fixed ratios | — | — | On-die, no inductor needed

Regulator response time is a digital design constraint.
 When a large synchronous block starts, it draws a current step; the regulator takes
 time to respond, and during that time the supply droops. The droop reduces gate drive
 and therefore increases delay, which can violate timing. Designers respond with
 di/dt management — staggering the release of clock gates so a block wakes
 in stages rather than all at once. This is a purely digital technique introduced to
 solve an analogue problem, and it must be specified: an IP that draws its full
 current in one cycle after an enable is harder to integrate than one that ramps.

[Table 119. Decoupling hierarchy]
Level | Capacitance | Effective range | Limit
On-die (MOS, MIM) | nF | >100 MHz | Area
Package | μF | 10–100 MHz | Package inductance
Board ceramic | μF | 1–10 MHz | ESL
Bulk electrolytic | 100 μF+ | The anti-resonance peak is a common cause of
 otherwise inexplicable failures. Package inductance and on-die capacitance form a
 parallel resonance at which the power delivery network's impedance is much higher than
 at neighbouring frequencies. A workload whose current draw happens to contain energy at
 that frequency — a loop running at the resonant rate, a burst-mode accelerator
 — produces supply noise far larger than the average current would suggest. The
 symptom is a design that passes all tests but fails on one specific piece of
 software. A digital block's current spectrum, not only its average power,
 is a system-level property.

L1. Semiconductor Physics: What Survives into Design

[그림] Figure 15. Band structure. The gap determines whether a material conducts, and silicon's 1.1 eV gap is what makes it useful.

[Table 120. Physical quantities and where a designer meets them]
Quantity | Symbol / value | Design consequence
Band gap of Si | 1.12 eV at 300 K | Falls with temperature → leakage rises, V TH falls
Intrinsic carrier density | n i ≈ 10 10 cm −3 | Doubles roughly every 8 K → junction leakage doubles with it
Thermal voltage | kT / q = 25.9 mV at 300 K | Sets the subthreshold slope : 60 mV/decade minimum
Mobility μ | ≈1400 (e), 450 (h) cm 2 /Vs | Why PMOS is sized ~2–3× wider than NMOS
Saturation velocity | ≈10 7 cm/s | Short-channel current becomes linear in overdrive
Oxide capacitance | C ox = ε ox / t ox | Thinner oxide → more drive and more gate leakage
Depletion width | ∝ √( V / N ) | Short-channel effects; junction capacitance

The 60 mV/decade subthreshold slope is a hard physical
 limit and it ended Dennard scaling. Below threshold, drain current depends
 exponentially on gate voltage with a slope of at best
 (kT/q) ln10 ≈ 60 mV per decade at room temperature,
 because the mechanism is thermal emission over a barrier. To keep leakage constant
 while lowering the supply, the threshold must fall by the same amount — but each
 100 mV of threshold reduction multiplies leakage by about fifty. This is why
 supply voltage stopped scaling near 0.8 V and why power density rose, which
 in turn is why the industry turned to specialised accelerators and therefore why the
 IP market grew. A thermodynamic constant is visible in a business model.

[Table 121. Devices beyond the planar MOSFET]
Device | Principle | Motivation
FinFET | Gate wraps a vertical fin on three sides | Better electrostatic control → less DIBL and leakage
GAA / nanosheet | Gate surrounds the channel completely | Further control; width quantised by sheet count
FD-SOI | Thin body on buried oxide | Low leakage; body bias as a live tuning knob
Tunnel FET | Band-to-band tunnelling | Can beat 60 mV/decade ; low on-current so far
Negative-capacitance FET | Ferroelectric gate stack | Internal voltage amplification; reliability unproven
2D materials | MoS 2 and similar | Ultra-thin body; research stage

L3. Thermal and Packaging

Segment | Symbol | Typical | Improved by

Hot spots are a floorplanning problem, and they couple
 back into timing. Average die temperature may be comfortable while a dense
 arithmetic block runs 20 K hotter than its surroundings. Since delay and leakage
 both depend on temperature, that block is slower and leakier than the sign-off corner
 assumed, and its leakage raises its temperature further — a positive feedback
 known as thermal runaway in the extreme. The design responses are spreading high-activity
 logic, inserting thermal sensors and throttling, and accounting for the gradient in
 timing analysis. For an IP vendor, a block with very high local power density
 should say so, because the customer's floorplanner needs to know.

[Table 123. Package types]
Package | Density | Thermal | Use
Wire-bond QFN/BGA | Low | Moderate | Cost-sensitive
Flip-chip BGA | High | Good (heat exits through the lid) | High performance
Silicon interposer (2.5D) | Very high | Good | HBM integration
3D stacking | Highest | Difficult — heat is trapped | Memory on logic
Fan-out wafer level | High | Moderate | Mobile
Chiplet in package | High | Manageable | Disaggregated designs

Thermal constraints are what limit 3D integration,
 not manufacturing. Stacking a logic die under another die places its heat behind a
 thermal barrier, so the achievable power density falls sharply. This is why current 3D
 products stack memory (low power) on logic rather than logic on logic, and why thermal
 modelling now appears early in architecture rather than at the end. The physical
 constraint determines the partitioning, which determines which interfaces are needed,
 which determines which IP is valuable.

장: M1. The Hardware–Software Interface
절: M1. The Hardware–Software Interface — 들어가며
글:
M1. The Hardware–Software Interface

An IP block is useless until software can drive it. The interface
 between them is a design artefact in its own right, and getting it wrong produces
 integration cost that dwarfs the block's development.

[Table 124. Interface mechanisms]
Mechanism | Direction | Cost | When appropriate
Memory-mapped registers | CPU → block | Low | Configuration, status; the default
Polling | CPU reads status | Wastes CPU cycles and power | Very short operations
Interrupt | block → CPU | Latency and context switch | Completion of long operations
DMA | block ↔ memory | Bus bandwidth | Bulk data; avoids CPU copying
Descriptor rings | — | Memory traffic | Streaming with many buffers (network, storage)
Mailbox / doorbell | bidirectional | Low | Command submission
Shared memory + fences | — | Coherence traffic | Tight coupling; requires a memory model

The single most consequential interface decision is
 who moves the data. A block that requires the CPU to write its input and read its
 output word by word can be limited by the CPU even when the block itself is fast; a
 DMA-capable block moves data in bursts and leaves the CPU free. The difference is
 frequently an order of magnitude in system throughput, and it is invisible in
 block-level benchmarks. For an IP vendor this means the example design matters as
 much as the block: a customer who integrates it through programmed I/O will measure
 disappointing performance and conclude the IP is slow.

[Table 125. Register map design rules]
Rule | Reason
Generate RTL, header, documentation and tests from one source | Three hand-maintained copies always diverge
Reserve and document unused bits | Forward compatibility
Make read-clear and write-one-clear behaviour explicit | Ambiguity here produces lost interrupts
Provide an identification and version register | Software can adapt to the actual hardware
Group by function, align to natural boundaries | Simplifies access
Avoid side effects on read where possible | A debugger that dumps registers must not change behaviour
State atomicity for wide registers | Prevents tearing

Read side effects break debuggers, and the failure is
 baffling when it happens. If reading a FIFO status register pops an entry, then
 attaching a debugger that displays the register window silently consumes data, and the
 bug disappears when the debugger is detached. Where a read side effect is genuinely
 required — a pop-on-read data port, for example — it must be isolated in
 its own register and clearly marked, so that a debug tool can be told to avoid it.
 This is a small documentation duty with a disproportionate payoff.

[Table 126. Driver and firmware concerns an IP vendor should anticipate]
Concern | What the IP must provide
Initialisation sequence | Exact required order, including any wait conditions
Reset semantics | What a soft reset does and does not clear
Error reporting | Sticky status bits with a defined clearing mechanism
Concurrency | Which registers may be accessed while the block is running
Endianness and bit order | Stated explicitly
Timeouts | Maximum time any operation can take
Low-power entry/exit | Sequence and state retention

M3. Image Signal Processing

[Table 127. The ISP pipeline]
Stage | Function | Why it is in hardware

Lens shading correction | Vignetting | Per-pixel with a gain surface
