Line buffers, not arithmetic, determine ISP cost. A
 5×5 neighbourhood operation at 4K resolution requires four lines of 3840 pixels
 each held on chip; at 12 bits per component that is roughly 184 kbit per stage
 before any compute. A pipeline with several such stages spends most of its silicon on
 storage. The architectural consequences are standard: process in tiles rather than
 full lines, fuse stages so that a neighbourhood is read once and used by several
 operations, and choose separable filters wherever possible. This is the same
 memory-versus-compute analysis as the roofline of Chapter J2, applied to a different
 domain.

[Table 128. Colour and vision concepts that reach the hardware]
Concept | Meaning | Implementation note
Bayer pattern | One colour per photosite | Demosaic must interpolate two of three
Colour space (sRGB, YCbCr) | — | YCbCr separates luma for chroma subsampling
Chroma subsampling (4:2:0) | Half resolution chroma | Exploits lower chroma acuity — halves the data
Gamma | Non-linear encoding | Must be undone before linear operations
HDR / tone mapping | Wide dynamic range compressed for display | Local operators need neighbourhood statistics
Rolling shutter | Rows exposed at different times | Motion artefacts; a system issue

Performing linear operations on gamma-encoded data is
 a persistent and quiet error. Gamma encoding is non-linear, so averaging two
 gamma-encoded pixels does not give the gamma encoding of their average. Scaling,
 blending and filtering must therefore be done in linear light, which means decoding
 before and re-encoding after. The visible symptom is subtly wrong brightness at edges
 — easy to miss in a test pattern and obvious on real images. Specify the
 colour encoding of every interface, in the same way and for the same reason that
 fixed-point formats must be specified.

장: M4. Measurement and Characterisation
절: M4. Measurement and Characterisation — 들어가며
글:
M4. Measurement and Characterisation

Everything in this book that is stated as a number came from a
 measurement, and the difference between a useful number and a misleading one is
 usually in the method rather than the instrument.

[Table 129. Instruments and what they actually measure]
Instrument | Measures | Principal limitation
Oscilloscope | Voltage versus time | Bandwidth and probe loading
Real-time versus sampling scope | — | Sampling scopes need a repetitive signal
Spectrum analyser | Power versus frequency | Resolution bandwidth changes the displayed noise floor
Vector network analyser | S-parameters | Calibration plane definition
BER tester | Errors per bit | Time: 10 −12 at 10 Gb/s takes ~100 s per point
Time interval analyser | Jitter statistics | Trigger accuracy
Logic analyser | Digital state | No analogue detail
Thermal camera | Surface temperature | Emissivity; not junction temperature
Power analyser / shunt | Current | Bandwidth versus resolution

Bathtub extrapolation exists because direct BER
 measurement does not scale. Confirming 10−15 by counting errors
 would take days per operating point, which is impossible for a characterisation sweep.
 Instead the eye is scanned at several sampling phases, the error rate is measured where
 it is high enough to be quick, and the Gaussian random-jitter tails are extrapolated to
 the target BER. The extrapolation is only valid if the random component really is
 Gaussian and has been correctly separated from the bounded deterministic component
 — which is why jitter decomposition is a required capability rather than a
 convenience, and why a reported margin should always name the method.

[Table 130. Characterisation practices]
Practice | Reason
Sweep, do not spot-check | A single operating point can be unrepresentative or accidentally favourable
Confirm the operating point is healthy first | Measurements taken on a broken setup look plausible
Obtain the same quantity a second way | An independent estimate catches methodological errors
List the trivial explanations and rule each out by measurement | A result that could be an artefact is a hypothesis, not a finding
Record conditions with every number | Temperature, voltage, part, instrument, settings
Report the condition under which the claim fails | A claim with no stated failure condition is advertising

Four measurement failures, each of which produced a
 plausible number that meant nothing. Taking the slope of a pulse at its peak
 — which is zero by definition — and reporting it as a sensitivity.
 Measuring residuals at an operating point where BER was already 0.49, so the link
 carried no information. Asking a tool for the longest path in an entire netlist when
 the quantity of interest was the delay around one feedback loop. Reporting a lookup
 table's accuracy at an operating point where the feedback taps were so small that the
 loop was effectively inactive, so the table was never exercised. In every case the
 instrument worked and the number was wrong, because the quantity measured was not the
 quantity intended. The four rules above are written to prevent exactly these.

장: M2. Machine Learning Hardware
절: M2. Machine Learning Hardware — 들어가며
글:
M2. Machine Learning Hardware

[Table 131. Operations that dominate inference]
Operation | Share of compute | Arithmetic intensity | Hardware mapping
Convolution | High in CNNs | High with tiling | Systolic array or vector units
Matrix multiply (GEMM) | Dominant in transformers | High | The universal accelerator primitive
Attention (QK T V) | Dominant in LLMs | Moderate | Memory bound at long sequence lengths
Element-wise / activation | Low compute | Very low | Memory bound; fuse with the previous layer
Normalisation | Low | Low | Fuse; needs reductions
Softmax | Low | Low | Needs exp and a reduction; numerically delicate
Embedding lookup | — | Very low | Random memory access

Fusion is the main architectural lever and it follows
 directly from the roofline. An activation function performs one operation per
 element and therefore has arithmetic intensity near zero — it is entirely memory
 bound. Executed as a separate pass it costs a full read and write of the tensor.
 Fused into the preceding matrix multiply's output stage it costs essentially nothing.
 Real accelerators therefore expose fused operations rather than primitive ones, and
 their compilers spend most of their effort deciding what to fuse. An IP block that
 implements a single layer type in isolation will underperform in a system for reasons
 that have nothing to do with its internal quality.

[Table 132. Quantisation approaches]
Approach | Accuracy loss | Effort | Hardware
Post-training, per-tensor INT8 | Moderate | Low | One scale per tensor
Post-training, per-channel INT8 | Small | Low | Per-channel scale multiply — usually worth it
Quantisation-aware training | Very small | High | Same as above
INT4 with grouping | Noticeable | High | Group-wise scales
Mixed precision | Small | Moderate | Sensitive layers kept wider
Binary / ternary | Large | High | XNOR–popcount; no multipliers

Quantisation is a fixed-point problem and the
 vocabulary of Chapter A3 applies unchanged. A per-tensor scale is a single Q
 format for the whole tensor; per-channel scaling is the recognition that different
 channels have different dynamic ranges, which is exactly the block-floating-point idea
 from the FFT chapter. Understanding this correspondence prevents an engineer from
 treating ML quantisation as a separate discipline: the questions — where to
 round, when to saturate, how dynamic range grows through a computation — are the
 same, and the answers are reached the same way.

[Table 133. Sparsity]
Kind | Speedup potential | Hardware feasibility
Unstructured (random zeros) | High in theory | Poor — irregular access defeats the memory system
Structured (2:4, block) | Moderate | Good — regular indexing
Channel / filter pruning | Moderate | Excellent — it is just a smaller dense model
Activation sparsity (ReLU) | Moderate | Dynamic; needs run-time detection

Unstructured sparsity is the clearest case of a
 metric that does not translate into hardware. A paper reporting 90% of weights
 pruned implies a tenfold reduction in operations, but realising it requires indexing
 individual non-zeros, which destroys the regular access patterns that give an
 accelerator its efficiency. The achieved speedup is commonly a small fraction of the
 nominal one, and can be below unity. Structured sparsity exists because hardware
 needs regularity more than it needs fewer operations — a principle that
 recurs whenever an algorithmic saving is proposed.

장: N1. Asynchronous and Globally Asynchronous Design
절: N1. Asynchronous and Globally Asynchronous Design — 들어가며
글:
N1. Asynchronous and Globally Asynchronous Design

Synchronous design — one clock, one timing constraint — is
 overwhelmingly dominant because it makes timing analysis tractable. Asynchronous
 techniques remain relevant in three specific places, and knowing which is which
 prevents both over-application and blind avoidance.

[Table 134. Asynchronous styles]
Style | Timing assumption | Property | Practical use
Bundled data | Matched delay line models the logic | Simple, small | Local handshakes, self-timed SRAM
Dual-rail / QDI | None (delay insensitive) | Robust to any delay; ~2× area | Extreme reliability, some security uses
Micropipelines | Bundled | Elastic pipelines | —
GALS | Synchronous islands, async between | Avoids a global clock tree | The practically important case — multi-domain SoCs
Self-timed memory | Internal | Hidden from the user | Nearly all SRAM

GALS is what most engineers actually encounter, usually
 without the name. Any SoC with several clock domains connected by asynchronous
 FIFOs is globally asynchronous and locally synchronous. Framing it that way is useful
 because it makes the design rules explicit: each island has its own timing closure,
 and every boundary between islands is a CDC problem requiring one of the techniques of
 Chapter C3. The failure mode of an undisciplined multi-domain design is not a
 timing violation but an intermittent data corruption, which is far harder to
 diagnose — which is why the boundaries must be enumerated and checked by a
 tool rather than by inspection.

[Table 135. Where fully asynchronous logic is genuinely used]
Application | Reason
SRAM internal timing | Self-timed sense amplifier control is faster than a clock
Security | No clock to glitch; power profile is less data-correlated
Ultra-low power / energy harvesting | No clock power when idle
Very wide dynamic voltage range | Works at whatever speed the supply allows
Reliability at extremes | Delay-insensitive circuits tolerate huge variation

The barrier to asynchronous design is tooling, not
 theory. Standard synthesis, static timing analysis, scan insertion and equivalence
 checking all assume a clock. An asynchronous block therefore needs custom flows, and
 — decisively for an IP vendor — the customer must be able to integrate,
 verify and test it in their flow. An asynchronous block is usually
 unsellable as RTL for this reason alone, regardless of its merits. Where the
 technique is used commercially it is nearly always hidden inside a hard macro with a
 synchronous interface.

장: N4. Optical Links and Photonics
절: N4. Optical Links and Photonics — 들어가며
글:
N4. Optical Links and Photonics

Beyond a few metres of copper, electrical links become impractical and
 the industry switches to optics. The digital blocks on either side — the FEC, the
 PCS, the DSP — are the same kind of IP discussed throughout this book, which is
 why the domain deserves a chapter.

[Table 136. Optical link components]
Component | Function | Impairment introduced
Laser (DFB, VCSEL) | Source | RIN, chirp, temperature drift
Modulator (direct, EML, MZM) | Impress data on light | Extinction ratio, chirp, nonlinearity
Fibre (SMF, MMF) | Transport | Chromatic dispersion, modal dispersion, attenuation, nonlinearity
Photodiode (PIN, APD) | Detect | Shot noise; APD adds excess noise
TIA | Current to voltage | Noise; bandwidth
Coherent receiver | Recover amplitude and phase | Requires a local oscillator and heavy DSP

[Table 137. Modulation and detection schemes]
Scheme | Detection | Reach | DSP required
NRZ / PAM4 IM-DD | Direct (intensity only) | ≤ 10 km | Equalisation, FEC — 802.3 territory
Coherent QPSK / 16-QAM | Coherent (amplitude and phase) | Long haul | Very heavy: CD and PMD compensation, carrier recovery
Probabilistic shaping | Coherent | Long haul | Shaping encoder/decoder

Chromatic dispersion compensation is where photonics
 becomes a large digital problem. Different wavelengths travel at slightly different
 speeds in fibre, so a pulse spreads over distance — and over hundreds of
 kilometres the spread reaches hundreds of symbol periods. Compensating it optically
 requires dispersion-compensating fibre; compensating it digitally requires a very long
 filter, which is implemented in the frequency domain because a direct FIR of that
 length is uneconomical. The result is that a coherent optical receiver contains one
 of the largest FFT blocks in commercial electronics, and the chapter on multirate
 and transform architectures applies directly. This is an unusually clear case of a
 physical-layer impairment creating a large, well-specified digital IP
 opportunity.

[Table 138. Co-packaged and silicon photonics]
Development | Motivation | Consequence
Pluggable optics | Serviceability | Electrical link to the module costs power
Co-packaged optics | Remove the electrical link | Large power saving ; serviceability and thermal challenges
Silicon photonics | CMOS-compatible fabrication | Integration density, cost
Optical I/O for chiplets | Bandwidth density | Research to early product

장: N2. Physical Design in More Depth
절: N2. Physical Design in More Depth — 들어가며
글:
N2. Physical Design in More Depth

[Table 139. Placement and routing concerns]
Concern | Cause | Symptom | Remedy
Congestion | More nets than routing tracks in a region | Routing failures, detours, timing loss | Spread cells, reduce utilisation, restructure logic
Timing/congestion conflict | Timing wants cells close; routing wants them apart | — | Iterate; sometimes an architectural change is needed
Antenna effect | Charge accumulation on a long metal segment during etch | Gate oxide damage | Diode insertion, layer jumping
Crosstalk delay and noise | Coupling between adjacent nets | Timing variation, glitches | Spacing, shielding, net ordering
Electromigration | Current density | Long-term failure | Wire widening, via arrays
IR drop | Grid resistance | Local slowdown | Grid strengthening, decap
Hold violations after CTS | Skew changes after the clock tree is built | — | Buffer insertion; usually many thousands

Utilisation is the number that governs the whole
 back-end schedule. Utilisation — the fraction of core area occupied by cells
 — trades area against routability. Below roughly 60% a design routes easily and
 wastes area; above roughly 80% congestion begins to dominate and each iteration
 becomes slower and less predictable. A block delivered with a recommended utilisation
 lets the customer floorplan correctly the first time. Omitting it is one of the
 common causes of "the IP does not meet timing in our flow", because the customer
 packed it at 85% while the vendor characterised it at 65%.

[Table 140. Standard cell library concepts]
Concept | Meaning | Selection consequence
Track height (e.g. 7.5T, 9T) | Cell height in routing tracks | Taller cells are faster and larger
Drive strength (X1, X2, X4…) | Transistor width multiplier | Higher drive for larger loads
Multi- V TH (LVT/SVT/HVT) | Threshold variants | Leakage versus speed, per cell
Characterisation corner | PVT point of the timing data | Must match the sign-off corner
NLDM / CCS | Delay model fidelity | CCS is needed at advanced nodes
Engineering change order cells | Spare gates scattered in the layout | Enable metal-only fixes after tape-out

Spare cells are cheap insurance that is often omitted
 and then badly missed. Scattering a small percentage of unused gates across the
 floorplan allows a post-silicon logic fix to be implemented by changing only the metal
 masks, which costs a fraction of a full mask set and weeks rather than months. The
 area cost is typically one or two percent. The decision is made at floorplan time
 and cannot be revisited, which is why it belongs on the checklist of Chapter
 W1 rather than being left to back-end judgement.

장: N3. Statistics for Silicon
절: N3. Statistics for Silicon — 들어가며
글:
N3. Statistics for Silicon

[Table 141. Variation sources]
Source | Scale | Correlation | Handled by
Lot to lot | Global | Fully correlated on a die | Process corners
Wafer to wafer | Global | Correlated | Corners
Die to die | Global | Correlated | Corners
Within die, systematic | Local | Position dependent | Layout-dependent effects, proximity rules
Within die, random | Local | Uncorrelated | OCV / AOCV / POCV derating
Random dopant fluctuation | Per device | None | σ ∝ 1/√( WL ) — matters most for small devices

The distinction between correlated and uncorrelated
 variation is what makes modern timing analysis tractable. If every device on a path
 varied independently, a long path would average out and show less relative
 variation than a short one — which is exactly what statistical on-chip variation
 (POCV) captures, and why it recovers pessimism that flat derating throws away. Flat OCV
 applies the same percentage to every path regardless of depth, which over-penalises
 long paths and under-penalises short ones (making hold analysis optimistic). The
 statistics are not a refinement; using the wrong model can make a design that signs off
 fail in silicon.

[Table 142. Statistical concepts used in characterisation]
Concept | Use
Mean, σ, ±3σ | Basic spread; 3σ ≈ 99.73%
6σ design | Memory bit cells — billions of instances require extreme tails to be safe
Importance sampling | Simulating a 6σ failure directly is infeasible; bias the sampling and correct
Monte Carlo | General variation analysis
Design of experiments | Efficient exploration of many parameters
Regression / response surface | Build a fast surrogate model
Confidence intervals | A measurement without one is an anecdote
Process capability C pk | Manufacturing margin

Memory bit cells illustrate why tail statistics matter
 so much. A 100 Mbit memory contains 108 cells; for the chip to
 yield, the per-cell failure probability must be well below 10−8,
 which corresponds to roughly 5.7σ. Plain Monte Carlo would need on the order of
 109 simulations to see such an event, so importance sampling —
 deliberately sampling the tail and reweighting — is mandatory. This is why
 memory design is a specialised discipline, and why memories come from compilers
 rather than being drawn by hand.

P3. The Gigabit Ethernet MAC and Its Transceiver Interfaces

Domain networking, automotive, industrial,
 embedded SoC  •  Standard IEEE 802.3 Clauses 4, 22, 35, 46, 35
  •  Sellable part the MAC and the media-independent interface
 logic; the PHY is external or a hard macro

장: P3. The Gigabit Ethernet MAC and Its Transceiver Interfaces
절: P3.1 What a MAC does
글:
P3.1 What a MAC does

[Table 143. GMAC functional blocks]
Block | Function | Notes
Transmit framer | Preamble/SFD insertion, padding to 64 B, FCS append, inter-frame gap | The IFG is 96 bit times and must be maintained exactly
Receive framer | Preamble detect, SFD align, FCS check, length check | Must distinguish a runt, a jabber and a valid short frame
CRC-32 | Frame check sequence, polynomial 0x04C11DB7 | Reflected input and output, initial value 0xFFFFFFFF, final XOR — all four conventions must match the standard
Address filter | Unicast, multicast hash, broadcast, promiscuous | Hash table sizing is a parameter
Flow control | PAUSE frames (802.3x), priority PAUSE (802.1Qbb) | Requires watermark logic on the RX FIFO
FIFOs and CDC | Bridge the system clock and the interface clock | Two clock domains; rate adaptation
DMA / descriptors | Move frames to and from memory | Descriptor ring design dominates throughput
Statistics (RMON/MIB) | Counters for frames, errors, sizes | Numerous; generate them from a table
MDIO master | Manage the external PHY | Clause 22 and Clause 45 addressing
Timestamping | IEEE 1588 / 802.1AS | Capture point accuracy is the spec

The CRC-32 conventions are a classic interoperability
 trap and deserve explicit treatment. Ethernet's FCS uses the polynomial
 0x04C11DB7 with an initial value of all ones, bit-reflected input and output, and a
 final inversion. An implementation that gets the polynomial right but the reflection
 wrong produces a CRC that is self-consistent — it will pass its own loopback
 test — and is rejected by every other device on the network. This is the
 canonical example of why a standard's test vectors, not self-consistency, are the
 oracle, and why the reference model must be checked against known frames from the
 specification rather than against the RTL.

장: P3. The Gigabit Ethernet MAC and Its Transceiver Interfaces
절: P3.2 Media-independent interfaces
글:
P3.2 Media-independent interfaces

[Table 144. The MII family]
Interface | Speeds | Signals | Clocking | Where used
MII | 10/100 | 4-bit each direction | 25 MHz from the PHY | Legacy
RMII | 10/100 | 2-bit | 50 MHz shared | Pin reduction
GMII | 1000 | 8-bit each direction | 125 MHz | Classic gigabit interface
RGMII | 10/100/1000 | 4-bit DDR | 125 MHz DDR | Halves the pins; introduces a clock-skew requirement
SGMII | 10/100/1000 | 1 serial lane | 625 MHz DDR / SerDes | Serial; needs a SerDes
XGMII / XLGMII | 10G / 40G | 32/64-bit | — | Higher speeds
1000BASE-X PCS | 1000 | — | — | 8b/10b + auto-negotiation, Clause 36/37

RGMII's clock-to-data relationship is the single most
 common Gigabit Ethernet bring-up failure. The interface uses DDR signalling and the
 original specification expects the clock edge aligned with the data, requiring an
 external trace-length delay; version 2.0 added an internal-delay option that the PHY
 may or may not implement, and that is often configured by strapping or by an MDIO
 register. The result is four plausible combinations of delay on each side, only some
 of which work. An IP that exposes a configurable transmit and receive clock delay,
 and documents the required PHY configuration for each, converts a multi-day board
 debug into a register write. This is a small feature with a very large support
 value.

장: P3. The Gigabit Ethernet MAC and Its Transceiver Interfaces
절: P3.3 Design decisions that matter
글:
P3.3 Design decisions that matter

[Table 145. GMAC architecture choices]
Decision | Options | Consequence
Store-and-forward vs cut-through | — | Store-and-forward can drop bad frames before transmitting ; cut-through has lower latency but forwards errors
FIFO depth | — | Must absorb the maximum frame plus system latency; underrun mid-frame is fatal
Datapath width | 8 / 32 / 64 bit | Width × clock must exceed 1 Gb/s with margin for IFG and preamble
Descriptor format | Ring vs list; scatter-gather | Throughput under small frames
Checksum offload | IPv4/TCP/UDP | Reduces host CPU load substantially
TSO / LRO | Segmentation offload | Large benefit; significant complexity
VLAN handling | Insert/strip/filter | Standard expectation
Jumbo frames | up to 9 kB | FIFO and descriptor sizing
1588 timestamping | — | The capture point must be at a defined layer boundary

Transmit underrun is the failure mode that defines FIFO
 sizing. Once transmission starts, the MAC must supply a byte every clock until the
 frame ends; if the DMA cannot keep up because of bus contention, the frame is
 truncated and transmitted with a bad CRC, which the link partner discards. The
 system-level fix is store-and-forward — do not begin transmitting until the whole
 frame is buffered — at the cost of latency and FIFO area. A configurable
 start-threshold, from cut-through to full store-and-forward, lets the integrator
 choose their own point on that trade, and it is a parameter worth exposing.

IEEE 1588 timestamping accuracy is determined by where
 the timestamp is taken, not by the counter's resolution. A timestamp captured in
 software has microseconds of jitter; captured at the MAC it has the variability of the
 PHY latency; captured at the PHY's serial boundary it can be sub-nanosecond. Since the
 PHY delay is not constant across speeds and link states, a MAC-level implementation
 must expose calibration registers for the ingress and egress delays. Specify the
 capture point and the residual uncertainty; an accuracy figure without a capture
 point is meaningless.

절: P3.4 Verification and deliverables
글:
P3.4 Verification and deliverables

[Table 146. GMAC verification plan]
Area | Stimulus | Oracle
Frame sizes | 64 (minimum) to 1518 and jumbo, plus every boundary | Golden model; runt, oversize and pad cases explicitly
CRC | Known frames from the standard | Standard vectors, not self-consistency
IFG and preamble | Back-to-back frames at line rate | Protocol checker
Address filtering | Unicast, multicast, hash collisions, broadcast | Model
Flow control | Trigger watermarks; receive PAUSE | Correct pause duration
Error injection | Bad CRC, truncated, symbol errors | Correct counters and discard
Underrun / overrun | Starve or stall the DMA | Defined behaviour, no lockup
Speed changes | 10/100/1000 transitions | Clean reconfiguration
MDIO | Clause 22 and 45 transactions | Timing and turnaround
Timestamping | Known packet timing | Accuracy within the stated bound
Interoperability | Against a real PHY on a board | The only test that finds RGMII delay problems

Deliverable note for all three interface blocks in
 this chapter. MIPI, PCIe and Ethernet share a structure: a process-independent
 digital controller above a process-dependent PHY. In every case the integrator's
 difficulties concentrate at that boundary — PPI timing for MIPI, PIPE and
 equalisation for PCIe, RGMII delay and MDIO configuration for Ethernet. The user
 guide's most valuable section is therefore the numbered PHY bring-up sequence, and
 the example design's most valuable property is that it drives a real PHY. An IP that
 has only ever been simulated against a PHY model will meet these problems at the
 customer's site rather than the vendor's.

장: P1. MIPI CSI-2 and DSI — Camera and Display Interfaces
절: P1. MIPI CSI-2 and DSI — Camera and Display Interfaces — 들어가며
글:
P1. MIPI CSI-2 and DSI — Camera and Display Interfaces

Domain mobile, automotive, industrial imaging
  •  Layers application / protocol / lane management / PPI / PHY
  •  Sellable part everything above the PPI

[그림] Figure 16. MIPI CSI-2 / DSI layering. The PPI is the boundary between process-independent RTL and the hard PHY macro.

장: P1. MIPI CSI-2 and DSI — Camera and Display Interfaces
절: P1.1 What the two specifications are
글:
P1.1 What the two specifications are

[Table 147. CSI-2 and DSI compared]
 | CSI-2 (camera) | DSI / DSI-2 (display)
Direction | Sensor → host (mostly unidirectional) | Host → panel, with a low-speed return path
Payload | Pixel data packets | Pixel data and command packets (DCS)
Modes | Continuous or non-continuous clock | Video mode (streaming) and command mode (panel with own memory)
Framing | Frame Start/End, Line Start/End short packets | Similar, plus timing packets (HSA/HBP/HFP)
Typical lanes | 1–4 (D-PHY), 1–3 trios (C-PHY) | 1–4
Error handling | ECC on the header, CRC on the payload | Same
Virtual channels | Up to 4 (16 in later versions) | Up to 4

The single most useful structural fact is that the
 packet header carries a Hamming ECC and the payload carries a CRC, and they do
 different jobs. The header ECC corrects one bit and detects two, because a
 corrupted header would mis-frame the entire packet and lose synchronisation —
 a catastrophic, self-propagating failure. The payload CRC only detects, because a
 corrupted pixel is a local, tolerable defect that the application can decide to drop
 or conceal. The protection strength is matched to the consequence of failure,
 which is a design principle worth carrying to other protocols: ask what a corruption
 of each field actually costs before choosing how to protect it.

장: P1. MIPI CSI-2 and DSI — Camera and Display Interfaces
절: P1.2 D-PHY and C-PHY, and what they force on the digital side
글:
P1.2 D-PHY and C-PHY, and what they force on the digital side

[Table 148. PHY options]
 | D-PHY | C-PHY
Signalling | Differential pairs; separate clock lane | Three-wire trios , embedded clock
Symbol | 1 bit per lane per UI | 2.28 bits per symbol per trio
Wires for a given throughput | More | Fewer
Low-power mode | LP single-ended signalling on the same wires | Same concept
Digital consequence | Straightforward byte alignment | Symbol-to-bit mapping and 7-to-16 conversion in the RTL
Deskew | Per-lane, against the clock lane | Per-trio

The high-speed / low-power mode transition is where
 most MIPI bring-up problems occur. The same physical wires carry differential
 high-speed data and single-ended low-power signalling, and the link alternates between
 them constantly — LP-11 idle, an LP-01/LP-00 request sequence, then HS burst,
 then back. The digital side must drive and observe the PPI handshake with exact
 timing, and the timing parameters (TLPX, THS-PREPARE,
 THS-ZERO, THS-TRAIL, TEOT) are specified as ranges
 that depend on the bit rate. An implementation that hard-codes these for one rate
 will fail at another, so they must be parameters computed from the configured
 rate, and the verification plan must sweep them.

장: P1. MIPI CSI-2 and DSI — Camera and Display Interfaces
절: P1.3 What to build, block by block
글:
P1.3 What to build, block by block

[Table 149. CSI-2 receiver: the blocks and what each must do]
Block | Function | Design notes
PPI interface | Byte-aligned data and valid per lane from the PHY | Clocked by the PHY byte clock; first CDC boundary
Lane aligner / deskew | Align lanes to a common byte boundary | Uses the sync sequence (0xB8) ; must tolerate inter-lane skew
Lane merger | Interleave N lanes into one byte stream | Byte n of the stream came from lane n mod N
Packet parser | Separate short and long packets, extract data type and VC | Short packets carry framing; long packets carry pixels
Header ECC | Correct one bit in the 24-bit header | Hamming; the correction must actually be applied, not just flagged
Payload CRC-16 | Detect payload corruption | Polynomial 0x1021, specified initial value — check against the spec
Pixel unpacker | RAW8/10/12/14, RGB888/565, YUV422 → aligned pixels | Bit-packing is the fiddliest part ; RAW10 packs 4 pixels in 5 bytes
Line buffer / output | Present pixels on a system interface | Usually AXI-Stream with a side channel for VC, data type, line/frame markers
Error reporting | ECC corrected/uncorrected, CRC fail, framing errors | Sticky status registers with defined clearing
Register file | Configuration and status | Generated from one source

The pixel unpacker is where most of the verification
 effort actually goes, and it is worth planning for. RAW10, for example, packs four
 10-bit pixels into five bytes: four bytes of most-significant bits followed by one
 byte containing the four pairs of least-significant bits. RAW12 packs two pixels in
 three bytes. Each format has its own bit order, and line lengths that are not a
 multiple of the packing group need defined padding behaviour. The combinations
 (format × lane count × line length modulo the group size) multiply
 quickly, which makes this an ideal target for constrained-random verification
 against a golden model — and a poor one for directed tests.

Area | Method | Oracle

장: P2. PCI Express, Generations 3 to 6
절: P2.1 What changes between generations
글:
P2.1 What changes between generations

[Table 152. PCIe generations]
Gen | Rate per lane | Encoding | Key addition | Digital consequence
1.0 | 2.5 GT/s | 8b/10b | — | 20% encoding overhead
2.0 | 5.0 GT/s | 8b/10b | — | —
3.0 | 8.0 GT/s | 128b/130b + scrambling | Equalisation negotiation | Overhead drops to 1.5% ; link training grows
4.0 | 16.0 GT/s | 128b/130b | Tighter channel budget | Retimers become common
5.0 | 32.0 GT/s | 128b/130b | — | Equalisation and margining become critical
6.0 | 64.0 GT/s | PAM4 , FLIT mode | Mandatory lightweight FEC + CRC | Fixed-size FLITs replace variable TLP framing; FEC in the datapath
7.0 | 128 GT/s | PAM4 | — | Further channel and FEC work

Generation 6 is the discontinuity, and it changes the
 controller, not only the PHY. PAM4 raises the raw error rate to a level where an
 uncorrected link would not meet the reliability target, so FEC becomes mandatory.
 Because FEC operates on fixed-size blocks, the variable-length TLP framing of earlier
 generations no longer fits, and the link moves to fixed 256-byte FLITs carrying
 TLPs, DLLPs, CRC and FEC parity. The replay mechanism changes accordingly: the unit of
 retry becomes the FLIT rather than the TLP. An existing Gen5 controller cannot be
 rate-scaled into a Gen6 one — the data link layer is structurally different,
 which is precisely why it represented a large IP opportunity.

장: P2. PCI Express, Generations 3 to 6
절: P2.2 The layers in implementation terms
글:
P2.2 The layers in implementation terms

[Table 153. What each layer must implement]
Layer | Responsibilities | Hardest part
Transaction | TLP assembly and decode; address routing; ordering rules ; credit-based flow control; completion tracking; tag management | The ordering rules (posted / non-posted / completion) and their interaction with relaxed ordering and ID-based ordering
Data link | Sequence numbers; LCRC; ACK/NAK; replay buffer ; DLLP generation; flow-control credit initialisation | Replay buffer sizing versus round-trip latency; credit accounting
Physical logical | Scrambling; 128b/130b (or FLIT) framing; lane-to-lane deskew; lane reversal and polarity inversion; LTSSM ; equalisation negotiation; margining | The LTSSM — a large hierarchical state machine with many timeouts and substates
Physical electrical | SerDes | Hard macro — not RTL

Ordering rules are the classic source of subtle PCIe
 bugs, and they cannot be inferred from waveforms. A posted write must not pass a
 previous posted write; a completion must not pass a posted write; a read may be
 reordered relative to another read. Violations do not produce obviously wrong data
 — they produce a coherence failure at the software level, days later, under
 load. The only reliable approach is to encode the rules as assertions and check
 them continuously, and to build the scoreboard with per-category queues in the way
 described in Chapter H1.4. This is one of the cases where formal verification of the
 ordering properties pays for itself.

장: P2. PCI Express, Generations 3 to 6
절: P2.3 The LTSSM
글:
P2.3 The LTSSM

[Table 154. Link Training and Status State Machine — principal states]
State | Purpose | Implementation note
Detect | Detect a receiver on the lanes | Uses electrical idle detection
Polling | Establish bit and symbol lock; exchange TS1/TS2 ordered sets | Lane polarity and reversal are resolved here
Configuration | Link and lane numbering; width negotiation; deskew | Where multi-lane bring-up problems appear
L0 | Normal operation | —
Recovery | Re-train after an error or a speed change | Equalisation for Gen3+ happens here ; substates are numerous
L0s / L1 / L2 | Low-power states | Entry and exit latency budgets
Disabled / Loopback / Hot Reset | Test and control | Required for compliance

The LTSSM is the best formal-verification target in the
 whole block. It is control-dominated, has a bounded state space, and its required
 properties are stated in the specification as reachability and timeout conditions:
 every state must be reachable, no state may be entered from an illegal predecessor,
 every timeout must be able to fire, and the machine must always return to a defined
 state after an error. Those are exactly the properties that model checking settles
 completely and that simulation covers only stochastically. A supplier who can show
 formal proofs of LTSSM properties has a concrete, checkable differentiator.

장: P2. PCI Express, Generations 3 to 6
절: P2.4 Parameters, compliance and deliverables
글:
P2.4 Parameters, compliance and deliverables

[Table 155. Controller parameters]
Parameter | Range | Effect
Link width | x1, x2, x4, x8, x16 | Datapath width and deskew logic
Maximum speed | Gen1–Gen6 | PHY choice; equalisation and FEC logic
Datapath width | 64/128/256/512 bit | Width × clock must exceed the line rate
Max payload size | 128–4096 B | Buffer sizing
Number of tags / outstanding reads | — | Throughput at high latency
Replay buffer depth | — | Must cover the worst-case round trip
Virtual channels | 1–8 | QoS; arbitration complexity
Functions / SR-IOV | — | Configuration space replication

Outstanding-read capacity, not link width, usually
 determines achieved throughput. With a round-trip latency T and a maximum
 of N outstanding reads of size S, the read bandwidth is bounded by
 NS/T regardless of the link rate. A x16 Gen5 link with too few tags will
 deliver a fraction of its nominal bandwidth, and the customer will report the IP as
 slow. Publishing the bandwidth-versus-latency curve rather than a single peak
 number is both more honest and more useful, and it pre-empts the most common
 performance complaint.

[Table 156. Compliance and interoperability]
Activity | What it establishes | Note
PCI-SIG compliance testing | Conformance to the specification | Required for the logo; a defined test suite
Interop testing | Works with real partners | Distinct from compliance
Lane margining | Receiver margin reporting | Mandatory from Gen4
Equalisation preset sweep | Link robustness | Gen3+
Error injection | Recovery behaviour | Replay, retrain, surprise removal

Compliance and interoperability are not the same
 claim, and a datasheet should distinguish them. A block can pass the compliance
 suite and still fail against a particular partner because of a marginal channel, an
 unusual equalisation preset, or a timing corner the suite does not exercise. Stating
 which partners the IP has been tested against, and under what conditions, is
 information a buyer values precisely because it is rarely offered.

장: Q3. Embedded Software Around the Hardware
절: Q3. Embedded Software Around the Hardware — 들어가며
글:
Q3. Embedded Software Around the Hardware

[Table 157. Software layers that touch an IP block]
Layer | Concern | What the hardware must provide
Boot ROM | Bring the system up | Deterministic reset state
Device driver | Register access, interrupts, DMA | A clean register map and a defined initialisation sequence
RTOS / kernel | Scheduling, memory management | Interrupt latency guarantees; cache coherence behaviour
Middleware | Protocol stacks | —
Application | — | —
Firmware in the block | Local control | Instruction memory, debug access

Cache coherence with a DMA-capable block is the
 interaction that produces the most confusing bugs. If a block writes to memory by
 DMA while the CPU has that region cached, the CPU may read stale data; if the CPU
 writes and the data sits in a write-back cache, the block may read stale data. On a
 coherent interconnect the hardware resolves this; on a non-coherent one the driver must
 invalidate before reading and clean before writing, and getting the order wrong
 produces intermittent corruption that looks like an IP defect. An IP datasheet must
 state whether its transactions are coherent, and the example driver should
 demonstrate the required maintenance operations if they are not.

[Table 158. Real-time considerations]
Concept | Meaning | Hardware implication
Interrupt latency | Event to first instruction of the handler | Interrupt controller design; cache and TLB state
Worst-case execution time | Upper bound, not average | Caches and branch prediction make it hard to bound
Priority inversion | Low-priority task blocks a high-priority one | Priority inheritance in locks
Jitter | Variation in response time | Deterministic arbitration helps
Scratchpad versus cache | — | Scratchpads give predictability; caches give average speed

The tension between average performance and worst-case
 predictability runs through the whole field. Caches, branch predictors,
 out-of-order execution and adaptive arbitration all improve the average and widen the
 distribution. Hard real-time systems therefore often disable or avoid them, accepting
 lower throughput for a bound that can be certified. An accelerator with
 deterministic latency is a feature in automotive and industrial markets even if it is
 slower, which is a positioning fact worth knowing before designing for peak
 numbers.

장: Q4. Electromagnetic Compatibility
절: Q4. Electromagnetic Compatibility — 들어가며
글:
Q4. Electromagnetic Compatibility

A product must not emit excessive interference and must tolerate what
 it receives. Both are system properties, but several of the levers are inside the
 digital design.

[Table 159. Emission mechanisms and mitigations]
Mechanism | Source | Mitigation | Where decided
Differential-mode radiation | Current loops on the board | Reduce loop area; ground planes | Board
Common-mode radiation | Cables driven by common-mode voltage | Balanced differential signalling; common-mode chokes | I/O design and board
Harmonics of clocks | Fast edges with periodic content | Spread-spectrum clocking; slew-rate control | Clock generator and I/O cells — a chip-level choice
Simultaneous switching | Many outputs toggling together | Stagger switching; use differential I/O | RTL and I/O planning
Power supply coupling | d I /d t | Decoupling; ramped enables | Chip and board

Spread-spectrum clocking is a direct trade of jitter for
 emissions. Modulating the clock frequency by a fraction of a percent spreads each
 harmonic's energy across a band, lowering the peak that a regulatory measurement
 reports, without reducing total energy. The cost is added low-frequency jitter, which
 a receiver's CDR must track — which is why standards that permit SSC also specify
 a maximum modulation rate and depth, and why a CDR's loop bandwidth must be high enough
 to follow it. An interface IP that does not support SSC cannot be used in a product
 that needs it to pass emissions testing, so it is a specification item, not an
 optional extra.

[Table 160. Immunity concerns]
Threat | Standard | Design response
ESD | IEC 61000-4-2, HBM/CDM | On-chip protection structures; careful I/O design
Radiated immunity | IEC 61000-4-3 | Shielding; filtering
Fast transients / surge | IEC 61000-4-4/5 | Board-level protection
Supply dips | IEC 61000-4-11 | Brown-out detection and clean reset
Latch-up | — | Guard rings; substrate contacts — a layout obligation

ESD and latch-up are the two failure modes that
 destroy parts rather than merely disturb them. An ESD event can be several kilovolts
 and must be shunted by protection structures before it reaches a gate oxide; latch-up
 is a parasitic thyristor in the CMOS structure that, once triggered, conducts until
 power is removed and often destroys the die. Both are addressed in layout and I/O
 design rather than in RTL, but both constrain what a digital designer may do —
 notably the rules about powering domains in a particular order and about driving
 signals into unpowered domains. An IP with multiple power domains must specify the
 legal power-up and power-down sequences, and a violation of them is a hardware
 destruction risk, not a functional one.

장: Q2. Compilers and High-Level Synthesis Internals
절: Q2. Compilers and High-Level Synthesis Internals — 들어가며
글:
Q2. Compilers and High-Level Synthesis Internals

HLS is often treated as a black box. Knowing what it does internally
 makes the difference between fighting the tool and directing it, and the internal
 steps are the same scheduling and binding problems that appear elsewhere in design.

[Table 161. The HLS pipeline]
Step | Function | What the designer controls
Front end | Parse to an intermediate representation | Language subset used
Optimisation | Constant folding, loop transforms, inlining | Code structure; pragmas
Scheduling | Assign operations to clock cycles | Target II and latency constraints; dependences
Allocation | Decide how many of each resource | Resource constraints, binding directives
Binding | Map operations to specific units, values to registers | Storage directives
Interface synthesis | Turn arguments into ports/protocols | Interface pragmas
RTL generation | Emit Verilog/VHDL | —

Scheduling is a constrained optimisation problem and
 that explains the tool's behaviour. Given a dependence graph and resource limits,
 the scheduler minimises latency or the initiation interval. Because the problem is
 NP-hard in general, tools use heuristics (list scheduling, modulo scheduling for
 pipelines, occasionally ILP for small regions). Two consequences follow. First, a
 small change in the source can produce a disproportionate change in the schedule,
 because the heuristic follows a different path — which is why HLS results can be
 unstable. Second, the tool cannot schedule around a dependence it cannot
 disprove, so telling it the truth about aliasing is the highest-leverage thing a
 designer does. That is what a dependence directive is: not an optimisation hint, but a
 fact the tool could not derive.

[Table 162. Directive families and what they actually do]
Family | Examples | Nature | Risk of misuse
Scheduling | pipeline, unroll, inline, loop_flatten, loop_merge | Requests — the tool may not achieve them | Silent failure to meet the target; check the report
Structural | array_partition, bind_storage, bind_op, dataflow, stream | Change what is built | Area explosion
Assertions | dependence, loop_tripcount | Facts the tool trusts | A false assertion produces silently wrong hardware
Interface | interface, axis, m_axi, s_axilite | Define ports | Protocol mismatch

The third family is categorically different from the
 other two and should be reviewed differently. A scheduling directive that cannot be
 satisfied produces a worse result and a report message. A structural directive produces
 a bigger design. A false dependence assertion produces hardware that computes the wrong
 answer, with no message and no simulation failure — because the C semantics are
 unaffected. Every dependence directive is therefore a proof obligation: the
 reviewer must be able to state why the asserted independence holds for every legal
 parameter value. Treating it as an optimisation switch is how silent bugs enter.

[Table 163. What HLS is good and bad at]
Suited | Reason | Unsuited | Reason
Loop-dominated datapaths | Regular dependence structure | Cycle-exact interface protocols | The tool owns the schedule
Design-space exploration | One source, many points | Control-dominated logic | Irregular; RTL is clearer
Filters, transforms, crypto rounds | Well-structured loops | Blocks needing precise latency | Latency is an output, not an input
Algorithm-level changes | Edit the C, not the RTL | Deep pipelines with feedback | The iteration bound still applies

장: Q1. Performance Modelling and Queueing
절: Q1. Performance Modelling and Queueing — 들어가며
글:
Q1. Performance Modelling and Queueing

Functional correctness is verified against a golden model; performance
 is predicted by a different kind of model entirely. Confusing the two is a common and
 expensive mistake, because a functionally perfect block can still fail its throughput
 requirement in a system.

[Table 164. Model types and what each answers]
Model | Question answered | Cost | Fidelity
Analytical (closed form) | Rough sizing, bounds | Minutes | Low but instant
Spreadsheet / static | Bandwidth and utilisation budgets | Hours | Adequate for first-order decisions
Queueing model | Latency under load, buffer sizing | Days | Good when arrivals are stochastic
Trace-driven simulation | Behaviour on real workloads | Days | High
Cycle-approximate (SystemC TLM) | System behaviour before RTL exists | Weeks | Good
Cycle-accurate | Exact cycle counts | Weeks–months | Highest
RTL simulation | Ground truth | — | Exact but far too slow for system studies

The practical value of the middle rows is that they
 exist before RTL does. An architecture decision — how deep a buffer, how many
 outstanding transactions, whether to double the datapath width — must be made
 months before there is anything to simulate. A cycle-approximate SystemC model built
 from the specification answers it in days, and being wrong by 10% is usually
 irrelevant when the alternatives differ by a factor of two. Insisting on
 cycle-accurate fidelity for an architectural question delays the decision until it is
 too late to act on.

[Table 165. Queueing results worth knowing]
Result | Statement | Use
Little's law | L = λ W | Occupancy = arrival rate × latency — sizes any buffer
M/M/1 latency | W = 1/(μ−λ) | Latency diverges as utilisation → 1
M/M/1 occupancy | ρ/(1−ρ) | At 90% utilisation the mean queue is 9
M/D/1 | Deterministic service | Half the waiting time of M/M/1
Erlang B | Blocking probability | Sizing a finite resource pool
Burstiness | — | Real traffic is burstier than Poisson — Poisson results are optimistic

Little's law is the single most useful formula in
 system design and it requires no assumptions about distributions. To sustain
 10 GB/s with a 500 ns round trip, the system must keep
 10×109×500×10−9 = 5 kB in
 flight; if the interface supports 32 outstanding 64-byte requests, that is 2 kB
 and the link will run at 40% of its rate no matter how fast it is. This is the
 quantitative form of the PCIe tag-capacity argument in Chapter P2, and the same
 calculation sizes DMA descriptor rings, memory controller queues and cache
 miss-status registers. Learning to apply it in thirty seconds is worth more than any
 simulator.

Designing for average load is designing to fail.
 The M/M/1 result shows latency rising hyperbolically with utilisation: at 50% the
 queue is 1, at 90% it is 9, at 99% it is 99. Systems provisioned at their average
 demand spend a substantial fraction of their time near saturation, where latency is
 dominated by queueing rather than service. Buffer sizing must be driven by the
 tail of the arrival distribution, not its mean, and a performance specification
 that quotes only average throughput is incomplete.

장: R1. Cryptographic Mathematics
절: R1.1 Number theory for public-key cryptography
글:
R1.1 Number theory for public-key cryptography

[Table 166. Results and the hardware they imply]
Result | Statement | Hardware consequence
Fermat's little theorem | a p −1 ≡ 1 (mod p ) | Inversion by exponentiation — avoids extended Euclid
Euler's theorem | a φ( n ) ≡ 1 (mod n ) | The basis of RSA
Chinese remainder theorem | Work modulo factors, recombine | RSA private operations run ~4× faster
Extended Euclid | Compute inverses | Needed for key setup
Montgomery reduction | Modular reduction without division | The core of every modular multiplier
Barrett reduction | Reduction by precomputed reciprocal | Alternative; good for fixed small moduli
Discrete logarithm hardness | — | Security of Diffie–Hellman and ECC
Elliptic curve group law | — | Point addition and doubling formulas

Montgomery multiplication is worth understanding
 because it explains why modular arithmetic is feasible in hardware at all. Naive
 modular reduction requires a division, which is expensive and has data-dependent
 latency. Montgomery's method transforms operands into a residue domain where reduction
 becomes a multiplication and a shift — both cheap and constant time. The cost is
 a conversion in and out of the domain, which is amortised when many operations are
 performed, exactly as in an exponentiation. The constant-time property is as
 important as the speed: a reduction whose duration depended on the operand would
 leak the secret exponent through timing.

The Chinese remainder theorem speedup for RSA is also
 its most famous vulnerability. Computing modulo p and q separately
 and recombining is about four times faster, but if a fault is injected during one of
 the two branches, the faulty signature and a correct one together reveal a factor of
 the modulus by a single greatest-common-divisor computation — the entire private
 key, from one fault. The standard countermeasure is to verify the signature before
 releasing it. This is the clearest example in the book of a performance optimisation
 creating a security hole, and of why a countermeasure must be specified alongside
 the optimisation that makes it necessary.

장: R1. Cryptographic Mathematics
절: R1.2 Post-quantum cryptography
글:
R1.2 Post-quantum cryptography

[Table 167. NIST post-quantum standards]
Standard | Scheme | Basis | Hardware character
FIPS 203 | ML-KEM (Kyber) | Module lattices (MLWE) | NTT over ℤ 3329 ; small coefficients
FIPS 204 | ML-DSA (Dilithium) | Module lattices | NTT over ℤ 8380417 ; rejection sampling
FIPS 205 | SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) | Hash-based | Many hash evaluations ; large signatures; conservative security
(FN-DSA) | Falcon | NTRU lattices | Floating-point Gaussian sampling — awkward in hardware

The shared kernel across the lattice schemes is the
 number-theoretic transform, and recognising this is how a design house covers several
 standards with one block. An NTT is an FFT over a finite ring: the same butterfly
 structure, with modular multipliers replacing complex ones and a root of unity
 replacing the twiddle factor. Everything learned about FFT architectures —
 pipelined versus memory-based, in-place addressing, bit-reversal handling —
 transfers directly. What is new is modular reduction in the datapath, and for the
 specific small primes used by these standards there are cheap reduction sequences.
 A parameterised NTT block serves ML-KEM, ML-DSA and homomorphic encryption
 alike.

Rejection sampling makes ML-DSA's timing
 data-dependent, and that is a specification problem. Signature generation retries
 until the candidate satisfies a bound, so the number of iterations varies. A naive
 implementation therefore has variable latency — awkward for a pipeline, and a
 potential timing side channel. Implementations must either run for a fixed number of
 iterations with the result masked, or ensure the timing variation reveals nothing about
 the secret. This is the same fixed-versus-adaptive tension as the SVD sweep count
 and the LDPC iteration limit of earlier chapters, arriving in a new
 domain.

장: R1. Cryptographic Mathematics
절: R1.3 Symmetric primitives and modes
글:
R1.3 Symmetric primitives and modes

[Table 168. Modes of operation and their hardware character]
Mode | Parallelisable | Needs | Note
ECB | Yes | — | Insecure for structured data — never use
CBC | Decrypt only | IV | Encryption is serial — a throughput limit
CTR | Fully, both directions | Unique counter | Preferred in hardware ; turns a cipher into a keystream generator
GCM | Yes | GF(2 128 ) multiplier | Authenticated encryption; the multiplier is a substantial block
XTS | Yes | Tweak | Storage encryption
CMAC / GMAC | — | — | Authentication only

Counter mode is the reason a high-throughput AES core
 is feasible. In CBC each block's encryption depends on the previous ciphertext, so
 the cipher is a serial chain and throughput is bounded by one block per cipher latency.
 In CTR the cipher encrypts a counter, independent of the data, so many blocks can be
 computed in parallel and the cipher becomes a pipelined keystream generator whose
 latency no longer matters. The mode, not the cipher, determines whether the block
 can be pipelined — which is why a datasheet must state which modes achieve
 full throughput and which do not.

장: R3. Quantum Computing: What a Hardware Engineer Should Know
절: R3. Quantum Computing: What a Hardware Engineer Should Know — 들어가며
글:
R3. Quantum Computing: What a Hardware Engineer Should Know

Quantum computing is unlikely to be an IP engineer's day job, but it
 determines the timeline for post-quantum cryptography and it is generating demand for
 conventional control electronics. This chapter covers only what is decision-relevant.

[Table 169. Concepts]
Concept | Meaning | Consequence
Qubit | Two-level quantum system | State is a superposition, not a bit
Superposition and entanglement | — | Source of the potential speedup
Decoherence | Loss of quantum state to the environment | The central engineering problem
Gate fidelity | Error per operation | Currently ~10 −3 –10 −4
Error correction | Many physical qubits per logical qubit | Overhead of 10 3 –10 4 ×
Shor's algorithm | Factoring in polynomial time | Breaks RSA and ECC — the reason for PQC
Grover's algorithm | Quadratic search speedup | Halves effective symmetric key strength — AES-256 remains adequate

The asymmetry between Shor and Grover is the fact that
 determines the migration plan. Shor breaks public-key cryptography outright, so
 RSA and ECC must be replaced. Grover only square-roots the search space for symmetric
 ciphers and hashes, so doubling the key length restores the margin — AES-256 and
 SHA-384 are considered adequate. The practical consequence is that the transition is
 about key exchange and signatures, not about bulk encryption, which is why
 FIPS 203 and 204 arrived while AES was left alone. An IP portfolio needs new
 asymmetric blocks, not new symmetric ones.

[Table 170. Conventional electronics needed by quantum systems]
Function | Requirement | Nature
Qubit control pulses | Precise microwave shaping | DAC + DSP — conventional high-speed design
Readout | Low-noise amplification and discrimination | ADC + classification
Real-time feedback | Error correction within the coherence time | Sub-microsecond latency — an FPGA or ASIC problem
Cryogenic operation | Operate at 4 K or below | Cryo-CMOS; extreme power limits
Classical control processor | Sequencing | Conventional

Quantum error correction is a real-time classical
 signal-processing problem, and that is where conventional IP meets the field.
 Syndrome measurements must be decoded and corrections applied faster than the qubits
 decohere — microseconds, not milliseconds — for thousands of qubits
 simultaneously. The decoders involved (minimum-weight perfect matching and its
 approximations) are graph algorithms with hard latency budgets, which is precisely the
 kind of problem the rest of this book is about. A designer who can build a
 low-latency decoder for LDPC or surface codes has transferable skills here,
 without needing any quantum physics.

장: R2. Manufacturing Test
절: R2. Manufacturing Test — 들어가며
글:
R2. Manufacturing Test

[Table 171. Fault models]
Model | Represents | Coverage target | Test method
Stuck-at | A node permanently 0 or 1 | >99% | Scan + ATPG
Transition / delay | A path too slow | >90% | At-speed scan (launch-on-capture or launch-on-shift)
Path delay | A specific critical path | Selected paths | Targeted patterns
Bridging | Short between nodes | — | Layout-aware ATPG
Open | Broken connection | — | —
IDDQ | Abnormal quiescent current | — | Less effective at advanced nodes — leakage swamps it
Cell-aware | Defects inside a standard cell | — | Requires cell-level fault dictionaries

Stuck-at coverage is a proxy, not a goal, and the
 distinction matters commercially. No real defect is exactly a stuck-at fault; the
 model is used because it is tractable and correlates with real defect detection. The
 correlation is imperfect, which is why transition and cell-aware models were added as
 geometries shrank. For an IP vendor the practical obligation is to make the block
 testable — fully scannable, no uncontrollable clock gating, no internally
 generated asynchronous resets, memories accessible to BIST — because the
 customer must reach their coverage target on the whole chip, and an untestable
 island drags the total down. Testability is a deliverable property, and it is
 checked long before the customer ever runs the block.

[Table 172. Test economics]
Factor | Effect | Lever
Tester time | Directly proportional to cost per part | Test compression (10–100× pattern reduction)
Pattern count | Drives tester time | ATPG effectiveness
Test escapes | Defective parts shipped | Higher coverage, better fault models
Yield loss (overkill) | Good parts rejected | Correct test limits
Burn-in | Screens infant mortality | Expensive; sometimes replaced by design margin
Known-good die | Essential for chiplets | Test before assembly or lose the whole package

Known-good-die testing is what makes chiplets
 economically possible, and its absence is what delayed them. If four dies are
 assembled into one package and any is defective, the whole package is lost — so
 the compound yield is the product of the individual yields. At 90% each, four dies give
 66%. Testing each die thoroughly before assembly restores the economics, but testing a
 bare die at speed is harder than testing a packaged part. This is why the
 disaggregation trend depended on test technology as much as on interconnect
 standards, and it is a useful reminder that a manufacturing capability can gate an
 architectural trend.

장: S3. Clock, Reset and Power Architecture of an IP Block
절: S3. Clock, Reset and Power Architecture of an IP Block — 들어가며
글:
S3. Clock, Reset and Power Architecture of an IP Block

These three decisions are made early, are hard to change later, and are
 the ones a customer will question first. They deserve their own chapter in the practice
 volume because they are specification items rather than implementation details.

[Table 173. Clock architecture decisions]
Decision | Options | Consequence for the integrator
Number of clock domains | One, or several | Each additional domain is a CDC verification obligation
Clock relationship | Synchronous ratio, asynchronous, or plesiochronous | Determines which CDC technique is legal
Who divides | Internal divider or external clocks | Internal is easier to use; external is easier to verify
Gating | Internal automatic, external enable, or none | Internal gating must be bypassable for scan
Clock enable versus gating | — | Enables are simpler; gating saves clock-tree power
DFT | — | Test clock must reach every flip-flop

Every clock domain you expose is a cost you impose on
 the customer. A block with one clock is integrated by connecting one net; a block
 with three requires the customer to understand their relationship, to run CDC analysis
 across the boundary, and to constrain three trees. If the second and third domains
 exist only because it was convenient internally, the block is harder to sell than it
 needs to be. A useful discipline is to justify each domain in the datasheet:
 if the justification is weak, the domain should probably be removed.

[Table 174. Reset architecture decisions]
Decision | Recommendation | Reason
Polarity | State it; be consistent | Mixed polarity causes integration errors
Synchronous or asynchronous | Async assert, sync de-assert | Works without a clock; avoids recovery/removal violations
One reset or several | As few as possible | Ordering between resets is a hazard
Minimum assertion width | Specify in cycles of each clock | Otherwise the customer guesses
Reset-less registers | Only where provably initialised by data | Saves area; creates an X-propagation obligation
Soft reset | Define exactly what it does and does not clear | Almost always under-specified

[Table 175. Power architecture decisions]
Decision | Options | Consequence
Single or multiple supplies | — | Level shifters; isolation cells
Power gating | Supported or not | Retention registers; wake sequencing; UPF
Retention | Full, partial, none | Area versus wake latency
DVFS | Supported or not | Timing must close at every operating point
Clock gating granularity | Block, module, register | Finer saves more and costs more verification states
Idle behaviour | Defined quiescent state | Predictable leakage

Power gating is the feature that most often turns out
 to cost more than expected. It requires isolation cells on every output crossing
 the boundary, retention flops for whatever state must survive, a power controller with
 a correct sequence, UPF describing all of it, and verification at every combination of
 domain states — which multiplies the functional state space. For an IP vendor the
 honest positions are either to support it fully, with the UPF and the verification
 evidence, or to state clearly that the block is not power-gateable. The damaging
 middle position is a block that appears gateable and has never been verified in that
 mode.

장: S2. Display and Audio Interfaces
절: S2. Display and Audio Interfaces — 들어가며
글:
S2. Display and Audio Interfaces

[Table 176. Display interfaces]
Interface | Layer | Notes
MIPI DSI | Mobile panel | Covered in P1; command and video modes
eDP / DisplayPort | Packetised, micro-packet | Lane count and rate negotiated; supports MST
HDMI | TMDS or FRL | Consumer; HDCP content protection
LVDS / FPD-Link | Parallel serialised | Automotive, industrial
V-by-One | — | Large panels
Parallel RGB | — | Simple small panels

The recurring structure is the same as everywhere else
 in this volume: a controller above a PHY. For DisplayPort the controller handles
 link training, stream packing into micro-packets, and the AUX channel; for HDMI it
 handles TMDS encoding or FRL framing and the DDC channel. In both cases the PHY is a
 hard macro and the controller is RTL. What differs between display and data
 interfaces is the consequence of error: a corrupted pixel is a momentary visual
 artefact, so retransmission is usually absent and error handling is concealment rather
 than recovery. That asymmetry changes the verification emphasis from data integrity to
 timing and synchronisation.

[Table 177. Audio interfaces]
Interface | Character | Design note
I2S | Simple serial, word clock + bit clock | Clock relationship is the whole protocol
TDM | Multi-channel over one data line | Slot assignment
SoundWire (MIPI) | Multi-drop, two wires | Control and data combined
S/PDIF | Self-clocking biphase-mark | Consumer digital audio
PDM | 1-bit oversampled from a MEMS microphone | Needs a decimation filter — a CIC plus compensation
USB Audio | — | Isochronous transfers; clock domain handling

A PDM microphone is a sigma-delta modulator without its
 decimator, and that decimator is the sellable block. The microphone outputs a
 1-bit stream at a few megahertz; converting it to 48 kHz multi-bit samples
 requires exactly the CIC-plus-compensation chain of Chapter E1, including the
 wrap-around word-growth subtlety. Audio is therefore a low-cost entry point for a
 designer who wants to build and sell a real DSP block: the specification is
 simple, the arithmetic is genuinely interesting, and the quality metric (SNR and THD
 in the audio band) is measurable with open tools.

[Table 178. Audio-specific signal processing]
Function | Purpose | Hardware note
Sample rate conversion | 44.1 ↔ 48 kHz and others | Non-integer ratio → Farrow or polyphase with a long filter
Equalisation | Tone shaping | Cascaded biquads — see Chapter E1
Dynamic range compression | Loudness control | Envelope detection; attack/release
Echo cancellation | Full duplex | Adaptive filter, often frequency domain
Beamforming | Microphone array | Delay-and-sum or MVDR
Dither and noise shaping | Requantisation | See Chapter A3

장: S4. Packaging an IP for Delivery
절: S4. Packaging an IP for Delivery — 들어가며
글:
S4. Packaging an IP for Delivery

[Table 179. Directory structure a customer expects]
Directory | Contents | Note
doc/ | Product brief, user guide, release notes, verification report | The first thing opened
rtl/ | Synthesisable sources plus a file list | Provide the file list in compile order
model/ | Reference model, build instructions | —
tb/ | Testbench, vectors, run scripts | Must run out of the box
syn/ | Synthesis scripts, SDC, reported results | Reproducibility
example/ | A minimal working system | Named target
sw/ | Headers, driver example | Generated from the register source
ipxact/ | Component description | Enables automated integration

The file list in compile order is a small item that
 saves every customer an hour. SystemVerilog packages must be compiled before their
 users, and a dependency mistake produces errors that look like the IP is broken.
 Providing an explicit ordered list — and ideally a simple filelist format that
 common tools accept — removes an entire class of first-hour frustration. The same
 applies to a documented minimum tool version: nothing damages confidence faster than an
 IP that does not compile.

[Table 180. IP-XACT: what it buys]
Element | Content | Enables
Component | Name, version, vendor | Identification in a catalogue
Ports | Names, widths, directions | Automated connection
Bus interfaces | AXI/APB mapping of ports | Automatic bus connection
Parameters | Names, types, ranges, defaults | Configuration UI
Memory maps | Registers, fields, access, reset values | Generation of RTL, headers, documentation and UVM RAL
File sets | Source files by purpose | Build automation

The memory map element is where the real value sits.
 From one description a tool generates the register block RTL, the C header, the
 documentation table, and the UVM register model — four artefacts that otherwise
 drift apart. Even a design house that does not ship IP-XACT should adopt the discipline
 internally, because the alternative is maintaining four hand-written copies of the same
 information. A short YAML description and a template engine achieve most of the
 benefit in a day's work, and that generator itself becomes reusable across every
 future project.

[Table 181. Release checklist]
Item | Check
Clean checkout | Does everything build and run from a fresh clone?
No absolute paths | Scripts must not reference the vendor's filesystem
Tool versions | Stated and tested
Licence headers | On every file
Third-party notices | Complete bill of materials
Version consistency | Version register, documentation and release note agree
Example runs | On the named target, from clean
Known issues | Listed, with severity and workaround
Regression evidence | Logs included, not just claimed

The last item is worth a sentence of its own. A
 verification report that states a coverage figure is a claim; one that ships the
 regression logs and the scripts that produced them is evidence. The difference costs
 nothing to provide and is immediately visible to a technical evaluator, who has almost
 certainly received the former from someone else.

장: S1. Storage Interfaces
절: S1. Storage Interfaces — 들어가며
글:
S1. Storage Interfaces

[Table 182. Storage interface families]
Interface | Physical layer | Protocol | Where
SATA | 1 lane, 1.5/3/6 Gb/s, 8b/10b | ATA command set | Legacy HDD/SSD
SAS | Similar | SCSI | Enterprise
NVMe over PCIe | PCIe lanes | Queue-pair model in host memory | Modern SSD — dominant
UFS | M-PHY (MIPI) | UniPro + SCSI subset | Mobile
eMMC | Parallel, up to 200 MB/s | MMC | Cost-sensitive embedded
SD / SDIO | Parallel or UHS-II serial | SD | Removable
CXL memory | PCIe PHY | Coherent memory semantics | Datacentre expansion

NVMe's design lesson is that the protocol, not the
 link, was the bottleneck. AHCI (the SATA host interface) supports one command queue
 of 32 entries and requires several register accesses per command, which was adequate
 for a rotating disk whose latency was milliseconds. Flash reduced device latency by
 three orders of magnitude and the host interface became the limit. NVMe replaced it
 with up to 64k queues of 64k entries each, placed in host memory so that submission
 costs one memory write and one doorbell write. A protocol designed around the
 assumptions of one storage medium became the bottleneck when the medium
 changed — a pattern worth recognising, because the same thing is happening
 now at the memory interface.

[Table 183. What a storage controller IP contains]
Block | Function | Difficulty
Host interface | PCIe/SATA link and protocol | Standard interface work
Command processing | Fetch, decode, dispatch, complete | Queue management; ordering
DMA engine | Move data between host memory and media buffers | Scatter-gather; alignment
Flash translation layer | Logical to physical mapping, wear levelling, garbage collection | Usually firmware — the real product differentiator
ECC (BCH or LDPC) | Correct raw flash errors | Raw BER rises as the flash wears — the code must be sized for end of life
Buffer manager | DRAM or SRAM buffering | Bandwidth
Power loss protection | Flush on power failure | Capacitor budget and sequencing

Flash ECC is sized for the end of the device's life,
 not its beginning. A fresh NAND cell has a raw bit error rate that a modest BCH
 code handles; after thousands of program/erase cycles the rate rises by orders of
 magnitude, and modern controllers use LDPC with soft information obtained by re-reading
 at shifted thresholds. This is why the decoder chapter's material is directly relevant
 to storage: the same min-sum architectures, the same fixed-point traps, and the same
 trade between average latency (few iterations) and worst-case correction (many).
 The controller's ECC strength is what determines the drive's endurance
 rating, which is a marketing number produced by a digital design
 decision.

장: T1. The MOSFET as Four Different Machines
절: T1. The MOSFET as Four Different Machines — 들어가며
글:
T1. The MOSFET as Four Different Machines

One device, four operating regions — and you design a different circuit in each.

읽기 전에 알아야 하는 것
전압 · 전류 · 저항 · 전기장 · 전하 · 전자 · 지수함수 · 로그 · 미분 · 옴의법칙

이 장에서 새로 나오는 것
문턱전압 · 차단영역 · 선형영역 · 포화영역 · 아문턱영역 · 온저항 · 아문턱기울기 · 누설전류 · 트랜스컨덕턴스 · 채널길이변조 · 출력저항 · 바디효과 · 게이트용량

A MOSFET is usually introduced as a switch, and for a first digital course
 that is enough. It is not enough to design production IP. The same four-terminal
 device behaves as four qualitatively different machines depending on the voltages you
 put on it, and a working designer moves between all four — often inside one block.
 A sampling front end uses the device as a resistor; the comparator behind it
 uses the device as an amplifier; the digital logic behind that uses it as a
 switch; and the leakage that drains the battery while all of it sits idle is
 the device acting as a very bad switch in the region nobody designed for.

This chapter establishes the four regions, then — for each — states where you
 use it, when you reach for it, how you apply it, and what the code that ships with a
 real IP deliverable looks like. Nothing here is included unless it is used later in
 this book.

장: T1. The MOSFET as Four Different Machines
절: T1.1 What the gate actually does
글:
T1.1 What the gate actually does

Before the regions, one physical fact, because every later equation rests on
 it. The gate is one plate of a capacitor. The channel — the thin sheet of silicon
 under the oxide — is the other. Between them sits an insulator a few atoms thick.

Gate oxide capacitance per unit area, Cox — εox/tox. With a physical oxide thickness of
 1.2 nm and εox ≈ 3.9 ε0, this is about
 16 mF/m² — roughly 1.60×1019 fF per square
 micrometre. Everything the transistor does is proportional to it.

유도 — Why gate voltage controls current at all

 | 이렇게 된다 | 왜냐하면
1 | Put a positive voltage on the gate of an NMOS. The gate is one plate of a capacitor, so it stores charge Q = C ox ·V per unit area. | That is the definition of capacitance. No transistor physics yet.
2 | The opposite charge must appear on the other plate — in the silicon, directly under the oxide. | A capacitor holds equal and opposite charge on its plates.
3 | In p-type silicon the mobile negative charge is electrons, which are scarce. Below some gate voltage the silicon supplies the required charge by pushing holes away instead, leaving fixed negative acceptor ions. | Depleting the majority carriers is cheaper than creating minority carriers.
4 | Above some gate voltage the depletion stops growing and the silicon starts supplying mobile electrons instead. That sheet of electrons is the channel. | Once the surface is pulled far enough, attracting electrons costs less energy than widening the depletion region.
5 | That crossover gate voltage is the threshold voltage V t . | It is not a switch trip point designed into the device; it is the voltage at which the silicon changes which kind of charge it supplies.
6 | Above V t , the mobile charge in the channel is Q ch = C ox (V GS − V t ) per unit area. | The first V t worth of gate voltage went into depletion; only the excess produces mobile charge.
7 | Current is charge times velocity, and velocity is mobility times field: I = W·Q ch ·μ·E. | Drift current, the same relation that gives Ohm's law in a resistor.

That last line is the whole device. Every equation below is this relation with
 a different assumption about how the field E varies along the channel. The quantity
 VGS − Vt appears so often it has a name: the
 overdrive, written Vov. When a designer says “I ran that
 device at 150 millivolts of overdrive”, this is the number.

Vt is not one number. It moves with temperature
 (roughly −1 mV/°C), with body bias, with channel length, with how close the
 neighbouring polysilicon is, and it differs from die to die and from transistor to
 transistor on the same die. A design that works only for the nominal Vt
 does not work. Chapter T27 makes this quantitative; for now, treat every
 Vt in this chapter as the centre of a distribution.

장: T1. The MOSFET as Four Different Machines
절: T1.2 Region 1 — cutoff: the switch that does not quite switch off
글:
T1.2 Region 1 — cutoff: the switch that does not quite switch off

Cutoff and subthreshold leakage

Below threshold the channel is not empty — it is exponentially sparse. The
 current does not stop; it falls by a factor of ten for every
 85 mV that VGS drops below Vt. That
 slope is the subthreshold swing, S, and it is the single most important
 number in a low-power design.

Ileak = I0 · 10(VGS − Vt)/S

S has a floor. The channel charge responds to the surface potential through a
 Boltzmann factor, so S ≥ (kT/q)·ln10 = 59.5 mV/decade
 at room temperature, and real devices land 20–40 % above that because part of the
 gate voltage is lost to the depletion capacitance. This floor is why leakage
 became the dominant power term as supplies scaled: you cannot lower
 Vt to keep speed without paying exponentially in leakage, and you
 cannot make the exponent steeper.

어디에 쓰나 | Standby power of every block you ship. Retention registers. Memory
 arrays (where leakage is multiplied by millions of cells). Power gating and the
 sizing of the header/footer switch. Any IP sold with a quoted standby current —
 which is most of them.
언제 쓰나 | Whenever you write a leakage number into a datasheet; whenever you choose
 between device flavours in synthesis; whenever a customer asks for a retention
 mode. Also whenever a block is mostly idle — an equaliser that runs for 3 % of the
 time is a leakage problem, not a dynamic-power problem.
어떻게 쓰나 | Get I off per micrometre of width from the foundry's
 characterisation at the worst corner (highest temperature, lowest V t ,
 highest supply — leakage worsens in the opposite direction from speed). Multiply
 by the total width in the block. Multiply again by the temperature factor — a rule
 of thumb is 2× per 10 °C, which follows directly from the S equation because S
 itself is proportional to T. Then decide: if the answer exceeds budget, move the
 non-critical paths to high-V t cells and re-time.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
// Liberty (.lib) — what the foundry actually ships you.
// This is the leakage the synthesiser reads. Note that it is
// state-dependent: a NAND2 leaks differently per input pattern,
