// because the stacked device changes the internal node voltage.

cell (NAND2_X1) {
 area : 1.596 ;
 cell_leakage_power : 4.2851e+03 ; // nW, the default
 leakage_power () {
 when : "!A1 & !A2" ;
 value : 1.8032e+03 ; // both off: stack effect helps
 }
 leakage_power () {
 when : "A1 & !A2" ;
 value : 4.9210e+03 ;
 }
 leakage_power () {
 when : "A1 & A2" ;
 value : 6.1104e+03 ; // both on: worst
 }
 ...
}

# Synthesis — trade leakage against timing by device flavour.
# The tool will use LVT only where it must to close timing.
set_db library [list sc9_base_svt.lib sc9_base_hvt.lib sc9_base_lvt.lib ]
set_db leakage_power_effort high
set_db dynamic_power_effort medium
# Forbid the leaky flavour outside the critical paths:
set_dont_use [get_lib_cells */*_LVT*]
# ... place and route, then selectively re-enable on failing paths:
set_dont_use -false [get_lib_cells */BUF_X*_LVT]
```

여기서 틀린다. Quoting leakage at nominal temperature. Leakage roughly doubles per
 10 °C, so a 25 °C number is 8–16× optimistic against a 125 °C automotive
 corner. A datasheet that says “standby 12 µA” without naming the
 temperature, supply and corner is not a specification — and a customer who
 discovers the real number at their thermal limit will not buy from you again.

예제 1. Leakage of a block, done the way a datasheet requires

주어진 것. A block with 40,000 gates, average device width 0.8 µm per gate
 (both n and p), Ioff = 0.01 nA/µm at VGS = 0,
 25 °C, typical corner. The customer runs it at 105 °C and asks for the
 worst-case standby current.

푸는 법. Total width, times Ioff per micrometre, times the
 temperature factor (2× per 10 °C), times the corner factor for fast-fast silicon
 (typically 2–3× on leakage).

답. Width = 40,000 × 0.8 = 32,000 µm. At 25 °C, typical:
 32,000 × 0.01 nA = 0.24 µA.
 Temperature: 105 − 25 = 80 °C, so 28 = 256×.
 Corner: ×2.5. Total ≈ 0.16 mA.

The factor-of-2-per-10 °C rule is an approximation of the exponential; for
 a real deliverable you read the number off the foundry's corner tables rather than
 extrapolating. The point of the estimate is to know, early, whether you are within
 a factor of two of the budget or a factor of fifty.

여기서 틀린다. The 25 °C typical number and the 105 °C fast number differ by
 640× here. Engineers quote the first because it is the one the tool prints
 by default. The second is the one the customer measures. Always state the
 triple — temperature, supply, process corner — next to the number; a leakage
 figure without it is meaningless.

장: T1. The MOSFET as Four Different Machines
절: T1.3 Region 2 — triode: the transistor as a resistor
글:
T1.3 Region 2 — triode: the transistor as a resistor

Triode (linear) region and on-resistance

Turn the gate well above Vt and hold the drain close to the
 source. Now the channel exists along its whole length and the field along it is
 nearly uniform, so the device behaves like a resistor whose value the gate
 controls:

ID = μCox(W/L)[(VGS − Vt)VDS
 − VDS²/2]

For small VDS the square term vanishes and the device is simply

Ron = 1 / [μCox(W/L)(VGS − Vt)]

Read that denominator. Ron is inversely proportional to
 overdrive. If the signal you are passing moves VS, then VGS
 moves with it, and the resistance changes with the signal. A
 signal-dependent resistance in a sampling path is distortion, and it is the
 reason bootstrapped switches exist.

어디에 쓰나 | Every transmission gate and pass gate. The sampling switch at the
 front of every ADC and every track-and-hold. Power-gating headers and footers.
 The programmable resistors in a CTLE. Write drivers in SRAM. Any place a digital
 signal must be routed rather than regenerated.
언제 쓰나 | When you need to connect two nodes rather than drive one.
 The moment you catch yourself writing “pass the signal through” rather
 than “buffer the signal”, you are in triode and R on 
 matters.
어떻게 쓰나 | Budget the settling first, then size from it. A switch with
 resistance R charging capacitance C settles with time constant τ = RC; to settle
 to N bits you need t settle ≥ RC·ln(2 N+1 ). Invert for R, then
 use R on = 1/[μC ox (W/L)V ov ] to get W/L. Then
 check R on at the worst signal level , not at mid-scale: for an
 NMOS passing a rising signal, V GS shrinks as the signal rises and
 R on blows up near V DD − V t .

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
* SPICE — the measurement you actually run on a sampling switch.
* You are not checking that it works; you are checking how Ron varies
* with the signal, because that variation is the distortion.

.param vin_val=0.45
M1 drain gate source bulk nch W=2u L=30n
Vg gate 0 DC 0.9
Vs source 0 DC 'vin_val'
Vd drain 0 DC 'vin_val+1m' $ 1 mV across the switch: stay in triode
.dc vin_val 0 0.9 0.01
.measure dc ron PARAM='1m/I(Vd)' $ R = V/I at each input level
.alter
.param boot=1 $ repeat with a bootstrapped gate
.end

// Verilog-AMS behavioural model used in mixed-signal top-level sims.
// A digital verification engineer meets this, not the SPICE deck.
module sw_nmos (inout d, inout s, input g);
 parameter real ron_nom = 250.0; // ohms at mid-scale
 parameter real roff = 1e12;
 analog begin
 // Ron rises as (Vgs - Vt) falls: this is the term that matters.
 real vgs, ron;
 vgs = V(g) - V(s);
 ron = (vgs > 0.35) ? ron_nom * 0.55 / (vgs - 0.35) : roff;
 I(d,s) 여기서 틀린다. Sizing the switch at mid-scale and declaring it done. Ron at
 the top of the input range can be several times its mid-scale value, and the
 settling error it causes is signal-dependent — which means it is harmonic
 distortion, not noise, and averaging will not remove it. Sweep Ron
 across the full input range and size for the worst point.

예제 2. Sizing a sampling switch from the settling requirement

주어진 것. A 10-bit converter samples onto C = 1 pF in 2 ns. Supply
 0.9 V, Vt = 0.3 V, and the worst-case input is
 0.5 V, so Vov = 0.9 − 0.5 − 0.35 = 0.1 V.

푸는 법. Settling to 10 bits needs the error below ½ LSB, i.e.
 e−t/τ < 2−11, so t/τ > 11·ln2 = 7.62. Use a 2× margin
 on τ for the rest of the path, then solve R from τ = RC, then W/L from
 Ron.

답. τ ≤ 2 ns / 7.62 = 262 ps. With 2× margin,
 τ = 131 ps. R = τ/C = 131 Ω.
 Then W/L = 1/(μCox·R·Vov) =
 317.

여기서 틀린다. Using Vov at the mid-scale input (0.45 V) instead of
 the worst-case input gives Vov = 0.1 V and a W/L
 about 2× smaller — and then the switch misses
 its settling target exactly where the signal is largest, which is where the
 distortion is most visible. Size switches at the worst signal level, not the
 average one.

장: T1. The MOSFET as Four Different Machines
절: T1.4 Region 3 — saturation: the transistor as a current source
글:
T1.4 Region 3 — saturation: the transistor as a current source

Saturation, transconductance, and output resistance

Raise VDS above the overdrive and the channel pinches off
 near the drain: the local VGS there falls to Vt and no more
 mobile charge exists. Beyond that point, raising the drain voltage no longer
 raises the current much. The device has become a current source controlled by the
 gate:

ID = ½ μCox(W/L)(VGS − Vt)²
 · (1 + λVDS)

Two derived quantities do all the work in analog design:

Transconductance gm = ∂ID/∂VGS
 = 2ID/Vov. How much current you get per volt of input —
 i.e. the gain-producing term.

Output resistance ro = ∂VDS/∂ID
 ≈ 1/(λID). How close to an ideal current source it is. The term λ
 exists because pinch-off moves with drain voltage — channel-length
 modulation — and it is worse for short channels, which is why analog blocks
 use devices several times the minimum length.

Their product gmro = 2/(λVov) is the intrinsic
 gain: the most voltage gain one transistor can give you. It falls as
 processes scale, which is why modern analog design leans on digital assistance
 rather than on raw gain.

어디에 쓰나 | Comparators and sense amplifiers — the pre-amp stage. Every current
 mirror and bias network. CTLE and the analogue front end of a SerDes. Level
 shifters during the transition. Ring-oscillator delay cells in a PLL. Anywhere the
 circuit must amplify rather than switch .
언제 쓰나 | When the question is “how much gain” or “how much
 current, independent of the load”. Also, unexpectedly, in digital 
 analysis: during a logic transition both devices pass through saturation, and the
 short-circuit current that flows then is the term T4 uses to explain why slow
 input edges cost power.
어떻게 쓰나 | Design with g m /I D rather than with W/L. Pick the
 g m you need from the gain or the noise requirement; pick
 g m /I D from the speed/power trade (high g m /I D 
 ≈ low overdrive ≈ efficient but slow; low g m /I D ≈ high
 overdrive ≈ fast but power-hungry); that fixes I D ; read W/L off the
 foundry's characterised g m /I D curves. This works across
 processes and does not rely on the square-law equation, which stops being accurate
 below about 100 nm.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
* The gm/ID sweep every analog team runs once per process,
* then reuses for every block. You are not simulating a circuit here;
* you are characterising the device so design becomes look-up.

.param L_val=100n
M1 d g 0 0 nch W=10u L='L_val'
Vg g 0 DC 0.5
Vd d 0 DC 0.45 $ hold Vds at VDD/2, in saturation
.dc Vg 0.2 0.9 0.005
.measure dc gm_id PARAM='deriv(I(Vd),V(g))/I(Vd)'
.measure dc ft PARAM='deriv(I(Vd),V(g))/(2*3.14159*cgg)'
.step param L_val list 30n 60n 100n 200n 500n
.end

// What a digital designer sees of all this: a characterised cell.
// The analog block arrives as a .lib timing/power view plus a
// behavioural model. You must still know what is inside, because
// the constraints you write depend on it.
cell (CMP_STRONGARM) {
 pin (CLK) { direction : input; clock : true; capacitance : 4.8; }
 pin (VINP) { direction : input; capacitance : 12.1; }
 pin (OUTP) { direction : output;
 timing () {
 related_pin : "CLK" ;
 timing_type : rising_edge ;
 cell_rise (delay_template) { ... }
 } }
 // The number a digital designer must not ignore:
 // the comparator has a metastability window like any bistable.
 // T14 derives it; the vendor states it here.
}
```

여기서 틀린다. Using the square-law equation for design in a modern process. Below
 roughly 100 nm the velocity of carriers saturates, the exponent drifts from 2
 toward 1, and the equation can be wrong by tens of percent. It remains excellent
 for reasoning — it tells you the right direction and the right
 sensitivity — and useless for numbers. Reason with the equation, size from
 the characterised curves.

장: T1. The MOSFET as Four Different Machines
절: T1.5 Region 4 — subthreshold as a design space, not only as leakage
글:
T1.5 Region 4 — subthreshold as a design space, not only as leakage

Subthreshold operation

The same exponential that produces leakage is a usable transfer
 characteristic. Biased below Vt, the device gives
 gm/ID at its maximum — about
 27.1 V⁻¹, set only by S — which is the best
 current efficiency any MOSFET can offer. The cost is speed: fT falls by
 orders of magnitude, and the exponential dependence on Vt means that
 device-to-device Vt mismatch turns into current mismatch of tens
 of percent.

So subthreshold is the region you choose when energy per operation dominates
 and speed does not, and the region you are forced into when a supply droops. It is
 also the region a retention circuit lives in: state is held by a device
 that is barely on.

어디에 쓰나 | Always-on domains — wake-up logic, watchdog timers, retention
 registers. Sensor front ends. Bias generators that must survive at very low
 current. And, negatively, every leakage path in every block you ship.
언제 쓰나 | When the duty cycle is very low and the energy budget is per-operation
 rather than per-second. When a customer asks for a retention mode with a quoted
 microamp figure. When you are asked to survive a supply that collapses toward
 V t .
어떻게 쓰나 | Accept that matching, not speed, will set your area. In strong
 inversion, current mismatch tracks V t mismatch through
 g m /I D ; in subthreshold g m /I D is at its
 maximum, so the same V t mismatch produces the largest 
 current mismatch. Size the devices from the matching requirement (T28's Pelgrom
 relation), then check speed, rather than the other way round.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
# UPF (Unified Power Format) — how the always-on domain is
# declared to the tools. A digital IP deliverable that supports
# retention ships this file, and it is as much a part of the
# product as the RTL.

create_power_domain PD_ALWAYS_ON -elements {u_wake u_timer}
create_power_domain PD_CORE -elements {u_dsp u_eq} -scope .

create_supply_net VDD_AON -domain PD_ALWAYS_ON
create_supply_net VDD_CORE -domain PD_CORE
set_domain_supply_net PD_CORE -primary_power_net VDD_CORE \
 -primary_ground_net VSS

# Retention: state survives while VDD_CORE collapses.
set_retention RET_CORE -domain PD_CORE \
 -retention_power_net VDD_AON -retention_ground_net VSS \
 -save_signal {u_dsp/ret_save high} \
 -restore_signal {u_dsp/ret_restore low}

# Isolation: outputs of a collapsed domain must not float into
# the always-on domain, or the always-on logic burns crowbar current.
set_isolation ISO_CORE -domain PD_CORE \
 -isolation_power_net VDD_AON -clamp_value 0 \
 -applies_to outputs
set_isolation_control ISO_CORE -domain PD_CORE \
 -isolation_signal u_pmc/iso_en -isolation_sense high
```

여기서 틀린다. Forgetting isolation. When a power domain collapses, its outputs drift
 to an intermediate voltage. Feed that into an always-on gate and both its
 devices conduct — the always-on domain then draws milliamps instead of microamps,
 and the retention mode you sold does not exist. This is one of the most common
 integration failures in low-power IP, and it is invisible in RTL simulation
 because RTL has no intermediate voltage.

장: T1. The MOSFET as Four Different Machines
절: T1.6 Two second-order effects you cannot ignore
글:
T1.6 Two second-order effects you cannot ignore

Body effect

Vt is quoted for source tied to bulk. Lift the source above the
 bulk and the depletion region under the channel widens, so more gate voltage is
 needed before inversion: Vt rises. The dependence is
 Vt = Vt0 + γ(√(2φF + VSB)
 − √(2φF)), and γ is a process constant of order 0.2–0.5 √V.

The practical consequence: a device whose source is not at the rail is
 weaker than the library says.

어디에 쓰나 | Stacked devices in NAND/NOR — the upper NMOS has its source above
 ground. Pass-gate chains. Cascode current sources. Multiplexer trees built from
 transmission gates. Any place transistors are in series.
언제 쓰나 | Whenever you stack. A 4-input NAND is not simply 4× slower than an
 inverter — it is worse, because the upper devices are body-effected. This is one
 reason wide gates are decomposed into trees rather than built flat.
어떻게 쓰나 | For hand analysis, add the V t shift and recompute the
 overdrive of the upper device. For real sizing, let the characterised library
 handle it — the .lib delay tables already contain the effect — but know it is
 there so that a stacked structure you invent is not assumed to scale
 linearly. If the stack is deep, insert a buffer instead.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
// Why you will not find `body effect` in an RTL file, but will
// feel it: the synthesiser's cell choice reflects it.
// These two are logically identical and time very differently.

assign y = ~(a & b & c & d); // maps to NAND4 — deep stack

wire ab = ~(a & b); // maps to NAND2 + NAND2 + NOR2
wire cd = ~(c & d); // shallower stacks, more cells
assign y = ~(~ab | ~cd) ? 1'b0 : 1'b1;

// Liberty shows the penalty directly. Compare the intrinsic delays:
// NAND2_X1 cell_rise (A1) ~ 0.021 ns
// NAND3_X1 cell_rise (A1) ~ 0.031 ns
// NAND4_X1 cell_rise (A1) ~ 0.045 ns 여기서 틀린다. Assuming a stack of n devices is n times slower. Body effect and the
 internal node capacitances make it super-linear, and above three or four the
 penalty grows fast. If a synthesised netlist contains NAND4s on a critical path,
 that is usually the first thing to restructure.

Gate capacitance — the load you are driving

The gate you drive is a capacitor: Cg ≈ Cox·W·L,
 plus overlap capacitance that does not scale with L. For
 1.2 nm oxide this is of order
 1.60×107 fF/µm² of gate area.

This single fact ties the whole of digital design together: the output of one
 gate must charge the input capacitance of the next, so delay is proportional to
 the ratio of load capacitance to drive strength. That ratio is the
 electrical effort of T3, and it is why sizing is a chain problem rather
 than a per-gate problem.

There is also a term that bites in analog and in high-speed digital: the
 gate-to-drain overlap capacitance Cgd appears at the output
 multiplied by the gain of the stage (Miller effect). In a comparator
 pre-amp this can dominate the load; in a digital gate it is why the input
 capacitance seen during a transition is larger than the static value.

어디에 쓰나 | Every delay calculation. Clock-tree power (the clock drives enormous
 total gate capacitance, which is why clock gating is the first power optimisation).
 Input capacitance you quote in a datasheet so a customer can budget their driver.
언제 쓰나 | Always, in digital. Specifically when you write the input capacitance
 line of an IP datasheet, and when you decide how many loads one cell may drive.
어떻게 쓰나 | Express loads in units of a minimum inverter's input capacitance and
 the arithmetic becomes tractable by hand — this is exactly what logical effort
 (T3) formalises. For the deliverable, state input capacitance per pin in the .lib
 and in the datasheet; integrators use it to size their drivers and to build the
 clock tree.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
// The datasheet line that comes from this, and the .lib it matches.
// If these two disagree, the customer's timing closure fails and
// they will find out before you do.

pin (D) {
 direction : input ;
 capacitance : 1.412 ; // fF — what the integrator budgets
 rise_capacitance : 1.455 ;
 fall_capacitance : 1.369 ;
 max_transition : 0.300 ; // ns — beyond this, delay tables
} // are extrapolated, not valid

// SDC the customer writes against your block:
set_load 0.0014 [get_ports eq_out*] ;# pF
set_driving_cell -lib_cell BUF_X4 [get_ports adc_data*]
set_max_transition 0.300 [current_design]
```

여기서 틀린다. Letting a net exceed max_transition. Beyond that point the
 library's delay tables are being extrapolated, and the timing report is no longer
 characterised data — it is a guess with a confident number next to it. Treat a
 max-transition violation as a hard error, not a warning.

장: T1. The MOSFET as Four Different Machines
절: T1.7 Which region, for which job
글:
T1.7 Which region, for which job

[표 1. The four regions as four design tools]
Region | Condition | The device behaves as | You use it for | The number that matters
Cutoff | V GS V t , V DS V t , V DS > V ov | a voltage-controlled current source | amplifiers, comparators, current mirrors, CTLE | g m , r o , g m /I D
Subthreshold | V GS slightly 실제로 난 일
A production sampling switch was sized from its mid-scale
 Ron and met its settling target in simulation at every corner. Silicon
 showed second-harmonic distortion 12 dB worse than simulated. The cause was that the
 verification sweep held the input at mid-scale while checking settling, and swept the
 input only while checking gain — so the combination that mattered, large input and
 tight settling, was never simulated. Nothing in the design was wrong; the
 verification grid was wrong. T30 turns this into a rule: sweep the axes
 together, not one at a time.

[표 2. 이 장의 개념이 실제로 쓰이는 자리]
개념 | 쓰이는 블록 | 무엇을 정하나
Subthreshold swing S | every block's standby spec | the leakage number in your datasheet, and whether retention is possible
R on and its signal dependence | sampling switch, pass gates, power switch | settling time, distortion, IR drop across the power switch
g m /I D | comparator pre-amp, CTLE, bias | gain and noise per unit of current — i.e. the power budget
Channel-length modulation λ | current mirrors, cascodes | how much the bias current moves with output voltage
Body effect γ | stacked logic, transmission-gate trees | why deep stacks are super-linearly slow
Gate capacitance C g | every delay and clock-power calculation | the input capacitance line of your datasheet

특허로 가는 길 — 이 주제에서 발명이 일어나는 자리

Device-level invention is largely closed to a fabless IP house — the
 foundry owns the device. What is open is how you choose among the devices
 you are given. Claims in shipping IP portfolios routinely read on
 selection and arrangement: a retention latch that uses high-Vt
 devices only on the state-holding node while the read path stays standard-Vt;
 a level shifter whose pull-up stack is sized so that the contention current is
 bounded across corners; a sampling switch whose bootstrap network holds
 VGS constant so that Ron is signal-independent. All three are
 device-region arguments, and all three are patentable as circuits. Read this
 chapter asking which region am I in, and what does that buy me — that
 question is where the claims come from.

장: T2. Delay — From One RC to a Whole Timing Path
절: T2. Delay — From One RC to a Whole Timing Path — 들어가며
글:
T2. Delay — From One RC to a Whole Timing Path

Every delay number a tool reports is one of four models. Know which one, or you will trust a number that was never about your circuit.

읽기 전에 알아야 하는 것
전압 · 전류 · 저항 · 미분 · 지수함수 · 옴의법칙 · 문턱전압 · 선형영역 · 포화영역 · 온저항 · 게이트용량 · 출력저항

이 장에서 새로 나오는 것
RC지연 · 엘모어지연 · 논리적노력 · 전기적노력 · 기생지연 · FO4 · 슬루 · 단락전류 · 배선지연 · 리피터 · 도착시각 · 요구시각 · 슬랙 · OCV · NLDM · 비선형지연모델

Ask four engineers what the delay of an inverter is and you get four answers,
 all correct, because they are answering with four different models. A SPICE user
 answers with a differential equation. A physical-design engineer answers with a
 two-dimensional lookup table from a Liberty file. A microarchitect answers in FO4.
 A synthesis engineer answers with a dimensionless number that has no picoseconds in
 it at all. These are not competing approximations of one truth; they are four tools
 with different jobs, and using the wrong one is how a design gets signed off on a
 number that was never about the path that failed.

This chapter builds them in order, each from the one before, and at every
 step states the regime in which that model is the right one to use. The numbers
 throughout come from one set of process constants declared at the top of this
 chapter's source — a 28 nm-class low-power node at 0.9 V —
 and every table below is computed from them, not typed in.

장: T2. Delay — From One RC to a Whole Timing Path
절: T2.1 The one model you can do in your head: switched RC
글:
T2.1 The one model you can do in your head: switched RC

A CMOS gate charges and discharges a capacitor through a transistor that is
 acting as a resistor. That is the whole of it. Everything else in this chapter is a
 refinement of that sentence, and every refinement exists because a specific
 assumption in it broke.

RC지연 (RC delay) — A gate's output node is a capacitance C driven through an equivalent resistance R. The node's voltage is a decaying exponential, and the delay is the time to cross the receiver's switching threshold — conventionally 50 % of VDD.

유도 — From the transistor to 0.69 RC

 | 이렇게 된다 | 왜냐하면
1 | A switching gate connects the output node either to V DD through the PMOS stack or to ground through the NMOS stack. | That is what a static CMOS gate is: two complementary networks, exactly one of which conducts in steady state.
2 | While it switches, the conducting transistor is not a resistor — it starts in saturation and ends in triode. | V DS starts at V DD and falls toward 0, so the device crosses regions during the transition (T1).
3 | We replace it anyway with a single equivalent resistance R eq , defined as the value that gives the same 50 % crossing time. | This is a fitted quantity, not a measured resistance — which is why it differs between textbooks and why you never compare R eq numbers across sources.
4 | Then V(t) = V DD ·e −t/RC for a falling output. | First-order linear ODE with a step excitation: the standard solution.
5 | Setting V = V DD /2 gives t = RC·ln 2 = 0.69 RC. | ln 2 = 0.693. This is where the 0.69 in every delay formula comes from — it is the 50 % point, nothing more.
6 | For 10–90 % rise/fall time the same solution gives t = RC·ln 9 = 2.2 RC. | Same exponential, different two crossings. 0.69 and 2.2 describe the same waveform — a delay and a slew are two readings of one curve.

[그림] 그림 1. The unit inverter. The pull-up and pull-down networks are the R in RC; the next stage's gate capacitance and the wire are the C.

τ = Req·Cg — the process's unit of time

Pick one reference device — the minimum-size inverter — and give it two
 numbers: an equivalent output resistance Req = 8 kΩ
 and an input capacitance Cg = 1 fF. Their product
 τ = 8 ps is the only absolute time in the rest of this chapter. Every other
 delay will be quoted as a multiple of it.

This is not a cosmetic choice. Ratios between gates are set by topology and
 are stable across process, voltage and temperature to within a few per cent;
 the absolute τ moves by 2× or more across corners. Separating the two is
 what lets you do architecture on paper and let the tool supply the picoseconds.

어디에 쓰나 | Every hand estimate of a critical path, every early architectural trade-off, every 'will this fit in one cycle' question before the RTL exists.
언제 쓰나 | Before synthesis — when there is no netlist to run STA on, and after STA, to check whether a reported number is even plausible.
어떻게 쓰나 | Express the path in τ, then multiply once at the end. A useful
 anchor is FO4 — an inverter driving four copies of itself —
 which in this process is 40 ps. A modern high-performance pipeline
 stage is roughly 12–20 FO4; a low-power one, 25–40.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
// A 'timing shell' exists so that the number you measure is about
// your logic, not about the pads. Synthesise the DUT inside registers:
module fir_shell (input clk, input rst, input signed [7:0] din, output signed [15:0] dout);
 reg signed [7:0] din_q;
 reg signed [15:0] dout_q;
 wire signed [15:0] y;
 always @(posedge clk) begin din_q 여기서 틀린다. Quoting Fmax from a design whose inputs and outputs are pins
 is the single most common false number in an IP datasheet. If a path has no
 launching and no capturing register, the tool has nothing to constrain and
 will report whatever combinational delay it found — often 10× optimistic.

장: T2. Delay — From One RC to a Whole Timing Path
절: T2.2 Elmore delay — when one RC becomes a chain of them
글:
T2.2 Elmore delay — when one RC becomes a chain of them

The single-RC model assumes the resistance is at one end and the capacitance
 at the other. A wire violates both: its resistance and its capacitance are
 distributed along it. Cutting it into N lumps and summing gives the Elmore delay,
 and the sum has a shape worth memorising, because it is the reason long wires do not
 scale.

[그림] 그림 2. A wire cut into four RC sections. Section 1's resistance pushes the capacitance of sections 1–4; section 4's pushes only its own.

유도 — Why wire delay grows with the square of length

 | 이렇게 된다 | 왜냐하면
1 | Cut a wire of length L into N equal sections, each with resistance R/N and capacitance C/N. | R = r·L and C = c·L, with r in Ω/µm and c in F/µm from the technology file.
2 | The charge for every capacitance downstream of section i must flow through section i's resistance. | Charge has only one path to reach them — that is the whole content of the Elmore model.
3 | So the delay is Σ i (R/N)·(N−i+1)(C/N) = RC·(N+1)/(2N). | Arithmetic series 1+2+…+N = N(N+1)/2. Substituting gives the closed form.
4 | As N → ∞ this tends to RC/2, and R and C are each proportional to L. | Hence t ∝ r·c·L² — doubling a wire's length quadruples its delay , while a gate's delay does not change at all.
5 | For this process, a 1, µm wire gives RC/2 = 90 ps, and the four-lump approximation gives 112 ps. | The coarse lump over estimates by 1.25×. Use the closed form for the distributed case and lumps only when the sections are real (a via, a branch, a tap).

[표 3. Lumping a distributed wire: how many sections are enough]
Sections N | Elmore delay | Error vs. distributed RC/2
1 | 18 ps | 1 %
2 | 135 ps | 50 %
4 | 112 ps | 25 %
8 | 101 ps | 12.5 %
16 | 95.6 ps | 6.25 %
32 | 92.8 ps | 3.12 %

Two facts hide in that table. First, a single lump is 100 % wrong
 — and a single lump is exactly what a naive spreadsheet does. Second, convergence is
 slow: even 8 sections is still 6 % high. This is why extraction tools do not lump
 at all; they solve the distributed network. Your hand estimate should use RC/2 and
 remember that it is a lower bound on what the extractor will report, because the
 extractor also sees coupling capacitance to neighbours.

Elmore delay

The first moment of the impulse response of an RC tree: for a node k,
 tk = Σi Rik·Ci, where Rik
 is the resistance shared by the path to node i and the path to node k. It is
 exact for a single RC, always an upper bound on the 50 % delay for an RC
 tree with a step input, and it ignores inductance entirely.

어디에 쓰나 | Clock-tree synthesis (balancing sinks), buffer and repeater insertion, and the delay model inside every placer's incremental timing engine — the placer cannot afford a full extraction per move.
언제 쓰나 | Whenever you need a delay that is monotone in the tree's structure and cheap to update. It is wrong by 10–30 % in absolute terms and right in its ordering, which is what an optimiser needs.
어떻게 쓰나 | Walk the tree from the driver; accumulate the shared resistance for each sink. Never use it to sign off timing — it is an optimisation objective, not a signoff model.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
# Extraction produces this; you read it when a net is suspect.
# SPEF, standard parasitic exchange format, one net:
*D_NET net_dout_3 1.84e-01 $ total capacitance, pF
*CONN
*I u_fir/Z O *L 0 *D INVX4 $ driver
*I u_reg/D I *L 1.02e-03 $ receiver pin cap, pF
*CAP
1 net_dout_3:1 2.31e-02
2 net_dout_3:2 net_clk:7 4.10e-03 $ COUPLING to an aggressor -- not in your hand estimate
*RES
1 net_dout_3:1 net_dout_3:2 1.79e+01 $ ohms
```

여기서 틀린다. Elmore is an upper bound for a step input. Real inputs have finite
 slew, and for a fast input into a long wire the true 50 % delay can exceed
 it. The bound you rely on is not the bound you were taught if the slew is
 large — which is the next section.

장: T2. Delay — From One RC to a Whole Timing Path
절: T2.3 Logical effort — delay with the picoseconds factored out
글:
T2.3 Logical effort — delay with the picoseconds factored out

Sizing a chain of gates by RC arithmetic works and is miserable. Logical
 effort removes the process from the problem entirely, leaving a dimensionless
 expression you can optimise in your head, and it answers the two questions that
 actually come up: how many stages, and how much bigger should each one
 be.

유도 — The normalised delay of one stage

 | 이렇게 된다 | 왜냐하면
1 | Write a gate's delay as d = (R gate ·C out ) + (R gate ·C self ). | The output node carries the load and the gate's own drain capacitance; both are charged through the same resistance.
2 | Divide through by τ = R inv C g . | We choose to measure everything relative to the minimum inverter. Nothing is lost; the units are.
3 | The first term becomes g·h: logical effort g = how much worse this topology is than an inverter at driving current, and electrical effort h = C out /C in . | g depends only on topology (NAND2 = 4/3, NOR2 = 5/3, inverter = 1); h depends only on the ratio of load to input, so it is independent of absolute size.
4 | The second term becomes p, the parasitic delay — the delay of the gate driving nothing. | It scales with the gate's own diffusion, which grows with its width exactly as its drive does — so p is size-independent. p inv ≈ 1.
5 | d = g·h + p. | Two multiplications and an addition, and no process constant anywhere.
6 | For a path of N stages, the total is minimised when every stage carries the same stage effort f = (G·B·H) 1/N . | Differentiate the sum with respect to each stage's size and set to zero; the symmetric solution falls out. G = Πg, H = C load /C in , and B accounts for branching off the path.

[그림] 그림 3. Four stages, each 4× the last. Equal stage effort is what makes the total minimal — not equal sizes, and not one huge final stage.

예제 3. Driving a 64× load: how many stages?

주어진 것. A 1× inverter must drive a load of 64·Cg (an on-chip bus with
 several receivers). Logical effort of an inverter chain is G = 1, no branching
 so B = 1, and H = 64, giving path effort F = 64.

푸는 법. Try each N, computing D = N·F1/N + N·pinv, and pick
 the smallest. The table below is computed, not recalled.

답. N = 3 stages, with stage effort f = 4
 and total delay 15·τ = 12 ps. A single stage would
 take 52 ps — 4.33× slower.

[표 4. Stage count versus total delay for F = 64]
Stages N | Stage effort f | Delay (τ) | Delay
1 | 64 | 65 | 52 ps
2 | 8 | 18 | 144 ps
3 | 4 | 15 | 12 ps
4 | 2.83 | 15.31 | 123 ps
5 | 2.3 | 16.49 | 132 ps
6 | 2 | 18 | 144 ps

여기서 틀린다. Reading the table's minimum as a sharp optimum. N = 3 and N = 4 differ by
 2.1 % — inside the
 noise of any real p. Take the cheaper of the two, not the nominally
 faster one; the extra stage costs area, leakage and a slew you must then drive.

[표 5. Logical effort of the cells you will actually instantiate]
Gate | g | p (τ) | Why g is what it is
Inverter | 1 | 1 | The reference
NAND2 | 4/3 | 2 | Two series NMOS: each must be 2× wider for the same pull-down current, so the input cap rises to 4/3 per input
NAND3 | 5/3 | 3 | Three in series — g grows linearly with stack depth
NOR2 | 5/3 | 2 | Series PMOS, and PMOS is the weaker device; this is why NOR is avoided in fast logic and NAND is not
NOR3 | 7/3 | 3 | Same reason, worse
XOR2 | 4 | 4 | Both polarities of both inputs are needed internally
MUX2 | 2 | 4 | Two transmission paths plus select drive
Tri-state inverter | 2 | 2 | The enable device is in series with the output — the classic bus driver

Logical effort, used as a design instrument

d = g·h + p. Total path delay D = Σ(gihi) + Σpi,
 minimised at equal stage effort f = F1/N, with the practical rule that
 f ≈ 4 (the true optimum for pinv = 1 is 3.6) and an extra stage
 is worth adding only while it removes more than p of delay.

어디에 쓰나 | Deciding how deep a pipeline stage can be before synthesis; choosing between a NAND-NAND and a NOR-NOR implementation; sizing a clock or reset distribution by hand; arguing with a synthesis result that looks wrong.
언제 쓰나 | At architecture time, and every time a tool's answer needs a sanity check. Synthesis does this internally but with a cost function that also weighs area and power, so its answer will differ — knowing the ideal tells you whether the difference is a trade or a mistake.
어떻게 쓰나 | Count G along the path, compute H from the real load, take F = G·B·H, then N ≈ log 4 F and f = F 1/N . Work backwards from the load to size each stage: C in,i = g i ·C out,i /f.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
# The synthesis constraint that makes the tool solve the same problem.
# Without a real load and a real driver, the tool optimises a fiction.
set_load 0.064 [get_ports dout*] ;# pF -- from the receiver's .lib
set_driving_cell -lib_cell INVX4 [get_ports din*] ;# not an ideal source
set_max_transition 0.150 [current_design] ;# ns -- bounds slew degradation
set_max_fanout 16 [current_design]
# And the one that is almost always missing on a first pass:
set_max_capacitance 0.200 [current_design]
```

여기서 틀린다. g is a property of the topology, not of the cell you picked from
 the library. A library's NAND2_X4 and NAND2_X1 have the same g; only Cin
 differs. Engineers who 'fix timing' by swapping to a bigger cell without
 changing the stage count are changing h for the previous stage — they move
 the problem upstream, and on a long chain it comes back.

장: T2. Delay — From One RC to a Whole Timing Path
절: T2.4 Slew, and why a delay has two arguments
글:
T2.4 Slew, and why a delay has two arguments

Both models so far take one input: the load. Every real timing tool takes
 two, because the delay of a gate depends on how fast its input moved. A slow
 input keeps both transistors partially on, wastes current through the stack, and
 starts the output late. That is the single largest correction to everything above,
 and it is why a Liberty file holds a table rather than a formula.

슬루 (slew / transition time) — The time for a signal to cross between two defined fractions of VDD, conventionally 10 %–90 % or 30 %–70 %. Which pair is a property of the library, and mixing libraries that use different pairs silently changes every delay in the design.

단락전류 (short-circuit current) — During a transition both the pull-up and pull-down networks conduct simultaneously, shorting VDD to ground through the stack. The charge lost this way is proportional to the input transition time; at normal slews it is 5–15 % of switching energy, and at degraded slews it can exceed the useful switching energy.

[표 6. The same inverter, four different 'delays' — an NLDM slice]
Input slew (ps) | Load 4 fF | Load 16 fF | Load 64 fF
20 | 16 ps | 40.4 ps | 137 ps
60 | 24 ps | 49.2 ps | 147 ps
120 | 36 ps | 62.4 ps | 162 ps
240 | 60 ps | 88.8 ps | 192 ps

That table is a model, not a measurement — the slew coefficients are
 illustrative. Say so. A real NLDM table is characterised by running SPICE at
 every grid point over the full corner set, typically 7×7 points per arc, per cell,
 per corner. What is real in the table is its shape: delay rises roughly linearly in
 load and roughly linearly in input slew, and the slew term is not small — at
 the light load it is the dominant term.

NLDM — the non-linear delay model, and what a tool actually reads

A Liberty (.lib) file gives, for each timing arc of each cell,
 two 2-D tables — one for delay and one for output slew — indexed by input
 transition time and total output capacitance. The tool bilinearly interpolates
 (and, at the edges, extrapolates) to get a number. Everything downstream —
 STA, synthesis cost, placement timing — is built on these tables.

Its successor, CCS (composite current source), stores a current waveform
 rather than a scalar, which matters when the receiver's input capacitance is
 itself voltage-dependent or when the net's resistance is large enough that the
 driver and the net interact. For an IP deliverable, state which model your
 numbers came from; they are not interchangeable at the 5 % level.

어디에 쓰나 | Every delay number in synthesis, STA, and place-and-route. Also in the IP datasheet, indirectly: your F max is only meaningful with the library and corner named.
언제 쓰나 | You read a .lib directly in exactly two situations: when a path's reported delay makes no sense and you want to see whether the tool extrapolated off the table, and when you are asked to support a library you have never seen.
어떻게 쓰나 | Find the arc, read index_1 (input slew) and index_2 (load), and check that your operating point is inside both. Off-table extrapolation is the standard cause of 'the tool says it passes and silicon says it does not'.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
/* Liberty, one arc of one cell -- this is what the tool reads. */
cell (INVX1) {
 area : 1.596 ;
 pin (A) { direction : input ; capacitance : 1.02 ; } /* fF */
 pin (Z) {
 direction : output ;
 function : "!A" ;
 max_capacitance : 64.0 ;
 timing () {
 related_pin : "A" ;
 timing_sense : negative_unate ;
 cell_fall (delay_7x7) {
 index_1 ("0.004, 0.012, 0.028, 0.060, 0.124, 0.252, 0.508"); /* input slew, ns */
 index_2 ("0.4, 1.6, 4.0, 8.8, 18.4, 37.6, 76.0"); /* load, fF */
 values ( "0.0091, 0.0142, 0.0241, 0.0431, 0.0812, 0.1574, 0.3098", \
 "0.0113, 0.0164, 0.0263, 0.0453, 0.0834, 0.1596, 0.3120", \
 /* ... five more rows, one per input slew ... */ );
 }
 fall_transition (delay_7x7) { /* the OUTPUT slew -- this feeds the next stage */ }
 }
 }
}
```

여기서 틀린다. Delay and output slew are two separate tables, and the output slew
 is the next stage's input slew. This is how one badly driven net poisons a
 whole path: each stage receives a worse slew, produces a worse slew, and the
 degradation compounds. set_max_transition exists to stop that
 compounding, and a design with no max_transition constraint can meet
 setup in the report and fail in silicon.

장: T2. Delay — From One RC to a Whole Timing Path
절: T2.5 The wire, and the repeater that saves it
글:
T2.5 The wire, and the repeater that saves it

Gate delay shrinks with each process node. Wire delay does not: r rises as
 wires get thinner, c stays roughly constant per micron, and the die does not shrink
 as fast as the transistors. Beyond a length that has been getting shorter every
 node, a wire dominates the path, and the fix is not a bigger driver — it is to stop
 the wire being long.

[그림] 그림 4. A long wire, and the same wire cut into segments by repeaters. The quadratic term shrinks by N; the buffer delay grows by N.

[그림] 그림 5. The full sweep for a 1, µm wire, each point at its own optimal
 repeater size. The minimum is shallow — N = 3, 4 and 5 are within
 2.1 % of each other — so take the one
 that routes.

유도 — Where the optimum comes from, and a check on it

 | 이렇게 된다 | 왜냐하면
1 | Cut the wire into k segments, each driven by an inverter of size h. | One repeater per segment; the last one drives the receiver.
2 | Each segment costs 0.7·(R inv /h)(C w /k + h·C g ) for the driver, 0.4·R s C s for the distributed wire, and 0.7·R s ·hC g for the far-end load. | The 0.4 and 0.7 are the standard distributed-RC coefficients — 0.4 for a wire driving its own capacitance, 0.69 for a lumped load.
3 | Sweeping k and h numerically gives 93.5 ps at k = 4, h = 38. | Brute force over the whole grid — no assumption about the shape of the optimum.
4 | The closed forms k = √(0.4R w C w / 0.7R inv C g ) and h = √(R inv C w / R w C g ) give k = 3.59, h = 37.9. | Independent cross-check. Two routes to the same answer, agreeing to 0.1 % in size. A single derivation that no one checked is how the wrong constant survives for years.
5 | Without repeaters, the same wire with its own best driver costs 131 ps. | So repeaters buy 1.4× here — and that is the honest headline , not a figure taken from the most favourable corner of the sweep.

Repeater insertion

Break a wire whose delay is quadratic in length into segments short enough
 that the quadratic term is comparable to a buffer delay. The optimum segment
 length is the one where the wire's RC per segment equals the buffer's own
 delay; past that, you are paying buffers to save nothing.

For this process the crossover is around a wire of
 25 µm — shorter than that and a repeater costs more than
 it saves.

어디에 쓰나 | Any net that leaves a block: block-to-block datapaths, clock spines, reset distribution, and the top-level assembly of an SoC where your IP's ports land.
언제 쓰나 | Decided in physical design, but constrained in your deliverable : if your IP's output has 200 ps of budget and the integrator's wire needs 300, the block fails through no fault of its RTL.
어떻게 쓰나 | Give the integrator a number, not a hope: state output delay, drive strength, and maximum load in the datasheet, and constrain both ends with set_output_delay / set_load. Then the repeater problem is theirs and is solvable.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
# What the integrator must be told, and what you must constrain.
# In your IP's SDC (shipped with the deliverable):
create_clock -name clk -period 4.000 [get_ports clk]
set_output_delay -max 1.200 -clock clk [get_ports {dout[*] dvalid}]
set_input_delay -max 1.000 -clock clk [get_ports {din[*] dvalid_i}]
set_load 0.064 [get_ports dout[*]] ;# what we assumed -- say it in the datasheet
# And in DATASHEET.md, the line that prevents the support call:
# Output timing assumes 여기서 틀린다. Repeaters are inverting. An odd number of them flips the polarity of the
 net, and the fix — using buffers (two inverters) instead — costs more delay
 than the inverter chain. Tools handle this, but hand-placed repeaters in a
 reset or scan-enable path are a classic bring-up bug: the block resets on
 the wrong polarity at one corner only, because that corner is the one where
 the inserted pair was optimised away.

장: T2. Delay — From One RC to a Whole Timing Path
절: T2.6 From cells to a path: what STA actually adds up
글:
T2.6 From cells to a path: what STA actually adds up

Static timing analysis does not simulate. It propagates two numbers through
 the graph — the earliest and latest time a signal can arrive — and compares them
 against what each endpoint requires. Everything above supplies one edge of that
 graph; this section is how the edges become a verdict.

유도 — Setup and hold, as one inequality each

 | 이렇게 된다 | 왜냐하면
1 | A launching flop puts data out at t launch = T clk,launch + t cq . | The clock arrives at the launching flop at its own time — clock delay is not the same at both ends of a path.
2 | It arrives at the capturing flop at t arrival = t launch + t logic . | t logic is everything this chapter has been computing.
3 | The capture edge occurs at T clk,capture + T period , and the data must be stable t setup before it. | That stability requirement is a property of the flop, characterised the same way as any other arc.
4 | Setup: t arrival ≤ T capture + T − t setup − t uncertainty . Slack is the difference. | Clock uncertainty absorbs jitter and the skew the tool cannot yet know (pre-CTS). Positive slack passes; negative fails.
5 | Hold: the fastest path must not arrive before the same capture edge's hold window: t arrival,min ≥ T capture + t hold . | Hold has no T in it. Slowing the clock does not fix a hold violation — this is the single most useful fact in the chapter for a first-time designer.

[표 7. The four ways a path's numbers get worse than your estimate]
Effect | What it does | Typical size | Where it is set
OCV / AOCV / POCV | Derates cell and net delays differently on the launch and capture clock paths, because two identical cells on the same die are not identical | 3–10 % of the clock path | set_timing_derate
Clock uncertainty | A flat subtraction standing in for jitter and, pre-CTS, for skew | 50–150 ps | set_clock_uncertainty
CPPR / CRPR | Gives back the derate double-counted on the shared part of the launch and capture clock paths | Recovers 10–50 ps | on by default in signoff STA; often off in synthesis
SI / crosstalk delay | An aggressor switching the other way stretches your transition | 5–15 % on long parallel nets | SI-aware STA with coupling from SPEF

Reading report_timing without being misled

A timing report is a ledger: clock path to the launch flop, cell and net
 delays along the data path, clock path to the capture flop, library setup, and
 the derates. The one line that decides whether the report is meaningful is
 the corner and mode it was run in — a report from the typical corner with
 ideal clocks is not evidence of anything.

어디에 쓰나 | Every timing signoff, every 'why is this failing' investigation, and every F max number you put in a datasheet.
언제 쓰나 | Read the whole path when slack is negative; read the startpoint and endpoint first when it is positive, to check that the tool timed the path you think it did. False paths and unconstrained endpoints show up here and nowhere else.
어떻게 쓰나 | Check: (1) is the endpoint a register, not a port; (2) is the clock real (propagated) or ideal; (3) what is the input transition at the worst cell — if it is at the end of the .lib index range, the number is extrapolated; (4) how much of the path is net delay. Above ~40 % net delay, the fix is placement, not logic.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
# Startpoint: u_fir/acc_reg[7] (rising edge-triggered flip-flop clocked by clk)
# Endpoint: u_fir/y_reg[15] (rising edge-triggered flip-flop clocked by clk)
# Corner: ss_0p81v_125c Check: setup Path Group: clk
# Point Incr Path
# clock clk (rise edge) 0.000 0.000
# clock network delay (propagated) 0.412 0.412 여기서 틀린다. clock network delay (ideal) in that report instead of
 (propagated) means no clock tree exists yet and the skew is a
 guess. Numbers from an ideal-clock report routinely improve by 200–400 ps at
 signoff — in the wrong direction. Never put an ideal-clock Fmax
 in a datasheet.

장: T2. Delay — From One RC to a Whole Timing Path
절: T2.7 What to do with this on Monday
글:
T2.7 What to do with this on Monday

[표 8. 이 장의 개념이 실제로 쓰이는 자리]
개념 | 쓰이는 블록 | 무엇을 정하나
RC지연 · τ · FO4 | Any block, before RTL exists | Whether the function fits in one cycle at the target frequency
엘모어지연 | Clock tree, reset tree, long datapath nets | Where a buffer must go, and which sink is the late one
논리적노력 | Critical-path restructuring, pipeline depth | Stage count and the size ratio between stages
슬루 · NLDM | Reading .lib, debugging an implausible delay | Whether the tool interpolated or extrapolated your operating point
배선지연 · 리피터 | Block boundaries and top-level assembly | The output-load and transition limits you publish in the datasheet
도착 · 요구 · 슬랙 | Every signoff | Whether the number you are about to sell is real

실제로 난 일
This repository measured its own FIR filter at 455 MHz and then
 at 47.4 MHz — a factor of 9.6 — from the same RTL. The
 difference was a timing shell. Without registers at the boundary, the tool reported
 the delay of a path from a pin to a pin, which is not a path that exists in a chip.
 Every number in this chapter is only as meaningful as the path it was measured on,
 and the cheapest way to be wrong by 10× is to time the wrong path.

The next chapter takes the one case this one cannot handle: what happens when
 the setup inequality is violated not by a slow path but because the data was never
 synchronous with the clock at all. The answer is not a longer delay but a
 probability, and it is the only timing quantity in this book that can never be made
 zero.

특허로 가는 길 — 이 주제에서 발명이 일어나는 자리

The delay of a gate is physics and is not patentable. The way a
 block arranges itself so that a delay stops mattering is. Look at what the
 claims in shipping IP actually cover: a speculative (unrolled) decision-feedback
 equaliser that moves a feedback multiply-add off the critical loop and replaces
 it with a precomputed mux — the arithmetic is unchanged, the loop delay is not;
 a carry-select adder that buys delay with area by computing both carries; a
 clock-tree scheme that deliberately skews two launch points so that a slow path
 borrows time from a fast one. In every case the invention is where the delay
 was moved, not how fast a transistor is. That is why this chapter spends as
 much time on which term dominates as on the formulae: you cannot move a
 term you have not identified.

장: T3. Metastability — the One Failure You Cannot Design Away
절: T3. Metastability — the One Failure You Cannot Design Away — 들어가며
글:
T3. Metastability — the One Failure You Cannot Design Away

Every other timing quantity can be made to pass. This one can only be made improbable, and you must say how improbable.

읽기 전에 알아야 하는 것
전압 · 전류 · 미분 · 지수함수 · 로그 · 확률 · 평균 · 트랜스컨덕턴스 · 출력저항 · 게이트용량 · RC지연 · 도착시각 · 요구시각 · 슬랙 · FO4

이 장에서 새로 나오는 것
준안정 · 결정시간상수 · 해결시간 · 준안정창 · MTBF · 동기화기깊이 · 다중비트문제 · 재수렴 · 그레이코드 · 핸드셰이크 · 비동기FIFO · 리셋동기화기 · 리커버리 · 리무벌 · CDC검증 · 준정적신호

A setup violation is a scheduling problem: the data was late, and if you slow
 the clock or shorten the logic, it is fixed. Metastability is not that. When a
 flip-flop samples an input that is changing at the moment of the clock edge, the
 output can sit between the two legal levels for an unbounded time. No amount of
 slowing down removes it — the sampling instant and the data transition are
 uncorrelated, so the bad coincidence will happen again. The only question is how
 often, and whether you have budgeted for it.

This chapter answers that question with a number, then spends the rest of its
 length on the more common failure: engineers who compute the number correctly, put in
 a two-flop synchroniser, and still ship a chip that hangs — because the thing that
 crossed the boundary was not one bit.

장: T3. Metastability — the One Failure You Cannot Design Away
절: T3.1 Why a decision can take unbounded time
글:
T3.1 Why a decision can take unbounded time

유도 — From the cross-coupled pair to an exponential

 | 이렇게 된다 | 왜냐하면
1 | A flip-flop's storage element is two inverters in a loop: the output of each drives the input of the other. | That loop is what holds state with no clock — it is the only structure in digital design that has memory without a capacitor being explicitly named.
2 | The loop has three equilibria: a solid 0, a solid 1, and a point in the middle where both inverters sit at their own switching threshold. | Plot V out1 vs V in1 and the mirrored curve for the second inverter; they cross three times. The middle crossing is the metastable point.
3 | The middle equilibrium is unstable : the loop gain there is A² > 1, so any deviation grows. | Each inverter has small-signal gain A = −g m (r o,n ∥ r o,p ) at its threshold, and T1 gave both terms.
4 | Linearise around it: C·dv/dt = (A − 1)·v/R, so v(t) = v 0 ·e t/τ with τ = RC/(A − 1). | This is where τ, the decision time constant, comes from . It is a circuit property — roughly the loop's RC divided by its excess gain — and it is not a specification you can choose.
5 | To resolve to a valid level the loop must grow the deviation from v 0 to about V DD /2, which takes t = τ·ln(V DD /2v 0 ). | The time is logarithmic in how close the sample landed to the centre — and v 0 can be arbitrarily small, so t is unbounded. There is no worst case to design for, only a distribution.
6 | The probability that a sample lands within a window that needs more than t r to resolve falls as e −t r /τ . | Uniform arrival within the clock period, and v 0 proportional to how close the edge was, give the exponential directly.

[그림] 그림 6. One of the two inverters in the loop. At the metastable point it sits at its own switching threshold with both devices in saturation — the highest-gain, highest-current, least-stable operating point it has.

Two consequences fall out of that derivation and both matter in
 practice. First, τ is a small-signal quantity, so it degrades exactly where
 gain degrades: slow corner, low voltage, high temperature. Second, the metastable
 point is where the flop burns the most current — both devices are on. A design
 that goes metastable often does not just fail logically; it draws current it was not
 budgeted for.

장: T3. Metastability — the One Failure You Cannot Design Away
절: T3.2 MTBF, and what every symbol in it actually is
글:
T3.2 MTBF, and what every symbol in it actually is

MTBF (mean time between failures) — The average time between two events in which a synchroniser fails to resolve within the time allowed. It is a rate, not a guarantee — a 1000-year MTBF does not mean the first failure is in year 1000; it means the failures are Poisson with that mean.

The MTBF expression

MTBF = etr/τ / (T0·fc·fd)

tr — resolution time: the time the synchroniser flop is
 given to settle before anything reads it. In a single-stage crossing that is
 Tclk minus the flop's own tcq, minus the setup of whatever
 reads it, minus any logic in between. τ — decision time constant, from
 T3.1, here 25 ps. T0 — the effective width of
 the aperture in which a sample can go metastable, here 1 ps;
 both are measured per cell per corner, not derived. fc —
 the sampling (destination) clock frequency. fd — the rate at
 which the asynchronous input changes.

Only tr is in the exponent, and that is the whole engineering
 content of this formula: everything you can do is linear, and the thing you
 cannot control is exponential. Doubling fd halves MTBF. Adding
 one synchroniser stage multiplies the exponent.

어디에 쓰나 | Every asynchronous boundary in the design: an external interrupt, a reset release, a pushbutton, a FIFO pointer crossing between clock domains, a PHY's recovered-clock domain meeting the core's.
언제 쓰나 | At architecture time you pick the depth; at signoff you state the number. An IP datasheet that claims 'CDC safe' without an MTBF and the conditions it was computed at has claimed nothing.
어떻게 쓰나 | Get τ and T 0 from the library's synchroniser cell characterisation (they are published per corner). Compute t r from the real path, not the ideal clock period. Then state MTBF at the slow corner , because τ is worst there.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
// The synchroniser, written so the tools recognise it.
// The attribute is not decoration: it tells the tool to keep the two flops
// adjacent and out of retiming, and it tells CDC checkers this is intentional.
(* ASYNC_REG = "TRUE" *) reg [1:0] sync_q; // Xilinx; Intel: altera_attribute
always_ff @(posedge clk_dst or negedge rst_n) begin
 if (!rst_n) sync_q 여기서 틀린다. Using set_false_path on a crossing is the single most common
 CDC constraint error. It silences the timing report, but it also removes any
 bound on the wire delay into the synchroniser — so the source can change
 arbitrarily close to the destination edge and the skew between the two
 bits of a bus becomes unbounded. Use set_max_delay -datapath_only.

[표 9. MTBF against clock frequency and synchroniser depth (τ = 25 ps, T₀ = 1 ps, f_d = f_c/10, overhead 15 ps)]
f_clk | t_r per stage | 1 stage | 2 stages | 3 stages
0.5 GHz | 1,85 ps | 1.7e+18 년 | 2.4e+50 년 | 3.3e+82 년
1 GHz | 85 ps | 1.85 년 | 1.1e+15 년 | 6.3e+29 년
2 GHz | 35 ps | 9.53×10 -10  년 | 0 년 | 1,378 년

예제 4. Why two stages is the default, and where it stops being enough

주어진 것. A 1 GHz destination clock, an input that changes at 100 MHz, and
 15 ps of overhead per stage, so tr =
 85 ps.

푸는 법. Put the numbers into the expression once per depth. The exponent scales with
 the number of stages because each stage gets its own full tr.

답. One stage: 1.85 년 — a failure every
 couple of years, per crossing. Two stages:
 1.1e+15 년. Three stages:
 6.3e+29 년.

[표 10. The same two-stage crossing at 1 GHz, as τ degrades]
τ | MTBF
1× | 1.08e+15 년
1.2× | 1.34e+09 년
1.5× | 1.54e+05 년
2× | 1.85 년

여기서 틀린다. Reading the two-stage number as a property of the design rather than of the
 corner. Recompute it with τ merely 2× worse — a plausible slow-corner,
 low-voltage degradation — and the same two-stage crossing gives
 1.85 년. The exponent
 collapsed. MTBF is exponentially sensitive to the one parameter you do not
 control, which is why the number must be quoted at the slow corner and why
 the third stage exists.

At 2 GHz the table says something worth pausing on: a
 single-stage crossing has an MTBF of
 0.0301 seconds. Not years — seconds. To reach 100 years
 with one stage at that frequency you would need tr =
 984.4 ps, which is longer than the
 clock period itself (500 ps). The requirement is not achievable in one
 cycle at all — this is the regime where depth stops being a safety margin and
 becomes the only way the circuit works.

장: T3. Metastability — the One Failure You Cannot Design Away
절: T3.3 A synchroniser is not a CDC solution
글:
T3.3 A synchroniser is not a CDC solution

Everything so far concerns one bit. The failures that actually reach silicon
 almost never come from a wrong MTBF; they come from designers who synchronised each
 bit of a bus correctly and still lost.

[그림] 그림 7. Two bits crossing through their own synchronisers. Each bit is individually safe. The pair is not: one resolves this cycle, the other next cycle, and the receiver sees a value that was never sent.

The multi-bit problem, and the three ways out

Independent synchronisers make independent decisions. If two bits change
 in the same source cycle, each may resolve on either side of the boundary, so
 the destination can observe an intermediate value — a code that the source
 never drove. A binary counter crossing 0111 → 1000 can be seen as 1111 or
 0000 or anything between. No MTBF calculation detects this: every flop behaved
 correctly.

어디에 쓰나 | Any bus, counter, pointer, status word or configuration field that crosses a clock boundary. In practice: FIFO pointers, interrupt status registers, and 'mode' fields written by a slow configuration domain and read by a fast datapath.
언제 쓰나 | The moment more than one bit crosses. The three-bit case is not safer than the thirty-two-bit case — it is the simultaneity that matters, not the width.
어떻게 쓰나 | Pick one: (1) Gray code — only one bit changes per increment,
 so an intermediate sample is either the old or the new value, both valid.
 Works for counters and pointers, not for arbitrary data. (2) Handshake 
 — hold the data stable and cross a single request bit; the receiver
 acknowledges. Costs round-trip latency, works for anything.
 (3) Asynchronous FIFO — a dual-port memory with gray-coded pointers;
 this is (1) and (2) combined and is what you ship for streaming data.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
// Gray-coded pointer crossing -- the standard async FIFO core.
// The pointer is converted to gray BEFORE crossing and back AFTER.
function automatic [PW:0] bin2gray(input [PW:0] b); return b ^ (b >> 1); endfunction

always_ff @(posedge wclk or negedge wrst_n)
 if (!wrst_n) {wbin, wgray} 여기서 틀린다. Gray code protects the pointer, not the data. The data path
 in an async FIFO is a dual-port RAM, and it is safe only because the read
 address is never allowed to reach a location the write side has not finished
 writing — that is what the conservative full/empty comparison buys. Copying
 the gray-code trick onto a data bus does nothing: consecutive data words
 differ in many bits.

실제로 난 일
A crossing can also fail with zero metastability events. If a
 source pulse is shorter than one destination clock period, the destination may never
 sample it — the synchroniser resolves cleanly to the old value, every time. This is
 not a probabilistic failure; it is a guaranteed one, and it is invisible to MTBF
 analysis. The rule that prevents it: a signal crossing into a slower domain must
 be held for at least one and a half destination periods, or converted to a
 level-toggle with a handshake back.

[표 11. What each crossing style costs and what it protects]
Style | Latency (dst cycles) | Throughput | Protects | Fails when
2-flop synchroniser | 2 | 1 bit / cycle | One bit, level-stable | More than one bit changes together; pulses shorter than 1.5 cycles
Pulse synchroniser (toggle) | 2–3 | 1 event / 3 cycles | Single events across any ratio | Events arrive faster than the round trip
Gray pointer | 2 | 1 increment / cycle | Monotone counters and pointers | Used on arbitrary data
Req/ack handshake | 4–6 round trip | 1 word / round trip | Arbitrary data of any width | Latency budget cannot absorb the round trip
Async FIFO | 2–3 + fill | 1 word / cycle sustained | Streaming data, rate mismatch | Depth is too small for the burst pattern
Quasi-static (config field) | 0 | written once | Fields that change only while the consumer is idle or in reset | Someone writes it while the datapath is running

준정적신호 (quasi-static signal) — A crossing signal that is guaranteed by protocol to change only while the destination is not using it — typically a configuration field written before the block is enabled. It needs no synchroniser, but it does need a written rule in the datasheet and a CDC waiver that says so. An undocumented quasi-static assumption is how an IP works in the lab and fails in the customer's system.

장: T3. Metastability — the One Failure You Cannot Design Away
절: T3.4 Reset: the crossing everyone forgets
글:
T3.4 Reset: the crossing everyone forgets

Reset is asynchronous by nature — it must work before any clock is running —
 and synchronous by necessity, because releasing it at the wrong instant violates the
 flop's recovery time and puts the state machine in a metastable state on its first
 cycle. The resolution is the same for every design and is worth memorising as a
 single sentence: assert asynchronously, release synchronously.

[그림] 그림 8. The reset synchroniser. The asynchronous assertion path has no clock in it; the release path runs through two flops clocked by the destination domain.

리커버리 · 리무벌 (recovery and removal)

Recovery time is the setup constraint on reset de-assertion: reset
 must be released at least trecovery before the active clock edge.
 Removal time is the corresponding hold constraint. They are characterised like
 any other timing arc and appear in the .lib — which means STA checks them
 only if the reset is a timed, synchronous signal at that flop.

An asynchronous reset that is released without a synchroniser has no such
 relation to the clock, so STA reports nothing, and the failure appears as a
 state machine that occasionally starts in an illegal state after power-up —
 typically at one corner, on some boards, after some power ramps.

어디에 쓰나 | Every clock domain. A design with three clocks needs three reset synchronisers, each clocked by its own domain and all fed by the same asynchronous source.
언제 쓰나 | Always. The cost is two flops per domain; the failure it prevents is the hardest class of bug to reproduce.
어떻게 쓰나 | Assert straight through (no clock), release through two flops. Then constrain it: the release is now a synchronous signal and STA will check recovery/removal on every flop it reaches.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
// Reset synchroniser -- one per clock domain.
module reset_sync (input clk, input arst_n, output rst_n);
 (* ASYNC_REG = "TRUE" *) reg [1:0] q;
 always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge arst_n)
 if (!arst_n) q 여기서 틀린다. Resetting the synchroniser's own flops with the synchronised reset
 is a loop with no way out: the block never leaves reset if the release edge
 is missed. The synchroniser must take the raw asynchronous reset on
 its clear pin. This is also why the two flops in a reset synchroniser reset
 to 0 and shift in 1, rather than the other way round.

장: T3. Metastability — the One Failure You Cannot Design Away
절: T3.5 What STA cannot check, and what a CDC tool does instead
글:
T3.5 What STA cannot check, and what a CDC tool does instead

[표 12. Two tools, two questions]
Question | STA | CDC analysis
Does this path meet setup at the given clock relation? | yes | no
Is there a clock relation at all? | assumes one | this is its job
Does every crossing have a synchroniser? | no | yes (structural)
Do multiple bits cross together? | no | yes — reconvergence and bus-coherency checks
Is the source stable long enough? | no | yes — protocol checks, usually as generated assertions in simulation
Is this crossing intentionally unsynchronised? | no | only if you waive it , by name, with a reason

The waiver file is the part of CDC signoff that decides whether the
 analysis meant anything. A tool run with two hundred waivers and a green summary is
 not evidence; it is two hundred assertions by an engineer. An IP deliverable
 should ship its CDC waivers as a readable document, one line of justification
 each, because the integrator inherits every one of them and cannot re-derive them
 from the netlist.

Proving a crossing in simulation as well as structurally

Structural CDC analysis proves a synchroniser exists. It cannot
 prove the source obeys the protocol the synchroniser assumes — that the data is
 stable while the request is high, that pulses are long enough, that a
 quasi-static field is not written while the datapath runs. Those are temporal
 properties, and they are checked by assertions, either hand-written or
 generated by the CDC tool.

The strongest available check adds metastability injection: the
 simulator randomly delays the synchroniser output by one cycle, so that a design
 which only works when the crossing resolves immediately fails in regression
 rather than in silicon.

어디에 쓰나 | Block-level verification of anything with more than one clock, and every IP you intend to sell into someone else's clocking scheme.
언제 쓰나 | Run structural CDC at every RTL freeze; run injection in the nightly regression. The two find different bugs and neither subsumes the other.
어떻게 쓰나 | Bind the assertions to the crossing module, run the regression with injection on, and record the result in the deliverable's verification section with the number of crossings and the number of waivers.

실제 코드는 이렇게 생겼다

```
// The protocol the handshake crossing assumes, stated as a checkable property.
property data_stable_while_req;
 @(posedge clk_src) disable iff (!rst_n)
 req |-> ##0 $stable(data) throughout (req [*1:$] ##1 ack_sync);
endproperty
assert property (data_stable_while_req)
 else $error("CDC: data changed while req was asserted -- the receiver may latch a mix");

// Metastability injection (simulation only): the synchroniser may take one extra cycle.
`ifdef CDC_INJECT
 always_ff @(posedge clk_dst)
 if ($urandom_range(0,99) 여기서 틀린다. Assertions written in the destination domain about source-domain signals
 are themselves a clock-domain crossing and can report failures that are
 artefacts of the testbench. Sample source signals in the source domain
 (@(posedge clk_src)) and cross only the boolean result.
