The number to carry from this chapter: at 12 bits a SAR's capacitor array is
 4.91× larger than noise alone would require,
 because matching sets it — and at 14 bits that factor is
 1.23, where noise has taken over. Design the 12-bit part
 from the matching requirement and the 14-bit part from kT/C, and you are sizing the
 same array by two different physics because the crossover sits between them.

The next chapters leave the converter and take up the circuit that decides
 when all of this happens — the phase-locked loop — where the same trade
 between noise, bandwidth and power appears in a feedback system rather than in a
 capacitor.

특허로 가는 길 — 이 주제에서 발명이 일어나는 자리

Converter patents cluster in three places and the pattern is worth
 seeing: switching schemes that lower the energy of a SAR's capacitive DAC
 (monotonic, split-cap, Vcm-based — all the same array, switched
 differently); calibration that measures a physical error once and
 subtracts it in the digital domain forever; and interleaving corrections
 for gain, offset and timing skew between slices. All three share a shape:
 accept the analog error and remove it somewhere cheaper. That is the most
 reliably patentable idea in mixed-signal design, and it is available in almost
 every block.

장: W3. Automation: Running Verification Around the Clock
절: W3. Automation: Running Verification Around the Clock — 들어가며
글:
W3. Automation: Running Verification Around the Clock

A solo developer cannot out-work a verification team, but can
 out-schedule one: machines run while people sleep. The objective is a loop that,
 unattended, generates stimulus, compares against the golden model, classifies
 failures, and leaves a prioritised queue for the morning.

장: W3. Automation: Running Verification Around the Clock
절: W3.1 The continuous verification loop
글:
W3.1 The continuous verification loop

[Table 184. Loop stages]
Stage | Action | Requirement
1. Generate | Random parameters and stimulus from declared legal ranges | Seeds recorded
2. Run model | Reference model produces expected output | Fast and deterministic
3. Run RTL | Open-source simulator (Verilator/Icarus) or vendor tool | Scriptable, headless
4. Compare | Scoreboard with the correct ordering semantics | See H1.4
5. Classify | Group failures by signature | Automated triage
6. Minimise | Shrink a failing case to a minimal reproducer | The single highest-value automation step
7. Report | Ranked queue with reproduction commands | —
8. Coverage | Accumulate and identify gaps | Feeds back into stage 1

Stage 6 is where automation earns its keep. A
 randomly generated failing case may be thousands of transactions long; a human cannot
 read it. Delta-debugging — repeatedly removing parts of the stimulus and
 re-running to see whether the failure persists — typically reduces such a case to
 a handful of transactions in a few minutes of machine time. The engineer then arrives
 to a minimal reproducer rather than a log file. This is the difference between an
 overnight run that produces work and one that produces guilt.

장: W3. Automation: Running Verification Around the Clock
절: W3.2 Where AI helps and where it must not be trusted
글:
W3.2 Where AI helps and where it must not be trusted

[Table 185. Machine assistance in an IP flow]
Task | Suitability | Condition
Writing testbench boilerplate | High | Reviewed; it is code like any other
Generating directed tests from a specification table | High | The table is the source of truth, not the model
Triage and clustering of failures | High | Statistical, low risk
Test case minimisation | High | Mechanical; verifiable by re-running
Documentation drafting | Moderate | Every number must be regenerated from data
Suggesting RTL fixes | Moderate | Must be re-verified from scratch
Writing the reference model | Low | It would share the same misreading as generated RTL — independence is lost
Judging whether coverage is sufficient | Low | Requires domain judgement
Deciding that an intermittent failure is benign | None | This is the judgement that must never be delegated

The independence argument constrains automation more
 than capability does. Verification works because two implementations were derived
 separately. If the same tool writes the model and the RTL from the same prompt, the
 two share every misunderstanding and the regression proves only internal consistency.
 Automation is therefore safest on the mechanical parts of the loop —
 generation, execution, comparison, minimisation, reporting — and least safe on
 the parts that define what correct means. Automate the pipeline; keep the oracle
 human or standards-derived.

장: W3. Automation: Running Verification Around the Clock
절: W3.3 Infrastructure a solo practice needs
글:
W3.3 Infrastructure a solo practice needs

[Table 186. Toolchain]
Function | Open-source option | Note
RTL simulation | Verilator (cycle-based), Icarus Verilog (event) | Verilator is fast enough for overnight regressions
Testbench | cocotb (Python) or plain SystemVerilog | cocotb lets the golden model and testbench share a language
Formal | SymbiYosys / Yosys | Sufficient for arbiters, FIFOs, protocol properties
Synthesis (estimation) | Yosys + an open PDK | Relative area/timing trends, not sign-off numbers
Lint | Verilator --lint-only , Verible | —
Coverage | Verilator coverage, simulator built-ins | —
Waveforms | GTKWave, Surfer | —
CI | Any runner | The regression must run on a clean checkout
Documentation | Generated from the same source as the RTL | See W2.3

On open-source synthesis results: report trends, not
 absolutes. Yosys with an open PDK will not reproduce a commercial tool's area or
 frequency, and quoting its numbers as a specification invites embarrassment. What it
 does reliably show is relative behaviour — that configuration B is
 40% larger than A, that removing a pipeline stage raises the critical path by 30%.
 Those comparisons are legitimate, useful during architecture, and free. State the
 tool and PDK next to every number and the report stays honest.

장: W7. Debug and Bring-Up
절: W7. Debug and Bring-Up — 들어가며
글:
W7. Debug and Bring-Up

The chapters so far describe how to avoid defects. This one describes
 what to do when one is present anyway, which is a distinct skill and the one most
 visibly separating experienced engineers from new ones.

장: W7. Debug and Bring-Up
절: W7.1 A debugging method
글:
W7.1 A debugging method

[Table 187. Systematic debugging]
Step | Action | Why this order
1 | Reproduce reliably | An unreproducible failure cannot be verified as fixed. Record the seed, the command and the environment
2 | Minimise | Shrink the stimulus until any further reduction removes the failure. Often reveals the cause without further work
3 | Bisect in time | Find the first cycle at which observed and expected diverge — not where the symptom appears
4 | Bisect in space | Move the observation point upstream until the signal is correct; the boundary contains the fault
5 | Bisect in history | If it worked before, bisect the revisions
6 | Form one hypothesis and test it | Changing several things at once destroys the evidence
7 | Explain the mechanism | A fix that works without an explanation has probably moved the bug
8 | Add the check that would have caught it | Otherwise the class of defect will recur

Step 7 is the one under schedule pressure most often
 skipped, and it is the one that causes recurrence. A change that makes a symptom
 disappear without an understood mechanism has frequently only altered timing or
 masking, leaving the defect present and less observable. The question that settles it
 is: can I re-create the failure on demand by undoing exactly this change, and does
 my explanation predict that? If not, the investigation is not finished.

장: W7. Debug and Bring-Up
절: W7.2 Observation techniques by level
글:
W7.2 Observation techniques by level

[Table 188. What can be observed where]
Level | Technique | Visibility | Cost
Simulation | Waveforms, printouts, assertions | Complete | Slow
Formal | Counterexample trace | Complete, minimal | Limited scope
Emulation | Trace buffers, triggers | Large but finite | Expensive
FPGA prototype | Integrated logic analyser | Small window | Compile time
Silicon | Scan dump, on-chip trace, debug bus | Very limited | Must be designed in beforehand
Silicon, physical | Laser probing, FIB, e-beam | Specialist | Very expensive

Observability in silicon is decided at design time, and
 it is decided by people who are not yet debugging. Once a chip exists, the only
 internal state visible is what someone chose to expose: scan chains, trace buffers,
 performance counters, a debug bus. A block that provides no status registers, no error
 counters and no way to inject or capture data is effectively opaque, and diagnosing a
 problem in it means diagnosing the whole subsystem. For an IP vendor, debug
 features are a support-cost investment: an error counter and a loopback mode cost
 a few hundred gates and can save a week of remote debugging on a customer's
 board.

장: W7. Debug and Bring-Up
절: W7.3 Bring-up
글:
W7.3 Bring-up

[Table 189. Bring-up order]
Stage | Check | If it fails
Power | Rails at expected voltages and sequence | Board or PMIC; no chip involvement
Clocks | Reference present; PLL locks | Check the reference before the PLL
Reset | Released cleanly, in the right order | Reset sequencing
Basic life | JTAG IDCODE reads back | If this fails, nothing else can be diagnosed
Debug access | Core halts and registers are readable | Debug module or its clocking
Memory | Write and read back patterns | Interface training
Boot | First instructions execute | ROM, fuses, boot mode pins
Console | UART output | From here the system can explain itself
Peripherals | One at a time | —
Performance | Against the model's prediction | Configuration or a real shortfall

The ordering is not arbitrary: each stage is the
 prerequisite for diagnosing the next. Chasing a peripheral fault before the console
 works means debugging blind. This is also why the UART and the debug module deserve
 disproportionate care in design and verification — they are the instruments with
 which everything else will be measured. A bug in the debug path costs far more than
 its size suggests, because it removes the means of finding other bugs.

장: W7. Debug and Bring-Up
절: W7.4 Classes of bug and where each is found
글:
W7.4 Classes of bug and where each is found

[Table 190. Bug taxonomy]
Class | Typical cause | Found by | Missed by
Functional | Misread specification | Model comparison | Directed tests alone
Protocol | Interface misuse | Protocol checkers, formal | Block-level tests
Corner case | Unusual combination | Constrained random, formal | Directed tests
Race / CDC | Missing synchroniser | CDC analysis, gate-level simulation | RTL simulation
Reset | Uninitialised state | X-propagation analysis | RTL with optimistic X
Timing | Path too long | STA | Any simulation
Power/IR | Local droop | Power analysis | All functional verification
Performance | Wrong architecture | System model | Block verification
Integration | Misunderstood interface | System simulation | Block verification
Specification | Requirement wrong | Review, prototype | All verification

The last row is the one no amount of verification can
 address. If the specification asks for the wrong thing, a perfectly verified
 implementation of it is still useless. This is the argument for early prototypes, for
 system models built before RTL, and for showing a specification to whoever will
 ultimately use the block. Verification answers "did we build it right"; only review
 and prototyping answer "did we build the right thing".

장: W8. Positioning, Pricing and Support
절: W8.1 Who buys IP and why
글:
W8.1 Who buys IP and why

[Table 191. Buyer motivations]
Buyer situation | What they are really buying | What convinces them
No in-house expertise | Capability | Evidence the block works; references
Expertise but no schedule | Time | Maturity; a working example design
Risk aversion | Someone to hold responsible | Verification evidence and support terms
Standard conformance needed | Conformance evidence | Test vector results, certification
Cost reduction | Lower total cost than building | A credible effort comparison
Second source | Supply security | Compatibility with the incumbent

The third row is the most common and the least
 discussed. An engineering manager who licenses a block has converted an internal
 schedule risk into a contractual relationship. That is worth paying for, and it
 explains why the verification report and the support agreement carry more weight in
 the decision than the RTL's elegance. It also explains why a first sale is so much
 harder than a second one to the same customer: the first requires establishing
 that the risk transfer is real.

[Table 192. Pricing inputs]
Factor | Direction | Note
Development cost | Floor | Must be recovered across expected licences
Customer's build-versus-buy cost | Ceiling | Their engineer-years times their rate
Value of the schedule saved | Raises the ceiling | Often larger than the build cost
Competitive alternatives | Anchors | Including open-source options
Volume | — | Royalty structures capture upside
Source access | Raises price substantially | Source enables the customer to fork
Support scope | Recurring revenue | Usually 15–20% of licence per year
Exclusivity | Large premium | Rarely wise for a small vendor

Free alternatives set the floor even when they are not
 equivalent. If an open-source block exists that does approximately the same thing,
 the value proposition must be stated against it explicitly: verification evidence,
 documentation, support, conformance testing, indemnity. “Ours is better”
 is not an argument a procurement process can act on; “here is the verification
 report and the conformance results that the open version does not have” is.
 This is another reason to invest in the evidence package rather than in additional
 features.

장: W8. Positioning, Pricing and Support
절: W8.2 Support
글:
W8.2 Support

[Table 193. Support categories and their true cost]
Category | Frequency | Cost driver | How to reduce it
Integration questions | High initially | Documentation gaps | Better user guide and example design
Configuration errors | High | Unclear parameter rules | Elaboration-time assertions
Environment differences | Moderate | Tool and version variety | State tested tool versions
Real defects | Low if verification was good | — | Verification investment
Feature requests | Moderate | — | Roadmap and paid customisation
Performance shortfalls | Moderate | Unstated assumptions | Document measurement conditions

Most support load is documentation debt, not defects.
 A useful discipline is to treat every support question as a documentation bug: when
 the answer is given, the document is updated so that the same question cannot be asked
 twice. Over a few customers this converges, and support cost per customer falls
 sharply. For a one-person practice this is the difference between a viable business
 and one that cannot take a second customer, because support is the cost that
 scales with customers rather than with product.

[Table 194. What to track from the first release]
Item | Why
Every question asked, and by whom | Reveals documentation gaps
Time spent per customer | Tells you whether the price is right
Defects found after release, and how | Shows what verification missed
Configurations actually used | Focuses future verification effort
Tool and version combinations | Compatibility matrix
Reasons for lost sales | Product direction

장: W6. Working on a Modelling Team
절: W6.1 The first week
글:
W6.1 The first week

[Table 195. Questions to ask, and what the answers reveal]
Question | What a good answer looks like | What a poor answer means
What is our golden model, and who owns it? | A named artefact with an owner | Correctness is decided ad hoc
How does the model connect to the RTL? | A defined trace interface (RVFI-like) or DPI harness | Building one is your first project
How often does the regression run, and how long does it take? | Nightly, under eight hours | Feedback is too slow to steer design
What is the specification? | A standard document or a maintained internal spec | The model is the specification — large responsibility
How is undefined behaviour handled? | Explicitly marked and masked in comparison | The model may have been tuned to match the RTL — independence lost
Who verifies the model? | Standard vectors, a second implementation, mutation testing | Nobody — this is your highest-value contribution
What escaped in the last year, and why? | A specific analysis | No escape analysis means no learning loop

The last question is the most informative one you can
 ask. An organisation that can describe a specific escape, its root cause, and the
 check that was added in response has a functioning improvement loop. One that cannot
 recall any escape either has not shipped much or does not trace failures back. The
 answer tells you more about how the team works than any description of its
 methodology.

장: W6. Working on a Modelling Team
절: W6.2 Habits that compound
글:
W6.2 Habits that compound

[Table 196. Working practices]
Practice | Effect
Annotate model code with specification section numbers | Makes the model auditable and survivable
Record the seed and the exact command with every failure | Turns an anecdote into a reproducible fact
Minimise a failing case before reporting it | Preserves the designer's trust and time
Suspect the comparison before the design | Most mismatches are scoreboard or timing issues
Write the check that would have caught it | Converts each bug into permanent coverage
Deliberately break things to test the tests | The only way to know a suite is alive
State confidence levels in reports | Distinguishes measured from assumed
Never close an unreproduced intermittent failure | Removes evidence, not the bug

“Suspect the comparison first” is worth
 making a reflex. In a mature project the ordering of likelihood is: the scoreboard
 or its timing assumptions, then the model, then the RTL. Reporting a suspected RTL bug
 that turns out to be a testbench issue twice in a row is enough to make the third
 report — the real one — go unexamined for a week. Running the model and the
 RTL separately on the same stimulus and reading both logs takes an hour and settles
 the question before anyone else is involved.

장: W6. Working on a Modelling Team
절: W6.3 Writing that gets read
글:
W6.3 Writing that gets read

[Table 197. Reporting a discrepancy]
Section | Content
One-line summary | What differs, where, under what condition
Minimal reproducer | Exact command, seed, and the shortest failing stimulus
Evidence | Model output and RTL output side by side, with the first differing cycle identified
Triage | Which of the three causes has been ruled out, and how
Specification reference | The clause or section that decides the question
Proposed disposition | Model change, RTL change, or specification clarification
Confidence | What you verified versus what you inferred

The last row is the habit that most distinguishes
 experienced engineers in written communication. A report that separates “I
 measured this” from “I believe this follows” can be acted on
 immediately; one that blends them forces every reader to re-derive the distinction.
 Over a project's life this single discipline saves more time than any tool.

장: W1. What a One-Person Design House Actually Sells
절: W1. What a One-Person Design House Actually Sells — 들어가며
글:
W1. What a One-Person Design House Actually Sells

The central proposition of this volume is that a customer does not buy
 RTL. They buy transferred risk. A competent customer could usually write the
 block themselves; what they cannot cheaply produce is the evidence that it is correct,
 the documentation that makes it integrable, and a commitment to fix it when it is not.
 Sellability is therefore a property of the evidence package, not of the code.
 Everything in this volume follows from that.

장: W1. What a One-Person Design House Actually Sells
절: W1.1 The deliverable set
글:
W1.1 The deliverable set

[Table 198. Minimum viable IP package]
# | Deliverable | Content | What its absence signals to a buyer
1 | Product brief (2–4 pp) | Function, performance, resources, interfaces, standards conformance | Not a product
2 | User guide | Parameters and legal combinations, ports with timing diagrams, register map, integration procedure, reset and clocking requirements | Integration will consume the vendor's time, not the customer's
3 | Synthesisable RTL | Parameterised, lint-clean, no tool-specific constructs | —
4 | Reference model (C/C++ or Python) | Bit-accurate; usable in the customer's own environment | The customer cannot verify integration independently
5 | Testbench and vectors | Self-checking, runnable on an open simulator if possible; standard vectors included | No acceptance test is possible
6 | Verification report | Method, coverage achieved, tests passed, known limitations | The most common omission and the most revealing
7 | Constraints (SDC) and synthesis scripts | Clock definitions, exceptions with justification, a reproduction recipe | Customer cannot reproduce the timing claim
8 | PPA report | Area, frequency, power — with process, library, corner, utilisation stated | The numbers are unusable
9 | Example design | Minimal system on a named FPGA board or simulation target | Evaluation takes weeks instead of a day
10 | Release notes and versioning | Change history, compatibility policy | No basis for a long-term commitment
11 | Licence and third-party notices | Scope of use, open-source bill of materials | Blocked in legal review
12 | IP-XACT metadata (recommended) | Machine-readable ports, parameters, register map | Manual integration

Stating known limitations increases the probability
 of a sale. This is counter-intuitive and consistently true. The reviewer is an
 engineer who knows that every block has boundaries; a report without them reads as
 either incomplete verification or concealment. A limitation stated precisely —
 "throughput is guaranteed only when the sink asserts ready at least once
 every four cycles" — is information the integrator needs, and it demonstrates
 that the vendor has characterised their own block.

장: W1. What a One-Person Design House Actually Sells
절: W1.2 Choosing the first product
글:
W1.2 Choosing the first product

[Table 199. Suitability screen for a solo developer]
Criterion | Good | Bad | Reason
Source of truth | Public standard with test vectors | Proprietary or informal | A solo developer cannot arbitrate correctness
Demand | Mandated by a standard | Nice to have | The customer must need it, not merely like it
Size | One function, 3–5 kLOC | Subsystem | Verification volume scales superlinearly
Domain | Digital, process-independent | Analogue/mixed-signal | PDK, tools and measurement equipment are out of reach
Interface | One standard bus | Custom protocol | Reuse and integration
Lifetime | Consumer/datacentre | Automotive/aerospace | 10–20 year support obligations
Novelty | Well-understood algorithm | Novel algorithm | Proving novelty costs more than implementing it

The last row is the one most often got wrong by technical
 founders. An IP business sells power, performance, area, interfaces, verification and
 support — not algorithmic novelty. A well-known algorithm has an external
 oracle, comparable prior implementations to benchmark against, and a customer who
 already knows they need it. A novel algorithm has none of these, and the first
 question every customer asks ("how do I know it works?") has no cheap answer.
 Existing implementations are an asset, not competition: they give you a baseline to
 quantify against.

장: W1. What a One-Person Design House Actually Sells
절: W1.3 Licensing and contracts
글:
W1.3 Licensing and contracts

[Table 200. Licence structures]
Model | Mechanics | Suits
Per-design licence | Fixed fee, one tape-out | Most common; predictable for both sides
Multi-use / site | Fee for unlimited designs in a period | Larger customers
Royalty per unit | Fee per shipped device | High-volume; requires audit rights
Hybrid | Reduced up-front plus royalty | Industry norm for significant IP
Source vs obfuscated | RTL source, encrypted RTL, or netlist | Source access materially increases price
Maintenance | 15–20% of licence per year | The recurring revenue that makes a solo practice viable

[Table 201. Contract clauses that matter most to a solo vendor]
Clause | Position to take | Why
Scope of use | Enumerate designs, derivatives, resale explicitly | The most frequent source of dispute
Acceptance criteria | Name the exact tests that constitute acceptance | Otherwise payment can be withheld indefinitely
Warranty period | Bounded (e.g. 12 months) defect correction | Unbounded is uninsurable
Limitation of liability | Cap at fees received | A consequential-damage claim on a tape-out would end a solo business
IP indemnity | ‘To the best of knowledge’, capped | Unlimited patent indemnity is not survivable
Third-party components | Disclose the open-source bill of materials | Legal review will ask
Escrow | Offer it | Removes the ‘what if you disappear’ objection cheaply
Support response | Define business-hours response, not resolution | Resolution cannot be promised

The indemnity clause deserves specific preparation.
 An unqualified promise that the IP infringes no patent exposes a one-person business
 to a liability unrelated to its size. The defensible position combines three things:
 a knowledge qualifier, a liability cap tied to fees received, and — crucially
 — evidence that a search was actually performed. A documented patent
 search, even a modest one, changes the character of any later dispute and is worth the
 few days it takes. Record the databases searched, the classification codes, the date,
 and the conclusions, exactly as you would record a verification campaign.

장: W4. Worked Exercises
절: W4. Worked Exercises — 들어가며
글:
W4. Worked Exercises

Each exercise below is a self-contained project that can be completed
 with open tools and produces an artefact of the kind described in W1. They are ordered
 so that each reuses the infrastructure built by the previous one.

장: W4. Worked Exercises
절: Exercise 1 — A verified GF(2 m ) arithmetic library
글:
Exercise 1 — A verified GF(2m) arithmetic library

[Table 202. Exercise 1]
Element | Specification
Objective | Parameterised finite-field arithmetic in software, with a test suite that verifies the field axioms rather than sample values
Deliverable | Library, test suite, short note on the primitive-polynomial requirement
Key decisions | Log/antilog tables versus direct reduction; whether the polynomial is a parameter or a constant
Tests that bite | Every non-zero element has an inverse and a · a −1 =1; the exponent table is a bijection onto the non-zero elements; a non-primitive polynomial is rejected rather than silently accepted; corrupting the multiply makes the axiom tests fail
Why it matters | Every code and cipher block rests on this. A silent error here is invisible everywhere above it

The non-primitive-polynomial test is the instructive
 one. An irreducible polynomial that is not primitive still defines a field, but
 α = x no longer generates the whole multiplicative group, so a
 log/antilog implementation built on it is wrong — and wrong in a way that
 ordinary arithmetic tests may not reveal, because most products are still correct.
 The defence is to verify at construction that the powers of α enumerate all
 2m−1 non-zero elements, and to refuse otherwise. A library
 that validates its own parameters is the difference between a component and a
 hazard.

장: W4. Worked Exercises
절: Exercise 2 — Reed–Solomon encoder and decoder (model)
글:
Exercise 2 — Reed–Solomon encoder and decoder (model)

[Table 203. Exercise 2]
Element | Specification
Objective | RS( n , k ) over the library from Exercise 1: systematic encoder, syndrome/BM/Chien/Forney decoder
Parameters | n , k , first consecutive root — all arguments, because the standard's values may not yet be confirmed
Tests that bite | Encoder output has zero syndrome; exactly t errors are always corrected with zero mis-corrections ; t +1 errors are never recovered , and the detected-versus-mis-corrected split is counted rather than assumed; a test with zero injected errors is explicitly flagged as meaningless; forcing the syndrome to zero makes the suite fail
Honest reporting | Do not claim that all errors beyond t are detected. Measure the mis-correction rate and state it

Parameterising the unknown constants is the
 professional move here. When the standard's field polynomial and first-root index
 have not been confirmed from the specification text, hard-coding a plausible value
 creates a model that is confidently wrong. Making them arguments, defaulting to a
 documented guess, and marking the guess as unverified in the code keeps the work
 moving without creating a false record. The tests verify properties —
 t corrected, t+1 not recovered — which hold for any legal
 parameter choice, so they remain valid when the constants are later confirmed.

장: W4. Worked Exercises
절: Exercise 3 — RTL and co-simulation
글:
Exercise 3 — RTL and co-simulation

[Table 204. Exercise 3]
Element | Specification
Objective | Synthesisable RTL for the Exercise 2 decoder's syndrome stage, co-simulated against the model
Method | DPI-C or cocotb; random vectors; seeds recorded
Tests that bite | Break the RTL deliberately and confirm the comparison fails; break the model deliberately and confirm it also fails — a harness that has only ever seen a correct design has not been tested
Extension | Sweep the parallelism parameter and plot cells versus throughput with Yosys; report the trend, not absolute area

장: W4. Worked Exercises
절: Exercise 4 — Fixed-point conversion
글:
Exercise 4 — Fixed-point conversion

[Table 205. Exercise 4]
Element | Specification
Objective | Convert a floating-point reference to fixed point and find the minimum word length meeting an accuracy target
Method | Sweep integer and fractional bits; measure the metric that matters (BER, SNR, residual) rather than raw error
Required experiments | Saturation versus wrap-around at each width; rounding mode comparison; reset-value alignment between model and RTL
Expected finding | The correct overflow policy is block-dependent: a CIC needs wrap, an LLR-based decoder needs saturation. Reproduce both results rather than accepting the claim

Check the operating point before believing any
 fixed-point result. If the floating-point baseline is already failing — BER
 near 0.5, a decoder not converging, a sampling phase misaligned — then every
 quantisation comparison made on top of it is meaningless, and the numbers will look
 plausible. The discipline is to sweep first for a healthy operating point, assert that
 the baseline metric lies in a sensible range, and only then vary word length. An
 assertion such as 0.02 < BLER < 0.6 in the test harness makes this
 automatic.

장: W4. Worked Exercises
절: Exercise 5 — A complete deliverable package
글:
Exercise 5 — A complete deliverable package

[Table 206. Exercise 5]
Element | Specification
Objective | Assemble the twelve deliverables of W1.1 for the Exercise 3 block
Hardest parts | The verification report's known limitations section; the PPA report's conditions ; the example design that runs from a clean checkout
Self-test | Hand the package to someone else and ask them to integrate it without speaking to you. Every question they ask is a documentation defect
Outcome | This is the artefact that demonstrates capability to an employer or a customer — not the RTL alone

장: W5. From Literature to a Block
절: W5.1 What published work is for
글:
W5.1 What published work is for

[Table 207. Four uses of literature in an IP practice]
Use | What to extract | Where to look | Trap
Architecture selection | Which structure, and under what conditions | JSSC, ISSCC, VLSI Symposia, DAC/ICCAD | Reported numbers come from the authors' best operating point
Algorithmic justification | Correctness conditions, convergence bounds | IEEE Transactions, arXiv | Confusing a theory paper with an implementable one
Attack awareness | Whether a countermeasure is already broken | CHES, CCS, USENIX Security, IACR ePrint | Mandatory for security IP
Standards rationale | Why a specification says what it says | Standards-body contribution archives | Contributions are proposals; not all were adopted

Standards contributions are the most under-used
 resource. The published standard states what; the working-group
 contributions that preceded it state why, with the measurements and the
 alternatives that were rejected. For IEEE 802 these are publicly archived. Reading the
 contributions for the clause you are implementing typically answers the questions the
 standard's terse language leaves open, and it does so faster than deriving the answer.
 It also reveals which parameter choices were contentious, which is exactly where
 implementations are most likely to differ.

장: W5. From Literature to a Block
절: W5.2 Reading efficiently
글:
W5.2 Reading efficiently

[Table 208. A triage procedure]
Step | Action | Decision
1 | Read the figures and tables first | What was measured?
2 | Find the experimental conditions | Is this comparable to my case?
3 | Identify the baseline | Is the comparison fair?
4 | Find the crossover | Where does the claimed advantage disappear?
5 | Only now read the method | How does it work?
6 | Read limitations and future work | What do the authors already know is wrong?

Record your confidence level with every citation.
 A note that says "full text read", "abstract only", or "search snippet only" costs
 nothing to write and prevents the most damaging failure mode in technical work:
 building a plan on a claim nobody actually verified. If a design decision rests on a
 paper you have not read in full, that fact should be visible in the document where
 the decision is recorded. Unverified citations propagate quietly and are discovered
 late.

장: W5. From Literature to a Block
절: W5.3 Turning a paper into a specification
글:
W5.3 Turning a paper into a specification

[Table 209. Translation checklist]
Question | Why it must be answered before design starts
What exactly is the input and output format? | Papers routinely omit scaling, ordering and normalisation conventions
What are the numerical requirements? | Most papers assume floating point; the word lengths are yours to determine
What is the initialisation? | Iterative methods rarely state the starting point; it affects convergence
What is the termination condition? | ‘Until converged’ is not implementable; fixed iteration counts are
Which parameters were tuned to the reported data set? | Those parameters will not transfer
What is the failure behaviour? | Papers report average performance; you must specify the worst case
Is there a patent? | Published does not mean free to use

The termination-condition question separates research
 from engineering. An algorithm described as iterating until a residual falls below
 a threshold has data-dependent latency, which a streaming datapath cannot accept. The
 engineering translation is a fixed iteration count chosen so that the worst case in
 the operating region still meets the accuracy requirement — and then the
 accuracy becomes a design-time constant rather than a run-time property. This is
 exactly what the Jacobi SVD does with a fixed sweep count, what an LDPC decoder does
 with a maximum iteration limit, and what K-best detection does relative to sphere
 decoding. Converting an adaptive algorithm into a fixed-latency one is a recurring
 and characteristic act of hardware design, and the specification must record the
 accuracy that the fixed budget guarantees.

장: W2. The Solo Process, Stage by Stage
절: W2. The Solo Process, Stage by Stage — 들어가며
글:
W2. The Solo Process, Stage by Stage

[그림] Figure 18. The development flow. What makes it a process rather than a sequence of activities is that each arrow has a written exit criterion.

[Table 210. Stage gates]
Stage | Output | Exit criterion (all must be true)
Select | Prior-art note | A named standard mandates it • prior implementations listed by name and size • the specification text is obtainable • a patent search has been performed and recorded
Specify | Specification document | Every parameter has a range and legal-combination rules • undefined behaviour is marked as such • word lengths, rounding, overflow policy and reset values are written down • reset and clocking requirements stated
Golden model | Reference model + self-tests | Standard vectors pass • deliberate mutation of the model turns the tests red • the model is deterministic • a second independent implementation or an external oracle agrees
RTL | Synthesisable RTL | Lint clean • no inferred latches • CDC static analysis clean • synthesises without warnings at the target frequency
Verify | Testbench, coverage, regression logs | Zero mismatches against the model • functional coverage goals met • no unexplained intermittent failures • mutation testing performed
Synthesise | PPA report | Timing closed at the stated corner • conditions fully documented
Document | The twelve deliverables | No section empty • the example design runs from a clean checkout
Deliver | Release | Acceptance tests defined and demonstrated

The gate that solo developers skip is the third one:
 verifying the reference model. Because the model defines correctness, there is a
 natural tendency to treat it as correct by definition. It is not, and an error there
 propagates into the RTL (which is written to match it) and into the testbench (which
 checks against it), so the regression is green and the silicon is wrong. The three
 cheap defences are standard vectors, a second independent implementation, and mutation
 testing of the model's own checks. In a one-person operation, where independence
 between designer and modeller cannot be organisational, these substitutes are the only
 thing standing in for it.

장: W2. The Solo Process, Stage by Stage
절: W2.1 Specification: the parts that are always missing
글:
W2.1 Specification: the parts that are always missing

[Table 211. Specification checklist for numerical blocks]
Item | Question to answer explicitly
Word lengths | Every signal's Q format, including internal accumulators
Rounding | Truncate, round-half-up, or round-half-even — at every reduction point
Overflow | Saturate or wrap , per signal — they are not interchangeable
Reset values | What is every state element after reset
Accumulation order | Fixed or unspecified — it matters under saturation
Latency | Exact cycle count, and whether it is data-dependent
Throughput | Initiation interval and any conditions on backpressure
Error behaviour | What happens on illegal input — and is it flagged
Undefined regions | Marked as such, with the expectation that DV masks them

A measured illustration of why reset values belong in
 the specification. In a feedback structure (DFE, IIR, accumulator), a mismatch in
 the initial register value causes the first outputs to differ, and the feedback carries
 the difference forward. In one measured comparison, 103 of 200 vectors mismatched;
 after aligning the model's and the RTL's reset value the count fell to 10, and the
 remaining ten had a separate cause. Half the apparent failures were one unwritten
 specification line. Debugging that without the specification costs days; writing
 it costs a sentence.

장: W2. The Solo Process, Stage by Stage
절: W2.2 Building the golden model
글:
W2.2 Building the golden model

[Table 212. Reference model construction rules]
Rule | Rationale
Do not use host arithmetic for fixed or floating point | Results become machine-dependent; use explicit integer or SoftFloat
Hide state access behind accessors | Allows the representation to change without touching every operation
One file (or function) per operation where possible | Extensions are additive; the Spike ISS is the model for this
Make it fast | It will run millions of times in regression
Make it deterministic | Seeded randomness only; no wall-clock, no hash order
Emit a trace | The DV team cannot compare what it cannot see
Annotate with specification section numbers | Three years later, this is the only record of why
Write tests that bite | Deliberately break the model and confirm the tests fail

A concrete pattern for “tests that bite”.
 For an error-correcting decoder, a test that injects zero errors passes even if the
 decoder does nothing at all. The useful test injects exactly t errors and
 requires full correction, injects t+1 and requires that the original is
 not recovered, and separately counts detected failures versus mis-corrections.
 Then it breaks the decoder on purpose — forcing the syndrome to zero — and
 asserts that the first test now fails. A suite that does not contain that last step
 has never been tested itself.

장: W2. The Solo Process, Stage by Stage
절: W2.3 Parameterisation
글:
W2.3 Parameterisation

[Table 213. Parameter design rules]
Rule | Mechanism | Effect
Expose orthogonal axes only | Design, not syntax | Prevents combinatorial explosion
Document legal combinations | A table in the user guide | Customer cannot guess
Enforce them at elaboration | $error inside generate ; static_assert in C++ | Illegal configurations fail to build rather than misbehave
Declare the verified set | A table of tested combinations | Honest scope statement; exhaustive testing is impossible
Safe defaults | Most conservative values | Wrong usage degrades, not breaks

Elaboration-time enforcement is the cheapest quality
 feature available. An illegal parameter combination that merely produces wrong
 behaviour will be discovered by the customer, late, and reported as a bug in your IP.
 The same combination rejected with a clear message at elaboration costs the customer
 five minutes. The difference in support burden over a product's life is large, and it
 requires perhaps twenty lines of code.

X10. Memory: The Block That Decides the Floorplan

In most IP blocks the memory is the largest single object, the slowest
 path, and the thing that cannot be changed late. It is also the part of a design that
 RTL hides most completely: a two-dimensional array in SystemVerilog becomes, in
 silicon, a compiled macro with a fixed aspect ratio, a fixed number of ports and its
 own timing model. This part computes what that substitution costs.

Worked example 1. The cost of forgetting to instantiate a RAM

Given. A 4 kB buffer, 32 768 bits. The 6T cell is 0.03 µm²; a flip-flop with its multiplexer occupies roughly 150× a bit cell once the write-enable logic is counted.

Method. Compute both areas and the array overhead. SRAM macros carry decoders, sense amplifiers and control that a small array cannot amortise; assume 40 % overhead at this size.

Bit-cell area | 983 µm²
Compiled macro with 40 % overhead | 1376 µm²
Same storage in flip-flops | 1.475×10 5  µm²
Ratio | 107×
Flip-flop clock power penalty (all bits clocked every cycle) | very large — every bit is on the clock tree

How this is got wrong. By writing an array in RTL and letting synthesis decide. Synthesis will infer flip-flops unless the coding style matches the inference template exactly — and the template differs between tools and between memory compilers. The failure is quiet: the design works, meets timing, and is a hundred times too large. Always check the synthesis report for inferred registers against your expected memory instances, and prefer explicit instantiation with a wrapper for anything above a few hundred bits.

절: X10.2 Aspect ratio, banking and the access-energy curve
글:
X10.2 Aspect ratio, banking and the access-energy curve

[Table 215. Same 32 768 bits, six aspect ratios (relative units)]
Words (depth) | Bits per word | Bit-line length | Word-line length | Relative access energy | Relative access delay
128 | 256 | 128 | 256 | 0.23 | 14.8
256 | 128 | 256 | 128 | 0.307 | 20
512 | 64 | 512 | 64 | 0.538 | 27.1
1,024 | 32 | 1,024 | 32 | 1.04 | 37
2,048 | 16 | 2,048 | 16 | 2.05 | 50.8
4,096 | 8 | 4,096 | 8 | 4.1 | 70

A tall narrow array has long bit lines, which cost energy and delay; a short wide one has long word lines and wastes energy activating bits it will not return. The optimum is in the middle and memory compilers know it, which is why a compiler refuses extreme aspect ratios and folds internally instead.

Sub-banking is why a 1 MB cache does not cost
 32× the energy of a 32 kB one. A large array is built as many small
 arrays with a hierarchical decoder, and an access activates one of them. Energy per
 access therefore grows roughly with the square root of capacity rather than
 linearly, and the same structure bounds the delay growth. This is the reason
 capacity-versus-energy intuitions borrowed from a small block do not transfer, and the
 reason a cache model that charges energy proportional to size will mispredict a
 memory-bound design badly. When you need real numbers, use a memory compiler's
 datasheet or a model such as CACTI — and state which, because the two
 disagree.

Worked example 2. A register file's port count is a quadratic cost

Given. A 32-entry × 64-bit register file for a 2-wide machine: 4 read ports and 2 write ports.

Method. Model the cell area as growing with the square of the total port count, which is the standard first-order model because each port adds a bit line and a word line to every cell.

Ports | 6

Bits | 2,048

How this is got wrong. By treating issue width as a free architectural parameter. Doubling it quadruples the register-file area and lengthens its access, which is one of the two reasons superscalar width stopped growing (the other is the scheduler's own quadratic wake-up logic). The architectural responses are all about avoiding the quadratic: clustering the register file and accepting a cross-cluster penalty, banking it by register number, or moving to a structure where most operands never enter the file at all. A cost model that is quadratic in a parameter is a signal to change the structure, not to tune the parameter.

절: X10.4 ECC: the arithmetic of protecting a memory
글:
X10.4 ECC: the arithmetic of protecting a memory

Why SECDED needs exactly the bits it needs

 | Step | Justification
1 | To correct a single error among k data bits, the syndrome must name one of k + r positions or say ‘no error’. | Every correctable case needs its own syndrome value.
2 | So 2 r ≥ k + r + 1. | The Hamming bound for single-error correction.
3 | Detecting double errors as well costs one more bit: an overall parity. | With it, a double error gives a non-zero syndrome and even overall parity, which single errors never do.
4 | SECDED overhead is r +1 bits for k data bits. | And because r grows logarithmically, wide words are far cheaper to protect than narrow ones — the single most useful consequence.

[Table 217. SECDED overhead against word width]
Data bits k | Hamming bits r | SECDED bits | Overhead (%) | Total stored bits
8 | 4 | 5 | 62.5 | 13
16 | 5 | 6 | 37.5 | 22
32 | 6 | 7 | 21.9 | 39
64 | 7 | 8 | 12.5 | 72
128 | 8 | 9 | 7.03 | 137
256 | 9 | 10 | 3.91 | 266
512 | 10 | 11 | 2.15 | 523

Protecting a 64-bit word costs 12.5 %; protecting a 512-bit line costs 2 %. This is why ECC is applied to cache lines and DRAM bursts rather than to bytes, and why a design that must protect narrow fields should consider grouping them first.

ECC changes the timing path and the failure modes,
 not only the area. The syndrome must be computed and the correction applied before
 the data is used, which inserts an XOR tree — typically 3 to 5 gate levels for a
 64-bit word — into the read path. At high frequency this forces the correction
 into a later pipeline stage, which means the consumer must be able to tolerate a
 late correction or be stalled, and that is an architectural decision, not an
 implementation detail. There is a second trap: a memory with ECC that is never
 scrubbed accumulates single-bit errors until two coincide in one word, at which point
 a correctable fault population becomes an uncorrectable event. Scrubbing is part of
 the ECC design, not an optional extra, and its period follows from the soft-error
 rate and the word count.

[Table 218. Soft-error arithmetic at 1000 FIT/Mbit (one failure per 10 9 device-hours per Mbit)]
Memory (Mbit) | Errors per hour | MTBF (years, one device) | Errors per device-year | Errors per year across a million units
1 | 1.00×10 -6 | 114 | 0.00877 | 8766
4 | 4.00×10 -6 | 28.5 | 0.0351 | 35064
16 | 1.60×10 -5 | 7.13 | 0.14 | 1.40×10 5
64 | 6.40×10 -5 | 1.78 | 0.561 | 5.61×10 5
256 | 2.56×10 -4 | 0.446 | 2.24 | 2.24×10 6

The last column is the one a product manager needs. A part that sees one upset per device-century produces thousands of field events per year across a large deployment, which is why ECC appears in consumer parts and not only in servers. The FIT figure itself depends on altitude, process and cell design and must come from the foundry.

Problem. Your block has a 2 kB configuration RAM written once at boot and read every cycle thereafter. Does it need ECC, and of what kind?
Solution. It needs protection more than a data buffer does, for a reason that has nothing to do with its size: a corrupted configuration bit is permanent and systematic, where a corrupted data word is transient. An upset in a filter coefficient degrades every subsequent output, silently, until the next reboot, and there is no downstream check that will catch it. The economical answer is usually parity plus a reload path rather than full SECDED: since the contents are known and re-writable, detection is enough — flag the error, interrupt, and have software rewrite the block. That costs one bit per word instead of eight and needs no correction logic in the read path, so it does not disturb the timing at all. Choose detection over correction whenever a recovery path exists; the recovery path is usually cheaper than the correction hardware, and it also covers failures the ECC cannot, such as a corrupted address.

Problem. Why does a FIFO built from a dual-port SRAM need its pointers in flip-flops rather than in the same memory?
Solution. Because the pointers must be readable in the same cycle they are compared, and a synchronous SRAM read has a cycle of latency. The full and empty conditions gate the write and read enables of the current cycle, so a pointer that arrives a cycle late produces a FIFO that overflows by one entry under back-to-back traffic — a bug that appears only at full rate, which is to say only in the system and never in the unit test that writes one word at a time. The general form of this trap is worth internalising: any state that participates in this cycle's flow-control decision cannot live behind a synchronous read port. It is the same reason a cache tag array is read a cycle ahead of the data array, and the reason credit counters in an interconnect are registers however large the credit table becomes.

X11. Interconnect: Arbitration, Flow Control and Deadlock

An IP block that talks to anything talks through an interconnect, and
 the interconnect's properties leak into the block's specification whether or not the
 specification mentions them. The three that leak hardest are how bandwidth is shared,
 how back-pressure propagates, and whether the system can lock up. All three are
 computable and the third is provable.

장: X11. Interconnect: Arbitration, Flow Control and Deadlock
절: X11.1 Credit-based flow control: sizing the buffer
글:
X11.1 Credit-based flow control: sizing the buffer

Why the buffer must cover the round trip

 | Step | Justification
1 | The sender may transmit only while it holds credits; each transmission consumes one. | Definition of credit-based flow control.
2 | A credit is returned when the receiver frees a buffer entry; the return takes t ret to arrive. | Physical delay: the return path is wires and pipeline stages like any other.
3 | For the sender never to stall while the receiver is draining, credits must outlast the round trip. | Otherwise there is an interval in which the sender has no credit and the receiver has space.
4 | N buf ≥ B · RTT , where B is the peak rate and RTT is forward latency plus return latency. | The bandwidth–delay product. It is the same formula as a TCP window and for exactly the same reason.
5 | Any shortfall shows up as a throughput loss of N buf /( B ·RTT), not as a functional failure. | Which is why an undersized buffer is found in performance bring-up rather than in verification — late, and by the customer.

[Table 219. Credit buffer needed against pipeline depth, one flit per cycle]
Forward stages | Return stages | Round trip (cycles) | Minimum credits | Buffer bytes at 32 B/flit | Throughput if only one credit is provided
1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 8 | 0.5
2 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 16 | 0.25
4 | 4 | 8 | 8 | 32 | 0.125
8 | 8 | 16 | 16 | 64 | 0.0625
16 | 16 | 32 | 32 | 128 | 0.0312

The last column is what an under-provisioned link actually delivers: one flit per round trip. A four-deep pipeline with one credit runs at an eighth of the wire's rate, and nothing in the design is broken.

Worked example 3. A block on a pipelined AXI interconnect

Given. A DMA engine issues read bursts across an interconnect with 6 cycles of forward latency and 6 of response, at 500 MHz, 128-bit data, and must sustain 6 GB/s.

Method. Convert the required bandwidth into outstanding transactions via the bandwidth–delay product, then check it against the interface's ID width, which is what actually limits outstanding transactions on AXI.

Bytes per beat | 16
Beats per second required | 3.750×10 8
Cycles per second | 5.000×10 8
Beats per cycle required | 0.75
Round-trip latency | 12 cycles
Outstanding beats needed | 9
If bursts are 16 beats: outstanding bursts needed | 1
Read data buffer required | 144 B

How this is got wrong. By sizing the buffer for the burst and not for the round trip. A common specification says ‘one burst of read data’, which permits exactly one outstanding burst and throttles the engine to burst-length divided by round-trip — here about a quarter of the wire rate. The second frequent error is to size for the average latency: the interconnect's latency has a tail whenever another master is active, and a buffer sized for the mean stalls whenever the tail occurs. Size for the latency at the load you will actually run at, and state that load in the datasheet, because a customer whose system is busier than your bench will not reach your quoted bandwidth.

Policy | M0 (busiest) | M1 | M2 | M3 (quietest)

[Table 221. Arbitration policies and what each guarantees]
Policy | Guarantees | Cost | Fails at
Fixed priority | Lowest latency for the top requester | A priority encoder — cheapest | Starvation : no bound for the bottom requester
Round robin | Bounded wait of n −1 grants | A rotating pointer | Does not respect differing bandwidth needs
Weighted round robin | Bandwidth in proportion to weights | Per-requester counters | Latency for a low-weight but urgent requester
Deficit round robin | Bandwidth proportion with variable-size requests | A deficit counter per requester | — this is the standard answer for packets

Lottery / randomised | Proportional in expectation | An LFSR | No bound , only an expectation — unacceptable for real-time

Quality of service is not a policy, it is two
 different requirements that must be separated before a policy can be chosen. A
 display controller needs guaranteed bandwidth and tolerates latency, because it
 has a line buffer; a CPU fetching a cache miss needs low latency and consumes
 little bandwidth. One arbiter cannot serve both well with a single knob, which is why
 real interconnects separate them: a bandwidth regulator (a token bucket or a deficit
 counter) enforces the first, and a priority class enforces the second, with the
 regulator demoting a requester that exceeds its allocation so that its priority cannot
 starve anyone. When writing an IP block's requirements, state which of the two you
 need; ‘high performance’ is not an interconnect requirement and cannot
 be designed against.

장: X11. Interconnect: Arbitration, Flow Control and Deadlock
절: X11.3 Deadlock: a property of the dependency graph
글:
X11.3 Deadlock: a property of the dependency graph

The four conditions, and which one hardware removes

 | Step | Justification
1 | Mutual exclusion: a resource is held by one holder at a time. | True of every buffer; not removable.
2 | Hold and wait: a holder may request another resource while holding one. | True of any pipelined request; removing it means allocating everything at once, which wastes buffers.
3 | No pre-emption: a buffer cannot be taken back. | Removable — by dropping and retrying , which is what a network does and what an on-chip fabric usually cannot afford.
4 | Circular wait : the wait-for graph contains a cycle. | This is the one hardware removes. Break every cycle and deadlock is impossible regardless of the other three.
5 | Virtual channels break cycles by splitting one physical buffer into several logically independent ones with an ordering between them. | A message may only move from a lower-numbered channel to a higher one, so the dependency graph becomes acyclic by construction.
6 | Dimension-ordered routing breaks cycles in a mesh by forbidding a turn. | X then Y: the turns that would close a cycle are simply not permitted. Cheap, and it costs path diversity , which costs throughput under adversarial traffic.

The most common on-chip deadlock has nothing to do
 with routing. It is a read response that cannot make progress because the response
 buffer is full of responses waiting behind a write that cannot complete because the
 write channel is blocked by a request from the same master. Protocol specifications
 address this with ordering rules — AXI's requirement that read and write
 channels be independent, and that a slave must not make a read response depend on a
 future write — and those rules are routinely broken by IP blocks that share
 one internal queue between the two channels. If your block merges AXI's read and
 write paths into a single ordered structure anywhere, you have created this deadlock,
 and it will appear in a customer's system and not in yours.

Problem. A bridge accepts an AXI write and must issue a read to fetch the rest of a partially written cache line, then complete the write. Why is this a deadlock hazard, and what are the fixes?
Solution. It creates a dependency from the write channel to the read channel. If the read travels through the same interconnect and that interconnect is congested with writes — including this one, which is holding a slot — the read cannot be issued and the write cannot retire. The wait-for graph has a cycle. Three fixes, in increasing order of cost and decreasing order of fragility. Reserve resources before accepting: do not accept the write until a read slot and a line buffer are already allocated, so the bridge never holds and waits. Use a separate virtual or physical channel for the fetch, so the read's path cannot be blocked by writes. Buffer the entire write and acknowledge it immediately, converting the dependency into a local one — which costs a full line of storage per outstanding write and changes the coherence behaviour. Whichever is chosen, the argument must be written down as an acyclicity claim about the dependency graph, because it is not something a simulation will refute reliably: deadlocks appear only under specific congestion, and the bench that would produce it is rarely the bench that is written.

Worked example 4. Bisection bandwidth decides, not link count

Given. A 16-node system, 128-bit links at 1 GHz. Compare a ring, a 4×4 mesh and a full crossbar under uniform random traffic, where on average half the traffic crosses the bisection.

Method. Compute the bisection bandwidth — the bandwidth across the worst cut that divides the network in half — and compare with the offered load. Bisection, not aggregate link bandwidth, is what limits uniform traffic.

Per-link bandwidth | 16 GB/s

The ring in this example has 16 links and 256 GB/s of aggregate link bandwidth, which sounds ample and is irrelevant: uniform traffic is limited by the two links at the cut. If the real traffic is nearest-neighbour, the ring's bisection never binds and it is the right answer; if it is all-to-all, only the bisection matters. X12. Data Converters and PLLs, Worked

Very few IP blocks are purely digital at their boundary. A SerDes has
 an analogue front end; a sensor interface has a converter; every synchronous block has
 a clock that came from a PLL. A digital designer does not have to design these, but
 does have to budget for them, and budgeting requires the same arithmetic the
 analogue designer uses. This part supplies it.

SNR, ENOB and the 6.02N+1.76 formula

 | Step | Justification
1 | Quantisation error is bounded by ±Δ/2 with variance Δ²/12, if it is uniform. | Part X1 established this and also measured where it fails.
2 | A full-scale sine of peak A = 2 N −1 Δ has power A ²/2. | RMS of a sinusoid.
3 | SNR = 10log 10 ( A ²/2 ÷ Δ²/12) = 6.02 N + 1.76 dB . | Substitute and simplify. The 1.76 is 10log 10 (1.5), the sine's crest-factor advantage over a uniform signal.
4 | Real converters fall short; the shortfall is expressed as ENOB = (SNDR − 1.76)/6.02 . | Invert the formula using the measured signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio. ENOB is a measurement, N is a pin count , and quoting the second as if it were the first is the standard datasheet deception.
5 | Aperture jitter adds a noise term SNR jitter = −20log 10 (2π f in σ t ). | The sampled error is the signal's slew times the timing error; slew is proportional to input frequency. This term does not depend on N at all and eventually dominates every high-speed converter.

Worked example 5. Specifying the clock for an ADC, backwards from the requirement

Given. A receiver needs 11 effective bits on a 500 MHz input. The converter's own thermal and distortion contribution is 13 ENOB.

Method. Convert the requirement to an SNR, subtract the converter's own contribution in the power domain to find the jitter budget, then invert the jitter formula.

Required SNDR | 67.98 dB
Converter's own SNR | 80.02 dB
Permitted jitter-noise SNR | 68.26 dB
Permitted RMS aperture jitter | 123 fs
Is that achievable with an on-chip PLL? | demanding — it is at the edge of a good integrated LC PLL

How this is got wrong. By subtracting decibels instead of powers. Noise contributions add in power, so budgets must be combined as 10−SNR/10 terms and only then converted back. Subtracting 11 from 13 in dB gives a meaningless number. The second error, subtler, is to forget that the clock buffer between the PLL and the sampler adds its own jitter, often more than the PLL, so a budget that spends the whole allowance on the PLL has already failed.

[Table 224. Converter architectures and where each lives]
Architecture | Resolution | Speed | Latency | Cost driver
Flash | 4–6 bits | Highest | 1 cycle | 2 N comparators — area doubles per bit
Pipelined | 10–14 bits | High | N /2 cycles | Op-amps; inter-stage gain accuracy
SAR | 8–16 bits | Moderate | N cycles | Capacitor matching; scales beautifully with process

Time interleaving is where the digital team earns its
 place in an analogue block. Running M converters in round robin multiplies

 spurs at multiples of fs/M; gain, which appears as spurs
 around the signal; and timing skew, which appears as signal-dependent spurs that grow

 three are corrected by digital background calibration that estimates the
 mismatch from the data and applies a correction. That estimator is a piece of DSP with
 a convergence time, a lock detector and a failure mode, and it is specified,
 modelled and verified by the digital side. A SerDes receiver's ADC is
 time-interleaved 32 or 64 ways, and its calibration loops are a substantial part of
 the digital block's area.

절: X12.2 Phase-locked loops: the transfer functions that matter
글:
X12.2 Phase-locked loops: the transfer functions that matter

Why a PLL is a lowpass for reference noise and a highpass for VCO noise

 | Step | Justification
1 | Open loop: G ( s ) = K pd F ( s ) K vco / s , divided by N . | Phase detector gain, loop filter, VCO as a phase integrator, feedback divider.
2 | Reference to output: N G /(1+ G ). | Standard feedback algebra. At low frequency G  ≫ 1 so this is N ; at high frequency it rolls off. Lowpass.
3 | VCO noise to output: 1/(1+ G ). | The VCO's noise enters after the phase detector. At low frequency the loop suppresses it; above the bandwidth it passes. Highpass.
4 | So the loop bandwidth is a crossover, not a quality setting. | Wide bandwidth tracks the reference and suppresses VCO noise; narrow bandwidth rejects reference noise and lets the VCO run free. The optimum is where the two noise densities cross, and that point is measured , not chosen by taste.
5 | Total output jitter is the integral of the combined phase-noise spectrum over the band of interest. | Which is why a jitter specification without an integration band is incomplete — the same part can be quoted at 200 fs or 2 ps depending on limits.

A PLL specification needs five numbers and is usually
 given two. Output frequency and jitter are not enough. The five are: output
 frequency range; integrated jitter with its integration band; spurious tone
 level, since a single reference spur can violate a mask that broadband jitter passes;
 lock time, which sets how long a power-gated block takes to become usable; and the
 input reference's own phase noise, since the PLL multiplies it by
 20log10N. A block that is specified without the fifth will work on
 the vendor's evaluation board with a laboratory clock source and fail in the
 customer's system with a crystal oscillator.

[Table 226. Reference phase noise is multiplied by the divide ratio]
Divide ratio N | 20log 10 N (dB) | Output noise from a −100 dBc/Hz reference | Output noise from a −130 dBc/Hz reference
2 | 6.021 | -93.98 | -124
4 | 12.04 | -87.96 | -118

In-band only — above the loop bandwidth the reference is filtered. This is the reason a high-speed SerDes wants a low reference multiplication, and the reason a 100 MHz reference often beats a 25 MHz one for the same output frequency.

Problem. A clock-and-data-recovery loop and a frequency-synthesis PLL are both PLLs. Why is the CDR's bandwidth chosen by a standard rather than by the designer?
Solution. Because in a CDR the loop bandwidth determines jitter tolerance, which is an interoperability property rather than a performance one. Jitter below the loop bandwidth is tracked by the receiver and causes no error; jitter above it is not tracked and eats the eye directly. So the receiver's bandwidth and the transmitter's permitted jitter spectrum are two halves of one specification: if each vendor chose its own bandwidth, a compliant transmitter and a compliant receiver could still fail together. Standards therefore specify a jitter tolerance mask — how much sinusoidal jitter the receiver must survive at each frequency — which constrains the loop bandwidth from below, and a jitter transfer limit, which constrains it from above so that jitter is not amplified around the loop's peaking and accumulated through a chain of repeaters. The designer's freedom is what remains between the two masks, and in modern standards that gap is narrow.

Problem. Why does a fractional-N synthesiser need a delta-sigma modulator, and what does it cost?
Solution. A divider divides by an integer. To reach a fractional average the divide ratio must be switched between neighbouring integers, and the pattern of switching determines where the resulting phase error lands in frequency. A simple periodic pattern puts it at a low frequency inside the loop bandwidth, where it appears as a fractional spur — a discrete tone that violates masks. A delta-sigma modulator chooses the pattern so that the quantisation error is shaped to high frequency, where the loop filters it. The costs are real: the shaped noise is larger in total than the unshaped noise, so the loop bandwidth must be kept below the point where the shaping rises; a higher-order modulator shapes harder but can produce idle tones if its input sits near a simple fraction, which is why implementations dither the input; and the divider must now handle a range of ratios, which complicates its design. This is a clean example of a digital block bought to relax an analogue constraint, which is the dominant trend in mixed-signal design and the reason the boundary keeps moving toward the digital side.

Neural-network accelerators are the largest category of new IP by
 value, and they are also the category where the gap between a quoted peak number and
 delivered performance is widest. The arithmetic that closes that gap is the roofline
 model and its refinements, and it is worth doing carefully because it decides the
 architecture before a line of RTL is written.

X13.3 Quantisation: where the bits actually go

[Table 229. Measured SQNR of a 512×512 int matrix product, per-tensor vs. per-channel weight scaling]
Bits | Per-tensor SQNR (dB) | Per-channel SQNR (dB) | Gain (dB) | Weight storage (kB)

Gaussian weights and post-ReLU activations, seed 21. Per-channel scaling is nearly free in hardware — one extra multiply per output channel, not per MAC — and buys several dB, which at low bit widths is the difference between a usable and an unusable network.

The outlier problem, and why it changed transformer
 accelerators. The table above uses Gaussian weights, for which max-based scaling
 is reasonable. Real transformer activations are not Gaussian: a few channels carry
 values tens of times larger than the rest, and a per-tensor scale chosen to contain
 them leaves the remaining channels occupying two or three bits. The measured
 consequence is that naive int8 quantisation of a large language model loses far more
 accuracy than the same procedure applied to a convolutional network, and the remedies
 — per-channel and per-group scales, keeping outlier channels in higher
 precision, or migrating the scale between activations and weights — all cost
 hardware that a convolution-era accelerator does not have. An accelerator's
 quantisation support is a workload-specific design decision, not a generic
 feature.

Problem. Why does int8 inference usually retain accuracy while int8 training does not?
Solution. Because the two use the numbers differently. Inference computes a forward pass whose outputs pass through nonlinearities that are insensitive to small perturbations, and errors do not accumulate across iterations — each inference is independent. Training computes gradients, which are (a) small differences of large numbers, so relative precision matters far more, (b) accumulated over many steps, so bias accumulates exactly as Part X1's truncating accumulator did, and (c) spread over an enormous dynamic range, because gradients of different layers differ by orders of magnitude. The practical resolution is the asymmetric one: low-precision multiplies with higher-precision accumulation and master weights, plus loss scaling to move small gradients out of the denormal region. bfloat16 exists for exactly the (c) reason — it sacrifices mantissa, which inference cares about, to keep exponent range, which training cares about.

Problem. A customer wants your accelerator to be ‘future proof’. What can you honestly offer?
Solution. Not architectural coverage of models that do not exist. What you can offer is specific and worth more than a vague claim: a programmable dataflow rather than a fixed one, so a new layer shape maps at some efficiency rather than not at all; a well-specified fallback path to a host or a DSP for operators the array cannot do, with measured numbers for that path so the customer can compute the Amdahl penalty themselves; a compiler that is open enough to extend, since in practice the compiler ages faster than the silicon; and measured utilisation on a set of named, versioned models, so the customer can extrapolate from evidence rather than from adjectives. Offering the measurement methodology is itself a differentiator: most datasheets in this field quote one peak number and one optimistic model, and a buyer who has been burned once recognises the difference immediately.

X14. Physical Design as the RTL Designer Sees It

A soft-IP vendor does not run place-and-route on the customer's chip,
 but the vendor's RTL determines whether that run succeeds. This part covers the
 physical facts that propagate back into RTL decisions, with the arithmetic that makes

Why a long wire gets relatively slower every generation

 | Step | Justification
1 | A wire's distributed RC delay is 0.38 rcL 2 for resistance r and capacitance c per unit length. | Elmore delay of a distributed line. Quadratic in length — the single most important fact in this chapter.
2 | Scaling reduces wire cross-section, so r rises roughly as 1/ S 2 while c stays roughly constant. | Thinner and narrower conductor, same dielectric spacing ratio.
3 | A wire of fixed physical length therefore gets slower as the process shrinks. | While gates get faster. The ratio moves against the wire every generation.
4 | Buffering breaks the quadratic: k equal segments give k ·( L / k ) 2 = L 2 / k plus k buffer delays. | Optimise over k and the delay becomes linear in L .
5 | So a long wire costs area and power, and it costs a fixed delay per millimetre that no amount of cleverness removes. | Which makes distance an architectural quantity. A design whose blocks must exchange data every cycle across a chip is not implementable at high frequency, however good the RTL.

At 3 GHz a signal crosses a fraction of a large die per cycle, so a chip-spanning bus is physically impossible at that frequency and the architecture must be pipelined, hierarchical, or both. This is the physical origin of networks-on-chip: not a preference for packets, but the observation that a global broadcast wire no longer exists. For an IP vendor the practical consequence is to keep the block's internal critical paths local and to register every boundary signal, so the customer's floorplanner has somewhere to put the pipeline stages the distance demands.

Synthesis can delete your synchroniser. The two
 flops of a synchroniser are functionally redundant to a tool that believes the input
 is a normal signal: it may merge them, retime through them, or move one across a
 boundary, any of which destroys the resolution time the MTBF calculation of
 Part X3 depends on. The defences are to mark the flops with a synthesis attribute
 that forbids merging and retiming, to place them in a module the tool is told not to
 ungroup, and to check the gate-level netlist that they are still there —
 a check that can be automated and belongs in the sign-off list. A design that relies on
 the tool's good behaviour here has an MTBF nobody has verified.

X14.3 Utilisation, congestion and the numbers that predict trouble

[Table 232. Relative routing difficulty against placement utilisation (heuristic model)]
Utilisation (%) | Relative difficulty | vs. 50 % | Practical verdict
50 | 2.828 | 1 | comfortable

The model is a heuristic, not a PDK number: difficulty grows as (1−u)−1.5. Its only job is to make the shape visible — the cost is mild to 70 % and then rises very fast, which is why floorplans target 65–75 % and why ‘we will just raise utilisation’ is rarely the answer to an area problem.

Congestion is caused by pin density and connectivity,
 not by cell area, and this distinction decides what an RTL designer can do about
 it. A block that is 60 % utilised can be unroutable if its cells are small
 and richly connected — a crossbar, a large multiplexer tree, a register file
 read network — because the routing demand per unit area is set by nets crossing
 a boundary, not by transistors under it. The RTL-level remedies are therefore about
 connectivity: reduce the radix of a switch and add a stage; replace a
 fully-connected structure with a hierarchical one; move a wide mux into a memory where
 the decoder is dense and local; and avoid the one-hot broadcast structures that
 look cheap in gate count and are expensive in tracks. An area report will not show
 any of this; a congestion map will.

Problem. Your block meets timing standalone at 800 MHz but the customer reports it fails at 600 MHz in their chip. Name four causes, in the order you would check them.
Solution. 1. Different constraints. Your standalone run may have used ideal clocks, no input/output delay, or a different corner set. Ask for their SDC and compare it with yours line by line; this is the cause more often than the other three together. 2. Boundary paths. Standalone runs frequently constrain inputs and outputs generously; in the chip your block's inputs arrive late and its outputs must arrive early. This is why registering every boundary is worth the latency — it makes your timing independent of their floorplan. 3. Physical context. In their chip your block may be stretched around a macro, sit far from its clock source, or share power rails with a noisy neighbour, all of which add delay your standalone run did not model. 4. A different library or corner. Same process, different vendor library or different Vt mix, and your critical path is no longer their critical path. The general lesson for a vendor is to ship the constraints and the conditions with the frequency claim; a frequency without them is not a specification, and this exact conversation is why.

Problem. Why do IP vendors quote area in gate equivalents rather than square micrometres?
Solution. Because square micrometres are meaningless without naming the process, the library and the utilisation, and a vendor who names all three has effectively told a competitor which foundry and library they used. A gate equivalent — conventionally the area of a two-input NAND in the same library — is a ratio, so it survives the translation between processes approximately, and it lets a customer scale to their own library by multiplying by their NAND area. The approximation is worse than it looks, because the ratio of flop area to NAND area and of SRAM bit-cell area to NAND area both vary between libraries, so a flop-heavy block converts less accurately than a logic-heavy one. The honest datasheet therefore gives gate equivalents, flop count and memory bits separately, which lets the customer do the conversion properly, and costs the vendor nothing.

X15. Hardware Security, Worked

Security is where a plausible-looking design is most often wrong,
 because the adversary is not a random input but a person who reads your datasheet.
 This part covers the parts of hardware security that are arithmetic — how many
 traces an attack needs, how much entropy a source really has, how long a key survives
 — because those are the parts a designer can actually bound.

절: X15.1 Side channels: the attack is a statistics problem

X15.1 Side channels: the attack is a statistics problem

Why correlation power analysis works, and how many traces it needs

 | Step | Justification
1 | Dynamic power depends on the number of bits that switch, which depends on the data being processed. | Part X7's α CV 2 f : α is data dependent.
2 | Choose an intermediate value v = f (plaintext, key guess) that the device computes, e.g. an AES S-box output. | It must depend on a small part of the key so the guesses can be enumerated.
