4 | Correlate the predicted leakage with the measured power across many traces, for every key guess. | The correct guess correlates; the others do not, because their predicted values are effectively random with respect to the device's actual computation.
5 | The number of traces needed is n ≈ 3 + 8( Z α /ln((1+ρ)/(1−ρ))) 2 . | Fisher's z-transform of the correlation coefficient. Quadratic in 1/ρ , which is why reducing the signal by a factor of ten costs the attacker a factor of a hundred in traces.

A masked implementation that is not verified at the
 gate level is usually not masked. Masking is a property of the computation,
 and synthesis optimises computations. If the tool finds that two shares are combined
 in a common subexpression — which is exactly the kind of optimisation it is good
 at — the shares meet in one gate and the first-order leakage returns, while the
 RTL still looks masked. There is a second, subtler failure: even without optimisation,
 a glitch in combinational logic can momentarily present a function of both

 construction rather than merely share-correct. The verification here is formal
 leakage analysis on the netlist, not inspection of the source.

X15.2 Entropy: counting what a random number generator really has

Worked example 8. A ring-oscillator TRNG, entropy per bit

Given. Two free-running ring oscillators, one sampled by the other. Jitter accumulates over the sampling interval; the accumulated timing uncertainty is σ = 12 ps and the sampled oscillator's period is T = 400 ps.

Method. The min-entropy of the sampled bit depends on how much of a period the uncertainty spans. A standard stochastic-model estimate is H ≈ 1 − (4/π2)e−4π2σ2/T2, which goes to 1 when the jitter covers a period and to 0 when it is small.

σ/ T | 0.03
Exponent argument | 0.03553
Estimated entropy per raw bit | 0.6089
Raw bits needed per full-entropy bit | 1.642
If σ falls to 3 ps (a quieter supply): entropy | 0.5956
Raw bits per full-entropy bit then | 1.679

How this is got wrong. By testing the output of the conditioner instead of the source. A cryptographic hash applied to a biased source produces output that passes every statistical test — that is what a hash does — while containing only as much entropy as went in. The test must be applied to the raw source, with an online health test that keeps checking it in the field, because the quantity being relied on (σ) depends on supply noise, temperature and ageing, and an attacker with access to the supply can reduce it deliberately. The second row from the bottom is that attack expressed as arithmetic.

Why the standards insist on min-entropy rather than
 Shannon entropy. Shannon entropy is an average; an adversary guesses the most
 likely value. A source that emits 0 with probability 0.9 has Shannon entropy 0.47 bits
 and min-entropy −log2(0.9) = 0.15 bits, and the second
 number is the one that bounds an attacker's success. For a key of k bits
 assembled from such a source, the attacker's work is 2 raised to the total
 min-entropy, not the total Shannon entropy — a factor of 20.32
 per bit, which over 256 bits is a factor of 1024. Using the wrong
 entropy measure is not conservative rounding, it is a wrong security
 claim.

장: X15. Hardware Security, Worked
절: X15.3 Fault attacks and the cost of detection
글:
X15.3 Fault attacks and the cost of detection

[Table 235. Fault-attack countermeasures]
Countermeasure | Mechanism | Catches | Overhead
None | — | 0 % | 0 %
Parity on registers | 1 bit per word | single-bit faults | 3–12 %
Duplication | Run twice, compare | any single fault | >100 %
Time redundancy | Run twice in sequence | transient faults only | 0 % area, 100 % time
Inverse check | Decrypt the ciphertext and compare | any fault in the datapath | ~100 % time
Infective computation | Spread the fault so the output is useless | prevents exploitation rather than detecting | moderate

The classic differential fault attack on RSA-CRT recovers the private key from one faulty signature, which is why the inverse check — verify the signature before releasing it — is standard there despite its cost. When one fault is enough, probabilistic countermeasures are not.

Problem. A customer asks for a ‘secure’ AES block. What do you ask them before quoting?
Solution. Four questions, because ‘secure’ alone does not specify anything. What is the attacker's physical access? A block in a server that an attacker cannot touch needs no side-channel countermeasures; a smart card that the attacker owns needs every one of them, and the area difference is a factor of three. How many operations per key? This bounds the traces available and therefore the required leakage reduction directly, via the table in X15.1. What certification is required? Common Criteria or FIPS levels prescribe specific countermeasures and specific evidence, and the evidence costs more than the design. What is the throughput and latency requirement? Masking costs randomness per cycle, and a design that must run at line rate may not be able to afford the randomness generation. A quote given without these answers will be wrong by a large factor in one direction or the other, and a vendor who asks them is demonstrating exactly the competence being bought.

Problem. Why is a hardware root of trust harder than storing a key in fuses?
Solution. Because the key is the easy part. A root of trust must establish, at every boot, that the first code to run is the code the owner intended — which requires immutable boot code, a verified signature chain, and protection of the verification itself from the fault and side-channel attacks above. It must survive the states nobody designs for: reset during an update, a power glitch mid-verification, a debug interface left enabled. It needs a way to revoke a compromised key and to roll forward a version counter that cannot be rolled back, which means monotonic storage, which means more fuses and a policy for them. And it must do all this while remaining debuggable in the field by the legitimate owner, which is the requirement that quietly reopens every door the rest closed. The key in fuses is perhaps five per cent of the work; the rest is the state machine around it, and that state machine is where the published attacks land.

X16. Reliability, Yield and Functional Safety, Worked

Three quantities decide whether a chip can be sold into an
 automotive, industrial or medical market, and all three are arithmetic: the fraction
 of dies that work, the rate at which working dies stop working, and the fraction of
 dangerous failures that are detected. A design house that can compute them can quote
 for markets that pay considerably more than consumer.

절: X16.1 Yield: the model and its parameter

X16.1 Yield: the model and its parameter

From defect density to die yield

 | Step | Justification
1 | Defects fall on the wafer at an average density D 0 per unit area. | Empirical; the foundry supplies it and it falls over a process's life.
2 | If defects were Poisson and independent, yield would be e − AD 0 . | Probability of zero defects in area A .
3 | They are not independent — defects cluster — so Poisson is pessimistic for large dies. | Clustering means some wafers are bad and others clean, which raises the average yield of the clean ones.
4 | The negative-binomial (Murphy/Seeds) model adds a clustering parameter α: Y = (1 + AD 0 /α) −α . | α ≈ 2–5 in practice; α → ∞ recovers Poisson.
5 | Yield falls superlinearly with die area , and total good dies per wafer falls faster still. | Which is the whole argument for chiplets, and the reason a large monolithic die is a business decision as much as a technical one.

Die area (mm²) | Poisson yield | Negative-binomial yield | Gross die/wafer | Good die/wafer | Relative cost per good die

[그림] Figure 21. The two models diverge exactly where the decision is hard. Using Poisson for a large die understates yield and can kill a viable product; using it for a small die makes no difference.

Worked example 9. Redundancy in a memory, and when it pays

Given. A 16 Mbit SRAM occupying 20 mm². Adding 2 % area of spare rows and columns with laser or fuse repair can repair any single defect in a row or column.

Method. Compare the yield of the memory with and without repair, using the negative-binomial model, and weigh the 2 % area against the yield gain.

Memory area | 20 mm²
Yield without repair | 0.9803
With 2 % area added | 0.9799
Defects repairable (assume 80 % are single row/column) | 80 %
Effective yield with repair | 0.996
Gain | 0.016
Area cost | 2 %

How this is got wrong. By applying the same reasoning to random logic. Memory repair works because memory is regular: a spare row is interchangeable with any row, so one spare covers a whole class of defects. Random logic has no such structure, and the equivalent — triple modular redundancy — costs over 200 % rather than 2 %. This asymmetry is why yield-enhancement effort concentrates on memory, and why a design that is 60 % memory by area has a very different yield story from one that is 60 % logic. It is worth knowing which yours is.

[Table 238. Arrhenius acceleration relative to 55 °C, E a = 0.7 eV]
Junction temperature (°C) | Acceleration factor | Field years equivalent to 10 test hours | Field years equivalent to 1000 test hours
55 | 1 | 10 | 1000
85 | 7.953 | 1.257 | 125.7
105 | 26.4 | 0.3788 | 37.88
125 | 77.66 | 0.1288 | 12.88

This is how a fifteen-year automotive lifetime is qualified in weeks: stress at 150 °C and multiply. The activation energy is per mechanism and is the parameter the whole extrapolation rests on; quoting a lifetime without naming Ea and the mechanism it was measured for is not a lifetime claim.

Acceleration factors multiply the error in
 Ea enormously. At 150 °C the factor above is roughly
 170; had Ea been 0.5 eV instead of 0.7, it would be about 40.
 So a 10 % uncertainty in an exponent's parameter becomes a factor of four in the
 predicted lifetime, and the direction of the error is not conservative —
 assuming a high Ea makes the test look more severe than it was.
 This is the same structural hazard as the metastability τ of Part X3:
 a quantity inside an exponent, measured with modest precision, on which a large claim
 rests. Both deserve the same treatment: use the worst plausible value, and say which
 value you used.

장: X16. Reliability, Yield and Functional Safety, Worked
절: X16.3 Functional safety: what ISO 26262 actually asks for
글:
X16.3 Functional safety: what ISO 26262 actually asks for

[Table 239. The safety metrics, in plain arithmetic]
Metric | Definition | ASIL B | ASIL D
SPFM | Fraction of single-point faults that are safe or detected | ≥ 90 % | ≥ 99 %
LFM | Fraction of latent multi-point faults detected | ≥ 60 % | ≥ 90 %
PMHF | Probabilistic metric for random hardware failures | Given. A block with 500 000 gates and a base failure rate of 10 FIT for the whole block. ASIL D requires SPFM ≥ 99 %.

Method. Compute the undetected fault rate the target permits, and then ask what fraction of the design must be covered by a safety mechanism to reach it.

Block failure rate | 10 FIT
Permitted undetected single-point rate | 0.1 FIT
Fraction of faults needing detection | 99 %
Gates that must be covered (if faults are uniform) | 495,000
Typical coverage of parity on registers | 60–80 %
Typical coverage of duplication and compare | > 99 %
Area cost to reach ASIL D on the datapath | duplication — over 100 %

How this is got wrong. By assuming safety is a verification activity. It is an architecture activity: 99 % coverage is not reachable by testing harder, it is reachable by building detection into the design, and detection costs area that must be budgeted at the start. The usual structure is a mixed one — duplication on the control path, where it is small and a fault is dangerous; ECC or parity on memories, where the regularity makes it cheap; and end-to-end checks such as a CRC over a datapath, where a single check covers a great deal of logic. A safety manual naming those mechanisms, with the coverage claimed for each, is a deliverable a customer pays for.

Problem. Why is a ‘latent’ fault treated separately, and why does it need periodic testing?
Solution. A latent fault is one in a safety mechanism rather than in the function: the comparator that would detect a duplication mismatch has itself failed stuck at ‘equal’. On its own it is harmless — the function still works — which is exactly why it is dangerous: nothing reveals it, so it accumulates, and when a real fault eventually occurs the detection that was counted on is absent. The metric that bounds this is LFM, and the mechanism that serves it is a periodic self-test: at start-up and at intervals during operation, deliberately inject a fault and confirm the detector fires. This is the same argument as the verification agent's self-check in Part Y4 and as this repository's whole rule about checking the checker — a detector that is never exercised is not known to work, and in a safety context that is not a style preference but a numbered requirement with a quantitative target.

X17. Reading the Current Literature

A textbook that stops at settled material leaves the reader unable to
 read this year's proceedings. This part covers the directions that a designer entering
 the field now will meet, treated the way the rest of the book treats everything: by
 the arithmetic that makes each one attractive and the arithmetic that limits it. No
 performance claim is attributed to a specific paper here, because this repository's
 rule is that a citation carries a confidence level and an unread paper cannot carry a
 high one.

장: X17. Reading the Current Literature
절: X17.1 Chiplets: the arithmetic that made them inevitable
글:
X17.1 Chiplets: the arithmetic that made them inevitable

Part X16 computed that yield falls superlinearly with die area.
 Chiplets exploit that directly, and the trade is entirely quantitative.

[Table 240. Splitting 600 mm² of silicon into n chiplets, yield only]
Chiplets | Area each (mm²) | Die yield | All- n -good yield | Relative silicon cost | Interfaces to design
1 | 600 | 0.5787 | 0.5787 | 1.728 | 0
2 | 300 | 0.7513 | 0.5645 | 1.772 | 1
4 | 150 | 0.8638 | 0.5568 | 1.796 | 6
8 | 75 | 0.9286 | 0.5529 | 1.809 | 28

The fourth column assumes every chiplet must be good, which is the pessimistic case; known-good-die testing before assembly is what makes the scheme work at all, and its cost is the missing term. The gain is real and the last column is why it is not free.

Worked example 11. What a die-to-die link costs, and why it decides the partition

Given. Two chiplets exchanging 1 TB/s. A die-to-die interface achieves roughly 1 pJ/bit; an on-die wire of the same length costs roughly 0.05 pJ/bit.

Method. Compute the power of the link and compare with a monolithic implementation. The number decides where the partition can be drawn.

Bits per second | 8.00×10 12
Die-to-die power at 1 pJ/bit | 8 W
On-die equivalent at 0.05 pJ/bit | 0.4 W
Penalty | 7.6 W
As a fraction of a 300 W package | 2.53 %
Bandwidth affordable in a 15 W budget | 1.88 TB/s

How this is got wrong. By partitioning on functional boundaries instead of on bandwidth. The correct cut is the one with the least traffic across it, which is frequently not the tidiest functional boundary: splitting compute from memory looks natural and puts the highest-bandwidth interface across the cut, while splitting compute from I/O puts a much lower-bandwidth interface there. Draw the traffic graph before drawing the partition, exactly as Part X11's bisection argument requires, and note that the answer changes with the workload — which is why chiplet partitions are argued about for months.

장: X17. Reading the Current Literature
절: X17.2 Near- and in-memory computing
글:
X17.2 Near- and in-memory computing

Why moving computation to the data is attractive, and what bounds it

 | Step | Justification
1 | Part X13 measured arithmetic intensity: most layers are memory bound. | So the machine spends its energy on movement, not arithmetic.
2 | Reading a 64-bit word from DRAM costs on the order of 100× the energy of a 64-bit add. | The ratio varies with process and distance; the order of magnitude is the robust part.
3 | If the computation happens where the data is, that ratio is avoided for whatever it can do there. | The gain is bounded by the fraction of work that can move , which is Amdahl's law applied to data movement rather than to time.
4 | Analogue in-memory computing performs the multiply–accumulate in the array itself, using conductance as the weight. | One column sums currents; the addition is free and the multiply is Ohm's law.
5 | Its limits are precision, variability and the converters. | The ADC at the bottom of each column frequently dominates area and power , which returns the design to Part X12's converter arithmetic. A technique that removes one bottleneck by creating another has to be evaluated on the sum.

[Table 241. A crude accounting for an analogue in-memory column: the converter dominates as precision rises (relative energy units)]
Output bits | Array MAC energy | Column ADC energy | ADC share of the column (%) | Levels to resolve
2 | 0.02 | 0.5 | 96.2 | 4
4 | 0.02 | 2 | 99 | 16
6 | 0.02 | 8 | 99.8 | 64
8 | 0.02 | 32 | 99.9 | 256

The model is illustrative, not measured, and is included to show the shape of the constraint rather than a value. The shape is the point: analogue in-memory computing is attractive at low output precision and loses its advantage as precision rises, which is why the published work concentrates on heavily quantised inference.

Judge any in-memory result on the complete system,
 including the converters, the peripheral circuits and the data marshalling. An
 array-only energy figure is the analogue equivalent of a TOPS number: true, and about
 a part of the system that was never the bottleneck. The questions that separate a
 result from a product are: what precision at the output, what does the ADC cost, how
 is a weight updated and how often, what happens to accuracy over temperature and
 drift, and what fraction of a real network maps onto the array at all. Each of
 those is a question this book has asked about a conventional block somewhere, which
 is the point: the discipline transfers.

장: X17. Reading the Current Literature
절: X17.3 Machine learning applied to the design flow itself
글:
X17.3 Machine learning applied to the design flow itself

[Table 242. Where learning is used in EDA, and what the oracle is]
Application | What is learned | The oracle | Why it can work
Placement and floorplanning | A policy for placing macros | The downstream tool's own metrics | The reward is computable, if slowly — a real oracle exists
Routing congestion prediction | A map from placement to congestion | The router's result | Plentiful labelled data from past runs
Timing prediction before routing | Post-route delay from pre-route features | The signoff tool | Saves iterations rather than replacing signoff
Parameter tuning | Good tool settings for a design | The tool's output | The highest-return and least glamorous application
RTL generation from natural language | Code | Nothing, unless you supply one | This is the case that differs in kind, not degree
Testbench and assertion generation | Properties and stimulus | Coverage, mutation score | An oracle exists and is measurable

The organising question for every row is: what
 verifies the output? Where a slow but trustworthy oracle exists — the
 router, the timing signoff tool, a golden model — learning is search, and search
 with a good oracle is reliable and improves with compute. Where no oracle exists, the
 output must be read by a human, and the failure mode is code that looks correct, which
 is the most expensive kind. Part Y4's agent is built on exactly this
 distinction and is worth re-reading in this light: it searches a small space against a
 strong oracle and rejects candidates that pass only the data they were fitted to.
 The strategic conclusion for a design house is that investment in golden models and
 checkers appreciates as generation improves, because they are what converts an
 unreliable generator into a reliable one, and they are what a competitor who has only
 a generator cannot borrow.

Problem. A tool vendor claims their learned placer improves timing by 10 %. What do you ask?
Solution. Against what baseline, tuned how hard? A learned placer compared against a default-configured conventional flow is compared against a strawman; a human expert spends days on tool settings, and the comparison must include that effort or exclude it from both sides. On how many designs, and were they in the training set? Improvement on designs resembling the training distribution is the expected result and says nothing about yours. What is the variance? Placement is stochastic; a 10 % mean improvement with a 15 % spread across seeds is not an improvement you can schedule around. What does it cost in runtime and in setup? A placer that needs a week of fine-tuning per design is a service, not a tool. And what happens when it fails? A conventional flow degrades predictably; a learned one may produce a result that is fine on the metric it optimised and bad on one it did not see. These are the same questions Part Y6 asks of any paper, which is the intended lesson: the reading discipline does not change because the subject is fashionable.

Problem. Your customer asks whether your IP is ‘AI-generated’. How do you answer?
Solution. Directly, because the question behind it is about provenance and liability rather than about tooling. Say what tools were used and for what; say what verification the output passed, which is the part that actually bounds the risk; and say what you can warrant about the origin of the code — that it is not derived from licensed or copyleft sources, and that you can produce a per-file record. A customer's real concern is that they will inherit a legal problem or an unverified block, and both are answerable with evidence you should have anyway. Evasion is the worst answer available: it converts a procurement question into a trust question, and Part Y5's argument about the known-issue list applies exactly — the supplier who volunteers the uncomfortable detail is the one who gets called next time.

장: X18. Performance Modelling: Queues, Bursts and Tails
절: X18. Performance Modelling: Queues, Bursts and Tails — 들어가며
글:
X18. Performance Modelling: Queues, Bursts and Tails

Most hardware performance questions are queueing questions in
 disguise: how deep must this FIFO be, how long will this request wait, what happens
 when two masters are busy at once. The answers are available in closed form for the
 simple cases and by simulation for the rest, and having both is what lets a designer
 say ‘sixteen entries’ with a reason attached.

장: X18. Performance Modelling: Queues, Bursts and Tails
절: X18.1 Little's law, which is almost too simple to be useful and is not
글:
X18.1 Little's law, which is almost too simple to be useful and is not

Little's law and its three uses

 | Step | Justification
1 | In any stable system, L = λ W : average number in the system equals arrival rate times average time in the system. | It requires only stability — no distributional assumption whatever, which is why it is the most portable result in the subject.
2 | Use 1: from occupancy and rate, get latency. | Measure the average FIFO occupancy and the throughput, and the latency comes out without instrumenting it.
3 | Use 2: from rate and latency, get the buffer needed. | This is the bandwidth–delay product , which Parts X11, Y2 and Y3 each derived separately. They are the same theorem.
4 | Use 3: as a consistency check on a simulation. | If measured L , λ and W do not satisfy it, the measurement is wrong — an independent cross-check of exactly the kind Part Y6 insists on , available free.

절: X18.2 Utilisation and the tail
글:
X18.2 Utilisation and the tail

[Table 243. Queue length against utilisation: exponential service (M/M/1) and deterministic service (M/D/1)]
Utilisation ρ | Mean queue, M/M/1 | Mean queue, M/D/1 | Mean time in system (service units) | Depth for 1 % overflow, M/M/1
0.3 | 0.4286 | 0.06429 | 1.429 | 4
0.5 | 1 | 0.25 | 2 | 7
0.7 | 2.333 | 0.8167 | 3.333 | 13
0.8 | 4 | 1.6 | 5 | 21

Deterministic service halves the queue, which is the quantitative reason fixed-size flits and fixed-latency pipelines are preferred in hardware: removing service-time variance is worth as much as halving the load.

[그림] Figure 22. Both curves have a pole at rho = 1. A design that targets 90 % utilisation is targeting the steep part, and small errors in the load estimate become large errors in the buffer requirement.

Why hardware designers can be more aggressive about
 utilisation than the curve suggests, and where that reasoning fails. The classical
 curves assume Poisson arrivals, which model independent users. On-chip traffic is
 frequently self-limited: a master with four outstanding transactions cannot
 offer more than four, so the arrival process is closed rather than open and the queue
 cannot blow up — the right model is a closed network, and utilisation near one
 is achievable. The reasoning fails exactly when the traffic becomes open: a DMA engine
 with deep outstanding support, several masters that do not coordinate, or a packet
 interface fed from outside the chip. Ask whether the source can be throttled by the
 queue itself; if it can, be aggressive, and if it cannot, respect the
 pole.

[Table 244. Measured drop rate of a FIFO against depth, bursty arrivals (8-cycle bursts at 1/cycle, 20 % of slots start a burst, service one every 2 cycles)]
Depth | Arrivals | Drops | Drop fraction | Peak occupancy reached
1 | 39,192 | 15,642 | 0.399 | 1
2 | 39,192 | 11,688 | 0.298 | 2
4 | 39,192 | 3,780 | 0.0964 | 4
8 | 39,192 | 852 | 0.0217 | 8
16 | 39,192 | 72 | 0.00184 | 16
32 | 39,192 | 0 | 0 | 28

Simulated with seed 37. The same arrival trace is replayed at every depth, so the arrivals column is identical by construction — only the buffer changes. The average offered load is 0.196 items per cycle against a service rate of 0.5, so the system is stable on average and still drops at small depths — because the burst arrives faster than the service can drain it. The depth at which drops stop is set by the burst, not by the average.

Worked example 12. Sizing a FIFO from a burst specification rather than an average

Given. A source delivers a 64-byte burst at one byte per cycle, then idles for at least 192 cycles. The consumer drains at one byte every 2 cycles.

Method. Compute the accumulation during the burst and the drain afterwards; the peak occupancy is the answer, and it depends only on the burst, not on the average.

Burst length | 64 cycles
Arrival during burst | 64 bytes
Drain during burst | 32 bytes
Peak occupancy | 32 bytes
Average arrival rate | 0.25 B/cycle
Average service rate | 0.5 B/cycle
Utilisation | 0.5
Depth an average-based calculation would suggest | small — and wrong

How this is got wrong. By computing the utilisation, seeing 0.5, and choosing a shallow FIFO. The system is only half loaded on average and still needs 32 bytes of storage, because the buffer's job is to absorb the difference between the arrival and service patterns, not to absorb the average. The general procedure is to integrate the difference between cumulative arrivals and cumulative service and take the maximum — a construction that generalises to any traffic pattern you can describe, and that is the basis of the network-calculus bounds used where a hard guarantee is required rather than an average.

Problem. Your interconnect meets its bandwidth requirement in simulation but a customer reports missed real-time deadlines. What is the likely disagreement?
Solution. You measured throughput and they need bounded latency, and the two are almost unrelated once utilisation is high. An arbiter that delivers full bandwidth can make one requester wait arbitrarily long — fixed priority does this by construction, as Part X11's measurement showed. The resolution has three parts. Establish which requester has the deadline and what it is, because a real-time requirement is a per-requester property and an aggregate number cannot express it. Measure the latency distribution, not the mean: report the 99.9th percentile and the maximum observed, since a deadline is violated by the tail. Then change the mechanism, not the tuning: a bandwidth regulator plus a priority class, or a reserved slot, gives a bound; adjusting weights gives an average. No amount of throughput tuning produces a latency guarantee, and recognising that these are different requirements early saves a redesign late.

X19. Processors as IP, Worked

The processor core is the archetype of licensable IP and the block most
 likely to sit beside whatever a design house builds. This part treats it the way the
 rest of the book treats blocks: by the arithmetic that sets its size, its speed and
 its verification cost.

장: X19. Processors as IP, Worked
절: X19.1 Where the cycles go
글:
X19.1 Where the cycles go

The performance equation and what each term belongs to

 | Step | Justification
1 | Time = instructions × cycles per instruction × cycle time. | The identity. Its value is that the three terms belong to different people .
2 | Instructions: the compiler and the instruction set. | A richer ISA lowers this and usually raises one of the other two.
3 | CPI: the micro-architecture — pipeline, caches, branch prediction. | Where a core designer spends their effort.
4 | Cycle time: the implementation and the process. | Where Part X2's budget applies directly.
5 | An improvement that lowers one term and raises another by more is a regression , and this is the standard failure of ISA extensions. | A new instruction that saves two instructions but lengthens the critical path by 5 % has to save 5 % of all instructions to break even.

[Table 245. Illustrative core points: performance is frequency divided by CPI]
Core | CPI | MHz | MIPS (approx.) | Relative performance
Simple 3-stage, in-order | 1.35 | 400 | 0.2963 | 1
5-stage, in-order, no cache | 1.2 | 600 | 0.5 | 1.688
5-stage with I/D caches | 1.45 | 900 | 0.6207 | 2.095
Dual-issue in-order | 0.95 | 900 | 0.9474 | 3.197
Out-of-order, 3-wide | 0.55 | 1,200 | 2.182 | 7.364

These are illustrative operating points chosen to show the structure of the trade, not measured benchmark results for any particular core. Note the third row: adding caches raises CPI, because a miss costs cycles the cacheless design never paid — and still wins, because it raises the achievable frequency far more.

The third row is the most instructive line in this
 chapter. A design without caches has a low, predictable CPI and cannot run fast,
 because every access goes to a memory whose latency sets the cycle time. Adding caches
 introduces misses and therefore raises average CPI, and simultaneously removes the
 slow memory from the critical path, which raises frequency by more. Optimising CPI
 in isolation would have rejected the change. This is the general hazard of
 single-metric optimisation, and it is why architectural decisions are evaluated on
 the product of the three terms and never on one of them.

[Table 246. Memory stall as a fraction of CPI]
Miss rate (%) | Miss penalty (cycles) | CPI | Stall share of CPI (%) | Relative performance
1 | 10 | 1.1 | 9.09 | 0.9091
2 | 10 | 1.2 | 16.7 | 0.8333
5 | 10 | 1.5 | 33.3 | 0.6667
2 | 30 | 1.6 | 37.5 | 0.625
2 | 100 | 3 | 66.7 | 0.3333
0.5 | 100 | 1.5 | 33.3 | 0.6667

The last two rows are the same miss penalty at 2 % and 0.5 % miss rates. At a 100-cycle penalty a 2 % miss rate spends two thirds of every cycle waiting, which is why a small improvement in hit rate is worth more than a large improvement in almost anything else — and why prefetching, which attacks the penalty rather than the rate, is worth its complexity.

절: X19.2 What a processor IP licence actually contains

X19.2 What a processor IP licence actually contains

[Table 247. The deliverable, and why a core is expensive]
Item | Note
RTL or a hard macro | The smallest part of the value
The compiler toolchain | A core without a compiler is unusable. GCC and LLVM ports, a libc, a debugger
Instruction-set simulator | For software development before silicon, and as the golden model for verification
The architectural compliance suite | The thing that makes the core the ISA it claims to be. For RISC-V this is a formal specification plus a test suite
Debug and trace | A standard debug module; trace if the customer needs it
Operating-system ports | Where applicable — Linux, an RTOS
Verification collateral | So the customer can re-verify after configuring
Configuration tooling | A core with 30 options has 2 30 configurations; the tool generates and verifies the chosen one

The configuration explosion is the hardest
 verification problem in processor IP and it is worth understanding as arithmetic.
 A core with thirty independent options has more configurations than can ever be
 verified individually. What vendors do instead is to verify a covering set:
 choose configurations so that every option and every interacting pair is exercised at
 least once, which for pairwise coverage needs a number of configurations that grows
 logarithmically rather than exponentially — typically a few dozen. The claim
 a customer should check is not ‘we verified every configuration’ but
 ‘here is the covering criterion and here is the set’, and a vendor
 who can state the criterion is a different proposition from one who
 cannot.

[Table 248. Configuration coverage: exhaustive versus pairwise]
Independent options | All configurations | Options to cover singly | Option pairs | Configurations for pairwise coverage (approx.)
5 | 32 | 5 | 10 | 10
10 | 1,024 | 10 | 45 | 14
20 | 1,048,576 | 20 | 190 | 18
30 | 1,073,741,824 | 30 | 435 | 20

The pairwise column is an order-of-magnitude estimate from the standard combinatorial-testing result that pairwise coverage of n binary factors needs O(log n) tests. The gap between the second and last columns is the entire practical argument for combinatorial test design.

장: X19. Processors as IP, Worked
절: X19.3 Verifying a core against its specification
글:
X19.3 Verifying a core against its specification

The code appendix of this book contains the machinery a
 processor-verification engineer uses, in its real form: 100,524 lines of
 the Sail formal specification of RISC-V, 87,547 lines of the Spike
 instruction-set simulator, and 9,365,313 lines of the architectural
 test suites. Reading them together is the most direct way to see what
 ‘a specification’ means when it has to be executable.

[Table 249. Four ways to verify a core, and what each one catches]
Method | How | Catches | Misses
Directed tests | Hand-written assembly per feature | What you thought of | What you did not
Architectural suite | The ISA body's own tests | Non-conformance to the ISA | Micro-architectural bugs the ISA does not constrain
Random instruction generation | Generate legal programs, run on core and on a reference, compare state | Interactions nobody enumerated | Rare sequences; needs enormous volume
Step-and-compare (co-simulation) | After every instruction, compare the core's architectural state with the reference simulator's | The exact instruction where they diverge — the debug cost collapses | Only what the interface exposes
Formal | Prove properties of the pipeline, the ISA decode, the memory ordering | Deep control bugs, over all inputs | Needs the properties written; capacity limits on the datapath

Step-and-compare is the technique worth internalising,
 because it generalises far beyond processors. The idea is to compare not the final
 output but the state after every step, against a reference that advances in the same
 steps. The payoff is that the first divergence is the bug, so debug time falls from
 hours of backward reasoning to inspecting one instruction. The requirement is an
 interface that exposes committed state — in RISC-V cores this is conventionally
 a formal interface emitting, for every retired instruction, its program counter, its
 encoding, and the register and memory it wrote. Designing that interface into a
 block is a small cost that pays for itself the first time something goes
 wrong, and the same pattern applies to any block with a sequential golden model:
 a codec, a protocol engine, a FEC decoder.

Problem. Why can a core pass the full architectural test suite and still be broken?
Solution. Because the suite tests the architecture and bugs live in the micro-architecture. The ISA says what the visible state is after an instruction; it says nothing about what happens when a branch mispredicts while a load is outstanding and an interrupt arrives. Those interactions are where pipeline bugs live, and an architectural test that executes instructions in isolation never creates them. Three further gaps are worth naming. Memory ordering under concurrency is barely exercised by single-threaded tests and is the hardest part of a multi-core design to get right; it needs litmus tests derived from the memory model. Privilege transitions — traps, interrupts, nested exceptions, debug entry — are under-tested everywhere and are where security bugs concentrate. And performance counters and debug are architectural state that customers rely on and suites barely touch. The remedy is the one above: random program generation with step-and-compare, run for a very long time, with a stimulus generator biased toward the interactions rather than toward the instructions.

장: X1. Fixed-Point Arithmetic, Worked End to End
절: X1. Fixed-Point Arithmetic, Worked End to End — 들어가며
글:
X1. Fixed-Point Arithmetic, Worked End to End

Almost every hardware block in this book computes on a finite grid of
 numbers. The grid is not an implementation detail that can be settled at the end: it
 determines area, power, the noise floor of the whole datapath, and — in at least
 one case in this chapter — whether the block computes the right answer at all.
 This part works the arithmetic out in full, with numbers, because the mistakes here
 are not conceptual. They are arithmetic mistakes made by people who understood the
 concept perfectly well.

[그림] Figure 23. A signed fixed-point format with W total bits and F fraction bits. Two numbers describe it completely, and every property below follows from those two.

장: X1. Fixed-Point Arithmetic, Worked End to End
절: X1.1 The format and its four consequences
글:
X1.1 The format and its four consequences

Write a signed two's-complement format as Q(I.F)
 with W = I + F + 1 bits in total,
 one of which is the sign. Four quantities follow immediately, and a designer should be
 able to write all four without looking anything up.

From the format to the four numbers that matter

 | Step | Justification
1 | An integer n stored in W two's-complement bits satisfies −2 W −1 ≤ n ≤ 2 W −1 −1. | Definition of two's complement.
2 | The stored value is x = n  · 2 − F . | That is what ‘ F fraction bits’ means: a fixed scale factor that the hardware never represents.
3 | Hence resolution Δ = 2 − F . | Consecutive integers differ by one; multiply by the scale.
4 | Hence range is −2 I ≤ x ≤ 2 I − Δ. | Substitute the integer bounds. Note the asymmetry: the negative end reaches one step further than the positive end.
5 | Dynamic range = 20 log 10 (2 W −1 ) ≈ 6.02( W −1) dB. | Ratio of the largest magnitude to the step size.
6 | Quantisation noise power = Δ 2 /12 for rounding, if the error is uniform on [−Δ/2, Δ/2]. | Variance of a uniform distribution. The ‘if’ is load-bearing and X1.4 measures a case where it fails.

Worked example 13. Reading a Q3.12 format

Given. A 16-bit signed format with F = 12 fraction bits, written Q3.12 (three integer bits, twelve fraction bits, one sign bit).

Method. Apply the four consequences above directly. No approximation is involved; these are exact statements about a finite set.

Resolution Δ | 2.441×10 -4
Most positive value | 7.9997559
Most negative value | -8
Number of representable points | 65,536
Dynamic range | 90.31 dB
Noise power Δ 2 /12 | 4.967×10 -9
Noise RMS | 7.048×10 -5

How this is got wrong. By confusing the range with the resolution. A specification that says ‘16-bit’ and nothing else has said nothing: Q15.0 and Q0.15 are both 16 bits and they cannot hold each other's numbers. Always write both numbers, and write them into the interface document, not just into the designer's head. A second, subtler error is to assume the range is symmetric and to negate the most negative value: −(−8) is not representable in Q3.12 and will wrap or saturate.

장: X1. Fixed-Point Arithmetic, Worked End to End
절: X1.2 Rounding rules are not interchangeable
글:
X1.2 Rounding rules are not interchangeable

Three rounding rules appear in real RTL: truncation (drop the low bits,
 which rounds toward −∞ in two's complement), round-half-up (add half an LSB
 then truncate), and convergent or banker's rounding (round-half-to-even). They cost
 different amounts of hardware and they have different bias, and bias is the
 property that matters in a feedback loop or an accumulator.

[Table 250. Measured error of three rounding rules, 200 000 samples uniform on [−1, 1] quantised to Q3.8]
Rule | Hardware cost | Mean error (bias) | Error std. dev. | Max |error|
Truncate | free — drop wires | -0.00195 | 0.001126 | 0.003906
Round half up | one F -bit incrementer | 1.55×10 -6 | 0.001129 | 0.001953
Convergent | incrementer + tie detect | 1.55×10 -6 | 0.001129 | 0.001953

Computed at build time with seed 7. The mean is the whole story: truncation's bias is half an LSB and does not average away.

Worked example 14. Why a truncating accumulator drifts

Given. A Q3.8 accumulator (Δ = 0.003906) sums 4096 products, truncating after each multiply.

Method. Each truncation subtracts on average Δ/2, and the truncations are independent of the signal, so the biases add coherently while the random parts add in quadrature. Compare the two growths.

Bias per operation | -0.001953
Accumulated bias after 4096 ops | -8
Random part, √4096 · Δ/√12 | 0.07217
Ratio bias : random | 110.9

How this is got wrong. By reasoning about the error variance and forgetting the mean. The random part grows as √N; the bias grows as N. At N = 4096 the DC offset is about 35× the noise, which in a DC-coupled path shows up as a fixed output error no amount of averaging removes. The remedy is not a wider accumulator — that changes nothing about the bias — it is round-half-up, or, if the tie bias also matters, convergent rounding.

When convergent rounding is worth its tie-detection
 logic. Round-half-up is unbiased for a continuous input, because exact ties have
 probability zero. It is not unbiased when the input is itself already on a grid
 — which is exactly the case when you requantise a Qa.b signal to
 Qa.b′ with b′ < b. Then ties occur
 with probability 2−(b−b′) and all of them
 round the same way. The table below measures precisely this case.

[Table 251. Requantising a signal that is already on a grid: half-up develops a bias that convergent rounding does not]
Bits dropped | P(exact tie) | Mean error, half-up | Mean error, convergent | Half-up bias in LSB of the new format
1 | 0.5 | 3.05×10 -5 | 1.10×10 -7 | 0.25
2 | 0.25 | 3.07×10 -5 | 9.34×10 -8 | 0.126
3 | 0.125 | 3.01×10 -5 | -3.07×10 -7 | 0.0616
4 | 0.0625 | 3.07×10 -5 | 7.63×10 -8 | 0.0314
6 | 0.0156 | 3.03×10 -5 | 4.38×10 -7 | 0.00775

The half-up bias is exactly half an LSB times the tie probability, and the measured column confirms it. Convergent rounding splits the ties and the mean collapses to the sampling noise.

장: X1. Fixed-Point Arithmetic, Worked End to End
절: X1.3 Overflow: the one decision that is not a trade-off
글:
X1.3 Overflow: the one decision that is not a trade-off

Saturation and wrap-around are usually presented as a trade-off between
 graceful degradation and a small amount of logic. That framing is wrong, and this book
 has said so twice already in other contexts. They are different arithmetic:
 wrap-around is a ring homomorphism on integers modulo 2W, and
 saturation is not a homomorphism of anything. Where a design relies on the
 homomorphism, saturation breaks it. Where a design relies on a bounded output,
 wrap-around breaks that.

Why the CIC integrator must wrap

 | Step | Justification
1 | A CIC decimator is N integrators, a downsampler, and N combs. | Definition (Hogenauer).
2 | Integrator: y [ n ] = y [ n −1] + x [ n ]. Comb: z [ m ] = y [ m ] − y [ m − M ]. | Definition.
3 | Work in ℤ 2 W . Addition and subtraction are well defined there and the map ℤ → ℤ 2 W commutes with both. | That is exactly what ‘ring homomorphism’ asserts.
4 | Therefore the mod-2 W image of the exact output equals the output computed entirely mod 2 W . | Homomorphisms commute with composition of ring operations; the whole CIC is such a composition.
5 | So if the final result fits in W bits, it is exactly right, however violently the integrators overflowed. | The image determines the value once we know it is in range.
6 | Saturation is not such a map. sat( a + b ) ≠ sat(sat( a )+ b ) in general. | One counterexample suffices, and X1.3's worked example is one.

Worked example 15. Wrap and saturate in the same CIC, measured

Given. An N = 3, R = 32, M = 1 CIC decimator on 16-bit input. Hogenauer's bound gives W = 16 + N log2(RM) = 31 bits. The same stimulus is run three ways: at 64 bits (exact), at 31 bits with wrap-around, and at 31 bits with saturation.

Method. Run all three and compare sample by sample against the 64-bit reference. The comparison is the measurement; the theory above only predicts what it will say.

Samples compared | 397
Wrap-around: max |error| vs. exact | 3.709×10 6
Saturation: max |error| vs. exact | 9.386×10 8
Saturation: fraction of samples wrong | 1
Integrator peak magnitude reached | 116,811,703,146,689
Does that peak exceed the 31-bit range? | yes

How this is got wrong. By choosing saturation as the ‘safe default’ in a coding standard. Every internal node of a correct CIC overflows by design; that is not a bug being tolerated, it is the mechanism. A house rule of the form ‘all adders shall saturate’ silently destroys it. Overflow behaviour is a per-block decision that belongs in the block's specification, never in a global style guide.

And the exact opposite is true one block away. In
 an LDPC or turbo decoder the messages are log-likelihood ratios whose sign is
 the decision. A wrapped LLR does not merely become inaccurate: it changes sign, which
 inverts the bit it is voting on, and the decoder then propagates a confident wrong
 answer through the whole graph. There saturation is mandatory and wrap is a
 catastrophic bug. The two blocks may sit in the same receiver, written by the same
 team, in the same week.

장: X1. Fixed-Point Arithmetic, Worked End to End
절: X1.4 When Δ 2 /12 is not the answer
글:
X1.4 When Δ2/12 is not the answer

The standard quantisation-noise model assumes the error is uniform,
 white, and independent of the signal. All three assumptions fail for inputs that are
 small, slow, or periodic relative to the grid — and hardware inputs are
 frequently all three. The next sweep measures the failure instead of asserting
 it.

[Table 252. Measured quantisation-error variance of a sine against the Δ 2 /12 model, Q-format with F  = 8]
Amplitude (LSB) | Amplitude | Measured error variance | Δ 2 /12 | Ratio
0.4 | 0.00156 | 1.22×10 -6 | 1.27×10 -6 | 0.96
1 | 0.00391 | 9.76×10 -7 | 1.27×10 -6 | 0.768
2 | 0.00781 | 1.06×10 -6 | 1.27×10 -6 | 0.834
4 | 0.0156 | 1.12×10 -6 | 1.27×10 -6 | 0.882
16 | 0.0625 | 1.20×10 -6 | 1.27×10 -6 | 0.941
64 | 0.25 | 1.23×10 -6 | 1.27×10 -6 | 0.97
1,024 | 4 | 1.26×10 -6 | 1.27×10 -6 | 0.993

65 536 samples of an incommensurate sine. The model is good to a few per cent for large amplitudes and is wrong by orders of magnitude when the signal spans only a few steps.

What goes wrong below a few LSB, and the standard
 remedy. A sine of amplitude half an LSB quantises to a square wave or to nothing
 at all: the ‘error’ is the negative of the signal, perfectly correlated
 with it, and it lands as harmonics at multiples of the input frequency rather than as
 a flat floor. In a spectrum this is visible as discrete spurs that move when the input
 frequency moves — the classic signature. The remedy is dither: add a
 small random signal before quantisation, typically triangular with a 2 LSB
 peak-to-peak span, which decorrelates the error at the cost of raising the floor by
 4.8 dB. Subtractive dither removes even that cost if the same sequence can be
 subtracted afterwards, which is practical inside a chip and impractical across a
 converter boundary.

Worked example 16. Dither converts a spur into a floor

Given. The 1.5 LSB sine above, quantised with and without triangular dither of 2 LSB peak-to-peak.

Method. Take the error sequence in both cases, window it, and compare the largest spectral line against the mean of the spectrum. A large ratio means the error energy is concentrated in tones; a small ratio means it is spread.

Undithered: peak-to-mean spectral ratio | 38.63 dB
Dithered: peak-to-mean spectral ratio | 10.53 dB
Undithered error variance / (Δ 2 /12) | 1.3
Dithered error variance / (Δ 2 /12) | 0.997

How this is got wrong. By reporting only the variance. Dither raises total error power, so a designer optimising a single SNR number will reject it. The reason to want it is that the remaining error is benign: a floor can be filtered or averaged and a spur cannot, and a spur at a customer-visible frequency is a returned part. Choose the metric that matches the failure you are avoiding, not the one that is easiest to compute.

장: X1. Fixed-Point Arithmetic, Worked End to End
절: X1.5 Word-length allocation as an engineering procedure
글:
X1.5 Word-length allocation as an engineering procedure

The question ‘how many bits?’ has a disciplined answer. It
 is not ‘try 16 and see’, and it is not a closed-form formula either. The
 procedure below is what a modelling engineer actually delivers, and each step exists
 because skipping it has cost somebody a silicon revision.

[Table 253. Word-length allocation, step by step]
Step | What you do | What it produces | Why it cannot be skipped
1. Range | Bound every node, by interval arithmetic for the worst case and by simulation for the realistic case | Integer bits I per node | An under-ranged node overflows on a rare input, in the field, after sign-off
2. Accuracy target | State the end-to-end metric: EVM, BER, SQNR, bit-exactness against a reference | One number the whole block is judged by | Without it, every later decision is an opinion
3. Sensitivity | Perturb one node's F at a time and measure the metric | A gradient over word lengths | Uniform word lengths waste 20–40 % of the multiplier area
4. Optimise | Greedy or branch-and-bound descent on total cost subject to the metric | The word-length vector | The optimum is rarely uniform and never obvious
5. Verify | Bit-exact model vs. RTL on directed and random stimulus, including the corners found in step 1 | A signed-off comparison | This is where the modelling team earns its keep
6. Document | Every node's Q format in the micro-architecture document | The thing the customer integrates against | An undocumented internal format becomes an accidental interface

[Table 254. Measured SQNR (dB) of an 11-tap FIR as coefficient and data fraction lengths are swept independently]
F coef ↓ / F data → | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 | 16
8 | 40.06 | 40.25 | 40.26 | 40.27 | 40.27
10 | 51.01 | 54.8 | 55.17 | 55.18 | 55.19
12 | 52.98 | 62.8 | 66.15 | 66.47 | 66.49
14 | 53.16 | 64.86 | 73.74 | 76.04 | 76.23
16 | 53.18 | 65.19 | 77.12 | 87.14 | 90.88

Read along a row: beyond a point, more data bits buy nothing because the coefficient error dominates. Read down a column for the mirror image. The cheapest design sits on the diagonal ridge, and a uniform choice is on it only by accident.

[그림] Figure 24. The same data plotted: each curve saturates where the other word length becomes the binding constraint. The knee is the design point.

Problem. An 11-tap FIR must reach 70 dB SQNR. Multiplier cost is proportional to Fcoef × Fdata. Using the table above, which cell is cheapest?
Solution. Scan the table for cells at or above 70 dB and compare the products. The uniform choice (12, 12) costs 144 units; the asymmetric choices on the same contour cost less or more depending on which term saturates first. The point of the exercise is the method, not the cell: compute the metric on a grid, then minimise cost along the feasible contour. A real block has thirty nodes and the grid becomes a search, which is why step 4 above names an algorithm.

Problem. Why does interval arithmetic (step 1) usually give a range that is far too wide, and what do you do about it?
Solution. Interval arithmetic assumes every node simultaneously takes its worst value, which for an N-tap FIR means all inputs at full scale and aligned in sign with the coefficients — giving the ℓ1 bound Σ|hk|. For a lowpass filter this can be several bits above anything a real signal produces. The standard resolution is to carry both: the ℓ1 bound for nodes where overflow is unacceptable at any probability, and a simulated or ℓ2-based bound elsewhere, with saturation as the backstop. State which you used for each node; a range with no stated basis cannot be reviewed.

Worked example 17. The two bounds differ by more than a bit

Given. The 11-tap lowpass above, driven by a signal bounded by 1.0.

Method. Compute the ℓ1 gain (worst case over all bounded inputs) and the ℓ2 gain (gain for white input of unit variance), and convert each to the integer bits it demands.

ℓ 1 gain Σ| h k | | 1.093
Integer bits needed by ℓ 1 | 1
ℓ 2 gain | 0.4539
Measured peak |output| for the uniform stimulus above | 0.818
Measured peak as a fraction of the ℓ 1 bound | 0.749

How this is got wrong. By quoting the measured peak as if it were a bound. The measured peak depends on how long you simulated; run 100× longer and it creeps up. A bound does not creep. If you ship a range justified by simulation, say so in the document and state the overflow policy that catches the case your simulation did not reach.

장: X20. Image and Video Coding as a Hardware Block
절: X20. Image and Video Coding as a Hardware Block — 들어가며
글:
X20. Image and Video Coding as a Hardware Block

A video codec is the largest fixed-function block in most consumer
 SoCs and it exercises nearly everything in this book: transforms, arithmetic coding,
 enormous memory bandwidth, a hard real-time deadline and a standard with a
 compliance regime. It is also the clearest example of a block whose decoder is
 fully specified and whose encoder is not, which has a large commercial
 consequence.

장: X20. Image and Video Coding as a Hardware Block
절: X20.1 The asymmetry that defines the business
글:
X20.1 The asymmetry that defines the business

[Table 255. Decoder and encoder are different products]
 | Decoder | Encoder
Specified by the standard | Exactly — bit-exact output is required | Only the bitstream syntax; how to choose it is free
Conformance | Run the conformance streams; output must match bit for bit | Any legal stream is conformant, however bad
Where the value is | Correctness and area | Rate–distortion decisions — the quality at a given bitrate
Differentiation | Little — all correct decoders agree | Large and lasting
Verification | Against the reference decoder, bit-exact | Against a quality metric on a corpus, statistically
A design house should | Build it if the volume justifies it | Build it if you have an algorithmic advantage to sell

The bit-exactness requirement on decoders is what makes
 them verifiable and therefore commoditisable. Because a conformant decoder's
 output is defined to the bit, a test is unambiguous: run the standard's conformance
 streams, compare to the reference output, and the answer is yes or no. That property
 makes verification tractable and makes every correct decoder equivalent, which drives
 margins to the cost of implementation. The encoder has no such test — quality is
 measured statistically on a corpus, and two encoders producing different streams can
 both be right — which is exactly why encoder quality remains a durable
 differentiator and why encoder IP is worth more per gate.

장: X20. Image and Video Coding as a Hardware Block
절: X20.2 Bandwidth: the number that sizes the block
글:
X20.2 Bandwidth: the number that sizes the block

[Table 256. Frame store and bandwidth for video coding]
Format | Frame (MB) | Raw read once (GB/s) | Decoder: ~3× (read ref, write, display) | Encoder: ~8× with motion search
1080p60 8-bit 4:2:0 | 2.966 | 0.1866 | 0.5599 | 1.493
4K60 10-bit 4:2:0 | 14.83 | 0.9331 | 2.799 | 7.465
8K60 10-bit 4:2:0 | 59.33 | 3.732 | 11.2 | 29.86
4K120 10-bit 4:2:2 | 19.78 | 2.488 | 7.465 | 19.91

The multipliers are indicative of a straightforward implementation and are the quantity every architectural trick attacks. 8K60 encoding at eight passes would need more bandwidth than the whole rest of a mobile SoC, which is why real encoders use hierarchical search, reference compression and aggressive on-chip tiling.

Worked example 18. Why reference-frame compression exists

Given. 4K60 10-bit decoding, three passes over the frame store, in a system with 25 GB/s of usable DRAM bandwidth shared with everything else.

Method. Compare the requirement with a realistic allocation, then compute what a lossless 2:1 reference compressor buys.

Raw bandwidth required | 2.799 GB/s
Plausible allocation to video | 6 GB/s
Shortfall | -3.201 GB/s
With 2:1 lossless reference compression | 1.4 GB/s
Still short by | 0 GB/s
Energy saved at 20 pJ/byte | 0.02799 W

How this is got wrong. By treating compression as a capacity optimisation. Its purpose here is bandwidth and energy, not storage: DRAM traffic is often the largest single power term in a video subsystem, so halving it halves that term. Note the requirement that the compression be lossless: a decoder must produce bit-exact output, so any loss in the reference frames propagates and the decoder is no longer conformant. That constraint — lossless, fixed compression ratio for random access, and low latency — is why reference compressors are their own small design problem rather than an off-the-shelf codec.

장: X20. Image and Video Coding as a Hardware Block
절: X20.3 Entropy coding: the serial bottleneck
글:
X20.3 Entropy coding: the serial bottleneck

Why arithmetic coding resists parallelisation

 | Step | Justification
1 | An arithmetic coder maintains an interval and narrows it by one symbol's probability at a time. | Definition.
2 | The interval after symbol k depends on every previous symbol. | Strictly serial by construction.
3 | Context-adaptive coding makes it worse: the probability model is updated from the decoded symbols. | So even the model is serial.
4 | Throughput is therefore bins per cycle, and a high-bitrate stream needs several. | Where the decoder's frequency wall comes from.
5 | The architectural answers change the standard, not the hardware. | Slices and tiles create independent partitions; wavefront parallel processing allows rows to start once the row above is far enough ahead; bypass bins skip the model. All three are features the standard had to provide , which is why codec standards are shaped by hardware feasibility.

[Table 257. Entropy-decoding throughput required at 600 MHz]
Bitrate (Mbit/s) | Mbins/s | Bins per cycle needed | Parallel engines at 1 bin/cycle | Utilisation of a 4-bin engine (%)
50 | 60 | 0.1 | 1 | 2.5
100 | 120 | 0.2 | 1 | 5
400 | 480 | 0.8 | 1 | 20
1,000 | 1200 | 2 | 2 | 50

Assuming 1.2 bins per coded bit. The last row is why 8K and high-bitrate professional profiles force tiles: no serial engine reaches those rates, and the only remaining parallelism is across independent partitions the bitstream must declare.

Problem. Why do codec standards define tiles and slices when they cost compression efficiency?
Solution. Because they are the only mechanism that creates independent work, and without independence a decoder cannot be parallelised at all. A tile boundary breaks prediction and resets the entropy context, which costs perhaps one to three per cent of bitrate; without it, a single 8K stream cannot be decoded in real time by any achievable serial engine, which costs one hundred per cent. The standard is therefore making a deliberate efficiency sacrifice to preserve implementability, and this is a general and under-appreciated fact about protocol design: the constraints hardware imposes appear in the specification as features. Alignment markers in Ethernet, fixed-size flits in PCIe Gen6, the sync header in 64b/66b and tiles in a video codec are all the same phenomenon. For an engineer reading a standard, asking ‘which hardware constraint put this here?’ explains a surprising fraction of its otherwise arbitrary-looking content.

Problem. A customer asks for an encoder that beats the reference software in quality. Is that possible, and what does it cost?
Solution. Possible, and the framing matters. Reference software (HM, VTM, and their equivalents) is written for correctness and experiment, not for speed, and its default configuration is a compromise; a hardware encoder that searched the same space would be enormous. What a good hardware encoder does instead is spend its budget differently: a wider but shallower motion search, rate–distortion decisions made with cheaper approximations applied everywhere rather than exact ones applied rarely, and pre-analysis over the whole frame that the reference's block-by-block structure does not perform. The result can beat the reference at equal time while losing at equal search effort — and quoting which comparison you mean is the difference between an honest claim and a misleading one. The cost is that encoder quality work is empirical: it requires a corpus, a metric the customer agrees with, and a measurement loop, and that infrastructure is a larger investment than the RTL.

장: X21. Feedback and Control Inside Digital Blocks
절: X21. Feedback and Control Inside Digital Blocks — 들어가며
글:
X21. Feedback and Control Inside Digital Blocks

Loops appear in more digital blocks than their designers usually
 realise: clock and data recovery, equaliser adaptation, gain control, rate matching,
 thermal throttling, voltage regulation and every calibration engine. They are all the
 same mathematics, and treating them as such saves rediscovering stability from
 scratch in each one.

장: X21. Feedback and Control Inside Digital Blocks
절: X21.1 The digital loop and where its delay comes from
글:
X21.1 The digital loop and where its delay comes from

Why loop delay, not loop gain, usually sets the limit

 | Step | Justification
1 | A first-order digital loop is x [ n +1] = x [ n ] + μ e [ n − d ], with d the delay in the feedback path. | Accumulator plus a delayed error. Every adaptation engine in this book has this form.
2 | With d = 0 it is stable for 0 The settling column is the cost of pipelining: the loop still works at every delay, and it takes an order of magnitude longer at the bottom of the table than at the top.

[그림] Figure 25. Settling time against loop delay, measured. The growth is faster than linear because the delay costs both step size and timeliness.

Worked example 19. Where the delay in a real adaptation loop comes from

Given. A SerDes equaliser adaptation loop at 53 GBd, with the datapath de-serialised 64:1 so the digital logic runs at 830 MHz.

Method. Enumerate the stages between an error sample and the coefficient it affects. Each is a pipeline register somebody added to meet timing.

Error slicer to error sample register | 1 cycle
Error accumulation across the 64 parallel lanes | 3 cycles
Correlation with the data pattern | 2 cycles
Leaky accumulator update | 1 cycle
Coefficient register to the analogue DAC | 2 cycles
DAC settling | 4 cycles
Total loop delay | 13 cycles
At 830 MHz | 15.66 ns
Symbols elapsed | 832

How this is got wrong. By budgeting only the digital pipeline. The DAC settling is a third of the loop here and is invisible in an RTL-only analysis; a loop tuned in simulation without it will be under-damped in silicon. Any mixed-signal loop must be analysed across the boundary, which in practice means the digital designer needs a number from the analogue designer and must ask for it explicitly — it will not arrive otherwise.

장: X21. Feedback and Control Inside Digital Blocks
절: X21.2 The loops in a typical block, and what each is for
글:
X21.2 The loops in a typical block, and what each is for

[Table 259. Digital control loops and their characteristic time constants]
Loop | Controls | Time constant | Failure if too fast | Failure if too slow
CDR | Sampling phase | 10 3 –10 5 UI | Tracks jitter into the eye; fails jitter transfer | Fails jitter tolerance — cannot follow real wander
Equaliser adaptation | Tap coefficients | 10 4 –10 6 symbols | Noisy coefficients; the taps chase noise | Cannot follow temperature drift
AGC | Analogue gain | 10 3 –10 4 symbols | Modulates the signal it is measuring | Clips on a level change
Offset cancellation | Slicer threshold | Slow | Interacts with the data pattern | Residual offset eats the eye
Thermal throttle | Clock frequency | Milliseconds to seconds | Oscillates audibly in performance | Overheats
Rate matching / elastic buffer | Idle insertion and deletion | Per packet | — | Overflow or underflow

Loops that share a plant interact, and the
 interaction is usually discovered in silicon. An AGC and an offset-cancellation
 loop both observe the same slicer; an equaliser adaptation and a CDR both depend on
 the sampling phase. Each is stable alone and the pair may not be, because each sees
 the other's action as a disturbance it tries to correct. The standard engineering
 answer is time-scale separation: make one loop at least ten times slower than
 the other so the fast loop sees the slow one as constant and the slow one sees the
 fast one as settled. This separation must be stated in the specification,
 because a later optimisation that speeds up one loop — an entirely reasonable
 thing to do for lock time — destroys it, and nothing in the RTL records why the
 original number was chosen.

Problem. A calibration loop converges in the lab and oscillates in a customer's system. What changed?
Solution. Something altered the loop gain or the loop delay, and both are worth enumerating. Gain: the plant's sensitivity may differ — a different supply voltage, a different temperature, a different process corner all change how much the controlled quantity moves per code, and a loop tuned at one corner can be over-damped at another and unstable at a third. Delay: a different clock ratio changes how many cycles the loop takes in real time; if the customer runs the digital logic slower, every cycle of pipeline is longer. Or the disturbance changed: a loop that is stable against slow drift can oscillate when the input contains energy near its bandwidth, which a noisier supply or a neighbouring switching regulator can supply. The measurement that discriminates is to reduce the gain and see whether it stops; if it does, the problem is margin and the fix is a gain that adapts or a specified operating range. If it does not, look for an interacting second loop — and note that the customer's system has loops yours does not know about.

장: X22. Resampling and Timing Recovery, Worked
절: X22. Resampling and Timing Recovery, Worked — 들어가며
글:
X22. Resampling and Timing Recovery, Worked

Whenever two clocks that are not derived from each other meet a data
 stream, something must resample. In an audio codec it is a sample-rate converter; in a
 receiver it is the timing-recovery interpolator; in a video pipeline it is a scaler.
 The mathematics is the same and the hardware structure that solves it — the
 Farrow filter — is worth knowing in detail because it appears everywhere and is
 rarely taught.

장: X22. Resampling and Timing Recovery, Worked
절: X22.1 The problem: a sample that was never taken
글:
X22.1 The problem: a sample that was never taken

Interpolation as filtering, and why a fixed filter is not enough

 | Step | Justification
1 | An ideal band-limited signal can be reconstructed exactly from its samples by convolution with a sinc. | Sampling theorem.
2 | So the value at any intermediate instant μ is a weighted sum of neighbouring samples, with weights sinc( k  − μ). | Evaluate the reconstruction at that instant. The weights depend on μ.
3 | For a fixed μ this is one FIR filter, and a set of L fixed filters gives L discrete phases. | The polyphase interpolator: fine when the phase set is known in advance.
4 | Timing recovery needs a μ that varies continuously and is not known in advance. | The sampling phase drifts with the frequency offset between transmitter and receiver, by an amount nobody can tabulate.
5 | Farrow's insight: approximate each weight as a polynomial in μ , h k (μ) = Σ c k,m μ m . | Then the interpolator becomes M +1 fixed FIR filters whose outputs are combined by Horner's rule in μ.
6 | The coefficients are constant; only μ changes. | So the multipliers can be constant-coefficient, and a continuously variable delay costs M general multiplies rather than a new filter per phase.

[Table 260. Measured worst-case error of a cubic Farrow interpolator against input frequency, swept over all fractional delays]
Normalised frequency | Fraction of Nyquist | Max |error| | Equivalent SNR (dB)
0.02 | 0.04 | 5.84×10 -6 | 104.7
0.05 | 0.1 | 2.24×10 -4 | 73.01
0.1 | 0.2 | 0.00353 | 49.03
0.2 | 0.4 | 0.0487 | 26.25
0.35 | 0.7 | 0.361 | 8.843
0.45 | 0.9 | 0.758 | 2.409

Computed directly by comparing against the exact sine. The interpolator is excellent well below Nyquist and degrades rapidly above about a third of it, which is the whole reason receivers oversample: the interpolator's accuracy, not the sampling theorem, sets the required rate.

[그림] Figure 26. Cubic Farrow interpolation accuracy. Choosing the oversampling ratio is choosing a point on this curve.

Worked example 20. How much oversampling does a link need for its interpolator?

Given. A receiver needs the interpolator to contribute no more than −40 dB of error, and the signal occupies the full symbol bandwidth.

Method. Read the required normalised frequency off the measured sweep and convert to an oversampling ratio.

Target interpolator SNR | 40 dB
Normalised frequency achieving it (from the sweep) | between 0.1 and 0.2
Oversampling ratio needed | roughly 5–10× the signal bandwidth
At 2 samples per symbol, signal edge sits at | 0.25
Verdict at 2 samples/symbol with a cubic | marginal — use a higher-order Farrow or more oversampling
Cost of a higher order | one more fixed FIR and one more Horner stage

How this is got wrong. By choosing the oversampling ratio from the sampling theorem alone. Nyquist says two samples per symbol suffices to represent the signal; it says nothing about reconstructing an intermediate sample with a short polynomial. The interpolator, not the theorem, sets the rate, and the trade is between ADC power (which scales with rate) and interpolator order (which scales with area). Modern high-speed receivers push toward the low end and pay with higher-order interpolators because the ADC is the expensive part.

장: X22. Resampling and Timing Recovery, Worked
절: X22.2 The timing-recovery loop around it
글:
X22.2 The timing-recovery loop around it

[Table 261. The pieces of a digital timing recovery loop]
Block | Job | Choice that matters
Interpolator | Produce a sample at the wanted instant | Order, from the sweep above
Timing error detector | Estimate how wrong the instant is | Gardner needs 2 samples/symbol and is modulation-independent; Mueller–Müller works at 1 sample/symbol and is the standard in high-speed links for exactly that reason
Loop filter | Proportional plus integral | The proportional term sets bandwidth, the integral term removes frequency offset
NCO / phase accumulator | Turn the filtered error into μ and a strobe | Its wrap handling is where the sample-slip logic lives

Why the integral term is not optional, stated
 precisely. A proportional-only loop has finite DC gain, so a constant frequency
 offset between transmitter and receiver produces a constant residual phase error
 — the loop settles to the wrong place and stays there. Adding an integrator
 gives infinite DC gain and drives the steady-state error to zero for a step in
 frequency, which is exactly the disturbance present. The cost is a second-order loop
 with the usual stability question, and the usual answer: the damping factor sets the
 overshoot and the natural frequency sets the tracking bandwidth, both bounded above by
 the loop delay from Part X21. Every CDR, PLL and equaliser adaptation in this
 book has this same second-order structure, and recognising it saves deriving the
 stability condition four times.

Problem. Why do high-speed SerDes receivers use Mueller–Müller timing detection rather than Gardner, when Gardner is simpler?
Solution. Because Gardner requires two samples per symbol and at 50 GBd that doubles the ADC rate, which is the single most expensive resource in the receiver. Mueller–Müller estimates the timing error from one sample per symbol and the decisions, using the correlation between the current decision and the previous sample; it is decision-directed, so it needs the decisions to be mostly correct, which is fine in a working link and is a chicken-and-egg problem during acquisition. The practical consequences are two: acquisition needs help — a frequency-acquisition aid, a training pattern, or a temporary alternative detector — and the detector's characteristic depends on the channel response, so the loop gain is not a constant of the design but varies with the equaliser state. That second point is the interacting-loops hazard of Part X21 in its most common real form: the timing loop's gain depends on the equaliser, and the equaliser's error depends on the timing.

장: X23. Complex Analysis and Transforms, for People Who Build Them
절: X23. Complex Analysis and Transforms, for People Who Build Them — 들어가며

X23. Complex Analysis and Transforms, for People Who Build Them

Every filter, every equaliser and every control loop in this book is
 described by a rational function of a complex variable. The mathematics is taught
 abstractly and used concretely, and the gap between the two is where designers lose
 confidence. This part closes it: each result is stated, derived, and then used to
 predict a number that is measured.

[그림] Figure 27. The z -plane. The unit circle is not a convention — it is the set of points where z = e jω , which is exactly the frequency response.

장: X23. Complex Analysis and Transforms, for People Who Build Them
절: X23.1 Why the z -transform is the right tool
글:
X23.1 Why the z-transform is the right tool

From a difference equation to a rational function

 | Step | Justification
1 | A linear time-invariant system obeys y [ n ] = Σ b k x [ n − k ] − Σ a k y [ n − k ]. | The general recursive filter. This is also literally the RTL : each delayed term is a register.
2 | Define X ( z ) = Σ x [ n ] z − n . | The z -transform. The only property we need is the next line.
3 | A delay by one sample multiplies the transform by z −1 . | Substitute and shift the summation index. So a register is a multiplication , which turns a difference equation into algebra.
4 | Therefore H ( z ) = Y / X = (Σ b k z − k ) / (1 + Σ a k z − k ). | Divide. The transfer function is a ratio of polynomials.
5 | Its zeros are where the numerator vanishes; its poles where the denominator does. | And the factored form tells you the response at a glance, which the coefficient list does not.
6 | Evaluating on z = e jω gives the frequency response; a zero near the circle makes a notch, a pole near it makes a peak . | Because | H | is a ratio of distances from the evaluation point to the zeros and poles. This geometric reading is the single most useful skill in filter design and it takes ten minutes to acquire.

[Table 262. Measured peak and bandwidth of a two-pole resonator as the pole radius approaches the unit circle (pole angle π/4)]
Pole radius r | Distance to circle | Peak | H | | Peak at ω/π | −3 dB bandwidth /π | Prediction 2(1− r )/π×π
0.5 | 0.5 | 1.886 | 0.1548 | 0.3849 | 1
0.8 | 0.2 | 3.928 | 0.242 | 0.1534 | 0.4
0.9 | 0.1 | 7.443 | 0.2481 | 0.06789 | 0.2
0.95 | 0.05 | 14.5 | 0.2496 | 0.03248 | 0.1
0.99 | 0.01 | 71.05 | 0.2501 | 0.006105 | 0.02

Computed by evaluating the transfer function on 4096 points of the unit circle. The last two columns are an independent cross-check: the textbook approximation says the bandwidth is about 2(1−r) radians, and the measurement confirms it as r → 1 and departs from it when the pole is far from the circle, exactly as the approximation's derivation requires.

Why this matters in fixed point, which is where the
 theory earns its keep. Quantising the coefficients moves the poles. For a
 high-order filter in direct form, the pole positions are an extremely sensitive
 function of the coefficients — the map from coefficients to roots is
 ill-conditioned, and for a narrow-band filter of order 10 or more, a few bits of
 coefficient error can move a pole outside the unit circle and make the filter
 unstable. This, not noise, is the reason high-order IIR filters are implemented as
 cascaded biquads: in a second-order section there are only two coefficients per
 pole pair and the root sensitivity is bounded. The structure choice is dictated by
 numerical conditioning, and a specification that says ‘10th-order elliptic’
 without saying ‘as five biquads’ has not specified an
 implementation.

[Table 263. Measured largest pole radius after quantising a Butterworth lowpass (cutoff 0.05×Nyquist) to 12 fraction bits]
Order | Direct form: max |pole| | Direct form verdict | Biquad cascade: max |pole| | Cascade verdict
2 | 0.894864 | stable | 0.894864 | stable
4 | 0.940012 | stable | 0.941787 | stable
6 | 1 | unstable | 0.96027 | stable
8 | 1.20313 | unstable | 0.969883 | stable
10 | 1.36193 | unstable | 0.975781 | stable

Roots computed from the quantised coefficients at 12 fraction bits. Direct form loses stability at high order while the cascade does not, on exactly the same filter with exactly the same word length — the cascade column is stable on every row, which is the finding, not a stuck measurement. The difference is entirely structural.
