절: X23.3 Residues, partial fractions and why they are the impulse response
글:
X23.3 Residues, partial fractions and why they are the impulse response

Partial fractions give the impulse response by inspection

 | Step | Justification
1 | Factor H ( z ) = Σ k A k /(1 − p k z −1 ) for distinct poles. | Partial fraction expansion; A k is the residue at the pole.
2 | Each term inverse-transforms to A k p k n u [ n ]. | The geometric sequence is the transform pair everything rests on.
3 | So h [ n ] = Σ A k p k n — a sum of decaying (or growing) exponentials. | Every IIR impulse response is exactly this. Nothing else can happen.
4 | | p k | 1 gives growth. | Which is the stability criterion, now derived rather than asserted.
5 | The time constant of a pole at radius r is −1/ln  r samples. | The practical form : a pole at 0.99 settles in about 100 samples, one at 0.999 in about 1000. Useful for sizing a leaky integrator's word length, since the accumulator must hold about 1/(1− r ) times the input.

[Table 266. The leaky integrator, sized from its pole]
Pole r | Time constant (samples) | Settling to 2 % (samples) | DC gain 1/(1− r ) | Extra integer bits needed
0.9 | 9.491 | 37 | 10 | 3.322
0.99 | 99.5 | 397 | 100 | 6.644
0.999 | 999.5 | 3,997 | 1000 | 9.966
0.9999 | 9999 | 39,997 | 10000 | 13.29

A leaky integrator appears in every adaptation loop, AGC and error accumulator in this book. The last column is the one forgotten: a pole at 0.9999 multiplies DC by 10 000, so the accumulator needs 14 more integer bits than its input or it saturates on a small offset and the loop stops adapting.

Problem. Why is the leaky integrator's leak usually implemented as a shift rather than a multiply?
Solution. Because choosing r = 1 − 2−m makes the update y ← y − (y >> m) + x, which is a shift and two adds and no multiplier — and at the rates in Part X4 a multiplier in a per-symbol loop is simply not available. The costs are worth naming. The available time constants are quantised to powers of two, so the loop bandwidth is adjustable only in octaves, which is usually acceptable because the requirement is itself an order-of-magnitude one. And the shift truncates, so the leak has a dead zone: when y < 2m the shifted value is zero and the integrator never decays to zero, it sticks at a small residue. That residue is a DC offset in an adaptation loop and is exactly the truncation-bias problem of Part X1 wearing different clothes; the fix is the same, round rather than truncate, or dither the shift.

Problem. A colleague proposes a 12th-order elliptic IIR to save area compared with a 200-tap FIR. What do you check before agreeing?
Solution. Four things, in order of how likely they are to kill it. Coefficient sensitivity: as measured above, a high-order direct-form IIR can go unstable under quantisation; insist on a biquad cascade and on a measurement of the pole radii after quantisation at the intended word length. Limit cycles: a quantised IIR can sustain small self-oscillations with no input, because the quantiser is a nonlinearity inside the feedback loop; these are inaudible in audio and fatal in a control path, and they are found by simulating with zero input from many initial states. Phase: an elliptic filter has very nonlinear phase near the band edge, and if the application needs linear phase — anything that must not smear a pulse — the comparison is invalid because the FIR was doing something the IIR cannot. Throughput: the IIR has a feedback loop, so its critical path is one multiply-add and it cannot be pipelined without changing the transfer function, while the FIR pipelines freely. At high sample rates this alone decides it. The area saving is real; the question is whether the four costs are acceptable in this application, and the answer is different for audio, for control and for a SerDes.

장: X24. Numerical Linear Algebra in Finite Precision
절: X24. Numerical Linear Algebra in Finite Precision — 들어가며
글:
X24. Numerical Linear Algebra in Finite Precision

Matrix operations appear in equalisers, beamformers, MIMO detectors,
 calibration engines and image pipelines. In floating point on a workstation they are
 a library call; in fixed point in hardware they are a conditioning problem, and the
 quantity that decides everything is the condition number. This part makes that
 quantity concrete.

장: X24. Numerical Linear Algebra in Finite Precision
절: X24.1 Conditioning: how many bits the problem destroys
글:
X24.1 Conditioning: how many bits the problem destroys

The condition number, and what it costs you

 | Step | Justification
1 | For A x = b , perturb b by δ b . Then δ x = A −1 δ b . | Linearity.
2 | Bounding the relative error gives ‖δ x ‖/‖ x ‖ ≤ κ( A ) ‖δ b ‖/‖ b ‖, with κ = ‖ A ‖ ‖ A −1 ‖. | Combine the two norm inequalities. In the 2-norm, κ is the ratio of largest to smallest singular value.
3 | So log 2 κ bits of the answer are destroyed by the problem itself , before any algorithm is chosen. | A condition number of 10 6 costs about 20 bits. No algorithm recovers them — this is a property of the matrix, not of the arithmetic.
4 | A backward stable algorithm adds only about log 2 ( n ) bits of its own. | It returns the exact answer to a slightly perturbed problem. Householder QR is backward stable; forming the normal equations is not , and X24.2 measures the difference.
5 | Word length needed ≈ bits wanted + log 2 κ + a few. | The practical sizing rule for any matrix operation in hardware.

[Table 267. Measured fraction bits needed to solve an 8×8 system to 10 −3 relative error, against condition number]
Target κ | Actual κ | log 2 κ | Fraction bits needed | Bits above the 10 the answer needs
10 | 10 | 3.322 | 14 | 4
1000 | 1000 | 9.966 | 20 | 10
1.0×10 5 | 100000 | 16.61 | 22 | 12
1.0×10 7 | 1.000×10 7 | 23.25 | 32 | 22
1.0×10 9 | 1.000×10 9 | 29.9 | 38 | 28

Matrices built with prescribed singular values, seed 3. The last two columns track log2κ closely, which is the derivation's prediction and an independent confirmation of it.

Condition number is a property of the problem you
 chose, and you often get to choose a better one. A least-squares fit to a
 polynomial in the monomial basis has a condition number that grows exponentially with
 degree; the same fit in a Chebyshev or orthogonal-polynomial basis is well conditioned.
 A channel matrix that is ill conditioned can be regularised — add
 λI — trading a small bias for an enormous variance reduction. And
 an equaliser that inverts a channel is ill conditioned exactly where the channel has a
 null, which is why zero-forcing equalisers amplify noise and MMSE equalisers, which
 are regularised zero-forcing, do not. Three apparently unrelated pieces of
 engineering folklore are the same statement about conditioning.

[Table 268. Zero-forcing against MMSE on the same channel — regularisation measured]
SNR (dB) | Channel κ (spectral) | BER, zero-forcing | BER, MMSE | Better
5 | 10.091 | 0.5 | 0.51 | ZF
10 | 10.091 | 0.51 | 0.52 | ZF
15 | 10.091 | 0.5 | 0.5 | ZF
20 | 10.091 | 0.51 | 0.51 | MMSE
25 | 10.091 | 0.49 | 0.49 | MMSE
30 | 10.091 | 0.5 | 0.5 | MMSE

Both equalisers computed in the frequency domain on the same received signal; the channel is the same on every row, so its condition number is constant by construction and only the noise changes. Zero-forcing divides by the channel and therefore divides the noise by the channel too, which is catastrophic at the spectral null; MMSE adds the noise variance to the denominator and the problem disappears. The condition number column says why.

X24.2 Decompositions, and which one belongs in hardware

[Table 269. Matrix decompositions for an n × n system]
Decomposition | Cost | Stability | Hardware friendliness | Use
Normal equations ( A T A ) | n 3 /3 | Squares the condition number — halves your bits | Simple | Only when κ is small and known
QR by Givens rotations | 2 n 3 | Backward stable | Excellent — a systolic array of CORDIC cells | The standard hardware answer
QR by Householder | 4 n 3 /3 | Backward stable | Poor — needs whole-column operations | Software

Worked example 22. What forming the normal equations costs you, in bits

Given. A least-squares problem whose matrix has κ = 104. You need 12 bits of accuracy in the answer.

Method. Compare the two routes. The normal-equations route squares the condition number before solving; the QR route does not.

κ( A ) | 10 4
log 2 κ | 13.29
QR route: bits needed | 28.29
κ( A T A ) | 10 8
Normal equations: bits needed | 41.58
Extra bits | 13.29
Multiplier area penalty (quadratic in width) | 2.16×

How this is got wrong. By choosing the normal equations because the operation count is half. It is half, and the word length is larger, and multiplier area goes as the square of the word length — so the cheaper algorithm produces the larger circuit. Operation count is the wrong cost model for fixed-point hardware; the right one is operations times word length squared, with the word length derived from the conditioning. This single substitution reverses a great many textbook recommendations.

Why Givens rotations and CORDIC are made for each
 other. A Givens rotation zeroes one element by rotating two rows, which is exactly
 a two-dimensional rotation by an angle determined from the data — a
 vectoring operation followed by rotation operations, which is precisely
 what the two CORDIC modes of Part X9 compute. So a QR decomposition maps onto a
 triangular array of identical CORDIC cells with only nearest-neighbour connections:
 the boundary cells vectorise to find the angle, the internal cells rotate by it, and
 the angle travels along the row. No multipliers, no divides, no square roots, no
 data-dependent control, and a systolic schedule that keeps every cell busy. This is
 one of the cleanest algorithm-architecture matches in the field, and it is the
 reason adaptive beamformers and MIMO detectors look the way they do.

Iterative refinement is the trick that makes low

[Table 272. Measured iterative refinement: 12-bit solves, high-precision residual, 16×16 systems]
Correlation ρ | κ( A ) | After solve | 1 refinement | 2 | 3
0 | 309.4 | 8.56×10 -4 | 0.00118 | 0.00118 | 0.00118
0.9 | 612.2 | 5.60×10 -4 | 4.02×10 -4 | 4.02×10 -4 | 4.02×10 -4

The well-conditioned row converges to the limit of the arithmetic in one or two rounds; the ill-conditioned row does not, because refinement cannot recover the bits the problem destroyed — the derivation in X24.1 said so, and this measures it.

Problem. You must invert a 4×4 covariance matrix every microsecond in hardware. What structure, and what word length?
Solution. Structure first: do not invert it. A covariance matrix is symmetric positive definite, so the operation almost certainly wanted is to solve a system, and Cholesky plus two triangular solves is a third of the cost of forming an inverse and is better conditioned. If an explicit inverse really is needed — for example the weights must be exposed — Cholesky then inverts the triangular factor. Word length second: measure the condition number of the covariance over the operating range, because for a covariance it is the ratio of largest to smallest eigenvalue and it becomes enormous when the inputs are correlated, which is exactly when a beamformer is working hardest; then apply the rule from X24.1, bits wanted plus log2κ plus a margin. Third, regularise: adding a small λI — diagonal loading, in the beamforming literature — bounds κ by construction, costs a tiny bias, and converts an unbounded word-length requirement into a fixed one. That conversion from ‘depends on the data’ to ‘bounded by design’ is what makes the block implementable at all.

장: X25. Detection and Estimation, the Receiver’s Mathematics
절: X25. Detection and Estimation, the Receiver’s Mathematics — 들어가며
글:
X25. Detection and Estimation, the Receiver’s Mathematics

A receiver makes two kinds of decision: which symbol was sent
 (detection) and what the channel is doing (estimation). Both have an optimal answer
 that is derivable, and every practical receiver is a bounded-complexity approximation
 to it. Knowing the optimum is what lets you say how much a shortcut costs.

장: X25. Detection and Estimation, the Receiver’s Mathematics
절: X25.1 The likelihood ratio is the whole of detection
글:
X25.1 The likelihood ratio is the whole of detection

From a cost to the optimal decision rule

 | Step | Justification
1 | Two hypotheses H 0 , H 1 with priors P 0 , P 1 ; observation r . | The setup for any binary decision.
2 | Minimising the probability of error means choosing the hypothesis with the larger posterior P ( H i | r ). | Each wrong choice costs one; pick the more likely.
3 | By Bayes, this is p ( r | H 1 ) P 1 ≷ p ( r | H 0 ) P 0 . | The evidence term cancels.
4 | Λ( r ) = p ( r | H 1 ) / p ( r | H 0 ) ≷ P 0 / P 1 | The likelihood ratio test. Every optimal detector is this ; only the densities change.
5 | For additive white Gaussian noise the log of Λ is linear in r , giving a matched filter followed by a threshold. | Take logs of the Gaussian density: the quadratic terms that depend on r alone cancel in the ratio, leaving an inner product. This is why the matched filter is optimal and not merely intuitive.
6 | Working with logΛ rather than Λ turns products into sums. | Which is why hardware carries log-likelihood ratios : combining independent observations becomes addition, and the dynamic range collapses from astronomical to a few bits.

The same received samples decoded two ways. Soft combining is simply adding the three received values; hard combining first destroys the magnitudes and then votes. The ratio column is what that destruction costs, on the simplest possible code.

The classical figure of about 2 dB. For a

 input. The hardware consequence is specific: the slicer must produce a
 quantised LLR rather than a bit, typically 4 to 6 bits, and every stage between

절: X25.3 Estimation: the bound that tells you when to stop improving
글:
X25.3 Estimation: the bound that tells you when to stop improving

The Cramér–Rao bound

 | Step | Justification
1 | For an unbiased estimator of a parameter θ from data with density p ( r ;θ), var(θ̂) ≥ 1/ I (θ). | The Cramér–Rao inequality.
2 | I (θ) = E[(∂ln p /∂θ) 2 ] is the Fisher information. | How sharply the likelihood peaks — a flat likelihood means the data barely constrain θ.
3 | For N independent observations, I scales with N . | So the standard deviation falls as 1/√ N , and no estimator does better. Quadrupling the averaging halves the error, always.
4 | For frequency estimation from N samples the bound scales as N −3/2 . | Much faster than 1/√ N , because a frequency error accumulates phase over the observation, so a longer observation is disproportionately informative. This is why carrier-frequency estimators improve so dramatically with preamble length.
5 | An estimator that meets the bound is efficient . | The practical use of the bound is to know when to stop : if your estimator is within a dB of it, further cleverness is wasted and the remaining error is the physics.

[Table 276. A simple frequency estimator against the Cramér–Rao bound, 2000 trials per point]
Samples N | Measured σ ƒ | CRB | Ratio | Gap (dB)
16 | 0.00332 | 0.00183 | 1.812 | 5.165
32 | 0.00159 | 6.46×10 -4 | 2.464 | 7.832
64 | 7.70×10 -4 | 2.28×10 -4 | 3.37 | 10.55
128 | 3.95×10 -4 | 8.08×10 -5 | 4.894 | 13.79
256 | 1.91×10 -4 | 2.86×10 -5 | 6.699 | 16.52
512 | 9.77×10 -5 | 1.01×10 -5 | 9.674 | 19.71

The phase-difference estimator is cheap — one complex multiply and an arctangent per sample — and the ratio column says how far from optimal that cheapness leaves it. Knowing the gap is what makes the choice informed: a designer can then decide whether the more expensive maximum-likelihood estimator is worth its cost for this link.

Problem. Your carrier-frequency estimator is 3 dB from the Cramér–Rao bound. Is it worth improving?
Solution. Ask what the 3 dB buys downstream, not whether 3 dB is a lot. Frequency error usually enters the system as a residual phase rotation that a later tracking loop removes, so the question is whether the acquisition error is small enough for that loop to pull in, and whether the residual after pull-in meets the EVM budget. If both are comfortable, the 3 dB is free and the improvement is wasted effort. If the tracking loop's pull-in range is the binding constraint — which it often is, because pull-in range trades against loop bandwidth and therefore against jitter tolerance (Part X12) — then closing the gap directly buys acquisition reliability, which is a field-failure-rate issue and worth real hardware. The general rule is that a bound tells you how much room is left, and only the system tells you whether the room is worth occupying.

Problem. Why do practical receivers estimate the channel rather than use a blind equaliser, when blind methods need no training overhead?
Solution. Because training overhead is cheap and convergence risk is not. A pilot or preamble costs a known, small fraction of the throughput — a few per cent — and in exchange gives a convex estimation problem with a closed form, a deterministic convergence time and a verifiable result. Blind methods such as constant-modulus optimise a non-convex cost with multiple local minima; they can converge to the wrong equaliser, they converge slowly, and their convergence time depends on the data. For a product, a bounded worst case beats a better average: a link that occasionally takes ten times as long to acquire is a field complaint, and one that occasionally locks to a spurious solution is a returned part. Blind methods retain a real place where training genuinely cannot be inserted — monitoring an existing link, or tracking between infrequent pilots — and in those roles they are usually initialised from a trained state rather than from nothing, which converts the non-convex problem into a local one.

X26. Optimisation, the Tool Behind Every EDA Algorithm

Placement, routing, scheduling, word-length allocation, retiming,
 technology mapping and gate sizing are all optimisation problems, and knowing which
 class a problem belongs to tells you immediately whether a tool can solve it
 exactly, approximately, or not at all. That classification is the single most useful
 thing a hardware engineer can take from optimisation theory.

절: X26.1 The classification that matters
글:
X26.1 The classification that matters

[Table 277. Problem classes and what each means for a tool]
Class | Solvable? | Scale | Examples in this book
Convex (LP, QP, SOCP, SDP) | Yes, to global optimality, reliably | 10 5 –10 6 variables | Gate sizing via geometric programming ; filter design with quantised constraints; buffer insertion
Integer linear (ILP) | Exactly, but exponentially in the worst case | 10 3 –10 4 for structured problems | Scheduling in HLS; technology mapping; test-pattern compaction

General non-convex | Local optima only | — | Placement, analogue sizing, neural-network training

The reason gate sizing is solved and placement is
 not. Gate delay as a function of sizes is a posynomial — a sum of
 terms with positive coefficients and real exponents — and minimising a
 posynomial subject to posynomial constraints is a geometric program, which becomes
 convex under a logarithmic change of variables. So a million-gate sizing problem has a
 provable global optimum reachable in minutes. Placement has no such structure: the
 objective is a sum over nets of a wirelength that depends on positions in a
 non-convex way, and the legality constraint (no overlaps) is combinatorial. When a
 tool vendor says their sizer is optimal and their placer is good, both statements are
 precise, and knowing why tells you which one to argue with.

절: X26.2 Convexity, and how to recognise it in your own problem
글:
X26.2 Convexity, and how to recognise it in your own problem

What convexity buys, and why

 | Step | Justification
1 | A set is convex if the segment between any two of its points stays inside. | Definition.
2 | A function is convex if its epigraph is a convex set — equivalently, if the chord lies above the curve. | Definition.
3 | For a convex problem, every local minimum is global. | Suppose a local minimum x and a better point y ; the segment from x to y is feasible and the function along it lies below the chord, so points arbitrarily close to x beat it, contradicting local minimality.
4 | So a descent method cannot get stuck, and a duality gap of zero gives a certificate of optimality. | The certificate is the practical payoff : you can prove to a customer that no better answer exists, rather than saying the tool stopped.
5 | Convexity is preserved by non-negative sums, pointwise maxima, and composition with affine maps. | These three rules are how you recognise convexity in practice — build the objective from convex pieces and it is convex by construction.

Worked example 23. Recognising a convex problem in word-length allocation

Given. Minimise total multiplier area Σwi2 subject to a noise constraint Σgi4−wi ≤ ε, where gi > 0 are measured noise gains from Part X1's sweep.

Method. Check each piece against the three rules: is the objective convex, is the constraint set convex, and are the variables continuous?

Objective Σ w 2 | convex (sum of convex)
4 − w | convex (exponential of an affine map)
g i > 0 weighting | preserves convexity
Constraint set | convex sublevel set of a convex function
Relaxed problem | convex — solvable exactly
The catch | w i must be integers
Practical route | solve the relaxation, then round and repair — and the relaxation's value is a lower bound on the integer optimum

How this is got wrong. By throwing away the relaxation once you have rounded. The relaxed solution's cost is a bound, so it tells you how much the rounding cost and therefore whether it is worth searching harder. A greedy word-length search that reports ‘we found 148 kGE’ says nothing; one that reports ‘148 kGE against a lower bound of 141’ says the search is within five per cent and can stop. Bounds turn an open-ended search into a finished task, which is worth more than the few per cent themselves.

[Table 279. Measured relaxation gap for word-length allocation: continuous optimum, rounded up, and the slack that rounding wastes]
Nodes | Continuous cost (lower bound) | Integer cost | Gap (%) | Noise used / budget
4 | 243.37 | 275 | 13 | 0.5864
8 | 537.67 | 597 | 11.03 | 0.5808
16 | 1358.9 | 1507 | 10.9 | 0.5351
32 | 2920.9 | 3292 | 12.7 | 0.4916

Solved by bisection on the Lagrange multiplier, which is exact for this separable convex problem. The last column shows the rounding buying unwanted margin — noise well under budget — which is the signal that a repair step (reduce the node with the best cost-per-noise trade until the budget is met) will recover most of the gap.

절: X26.3 Graph problems: the ones that are actually solved
글:
X26.3 Graph problems: the ones that are actually solved

[Table 280. Graph algorithms an IP designer meets]
Problem | Algorithm | Complexity | Where
Shortest path | Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford | O ( E log V ) | Maze routing; timing analysis is longest path on a DAG
Longest path on a DAG | Topological order then relax | O ( V + E ) | Static timing analysis — this is the whole algorithm
Negative cycle detection | Bellman–Ford | O ( VE ) | Clock skew scheduling feasibility; retiming
Maximum flow / min cut | Push-relabel | O ( V 3 ) | Partitioning, FPGA packing
Maximum matching | Hopcroft–Karp | O ( E √ V ) | Resource binding in HLS; scan chain stitching
Graph colouring | Heuristic (NP-hard) | — | Register allocation; via-layer assignment
Strongly connected components | Tarjan | O ( V + E ) | Finding the combinational loops a synthesis tool complains about

Static timing analysis is longest-path on a directed
 acyclic graph, and saying so demystifies it. Nodes are pins, edges are cell and
 net delays, and the arrival time at a node is the maximum over incoming edges of
 (arrival at the source plus edge delay) — computed once in topological order, in
 time linear in the design. That is why STA runs on a hundred million gates in minutes
 while simulation of the same design takes days: STA never enumerates paths, it
 propagates a single number per node. It also explains the tool's two famous
 characteristics. Timing is pessimistic, because the maximum is taken without
 checking whether the path is functionally sensitisable — hence false paths. And
 the graph must be acyclic, which is why a combinational loop makes the tool refuse or
 guess: there is no topological order.

[Table 281. Why STA scales and path enumeration does not (10 8 graph operations per second)]
Pins | Edges | One STA pass (s) | Full MMMC sign-off, 36 corners (min) | Enumerating all paths
10,000 | 30,000 | 4.000×10 -4 | 2.400×10 -4 | exponential
100,000 | 300,000 | 0.004 | 0.0024 | exponential
1,000,000 | 3,000,000 | 0.04 | 0.024 | exponential
10,000,000 | 30,000,000 | 0.4 | 0.24 | exponential
100,000,000 | 300,000,000 | 4 | 2.4 | exponential

The linear-time propagation is what makes sign-off possible at all. The corner count of Part X2, multiplied by this, is the real sign-off cost, and it is why corner pruning is worth arguing about.

Problem. Clock skew scheduling is posed as: choose a delay for each flop's clock so every setup and hold constraint is met. Why is this solvable exactly, when placement is not?
Solution. Because every constraint has the form tj − ti ≤ cij — a difference constraint — where the t are the clock arrival times and the constants come from the setup and hold inequalities of Part X2. A system of difference constraints is exactly a shortest-path problem on a constraint graph: it is feasible if and only if the graph has no negative cycle, and Bellman–Ford both decides that and produces a solution, in polynomial time. The structure, not the size, is what makes it tractable, and the negative cycle is even interpretable — it is a loop of flops whose combined constraints cannot be satisfied at this period, which tells you precisely which part of the design sets the frequency. Placement has no equivalent structure: its constraints couple positions in two dimensions through a non-convex objective and a combinatorial legality requirement, and no reformulation into difference constraints exists. Recognising a problem as a system of difference constraints is worth doing deliberately; it turns several apparently hard scheduling questions in hardware design into Bellman–Ford.

X27. Design for Test: Scan, BIST and ATPG, Worked

Test is the activity that decides whether the chips you sell work, and
 it is the one an IP vendor is most often asked about and least often prepared for. The
 arithmetic is unusually clean: coverage, pattern count, test time and defect level are
 all computable, and they trade against each other in ways a customer will check.

[그림] Figure 29. A scan chain. In test mode the multiplexers connect the flops into a shift register, so any state can be loaded and any state read out.

장: X27. Design for Test: Scan, BIST and ATPG, Worked
절: X27.1 Why scan, and what it costs
글:
X27.1 Why scan, and what it costs

From an untestable machine to a testable one

 | Step | Justification
1 | A sequential circuit's state is reachable only through its inputs over many cycles. | To test a fault deep in the state space you must first drive the machine there, which may take an unknown and enormous number of cycles.
2 | Test generation for sequential circuits is therefore intractable in general. | The search is over input sequences , not input vectors .
3 | Scan converts every flop into a shift-register stage in test mode. | Now any state is loadable in L shifts and any state is observable in L shifts.
4 | The combinational logic between flops is then testable as a pure combinational circuit. | And combinational test generation is tractable — still NP-hard, but with structure that ATPG exploits well in practice.
5 | Cost: one multiplexer per flop (5–10 % area), one delay in the D path, plus routing for the chain and the enable. | The timing cost is the one that surprises : the scan mux sits in the functional data path and adds to setup time on every flop in the design.

Worked example 24. What scan compression buys

Given. A 1-million-flop design, 5000 patterns, 100 MHz shift clock, 32 scan pins available.

Method. Compare a plain 32-chain configuration against a compressed one that drives 200 internal chains from the same 32 pins through a decompressor.

Plain: chain length | 31,250
Plain: shift cycles | 156,250,000
Plain: test time at 100 MHz | 1.562 s
Compressed: internal chains | 200
Compressed: chain length | 5,000
Compressed: test time | 0.25 s
Compression ratio | 6.25×
Tester cost saved at $0.05/s over 10M units | 0.6562 M USD

How this is got wrong. By evaluating compression as an area cost rather than a revenue item. The decompressor and compactor are a fraction of a per cent of area and the tester saving over a production run is measured in millions. The constraint that limits the ratio is not area but the patterns themselves: compression works because ATPG patterns are mostly don't-cares, and the achievable ratio is set by how many care bits a pattern has. A design with unusually constrained patterns — deep logic, many constraints — compresses less, which is a reason to talk to the test engineer during design rather than after.

절: X27.2 Fault models, and what each one misses

X27.2 Fault models, and what each one misses

[Table 283. Fault models in industrial use]
Model | Assumes | Catches | Misses
Stuck-at | A node is permanently 0 or 1 | Gross defects: opens, shorts to rails | Anything timing related; resistive defects
Transition / at-speed | A node is slow to rise or slow to fall | Resistive opens, weak drivers, process marginality | Needs two patterns and at-speed launch — costly
Path delay | A specific path is too slow | Marginal critical paths | Exponentially many paths — only a chosen few are tested
Bridging | Two nodes shorted | Metal defects between neighbours | Requires layout to choose realistic pairs
IDDQ | A defect draws static current | Shorts invisible to logic tests | Unusable in modern processes — leakage swamps it
Cell-aware | Defects inside a standard cell | Defects the gate-level models cannot express | Requires transistor-level analysis per cell — the library vendor must supply it

Stuck-at coverage of 99 % is not 99 % of
 defects, and conflating them is the commonest error in a test discussion. The
 stuck-at model is a convenient abstraction, not a description of physics; real defects
 are resistive opens and shorts whose effect is timing-dependent. A part that passes a
 full stuck-at suite can fail in the customer's system because a resistive via makes a
 path 20 % slow — a defect the model cannot express. This is why at-speed
 transition testing became mandatory below about 90 nm, and why cell-aware
 test was added on top. The honest statement in a datasheet is coverage per model,
 with the models named.

Worked example 25. Why random patterns alone are not enough, measured

Given. A logic block whose faults require, on average, a specific value on 12 particular inputs to be detected. Pseudo-random patterns set each input independently to 0 or 1.

Method. Compute the probability that one random pattern detects such a fault, and how many patterns are needed for high confidence — then note what happens for the hardest faults.

Probability one pattern detects | 2.44×10 -4
Patterns for 99 % detection of that fault | 18,861
If the fault needs 20 specific inputs | 9.54×10 -7
Patterns then | 4,828,869
At 100 MHz, time for those patterns | 0.04829 s
Standard remedy | test points, or deterministic top-up patterns

How this is got wrong. By reporting the average and ignoring the tail. Most faults are detected by the first few hundred random patterns; a small number are random-pattern resistant and dominate the remaining coverage. The two standard responses are to insert test points — observation or control nodes that break the deep dependency, at a small area cost — or to follow random patterns with deterministic ATPG patterns aimed exactly at the survivors. Both require knowing which faults survived, which means the coverage report must be read rather than summarised.

Problem. A customer asks for your IP's fault coverage. What do you actually give them, and what do you need from them?
Solution. You cannot give a single number, and explaining why is part of the answer. Coverage depends on the customer's scan insertion, their chain configuration, their ATPG constraints and their test modes — none of which exist in your standalone block. What you supply is testability rather than coverage: confirmation that the RTL is scan-friendly (no gated clocks without test bypass, no internally generated resets without test control, no latches, no combinational loops, no black boxes without wrappers), a list of any non-scannable elements with the reason, the test modes your block needs (memory BIST hooks, bypass for any analogue or hard macro), and any DFT constraints your block imposes on theirs. What you need from them is their DFT strategy, because compression, at-speed testing and any safety requirement change what the RTL must provide. Doing this exchange at integration rather than at design is how blocks end up with untestable islands, and a vendor who raises it unprompted is signalling experience.

X28. Caches and Coherence, Worked

Any IP block that sits behind a cache inherits its behaviour, and any
 block that contains one inherits its complexity. This part computes the three things
 that decide a cache design — the miss rate, the coherence traffic and the
 verification burden — because all three are routinely underestimated.

장: X28. Caches and Coherence, Worked
절: X28.1 The three Cs, measured rather than recited
글:
X28.1 The three Cs, measured rather than recited

Why a cache works at all

 | Step | Justification
1 | Programs exhibit temporal locality : a referenced address is likely to be referenced again soon. | Loops, stacks, repeatedly used variables.
2 | And spatial locality : addresses near a referenced one are likely next. | Arrays, instruction streams, structures.
3 | A cache exploits the first by keeping recent data and the second by fetching a whole line. | The line size is the knob that trades one against the other.
4 | Misses classify as compulsory (first touch), capacity (working set exceeds the cache) and conflict (associativity too low). | Hill's three Cs. Each has a different fix , which is why the classification is worth measuring rather than guessing.
5 | Compulsory misses fall with line size; conflict misses fall with associativity; capacity misses fall only with capacity. | So a miss-rate problem must be classified before it can be addressed. Doubling associativity does nothing for a capacity problem, and the tool will not tell you which you have.

 | 4 | 256 | 0.008533 | 256 | 0 | 0

Each miss is classified by running a fully associative cache of the same capacity alongside: a miss the fully associative cache would have hit is a conflict miss. The two streams are the two regimes. The first is capacity-bound — it touches far more data than fits, so associativity buys almost nothing (59 conflict misses out of 33 707). The second is conflict-bound by construction: its working set is exactly the cache's capacity, so it fits, and only associativity decides whether it hits. A miss-rate number without this breakdown cannot tell you which you have, and the two have different fixes.

Worked example 26. Two caches, one better miss rate, and the wrong winner

Given. Cache A: 2 % miss rate, 2-cycle hit. Cache B: 1.4 % miss rate, 3-cycle hit (it is larger and more associative). Miss penalty 60 cycles.

Method. Average memory access time is hit time plus miss rate times penalty. Compute both and then find the penalty at which they cross.

Cache A AMAT | 3.2 cycles
Cache B AMAT | 3.84 cycles
Winner at 60-cycle penalty | A
Crossover penalty | 166.7 cycles
Winner at 200-cycle penalty (DRAM) | B — 5.8 vs 6
What this depends on | the memory system, which is the customer's, not yours

How this is got wrong. By optimising the miss rate. Miss rate is a property of the cache and the workload; AMAT is a property of the whole system, and the two rank designs differently whenever the hit time changes. The crossover above is at 167 cycles, so the same two caches swap places between an SRAM-backed system and a DRAM-backed one. An IP block containing a cache must therefore state the miss penalty its configuration was chosen for, and ideally make the configuration a parameter, because the customer's penalty is not yours.

장: X28. Caches and Coherence, Worked
절: X28.3 Coherence: the protocol and its traffic
글:
X28.3 Coherence: the protocol and its traffic

[Table 289. MESI states and what each permits]
State | Meaning | Read hit | Write hit | On a remote read
M odified | Dirty, exclusive | Yes | Yes, silently | Write back, go to S
E xclusive | Clean, exclusive | Yes | Yes, silently — this is why E exists | Go to S
S hared | Clean, possibly shared | Yes | No — must invalidate others first | Stay S
I nvalid | Not present | Miss | Miss | —

The E state exists entirely to make private data
 cheap. Without it, a line loaded by a read would be S, and the first write to it
 would need a bus transaction to invalidate copies that do not exist. Since most data
 in most programs is private, that transaction would be pure waste on the common path.
 E says ‘clean and I am the only holder’, so the write is silent. The cost
 is that the interconnect must be able to tell a requester whether anyone else has a
 copy — a shared signal on a bus, or a directory lookup — which is a real
 structural requirement that exists solely to support this optimisation. It is a
 good example of a protocol state that looks redundant on a state diagram and is
 load-bearing in the traffic.

[Table 290. Coherence cost against core count]
Cores | Snoop messages per miss (all-to-all) | Snoops each cache must absorb | Directory bits per line (full bit vector) | Directory overhead (% of line) | Practical choice
2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 0.3906 | snoop
4 | 12 | 3 | 4 | 0.7812 | snoop
8 | 56 | 7 | 8 | 1.562 | snoop
16 | 240 | 15 | 16 | 3.125 | directory
32 | 992 | 31 | 32 | 6.25 | directory
64 | 4,032 | 63 | 64 | 12.5 | directory

Snooping broadcasts, so its traffic is quadratic in cores and every cache must absorb every other cache's misses — which becomes the bottleneck long before the wires do. A directory is linear in traffic and pays a storage overhead, and the crossover in practice is around eight to sixteen cores.

Coherence is where verification cost explodes, and
 the reason is combinatorial. A four-state protocol with four caches has
 44 combinations of state for one address, and the interesting bugs involve
 two addresses, an eviction in flight, and a request that arrives between the two
 halves of another transaction. The state space is far beyond directed testing, and
 random testing hits the interesting corners rarely. This is the clearest case in
 the book for formal verification: a coherence protocol is exactly the kind of
 deep, narrow state space that model checking handles and simulation does not, and
 proving the protocol at the specification level — before any RTL — is
 standard practice at companies that ship coherent systems. What formal cannot do is
 prove the implementation matches the protocol at scale, so both are
 needed.

Problem. Your accelerator has a private cache and the host writes its input buffer. What are the choices, and what does each cost?
Solution. Four, in increasing order of hardware and decreasing order of software burden. Uncached access: the accelerator does not cache the buffer at all; correct by construction, and it gives up locality entirely, which for a streaming accelerator that touches each byte once is often the right answer. Software coherence: the driver flushes and invalidates around each transfer; cheap in hardware, and it is a source of extremely nasty bugs because a missing invalidate is intermittent and data-dependent, and the failure appears in the customer's driver rather than in your block. IO coherence (one-way): the accelerator's accesses snoop the host caches but not the reverse; this is what most SoC interconnects offer today, it removes the flush burden for host-written data, and it costs interconnect support rather than accelerator complexity. Full coherence: the accelerator participates in the protocol as a peer, which gives the best performance for fine-grained sharing and costs a coherent cache controller plus the verification burden described above. For a design house the recommendation is usually the third option: it captures most of the benefit, the complexity lives in the customer's interconnect where it already exists, and it does not put a protocol state machine into your verification scope.

X29. LDPC and Polar Codes, Worked

These are the codes that reach within a fraction of a decibel of
 capacity and they are, between them, the error correction of 5G, Wi-Fi, high-speed
 Ethernet and modern storage. Their hardware is dominated by memory and interconnect
 rather than arithmetic, which makes them an unusually good case study in the gap
 between an algorithm's operation count and its silicon.

[그림] Figure 31. A Tanner graph. The code is the graph; the decoder is message passing on it.

장: X29. LDPC and Polar Codes, Worked
절: X29.1 Belief propagation, and the approximation everyone ships
글:
X29.1 Belief propagation, and the approximation everyone ships

From the check equation to the min-sum rule

 | Step | Justification
1 | A check node enforces that the XOR of its connected bits is zero. | Parity check.
2 | The log-likelihood ratio of a XOR of independent bits satisfies tanh( L /2) = Π tanh( L i /2). | The standard identity: probabilities of a parity multiply in the tanh domain.
3 | So the exact check update is L = 2 tanh −1 (Π tanh( L i /2)). | Accurate and unimplementable : a transcendental function per edge, at hundreds of gigabits per second.
4 | Because tanh saturates, the product is dominated by its smallest term. | Every factor with large | L | is close to ±1.
5 | Min-sum: L ≈ (Π sgn L i ) · min | L i |. | A comparison and a sign product — no multipliers, no tables.
6 | Min-sum overestimates the magnitude, so it is scaled or offset: α·min or max(min − β, 0). | One constant recovers most of the loss , and X29.2 measures how much.

[Table 291. Measured bit error rate of a (96,  d v =3, d c =6) LDPC code under three check-node rules, 8 iterations, 60 trials per point]
SNR (dB) | Uncoded (last trial) | Plain min-sum | Scaled min-sum (α=0.75) | Offset min-sum (β=0.5)
1 | 0.146 | 0.106 | 0.0767 | 0.0774
2 | 0.0625 | 0.0436 | 0.024 | 0.0234
3 | 0.104 | 0.00955 | 0.00642 | 0.00712
4 | 0.0938 | 0 | 0 | 0

Decoded by a direct implementation of the message-passing rules, all-ones codeword. The scaling and offset constants cost one multiplier or one subtractor in the whole decoder and recover a measurable part of the loss; this is the cheapest improvement available in an LDPC decoder and it is universal in shipping designs.

Why the all-ones codeword is a legitimate test and
 not a shortcut. For a linear code over a symmetric channel, the error probability
 is independent of the transmitted codeword: the decoder's behaviour depends only on
 the noise realisation relative to the sent word, and the code's symmetry makes every
 word equivalent. So simulating the all-zero (or all-ones, under the sign convention
 used here) word is exact, not approximate, and it removes the encoder from the
 simulation entirely. The condition to check is that the decoder is genuinely
 symmetric — a quantised implementation with an asymmetric saturation or a
 biased rounding rule is not, and then the shortcut becomes invalid. That is a real
 trap in fixed-point LDPC verification and a good reason to run a full encoder at
 least once against the shortcut.

절: X29.2 Where the hardware cost actually is
글:
X29.2 Where the hardware cost actually is

[Table 292. LDPC decoder memory and interconnect, 6-bit messages]
Block length n | Rate | Checks m | Edges | Message memory (kB) | Message accesses per iteration
648 | 0.5 | 324 | 1,944 | 1.4238 | 3,888
1,944 | 0.5 | 972 | 5,832 | 4.2715 | 11,664
8,448 | 0.8 | 1,689 | 33,792 | 24.75 | 67,584
26,112 | 0.86 | 3,655 | 104,448 | 76.5 | 208,896

The edge count sets everything. A decoder is a memory with comparators attached: the message memory dominates area, and moving those messages between the variable and check phases dominates power. Arithmetic — comparisons and adds — is almost free by comparison.

[Table 293. Decoder architectures]
Architecture | Parallelism | Memory | Throughput | Where used
Fully parallel | Every edge has wires | Registers | Highest | Short codes; the interconnect is the limit and routing congestion sets the block length
Layered / row-parallel | One block-row of the parity matrix at a time | SRAM banks | High; roughly halves the iterations needed | The standard for 5G and Wi-Fi quasi-cyclic codes
Serial | One check at a time | Single memory | Low | Area-critical, low-rate applications
Flooding | All checks then all variables | Two message arrays | Moderate | Simple; needs about twice the iterations of layered

Why quasi-cyclic codes are the ones that get
 standardised. A quasi-cyclic parity-check matrix is built from circulant blocks
 — identity matrices shifted by a stored amount. Three consequences follow, and
 all three are hardware consequences rather than coding ones. The matrix is described
 by a small table of shift values instead of a full incidence list, so the code fits in
 a few hundred bytes of ROM. A whole block-row can be processed in parallel with
 perfectly regular addressing, because a circulant is a barrel shifter. And the same
 hardware serves many block lengths by changing the circulant size, which is what lets
 one decoder cover a standard's whole rate and length family. The structure exists
 for the decoder's benefit, at a small cost in threshold performance, and that
 trade is why every modern LDPC standard is quasi-cyclic.

장: X29. LDPC and Polar Codes, Worked
절: X29.3 Polar codes, and why they won the control channel
글:
X29.3 Polar codes, and why they won the control channel

Channel polarisation in one page

 | Step | Justification
1 | Combine two uses of a channel W as u 1 ⊕ u 2 and u 2 . | The basic 2×2 transform.
2 | Decoding u 1 first sees a worse channel; decoding u 2 given u 1 sees a better one. | The mutual information is conserved but redistributed: I ( W − ) + I ( W + ) = 2 I ( W ).
3 | Recurse n times over 2 n uses. | The fraction of synthetic channels that are nearly perfect tends to I ( W ) and the rest tend to useless.
4 | Put information on the good channels and freeze the rest to known values. | That is the entire code construction — no search, no optimisation, and it provably achieves capacity as the length grows.
5 | Decoding is successive cancellation: decide bits in order, using earlier decisions. | Inherently serial , which is the hardware problem; latency grows with block length even though the operation count is N log N .
6 | Adding a CRC and keeping L candidate paths (SCL) closes most of the gap to maximum likelihood. | At L × the memory and the sorting network , which is what 5G specifies for control channels.

[Table 294. Successive-cancellation list decoding cost]
N | List size L | SC latency (cycles, unoptimised) | Path memory (bytes, 6-bit LLR) | Sorter comparisons per stage
128 | 1 | 254 | 96 | 7
128 | 2 | 254 | 192 | 14
128 | 4 | 254 | 384 | 28
128 | 8 | 254 | 768 | 56
256 | 1 | 510 | 192 | 8
256 | 2 | 510 | 384 | 16
256 | 4 | 510 | 768 | 32
256 | 8 | 510 | 1536 | 64
512 | 1 | 1,022 | 384 | 9
512 | 2 | 1,022 | 768 | 18
512 | 4 | 1,022 | 1536 | 36
512 | 8 | 1,022 | 3072 | 72
1,024 | 1 | 2,046 | 768 | 10
1,024 | 2 | 2,046 | 1536 | 20
1,024 | 4 | 2,046 | 3072 | 40
1,024 | 8 | 2,046 | 6144 | 80

Latency is the polar decoder's problem and list size is its area problem. The published architectural work is almost entirely about shortening the serial schedule — recognising sub-blocks that can be decoded in one step rather than bit by bit.

Problem. 5G uses polar codes for control channels and LDPC for data. Why not one code for both?
Solution. Because the two channels have opposite requirements and each code is better at one of them. Control messages are short — tens of bits — and at those lengths LDPC's performance degrades badly, because the Tanner graph cannot avoid short cycles and the asymptotic analysis that makes LDPC excellent does not apply. Polar codes with CRC-aided list decoding are close to optimal at short lengths, and their error detection is excellent, which matters enormously for control: a mis-decoded control message is worse than a detected failure, exactly as Part X5 argued for Reed–Solomon. Data blocks are long and need throughput, and there LDPC's parallel decoding wins decisively while polar's serial successive cancellation would set a latency floor. The standard is not being indecisive; it is applying the right tool at each length, and the lesson generalises: code choice is dominated by block length and by whether detection or throughput is the binding requirement.

절: X2.1 The two inequalities
글:
X2.1 The two inequalities

Setup and hold from first principles

 | Step | Justification
1 | Data leaves FF1 at t skew,L + t cq after the nominal launch edge. | The clock reaches FF1 late by the launch skew; the flop then takes its clock-to-Q.
2 | It arrives at FF2 at t skew,L + t cq + t logic . | Add the combinational delay.
3 | FF2 samples at T + t skew,C and needs the data stable t su before that. | Definition of setup time, one period later.
4 | Setup: t skew,L + t cq + t logic + t su ≤ T + t skew,C . | Arrival no later than required.
5 | Rearranged: slack su = T − t cq − t logic − t su + t skew , with t skew = t skew,C − t skew,L . | Only the difference of the skews appears. Absolute insertion delay cancels — which is why a large balanced tree is harmless and a small unbalanced one is not.
6 | For hold, the same edge must not be overtaken: t skew,L + t cq,min + t logic,min ≥ t skew,C + t h . | New data must not reach FF2 before the old data has been captured.
7 | slack h = t cq,min + t logic,min − t h − t skew . T does not appear. | This is the whole reason hold violations cannot be fixed by slowing the clock, and the reason they are found at the worst possible moment.

Setup slack | 270 ps

Flop overhead (tcq + tsu)
 is roughly fixed by the library; the period is not. The consequence is the single most

 table rather than as a feeling.

[Table 295. Budget left for logic after fixed flop overhead of 140 ps]
f (GHz) | T (ps) | overhead (ps) | logic budget (ps) | overhead as % of T | FO4 levels at 25 ps

1 | 1000 | 140 | 860 | 14 | 34

Skew and jitter are excluded, so these are optimistic. Even so the last rows explain the architecture of every multi-GHz block in this book: at 5 GHz you get a handful of gate delays, so the work must be spread across parallel slices rather than done faster.

[그림] Figure 34. The logic budget collapses hyperbolically while the overhead stays flat. Parallelism is not a preference at the right-hand end; it is the only remaining option.

The consequence for IP architecture. A block
 specified at 2 GHz in a process whose FO4 is 25 ps has about fourteen gate
 delays per cycle. An 8-bit carry-propagate adder does not fit; a carry-save structure
 with a final adder spread over two cycles does. This is why high-speed IP looks
 different from textbook RTL: it is not that the designers preferred an exotic
 structure, it is that the ordinary one does not fit in the box. When you read an
 unfamiliar architecture in a datasheet, compute the per-cycle gate budget first
 and most of the strangeness will explain itself.

장: X2. Timing Closure Arithmetic, Worked
절: X2.3 Corners, derates and the multiplication of runs
글:
X2.3 Corners, derates and the multiplication of runs

Sign-off is not one analysis. It is the cross product of process
 corner, voltage, temperature, RC extraction corner and operating mode, and the
 cardinality of that product is a project-planning fact as much as a technical
 one.

Worked example 28. How many sign-off runs is ‘sign-off’?

Given. 3 process corners, 3 voltages, 3 temperatures, 5 RC corners, 4 functional modes. A single run takes 6 hours on 16 cores.

Method. Multiply. Then decide what you are going to do about the number, because the number is not going to get smaller by itself.

Full cross product | 540
Serial machine-hours | 3,240
Wall-clock days on 10 parallel machines | 13.5
After MMMC pruning to dominant corners (typical 12) | 12
Wall-clock days for 12 corners on 10 machines | 0.3

How this is got wrong. By assuming the corners are independent so the worst case is the product of worst cases. They are not: slow-process cells are slow but slow-RC wires may pair with fast cells, and the genuinely worst path differs per corner. Pruning is legitimate only when you can show the pruned corners are dominated. Record the dominance argument; ‘we always run these twelve’ is not one, and it is how a corner quietly stops being covered after a library update.

[Table 296. What each corner axis is actually modelling]
Axis | Physical cause | Hurts setup when | Hurts hold when
Process (SS/TT/FF) | Threshold voltage and mobility spread across wafers and lots | Slow | Fast
Voltage | IR drop, regulator tolerance, di/dt droop | Low | High
Temperature | Mobility falls with heat; threshold falls too | Hot — usually | Cold
RC extraction | Metal width/thickness and dielectric variation | Cmax / RCmax | Cmin / RCmin
OCV / AOCV / POCV | Within-die variation along one path | Derated launch vs. capture | The reverse

Temperature inversion makes the ‘hot is
 slow’ rule false at low voltage. Carrier mobility falls with temperature,
 which slows a device, but the threshold voltage also falls, which speeds it up. Above
 roughly 0.8 V in mature nodes the mobility term wins and hot is slow. Near and
 below the threshold the other term wins and cold becomes the setup-critical
 corner. Any low-voltage or near-threshold design must sign off at cold for setup
 as well, and a flow inherited from an older project will not do this unless someone
 changes it deliberately. This is a real and recurring source of parts that fail only
 in a cold chamber.

장: X2. Timing Closure Arithmetic, Worked
절: X2.4 Statistical slack: what a 3σ margin buys
글:
X2.4 Statistical slack: what a 3σ margin buys

Corner-based timing answers a yes/no question. Yield is a probability,
 so at some point the two have to be connected. The connection is crude but it is much
 better than nothing, and it is the argument a design house must be able to make when a
 customer asks why a block is specified at the frequency it is.

[Table 297. Monte-Carlo path yield as the target frequency is raised (200 000 trials, σ logic = 35 ps)]
f (GHz) | T (ps) | mean slack (ps) | slack / σ | P(path fails) | Yield of 20 000 such paths
1 | 1000 | 270 | 7.71 | Why the last column is the honest one, and why it is
 still optimistic. Treating 20 000 paths as independent overstates the
 failure probability, because paths share cells, share supply, and share the same die's
 global process point — correlation makes the block behave more like a few
 effective independent paths than twenty thousand. Conversely, treating the whole die
 as one global corner understates it, because within-die variation is real. Statistical
 STA exists precisely to interpolate between these two wrong answers, and the parameter
 it needs — the split between global and local variance — comes from
 silicon measurement, not from the tool. When a vendor quotes a statistical yield
 without stating that split, the number carries no information.

Problem. A block has 20 000 timing paths. You need 99 % of dies to have every path passing. Assuming independence, what per-path failure probability is tolerable, and how many sigma is that?
Solution. Require (1−p)20000 ≥ 0.99, so p ≤ −ln(0.99)/20000 ≈ 5.03×10-7. For a Gaussian that is about 4.4σ (the exact quantile is Φ−1(1−p)). Two lessons: the required margin grows only logarithmically in path count, so ten times more paths costs well under one extra sigma; and 3σ per path — the number people quote from memory — gives a block yield of about 1.85×10-12, which is zero. Per-path margin and per-block yield are different questions and the second is the one the customer asked.

절: X2.5 Fixing what the report says is broken
글:
X2.5 Fixing what the report says is broken

[Table 298. Failure mode → remedy, with the cost of each remedy]
Symptom | Which term is short | Remedies, cheapest first | What it costs
Setup fails by 20–80 ps on many paths | t logic | Upsize cells on the critical path; restructure the logic; useful skew; retime; add a pipeline stage | Power; then area; then latency and a verification change
Setup fails by >200 ps on a few paths | Architecture, not cells | Re-architect that path; the tool cannot buy 200 ps | Schedule — treat as a design bug, not a closure task
Hold fails after CTS | t logic,min vs. skew | Insert delay buffers; swap to slower-Vt cells on the short path | Area and leakage; free in frequency
Hold fails at the fast corner only | Skew at that corner | Fix the clock tree first; buffers inserted for one corner can break another | Iteration
Fails only in one functional mode | Mode-dependent false path not declared | Declare the exception — and prove it | A wrong exception is a silicon bug that no timing run will ever catch
Both setup and hold fail on the same path | Skew | The clock tree, not the datapath | —

Timing exceptions are assertions about behaviour, and
 the timing tool cannot check them. A set_false_path tells the tool to
 stop looking. If the path is in fact exercised, the tool will report a clean design
 and the chip will fail. Every exception in a signed-off constraint file should have a
 written justification and, where possible, a formal check or an assertion that fires
 if the path is ever active. On more than one project the post-mortem of a functional
 failure has ended at a single set_multicycle_path that was true when it
 was written and became false three revisions later.

Problem. A path fails setup by 40 ps. Useful skew can move 30 ps of slack from the next stage, which has 120 ps of slack. Is this a good fix?
Solution. Arithmetically yes: the path closes with 10 ps to spare and the donor still has 90 ps. Two cautions make it a conditional yes. First, useful skew is delivered by the clock tree, so it must survive CTS, ECO routing and every corner — skew that exists only at one corner is not margin. Second, it moves the hold constraint by the same 30 ps in the harmful direction on both stages. Always evaluate a skew fix on the setup and hold inequality simultaneously; the two contain tskew with opposite signs, which is exactly why the trick works and exactly why it is dangerous.

장: X30. OFDM and MIMO, Worked
절: X30. OFDM and MIMO, Worked — 들어가며
글:
X30. OFDM and MIMO, Worked

Every wireless standard of the last twenty years is OFDM, and most are
 MIMO. Both are, from a hardware point of view, ways of converting a hard problem into
 a large number of easy ones — and the conversion has costs that are computable
 and are the subject of most of the implementation literature.

장: X30. OFDM and MIMO, Worked
절: X30.1 Why OFDM turns equalisation into division
글:
X30.1 Why OFDM turns equalisation into division

The cyclic prefix is the whole trick

 | Step | Justification
1 | A multipath channel convolves the transmitted signal with an impulse response of length L . | Linear convolution.
2 | Circular convolution in time is multiplication in the DFT domain. | The convolution theorem — but only for circular convolution.
3 | A channel performs linear convolution, which is not circular, so the theorem does not apply. | The blocks bleed into each other.
4 | Prepend the last L −1 samples of each block to itself. | Now the tail that bleeds in is the same as what would have wrapped around, so over the retained window the linear convolution is circular.
5 | Therefore Y k = H k X k + N k , one complex multiply per subcarrier. | Equalisation becomes one complex division per subcarrier , replacing a time-domain equaliser of length L . This is the entire reason OFDM exists.
6 | Cost: the prefix is redundancy, so the rate falls by N /( N + L −1). | And the peak-to-average ratio rises , because a sum of many independent subcarriers is nearly Gaussian — X30.2.

[Table 299. Cyclic-prefix overhead and the delay spread it tolerates]
Standard | FFT size | CP samples | Rate lost (%) | Symbol duration (µs) | Max echo path (m)
802.11a | 64 | 16 | 20 | 4 | 240
802.11ax | 256 | 32 | 11.11 | 14.4 | 480
LTE 20 MHz | 2,048 | 144 | 6.569 | 109.6 | 2160
5G NR 100 MHz SCS30 | 4,096 | 288 | 6.569 | 43.84 | 864

The last column is the design driver: the prefix must exceed the channel's delay spread, and delay spread is set by the environment — tens of metres indoors, kilometres in a large cell. The prefix is therefore not a free parameter but a property of the deployment, which is why standards define several and negotiate.

Worked example 29. Sizing an OFDM receiver's FFT from the standard

Given. 5G NR, 100 MHz channel, 30 kHz subcarrier spacing, 4096-point FFT, 14 symbols per slot, 0.5 ms slot.

Method. Compute the FFT rate the receiver must sustain, then apply Part X6's resource arithmetic to see what that implies.

Symbols per second | 28000
FFT size | 4,096
Complex multiplies per FFT | 24,576
Complex multiplies per second | 6.88×10 8
At 500 MHz, multipliers needed | 2
Memory accesses per second (4 per butterfly) | 2.75×10 9
SRAM ports needed at 500 MHz | 6

How this is got wrong. By sizing for one FFT and forgetting the antennas and the layers. A four-antenna receiver needs four of these, and channel estimation needs more transforms again. The multiplier count is modest and the memory port count is not — which is Part X6's conclusion arriving in a specific product, and the reason an OFDM receiver's floorplan is dominated by buffer SRAM rather than by arithmetic.

PAPR is a power-amplifier problem, and the power
 amplifier is the most expensive and least efficient thing in a radio. An amplifier
 must be operated below its compression point by the PAPR or the peaks clip, generating
 out-of-band emission that violates the spectral mask. Backing off 8 dB means
 operating at a small fraction of the amplifier's capability, and amplifier efficiency
 falls steeply with back-off — which in a handset is battery life and in a base
 station is the electricity bill and the cooling. This is why PAPR reduction
 (clipping and filtering, tone reservation, selected mapping) and digital
 pre-distortion exist, and why single-carrier FDMA was chosen for the LTE uplink:
 the handset's amplifier is the constraint, so the uplink gave up OFDM's convenience to
 get several dB of PAPR back. An architectural decision in a standard, driven
 entirely by one analogue component's efficiency curve.

Why multiple antennas multiply capacity

 | Step | Justification
1 | With N t transmit and N r receive antennas, y = Hx + n . | H is N r × N t complex.
2 | Decompose H = UΣV H ; the channel becomes min( N t , N r ) parallel scalar channels with gains σ i . | The singular value decomposition of Part X24, used as a change of basis.
3 | Capacity = Σ log 2 (1 + P i σ i 2 / N 0 ). | Sum of parallel Gaussian channels, with power allocated by water-filling.
4 | So capacity grows linearly with min( N t , N r ) , not logarithmically with power. | This is the whole point : spatial multiplexing buys rate that more power cannot.
5 | It requires the σ i to be comparable — a well-conditioned H . | Line-of-sight channels are ill conditioned and give almost no multiplexing gain. Rich scattering, which sounds like a bad channel, is what makes MIMO work — and Part X24's condition number is again the deciding quantity.

[Table 302. Measured ergodic capacity at 10 dB SNR: rich scattering against pure line of sight, 400 channel realisations]
Configuration | Rich scattering (bit/s/Hz) | Line of sight | Ratio | min( N t , N r )

2×2 | 5.618 | 4.392 | 1.279 | 2
4×4 | 11 | 5.358 | 2.054 | 4

[Table 303. MIMO detectors, and what each costs]
Detector | Complexity | Performance | Hardware
Zero forcing | O ( N 3 ) once per channel | Poor at low SNR — noise enhancement (Part X24) | A matrix inverse
MMSE | Same | Better; regularised | Same plus a diagonal add
Ordered SIC (V-BLAST) | N passes | Noticeably better than linear | Sequential — latency grows with N ; error propagation
Sphere / K-best | Tree search, bounded | Near maximum likelihood | A sorter and a tree walk — the standard hardware compromise
Maximum likelihood | M N t candidates | Optimal | Infeasible beyond small cases: 16-QAM 4×4 is 65 536 candidates per symbol

Problem. Why does massive MIMO make the detector easier rather than harder, despite having far more antennas?
Solution. Because when Nr is much larger than Nt the columns of H become nearly orthogonal — a consequence of concentration of measure, since independent high-dimensional random vectors are nearly orthogonal with high probability. Nearly orthogonal columns mean HHH is nearly diagonal, so the simple matched filter (conjugate beamforming) is nearly optimal and the noise enhancement that makes zero forcing bad at low SNR essentially vanishes. The hard detector problem is a symptom of having barely enough antennas, and adding antennas at the base station — where size and power are affordable — dissolves it. The cost moves elsewhere and should be named: channel estimation for many antennas needs pilot resources and becomes the limiting factor (pilot contamination), the number of RF chains dominates cost and power, and the digital front end must move enormous sample rates from the antennas to the processing. Massive MIMO trades a detection problem for an interconnect and calibration problem, which is a trade the digital designer should recognise as favourable and should be ready to quantify.

X31. Analogue Building Blocks, Budgeted

A digital designer does not size transistors, but does have to say
 whether an analogue requirement is reasonable before committing to an architecture.
 The quantities that answer that are few and computable: thermal noise, matching,
 gain-bandwidth and settling. This part gives them.

장: X31. Analogue Building Blocks, Budgeted
절: X31.1 kT / C — the noise floor you cannot design away
글:
X31.1 kT/C — the noise floor you cannot design away

Why sampled noise depends only on the capacitor

 | Step | Justification
1 | A switch has resistance R ; its thermal noise density is 4 kTR V²/Hz. | Johnson–Nyquist.
2 | The RC network's noise bandwidth is 1/(4 RC ). | Integrating a single-pole response gives π/2 times the 3 dB bandwidth.
3 | So the sampled noise power is 4 kTR · 1/(4 RC ) = kT / C . | The resistance cancels. A better switch does not help; only a bigger capacitor does.
4 | Doubling resolution means halving the noise voltage, which means quadrupling the capacitor . | And capacitance is area, and it is also the load the driver must charge, so power rises too.
5 | Each extra bit of a sampled system costs 4× the capacitor and roughly 4× the power. | This single relation explains the shape of every converter's energy-per-conversion curve above about 10 bits.

[Table 304. kT / C noise and the resolution it permits (1 V full scale, 300 K)]
Capacitance (fF) | RMS noise (µV) | SNR (dB) | ENOB | Approx. area (µm² at 2 fF/µm²)
10 | 643.58 | 54.8 | 8.81 | 5
100 | 203.52 | 64.8 | 10.47 | 50
1000 | 64.358 | 74.8 | 12.13 | 500
10000 | 20.352 | 84.8 | 13.79 | 5000
1.0000×10 5 | 6.4358 | 94.8 | 15.45 | 50000

Computed from kT/C alone, ignoring every other noise source, so these are optimistic. A 14-bit sampled system needs picofarads, and the area and power that implies is why high-resolution converters are large and why oversampling architectures, which trade speed for resolution, exist.

Worked example 30. Can this ADC specification be met?

Given. A customer asks for a 16-bit, 100 MS/s SAR ADC on 1 V supply, ‘small area’.

Method. Work the kT/C requirement, then the settling requirement, then compare against what the process offers.

Required SNR for 16 bits | 98.08 dB
Signal RMS at 1 V full scale | 353.6 mV
Permitted noise RMS | 4.41 µV
Required capacitance | 212.96 pF
Array area at 2 fF/µm² | 1.0648×10 5  µm²
Settling time available at 100 MS/s, 16 SAR cycles | 625 ps
Time constants needed for 16-bit settling | 11.09
Required RC | 56.36 ps
Verdict | the capacitor and the settling requirement are in direct conflict

How this is got wrong. By treating ‘16-bit’ and ‘100 MS/s’ as independent requirements. The noise requirement forces a large capacitor; the speed requirement forces that capacitor to settle in picoseconds, which forces a very low switch resistance and therefore an enormous switch, which loads the previous stage. This is why 16 bits at 100 MS/s is a time-interleaved or pipelined architecture and not a single SAR, and why the answer to the customer is a question about their actual SNR requirement in the signal band — if they need 16 bits over 1 MHz rather than over 50 MHz, oversampling changes the arithmetic completely.

X31.2 Matching: why analogue area is set by statistics

Pelgrom's law

 | Step | Justification
1 | Threshold voltage varies between nominally identical devices because of random dopant fluctuation and line-edge roughness. | A counting phenomenon: fewer dopants under a smaller gate means larger relative variation.
2 | The standard deviation of the mismatch between two devices is σ Δ V th = A VT /√( WL ). | Pelgrom's law, verified across many processes. A VT is a process constant of a few mV·µm.
3 | So halving the mismatch requires four times the area. | The same 4× law as kT / C , arriving from a completely different mechanism.
4 | A comparator's input-referred offset is this mismatch; a current mirror's error is proportional to it. | Which sets the minimum size of every matched pair in a converter.
5 | Digital calibration converts area into computation. | Measure the offset once, store it, subtract it. This is the dominant trend in mixed-signal design and the reason the digital content of converters keeps growing.

[Table 305. Pelgrom matching against device area ( A VT = 3.5 mV·µm)]
WL (µm²) | σ Δ V th (mV) | 3σ spread (mV) | Bits resolvable without calibration at 1 V FS | Pair area (µm²)
0.01 | 35 | 210 | 2.252 | 0.02
0.1 | 11.07 | 66.41 | 3.913 | 0.2
1 | 3.5 | 21 | 5.573 | 2
10 | 1.107 | 6.641 | 7.234 | 20
100 | 0.35 | 2.1 | 8.895 | 200

Without calibration, matching alone limits an uncalibrated comparator to about eight bits at sane areas. Every converter above that resolution calibrates, and the calibration engine is digital — which is how a digital designer ends up owning a large part of an analogue block.

The calibration trade, stated as arithmetic. Suppose
 a comparator needs 1 mV of offset. Pelgrom says that costs about
 12 µm² of gate area per device, and in a 64-way time-interleaved ADC
 that is repeated 64 times, in the fastest and most power-hungry part of the chip.
 Alternatively, build a minimum-size comparator with 10 mV of offset and add a
 trim DAC plus a digital loop that measures and cancels it. The trim DAC is small, the
 loop is a counter and a comparator, and the whole thing is synthesised. The
 crossover is far to the digital side and moves further every process node, because
 digital area shrinks and AVT improves only slowly. This is the
 single clearest instance of the general trend this book keeps meeting: buy analogue
 precision with digital computation.

[Table 307. The analogue specifications a digital architect should be able to sanity check]
Quantity | Rule of thumb | If the requirement exceeds it
Sampled SNR | kT / C ; 14 bits needs >1 pF at 1 V | Oversample, or relax full scale, or use a different architecture
Uncalibrated comparator offset | Pelgrom; ~8 bits at sensible area | Add digital calibration
Amplifier DC gain | ~6 dB per bit | Gain boosting, or a correlated-double-sampling scheme
Aperture jitter | SNR = −20log(2π f in σ t ) — Part X12 | A better clock, not a better converter
Reference noise | Appears directly at the output | Filter it; and remember the filter capacitor is area too
Supply rejection | Falls with frequency; poor above the loop bandwidth | This is why the PDN of Part X32 matters to analogue blocks

Problem. Your digital block shares a supply with an ADC and the customer reports spurs at your clock frequency. Whose problem is it?
Solution. Both of yours, and the useful response is to find out which mechanism rather than which party. There are three paths and they are distinguishable by measurement. Supply coupling: your switching current modulates the shared rail, and the converter's finite power-supply rejection turns that into an input offset; test by changing your block's activity and watching whether the spur amplitude tracks, and by separating the supplies if the board permits. Substrate coupling: switching current injects into the substrate and reaches the converter's sensitive nodes; this is layout, and the remedies are guard rings, deep n-well isolation and distance. Clock coupling: your clock capacitively couples into the sampling network, which is the worst of the three because it lands exactly at a fixed frequency and its harmonics. The digital side's contribution, and it is a real one, is to reduce di/dt: spread the clock tree's switching with deliberate skew, gate clocks aggressively so the average current is lower, add on-chip decoupling, and avoid large simultaneous switching events. None of that is exotic, and all of it is far cheaper than asking the analogue designer for another 20 dB of supply rejection, which may not be available at any price.

X32. The Power Delivery Network, Worked

Every timing number in Part X2 assumed a supply voltage. The
 network that delivers it is a distributed RLC structure whose impedance must be low
 across six decades of frequency, and when it is not, the result is a voltage droop
 that shows up as a timing failure nobody can reproduce. This is a digital designer's
 problem even though it looks like an analogue one.

[그림] Figure 35. The power delivery hierarchy. Each element handles a different timescale because each is limited by its own parasitic inductance.

절: X32.1 Target impedance, and where the number comes from

X32.1 Target impedance, and where the number comes from

From a droop budget to an impedance specification

 | Step | Justification
1 | The supply must stay within ±δ of nominal for the timing libraries to apply. | Typically 5 %. Outside it, the delays are not the ones you signed off with.
2 | A current step Δ I produces a voltage Z ( f )Δ I . | Ohm's law for an impedance.
3 | Target impedance Z t = δ V dd /Δ I max . | The one number the whole PDN is designed to , and it must be met at every frequency, not on average.
4 | Δ I max is the worst-case step, not the average current. | A clock-gated block waking up, or a test pattern that toggles everything, is a far larger step than any functional average — which is why maximum-toggle test patterns can fail a part that works in its application.
5 | Falling voltage and rising current per node make Z t shrink every generation, quadratically. | This is why PDN design has become progressively harder rather than benefiting from scaling.

[Table 308. Target impedance across process generations (5 % droop budget)]
Node | V dd (V) | Peak current (A) | Z t (mΩ) | Peak power (W) | Droop budget (mV)
180 nm | 1.8 | 2 | 45 | 3.6 | 90
90 nm | 1.2 | 10 | 6 | 12 | 60
28 nm | 1 | 40 | 1.25 | 40 | 50
7 nm | 0.8 | 120 | 0.3333 | 96 | 40

Worked example 31. Sizing on-die decoupling capacitance

Given. A block draws 5 A when active and is clock-gated. On wake-up the current rises in 2 ns. The package inductance is 100 pH and the droop budget is 40 mV.

Method. The package cannot supply current faster than its inductance allows, so on-die capacitance must cover the interval until the package catches up. Compute the charge needed and hence the capacitance.

Current step | 5 A
Rise time | 2 ns
L d i /d t if the package had to supply it | 250 mV
Droop budget | 40 mV
Verdict | the package alone exceeds the budget by 6×
Charge to supply during the step | 5 nC
Capacitance for a 40 mV droop | 125 nF
Area at 10 fF/µm² (MOS cap) | 12.5 mm²

How this is got wrong. By budgeting only the resistive drop. At a nanosecond timescale the package is an inductor, not a wire, and Ldi/dt dominates the static IR term by a large factor. The remedy is not lower resistance but local charge storage, and the area it costs is real — on-die decoupling is commonly several per cent of die area and in some designs more than ten. A second, cheaper remedy belongs to the digital designer: ramp the current instead of stepping it, by staging the clock-gate release across several cycles, which is a few gates of logic and can reduce the required capacitance by a large factor.

절: X32.2 Resonance: the peak that puts the droop where you are not looking
글:
X32.2 Resonance: the peak that puts the droop where you are not looking

[Table 309. Resonant peaks formed by each inductance with the capacitance below it]
L (pH) | C (nF) | R (mΩ) | Resonant frequency (MHz) | Q | Peak impedance (mΩ)
1000 | 100 | 5 | 15.915 | 20 | 100
1000 | 1000 | 5 | 5.0329 | 6.325 | 31.62
100 | 100 | 2 | 50.329 | 15.81 | 31.62
100 | 10 | 2 | 159.15 | 50 | 100
10 | 100 | 1 | 159.15 | 10 | 10

Every inductance in the hierarchy resonates with the capacitance on the load side of it, and at resonance the impedance is Q times the series resistance. A high-Q peak is the dangerous case: if the current spectrum has energy there, the droop is far worse than the target impedance suggests.

The first-droop, second-droop, third-droop language
 engineers use is just this resonance hierarchy, and the dangerous one is usually the
 mid-frequency droop. The first droop (hundreds of megahertz) is handled by on-die
 capacitance; the third (kilohertz) by the regulator's control loop. The second —
 tens to a couple of hundred megahertz, set by package inductance against on-die
 capacitance — sits in a gap between the two remedies and is where the highest-Q
 peak usually lands. It is also, unhelpfully, right where a processor's activity
 changes: a loop that alternates between a heavy and a light phase at that rate
 excites it directly, which is the origin of the classic ‘this benchmark fails
 and that one does not’ report. The digital remedies are to add damping (series
 resistance in some decoupling, deliberately), to spread activity in time, and to use
 an adaptive clock that stretches the period when a droop is detected — which
 converts a functional failure into a small performance loss and is now common in
 large processors.
