The useful content is the third column: a few milliamps per micron of width is the order of magnitude, so a 5 A block needs of the order of a millimetre of total metal width to feed it — which is why power grids are wide, numerous and on the thick upper metal layers.

Problem. Your block passes timing in every corner and fails intermittently in silicon at high activity. How do you decide whether it is the PDN?
Solution. Look for the signature, which is specific and distinguishable. A PDN-induced failure is activity dependent rather than pattern dependent: it appears when many things switch at once, not when a particular logical case occurs, so a test that toggles a lot fails while a functionally harder but quieter test passes. It moves with supply and with frequency in a particular way: raising the supply helps more than it should for a simple timing problem, because it increases the margin against droop as well as speeding the logic. It correlates with di/dt, not with average power, so a test with the same average current but smoother activity passes. The measurements that settle it are an on-die droop monitor if one exists — and if none exists, that is the lesson for the next design, because a ring-oscillator-based droop detector is a few hundred gates — and an experiment that staggers the wake-up of the block's clock-gating domains, which changes only di/dt. If staggering fixes it, the PDN is the cause and the cheapest fix is the staggering you just used to diagnose it.

장: X33. Boolean Reasoning: BDDs, SAT and Equivalence Checking
절: X33. Boolean Reasoning: BDDs, SAT and Equivalence Checking — 들어가며

X33. Boolean Reasoning: BDDs, SAT and Equivalence Checking

Three tools an IP designer uses every week — logic equivalence
 checking, formal property verification and automatic test pattern generation —
 are the same engine underneath: a decision procedure for Boolean formulas. Knowing
 what that engine can and cannot do explains why one proof finishes in seconds and
 another never finishes, which is otherwise the most frustrating thing about these
 tools.

장: X33. Boolean Reasoning: BDDs, SAT and Equivalence Checking
절: X33.1 Representations, and why the choice is everything
글:
X33.1 Representations, and why the choice is everything

[Table 311. Ways to represent a Boolean function]
Representation | Size | Equivalence check | Where it is used
Truth table | 2 n always | Trivial | Small cells; library characterisation
Sum of products | Can be exponential | Hard | Two-level minimisation, PLAs
BDD (reduced, ordered) | Canonical — and variable-order dependent | Pointer comparison | Symbolic model checking; some equivalence checking
AIG (and-inverter graph) | Linear in the circuit | Needs a solver | The working representation of every modern synthesis and verification tool
CNF for SAT | Linear via Tseitin encoding | NP-complete, and fast in practice | Formal verification, ATPG, equivalence

Canonicity is the property that makes BDDs both
 magical and fragile. Two functions are equal if and only if their reduced ordered
 BDDs are the identical graph, so equivalence is a pointer comparison rather than a
 search. The price is that the size depends catastrophically on the variable order: the
 same function can be linear under one order and exponential under another, and finding
 the best order is itself NP-hard. The canonical example is a multiplier, whose BDD is
 exponential under every order — which is exactly why BDD-based equivalence
 checking fails on datapaths and why modern tools use AIGs plus SAT instead. When a
 tool reports that it is ‘building BDDs’ and then runs out of memory, this
 is what happened, and the remedy is a different engine rather than a bigger
 machine.

[Table 312. Measured decision-diagram size for x 0 y 0 + x 1 y 1 + … under two variable orders]
Variables | Product terms | Interleaved order (nodes) | Separated order (nodes) | Ratio
4 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 1.5
8 | 4 | 8 | 30 | 3.75
12 | 6 | 12 | 126 | 10.5
16 | 8 | 16 | 510 | 31.88

Built by exhaustive construction with subfunction sharing, which is what reduction does. The interleaved column is exactly n; the separated column is 2n/2+1−2. Linear against exponential, on the same function with the same tool. The ratio is modest at these sizes because the exponent is small — at 40 variables it is a factor of 52 000 — (221−2)/40 — which is the difference between a second and a week. This is the whole of BDD practice in one table.

장: X33. Boolean Reasoning: BDDs, SAT and Equivalence Checking
절: X33.2 Why SAT is fast even though it is NP-complete
글:
X33.2 Why SAT is fast even though it is NP-complete

What a modern SAT solver actually does

 | Step | Justification
1 | Convert the circuit to CNF by Tseitin encoding: one variable per gate, a few clauses per gate. | Linear in circuit size — no blow-up here, unlike naive expansion.
2 | Search by assigning variables, propagating implications, and backtracking on conflict. | DPLL. The naive version is hopeless.
3 | On conflict, derive a new clause that explains it (clause learning) and add it. | This is the single change that made SAT practical. The learned clause prunes an entire region of the search space, not just the current branch.
4 | Backjump non-chronologically to the level the conflict actually came from. | Rather than undoing one decision at a time.
5 | Restart periodically, keeping the learned clauses. | Escapes a bad region of the search while retaining what was learned.
6 | Result: industrial instances with millions of variables solve in seconds , while small random instances at the hardness threshold do not. | Structure, not size, decides. Circuits have enormous structure; that is why circuit problems are the easy case and why a tool's runtime is unpredictable in the specific way engineers observe.

Worked example 32. Why equivalence checking succeeds where simulation cannot

Given. Comparing a 64-bit multiplier's RTL against its gate netlist.

Method. Compare the exhaustive-simulation cost with what an equivalence checker does instead.

Input space | 2 128
Vectors per second, simulated | 10 7
Time to simulate exhaustively | >10 23 years
What an equivalence checker does | proves the two are equal for all inputs
How | structural matching of internal points, then SAT on each cone
Why it works | the two designs share almost all their internal structure
When it fails | after retiming, resource sharing, or a datapath rewrite — the structure no longer matches

How this is got wrong. By assuming equivalence checking always works. It works because it finds internal equivalence points and cuts the problem into small cones; a transformation that destroys that correspondence — retiming across register boundaries, sequential optimisation, a multiplier architecture change — leaves the tool with one enormous cone and it fails. The practical consequence is a rule for the synthesis flow: turn on transformations that break equivalence checking only when you are prepared to verify the result another way, and know which ones they are before the schedule depends on them.

[Table 313. Why cone size, not design size, decides an equivalence check]
Situation | Cones | Typical cone size (gates) | Total gates | Difficulty
Control logic | 50,000 | 40 | 2,000,000 | easy
Datapath adders | 2,000 | 200 | 400,000 | easy
Multiplier (structural match) | 500 | 2,000 | 1,000,000 | easy
Multiplier (after rewrite) | 1 | 500,000 | 500,000 | the hard case

Illustrative structure counts. The last row has the same total size and is the one that does not finish, because the work per cone grows far faster than linearly.

장: X33. Boolean Reasoning: BDDs, SAT and Equivalence Checking
절: X33.3 Model checking: proving something about all time
글:
X33.3 Model checking: proving something about all time

Bounded model checking, and what ‘bounded’ costs

 | Step | Justification
1 | Unroll the design's transition relation k times. | Copy the combinational logic k times, chaining state.
2 | Assert the initial state and the negation of the property. | If satisfiable, the assignment is a counterexample trace of length ≤ k .
3 | Hand the whole thing to SAT. | A bug of depth ≤ k is found; a bug of depth k +1 is not.
4 | So BMC is a very good bug hunter and not a proof . | This is the distinction that matters when reading a tool's report: ‘proven to depth 40’ is not ‘proven’.
5 | A full proof needs induction, interpolation or IC3/PDR, which find an inductive invariant. | These do give unbounded proofs , and they are what a tool means by ‘proven’ without a depth.
6 | The bound needed for confidence is the design's diameter — how many cycles to reach any reachable state. | Usually unknown, and for a design with a large counter it is astronomically large. Which is why counters are abstracted before proving anything around them.

The three ways a formal proof lies to you, in order
 of frequency. Over-constraint: an assumption excludes the input that would
 have failed, so the property is proven about a machine that is not yours. This is the
 formal equivalent of a disabled checker and is by far the commonest; the defence is to
 check that the constraints are satisfiable together with interesting behaviour, which
 good tools report as ‘assumption coverage’. Vacuity: the property's
 antecedent never occurs, so it holds trivially — ‘if a grant is given
 without a request…’ proven because no grant is ever modelled. A
 bounded result read as a proof, as above. All three report green, which is
 why this book's rule applies with full force here: a proof whose assumptions have not
 themselves been checked is an unexamined green light.

Problem. Where should a design house spend its formal effort, given that it cannot afford to prove everything?
Solution. On the properties whose failure is catastrophic and whose state space is deep and narrow, which is where formal has the advantage over simulation. In practice that means, in order: arbiters and any structure that can starve, because starvation is a liveness property and simulation can never prove its absence; FIFOs, credit counters and flow control, where overflow and underflow are provable and the bugs appear only at full rate; protocol interfaces, where a vendor-supplied assertion set exists and proving compliance at the boundary is worth more than any amount of traffic; clock-domain crossing structures, where the interesting cases are timing-related and simulation is blind to them; and security properties, where the question is whether information can flow between two places and the answer must hold for all inputs. What not to spend it on: datapath equivalence at the algorithm level — a bit-exact reference model plus random simulation gets there faster — and anything with a large counter in the cone, until the counter has been abstracted.

X34. Logic Synthesis: What the Tool Is Actually Doing

Synthesis is the step an IP designer has least visibility into and
 most dependence on. Its behaviour is not arbitrary: it is a sequence of well-defined
 transformations with known strengths, and knowing them turns ‘the tool did
 something odd’ into a specific diagnosis.

장: X34. Logic Synthesis: What the Tool Is Actually Doing
절: X34.1 The pipeline, stage by stage
글:
X34.1 The pipeline, stage by stage

[Table 314. What each synthesis stage does and what it cannot do]
Stage | Input → output | Optimises | Cannot
Elaboration | RTL → generic netlist | Nothing — it interprets the language | Fix a coding style that infers a latch
Datapath extraction | Operators → architectures | Picks adder and multiplier structures from a library | Restructure an algorithm you wrote out by hand as gates
Technology-independent optimisation | Generic netlist → smaller generic netlist | Factoring, common subexpressions, constant propagation, redundancy removal | Know anything about delay in picoseconds
Technology mapping | Generic → library cells | Covers the network with cells at minimum cost — solvable optimally on a tree | Change the network's structure much
Timing-driven restructuring | Netlist → netlist | Balances the critical path, duplicates, remaps | Buy more than a limited amount — see Part X2
Sizing and buffering | Netlist → sized netlist | Convex, near-optimal (Part X26) | Fix a structural problem

Technology mapping is optimal on trees and heuristic
 on graphs, and that single fact explains most of what a synthesis tool does well.
 The classic formulation covers a Boolean network with library cells at minimum cost.
 If the network is a tree, dynamic programming over the nodes gives a provably optimal
 cover in linear time. Real networks are DAGs with reconvergent fanout, so the tool
 partitions them into trees at multiple-fanout points, maps each optimally, and accepts
 that the partition itself was a heuristic choice. The practical consequence is that
 logic with heavy reconvergence maps worse than logic without it, and that
 restructuring an expression to reduce fanout — which looks cosmetic in RTL
 — can measurably change the result.

[Table 315. A balanced tree of two-input gates: the structure mapping likes]
Depth | Gates | Logic levels | DP table entries (4 cells/node) | Gate delays at 2 per level
2 | 3 | 2 | 12 | 5
4 | 15 | 4 | 60 | 9
6 | 63 | 6 | 252 | 13
8 | 255 | 8 | 1,020 | 17
10 | 1,023 | 10 | 4,092 | 21
12 | 4,095 | 12 | 16,380 | 25

Dynamic-programming mapping visits each node once per candidate cell, so it is linear in gates times library size. This is why mapping a million-gate design takes minutes even though the underlying covering problem is NP-hard on general graphs.

X34.2 What your RTL controls, and what it does not

[Table 316. RTL constructs and what the tool does with them]
You write | The tool produces | You control it by
a + b | An adder chosen from an architecture library | The timing constraint — not by writing the adder yourself
a * b | Booth or array multiplier, possibly shared | Constraints, and set_dont_use if the choice is wrong
case (full) | A multiplexer tree | Ordering and priority annotations
case (incomplete, no default) | A latch — almost never what you meant | Write the default; lint for it
if chain | Priority logic — deep and slow | Use case when the conditions are mutually exclusive
A for loop | Unrolled combinational logic | The loop bound; there is no hardware loop
x Given. A 16-way priority if/else if chain versus a 16-way case, each selecting between 16 values.

Method. Count the logic levels. A priority chain is a serial selection; a case is a balanced tree, because the tool knows the conditions are mutually exclusive.

Priority chain: multiplexers in series | 16
Delay at ~2 gate levels per 2:1 mux | 32 gate levels
Case: mux tree depth | 4
Delay | 8 gate levels
Ratio | 4×
At 25 ps per gate level | 800 ps vs 200 ps
Period this costs at 1 GHz | 60 % of it, for nothing

How this is got wrong. By assuming the tool will notice the conditions are exclusive. Sometimes it does, and it cannot in general — proving exclusivity is a Boolean problem it does not always attempt. Writing case, or annotating the chain as parallel, tells it directly. This is the single highest-value RTL coding habit for timing, and it costs nothing; a priority structure should appear only where priority is actually meant, and then the depth is a deliberate cost rather than an accident.

장: X34. Logic Synthesis: What the Tool Is Actually Doing
절: X34.3 Retiming: moving registers without changing behaviour
글:
X34.3 Retiming: moving registers without changing behaviour

Why retiming is a graph problem with an exact answer

 | Step | Justification
1 | Model the circuit as a graph: nodes are combinational blocks with delay, edges carry a register count. | The standard retiming model.
2 | Retiming assigns each node an integer r v : move r v registers from its outputs to its inputs. | Registers on edge ( u , v ) become w + r v − r u .
3 | Legality requires every edge to keep a non-negative count: r u − r v ≤ w . | A system of difference constraints — exactly the structure Part X26 identified as solvable.
4 | Achieving period P adds more difference constraints between node pairs. | Derived from the longest combinational path between them.
5 | So ‘is period P achievable by retiming?’ is a negative-cycle test, and binary search over P finds the optimum. | Polynomial, exact, and implemented in every synthesis tool.
6 | What it cannot do: change the number of registers on any cycle. | The latency around a feedback loop is invariant under retiming , which is why retiming cannot fix a loop that is too long — Part X4's DFE problem is exactly this, and the answer there was unrolling, which changes the graph.

Retiming is exact and is nevertheless often turned
 off, for reasons worth knowing. It renames and moves registers, which breaks the
 structural correspondence equivalence checking depends on (Part X33), so
 verification becomes sequential equivalence checking — a much harder problem
 that may not complete. It also destroys the correspondence between RTL signal names
 and netlist nodes, which makes debug and ECOs painful, and it can interact badly with
 scan insertion and with clock gating. The common compromise is to retime within
 a clearly delimited pipeline and to verify that block by simulation against its
 pre-retiming version, rather than enabling it design-wide.

Problem. Synthesis reports your block at 620 MHz against a 700 MHz target. List what you would try, in order of cost.
Solution. Cheapest first, because the early items often suffice. Check the constraints before the design: an over-constrained input delay, a missing multicycle path, or a clock defined without its uncertainty will each produce a believable-looking failure that no RTL change fixes. Read the critical path and classify it — if it crosses a whole datapath it is structural, if it is a long priority chain it is X34.2, if it starts or ends at a boundary it is a constraint issue, and each has a different fix. Try the free restructuring: turn an if-chain into a case, split a wide comparison, move a constant multiplication to a shift-add, precompute something that depends only on slowly changing inputs (Part X9's rule). Then pipeline — one more stage, which costs latency and a verification change and is usually decisive. Then re-architect: parallel slices at a lower rate, which is Part X7's energy argument arriving as a timing fix. What not to do first is instantiate gates by hand; it is slow, it does not port, and the tool is better at it than you are except in the rare case where you know something it cannot — and then you should be telling it, through a constraint, rather than bypassing it.

X35. Hardware Data Structures: CAM, Hashing and Bloom Filters

Networking, storage and security IP spend most of their logic looking
 things up. The structures that do it are a small, well-understood family with sharply
 different cost profiles, and choosing among them is one of the clearest cases in this
 book where an architectural decision is settled by arithmetic rather than by
 preference.

장: X35. Hardware Data Structures: CAM, Hashing and Bloom Filters
절: X35.1 The lookup family
글:
X35.1 The lookup family

[Table 317. Lookup structures compared]
Structure | Query | Area per entry | Power | Updates | Used for
RAM (direct index) | 1 cycle | 1 bit/bit | Low | 1 cycle | Small, dense key spaces
Binary CAM | 1 cycle, all entries in parallel | ~8–10 transistors per bit | Very high — every cell compares every cycle | 1 cycle | MAC address tables, tag matching
Ternary CAM | 1 cycle, with don't-cares | ~16 transistors per bit | Higher still | Needs priority ordering — insertion can require moving entries | Longest-prefix routing, ACLs
Hash table | 1–2 cycles typical | ~1 bit/bit plus load factor | Low | 1 cycle, except on collision | Flow tables, caches
Cuckoo hash | d parallel probes, worst case bounded | ~1.05 bits/bit at high load | Low | Insertion can cascade | Flow tables where a bounded query time is required
Trie / tree | log n memory accesses | Pointer overhead | Low | Simple | Prefix matching in software
Bloom filter | k probes | ~10 bits per entry for 1 % false positive | Low | Insert only | A cheap pre-filter in front of an expensive lookup

TCAM is the structure that decides the cost of a
 router, and it is worth knowing why it is so expensive. A ternary cell stores
 three states — 0, 1 and don't-care — which needs two storage bits plus
 comparison logic, roughly sixteen transistors against six for SRAM. Worse, every cell
 compares on every lookup, so power is proportional to the whole table rather than to
 the entry found: a large TCAM can dissipate tens of watts doing nothing but matching.
 The architectural responses all reduce the number of cells that must compare
 — partition the table by prefix length and activate only relevant banks, put a
 small filter in front, or replace TCAM with an algorithmic trie in SRAM and accept
 multiple accesses. Every high-end switch datasheet's power figure is substantially a
 statement about this one structure.

[Table 318. TCAM cost against table size, 144-bit keys (indicative 16 T/cell against 6 T SRAM, 1 GHz lookup)]
Entries | Key bits | SRAM-equivalent (MB) | TCAM area as SRAM-equivalent (MB) | Match-line power (W, indicative)
1,000 | 144 | 0.01717 | 0.09155 | 1.728×10 -4
10,000 | 144 | 0.1717 | 0.9155 | 0.001728
100,000 | 144 | 1.717 | 9.155 | 0.01728
1,000,000 | 144 | 17.17 | 91.55 | 0.1728

Indicative constants, not a vendor datasheet. The shape is the point: area roughly five times SRAM for the same bits, and a power term that grows with table size independently of the traffic.

절: X35.2 Hashing: the birthday problem decides your table size
글:
X35.2 Hashing: the birthday problem decides your table size

Why a hash table needs to be much larger than its contents

 | Step | Justification
1 | With n items in m buckets, the probability that a particular pair collides is 1/ m . | Uniform hashing assumption.
2 | There are n ( n −1)/2 pairs, so the expected number of colliding pairs is about n 2 /(2 m ). | Linearity of expectation.
3 | Collisions start appearing when n ≈ √ m , not when n ≈ m . | The birthday paradox. This is the fact that surprises people sizing tables.
4 | The longest chain with n = m is Θ(log n /log log n ) — about 5–8 for realistic sizes. | So a single-probe hardware lookup fails often enough to matter.
5 | Two hash functions and a choice of the emptier bucket reduces the longest chain to log log n . | The power of two choices: an exponential improvement from one extra probe. This is why hardware hash tables are multi-way.

[Table 319. Measured longest bucket in a 4096-bucket table, one hash against two-choice hashing, 30 trials per point]
Load factor | Keys | Longest bucket, 1 hash | Longest bucket, 2 choices | Ratio
0.25 | 1,024 | 3.5 | 2.1 | 1.667
0.5 | 2,048 | 4.367 | 3 | 1.456
0.75 | 3,072 | 5.5 | 3.4 | 1.618
0.9 | 3,686 | 6.133 | 3.9 | 1.573
0.95 | 3,891 | 6.2 | 4.033 | 1.537

Simulated with random keys, seed 13. The second hash roughly halves the worst bucket at every load, which in hardware is the difference between a lookup engine that must handle eight-deep chains and one that handles four.

Worked example 34. Sizing a flow table for a bounded lookup time

Given. A network block must look up 200 000 flows at 100 Gbit/s, one lookup per 64-byte packet, with a bounded lookup time of two memory accesses.

Method. Bounded worst case rules out chaining. Compute what a 4-way cuckoo table costs at a load factor it can sustain.

Packet rate at 64 B | 148.8 Mpps
Lookups per second | 1.49×10 8
Flows | 200,000
Cuckoo load factor achievable at 4 ways | 0.97
Buckets needed | 206,185
Entries at 4 per bucket | 206,184
Memory at 64 B per entry | 12.58 MB
Probes per lookup | 4 (parallel, one bucket read)
Worst-case accesses | 2

How this is got wrong. By choosing the average-case structure for a worst-case requirement. Chained hashing has a superb average and an unbounded tail, and a networking datapath is judged on the tail: a lookup that occasionally takes eight accesses either stalls the pipeline or drops the packet. Cuckoo hashing buys a bounded query at the cost of a potentially long insertion, which is the right trade because insertions are rare and can be handled by a slow path. Recognising which operation must be bounded is the whole of the design decision.

장: X35. Hardware Data Structures: CAM, Hashing and Bloom Filters
절: X35.3 Bloom filters: paying memory for certainty in one direction
글:
X35.3 Bloom filters: paying memory for certainty in one direction

The false-positive rate, and the optimal number of hashes

 | Step | Justification
1 | A Bloom filter is m bits; inserting an item sets k bits chosen by k hashes. | No item is stored — only its fingerprint in the bit array.
2 | After n insertions, the probability a given bit is still zero is (1−1/ m ) kn ≈ e − kn / m . | Independent settings.
3 | A query gives a false positive when all k bits happen to be set: p = (1−e − kn / m ) k . | Never a false negative — that asymmetry is the whole value.
4 | Minimising over k gives k = ( m / n )ln 2. | And then p = 2 − k .
5 | So about 1.44 log 2 (1/ p ) bits per item, regardless of how large the items are. | A 1 % filter costs about 10 bits per item whether the items are 32-bit or 1500-byte. That independence from key size is why it is used in front of expensive lookups.

[Table 320. Bloom filter false-positive rate against bits per item]
Bits/item | Optimal hashes k | False positive | (%) | Memory for 10 6 items (MB)
4 | 3 | 0.147 | 14.7 | 0.4768
8 | 6 | 0.0216 | 2.16 | 0.9537
10 | 7 | 0.00819 | 0.819 | 1.192
12 | 8 | 0.00314 | 0.314 | 1.431
16 | 11 | 4.59×10 -4 | 0.0459 | 1.907
20 | 14 | 6.71×10 -5 | 0.00671 | 2.384

Computed from the closed form. Ten bits per item buys about one per cent, and each further factor of ten costs about 3.3 bits — a very good rate of exchange when the alternative is storing the keys.

Problem. Where does a Bloom filter belong in an IP block, and where does it not?
Solution. It belongs wherever a negative answer is common and an expensive lookup can be skipped, and where a false positive costs only wasted work rather than a wrong result. Concretely: in front of a TCAM or an off-chip table, to avoid the access entirely for the majority of keys that are absent; in a cache to avoid probing a way; in a coherence directory to avoid a snoop. In each case the filter is an optimisation and the real structure still answers. It does not belong anywhere the answer is used directly, because a false positive is then a wrong answer — and it does not belong where deletions are needed, because a plain Bloom filter cannot delete (clearing a bit may un-insert another item); that needs a counting Bloom filter at four times the memory, and at that point a small hash table is often better. The design question to ask is: what is the measured fraction of negative queries? A filter in front of a table that is usually hit is pure cost, and that fraction is a property of the customer's traffic, which means it belongs in the datasheet as an assumption.

X36. Cryptographic Engines, Sized

Crypto IP is one of the most commonly licensed categories, and it is
 unusual in that its correctness is binary, its specifications are published and
 testable, and its cost is dominated by a small number of arithmetic primitives. That
 combination makes it a good first product for a design house and a good subject for
 exact sizing.

장: X36. Cryptographic Engines, Sized
절: X36.1 The three primitive families and their costs
글:
X36.1 The three primitive families and their costs

[Table 321. What each family needs from the hardware]
Family | Examples | Core operation | Cost driver | Typical area
Block ciphers | AES, ChaCha, SM4 | Substitution and permutation over a small state | The S-box, replicated | 5–50 kGE
Hashes | SHA-2, SHA-3, BLAKE | A compression function over a message block | Adders and rotations; long carry chains in SHA-2 | 10–30 kGE
Public key | RSA, ECC, Diffie–Hellman | Modular exponentiation or point multiplication | The modular multiplier — dominates everything | 50–500 kGE
Post-quantum | ML-KEM (Kyber), ML-DSA (Dilithium) | Polynomial arithmetic in a ring, NTT | NTT butterflies and modular reduction — Part X6's FFT with a different field | 50–200 kGE
MAC / AEAD | GCM, Poly1305, CMAC | Carry-less or modular multiply-accumulate | GF(2 128 ) multiplier for GCM | 10–40 kGE

Post-quantum cryptography is an opportunity for
 design houses precisely because it is new. The standards are recent, the hardware
 literature is thin, the incumbent crypto-IP vendors' portfolios were built for RSA and
 ECC, and the core operation — the number-theoretic transform — is an FFT
 over a finite field, which means Part X6's entire architectural analysis
 transfers: the same radix choices, the same twiddle-ROM symmetries, the same
 memory-versus-multiplier trade. A team that has built an FFT has most of what an
 NTT needs, with the arithmetic replaced by modular arithmetic, and that is an
 unusually direct path from an existing competence to a new market.

장: X36. Cryptographic Engines, Sized
절: X36.2 AES: where the area actually goes
글:
X36.2 AES: where the area actually goes

The S-box is the block

 | Step | Justification
1 | AES-128 is ten rounds of SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, AddRoundKey. | Specification.
2 | ShiftRows is wiring; AddRoundKey is 128 XORs; MixColumns is a fixed GF(2 8 ) matrix — shifts and XORs. | All three are nearly free.
3 | SubBytes applies a 256-entry nonlinear substitution to each of 16 bytes. | This is the whole cost.
4 | As a table it is 16 × 2048 bits of ROM or 16 × ~700 gates synthesised. | The naive implementation.
5 | Or compute it: the S-box is inversion in GF(2 8 ) plus an affine map, and inversion decomposes through GF((2 4 ) 2 ). | Canright's tower-field construction reduces the S-box to roughly a third of the table's area, at the cost of more logic depth. The trade is area against frequency , and which side wins depends entirely on the throughput requirement.
6 | A round can use 16 S-boxes (one cycle per round), 4, or 1. | Throughput scales linearly with S-box count and so does area , which makes AES one of the cleanest area/throughput families to parameterise — and therefore a good product, because one design serves many customers.

[Table 322. AES-128 area and throughput against S-box count, at 1 GHz]
S-boxes | Cycles per block | bits/cycle | Gbit/s | Approx. gates | Mbit/s per kGE
16 | 10 | 12.8 | 12.8 | 13,200 | 969.7
8 | 20 | 6.4 | 6.4 | 7,600 | 842.1
4 | 40 | 3.2 | 3.2 | 4,800 | 666.7
1 | 160 | 0.8 | 0.8 | 2,700 | 296.3

Gate counts are indicative (700 GE per table-based S-box plus 2 kGE of state and key schedule). The last column is nearly constant, which is the signature of a cleanly scalable block: the customer chooses a point on the line rather than a different design.

Worked example 35. Which AES configuration does a 400 Gbit/s link need?

Given. MACsec on a 400 Gbit/s Ethernet port, AES-GCM, digital logic at 800 MHz.

Method. Work out bits per cycle, then how many parallel AES cores that implies, then check the GCM multiplier alongside it.

Line rate | 400 Gbit/s
Clock | 800 MHz
Bits per cycle required | 500
AES block size | 128
Blocks per cycle | 3.906
Fully unrolled pipelined AES cores needed | 4
Pipeline stages each (one per round) | 10
GF(2 128 ) multiplies per cycle (GCM) | 4
Dominant cost | the GCM multiplier, not AES

How this is got wrong. By sizing AES and forgetting the mode. Counter mode parallelises perfectly — each block's keystream is independent — so AES scales by replication. The GCM authentication tag is a sequential multiply-accumulate in GF(2128), which does not parallelise naively; making it keep up requires the standard trick of precomputing powers of the hash key and processing several blocks at once, which costs several 128-bit carry-less multipliers and their key storage. At high line rates the authenticator is larger than the cipher, and a datasheet that quotes only AES throughput has quoted the easy half.

장: X36. Cryptographic Engines, Sized
절: X36.3 Public key: modular multiplication is the whole problem
글:
X36.3 Public key: modular multiplication is the whole problem

Montgomery multiplication, and why division disappears

 | Step | Justification
1 | Modular multiplication needs ab mod n ; the reduction is a division, which is expensive (Part X9). | And it is needed thousands of times per operation.
2 | Montgomery's idea: work with a ̅ = aR mod n for R = 2 k > n . | A change of representation.
3 | Then REDC( x ) = ( x + ( xn ′ mod R ) n )/ R reduces using only multiplications and shifts , because dividing by R is a shift. | The division is gone. n ′ is precomputed once.
4 | Conversion in and out costs two extra multiplications, amortised over the whole exponentiation. | Negligible over thousands of operations.
5 | So an RSA engine is: a wide multiplier, an adder, a shifter, and a controller. | And the wide multiplier is 80–90 % of the area , which is why the literature is about multiplier architectures and not about protocols.

[Table 323. Public-key work, measured in modular multiplications and cycles (64-bit multiplier, schoolbook, 500 MHz)]
Operation | Modulus bits | Modular multiplies | 64-bit words | Cycles (approx.) | Time (ms)
RSA-2048 (CRT) | 1,024 | 3,072 | 16 | 196,608 | 0.3932
RSA-4096 (CRT) | 2,048 | 6,144 | 32 | 1,572,864 | 3.146
ECC P-256 | 256 | 3,993 | 4 | 15,974 | 0.03195
ECC P-384 | 384 | 5,990 | 6 | 53,913 | 0.1078
X25519 | 255 | 3,315 | 4 | 13,260 | 0.02652

The multiplication counts are the standard estimates: square-and-multiply for RSA with the Chinese remainder theorem halving the modulus, and roughly a dozen field operations per elliptic-curve point addition. The table explains the industry's migration: ECC at 256 bits gives comparable security to RSA at 3072 and costs orders of magnitude less work.

A public-key engine that is merely correct is
 dangerous. The classical attacks are not on the mathematics but on the
 implementation: a square-and-multiply loop that branches on key bits leaks the key
 through timing and through power (Part X15), and a Montgomery ladder —
 which performs the same operations regardless of the bit — costs perhaps
 30 % more work and removes the leak. Likewise a conditional subtraction at the
 end of a reduction is a data-dependent branch, so implementations make it
 unconditional. Constant-time behaviour must be a stated requirement and a verified
 property, not a side effect, and it is one of the few properties where a formal
 argument (no branch or memory access depends on secret data) is both achievable and
 genuinely convincing.

Problem. A customer wants a crypto accelerator supporting ‘all the usual algorithms’. How do you scope it?
Solution. Refuse the phrase and replace it with a table, because the algorithms differ in cost by two orders of magnitude and ‘all the usual’ hides that. Ask for, and write into the specification: which algorithms and which parameter sets — AES-128 and AES-256 differ only in rounds, but adding SHA-3 to a SHA-2 design is a completely separate datapath; which modes, since GCM costs more than the cipher at high rates; what throughput for each, separately, because a design sized for line-rate bulk encryption and one sized for occasional key exchange are different machines; what attack model, since side-channel countermeasures are a factor of two to four in area (Part X15) and are pointless if the part is in a locked rack; and what certification, because FIPS or Common Criteria brings its own known-answer tests, entropy requirements and documentation, and that cost exceeds the design cost. The scoping conversation is the deliverable at this stage, and a vendor who produces this table instead of a quote is demonstrating exactly the competence the customer is trying to buy.

X37. Bus Protocols: Ordering, Outstanding Transactions and Exclusives

Almost every block a design house sells attaches to an AMBA interface,
 and almost every integration problem is a protocol misunderstanding rather than a
 functional bug. The protocol's subtle points are few and they recur; this part works
 through them.

[그림] Figure 36. The five AXI channels.

장: X37. Bus Protocols: Ordering, Outstanding Transactions and Exclusives
절: X37.1 The handshake, and the one rule that is always broken
글:
X37.1 The handshake, and the one rule that is always broken

VALID/READY, and why VALID may not wait

 | Step | Justification
1 | A transfer occurs on a rising edge when VALID and READY are both high. | The basic handshake, shared by AXI, AXI-Stream, TileLink and CHI.
2 | Once VALID is asserted it must stay asserted until the transfer occurs , and the payload must not change. | Otherwise the receiver cannot rely on what it sampled.
3 | VALID must not depend combinationally on READY. | This is the rule that is broken. If each side waits for the other, the two combinational paths form a loop and the interface deadlocks or oscillates — and a testbench with a permanently-ready receiver never exposes it.
4 | READY may depend combinationally on VALID. | The asymmetry is deliberate: it lets a receiver accept in the same cycle, which is where the throughput comes from.
5 | A registered-output, registered-ready skid buffer breaks any timing path across the interface at the cost of one cycle and two entries of storage. | The standard remedy, and the right default for an IP boundary — Part X14's advice to register every boundary, in protocol form.

The testbench that hides this bug is the default
 one. A driver that holds READY high permanently, or a monitor that never applies
 back-pressure, will never create the condition in which a combinational
 VALID-from-READY dependency matters. Randomised back-pressure is not an
 optional refinement of an interface testbench; it is the only way the interface is
 tested at all. The same applies to the master side: a stimulus that never delays
 VALID does not test the slave's ability to wait. Both are one line of constrained
 randomisation and both routinely go missing.

[Table 324. Interface buffering options and what each costs]
Structure | Added latency (cycles) | Throughput (transfers/cycle) | Timing path across the boundary | Full rate?
Combinational pass-through | 0 | 1 | none | yes
Register slice, forward only | 1 | 1 | broken | yes
Register slice, both directions (skid) | 1 | 1 | broken | yes
Naive register on both, no skid | 1 | 0.5 | broken | halved
Two-deep FIFO | 2 | 1 | broken | yes

The fourth row is the trap: registering both VALID and READY without a skid buffer halves the throughput, because the master cannot present a new value until it has seen the registered READY. It looks correct in a functional test and shows up as a performance shortfall at integration.

장: X37. Bus Protocols: Ordering, Outstanding Transactions and Exclusives
절: X37.2 Ordering: what the protocol guarantees and what it does not
글:
X37.2 Ordering: what the protocol guarantees and what it does not

[Table 325. AXI ordering rules, and the integration failures each one causes]
Rule | What it means | The bug it causes when forgotten
Same ID, same direction → ordered | Responses come back in order for one ID | A slave that reorders within an ID breaks masters that rely on it
Different IDs → no order guarantee | Responses may interleave arbitrarily | A master that assumes order across IDs corrupts data
Reads and writes are not ordered relative to each other | A read issued after a write may complete first | Read-after-write hazards in a customer's driver ; needs an explicit barrier or a completion wait
Write response means accepted, not visible | B arrives when the slave takes responsibility | Assuming data is observable by another master — it may not be
Bursts must not cross 4 kB boundaries | A page-crossing burst is illegal | A DMA that ignores it produces a protocol violation the interconnect may not check
Narrow transfers use strobes | WSTRB selects lanes | A slave ignoring WSTRB corrupts neighbouring bytes

Worked example 36. How many IDs does a master need?

Given. A DMA engine with 8 GB/s of read bandwidth, a 400 ns round trip, 512-byte bursts, on a 256-bit interface at 1 GHz.

Method. Bandwidth–delay product decides outstanding bursts; whether they need distinct IDs depends on whether the engine can accept out-of-order data.

Bytes in flight needed | 3.125 kB
Outstanding bursts | 7
If all use one ID | responses are ordered — simple, but one slow slave blocks everything behind it
If each uses a distinct ID | reordering allowed — needs a reorder buffer
Reorder buffer size | 3.125 kB
ID bits needed | 3
Recommended | a few IDs, grouped by destination

How this is got wrong. By choosing one extreme. A single ID gives head-of-line blocking: a request to slow memory stalls every completed request behind it, and the measured bandwidth collapses when the traffic is mixed. Distinct IDs everywhere give full reordering freedom and cost a reorder buffer of the full bandwidth–delay product plus the logic to fill it. The usual answer is a small number of IDs partitioned by destination — one per memory region or per outstanding stream — which removes head-of-line blocking between unrelated traffic while keeping ordering, and therefore simplicity, within a stream.

장: X37. Bus Protocols: Ordering, Outstanding Transactions and Exclusives
절: X37.3 Exclusive access, and why it is harder than it looks
글:
X37.3 Exclusive access, and why it is harder than it looks

Load-linked / store-conditional in bus form

 | Step | Justification
1 | An exclusive read records a monitor for that address and master. | AXI's ARLOCK exclusive, or the processor's load-linked.
2 | An exclusive write succeeds only if the monitor is still set. | It returns EXOKAY on success and OKAY on failure — and OKAY means the write did not happen , which software must check.
3 | Any intervening write to the address by anyone clears the monitor. | That is what makes it atomic.
4 | The monitor is in the slave or the interconnect, not the master. | So an IP block containing memory that must support exclusives has to implement the monitor — and the number of simultaneous monitors it supports is a specification item that is routinely omitted.
5 | Monitors may be granted at a granularity coarser than one address. | Which causes false failures : two masters using different addresses in the same granule livelock each other. The granule size must be documented.
6 | Spurious failure is always permitted, so software must loop. | Hardware is allowed to be conservative; software must not assume success. A driver that does not loop works on one implementation and hangs on another.

Atomics moved from the master to the interconnect, and
 an IP vendor should know which era their customer is in. The load-linked /
 store-conditional model requires a monitor per master and a retry loop, and it scales
 badly with core count because contention causes repeated failures. Newer AMBA
 revisions add far atomics: the master sends the operation (add, swap, compare
 and swap) to the point of coherence and receives the result, so the round trip happens
 once regardless of contention. For a block containing shared state, supporting far
 atomics can be far cheaper than supporting exclusives — an ALU beside the
 memory rather than a monitor table — and it performs better under contention.
 Asking the customer which their system uses is a scoping question worth raising
 early.

Problem. Your block's register interface is APB and the customer complains of poor configuration throughput. What do you say?
Solution. That APB is doing exactly what it is for, and then offer the two real options. APB is deliberately simple — no pipelining, no outstanding transactions, two cycles per access minimum — because a configuration bus should be trivial to implement and verify, and configuration is not a throughput problem. If the customer is writing thousands of registers at boot and it matters, the causes are usually not the bus: a slow bridge clock ratio, a synchroniser per access, or software doing read-modify-write where a write would do. Measure before changing the interface. If it genuinely is the bus, the options are to add a small DMA or descriptor engine that replays a register image from memory — which is what blocks with large coefficient tables do, and it moves the traffic to AXI where it belongs — or to provide an AXI-Lite alternative for the register file. Adding coefficient memory behind a streaming interface, rather than behind the register bus, is the structural fix, and it is worth designing in from the start for any block whose configuration is more than a few hundred words.

장: X38. Colour, the ISP Pipeline and Display Processing
절: X38. Colour, the ISP Pipeline and Display Processing — 들어가며
글:
X38. Colour, the ISP Pipeline and Display Processing

Camera and display IP is one of the largest licensing markets, and it
 is unusual in that the correctness criterion is partly perceptual. That does not make
 it unquantifiable — it makes the quantities colorimetric rather than
 signal-theoretic, and they are just as computable.

[그림] Figure 37. A minimal image signal processor. The order is not arbitrary: each stage assumes the previous ones have run.

장: X38. Colour, the ISP Pipeline and Display Processing
절: X38.1 Why the pipeline is in that order
글:
X38.1 Why the pipeline is in that order

[Table 326. Each stage, what it corrects, and why it must come where it does]
Stage | Corrects | Why here
Black level | Sensor pedestal and dark current | First — everything downstream assumes zero means zero
Defect pixel | Stuck sensor pixels | Before demosaic, or the defect spreads to neighbours
Lens shading | Vignetting, colour shading | Before white balance, because the shading is colour dependent
Demosaic | One colour per pixel → three | The data rate triples here ; everything possible is done before it
White balance | Illuminant colour | Per-channel gains; conventionally applied on the Bayer data for cost
Colour correction matrix | Sensor spectral response → a standard space | Needs three channels, so after demosaic
Gamma / tone | Perceptual coding | After all linear operations — averaging gamma-encoded values is wrong, and doing it is the commonest ISP bug
Sharpen, noise reduction | Perceptual quality | After tone mapping, because the visibility of noise is nonlinear

Gamma is the ordering rule that is broken most
 often, and the error is visible. Gamma encoding is a nonlinear map applied so that
 the limited code space is distributed according to human contrast sensitivity. Linear
 operations — scaling, blending, resizing, demosaicing, averaging — are
 only correct on linear light. Resizing a gamma-encoded image darkens edges and
 shifts colours; alpha-blending gamma-encoded values produces halos. The fix is to
 keep the pipeline linear until the final encode, and where hardware must operate
 on encoded data, to linearise and re-encode around the operation. This is a real and
 recurring defect in shipped display and camera pipelines, and it is worth an explicit
 statement in an IP block's datasheet about which domain its input and output are
 in.

[Table 327. Measured error from averaging in the gamma domain (γ = 2.2), linear light values]
Value A | Value B | Correct average (linear) | Average of encoded values, decoded | Error (%)
0 | 1 | 0.5 | 0.2176 | -56.47
0.2 | 0.8 | 0.5 | 0.4454 | -10.93
0.4 | 0.6 | 0.5 | 0.4945 | -1.102
0 | 0.5 | 0.25 | 0.1088 | -56.47
0.5 | 1 | 0.75 | 0.7266 | -3.121

Computed directly. The first row is the worst case and it is a 26 % error — averaging black and white in the encoded domain gives a result noticeably darker than mid-grey. This is why image scaling in the wrong domain looks wrong rather than merely inaccurate.

절: X38.2 Colour spaces as matrices
글:
X38.2 Colour spaces as matrices

Why colour conversion is a 3×3 matrix and when it is not

 | Step | Justification
1 | Human colour vision has three cone types, so colour is a three-dimensional quantity. | Trichromacy. Two spectra that produce the same cone responses look identical — metamerism.
2 | A display's primaries span a triangle in chromaticity space; its gamut is that triangle. | Any colour inside is reproducible; outside is not.
3 | Converting between two sets of primaries is a change of basis: a 3×3 matrix on linear tristimulus values. | Linear is load-bearing — see X38.1.
4 | So BT.709 to BT.2020, or camera RGB to XYZ, is one matrix multiply per pixel. | Nine multiplies and six adds — trivial hardware, which is why colour conversion is never the bottleneck.
5 | It stops being a matrix when the gamut does not contain the colour, or when the transfer function is not a power law. | Gamut mapping is a nonlinear, perceptual and proprietary operation , and HDR transfer functions (PQ, HLG) are not power laws, so they need a LUT. Those two are where display IP actually differentiates.

[Table 328. Gamut areas in CIE xy, computed from the primaries]
Space | Red (x,y) | Green (x,y) | Blue (x,y) | Triangle area | Relative to BT.709 (%)
BT.709 / sRGB | 0.64, 0.33 | 0.3, 0.6 | 0.15, 0.06 | 0.112 | 70.83
DCI-P3 | 0.68, 0.32 | 0.265, 0.69 | 0.15, 0.06 | 0.152 | 96.08
BT.2020 | 0.708, 0.292 | 0.17, 0.797 | 0.131, 0.046 | 0.2119 | 133.9
Adobe RGB | 0.64, 0.33 | 0.21, 0.71 | 0.15, 0.06 | 0.1512 | 95.54

Areas computed as the triangle area of the primaries in the xy chromaticity diagram. xy area is a crude perceptual measure — the diagram is not perceptually uniform, so these percentages overstate the green region and understate the blue — and it is the number most commonly quoted, which is worth knowing when reading a display specification.

절: X38.3 Line buffers: the memory that sets ISP area
글:
X38.3 Line buffers: the memory that sets ISP area

Worked example 37. Why an ISP is mostly SRAM

Given. A 4K (3840-wide) pipeline, 12 bits per channel. The stages need vertical neighbourhoods: demosaic 5 lines, noise reduction 7, sharpening 5, lens shading 1, scaler 4.

Method. Each stage that looks at neighbouring rows must buffer those rows, because the sensor delivers one row at a time. Count the lines and the bits.

Line width | 3,840
Bits per pixel (Bayer, pre-demosaic) | 12
Demosaic: 5 lines | 28.12 kB
Noise reduction: 7 lines (RGB, 36 bit) | 118.1 kB
Sharpen: 5 lines (RGB) | 84.38 kB
Scaler: 4 lines (RGB) | 67.5 kB
Total line buffers | 298.1 kB
As a fraction of a typical ISP's area | the majority

How this is got wrong. By counting arithmetic and not lines. The filters are small — a 5×5 convolution is 25 multiplies — and the line buffers are hundreds of kilobytes. Two consequences follow and both are architectural. Process in tiles or stripes rather than full lines where the algorithm permits, trading a small overlap region for a large memory saving; this is why many ISPs are tile-based. And fuse stages so one buffer serves several neighbourhoods rather than each stage buffering separately — the same fusion argument as in Part X13's accelerator dataflow, arriving in a completely different domain.

[Table 329. Line-buffer memory against tile width (8-pixel halo)]
Image width | Tile width | Line buffer (kB) | Overlap overhead (%) | Memory vs. full line (%)
1,920 | full line | 149.06 | 0 | 100
1,920 | 256 | 19.875 | 3.12 | 13.33
1,920 | 512 | 39.75 | 1.56 | 26.67
3,840 | full line | 298.12 | 0 | 100
3,840 | 256 | 19.875 | 3.12 | 6.667
3,840 | 512 | 39.75 | 1.56 | 13.33
7,680 | full line | 596.25 | 0 | 100
7,680 | 256 | 19.875 | 3.12 | 3.333
7,680 | 512 | 39.75 | 1.56 | 6.667

Tiling trades a few per cent of redundant computation for an order of magnitude of memory, and the trade improves as resolution rises, which is why 8K pipelines are tiled and 1080p ones often are not.

Problem. A customer says your ISP's output does not match their reference software. Where do you look?
Solution. Almost always at a convention rather than at the arithmetic, and the candidates are few enough to enumerate. Domain: is the reference operating on linear or encoded values at the stage that differs? X38.1's error is large and looks like a gain error. Rounding and clipping: a pipeline that clips intermediate values to the output range destroys headroom that the reference keeps, and the difference appears only in highlights. Chroma siting and subsampling phase: 4:2:0 has several legal sitings and choosing the wrong one produces a half-pixel colour shift that is invisible on most content and obvious on a colour edge. Matrix coefficients and range: limited versus full range, and BT.601 versus BT.709 coefficients, are four combinations and three of them are wrong. Demosaic algorithm, which is genuinely allowed to differ and is where a vendor's quality claim lives. Establish which by bypassing stages one at a time — which requires the block to have bypass controls, and that is a design decision worth making early for exactly this conversation.

장: X39. Clock Generation, Distribution and Time Synchronisation
절: X39. Clock Generation, Distribution and Time Synchronisation — 들어가며
글:
X39. Clock Generation, Distribution and Time Synchronisation

Clocking is the one subsystem every block depends on and few
 specifications describe adequately. This part covers the three parts an IP designer
 must be able to reason about: how the clock is made, how it is delivered, and how time
 is agreed between chips.

장: X39. Clock Generation, Distribution and Time Synchronisation
절: X39.1 Spread spectrum: trading a specification for a specification
글:
X39.1 Spread spectrum: trading a specification for a specification

Why modulating the clock reduces measured emissions

 | Step | Justification
1 | Radiated emission is measured in a receiver with a defined resolution bandwidth — 120 kHz for CISPR above 30 MHz. | The regulation specifies the measurement, not the physics.
2 | An unmodulated clock puts all its harmonic energy in one line, far narrower than that bandwidth. | So the receiver sees the whole harmonic.
3 | Modulating the frequency by ±0.5 % spreads each harmonic over ±0.5 % of its frequency. | The n th harmonic spreads n times as far, so higher harmonics benefit more.
4 | The receiver now sees only the fraction of the energy inside its bandwidth , so the reading falls by roughly 10 log 10 (spread/RBW) dB. | The total radiated energy is unchanged. The compliance number improves; the physics does not.
5 | Cost: the clock period now varies, so every synchronous budget must hold at the fastest excursion, and any PLL downstream must track the modulation. | Which is why a SerDes reference clock's spread must be negotiated — the CDR's loop bandwidth must exceed the modulation rate or it cannot follow.

[Table 330. Spread-spectrum reduction in a 120 kHz measurement bandwidth]
Clock (MHz) | Spread (±%) | Harmonic | Spread width (MHz) | Reading reduced by (dB)
100 | 0.5 | 1 | 1 | 9.208
100 | 0.5 | 5 | 5 | 16.2
100 | 0.5 | 10 | 10 | 19.21
100 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 12.22
100 | 1 | 5 | 10 | 19.21
100 | 1 | 10 | 20 | 22.22
1000 | 0.5 | 1 | 10 | 19.21
1000 | 0.5 | 5 | 50 | 26.2
1000 | 0.5 | 10 | 100 | 29.21
1000 | 1 | 1 | 20 | 22.22
1000 | 1 | 5 | 100 | 29.21
1000 | 1 | 10 | 200 | 32.22
5000 | 0.5 | 1 | 50 | 26.2
5000 | 0.5 | 5 | 250 | 33.19
5000 | 0.5 | 10 | 500 | 36.2

Computed from the ratio of spread width to resolution bandwidth. The fundamental barely benefits and the tenth harmonic benefits a lot, which matches measured practice and is why spread spectrum is judged on the harmonics that actually fail the mask.

Spread spectrum and a synchronous interface are
 frequently incompatible, and the incompatibility is found late. Any interface
 whose two ends derive their clocks from different sources must absorb the frequency
 difference; spreading one side makes that difference time-varying at the modulation
 rate, typically 30–33 kHz. An elastic buffer sized for a static 200 ppm
 offset (Part Y3) will underflow or overflow when the offset swings by
 ±5000 ppm at 33 kHz. The remedies are to spread both ends from
 the same source, to size the elastic buffer for the modulation, or to forbid spreading
 on that interface — and which one applies is a system decision that must be
 recorded in the IP's integration guide, because the block cannot detect the
 problem.

[Table 331. Clock tree cost at 1 GHz, 0.8 V (indicative 5 fF per flop clock pin, fanout 4)]
Flops | Buffer levels | Buffers | Total clock capacitance (pF) | Clock power (W) | Insertion delay (ps)
10,000 | 7 | 3,333 | 60 | 0.0384 | 210
100,000 | 9 | 33,333 | 600 | 0.384 | 270
1,000,000 | 10 | 333,333 | 6000 | 3.84 | 300
10,000,000 | 12 | 3,333,333 | 60000 | 38.4 | 360

Indicative constants. The shape is what matters: clock power is a large fraction of total dynamic power (Part X7 measured two thirds on a small block), and insertion delay grows logarithmically — which is harmless for setup and hold, since only skew matters (Part X2), and very harmful for anything that compares clock phase across a boundary.

[Table 332. Clock distribution styles]
Style | Skew | Power | Where
Balanced H-tree | Low by construction | High — long wires | Top-level distribution in large chips
Buffered tree from CTS | Tool-balanced, a few tens of ps | Moderate | The default for a block
Mesh / grid | Very low | Highest — the whole grid switches | High-performance processors
Clock gating (integrated cell) | Adds a level | Saves 20–40 % | Everywhere — Part X7
Resonant / rotary | Low | Potentially much lower | Research and a few products; needs inductors

Why a block should provide one clock input and do its
 own gating, rather than accepting several clocks. Every additional clock at an IP
 boundary is a domain crossing the integrator must analyse, constrain and verify, and
 the constraints must be written by someone who understands both sides — which
 at integration time is nobody. A block that takes one clock and derives its internal
 enables is far easier to integrate, and the power saving from gating is identical.
 Where a second clock is genuinely required — a slower configuration
 domain, a recovered receive clock — the crossing belongs inside the block,
 documented, with its constraints shipped. That is a concrete piece of value a
 vendor adds, and its absence is a concrete integration cost.

장: X39. Clock Generation, Distribution and Time Synchronisation
절: X39.3 Agreeing on time: IEEE 1588 and the hardware it needs
글:
X39.3 Agreeing on time: IEEE 1588 and the hardware it needs

Why timestamping must be in the PHY

 | Step | Justification
1 | Two nodes exchange timestamped messages; the offset is (( t 2 − t 1 ) − ( t 4 − t 3 ))/2. | The standard two-way exchange.
2 | This assumes the path is symmetric . | Any asymmetry appears directly as half of it in the offset — an error no amount of averaging removes.
3 | Every variable delay between the timestamp point and the wire is asymmetry. | Software stacks, driver queues, interconnect arbitration, and even FIFO occupancy in the MAC.
4 | So the timestamp must be taken as close to the wire as possible , in hardware, at a defined reference plane. | Typically the start-of-frame delimiter crossing the MII interface, which is why PTP support is a PHY and MAC feature rather than a software one.
5 | Residual asymmetry (different cable lengths, different PHY latencies for TX and RX) must be calibrated and subtracted. | Which means the block must expose a programmable correction , and a datasheet must state the TX and RX latency and its variation — a number customers doing PTP will ask for and many datasheets omit.

[Table 333. Where the timestamp is taken decides the achievable accuracy]
Timestamp point | Delay variation (ns) | Offset error contribution (ns) | Equivalent distance error (m)
Software timestamp | 1.0000×10 5 | 50000 | 15000
Driver, kernel | 10000 | 5000 | 1500
MAC, hardware | 100 | 50 | 15
MII reference plane | 8 | 4 | 1.2
PHY, sub-ns aware | 1 | 0.5 | 0.15

Indicative figures for each point in the stack. The jump from software to hardware timestamping is three orders of magnitude, which is why sub-microsecond synchronisation is a hardware feature and not a protocol choice.

Problem. Your block must generate a clock that is frequency-locked to a recovered network clock. What are the options?
Solution. Three, and they differ in what they require from the system rather than in accuracy. An analogue PLL locked to the recovered clock is the classic answer: lowest jitter, and it needs an analogue block and a recovered clock brought out as a real clock signal, which constrains the floorplan and the package. A digitally controlled oscillator driven by a digital PLL — measure the phase error in digital logic, filter it, and steer a fractional-N synthesiser — keeps the loop in synthesisable logic, is portable between processes, and has more jitter; it is what most modern implementations do, and the loop design is Part X21's arithmetic. Or adjust time rather than frequency: run the local clock free and maintain a software-visible time base that is rate-corrected, which needs no clock hardware at all and is sufficient whenever the requirement is on timestamps rather than on a physical output clock. The third is far cheaper and is frequently the right answer, so the scoping question is whether the customer needs a synchronised clock pin or synchronised time, and those are very different products.

장: X3. Metastability and Clock-Domain Crossing, Worked
절: X3. Metastability and Clock-Domain Crossing, Worked — 들어가며
글:
X3. Metastability and Clock-Domain Crossing, Worked

A flip-flop sampled while its input is changing may enter a
 metastable state whose resolution time is unbounded. ‘Unbounded’ is the
 word that matters: there is no settling time that guarantees correctness, only a
 settling time that makes failure rare enough. Designing a synchroniser therefore means
 choosing a number of years, which is a much more concrete decision than it first
 sounds.

[그림] Figure 38. A two-flop synchroniser. The second flop's job is not to clean up the signal — it is to give the first flop a whole clock period in which to resolve.

장: X3. Metastability and Clock-Domain Crossing, Worked
절: X3.1 The MTBF expression and what each symbol is
글:
X3.1 The MTBF expression and what each symbol is

Where the exponential comes from

 | Step | Justification
1 | A metastable flop's output separates from the balance point exponentially: Δ V ( t ) = Δ V 0 e t /τ . | Small-signal analysis of the cross-coupled pair: the loop has a positive real pole, and τ is its inverse.
2 | Resolution by time t requires Δ V 0 larger than some Δ V min e − t /τ . | Invert the exponential.
3 | Δ V 0 is proportional to how far the data edge was from the sampling point, and that offset is uniformly distributed. | Asynchronous input: no phase relationship, so all offsets equally likely.
4 | So P(unresolved after t ) ∝ e − t /τ , with a constant T 0 carrying the aperture width. | Uniform measure times an exponentially shrinking target window.
5 | Failures occur at rate f clk f data T 0 e − t r /τ . | Each clock edge is a trial; each data edge supplies an opportunity.
6 | MTBF = e t r /τ ⁄ ( T 0 f clk f data ) | Reciprocal of the rate. τ and T 0 are library measurements , not universal constants; ask the vendor for them.

2 | 1000 | 1880 | 10 34.8 | 10 27.3

[그림] Figure 39. MTBF in years, log scale, against depth. A straight line on this axis is the exponential: each stage adds the same number of decades, and that number shrinks as the period shrinks.

Worked example 38. Choosing the depth for a 1 GHz interface

Given. τ = 20 ps, T0 = 10 ps, fclk = 1 GHz, data edges at 100 MHz. Setup plus clock-to-Q consume 120 ps of each period.

Method. Compute MTBF for two and three stages, then compare against a target. A reasonable target for a part shipping in volume is not ‘longer than the product's life’ — it is longer than the product's life multiplied by the number of units in the field.

Resolution time, 2 stages | 1880 ps
MTBF, 2 stages | 10 27.3 years
MTBF, 3 stages | 10 49.0 years
2-stage MTBF across a 10-million-unit fleet | 10 20.3 years
Same, but with τ doubled at the cold/low-V corner | 10 -0.1 years

How this is got wrong. By evaluating the MTBF for one chip. The failure rate is additive over units, so a fleet of ten million divides the MTBF by ten million. A synchroniser that is comfortable in the lab can produce a field return every few weeks. The second common error is to use τ from a different library, or from a conference slide: τ varies by a factor of several between libraries and corners, and it sits in an exponent.

τ degrades at low voltage and cold, and the
 degradation is exponential in effect. A synchroniser characterised at nominal may
 have a τ 1.5–2× larger at the low-voltage corner; with
 tr/τ halved, an MTBF of 109 years becomes
 104. Evaluate the MTBF at the worst corner for τ, not the typical
 one — and note that this is a corner the timing tool does not analyse for
 you, because the synchroniser path is one you told it to ignore.

절: X3.2 A synchroniser is not a CDC solution
글:
X3.2 A synchroniser is not a CDC solution

Two flops make one bit safe. They do nothing for the problem
 that actually causes CDC bugs, which is that several bits crossing together may be
 sampled on different edges and produce a value that never existed in the source
 domain.

[Table 335. Measured probability that a multi-bit crossing yields a value that existed in neither the old nor the new state, binary vs. Gray coding]
Bits | P(bogus), binary | P(bogus), Gray | Bogus samples, binary | Bogus samples, Gray
1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0
2 | 0.248 | 0 | 49,651 | 0
4 | 0.329 | 0 | 65,732 | 0
8 | 0.334 | 0 | 66,771 | 0
16 | 0.334 | 0 | 66,704 | 0

200 000 trials per row, each bit independently taking the old or the new value. Gray coding makes the bogus count exactly zero, because consecutive Gray codes differ in one bit and a single bit can only be old or new.

Worked example 39. Why Gray code is not optional in an asynchronous FIFO

Given. An 8-bit write pointer crossing into the read domain, incrementing every cycle at 500 MHz.

Method. Take the measured binary bogus probability from the row above and turn it into a rate. Then ask what a bogus pointer does.

P(bogus sample), 8 bits binary, measured above | 0.334
Crossings per second | 5.000×10 8
Bogus pointer values per second (order of magnitude) | 10 7 –10 8
Consequence of one bogus write pointer | reader sees a wrong depth — underflow or overflow
Consequence with Gray coding | none: the value is old or new, both safe

How this is got wrong. By assuming the synchroniser flops fix it. They do — per bit. The failure is a composition failure across bits, and no amount of depth on individual bits addresses it. The other frequent error is to Gray-code the pointer and then do arithmetic on it in the destination domain before converting back to binary; Gray codes do not add, and a comparison of Gray values is not a comparison of the numbers they encode except in the specific equality test that the standard FIFO empty/full logic uses.

[Table 336. CDC schemes and what each is actually for]
Scheme | Carries | Throughput | Latency | Fails if
Two-flop synchroniser | one bit, slowly changing | The pulse-loss trap, stated precisely. A
 synchroniser samples; it does not detect edges. If the source asserts a signal for one
 source-clock cycle and the destination clock is slower, the destination may simply
 never see it. The rule is that a level crossing into a slower domain must be held for
 at least one full destination period plus the source's own uncertainty — in
 practice three destination cycles is the usual specification. When the ratio is not
 known at design time, because the customer sets both frequencies, a level crossing
 is unimplementable and the crossing must be a toggle or a handshake. This is a
 frequent finding in IP integration: the block worked at the vendor's ratio and fails
 at the customer's.

Problem. A configuration register is written in a 100 MHz APB domain and read by a 1 GHz datapath. The 32 bits change together. What is the correct structure, and what is wrong with synchronising each bit?
Solution. Synchronising each bit independently is wrong for the reason measured above: the datapath can observe a mixture of old and new fields. The standard structure is data hold with a synchronised enable: the APB domain writes the 32 bits into a holding register and then toggles a single control bit; that one bit crosses through a two-flop synchroniser; the datapath samples the 32 bits only when it sees the toggle. The data bits themselves never need synchronisers because they are guaranteed stable for several destination cycles before and after the sampling point — a guarantee that must be written into the constraint file as a set_max_delay -datapath_only, or the tool will either flag it or, worse, silently optimise the holding register away.

Problem. A reviewer says ‘add a third flop, it is nearly free’. When is that the wrong advice?
Solution. When the crossing's problem is not metastability. A third flop buys MTBF and costs one cycle of latency; if the observed bug is pulse loss, bus coherency or a missing constraint, the third flop changes nothing except the latency, and it can make a reconvergence problem worse by lengthening one path relative to another. Establish which of the four CDC failure modes you have before reaching for depth: metastability, pulse loss, incoherent multi-bit sampling, and reconvergence of separately synchronised signals. Only the first is helped by more stages.
