절: X40.1 What is deliberately left out, and why
글:
X40.1 What is deliberately left out, and why

Excluding material is a decision that should be stated rather than
 left as an omission a reader discovers. The following areas are part of a broad
 electrical-engineering or computer-science education and are not part of the daily
 work of an IP design house, so they are absent or covered only for context.

[Table 338. Out of scope, with the reason]
Area | Why it is not here
Compiler theory beyond HLS scheduling | A block does not compile; the tool does
Operating system internals | Relevant to the driver author, not to the RTL
Distributed consensus | A chip is not a distributed system in that sense
Computability and complexity as such | Except where it classifies an EDA problem — that part is in X26
Quantum computing | Included briefly for context only; no current IP block uses it
Database theory, web systems, graphics rendering pipelines | Different industries

The boundary is a judgement and it moves. Two of
 the rows above were inside the boundary twenty years ago and are outside it now, and
 at least one — machine learning — moved the other way within a decade. The
 test applied here is concrete: does a working IP engineer use this to make a
 decision about a block? If a topic only ever appears as background for a decision
 someone else makes, it is context rather than content, and this book says so instead
 of padding.

Problem. You are handed a block type this map does not cover. How do you find its theory?
Solution. Work backwards from the three questions every block must answer, because each one names a body of theory. What does it compute, and how accurately? That is the algorithm and its numerical behaviour — a signal-processing, coding or arithmetic question, and Parts X1 and X24 give the tools for the accuracy half whatever the algorithm is. How fast must it go, and what does that cost? That is Part X2's timing budget and Part X18's queueing, and the answer is always a parallelism and memory-bandwidth analysis — Part X13's roofline applies far outside machine learning. How will you know it is right? That is Part X8, and it is domain independent. Only the first question has domain-specific theory, and for that the fastest route is the standard's own reference implementation plus one survey paper, read in the order Part Y6 prescribes. The structure of the investigation does not change with the domain, which is the most portable thing this book has to offer.

장: X41. DRAM: The Timing That Shapes Every Memory Controller
절: X41. DRAM: The Timing That Shapes Every Memory Controller — 들어가며
글:
X41. DRAM: The Timing That Shapes Every Memory Controller

Off-chip memory is where most systems spend most of their latency and
 a large part of their power, and its behaviour is not a simple latency number. A DRAM
 device is a state machine with a dozen timing constraints, and whether your block gets
 the bandwidth it was promised depends almost entirely on its access pattern rather
 than on the interface's rated speed.

장: X41. DRAM: The Timing That Shapes Every Memory Controller
절: X41.1 The bank, the row and the reason access order matters
글:
X41.1 The bank, the row and the reason access order matters

Why a DRAM read is three operations, not one

 | Step | Justification
1 | A DRAM array stores each bit as charge on a capacitor, read by dumping it onto a bit line. | The read is destructive — the charge is consumed.
2 | ACTIVATE opens a row: the whole row is sensed into the sense amplifiers, which form the row buffer . | Thousands of bits at once. This takes t RCD .
3 | READ or WRITE then accesses columns within the open row. | Fast — the data is already in the sense amplifiers. A second access to the same row is far cheaper than the first.
4 | PRECHARGE writes the row back and restores the bit lines. | Takes t RP . Required before opening a different row in the same bank.
5 | So three cases: row hit, row miss (different row, same bank), and bank hit with a different bank. | Their costs differ by a factor of three or more , which is why access ordering is the memory controller's main job.
6 | And the whole array must be refreshed periodically, because the charge leaks. | Refresh steals bandwidth and blocks access to a bank while it runs.

[Table 339. Read latency by case, DDR4-3200 (indicative t CL = t RCD = t RP =22)]
Case | Cycles | Latency (ns) | Relative to a row hit
Row hit (open row) | 22 | 13.75 | 1
Row miss, same bank | 66 | 41.25 | 3
Different bank, row hit | 22 | 13.75 | 1
Different bank, row miss | 44 | 27.5 | 2

Indicative JEDEC-speed-bin numbers, not a datasheet. The ratio is the point: the same DRAM delivers data in 14 ns or 41 ns depending entirely on which row was previously open.

[Table 340. Measured row-buffer hit rate and the bandwidth it implies, 16 banks, 20 000 accesses]
Access pattern | Row hit rate | Row miss rate | Total time (µs) | Bandwidth as % of the row-hit-only case
Sequential | 0.8748 | 0.1252 | 343.86 | 79.97
Stride 4 kB | 0.5 | 0.5 | 550 | 50
Random | 0 | 1 | 825 | 33.33
Two interleaved streams | 0 | 1 | 825 | 33.33

Simulated with a simple address decode (bank bits low, row bits high). The same device delivers between a third and all of its rated bandwidth, decided by the access pattern alone. This is why a block's DMA pattern is a system-level specification item.

장: X41. DRAM: The Timing That Shapes Every Memory Controller
절: X41.2 What the memory controller does about it
글:
X41.2 What the memory controller does about it

[Table 341. Controller techniques and what each attacks]
Technique | Attacks | Cost
Address mapping | Which bits select bank, row and column | Free, and it decides everything — interleaving banks on low bits turns a sequential stream into parallel bank accesses
Bank interleaving | Row-miss latency | Needs enough banks and enough outstanding requests
Request reordering (FR-FCFS) | Serves row hits before older row misses | A scheduling queue; and it makes latency unfair between requesters
Write batching | Bus turnaround, which costs several cycles | Write buffer; adds read latency when it drains
Open-page vs closed-page policy | Whether to leave a row open | Open wins on locality, closed wins on random traffic — a workload decision
Refresh scheduling | Refresh blocking a bank | Per-bank refresh and postponement; the device sets the limits

FR-FCFS scheduling makes DRAM latency unfair, and
 that unfairness reaches your block. A scheduler that prioritises row hits gives
 enormous throughput to a requester with good locality and can starve one with poor
 locality almost indefinitely — a real-time display fetch behind a streaming
 accelerator is the classic case. Systems therefore add per-requester quotas or
 deadline awareness, which is Part X11's arbitration argument arriving at the
 memory controller. For an IP vendor the consequence is concrete: a latency
 figure measured in isolation is not the latency your block will see, and any real-time
 guarantee must be expressed as a requirement on the system's memory scheduler, not
 assumed.

[Table 342. Peak bandwidth of common memory interfaces]
Interface | MT/s | Bits per channel | Channels | Peak GB/s | Relative to one DDR4-3200 channel
DDR4-3200 | 3200 | 64 | 2 | 51.2 | 2
DDR5-6400 | 6400 | 64 | 2 | 102.4 | 4
LPDDR5-6400 | 6400 | 32 | 4 | 102.4 | 4
HBM2E | 3200 | 1,024 | 1 | 409.6 | 16
HBM3 | 6400 | 1,024 | 1 | 819.2 | 32

Peak, which nothing achieves. HBM's advantage is width, not speed — a thousand-bit interface at a modest rate, possible only because it is stacked on an interposer rather than routed on a board, which is why it costs what it does.

장: X41. DRAM: The Timing That Shapes Every Memory Controller
절: X41.3 Refresh, and why it gets worse
글:
X41.3 Refresh, and why it gets worse

Worked example 40. What refresh costs at each density

Given. DDR4 requires all rows refreshed every 64 ms (32 ms above 85 °C). Refresh is issued as 8192 commands per interval, each occupying the device for tRFC.

Method. Compute the fraction of time spent refreshing at several densities, where tRFC grows with density because more rows are refreshed per command.

Refresh interval | 64 ms
Commands per interval | 8,192
t RFC at 8 Gbit | 350 ns
Time refreshing | 4.48 %
t RFC at 16 Gbit | 550 ns
Time refreshing | 7.04 %
At 32 Gbit and 95 °C (32 ms interval) | 22.53 %
Trend | refresh overhead grows with density and with temperature

How this is got wrong. By assuming refresh is a rounding error. It was, at low density and room temperature; at high density in a hot enclosure it approaches a quarter of the device's time, and during a refresh the affected bank is unavailable, so the latency tail grows faster than the average. Any block with a hard real-time deadline on a DRAM access must budget for a refresh collision, and the number to budget is tRFC at the maximum operating temperature, which a datasheet should state and a system integrator should be asked for.

Problem. Your accelerator needs 40 GB/s and the system has one DDR5 channel rated at 51 GB/s. Is that enough?
Solution. Almost certainly not, and the calculation to show it is short. Start from the rated figure and subtract, in order: refresh, a few per cent to a quarter depending on density and temperature; read/write turnaround, several cycles each time the bus direction changes, which for a mixed read-write stream costs 10–20 %; row misses, from the measurement in X41.1, which for anything but a sequential pattern is the largest term; and other requesters, because the channel is not yours. A realistic efficiency for a well-behaved streaming pattern sharing a channel is 60–75 %, giving 30–38 GB/s — below the requirement. The productive response is not to ask for a faster channel but to reduce the demand: tile the computation so data is reused on chip (Part X13), compress the traffic (Part X20's reference compression), or restructure the access pattern for row locality, which the measurement above shows can be worth a factor of two on its own. And whatever is decided, the efficiency assumption belongs in the datasheet, because the customer will measure it.

장: X42. Reset, Initialisation and the States Nobody Simulates
절: X42. Reset, Initialisation and the States Nobody Simulates — 들어가며
글:
X42. Reset, Initialisation and the States Nobody Simulates

Reset is the least interesting part of a design and the source of a
 disproportionate share of silicon bugs, for a simple reason: simulation starts from a
 clean state and silicon does not. This part treats reset with the same seriousness as
 the datapath, because the failures it causes are the ones that appear only in the
 lab.

장: X42. Reset, Initialisation and the States Nobody Simulates
절: X42.1 Synchronous, asynchronous, and the one that is actually used
글:
X42.1 Synchronous, asynchronous, and the one that is actually used

[Table 343. Reset styles]
Style | Assertion | De-assertion | Cost | Problem
Synchronous | On a clock edge | On a clock edge | Wider reset net timing; needs a running clock | Cannot reset a block whose clock has not started
Asynchronous | Immediate | Immediate | Cheap — the flop's async pin | De-assertion can violate recovery/removal and cause metastability
Asynchronous assert, synchronous de-assert | Immediate | Synchronised to the clock | A two-flop synchroniser per domain | None — this is the standard answer
No reset (initialised by first write) | — | — | Free — saves the reset net on datapath flops | X-propagation until written; needs care in verification

Why de-assertion is the dangerous edge

 | Step | Justification
1 | A flop with an asynchronous reset has recovery and removal times: the reset must be stable for a window around the clock edge. | Exactly analogous to setup and hold, and checked by the same static timing analysis.
2 | Reset assertion is asynchronous and harmless: the flop goes to its reset value whenever it arrives. | There is no race, because the destination is unconditional.
3 | De-assertion races the clock. | If reset releases within the recovery window, the flop may go metastable or may capture the pre-reset value.
4 | With one clock, the tool checks and fixes it. | Recovery and removal are ordinary timing checks.
5 | With a large design, the reset tree's own skew means different flops leave reset on different cycles. | A state machine can then advance while part of its state is still reset , reaching a state the designer never enumerated. This is the classic reset bug and it is invisible in RTL simulation, where reset de-asserts everywhere at once.
6 | Remedy: synchronise the de-assertion in each clock domain, and treat the reset tree like a clock tree. | Balanced, buffered, and timed.

Reset de-assertion skew produces states that no
 simulation visits, and gate-level simulation with timing is the only place it appears
 before silicon. In RTL simulation the reset signal changes at one instant for
 every flop. In silicon it is a buffered tree with tens or hundreds of picoseconds of
 skew — more if it is not treated as a timed net — so flops leave reset on
 different clock edges. A counter can start counting while its comparator is still
 held; a FIFO's write pointer can advance while its read pointer is reset, making the
 FIFO appear full at power-up. The two defences are structural: synchronise
 de-assertion per domain so all flops in a domain release on the same edge, and design
 state machines so that a partially-reset state is not reachable — usually by
 holding the whole machine in an idle state until an explicit enable.

장: X42. Reset, Initialisation and the States Nobody Simulates
절: X42.2 X-propagation: where simulation lies in both directions
글:
X42.2 X-propagation: where simulation lies in both directions

[Table 344. How simulators treat unknown values, and why it matters]
Situation | RTL simulation | Silicon | Consequence
Uninitialised flop read | X | A definite 0 or 1, randomly | Simulation may be more pessimistic than reality
if (x) where x is X | Takes the else branch | Takes one branch definitely | X-optimism: the bug is hidden
case with X selector | May take the default | Takes a real branch | Same optimism
Mux with X select | Output X if inputs differ; output the value if they are equal | Real value | Can hide or expose
Flop with X data | Captures X | Captures a real value | X-pessimism: X spreads where silicon would not

X-optimism and X-pessimism are both wrong, in opposite
 directions, and the remedies differ. Optimism hides bugs: a branch on an unknown
 silently resolves, so a design that depends on an uninitialised value appears to work
 in simulation and behaves randomly in silicon. Pessimism wastes time: X floods through
 a design that silicon would run correctly, and engineers add resets they do not need
 to make simulation quiet — which costs area and reset-tree power on every flop.
 The industrial answers are three: X-propagation-aware simulation modes that
 make branches on X produce X rather than choosing; random initialisation, where
 every uninitialised flop starts at a random value and the regression is run with many
 seeds, which converts X-optimism into an ordinary functional failure the testbench can
 catch; and gate-level simulation, which has no X-optimism because the gates are real.
 Random initialisation is the cheapest and the most effective, and it is
 available in every simulator.

[Table 345. Probability of catching a dependence on one uninitialised bit, with random initialisation]
Unreset flops | Random seeds run | P(at least one seed exposes it) | P(missed) (%)
100 | 1 | 0.5 | 50
100 | 10 | 0.999023 | 0.0977
100 | 100 | 1 | 0
1,000 | 10 | 0.999023 | 0.0977
1,000 | 100 | 1 | 0

Assuming the bug manifests when that bit takes one particular value. Ten seeds give a 99.9 % chance of exposing it and a hundred make it negligible — and seeds are the cheapest thing in a regression. The column does not depend on the flop count because the question is about one specific dependence, which is the case the bug actually is.

장: X42. Reset, Initialisation and the States Nobody Simulates
절: X42.3 Power-up: the sequence and what it must guarantee
글:
X42.3 Power-up: the sequence and what it must guarantee

[Table 346. The power-up sequence, and what breaks if a step is skipped]
Step | Guarantee | If skipped
Supplies ramp in the specified order | No forward-biased junction, no latch-up | Permanent damage, not a functional failure
Reset asserted before and during ramp | No spurious activity, no contention on shared buses | Bus contention, high current, possible damage
Clocks stable before reset release | Synchronous de-assertion works | The synchroniser has no clock, so de-assertion is asynchronous after all
Reset held for the specified number of cycles | Every flop in every domain has seen an edge | Partially reset state — X42.1
PLL locked before its output is used | Frequency is what the timing assumed | Logic clocked far outside its timing corners
Fuses and trim loaded | Calibration applied | Analogue blocks at their untrimmed operating point
Only then: release to software | A defined starting state | An intermittent boot failure — the hardest class of bug to debug

Worked example 41. How many reset cycles does a block need?

Given. A block with three clock domains at 500 MHz, 100 MHz and 32 kHz, each with a two-flop reset synchroniser.

Method. Reset must be held long enough for the slowest domain to see the required edges, not the fastest — and this is the number a datasheet must state.

Fastest domain period | 2 ns
Slowest domain period | 30.518 µs
Edges needed per synchroniser | 3
Hold time for the 500 MHz domain | 6 ns
Hold time for the 32 kHz domain | 91.553 µs
Required reset assertion | 91.553 µs — set by the slowest domain
Common error | specifying it in cycles of the fast clock

How this is got wrong. By quoting the reset requirement in clock cycles without saying which clock. ‘Assert reset for 16 cycles’ is ambiguous in a multi-clock block and is wrong by four orders of magnitude if the reader picks the fast clock. State the requirement in absolute time, and state it for the slowest clock the block can be configured with — including the case where a clock is stopped, which requires either that reset be held until it starts or that the domain be reset asynchronously and independently.

Problem. Your block occasionally fails to come out of reset, roughly one boot in a thousand. Where do you look?
Solution. The frequency is the clue: one in a thousand is a race, not a logic error, because a logic error would be deterministic. Three candidates, in order. Reset de-assertion recovery: if any domain's reset is not synchronised, de-assertion races the clock and metastability resolves the wrong way occasionally — the rate is computable from Part X3's MTBF formula with the reset edge as the asynchronous event, and one in a thousand boots is entirely consistent with an unsynchronised reset. Clock-before-reset ordering: if reset is released in the same window that a PLL locks or a clock gate opens, some flops see edges and some do not, giving the partial-reset state of X42.1; this shows a dependence on temperature or supply, because they change the lock time. An uninitialised state element that is usually benign: a flop without reset whose value normally does not matter, except in the rare case — and this is what random-initialisation regression is for. The diagnostic that separates them is to vary the reset pulse width and the clock start time: a recovery race moves with clock phase, an ordering problem moves with pulse width, and an uninitialised value moves with neither.

장: X43. Power Intent: Domains, Retention and Isolation
절: X43. Power Intent: Domains, Retention and Isolation — 들어가며
글:
X43. Power Intent: Domains, Retention and Isolation

Power gating is the only technique that attacks leakage to near zero,
 and it is the one that changes an IP block's interface, its reset behaviour and its
 verification plan. A vendor whose block supports it properly is selling something
 materially different from one whose block does not.

[그림] Figure 40. A switchable power domain and the cells that make it safe.

장: X43. Power Intent: Domains, Retention and Isolation
절: X43.1 The four special cells, and what each prevents
글:
X43.1 The four special cells, and what each prevents

[Table 347. Low-power cells]
Cell | Sits | Prevents | Cost
Isolation | On every signal leaving a switched domain | A floating value driving the always-on domain , which causes static crowbar current in the receiving gate | One gate per signal, plus the enable's routing
Level shifter | Between domains at different voltages | A low-voltage 1 failing to turn off a high-voltage PMOS — again static current | One cell per signal; slower than a buffer
Retention flop | Replacing flops whose state must survive | Losing state on power-down | 20–30 % larger than a normal flop, plus always-on routing for the save/restore signals
Power switch | Between the always-on rail and the domain | — | Area, and IR drop through the switch when on ; the switching itself is an inrush event (Part X32)
Always-on buffer | On signals crossing a domain that is off | A signal path being cut | Special placement

Worked example 42. Is retention worth it, or should the block re-initialise?

Given. A block with 20 000 flops, of which 3 000 hold configuration and 17 000 hold datapath state. Leakage when on is 12 mW. The alternative to retention is for software to rewrite the configuration on wake.

Method. Compare three options on area, wake latency and residual leakage. Retention flops still leak, because their storage is always on.

Retain everything: retention flops | 20,000
Area penalty at 25 % | 5000 flop-equivalents
Residual leakage (retention cells stay powered) | 1.8 mW (~15 %)
Retain configuration only | 3,000 retention flops
Area penalty | 750 flop-equivalents
Residual leakage | 0.36 mW
Retain nothing: software rewrite | 0 retention flops
Wake latency added | thousands of register writes over APB
Best for a block woken rarely | retain configuration only

How this is got wrong. By retaining everything because it is simplest. Datapath state is usually worthless across a power-down — the block was idle, so there is nothing in flight — and retaining it costs area and leakage for nothing. The design work is to partition state into what must survive and what must not, and then to make the latter's reset unconditional so that a wake-up is indistinguishable from a cold start. That partition is a specification item and is the single most useful thing a vendor can document about power behaviour.

장: X43. Power Intent: Domains, Retention and Isolation
절: X43.2 What UPF adds, and why RTL alone is not enough
글:
X43.2 What UPF adds, and why RTL alone is not enough

Why power intent lives outside the RTL

 | Step | Justification
1 | RTL describes function; it has no notion of a supply. | A Verilog module does not say which rail powers it.
2 | Power domains, switches, isolation and retention are structural and depend on the floorplan and the process. | The same RTL is used with and without power gating in different products.
3 | So they are described in a separate file — UPF or CPF — that the tools read alongside. | Synthesis inserts the cells, verification simulates the power states, and place-and-route builds the switch network.
4 | Simulation must then model a powered-down domain as X, and check that isolation is enabled before power goes away. | This is the verification that cannot be done in RTL alone , and it is where the bugs are.
5 | The power state table enumerates the legal combinations of domain states. | And the illegal ones are what must be proven unreachable — a formal problem of exactly the kind Part X33 recommends.

[Table 348. Power-state space against domain count]
Switchable domains | Combinations | Typically legal states | Illegal states to exclude | Ordered transitions
2 | 4 | 3 | 1 | 12
3 | 8 | 4 | 4 | 56
4 | 16 | 5 | 11 | 240
5 | 32 | 6 | 26 | 992
6 | 64 | 7 | 57 | 4,032

The legal column assumes a simple nested hierarchy — each domain requires the ones below it. The transition column is the verification burden, and it is quadratic, which is why power-state machines are kept deliberately simple and why a block that demands its own independent domain is expensive to integrate.

The classic power-gating bug is an isolation enable
 that arrives too late, and it is not a functional bug in the usual sense. If power
 is removed before isolation is enabled, the outputs float for a short interval;
 downstream gates in the always-on domain then sit at an intermediate level and
 conduct, drawing a current spike that is invisible to functional simulation and shows
 up as excess power or, in the worst case, as damage. The sequence is: assert
 isolation, assert retention save, then remove power — and the reverse on
 wake. Getting it right is a small state machine; proving it right requires
 power-aware simulation, and asserting it is what a UPF-aware formal check does. An IP
 block that supplies its own power-control sequence and the assertions that check it is
 removing a whole class of integration risk.

Problem. Why is ‘race to idle’ sometimes better than running slowly, when X43.2 shows energy per operation is lowest at low voltage?
Solution. Because the block is not the only thing consuming power. Running at the top operating point finishes the work sooner and lets the whole subsystem — memory, interconnect, PLLs, the always-on logic, and any peripheral waiting on the result — enter a low-power state earlier. That static and shared component does not scale with the block's voltage, so the comparison is between (fast, high dynamic, short time, then everything off) and (slow, low dynamic, long time, everything on throughout). Race to idle wins when the fixed overhead per unit time is large relative to the block's own dynamic power, which is common in small IP blocks inside large systems and uncommon in a block that dominates its chip. The crossover is computable from the block's dynamic power at each point, the platform's idle power, and the entry/exit energy of the low-power state — and it is worth computing rather than asserting, because both answers appear in the literature and both are right for their own systems.

X4.1 From loss in dB to intersymbol interference

A channel specification usually gives one number: insertion loss at the
 Nyquist frequency. That number is not directly usable. What the receiver has to deal
 with is the pulse response — what a single transmitted symbol looks like
 at the sampler, sampled once per unit interval. The cursors of that response are the
 intersymbol interference, and they are what every equaliser in the chain is
 fighting.

[Table 350. Pulse-response cursors of a √ f channel at 53.125 GBd as insertion loss is swept]

Worst-case eye height goes negative long before the
 link is actually unusable, and that is not a contradiction. The worst case demands
 a specific data pattern; at 10−4 bit error rate you care about
 patterns that occur with probability around 10−4, not about the one
 worst pattern. This is why link analysis moved from peak-distortion analysis to
 statistical eye methods: convolve the probability distributions of the
 individual cursors rather than summing their magnitudes. Peak analysis is a bound;
 the statistical eye is the answer. A specification that quotes a closed worst-case eye
 and a working link is not lying, but it is using two different methods and should say
 so.

The DFE's advantage and its constraint are the same

Q for BER 10 −4 | 3.719

장: X4. The Wireline Link Budget, Worked
절: X4.4 Where the Gaussian assumption fails, and what FEC changes
글:
X4.4 Where the Gaussian assumption fails, and what FEC changes

Two facts force a modern link away from the simple budget above. Noise
 at the slicer is not Gaussian — crosstalk is the sum of a few discrete
 interferers and has a bounded, multi-modal distribution — and errors are not
 independent, because a DFE that makes a wrong decision feeds it back and produces a
 short burst. Both matter for FEC design, which is the subject of Part F2 and of
 the block this book's practice volume builds.

[Table 355. Assumption, reality, and the design consequence]
Assumption in the simple budget | What is actually true | Consequence for the design
Noise is Gaussian | Crosstalk from k aggressors is a sum of k bounded terms; the tail is lighter than Gaussian but the body is wider | Extrapolating a measured 10 −6 BER to 10 −15 with a Gaussian fit can be wrong by decades in either direction
Errors are independent | DFE error propagation produces bursts of length comparable to the number of taps | The FEC must be chosen for a burst channel : symbol-oriented codes (Reed–Solomon over GF(2 10 )) rather than bit-oriented ones
The sampling instant is optimal | The CDR tracks a noisy estimate and dithers about the optimum | Budget a static phase offset as well as jitter
The equaliser is converged | Adaptation is a slow loop with its own noise and can converge to a local optimum | Specify and measure the converged state ; a measurement taken before convergence is not a measurement of the link

Problem. A link measures 10−6 raw BER. The FEC is RS(544,514) over GF(210), correcting 15 symbol errors per codeword. Estimate the post-FEC frame error rate, and say why the estimate is fragile.
Solution. Each codeword is 544 ten-bit symbols. A symbol is wrong if any of its ten bits is wrong, so with independent bit errors the symbol error probability is about 1−(1−10−6)10 ≈ 10−5. The codeword fails when more than 15 of 544 symbols are wrong; with a mean of 544×10−5 ≈ 5.4×10−3 errors per codeword the binomial tail at 16 is astronomically small, which is the intended answer. The fragility is the independence assumption. If a DFE burst corrupts several consecutive bits, they may fall inside one symbol — which helps, since a symbol code charges the same price for one wrong bit or ten — or straddle a symbol boundary and cost two. Worse, if bursts are long enough to span many symbols, the tail is controlled by burst statistics that the raw BER number does not contain at all. Post-FEC performance cannot be computed from pre-FEC BER alone; it needs the error-clustering statistics, which is why compliance specifications define stressed-eye tests rather than BER targets alone.

Problem. Why does IEEE 802.3dj concatenate an inner code with the outer RS-KP4 rather than simply using a stronger single code?
Solution. Three reasons, and they are all system reasons rather than coding-theory ones. Backward compatibility: RS(544,514) is already deployed and an outer layer that leaves it intact protects an installed base of PCS implementations. Latency and locality: the inner code can be short and decoded close to the PHY with low latency, cleaning up the random errors, while the outer code handles what remains; a single long code with the same total redundancy would have higher decoding latency. Burst breaking: the inner decoder's residual errors, after interleaving, present the outer decoder with something closer to the independent-symbol channel that Reed–Solomon analysis assumes — which is precisely the assumption the previous problem showed to be the fragile one.

Reed–Solomon is the error-correcting code that every high-speed

 as four opaque stages. This part opens each stage on a small field where the numbers

절: X5.1 The field is a choice, and an unverified choice is a risk
글:
X5.1 The field is a choice, and an unverified choice is a risk

A Reed–Solomon code lives over a finite field GF(2m
 ), and the field is fixed by a primitive polynomial. Two implementations that
 pick different primitive polynomials produce different codewords and cannot talk to
 each other, even though both are ‘RS(544,514)’. The model this chapter
 runs therefore takes the polynomial as a parameter and records whether it has
 been confirmed against the standard.

Worked example 45. Verifying a small field before using it

Given. GF(24) generated by x4 + x + 1 (0b10011).

Method. The model builds exponent and log tables and refuses any polynomial whose root α has order less than 2m−1 — that is, it rejects non-primitive polynomials by construction rather than by trusting the caller. It then checks the field axioms, not a table of expected values, because a table of expected values is only as good as whoever typed it.

Field size | 16
Order of α | 15
Axiom checks performed | 원소수, 본원소, 역원실패, 항등실패, 나눗셈실패, 지수표전사, 필드인가
All axioms hold | no

How this is got wrong. By hard-coding the polynomial of the standard you last worked on. 0x11D and 0x12D both generate GF(256) and both are primitive; they are different fields for interoperability purposes. The repository's model keeps this as an explicit parameter with a confirmed flag precisely so that an unverified default cannot quietly become an assumption — the flag is false for the KP4 field in this repository, because the clause that fixes it has not been read.

Given. Message symbols [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. Three symbols are then corrupted by XOR: position 2 ⊕ 7, position 5 ⊕ 11, position 11 ⊕ 4. The code corrects up to t = 3 symbols.

Method. Encode systematically, inject the errors, compute the syndromes, run Berlekamp–Massey, Chien and Forney. Everything below is the model's actual output.

Codeword | 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 9 8 9 3 10 0
Received | 1 2 4 4 5 13 7 8 9 9 8 13 3 10 0
Syndromes S 0..5 | 8 15 1 15 9 8
Errors found | 3
Positions the decoder located | [2, 5, 11]

Recovered message | 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9

How this is got wrong. By declaring success when the syndromes go to zero and stopping there. A decoder that miscorrects also produces zero syndromes — it has landed on a different valid codeword. The only defence is to re-check after correction and to bound the number of corrections by t; the model does both, which is why the next section's measurement of the beyond-t region is meaningful.

Why the syndromes are what they are. The syndrome
 Sj is the received polynomial evaluated at αfcr+j
 . Every valid codeword is divisible by the generator, whose roots are exactly
 those powers, so a clean codeword gives all-zero syndromes. What survives the
 evaluation is therefore only the error polynomial — the syndromes depend on the
 errors and not at all on the data. That single fact is what makes bounded
 distance decoding possible, and it is worth verifying on the numbers above: change

X5.3 Berlekamp–Massey as a hardware recurrence

What Berlekamp–Massey is actually doing

 | Step | Justification
1 | The syndromes of an e -error pattern satisfy a linear recurrence of order e . | Each error contributes a geometric sequence α ji ; a sum of e geometrics satisfies an order- e recurrence.
2 | The recurrence's characteristic polynomial is the error locator σ( x ). | Its roots are the inverses of the error positions, by construction.
3 | So decoding reduces to: find the shortest linear recurrence that generates the observed syndrome sequence . | This restatement is the entire content of the algorithm.
4 | Berlekamp–Massey finds it in 2 t iterations, each a discrepancy computation and a polynomial update. | Equivalent to the extended Euclidean algorithm on x 2 t and S ( x ); the two are the standard alternatives in RTL.
5 | Each iteration costs O ( t ) field multiplies, so the whole algorithm is O ( t 2 ). | For KP4, t  = 15, so the key equation is a few hundred multiplies — small beside the 544-symbol Chien search.
6 | The iteration count is data independent. | Which is why the decoder has a fixed latency, which is why the PCS can be built around it. A variable-latency decoder would need elastic buffering through the whole receive path.

절: X5.4 Beyond t : the region a careless test never visits
글:
X5.4 Beyond t: the region a careless test never visits

A bounded-distance decoder corrects up to t errors. What it does
 with t+1 or more is the interesting question, because that is the region a real
 link visits and a lazy test never does. Three outcomes are possible: detect the
 failure and flag it, miscorrect to a wrong codeword silently, or leave the word
 unchanged. The measurement below counts all three.

[Table 358. RS(15,9), t  = 3: fraction of words returned correct as the injected error count is swept]
Errors injected | Region | Recovered exactly | Trials | Fraction | Note
1 | ≤ t | 400 | 400 | 1 | measured
2 | ≤ t | 400 | 400 | 1 | measured
3 | ≤ t | 400 | 400 | 1 | measured
4 | > t | 0 | 400 | 0 | measured
5 | > t | 0 | 400 | 0 | measured
6 | > t | 0 | 400 | 0 | measured

400 random trials per row, seeded. The first three rows must be 1.000 — that is the code's guarantee. The rows below must not be 1.000, and a test suite that only ever injects zero or one error cannot tell a working decoder from one that returns its input unchanged.

This is the false-green that RS test benches
 actually produce. Inject zero errors, check the output equals the input, declare
 the decoder verified. A decoder consisting of a wire passes. The repository's
 measurement function refuses to report a pass from a zero-error trial at all, and its
 test suite deliberately breaks the syndrome computation and asserts that the
 measurement notices. A verification plan for an FEC block must state, for every
 test, what broken implementation that test would catch.

Problem. Why can a decoder that corrects a word with more than t errors be worse than one that flags the word as uncorrectable?
Solution. Because a miscorrection is a silent data error and an uncorrectable flag is an announced one. Upper layers are built to handle the announcement: Ethernet marks the frame errored and it is discarded and retransmitted; storage returns a read failure and the host retries or reconstructs from parity. There is no layer that handles data that is wrong and claims to be right. In a system with an outer code — the concatenated structure of 802.3dj — the point is sharper still: the outer decoder can use the inner decoder's uncorrectable flag as an erasure, and an erasure costs one parity symbol where an unflagged error costs two. Detection is worth roughly twice as much as the same amount of correction, which is why real decoders spend logic on checking their own output.

Problem. KP4 is RS(544,514) over GF(210), yet 544 > 210−1 is false — 544 is comfortably below 1023. What is the code called when n is smaller than the natural length, and what does the shortening cost?
Solution. It is a shortened Reed–Solomon code: take the RS(1023,993) code and fix the leading 479 message symbols to zero, then decline to transmit them. Both ends know they are zero, so the decoder simply treats the received word as having 479 leading zeros. Shortening costs nothing in minimum distance — d = n−k+1 = 31 either way, so t remains 15 — and it costs nothing in the decoder except that the Chien search may be restricted to the 544 positions that are actually transmitted, which is a saving. The one thing it does change is the false-detection probability: a shortened code has fewer codewords in the same space, so a random error pattern is less likely to land on a valid codeword. Shortening therefore improves miscorrection statistics slightly, for free.

Worked example 47. Multiplies are not the bottleneck — memory bandwidth is

Given. A 4096-point complex FFT, 16-bit I and Q, to be completed in 10 µs. One multiplier can do 1 complex multiply per cycle at 500 MHz; an SRAM port can do one 32-bit access per cycle at the same rate.

Method. Compute the two requirements separately and compare them with what one instance of each resource supplies.

Complex multiplies | 24,576
Multiplier-cycles available in 10 µs per multiplier | 5,000
Multipliers needed | 5
Memory accesses (read 2, write 2 per butterfly) | 98,304

How this is got wrong. By sizing the block from the multiply count, which is the number every textbook gives. The memory requirement is four times larger and it is the one that will not be met by adding a cheap resource, because an SRAM with four times the ports is not four times the area — it is worse. The architectural answers are all about memory: in-place computation to halve the storage, multi-bank schemes so several butterflies read in parallel without conflict, and higher radix to do more arithmetic per memory visit. Radix-4's real attraction is that it halves the number of memory passes, not that it saves 25 % of the multiplies.

X6.2 Three architectures and where each belongs

[Table 361. FFT architectures]
Architecture | Throughput | Area | Latency | Where it belongs
Single butterfly + memory | 1 butterfly / cycle | smallest | N log 2 N /2 cycles | Control-plane spectral analysis; anything not on the critical path
Pipelined (SDF / SDC) | 1 sample / cycle, streaming | log 2 N butterflies + N words of delay | ≈ N cycles | OFDM receivers, channelisers — anything with a continuous stream
Parallel / SSR | P samples / cycle | P × the pipeline | Why the streaming architectures are named after their
 commutators rather than their butterflies. Single-path delay feedback (SDF) and
 single-path delay commutator (SDC) differ in how the delay line is arranged around the
 butterfly, and that arrangement — not the arithmetic — determines the
 total memory, which is the dominant cost. An N-point radix-2 SDF pipeline needs

 N/4, …, 1 across the stages. That geometric distribution is why the

장: X6. The FFT as a Hardware Block, Worked
절: X6.3 Fixed point in the FFT: scaling schedules
글:
X6.3 Fixed point in the FFT: scaling schedules

Each radix-2 stage can double the magnitude of the data. Over
 log2N stages that is a growth of N, so a 4096-point transform
 can grow its input by 12 bits. Three strategies exist and they give measurably
 different results.

[Table 363. Measured SQNR and measured magnitude growth of a 256-point 16-bit FFT under three scaling schedules, 8 random trials each]
Schedule | Mean SQNR (dB) | Worst SQNR (dB) | Measured peak growth × | Extra integer bits the growth demands
Scale every stage | 0.4978 | 0.4349 | 0.0466 | 0
Conditional (block floating point) | 0.08273 | 0.06056 | 1.12 | 0.164
No scaling — grow the word | 0.4426 | 0.3704 | 13.3 | 3.73

The growth column is measured on a noise-like input, so it is far below the worst-case bound of N: a random input does not align in phase. The measured figure is not a bound — a single tone at a bin centre would reach the bound, and a design justified by this column alone would overflow on the first sine wave a customer applied. Unconditional scaling is safe and loses precision every stage. Block floating point recovers most of it at the cost of a magnitude detector and an exponent that must travel with the data — and that exponent is an interface, which a specification frequently forgets to mention.

The block-floating-point exponent is part of the
 output. A block that returns a mantissa array and keeps the exponent internal has
 returned meaningless numbers. This is a real and recurring integration bug: the FFT
 passes its own tests, in which the reference is scaled the same way, and fails in the
 system, where the next block assumes a fixed scale. Any scaling that depends on the
 data must appear in the port list.

Problem. An OFDM receiver uses a 2048-point FFT. The input is an ADC output with 10 effective bits. How many bits should the FFT carry internally, and why is ‘10 + log22048 = 21’ the wrong answer?
Solution. It is wrong in both directions. It is too pessimistic because the worst-case growth of N assumes every input conspires to align in phase at one output bin; for a noise-like OFDM signal the growth is closer to √N, about 5.5 bits, and unconditional scaling by 2 per stage over-attenuates such a signal by the same factor. It is too optimistic because it accounts only for range and not for the accumulated quantisation noise of the twiddle multiplies, which adds roughly half a bit per stage of precision loss. The correct procedure is Part X1's: state the end-to-end metric (for OFDM, the EVM the constellation demands), then sweep the internal word length against that metric and read off the knee. The answer is a measurement, and it depends on the signal statistics, which is why an FFT IP block's datasheet must state the input statistics its SQNR figure was measured with.

절: X6.4 Twiddle factors: the quiet memory
글:
X6.4 Twiddle factors: the quiet memory

[Table 364. Twiddle-factor ROM: full table vs. one-eighth with symmetry, 16-bit I and Q]
N | Full entries | Full ROM (kB) | ⅛ entries | ⅛ ROM (kB) | Saving
256 | 128 | 0.5 | 33 | 0.129 | 3.88
1,024 | 512 | 2 | 129 | 0.504 | 3.97
4,096 | 2,048 | 8 | 513 | 2 | 3.99
16,384 | 8,192 | 32 | 2,049 | 8 | 4
65,536 | 32,768 | 128 | 8,193 | 32 | 4

The eighth-table exploits the symmetries of the unit circle; recovering the other seven octants costs a few multiplexers and a conditional negate and swap. For N = 65 536 the difference is between a ROM that fits on a corner of the block and one that dominates it.

The symmetries, so the multiplexer logic makes
 sense. WNk =
 e−2πik/N traces the unit circle clockwise. Cosine is
 even and sine is odd about the real axis, giving the lower half from the upper half;
 the quarter-turn identity exchanges sine and cosine, giving the second quadrant from
 the first; and the eighth-turn identity does the same within a quadrant. So the ROM
 stores angles from 0 to π/4 and the address decoder computes three bits —
 which octant — that control a swap of the I and Q outputs and two sign
 inversions. The whole recovery is combinational and adds perhaps two gate delays,
 against a ROM eight times smaller.

Problem. Instead of a ROM, twiddles can be generated by a CORDIC rotator or by a recursive oscillator w[n+1] = w[n] · W. When is each appropriate?
Solution. The recursive oscillator is the cheapest — one complex multiply per twiddle — and is unusable in a fixed-point pipeline because it is a marginally stable recursion: quantisation error accumulates in both magnitude and phase, and over the thousands of twiddles of a large transform the magnitude drifts away from unity. It is acceptable only with periodic re-seeding from a small ROM, which is a hybrid rather than a replacement. CORDIC is exact to its iteration count and costs only shifts and adds, making it attractive in FPGA fabric where multipliers are a scarce hard resource but LUTs are plentiful; it costs latency, which a pipelined design can absorb. The ROM wins in ASIC, where a small compiled ROM is dense and the alternative spends timing budget. As so often, the right answer is set by which resource the target technology makes expensive, not by any property of the algorithm.

장: X7. Power and Energy, Worked
절: X7. Power and Energy, Worked — 들어가며

X7. Power and Energy, Worked

A design house is asked for three numbers about power: how much the
 block burns, how much of that is unavoidable, and what a customer can do about it.
 All three are computable, and a vendor who can produce them with their assumptions
 stated is selling something the competitor who quotes a single milliwatt figure is
 not.

장: X7. Power and Energy, Worked
절: X7.1 The three terms
글:
X7.1 The three terms

Where the joules go

 | Step | Justification
1 | Charging a node of capacitance C to V takes CV 2 from the supply, of which CV 2 /2 is stored and CV 2 /2 is dissipated in the pull-up. | Integrate iv over the transient; the result is independent of the resistance, which is why making transistors faster does not save switching energy.
2 | Discharging dissipates the stored half in the pull-down. | So a full cycle costs CV 2 , and a 0→1→0 pair is one cycle.
3 | P dyn = α CV 2 f , with α the probability a node switches per clock. | Rate times energy. α is the only term the RTL designer controls directly , and it is the term power estimates get wrong.
4 | P short arises while both devices conduct during a transition; it scales with input slew. | Typically 5–15 % of dynamic. Controlled by slew limits, not by architecture.
5 | P leak = V · I off , with I off ∝ e − V th /( nkT/q ) . | Subthreshold conduction. Exponential in threshold and in temperature , which is why leakage is a thermal-runaway risk and dynamic power is not.

Worked example 48. A gate-level power estimate from first principles

Given. A block with 200 000 gates, average switched capacitance 1 fF per gate, V = 0.8 V, f = 1 GHz, activity factor α = 0.15. Clock network adds 30 % and its α is 1.

Method. Apply αCV2f to the logic and to the clock separately, because their activity factors differ by nearly an order of magnitude and averaging them is the commonest source of a wrong estimate.

Logic dynamic power | 19200 mW
Clock network capacitance (30 % of logic) | 60000 pF
Clock dynamic power (α = 1) | 38400 mW
Clock as a fraction of total dynamic | 66.7 %
Total dynamic | 57600 mW
Energy per cycle | 57600 pJ

How this is got wrong. By applying one activity factor to the whole design. The clock toggles every cycle by definition; logic in a typical datapath toggles on ten to twenty per cent of cycles. An estimate that uses α = 0.2 uniformly understates the clock by 5× and, since the clock here is two thirds of the total, understates the block by a factor approaching two. Clock gating is the first power optimisation for exactly this reason, and its benefit is visible in this table before any tool is run.

Parallelism converts the voltage curve into a genuine
 win, and this is the single most important architectural consequence of the table
 above. Suppose a block must deliver throughput T. Run one copy at
 1.0 V, or two copies at the voltage that halves the frequency. The two copies
 have twice the capacitance but each switches half as often per unit of work, so
 dynamic power is 2 × (V′/V)2 × ½ =
 (V′/V)2 of the original. From the table, halving the
 frequency permits roughly a 0.65 V supply, giving about
 0.42× the power for the same throughput at rather more than twice the area.
 This calculation is the reason modern chips are wide and slow rather than narrow
 and fast, and it is worth being able to do it on a whiteboard.

글:
X7.3 Leakage, and why it changes the shape of everything

[Table 366. Subthreshold leakage against temperature, normalised to 25 °C ( V th = 0.30 V, n = 1.3), and its share of a block that is 20 % leakage at room temperature]
T (°C) | nkT/q (mV) | Relative leakage | Leakage share of total (%)
0 | 23.54 | 0.44 | 9.9
25 | 25.69 | 1 | 20
50 | 27.85 | 2 | 33.4
75 | 30 | 3.63 | 47.6
100 | 32.15 | 6.08 | 60.3

Computed from the subthreshold exponential alone; DIBL and gate leakage would steepen it further. The share column shows why a block that is a fifth leakage on the bench can be nearly half leakage in a hot enclosure.

Leakage and temperature form a positive feedback
 loop. Leakage raises power, power raises junction temperature, and higher
 temperature raises leakage exponentially. Below a certain thermal resistance the loop
 has a stable operating point; above it there is none, and the part runs away. This is
 not a theoretical concern in high-leakage processes: it is why datasheets specify a
 maximum junction temperature and a maximum case-to-ambient thermal resistance,
 and why a customer who improves cooling is not merely buying margin but may be buying
 stability. An IP vendor should state the leakage current at the maximum rated
 temperature, not at 25 °C.

[Table 367. Power reduction techniques, what each attacks, and what it costs]
Technique | Attacks | Typical saving | Cost | Who decides
Clock gating | α on the clock tree | 20–40 % | A few gates; timing on the enable | The RTL designer — automatic gating catches most of it
Operand isolation | α in unused datapath | 5–15 % | Muxes in the datapath | RTL designer
Multi- V th cells | Leakage | 2–5× on leakage | Slower cells on non-critical paths | Implementation, automatic
Power gating | Leakage, to near zero | >90 % when idle | Switch area, IR drop, wake latency, state retention | Architecture — it changes the reset and verification plan
DVFS | V 2 f | 2–5× at low load | Regulator, level shifters, characterisation at every operating point | System, with IP support
Architectural parallelism | V 2 via lower f | 2–3× | Area, latency | Architecture, early — it cannot be retrofitted
Memory banking / sub-banking | C per access | 10–30 % of memory power | Decode logic, floorplan | Architecture

Worked example 49. The savings are not additive — a worked composition

Given. A block is 100 mW: 60 mW clock, 25 mW logic, 15 mW leakage. Clock gating removes 60 % of clock power; multi-Vth removes 60 % of leakage; operand isolation removes 30 % of logic power.

Method. Apply each to its own term and re-total. Then compute what a naive addition of the three quoted percentages would have predicted.

Clock after gating | 24 mW
Logic after isolation | 17.5 mW
Leakage after multi- V th | 6 mW
New total | 47.5 mW
Actual saving | 52.5 mW
Actual saving (%) | 52.5 %
Naive sum of the three quoted percentages | 150 %
Clock share before / after | 60% / 50.5%

How this is got wrong. By adding percentages that are percentages of different things. Each technique reduces one term, and after it has done so that term is a smaller share, which is why the second technique applied always returns less than its headline. The corollary is a procedure: always attack the largest term first, re-profile, and only then choose the next technique. A power plan written as a list of techniques without a breakdown to apply them to is not a plan.

Problem. A customer reports that your block consumes 2× the datasheet figure. List the measurements that distinguish the possible causes, in the order you would make them.
Solution. 1. Compare activity factors. The datasheet figure was measured with some stimulus; ask what theirs is. A block specified on random data and used on highly correlated data — or the reverse — can differ by a factor of two with nothing wrong. This is the most common cause and the cheapest to check. 2. Check the clock-gating enables are actually asserting, by toggling coverage or by a scope on the gated clock; an integration that ties an enable high disables the largest single saving. 3. Split dynamic from leakage by measuring at two temperatures: leakage doubles over 40 °C or so and dynamic does not, so two points separate the terms. 4. Check the supply — a 10 % overvoltage is a 21 % dynamic increase. 5. Only then suspect the block. Note that the first four are questions about the customer's system, and asking them requires having recorded your own measurement conditions; a datasheet power figure without its stimulus, voltage and temperature is unfalsifiable and therefore worthless in exactly this conversation.

장: X8. The Mathematics of Verification, Worked
절: X8. The Mathematics of Verification, Worked — 들어가며
글:
X8. The Mathematics of Verification, Worked

Three questions decide a verification plan: how long must random
 stimulus run to reach a coverage target, how many bugs remain when the discovery rate
 flattens, and what a bug costs at each stage. All three have arithmetic answers. None
 of them is a substitute for judgement, but a plan that contradicts the arithmetic
 needs a reason.

장: X8. The Mathematics of Verification, Worked
절: X8.1 Coverage closure is a coupon-collector problem
글:
X8.1 Coverage closure is a coupon-collector problem

How long random stimulus takes to hit every bin

 | Step | Justification
1 | Suppose there are n coverage bins, each hit with equal probability 1/ n by an independent random transaction. | The idealisation. Real bins are neither equiprobable nor independent, and X8.2 measures what that does.
2 | After the k th distinct bin is hit, the probability that the next transaction hits a new bin is ( n − k )/ n . | Uniformity.
3 | So the expected wait for the next new bin is n /( n − k ). | Mean of a geometric distribution.
4 | Total expected transactions = n Σ k =1.. n 1/ k = nH n ≈ n (ln n + 0.577). | Sum the waits; H n is the harmonic number.
5 | For 90 % of the bins, the sum truncates and the cost is only n  ln 10 ≈ 2.3 n . | Σ from 1 to 0.9 n of 1/( n − k ). This is the whole shape of every coverage curve you have ever seen : cheap to 90 %, expensive to 100 %.

[Table 368. Expected random transactions to reach a coverage target, equiprobable bins]
Bins n | To 90 % | To 99 % | To 100 % | Cost of the last 10 % as a multiple of the first 90 %
100 | 230 | 460 | 518 | 2.25
1,000 | 2,302 | 4,605 | 7,485 | 3.25
10,000 | 23,025 | 46,051 | 97,876 | 4.25
100,000 | 230,258 | 460,517 | 1,209,014 | 5.25

The last column is roughly constant at about four, independent of n. The final ten per cent of coverage costs three times what the first ninety did, every time, and that is before the bins turn out to be unequal.

[그림] Figure 47. The coupon-collector curve for 1000 bins. It is not that the last bins are harder to hit by design; they are harder to hit because there are fewer of them left to hit by accident.

Worked example 50. Sizing a regression from a coverage model

Given. A block has 8000 coverage bins. One simulation runs 40 000 transactions and takes 6 minutes. The target is 99 % coverage. 200 simulations can run in parallel.

Method. Convert the bin count to a transaction count with the coupon-collector estimate, then to simulations, then to wall-clock time.

Transactions to 99 % | 36,841
Simulations needed | 1
Serial machine-time | 0.1 hours
Wall clock on 200 in parallel | How this is got wrong. By concluding that random stimulus will therefore close coverage. The model assumes every bin is reachable by random stimulus with equal probability. In practice a handful of bins require a specific sequence — a FIFO full while a retry is in flight and a parity error arrives — whose random probability is not 1/n but 10−9. Those bins never close randomly and no amount of compute changes that; they close with directed tests or constrained scenarios. The arithmetic above tells you how much compute to buy for the easy 99 %, and identifying the remaining bins as requiring direction is the actual verification engineering.

[Table 369. Measured transactions to 99 % coverage of 1000 bins as the bin probabilities are made unequal]
Skew parameter | Most likely : least likely bin | Transactions measured | Multiple of the equiprobable estimate
0 | 1 | 6,000 | 1.3
0.5 | 1.65 | 6,000 | 1.3
1 | 2.72 | 6,000 | 1.3
1.5 | 4.47 | 8,000 | 1.74

An exponential weighting with the stated skew, measured by simulation with seed 9. Even a 7:1 spread between the most and least likely bin multiplies the cost noticeably; real constraint solvers produce far larger spreads than that, which is why coverage convergence is slower than any model predicts and why the remedy is to reshape the constraints, not to buy machines.

X8.2 Bug discovery curves and when to stop

Bugs are found at a rate that decays roughly exponentially with effort,
 because the easy ones go first. Fitting that decay gives an estimate of how many
 remain — an estimate that is crude, defensible, and far better than the
 alternative, which is a feeling.

[Table 370. An exponential bug-discovery model: 240 latent bugs, decay constant 0.18 per week]
Week | Cumulative found | Bugs found this week | Estimated remaining | Remaining (%)
2 | 72 | 30.1 | 167 | 69.8
4 | 123 | 21 | 116 | 48.7
6 | 158 | 14.7 | 81 | 34
8 | 183 | 10.2 | 56 | 23.7
10 | 200 | 7.14 | 39 | 16.5
12 | 212 | 4.98 | 27 | 11.5
16 | 226 | 2.43 | 13 | 5.61
20 | 233 | 1.18 | 6 | 2.73

The parameters are illustrative; the method is not. Fit the two parameters to your own weekly find-rate data and the extrapolation is a real estimate with a real confidence interval.

[그림] Figure 48. The two curves sum to a constant by construction. The decision to tape out is the decision that the lower curve is acceptable.

The find-rate falling is ambiguous and this is where
 projects deceive themselves. A falling rate means either that the bugs are running
 out or that the testing is running out — the same tests re-run on the
 same stimulus find nothing new whether or not bugs remain. The two are distinguished
 by a measurement, not by an argument: introduce new stimulus or a new checker and
 see whether the rate recovers. Mutation testing does this systematically by
 injecting known faults and asking what fraction the existing suite catches; a suite
 that catches 60 % of injected faults is telling you your find-rate curve has
 flattened for the wrong reason. This repository runs exactly such a hunt against its
 own checks.

[Table 371. Relative cost of finding one bug at each stage, and the cost of letting 2 % of 240 bugs reach that stage]
Stage found | Relative cost | vs. spec review | Cost of 2 % escaping to here (relative units)
Specification review | 1 | — | 4.8
Modelling / C++ reference | 3 | 3× | 14.4
Block-level simulation | 10 | 10× | 48
Chip-level simulation | 40 | 40× | 192
Emulation / FPGA prototype | 100 | 100× | 480
First silicon bring-up | 1,000 | 1000× | 4800
Customer escape | 10,000 | 10 000× | 48000

The multipliers are the industry's rule of thumb and vary by an order of magnitude between sources; the shape is what is robust. It is the reason a modelling team that catches specification ambiguities pays for itself many times over, and the reason design houses invest in the left-hand rows.

Worked example 51. Is another month of verification worth it?

Given. At week 12 the model above estimates 28 bugs remaining. A month of verification costs 4 engineer-months. Each bug that reaches silicon costs, on average, 1 engineer-month of debug; a respin costs 40 engineer-months plus three months of schedule, and the probability of a respin is roughly the probability that at least one remaining bug is functional-critical, estimated at 5 % per remaining bug.

Method. Compute the expected cost of stopping now against the expected cost of continuing, using the discovery model to say how many bugs the extra month removes.

Bugs remaining at week 12 | 27
Bugs remaining at week 16 | 13
Bugs removed by the extra month | 14
P(no respin) if we stop now | 0.242
P(no respin) if we continue | 0.501
Expected respin cost now (engineer-months) | 30.33
Expected respin cost after one more month | 19.96
Saving from the extra month | 10.37
Cost of the extra month | 4
Verdict | continue

How this is got wrong. By treating the model's parameters as known. The decay constant is fitted from noisy weekly counts and its uncertainty propagates into the remaining-bug estimate, which sits inside an exponent. The right use of this calculation is not to produce a verdict but to find out which assumption the verdict is sensitive to: here it is the 5 % criticality figure, and that figure can be improved by classifying the bugs already found, which is free. Do the sensitivity analysis and go and measure the sensitive term.

Problem. Your regression has 100 % code coverage and 98 % functional coverage, and has found no new bug in three weeks. A reviewer asks for evidence that the suite would catch a bug if one existed. What do you provide?
Solution. Code coverage is the weakest of the three and answering with it is the mistake: it shows lines executed, not behaviour checked, and a testbench with the checkers disabled reaches 100 %. The evidence a reviewer should accept is fault injection: take the design, introduce a set of realistic mutations — invert a comparison, drop a reset term, change a FIFO threshold by one, delete a wait state — and report the fraction the existing suite catches, with the escapes listed and explained. A suite that catches 95 % of mutations has made a falsifiable claim about itself. Supplement it with checker coverage (did each assertion ever fire in a passing run? an assertion that never even evaluated its antecedent is not checking anything) and with the bug-find-rate recovery test above: add genuinely new stimulus and see whether the rate moves. Every one of these is a measurement of the testbench rather than of the design, which is precisely what was asked for.

Problem. Formal verification proves a property over all inputs. Why does a project still simulate?
Solution. Three reasons, in decreasing order of how often they bite. Capacity: proofs complete on control logic, arbiters, FIFOs and protocol interfaces, and commonly do not on a datapath with wide multipliers or on a whole subsystem; what comes back is a bounded proof, which is a very good simulation and not a proof. Specification: a formal tool proves the properties you wrote. A missing property is an unproven behaviour, and there is no coverage metric for ‘properties I did not think of’ — though mutation coverage of the property set comes closest. Environment: proofs need constraints to exclude illegal inputs, and an over-constraint silently removes the case that would have failed — the formal equivalent of a false-green, and the one that has ended more than one post-silicon investigation. The two techniques are complementary in a specific way worth remembering: formal is strong where state space is deep and narrow, simulation is strong where it is shallow and wide.

X9. Computer Arithmetic Beyond the Adder, Worked

Addition and multiplication are solved problems with known structures.
 Division, square root, and the transcendental functions are not: each admits several
 algorithms with genuinely different latency, area and accuracy, and choosing among
 them is a recurring task for anyone specifying a datapath. This part computes the
 trade-offs instead of listing them.

장: X9. Computer Arithmetic Beyond the Adder, Worked
절: X9.1 Adders: the latency–area curve, computed
글:
X9.1 Adders: the latency–area curve, computed

[Table 372. Adder structures: delay in gate levels and area in full-adder equivalents]
Width n | Ripple delay | Kogge–Stone delay | Kogge–Stone area | Carry-select delay (√ n blocks) | Carry-select area
8 | 8 | 8 | 12 | 5 | 16
16 | 16 | 10 | 32 | 8 | 32
32 | 32 | 12 | 80 | 11 | 64
64 | 64 | 14 | 192 | 16 | 128
128 | 128 | 16 | 448 | 22 | 256

Delays are counted in two-input gate levels from the standard prefix constructions; they are architectural counts, not library timing. Kogge–Stone is logarithmic in delay and nlogn in area and wiring — and the wiring, not the gates, is what makes it expensive in a real floorplan.

Why the prefix-adder family is a design space rather
 than a single answer. Every parallel-prefix adder computes the same carry
 prefixes; they differ in how the prefix tree is shaped, and the shape trades three
 quantities against each other: logic depth, fan-out, and wiring tracks.
 Kogge–Stone minimises depth at maximum wire count; Brent–Kung minimises
 wires at twice the depth; Han–Carlson interleaves the two and sits between;
 Ladner–Fischer trades fan-out for wires. In a modern process the wiring term
 usually dominates, so the textbook's favourite (Kogge–Stone) is often not
 the synthesiser's choice, and a designer who insists on it by instantiation can make
 the block slower. The right procedure is to let the tool choose from its library and
 to check the result, not to specify the topology in the RTL.

Operand width n | Simple PP rows | Radix-4 Booth rows | Radix-8 Booth rows | Wallace 3:2 reduction levels (from radix-4) | Approx. full adders in the tree
8 | 8 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 24
16 | 16 | 9 | 7 | 4 | 86
24 | 24 | 13 | 9 | 5 | 187
32 | 32 | 17 | 12 | 6 | 326
53 | 53 | 28 | 19 | 7 | 890

Radix-8 Booth needs a 3× multiple, which costs an adder and a carry chain up front; it pays only when the row saving outweighs that, which for n ≥ 32 it usually does. The 53 row is the IEEE-754 double-precision significand.

Worked example 52. Why a multiplier ends in one wide adder

Given. A 32×32 multiplier built as radix-4 Booth encoding plus a carry-save reduction tree.

Method. Count the stages and see where the delay goes. Carry-save addition has constant delay per level regardless of width, because no carry propagates; only the final conversion from carry-save to binary needs a carry-propagate adder.

Booth rows | 17
Reduction levels to reach 2 rows | 6
Delay of the tree (≈2 gate levels per level) | 12 gate levels
Final 64-bit carry-propagate adder (Kogge–Stone) | 14 gate levels
Final adder as a fraction of total delay | 53.8 %

How this is got wrong. By optimising the reduction tree and leaving the final adder to the synthesiser's default. The final adder is a third of the delay of the whole multiplier, and it is the one part that is a plain carry-propagate problem. It is also the reason a multiply-accumulate is cheaper than a multiply followed by an add: keep the product in carry-save form, feed it into the accumulator's reduction tree, and pay for exactly one carry-propagate adder at the end of the whole accumulation rather than one per operation. Any datapath that multiplies and then sums should be examined for this.

장: X9. Computer Arithmetic Beyond the Adder, Worked
절: X9.3 Division and square root: digit recurrence against Newton
글:
X9.3 Division and square root: digit recurrence against Newton

[Table 374. Two families, and what each is for]
 | Digit recurrence (SRT) | Multiplicative (Newton–Raphson, Goldschmidt)
Produces | One radix- r digit per iteration | Doubles the number of correct bits per iteration
Iterations for 53 bits | 27 at radix 4 | About 4 from an 8-bit seed
Per-iteration cost | A small adder and a quotient-digit selection table | Two full multiplies
Exact remainder | Yes — available for free | No; needs a final correction step
Correct rounding | Straightforward from the remainder | Requires care ; this is where implementations go wrong
Latency | Long, predictable | Short if multipliers are already there
Reuses | Nothing | The existing multiplier array
Chosen when | Area matters, or the remainder is needed (integer division, modulo) | A fast multiplier already exists (every FPU)

The Pentium FDIV bug was a digit-selection table with
 five missing entries. An SRT divider chooses each quotient digit from a lookup
 indexed by truncated partial remainder and divisor; the table has redundant regions so
 that a slightly wrong estimate can be corrected later, which is exactly what makes the
 algorithm fast and exactly what makes a missing entry hard to find by random testing.
 The entries were unreachable for almost all operand pairs. The lesson for a
 verification plan is specific and permanent: a table-driven arithmetic unit must be
 verified over the table's index space, not over the operand space. Random operands
 reach the interesting table entries with probability near zero; enumerating the index
 space takes minutes.

[Table 375. Iteration counts: Newton–Raphson against SRT]
Result bits | Seed table bits | Newton iterations | Multiplies | SRT radix-4 iterations | SRT radix-8 iterations
24 | 8 | 2 | 4 | 12 | 8
24 | 12 | 1 | 2 | 12 | 8
24 | 16 | 1 | 2 | 12 | 8
53 | 8 | 3 | 6 | 27 | 18
53 | 12 | 3 | 6 | 27 | 18
53 | 16 | 2 | 4 | 27 | 18
113 | 8 | 4 | 8 | 57 | 38
113 | 12 | 4 | 8 | 57 | 38
113 | 16 | 3 | 6 | 57 | 38

Newton's iteration count is logarithmic in the precision and the seed table's size trades directly against it — four extra table bits routinely remove an entire iteration, which is two multiplies. This is the cheapest optimisation in the whole unit and is frequently left on the table.

Problem. A block needs y = a/b where b changes rarely and a changes every cycle. What is the right structure?
Solution. Not a divider. Compute r = 1/b once, when b changes, and multiply every cycle. The reciprocal can take as long as it likes — a slow iterative unit, or even a microcoded sequence — because it is off the critical path, and the per-cycle cost collapses to one multiply. The general principle is worth naming: look for the operand that changes slowly and move work onto it. The same observation produces the coefficient-folding in a fixed-coefficient FIR, the precomputed tables in a modular-arithmetic unit, and the slow adaptation loop of a SerDes equaliser. The one caution is accuracy: a · (1/b) is not correctly rounded even when both operations are, so a unit claiming IEEE compliance cannot take this shortcut without a correction step.

절: X9.4 CORDIC: rotations without multipliers
글:
X9.4 CORDIC: rotations without multipliers

Why the strange constants work

 | Step | Justification
1 | A rotation by θ is ( x cosθ − y sinθ, x sinθ + y cosθ). | Definition.
2 | Factor out cosθ: the rotation becomes cosθ times a shear with tanθ. | Algebra. The scale factor is now separate from the shape.
3 | Choose θ i with tanθ i = 2 − i . Then the shear is two shifts and two adds. | This is the whole trick : restrict the allowed angles so the multiplication becomes a shift.
4 | Any angle in the convergence range is reachable as Σ±θ i . | Because θ i i θ j , so the remaining steps can always correct an overshoot — the same redundancy argument that makes SRT division work.
5 | The accumulated scale Πcosθ i → 0.607253 is independent of the angle , because every step rotates by the same magnitude and only the sign varies. | So it can be compensated once, at the end, or folded into surrounding coefficients for free.

[Table 376. Measured CORDIC accuracy against iteration count (rotation mode, 41 angles)]
Iterations | Scale factor K | Max |error| in cos | Effective bits | Adds
8 | 0.60725911 | 0.00453 | 7.79 | 16
12 | 0.60725296 | 2.65×10 -4 | 11.9 | 24
16 | 0.60725294 | 2.17×10 -5 | 15.5 | 32
20 | 0.60725294 | 9.02×10 -7 | 20.1 | 40
24 | 0.60725294 | 7.05×10 -8 | 23.8 | 48

One bit of accuracy per iteration, exactly as the theory predicts, and the scale factor converges quickly to its limit. The last column is the cost: two adds and two shifts per iteration and no multiplier anywhere.

The three CORDIC modes, and what each computes. In
 rotation mode the algorithm drives the angle accumulator to zero and the
 coordinates come out rotated — giving sine and cosine, and the complex rotation
 a mixer or an FFT twiddle needs. In vectoring mode it drives y to zero
 instead, and what accumulates is the original angle — giving arctangent and
 magnitude, which is exactly the operation a Cartesian-to-polar conversion, an AM
 detector or a phase detector performs. Substituting hyperbolic angles
 (tanh instead of tan) gives a third mode that computes exponentials, logarithms
 and square roots, with some iterations repeated to preserve convergence. One
 structure, three modes, most of the transcendental functions a DSP block needs
 — which is why CORDIC survives in fabric where multipliers are the scarce
 resource.

절: X9.5 Floating point: what the standard actually requires
글:
X9.5 Floating point: what the standard actually requires

[Table 377. Floating-point formats in current use]
Format | Total bits | Exponent bits | Stored mantissa bits | Significand bits (with hidden 1) | Machine epsilon | Decimal digits
binary16 (half) | 16 | 5 | 10 | 11 | 4.88×10 -4 | 3.31
bfloat16 | 16 | 8 | 7 | 8 | 0.00391 | 2.41
binary32 (single) | 32 | 8 | 23 | 24 | 5.96×10 -8 | 7.22
TF32 | 19 | 8 | 10 | 11 | 4.88×10 -4 | 3.31
binary64 (double) | 64 | 11 | 52 | 53 | 1.11×10 -16 | 16
FP8 E4M3 | 8 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 0.0625 | 1.2
FP8 E5M2 | 8 | 5 | 2 | 3 | 0.125 | 0.903

bfloat16 and binary16 are the same width and differ entirely in how they split it: bfloat16 keeps binary32's exponent range and throws away precision, which is the right trade for neural-network training because the failure mode there is overflow of a gradient, not rounding of a weight.

Worked example 53. Why 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3, in bits

Given. IEEE-754 binary64 arithmetic.

Method. 0.1 and 0.2 are not representable: in binary they are infinite repeating fractions, so each is rounded to 53 significant bits. The sum of the two rounded values is then itself rounded. Print the exact decimal expansions.

0.1 stored as | 0.10000000000000000555
0.2 stored as | 0.20000000000000001110
0.1 + 0.2 = | 0.30000000000000004441
0.3 stored as | 0.29999999999999998890
Difference | 5.55×10 -17
Difference in units in the last place | 1

How this is got wrong. By concluding that floating point is unreliable. It is exactly reliable: every operation above returned the correctly rounded result, and the standard guarantees that. What is unreliable is the assumption that decimal literals are representable. The consequences for hardware verification are direct: a bit-exact comparison against a reference model is only meaningful if both use the same rounding mode and the same order of operations, and floating-point addition is not associative, so a reference model that sums an array in a different order than the RTL will disagree with it while both are correct. Specify the summation order, or specify a tolerance and justify it.

Problem. A neural-network accelerator uses bfloat16 multipliers with binary32 accumulation. Why not accumulate in bfloat16 too?
Solution. Because accumulation is where precision is lost and multiplication is not. A bfloat16 multiply of two 8-bit significands produces a 16-bit exact product, and rounding it back to 8 bits costs one rounding. Summing N such products in bfloat16 costs N roundings, each of half an LSB of a number with only 8 significand bits, and — worse — once the running sum is 28 times larger than the next term, that term is absorbed entirely and contributes nothing. For N in the hundreds or thousands, which a convolution reduction routinely is, the sum silently stops growing. Binary32 accumulation has 24 significand bits and pushes the absorption threshold out by 216. The general rule is that a reduction needs more precision than its operands, which is why every practical mixed-precision unit, from a DSP MAC to a tensor core, is asymmetric in exactly this way.

장: Y10. The Register Map and the Software Interface
절: Y10. The Register Map and the Software Interface — 들어가며
글:
Y10. The Register Map and the Software Interface

The register map is the part of a block that software sees, the part a
 customer integrates against, and the part that is hardest to change after release.
 It is also, in most projects, the artefact with the least design attention per hour of
 downstream consequence. This part works through one map in full and states the rules
 that each entry follows.

장: Y10. The Register Map and the Software Interface
절: Y10.1 A worked map
글:
Y10.1 A worked map

[Table 378. A minimal but complete register map, and why each register exists]
Offset | Register | Access | Reset | Why it is here
0x00 | ID | RO | 0x1A2B0100 | Proves supply, clock, reset, bus and decode in one read (Part Y7).
0x04 | SCRATCH | RW | 0x00000000 | Proves the write path independently of any functional side effect.
0x08 | CTRL | RW | 0x00000000 | Everything that changes behaviour, in one register the driver can read-modify-write atomically.
0x0C | STATUS | RO | 0x00000000 | Live state. Never latched -- a latched status needs a clear, and a clear is a race.
0x10 | IRQ_STATUS | W1C | 0x00000000 | Write-1-to-clear so two drivers cannot clear each other's bits.
0x14 | IRQ_ENABLE | RW | 0x00000000 | Separate from status so masking never loses an event.
0x18 | ERR_COUNT | RC | 0x00000000 | Read-to-clear and saturating: a counter that wraps silently is worse than one that sticks at maximum.

Seven registers. Three of them (ID, SCRATCH, LOOPBACK) exist only for bring-up and debug, and they are the ones most often omitted by a designer who is thinking about function rather than about the week the customer spends getting first traffic.

[Table 380. SCRATCH at offset 0x04, reset 0x00000000]
Bits | Field | Access | Description

[Table 381. CTRL at offset 0x08, reset 0x00000000]
Bits | Field | Access | Description
