1 | SOFT_RESET | W1S | Self-clearing; resets the datapath only
2 | LOOPBACK | RW | Internal loopback for bring-up

[Table 382. STATUS at offset 0x0C, reset 0x00000000]
Bits | Field | Access | Description

장: Y10. The Register Map and the Software Interface
절: Y10.2 Access types, and the race each one prevents
글:
Y10.2 Access types, and the race each one prevents

[Table 383. Register access types]
Type | Behaviour | The problem it solves | Where it goes wrong
RO | Read only | — | Writing is silently ignored — specify that, or software will assume it faulted
RW | Read and write | — | Read-modify-write on a register hardware also writes loses the hardware's update
W1C | Write 1 to clear a bit | Two drivers clearing different bits do not clobber each other | A driver that writes 0xFFFFFFFF clears events it never handled
W1S / W1T | Write 1 to set / toggle | Same, for setting | —
RC | Read clears | A counter read without a separate write | A debugger that reads registers disturbs state — mark such registers so tools skip them
WO | Write only | Command registers | Unreadable state cannot be restored after suspend; prefer RW with a self-clearing bit
RW1 | Writable once until reset | Lockable configuration | Software must know the lock exists

The read-modify-write race is the defect this table
 exists to prevent, and it is worth stating concretely. Suppose STATUS bits lived
 in CTRL. A driver reads CTRL, changes ENABLE, and writes it back. Between the read and
 the write, hardware set an error bit. The write puts back the old value of that bit
 and the error is lost — silently, rarely, and only under load. The rule is
 structural: never mix software-written and hardware-written bits in one register,
 and where an event must be cleared by software, use W1C so that the write names
 exactly the bits it intends. This costs one extra register and removes a class of bug
 that is close to undebuggable in the field.

장: Y10. The Register Map and the Software Interface
절: Y10.3 One source, many outputs
글:
Y10.3 One source, many outputs

A register map appears in at least six places. Maintaining them by hand
 guarantees they diverge, and the divergence is discovered by a driver author at the
 worst moment.

[Table 384. What is generated from the register description, and who consumes it]
Artefact | Consumer | What divergence costs
RTL register file | The design | —
C header with offsets and field masks | The driver author | A driver that writes the wrong bit
IP-XACT or SystemRDL | The customer's integration tooling | Manual integration — increasingly a purchase blocker
Documentation tables | Everyone | A datasheet that lies
UVM register model | Verification | Tests that pass against a stale model
Debugger description | Bring-up | Wrong values read during the week they matter most

Worked example 54. The cost of maintaining six copies by hand

Given. A 60-register map, six artefacts, and a change rate of roughly 8 register changes per month during development.

Method. Count the edits and the probability that at least one is missed, assuming a 2 % chance of missing any individual edit.

Artefacts | 6
Edits per month | 48
Edits over a 9-month project | 432
P(no edit missed) at 2 % per edit | 1.62×10 -4
Expected number missed | 8.64
Effort to build a generator | 1–2 weeks
Effort saved | 0.54 weeks, plus the bugs

How this is got wrong. By evaluating the generator against the edit effort alone. The edits are cheap; the missed ones are not, and the expected count here is about nine. Each is a divergence between what software believes and what hardware does, found at integration. The generator's value is in the defects it removes, not the keystrokes, and stating it that way is also how to justify the two weeks to a manager who sees only the keystrokes.

Problem. What should a register do when software writes a reserved bit?
Solution. Define it, and define it in the direction that leaves you room. The two defensible choices are ‘reserved, write zero, read undefined’ and ‘reserved, preserve on write, read as written’. The second is much better for forward compatibility: software does a read-modify-write and unknowingly preserves bits a future version defines, so an old driver keeps working with new hardware. The first is simpler and breaks that property. What is not acceptable is leaving it unspecified, because software will discover the behaviour empirically and depend on it, and you will then be unable to change it. The same principle applies to every ‘don't care’ in a specification: an unspecified behaviour is not free, it is a behaviour your customers will come to rely on before you have decided what it should be.

Problem. Your block is in a power domain that can be switched off. What does that do to the register map?
Solution. It adds a requirement that is easy to miss and expensive to retrofit: every register software may need after resume must be restorable. That means no write-only registers whose value cannot be read back, no state that exists only in hardware counters software cannot reconstruct, and a documented save/restore list telling the driver exactly which offsets to store. It also raises a design question about which registers should be in an always-on domain — typically the ones controlling wake-up and the power sequence itself, since a register that controls power-up cannot live in the domain being powered up. Getting this wrong produces a block that works until the first suspend/resume cycle, which in a mobile or automotive product is within minutes of the customer first running real software on it.

절: Y11. The Modelling Engineer’s Working Day — 들어가며
글:
Y11. The Modelling Engineer’s Working Day

This book was written for someone joining a modelling team. This part
 describes the job concretely: what is produced, how it is judged, what the first
 ninety days look like, and the specific habits that distinguish a modelling engineer
 whose work is trusted from one whose work is checked.

[그림] Figure 49. The three roles and the place of the model. The dashed line is the comparison that defines a bug.

장: Y11. The Modelling Engineer’s Working Day
절: Y11.1 What a modelling engineer produces
글:
Y11.1 What a modelling engineer produces

[Table 385. The deliverables, in the order they are usually needed]
Deliverable | Form | Judged by
Algorithm study | Python or MATLAB, plots, a written recommendation | Whether the architecture chosen from it survives implementation
Bit-accurate reference model | C or C++, callable from the testbench | Whether it agrees with the RTL, and whether it is right when it does not
Word-length study | A sweep and a recommendation per node | Area saved against the metric held
Performance model | A cycle-approximate or cycle-accurate model | Whether the predicted throughput matches silicon
Test vectors | Stimulus and expected output | Coverage of the corners the RTL must handle
The specification's numbers | Tables in the micro-architecture document | Whether anyone has to re-derive them later

The bit-accurate model is the deliverable the role is
 named for, and its value rests entirely on one property: independence. It must
 encode the specification's behaviour, not the design's. A model written by
 reading the RTL is a paraphrase, and a paraphrase agrees with the original for exactly
 the wrong reason. The practical discipline is to write it from the standard or the
 algorithm description before the RTL exists, and to resist the pressure — which
 is constant and comes from everyone — to ‘just make the model match’
 when the two disagree near a deadline. Every time you make the model match, you
 delete a check that cannot be recovered, and nobody will remember later which
 checks were deleted.

장: Y11. The Modelling Engineer’s Working Day
절: Y11.2 Fixed point is most of the work
글:
Y11.2 Fixed point is most of the work

The floating-point algorithm is usually short. Turning it into
 something implementable is not, and that conversion is where a modelling engineer
 spends most of their time. Part X1 gives the arithmetic; this is the
 workflow.

[Table 386. The six models, and what each one answers]
Stage | Model | Question | Output
1 | Floating-point reference | Does the algorithm work at all? | A plot against the metric
2 | Range analysis | What does each node hold? | Integer bits per node, with the basis stated
3 | Quantised model with parameterised word lengths | How does the metric degrade? | A sweep, as in Part X1
4 | Word-length optimisation | What is the cheapest point that passes? | A vector of word lengths and the cost model used
5 | Bit-exact model | Exactly what the RTL must produce, every bit | The reference the testbench compares against
6 | Corner vectors | What must the RTL handle that random stimulus will not reach? | A directed vector set

These are six models, not one model in six states. Keeping them separate means the floating-point reference remains available to answer ‘is the algorithm wrong or is the quantisation wrong?’ — a question that arises constantly and is unanswerable once the models have been merged.

Worked example 55. A disagreement, diagnosed properly

Given. The RTL and the bit-exact model differ on 3 samples in 100 000, always by one LSB, always when the input is near full scale.

Method. Do not guess. Use the model hierarchy: compare the bit-exact model against the quantised model, and the quantised against floating point, on the same three inputs. The stage where the discrepancy appears names the cause.

Differing samples | 3 / 100,000
Magnitude | 1 LSB
Correlated with | near-full-scale input
First hypothesis | rounding at a saturation boundary
Test | compare rounding mode at the saturating node in both
Second hypothesis | the RTL saturates before rounding, the model after
Which is right? | whichever the specification says — check

How this is got wrong. By deciding which is right from which is easier to change. The order of rounding and saturation is a real specification question with a real answer, and getting it wrong produces a block that differs from every other implementation by one LSB at full scale — which will be found by a customer comparing against a competitor. One-LSB disagreements are the ones most often waved away and most often genuine; the discipline is that a disagreement is closed by a citation to the specification, not by a judgement about magnitude.

장: Y11. The Modelling Engineer’s Working Day
절: Y11.3 The first ninety days
글:
Y11.3 The first ninety days

[Table 387. A first quarter that builds credibility]
When | What | Why this and not something more impressive
Week 1–2 | Build and run the existing models and the regression | You cannot contribute to a flow you cannot run. Fix the first thing that does not build — it is a real contribution and it teaches the flow
Week 2–4 | Read the specification of the block you will model, and the existing model beside it | Note every place the model differs from your reading; some are your misunderstanding and some are bugs
Week 4–6 | Take a small, complete piece — one function, one corner case, one test | Complete and small beats large and partial ; the goal is a closed loop through review and merge
Week 6–10 | Own a module's model end to end | Including its verification against the RTL and its documentation
Week 10–13 | Find something the process misses and fix it | A missing check, an unreproducible result, a manual step. This is what distinguishes you

The pattern is deliberate: run before reading, read before writing, small before large, and process improvement last — because a process criticism from someone who has not yet shipped anything through the process is ignored, and the same criticism after ten weeks is acted on.

The failure mode of a new modelling engineer is
 silent disagreement. You read the specification, you believe the existing model is
 wrong, and you say nothing because you assume the experienced people have a reason.
 Sometimes they do, and hearing it is how you learn. Sometimes they do not, and the bug
 ships. The correct move is neither silence nor an accusation: it is a question with
 the clause number attached. ‘Clause 7.3.2 says the rounding happens before
 saturation and I read the model as doing the reverse — what am I missing?’
 costs nothing if you are wrong and is extremely valuable if you are right. Engineers
 who ask this way get answers; engineers who assert get arguments.

Problem. You are asked to model a block whose specification is an internal document written by an architect who has left. What do you do?
Solution. Treat the gap as the first deliverable. Write down what the document does not determine — every place where two readings are possible, every constant with no stated basis, every behaviour on an illegal input — and circulate that list. It is immediately useful to everyone and it is the cheapest thing you can produce in week one. Then resolve the list by evidence in this order: existing RTL or a previous generation, since what shipped is a fact; test vectors or captured data, which settle behaviour without settling intent; the people who integrated against it, who know what they relied on; and finally a decision recorded as a decision, with your name and the date, for the items nothing resolves. What you must not do is make the choices silently inside the model. A model containing twenty undocumented decisions is not a reference; it is a second design, and when it disagrees with the RTL nobody will be able to say which is right.

Problem. Your model and the RTL agree perfectly on the first day of integration. Is that good news?
Solution. It is news that needs checking before it is good. Perfect agreement on day one has three explanations and only one of them is happy. The comparison may not be running — a checker that is disabled, a stimulus that never reaches the block, a comparison of two constants; this is the first thing to rule out, and the way to rule it out is to break something deliberately and confirm the comparison notices, which is the same self-check the agent in Part Y4 performs every round. The model may have been written from the RTL, in which case agreement is tautological. Or the block may genuinely be simple and correct, which does happen. Establishing which costs half an hour and is the single highest-value half hour in an integration, because everything downstream rests on the answer.

장: Y12. High-Level Synthesis in a Small Design House
절: Y12. High-Level Synthesis in a Small Design House — 들어가며
글:
Y12. High-Level Synthesis in a Small Design House

High-level synthesis promises to turn C++ into RTL, which for a
 one-person house sounds like a way to multiply headcount. It is a real tool with a
 real place, and the place is narrower than the marketing and wider than the
 scepticism. This part states where it wins, where it does not, and what this
 repository measured when it tried to synthesise a production C++ library with an
 open-source tool.

장: Y12. High-Level Synthesis in a Small Design House
절: Y12.1 What HLS actually decides for you
글:
Y12.1 What HLS actually decides for you

The three transformations, and which one is the hard one

 | Step | Justification
1 | Scheduling : assign each operation to a clock cycle, respecting data dependences and the target period. | The tool solves a constrained scheduling problem, typically with a list-scheduling heuristic or an ILP formulation for small regions.
2 | Allocation : decide how many of each resource exist. | Two multiplies in different cycles may share one multiplier.
3 | Binding : assign operations to specific resource instances, and variables to registers or memories. | Introduces multiplexers, which is where a naive binding loses the timing the scheduler thought it had.
4 | All three are driven by pragmas , not by the C++ semantics. | This is the fact that determines everything else. The same C++ with different pragmas produces designs differing by orders of magnitude in area and throughput, which means the C++ is not the design — the C++ plus the pragmas plus the tool version is the design.
5 | So HLS source is not portable between tools in any practical sense. | The pragma dialects differ, the library types ( ap_fixed , hls::stream ) differ, and the scheduling behaviour differs. Measured in this repository : a production Xilinx Vitis library did not build under an open-source HLS tool without modification.

[Table 388. Where HLS wins and where it does not]
Situation | HLS | Why
Datapath-heavy, regular loops (filters, transforms, linear algebra) | Strong | Scheduling a loop nest is exactly what the tool is good at
Design-space exploration — ten variants of one algorithm | Very strong | Changing a pragma is minutes; rewriting RTL is days. This is the best argument for HLS
Algorithm still changing | Strong | The C++ stays readable as the algorithm moves
Control-dominated protocol logic | Weak | A state machine expressed as C++ control flow is harder to read and to verify than the FSM it becomes
Cycle-exact interface timing | Weak | The tool owns the schedule; you are negotiating with it
Area- or timing-critical blocks at the frequency limit | Weak | The last 20 % needs control the abstraction removes
Code you must hand to a customer as portable RTL | Fine | Ship the generated RTL; the customer never needs the C++

The strongest case for HLS in a small house is
 exploration, not production. The question ‘what does this algorithm cost at
 four different parallelism factors?’ takes an afternoon in HLS and a fortnight
 in RTL, and the answer changes the architecture. Having taken the decision, writing
 the production block in RTL is often still the right call — and the HLS model
 remains useful as a golden reference, since it is C++ that is known to produce the
 same numbers. Used this way, HLS is a modelling tool that happens to emit
 RTL, which fits the role this book is written for.

장: Y12. High-Level Synthesis in a Small Design House
절: Y12.2 What this repository measured
글:
Y12.2 What this repository measured

This repository built an open-source HLS tool from source and
 attempted to synthesise a production vendor C++ library with it. The findings
 are recorded in survey/synth/합성결과.md
 (144 lines) and are summarised here because they are the kind of result that
 is rarely written down.

[Table 389. Three independent blockers, isolated by single-variable experiments]
Blocker | Evidence | What it means for a user
Pragma dialect | Vendor pragmas are not recognised by the other tool; the code compiles and schedules differently | HLS source does not port. Budget a rewrite, not a recompile
Library types | A crash in the tool's own pass while handling a streaming class passed by value | The vendor's stream and fixed-point classes are part of the vendor's tool, not part of C++
Template instantiation cost | Heavily templated fixed-point code expands enormously before synthesis begins | Compile time can exceed the time budget before any hardware is generated

Two lessons from that exercise are worth more than
 the result itself. First, the blockers were only separable by controlled
 experiments: all three appeared as ‘it does not work’ until each was
 isolated with one variable changed at a time, and before that isolation it would have
 been easy — and wrong — to report a single cause. Second, an early
 attempt to name the cause was withdrawn because the run had timed out before reaching
 the pass in question, so the claim was a guess and not a measurement. The rule that
 produced both corrections is the one this whole book applies: a number or a cause you
 have not measured is not a finding, however confident you are.

장: Y12. High-Level Synthesis in a Small Design House
절: Y12.3 Verifying HLS output
글:
Y12.3 Verifying HLS output

[Table 390. The three levels of HLS verification]
Level | What it compares | Catches | Cost
C simulation | The C++ against your test vectors | Algorithm bugs | Seconds — run constantly
C/RTL co-simulation | The generated RTL against the same C++ on the same vectors | Tool bugs and pragma misunderstandings | Minutes to hours
RTL verification | The generated RTL in its real environment | Interface and integration problems the co-simulation harness hides | As for any RTL

Why C/RTL co-simulation is not optional. It is
 tempting to reason that if the C++ is correct and the tool is correct then the RTL is
 correct. The second premise is the problem: HLS tools have bugs, and more commonly the
 pragmas do not mean what the writer thought — a dependence the tool was
 told to ignore was real, a loop it was told to pipeline could not be, an interface
 protocol was inferred differently from what the integrator expects. Co-simulation
 catches all of these for the cost of running the vectors twice. It is also the only
 thing that makes the C++ usable as a golden model afterwards, since it establishes
 that the two really do agree.

Worked example 56. When HLS pays for itself, as arithmetic

Given. An exploration of one algorithm at four parallelism factors and three word lengths — twelve design points. RTL: 3 days per point. HLS: 2 days to set up plus 2 hours per point. Both need the results to be trustworthy.

Method. Count the days for each route, including the HLS learning and verification overhead that is easy to omit.

Design points | 12
RTL route, days | 36
HLS setup, days | 2
HLS per point, days | 0.25
HLS route, days | 5
Plus co-simulation of the chosen point, days | 2
HLS total | 7
Saving | 29 days

How this is got wrong. By counting the saving and then shipping the HLS output without the verification days. The arithmetic above holds only because the last two rows are included; an HLS flow without co-simulation is faster and produces RTL nobody should trust. The second common error is to count the setup as a one-off when it is per-project: tool versions, library versions and pragma behaviour change, and a flow that worked last year needs re-establishing. Budget the setup every time and the saving is still large for exploration and small or negative for a single production block — which is exactly the recommendation in Y12.1, now with numbers behind it.

Problem. A customer asks whether your block was written in RTL or generated from HLS. Does it matter, and how do you answer?
Solution. It matters to them for three legitimate reasons and you should answer plainly. Maintainability: if they must modify the block, generated RTL is unpleasant to edit, so they need either the C++ and the flow, or a commitment that you will make changes. Quality of results: generated RTL is usually larger and slower than good hand RTL at the same function, and if they are area- or frequency-constrained that is their business. Predictability: regenerating with a different tool version can change the result, so they will want to know the RTL they receive is frozen and verified as delivered, not regenerated on demand. The answer that satisfies all three is to ship frozen, verified RTL with its synthesis and timing reports, and to state the provenance. Concealing it is the bad option: it is discoverable from the generated code's shape in about five minutes, and being caught concealing something harmless costs more than the thing concealed.

장: Y13. Getting Hired into a Modelling Team
절: Y13. Getting Hired into a Modelling Team — 들어가며
글:
Y13. Getting Hired into a Modelling Team

This part is about the interview and the portfolio, treated as an
 engineering problem: what does the hiring side actually need to learn about you, and
 what evidence answers it fastest? The answer is unusually concrete for this kind of
 advice, because modelling work produces artefacts that can be shown.

장: Y13. Getting Hired into a Modelling Team
절: Y13.1 What the interviewer is trying to find out
글:
Y13.1 What the interviewer is trying to find out

[Table 391. The four questions behind a modelling interview]
The question | How it is usually asked | What actually answers it
Can you write a correct model? | A coding exercise, often a fixed-point or protocol task | Code that handles the corners and says which it handles
Do you know why the model exists? | ‘How would you verify this block?’ | An answer that mentions independence and what a disagreement means
Do you understand the hardware? | ‘Why is this architecture like this?’ | Reasoning from timing, area or bandwidth — numbers, not adjectives
Will you say when something is wrong? | ‘Tell me about a time…’, or a deliberately flawed premise in a question | Noticing the flaw and saying so, politely, is the whole test

The fourth question is weighted more heavily than
 candidates expect, and it is the one this book's discipline speaks to directly. A
 modelling engineer's value is that they are an independent check. An engineer who
 defers to the design team's reading of the specification is not performing the
 function they were hired for, however good their code is. Interviewers probe this
 deliberately — a question with a wrong assumption embedded, a requirement that
 contradicts an earlier one — and the answer they want is neither silence nor
 combativeness but the thing this book keeps recommending: name the discrepancy,
 cite the source, and ask.

장: Y13. Getting Hired into a Modelling Team
절: Y13.2 A portfolio that is evidence rather than assertion
글:
Y13.2 A portfolio that is evidence rather than assertion

[Table 392. Portfolio items, ordered by what they prove per hour of effort]
Item | Concretely | What it proves
A bit-accurate model of a standard block | RS or BCH decoder, a CIC decimator, a 64b/66b PCS | Shows you can read a specification and produce something checkable
Its test suite, with mutation results | ‘These 14 injected faults; the suite catches 13; here is the escape and why’ | Almost nobody does this, and it is the single most convincing artefact
A word-length study | A sweep, a cost model, a chosen point with a reason | Shows you understand the actual daily work
An RTL block compared against the model | Even a small one, with the comparison automated | Shows you have closed the loop end to end
A written page on a bug you found | Symptom, hypotheses, the measurement that discriminated, the fix | Demonstrates method, which is what is being hired
A contribution to an open project | A fix, a test, a documentation improvement in a real codebase | Independent evidence that someone reviewed and merged your work

Depth beats breadth here. One block modelled properly, with its verification and its written reasoning, is worth more than six half-finished repositories — because the thing being assessed is whether you finish and whether you check, and only a finished, checked thing can show that.

Worked example 57. Where the hours go, and what each hour buys

Given. 120 available hours over three months, to be spent on a portfolio.

Method. Allocate against the four interview questions, weighting by how much evidence each hour produces.

Model of one standard block | 40 h
Test suite with mutation measurement | 30 h
Small RTL implementation and comparison | 25 h
Written documentation and a bug write-up | 15 h
Polish, README, reproducibility | 10 h
Total | 120 h
Questions from Y13.1 this evidences | all four

How this is got wrong. By spending all 120 hours on the model. A beautiful model with no test suite answers one of the four questions; the same model with 30 hours moved into verification answers three. The most common portfolio failure is an imbalance in exactly this direction, because modelling is the enjoyable part. The hours spent proving the model is right are the hours that differentiate, precisely because they are the ones most candidates skip.

장: Y13. Getting Hired into a Modelling Team
절: Y13.3 Interview questions you should expect, and how to think about them
글:
Y13.3 Interview questions you should expect, and how to think about them

[Table 393. Common questions and the shape of a good answer]
Question | What they want to hear
‘How do you know your model is right?’ | Independence of source; a third-party reference where one exists; property-based checks rather than sample values; fault injection to prove the checks bite
‘The RTL and your model disagree. What now?’ | Reproduce minimally, then go to the specification. Do not edit the model to match , and say so
‘How many bits does this filter need?’ | ‘Against what metric?’ — then range, then sweep, then the knee. Asking for the metric first is most of the answer
‘Why not just use floating point?’ | Area, power and determinism; then the accumulation and associativity arguments from Part X9
‘Our coverage is 100 %. Are we done?’ | Code coverage measures execution, not checking. Offer mutation score and checker coverage as the evidence that would settle it
‘Tell me about a hard bug.’ | The method, not the heroics: hypotheses, the measurement that discriminated, what you changed in the process afterwards

One answer to avoid: ‘I would add more
 tests.’ It is the reflex response to every verification question and it is
 almost never the best one, because it does not say which tests or how you would
 know they were enough. The answers that distinguish a candidate name a measurement:
 mutation score, checker coverage, a comparison against an independent reference, a
 property that holds for all inputs rather than a vector that holds for one. Every
 one of those is something this book has computed somewhere, and being able to say
 ‘I would measure X and here is what X would tell us’ is the difference
 between sounding careful and being useful.

Problem. You are asked to estimate something you do not know — how many gates a block needs, how long a task takes. What do you do?
Solution. Estimate out loud, from decomposition, and say what would sharpen it. The interviewer is not testing recall of a number; they are watching whether you can bound an unknown, which is most of engineering judgement. A good answer names the decomposition (‘the multiplier array is about n² full adders, a full adder is about six gates, so…’), states the assumption that matters most, gives a range rather than a point, and ends with the measurement that would collapse the range. Refusing to estimate is the worst answer and a confident unqualified number is the second worst; the habit being looked for is the one Part X1 applies to word lengths and Part Y8 to schedules — a bound, its basis, and what would improve it.

Problem. You have no industry experience and no degree from a famous university. What actually compensates?
Solution. Artefacts, and one specific kind of them. A repository containing a model, its test suite, a mutation measurement of that suite, and a written page explaining a bug it caught is evidence that nobody can produce without having done the work — and it is checkable in ten minutes by the person deciding whether to interview you. Two things amplify it. Contributions to a real open project carry an independent review signal: someone with no reason to flatter you merged your change. And a written explanation of something difficult — a blog post deriving a result, a clear note on a standard's ambiguity — demonstrates the communication half of the job, which is half of it. What does not compensate is a list of technologies; every candidate has one, and it distinguishes nobody. Build one thing completely and write down how you know it works.

장: Y14. The Flow a One-Person House Can Actually Run
절: Y14. The Flow a One-Person House Can Actually Run — 들어가며

Y14. The Flow a One-Person House Can Actually Run

Commercial EDA licences cost more per year than a one-person house
 earns. That fact shapes what such a house can sell, and the honest answer is that a
 great deal is possible with free tools and one thing is not. This part sets out which
 is which, and measures what is actually installed in the environment this book was
 built in.

장: Y14. The Flow a One-Person House Can Actually Run
절: Y14.2 What the free flow can and cannot do
글:
Y14.2 What the free flow can and cannot do

[Table 395. Capability, honestly assessed]
Activity | Free flow | Note
Modelling and algorithm work | Complete | Python, NumPy, C++ — nothing is missing
RTL simulation | Complete for most purposes | Verilator is fast; Icarus handles constructs Verilator does not
UVM | Partial | UVM needs constrained randomisation and full class support; free simulators have improved but are not equivalent. cocotb is a viable different answer
Formal property checking | Usable | SymbiYosys and its solvers; capacity below commercial tools
Lint and CDC | Partial | Verilator lint is good; dedicated CDC sign-off tools have no free equivalent
Synthesis to a gate netlist | Yes | Yosys, with open cell libraries
Place and route | Yes for open PDKs | OpenROAD and the open PDK flows
Sign-off STA in a commercial process | No | Needs the foundry's timing libraries, which come with an NDA and a commercial tool
Tape-out to a commercial foundry | No | This is the line a free flow does not cross

The line falls exactly where a soft-IP business
 wants it. Everything on the seller's side of a soft-IP transaction —
 modelling, RTL, verification, and enough synthesis to quote area and frequency
 credibly — is reachable with free tools. Everything on the buyer's side
 — sign-off in their process, with their libraries, in their flow — is
 theirs to run and they already have the licences. A design house selling RTL
 therefore does not need a tape-out flow, and recognising that is the difference
 between a viable plan and one that requires six figures of tooling before the first
 sale. The caveat to state to customers is equally clear: your frequency and area
 numbers come from an open flow and an open library, and they will re-run them; give
 them the scripts so they can.

Worked example 58. What credible area and frequency numbers cost to produce

Given. You want to quote ‘150 kGE at 500 MHz’ for a block, with evidence, using only free tools.

Method. Enumerate what is needed and what each step actually establishes.

Synthesis with Yosys to an open library | area in gate equivalents
Static timing with OpenSTA on that netlist | a frequency, in that library
What this does not establish | performance in the customer's process
What makes it credible anyway | the ratio transfers; publish the library and the scripts
Additional cost | 0 USD
What a customer will still do | re-run it in their flow
What they are really buying | the assurance that the number is not invented

How this is got wrong. By quoting a number from an open flow as though it were a sign-off number. It is not, and a customer who discovers the elision stops trusting the rest of the datasheet. The correct presentation names the library, the tool and the version, states that it is a pre-layout estimate in an open process, and offers the scripts. That presentation is more persuasive than an unattributed larger claim, for the same reason the known-issue list of Part Y5 is: it is checkable.

장: Y14. The Flow a One-Person House Can Actually Run
절: Y14.3 A regression setup that survives one person
글:
Y14.3 A regression setup that survives one person

[Table 396. What to automate first, in order of return]
Automate | Why it is first | Effort
One command that runs everything | If the regression is three commands, it will be run less often, and the one that is skipped is the one that would have caught it | Hours
Deterministic seeds recorded with results | A failure you cannot reproduce is a failure you cannot fix | Hours
A self-check that the checkers bite | Otherwise a green regression means nothing — the theme of this entire book | A day
Results to a ledger, not to a terminal | You will be asked what changed between last week and now | A day
Overnight running with the correct detachment | Part Y4's setsid / nohup / disown pattern — the obvious way silently does nothing | Hours
Mutation testing of the suite | Turns ‘we have tests’ into a number you can quote | Days — and it is what a customer remembers

The failure that ends solo projects is not a hard
 bug; it is losing the ability to reproduce. Six months in, with several branches,
 a half-changed model and results in a terminal scrollback, the question ‘did
 this ever pass?’ becomes unanswerable, and from that point every decision is a
 guess. The defence is cheap and must be built before it is needed: every run
 records its commit, its seeds, its tool versions and its results to a file that is
 committed. This book's own repository does exactly this, and the rule that
 produced it is worth repeating: a check that leaves no record is a check nobody can
 audit, including you.

Problem. Which free simulator should a one-person house standardise on?
Solution. Both, for different jobs, and the reasoning generalises. Verilator for the bulk regression: it compiles to C++ and runs one to two orders of magnitude faster than event-driven simulation, which is what makes an overnight run worth having; its restrictions (two-state by default, synthesisable subset, no timing constructs) are mostly acceptable for a testbench driven from C++ or cocotb. Icarus for the cases Verilator refuses: four-state X-propagation, gate-level simulation with delays, and legacy constructs. The important discipline is to keep the RTL compiling under both, because each catches things the other permits — Verilator's lint is stricter than most commercial tools, and Icarus's four-state semantics catch reset and initialisation bugs that a two-state run hides. Two simulators disagreeing about your design is information, and it is free.

장: Y15. A Complete Worked Project: RS-KP4
절: Y15. A Complete Worked Project: RS-KP4 — 들어가며

Y15. A Complete Worked Project: RS-KP4

This part takes one block from a specification through to a delivery
 package, with the numbers computed rather than estimated. It uses the code that is
 already in this repository — the field arithmetic and the decoder of
 Part X5 — and it states, at each step, what exists and what does not, so
 the reader can see the difference between a worked example and a finished
 product.

[그림] Figure 50. The decoder architecture. The delay FIFO is the block's dominant memory and the reason latency is quoted in codewords.

장: Y15. A Complete Worked Project: RS-KP4
절: Y15.1 The parameters, and which are still unconfirmed
글:
Y15.1 The parameters, and which are still unconfirmed

[Table 397. The parameter set, with the confidence of each entry]
Parameter | Value used | Confidence | Where it is fixed
Field | GF(2 10 ) | confirmed by the code length | —
Primitive polynomial | 0x409 assumed | NOT confirmed | Fixed by IEEE 802.3 Clause 91, which this repository has not read
First consecutive root fcr | 0 assumed | NOT confirmed | Same clause
Symbol bit order | MSB first assumed | NOT confirmed | Same clause
n , k | 544, 514 | confirmed — the code's name | —
t | 15 | derived: ( n − k )/2 | —

Three of six are assumptions. The model in this repository takes all three as arguments with the assumption marked, and its tests check properties that hold whatever the values are — that up to t errors are always corrected and that beyond t the decoder does not silently return the input. When the clause is obtained, only the defaults change.

This is what it looks like to build honestly on an
 unread specification. The alternative — pick a polynomial, hard-code it,
 and proceed — produces a block that works perfectly against itself and fails at
 the first interoperability test, with the cause buried in a constant nobody
 questions. Parameterising costs nothing and the marked confidence costs one column in
 a table. What it buys is that the unread clause remains visible instead of
 dissolving into an assumption, which is precisely the failure Part Y6 is written
 to prevent.

장: Y15. A Complete Worked Project: RS-KP4
절: Y15.2 Sizing the block from the standard's rate
글:
Y15.2 Sizing the block from the standard's rate

[Table 398. Parallelism required at 53.125 GBd, one symbol per 10 bits]
De-serialisation | Digital clock (MHz) | Symbols per clock | Symbols processed in parallel | Datapath width (bits) | Clocks per codeword
4 | 830 | 64.01 | 65 | 650 | 8.369
8 | 415 | 128 | 129 | 1,290 | 4.217
16 | 208 | 255.4 | 256 | 2,560 | 2.125
32 | 104 | 510.8 | 511 | 5,110 | 1.065

The third column is the block's fundamental parallelism: at 830 MHz the decoder must absorb 64 symbols every cycle. Every stage of the architecture must be replicated or restructured to that width, and that replication, not the algorithm, is where the area goes.

Worked example 59. Where the area actually goes

Given. RS(544,514), t = 15, 64 symbols per cycle at 830 MHz.

Method. Count the three structures separately: the syndrome computation (parallel, wide), the key equation (serial, narrow) and the Chien search (parallel, wide). The asymmetry is the architectural fact.

Syndromes to compute | 30
GF multipliers for syndromes, unparallelised | 30
At 64 symbols per cycle | 1,920
Berlekamp–Massey multipliers (serial, ~2 t ) | 30
BM cycles per codeword | 30
Chien: evaluate σ at 64 positions per cycle | 960
Ratio of wide structures to the key equation | 96×
Delay FIFO | 5,440 bits per codeword in flight

How this is got wrong. By optimising Berlekamp–Massey. It is the algorithmically interesting stage, it is what the literature discusses, and here it is about one per cent of the multipliers. The syndrome and Chien stages dominate because they are replicated 64 ways and BM is not. The architectural leverage is therefore in sharing and folding those wide stages — the standard techniques being common-subexpression sharing across the syndrome constants and a folded Chien search — and in nothing else. Compute the replication factor before deciding what to optimise, in any block.

Item | State | Where

Listing what does not exist is the point of this
 section. A worked example that presents a partial project as a finished one
 teaches the wrong lesson twice: it misleads about the effort, and it models the
 behaviour — quiet omission of the incomplete parts — that this book spends
 two chapters warning against. The honest summary is that this repository contains a
 verified reference model and one verified RTL primitive for a block whose
 full implementation is most of Part Y8's 39-week plan, and that three of its
 parameters await a document that must be purchased.

Problem. Given that state, what are the next three actions, in order?
Solution. First, obtain the clause. Three unconfirmed constants block every downstream claim of interoperability, and no amount of RTL removes that block; until they are confirmed the project can produce a correct decoder for a code that may not be the standard's. This is a purchase and a fortnight of reading, and it is the highest-value action available. Second, build the syndrome stage at full parallelism and verify it against the model, because the sizing example above says that stage dominates the area, so the area and frequency claims — the numbers a customer asks for first — are determined by it. One wide stage, synthesised and timed, converts an estimate into a measurement. Third, find a customer conversation before writing the key equation, because everything after the syndrome stage is a large effort whose requirements (latency budget, code rate set, concatenation) the customer determines, and guessing them is how the 39 weeks turn into 60. Note that the technically interesting work is third on this list, which is usually where it belongs.

Y1. MIPI CSI-2 and DSI, Worked as a Deliverable

Every phone camera, most automotive cameras and a large fraction of
 embedded vision sensors speak CSI-2; every phone display and most embedded panels
 speak DSI. The two share a PHY and a packet structure, which is why a design house
 that builds one has most of the other. This part works the numbers a customer will
 ask for, and states where the answers come from.

절: Y1.1 Bandwidth: from a sensor specification to a lane count
글:
Y1.1 Bandwidth: from a sensor specification to a lane count

This is the first calculation a customer will do with your datasheet,
 so it must be the first one in it. It is also the calculation that decides whether
 your block is in the design at all.

[Table 400. Required D-PHY bandwidth and lane count at 2.5 Gbps per lane]
Mode | Mpixel/s | bits/pixel | Payload (Gbps) | With 15 % overhead (Gbps) | Lanes at 4 Gbps/lane | Lanes at 2.5 Gbps/lane
1080p30 | 62.21 | 12 | 0.7465 | 0.8585 | 1 | 1
1080p60 | 124.4 | 12 | 1.493 | 1.717 | 1 | 1
4K30 | 248.8 | 12 | 2.986 | 3.434 | 1 | 2
4K60 | 497.7 | 12 | 5.972 | 6.868 | 1 | 3
8MP automotive 30 | 248.8 | 16 | 3.981 | 4.579 | 1 | 2
12MP still burst | 360 | 14 | 5.04 | 5.796 | 1 | 3

The 15 % allowance covers line blanking, packet headers and footers, and the low-power intervals between bursts. It is an assumption and it belongs in the datasheet beside the number it produced; a customer with a different blanking ratio will get a different lane count and should be able to see why.

Worked example 60. Why the overhead is not a fixed percentage

Given. A 1920×1080 frame, 12 bits per pixel, RAW12 packing. Each line is one long packet: 4 bytes of header, the payload, and 2 bytes of footer. Between lines the link may drop to low-power state and return, costing TLPX + THS-PREPARE + THS-ZERO + sync, taken here as 300 ns.

Method. Compute the per-line overhead in bytes and in time, then express it as a fraction. The fraction depends on the line length, which is why a single percentage cannot be right for every mode.

Payload bytes per line | 2,880
Packet header + footer | 6 bytes
Packet overhead | 0.208 %
Line payload time at 4 lanes × 2.5 Gbps | 2.304 µs
LP transition cost per line | 0.3 µs
Transition overhead | 13 %
Total overhead for this mode | 13.2 %
Same for a 320-pixel-wide line | 79.4 %

How this is got wrong. By quoting one efficiency figure for the whole product. The overhead is dominated by a per-line constant, so efficiency collapses for short lines: a narrow region-of-interest readout — exactly what a machine-vision customer does — can spend more time in transitions than in data. The design response is to stay in high-speed state across lines when the blanking interval is short, which the specification permits and which many controllers do not implement. That feature is worth naming in a datasheet because a competitor's block that lacks it will lose the ROI benchmark.

장: Y1. MIPI CSI-2 and DSI, Worked as a Deliverable
절: Y1.2 The D-PHY state machine and its timing parameters
글:
Y1.2 The D-PHY state machine and its timing parameters

[Table 401. D-PHY lane states and what each costs]
State | Electrical | Purpose | Entry cost
LP-11 (Stop) | Both lines high, 1.2 V single-ended | Idle | —
LP-01 / LP-00 | Low-power signalling | Request and bridge states | T LPX per transition, min 50 ns
HS-0 / HS-1 | 200 mV differential about a 200 mV common mode | Data burst | T HS-PREPARE + T HS-ZERO + sync, 150–300 ns
ULPS | LP-00 held | Ultra-low power; clock may stop | T WAKEUP ≥ 1 ms — a millisecond, not a microsecond
Escape mode | LP pulse-coded | Trigger, LPDT side-channel | Slow by design

The 1 ms ULPS wake-up is a system-level number
 that routinely surprises integrators. A design that powers the link down between
 frames to save energy cannot wake it in a line blanking interval; it can only wake it
 in a frame interval, and only if the frame rate leaves a millisecond spare.
 30 fps gives 33 ms per frame, so it fits; a 240 fps burst mode does
 not. Power state transitions have latencies that are three to five orders of
 magnitude apart — 50 ns for LPX, 1 ms for ULPS — and a power
 management policy that treats them as interchangeable will either waste energy or
 drop frames.

[Table 402. D-PHY timing parameters evaluated at three lane rates (ns)]

On quoting a specification you have not read.
 The table above is deliberately marked. A design house that builds a MIPI controller
 buys the specification; there is no substitute and no legitimate way around it.
 Writing formulae from secondary sources into RTL is how a block comes to fail
 interoperability at a plugfest, and the failure is expensive precisely because it is
 found late and in public. The correct entry in a project plan is a line item for
 the specification and for membership, not an assumption that the numbers can be
 inferred.

장: Y1. MIPI CSI-2 and DSI, Worked as a Deliverable
절: Y1.3 Packet structure, ECC and CRC — and why both exist
글:
Y1.3 Packet structure, ECC and CRC — and why both exist

Why the header has ECC and the payload has CRC

 | Step | Justification
1 | The short packet header is 4 bytes: data identifier, two word-count bytes, and one ECC byte. | CSI-2 packet structure.
2 | The ECC is a Hamming code over the preceding 24 bits, giving single-error correction and double-error detection. | From Part X10's bound: 24 data bits need r = 5 for correction, plus one overall parity, which fits in the byte with two bits spare.
3 | A corrupted header is unrecoverable at any higher layer , because the word count tells the receiver where the packet ends. | A wrong length desynchronises the stream for the remainder of the frame. Correction, not detection, is therefore required here.
4 | The payload carries a 16-bit CRC and no correction . | A corrupted pixel is one bad pixel; the frame continues. Detection lets the application decide, and correction would cost far more for far less.
5 | The asymmetry is a design principle, not a quirk of this standard. | Spend correction where a failure is structural and detection where it is local. The same reasoning produced the parity-plus-reload answer for configuration memory in Part X10.

Problem. A customer reports occasional frame corruption that disappears when they reduce the lane rate. Your ECC error counter is zero and your CRC counter is non-zero. What does that tell you, and what would the opposite pattern tell you?
Solution. CRC errors without ECC errors mean the payload is being corrupted while the headers survive. That is a strong hint, because headers and payload travel the same wires but not the same way: headers occur at the start of a burst, just after the HS settle time, and are short; payload is long and continuous. Corruption that spares the header and hits the payload points at something that accumulates over a burst — clock drift or an under-specified THS-SETTLE window that is fine for the first bytes and drifts later, or an SSC/jitter interaction, or simply insufficient eye at the sampling point for long runs. The opposite pattern, ECC errors without CRC errors, would point at the transition: the receiver is mis-sampling the first bytes after leaving low-power state, which is the classic symptom of an incorrect settle-time programming or of a PHY that reports ready too early. The instrumentation that makes this diagnosis possible — separate, readable counters for header and payload errors, with the ability to capture the first failing packet — is a feature to design in, not a debug hack; it is also a strong differentiator in a datasheet.

Y2. PCI Express, Generations 3 to 6, Worked

PCIe is the interface a design house is most likely to be asked for and
 least likely to build from scratch, because the controller is enormous and the
 compliance burden is severe. It is nevertheless worth understanding in detail, because
 almost every block a design house sells will sit behind one, and the properties of
 that link — its latency, its credit behaviour, its error model — propagate
 into the specification of whatever is attached.

장: Y2. PCI Express, Generations 3 to 6, Worked

글:
Y2.1 The rate table, computed rather than remembered

[Table 405. PCIe generations: raw rate, encoding and usable bandwidth]
Generation | GT/s per lane | Encoding | Encoding efficiency | GB/s per lane (one direction) | GB/s at x16 | Modulation
Gen1 | 2.5 | 8b/10b | 0.8 | 0.25 | 4 | NRZ
Gen2 | 5 | 8b/10b | 0.8 | 0.5 | 8 | NRZ
Gen3 | 8 | 128b/130b | 0.9846 | 0.9846 | 15.75 | NRZ
Gen4 | 16 | 128b/130b | 0.9846 | 1.969 | 31.51 | NRZ
Gen5 | 32 | 128b/130b | 0.9846 | 3.938 | 63.02 | NRZ
Gen6 | 64 | 242B FLIT / PAM4 | 0.9453 | 7.562 | 121 | PAM4

Computed from the transfer rate and the encoding efficiency alone; protocol overheads (TLP headers, DLLPs, ordered sets) are additional and Y2.3 computes them. The 8b/10b to 128b/130b change at Gen3 is why Gen3 is more than 1.6× Gen2 despite the rate being only 1.6×.

Worked example 61. Why Gen6 went to PAM4 and what it cost

Given. Gen5 runs 32 GT/s NRZ; Gen6 runs 64 GT/s. The channel budget is roughly unchanged, because the connectors and boards are the same.

Method. Compare the Nyquist frequency each modulation requires and the eye each produces, then note what follows.

Gen5 NRZ Nyquist | 16 GHz
Gen6 at 64 GT/s with NRZ would need | 32 GHz
Gen6 PAM4 symbol rate | 32 GBd
Gen6 PAM4 Nyquist | 16 GHz
PAM4 levels | 4
Eye height relative to NRZ at equal amplitude | 0.333
SNR penalty | 9.542 dB
Consequence | a raw BER near 10 −6 , so FEC becomes mandatory

How this is got wrong. By reading PAM4 as free bandwidth. It keeps the Nyquist frequency — and therefore the channel loss — unchanged, which is the whole point, and it pays 9.5 dB of eye for it. That payment forces three things into the specification at once: forward error correction, which adds latency; a flit-based protocol, because FEC needs fixed-size blocks and the old variable-length TLP framing does not provide them; and retry at the flit level rather than the packet level. Gen6 is therefore not an incremental speed bump but a protocol change, and any IP behind it sees different latency statistics.

Y2.2 Link training: the LTSSM as a bring-up tool

[Table 406. LTSSM states a bring-up engineer actually watches]
State | What it establishes | Stuck here means

Polling | Bit lock and symbol lock at 2.5 GT/s | Reference clock, PHY configuration, or gross signal integrity
Configuration | Lane numbering, link width, lane reversal, polarity inversion | Lane mapping error in the board or the controller
Recovery | Speed change and equalisation | The commonest stall: the link comes up at Gen1 and will not train higher
L0 | Normal operation | —
L0s / L1 / L2 | Power states | Exit latency violations, or a partner that does not support the state
Hot Reset / Disabled | Explicit teardown | Software

‘Trains at Gen1, fails at Gen3’ is a
 diagnosis, not a symptom, and it is worth knowing why. Every PCIe link starts at
 2.5 GT/s with no equalisation, because both ends must be able to talk before they
 can negotiate. The move to Gen3 and beyond runs a four-phase equalisation procedure in
 Recovery in which each end requests transmitter coefficient settings from the other
 and evaluates the result. A link that trains at Gen1 and fails above it has working
 wires and a failing equalisation: the channel is worse than the preset assumes, the
 far end's coefficient requests are being ignored or mishandled, or the receiver's
 evaluation is reporting success when the eye is marginal. The debug sequence is
 therefore: read the link status registers for the actual speed and width; read the
 lane error status; capture the equalisation phase the link fails in; and only then
 look at the board. Controllers that expose per-phase equalisation status are much
 faster to bring up, and this is a feature worth asking a vendor for.

Gen5 | 32 | 31.25 | 9.38 | 3.13 | 28

[Table 408. TLP efficiency against maximum payload size, Gen5 x16]
Max payload (B) | Overhead bytes | Total bytes | TLP efficiency | × encoding efficiency | Usable GB/s
64 | 24 | 88 | 0.7273 | 0.7161 | 45.83
128 | 24 | 152 | 0.8421 | 0.8291 | 53.07
256 | 24 | 280 | 0.9143 | 0.9002 | 57.61
512 | 24 | 536 | 0.9552 | 0.9405 | 60.19
4,096 | 24 | 4,120 | 0.9942 | 0.9789 | 62.65

The overhead figure counts a 12-byte header, sequence number, LCRC and framing; it ignores DLLP acknowledgements and flow-control updates, which consume a further few per cent. The lesson is the first column: a device restricted to 128-byte payloads gets roughly three quarters of the bandwidth of one that negotiates 512, and maximum payload size is negotiated to the minimum of the whole path, so one old switch in the chain sets it for everybody.

Worked example 62. Why a DMA engine behind PCIe needs deep outstanding-read support

Given. A Gen4 x8 link, 4 µs round-trip read latency to host memory, requesting 512-byte reads. The engine must sustain 12 GB/s.

Method. Bandwidth–delay product again, exactly as in Part X11 — the formula does not care that the wire is now a PCIe link.

Gen4 x8 usable bandwidth | 15.75 GB/s
Required bandwidth | 12 GB/s
Bytes in flight needed | 46.88 kB
512-byte reads outstanding | 94
Tag space needed (10-bit tags allow 768) | 94 of 768
Completion buffer required | 46.88 kB

How this is got wrong. By sizing from the link rate and ignoring the latency. A device with 32 outstanding reads on this link achieves 512 × 32 / 4 µs = 4 GB/s regardless of the link being capable of 15. The second trap is the completion buffer: those bytes in flight must land somewhere, so the buffer is not optional and it is tens of kilobytes. Outstanding-transaction capability and completion-buffer size are the two numbers that decide whether a PCIe device performs, and they belong on the first page of its datasheet, not in an appendix.

절: Y2.4 What the corpus contains, and what it does not
글:
Y2.4 What the corpus contains, and what it does not

This book's code appendix includes 198,332 lines of a
 working open-source PCIe datapath: DMA engines, TLP generation and parsing, and
 AXI bridging. It is genuinely useful and it is worth being precise about what it
 is. It is the transaction and data-link layer above a vendor hard macro
 — the PHY, the LTSSM, the equalisation procedure and the serialiser are not
 in it and cannot be, because they are analogue and foundry-specific.

[Table 409. Where PCIe functionality actually comes from, and who can sell it]
Layer | Implemented as | Who supplies it | Can a small design house sell this?
Serialiser, CDR, equaliser | Hard macro in a specific process | PHY vendor or foundry | No — requires analogue design and process access
PIPE interface | Defined digital interface | Boundary between the two | —
LTSSM, lane management | RTL | Controller vendor | In principle; compliance is the barrier
Data link layer: ack/nak, flow control | RTL | Controller vendor | Yes, with effort
Transaction layer, config space | RTL | Controller vendor | Yes
Application logic behind the controller | RTL | Anyone | Yes — and this is where a design house should be

Compliance is the commercial fact about PCIe.
 A controller that works is not a controller that can be sold: the PCI-SIG compliance
 programme, its test fixtures, its interoperability workshops and the membership that
 permits them are a substantial and recurring cost, and a customer buying a PCIe
 controller is buying that compliance as much as the RTL. For a one-person design
 house the rational position is above the controller, not inside it — build
 the accelerator, the DMA engine, the protocol offload that sits behind a licensed
 controller, and let the customer bring the controller they have already
 qualified.

Problem. A customer asks you to quote for ‘a PCIe Gen4 endpoint with a custom accelerator’. How do you structure the quote?
Solution. Split it explicitly, and say why in the quote itself. Item one: the accelerator — your design, your verification, your price. Item two: integration with a controller the customer licenses, quoted as integration effort with the controller named, because the effort depends heavily on which one; a controller with a clean AXI-Stream application interface is a fortnight and one with an idiosyncratic interface is two months. Item three: what you are not supplying — the controller licence, the PHY, the compliance testing, and the driver, each listed with who you expect to provide it. A quote that silently includes the controller either loses on price to competitors who excluded it, or wins and then discovers the licence costs more than the project. Being explicit about scope is not a weakness in a proposal; it is the clearest signal that the quoter has done this before, and experienced buyers read it that way.

Problem. Gen6 introduced FEC. What does that do to the latency your block sees, and why can the FEC not simply be made stronger to allow a cheaper channel?
Solution. FEC operates on fixed-size flits, so the receiver must collect a whole flit before it can correct it, and the correction itself takes time. The added latency is small in absolute terms — tens of nanoseconds — but it is added to every transaction, and for a latency-sensitive accelerator performing fine-grained host synchronisation it can matter more than the doubled bandwidth helps. It also changes the distribution: retries now happen at flit granularity with a different tail than Gen5's packet-level replay. Stronger FEC is not the answer to a worse channel because latency is the constraint that a stronger code violates first: a longer code corrects more and waits longer, and PCIe's entire value proposition rests on being a low-latency load/store fabric rather than a network. The design point was chosen to bound added latency, and the code strength followed from that bound — not the other way round, which is the usual direction in communications and the reason PCIe's FEC looks weak to someone arriving from Ethernet.

Y3. The Ethernet MAC and Its Transceiver, Worked

The Gigabit MAC is the most-integrated communications block in
 existence and a good vehicle for the whole of this book: it has a datapath with hard
 real-time constraints, a protocol with a long tail of options, a clock-domain problem
 at its centre, and an interface stack whose names (GMII, RGMII, SGMII, QSGMII) encode
 a series of commercial compromises worth understanding.

절: Y3.1 Frame timing: the arithmetic that sets every buffer
글:
Y3.1 Frame timing: the arithmetic that sets every buffer

[Table 410. Frame times, packet rates and the inter-packet gap]
Rate | Mbit/s | Min frame + preamble + IPG (ns) | Max frame + overhead (µs) | Max frames/s (M) | IPG (ns)
10BASE-T | 10 | 67200 | 1230 | 0.01488 | 9600
100BASE-TX | 100 | 6720 | 123 | 0.1488 | 960
1000BASE-T | 1000 | 672 | 12.3 | 1.488 | 96
2.5GBASE-T | 2500 | 268.8 | 4.922 | 3.72 | 38.4

25GBASE-R | 25000 | 26.88 | 0.4922 | 37.2 | 3.84

Computed from 8 bytes of preamble and start delimiter, 12 bytes of inter-packet gap, and the frame itself. The fifth column is the number that sizes the control path: at 25 Gbit/s a new frame can start every 33 ns, so any per-frame decision — a lookup, a filter, a statistics update — must complete in that time or be pipelined.

Worked example 63. Why a MAC at 10 Gbit/s cannot process one byte per cycle

Given. 10 Gbit/s line rate. The digital logic runs at 156.25 MHz, which is the standard XGMII clock.

Method. Divide the bit rate by the clock to find the datapath width, then check what that width does to frame alignment.

Bits per clock | 64
Datapath width | 64 bits = 8 bytes
Bytes per clock | 8
Minimum frame (64 B) in clocks | 8
Can a frame start mid-word? | yes — the IPG is 12 bytes, not a multiple of 8
Alignment cases the datapath must handle | 8
At 25 Gbit/s on the same clock: width | 160 bits

How this is got wrong. By designing the datapath for aligned frames. Because the inter-packet gap is 12 bytes and the datapath is 8 wide, successive frames start at different byte lanes, so every parser, every CRC engine and every filter must handle all eight alignments. This is the single largest source of complexity in a wide Ethernet MAC and it is invisible in a specification that describes the protocol in bytes. A block that assumes alignment will pass a test bench that sends one frame at a time and fail on back-to-back traffic at line rate — which is the only traffic that matters.

[Table 411. MAC-to-PHY interfaces: the same function, very different pin counts]
Interface | Data bits each way | Clocking | Carries | Approx. pins
MII | 4 | 25 MHz | 100 Mbit/s | 16
GMII | 8 | 125 MHz | 1 Gbit/s | 24
RGMII | 4 | 125 MHz DDR | 1 Gbit/s | 12
SGMII | 1 | 625 MHz DDR serial | 1 Gbit/s | 4
QSGMII | 1 | 5 Gbit/s serial | 4 × 1 Gbit/s | 4

The progression is one long trade of pins against signalling difficulty. RGMII halves GMII's pins by clocking on both edges and pays with a notorious source-synchronous timing problem: the specification's delay requirement is met either by the board, by the PHY or by the MAC, and mismatched assumptions between the three are the most common Gigabit Ethernet bring-up failure in existence.

The RGMII delay question, stated once so it can be
 checked. RGMII requires the clock to be delayed relative to the data by roughly
 1.5–2 ns at the receiver. That delay may be provided by a long clock trace
 on the board, by the PHY's internal delay (enabled by strap or register), or by the
 MAC's output delay. Exactly one of the three must provide it. Zero gives a
 link that does not pass traffic or passes it only at 10 Mbit/s; two gives the
 same symptom for the opposite reason. Because each is configured by a different party
 — layout, PHY firmware, RTL — nobody owns the question, and it is worth
 writing the answer into the integration guide of any MAC a design house ships, along
 with the register bits that set it.

Why 64b/66b replaced 8b/10b

 | Step | Justification
1 | 8b/10b maps each byte to a 10-bit symbol chosen for DC balance and transition density. | Original Gigabit encoding.
2 | Overhead is 25 %: a 1.25 GBd line carries 1 Gbit/s. | 10/8. At 10 Gbit/s that would demand 12.5 GBd , which the channel of the day could not support.
3 | 64b/66b prefixes two bits of sync header to 64 bits of scrambled payload. | Overhead 3.1 %.
4 | Transition density comes from a self-synchronous scrambler ( x 58 + x 39 +1), not from the code. | The sync header is the only guaranteed transition , which is enough for a CDR with a long time constant and would not have been enough for the receivers of 1998.
5 | The scrambler is self-synchronising, so a single bit error produces three errors at the descrambler. | The error is fed back at the two tap positions. This multiplication is the reason the FEC above it is symbol-oriented , and it is a fact a link budget must account for.

[Table 412. Line-rate consequences of the encoding choice]
Encoding | Expansion | Payload Gbit/s | Line GBd (NRZ) | Overhead (%)
8b/10b | 1.25 | 1 | 1.25 | 25
64b/66b | 1.0312 | 10 | 10.312 | 3.12
64b/66b | 1.0312 | 25 | 25.781 | 3.12
256b/257b + RS-FEC | 1.0625 | 50 | 53.125 | 6.25
256b/257b + RS-FEC | 1.0625 | 100 | 106.25 | 6.25

The last two rows include the RS(544,514) FEC expansion, which is why 100 Gbit/s per lane runs at about 53.125 GBd — the number Part X4's link budget used.

Where the design-house opportunity is in this
 stack. The PMA — serialiser, CDR, equaliser — is a hard macro and is
 not available to a soft-IP vendor. The MAC is a commodity: dozens of implementations
 exist, several of them open, and margins are thin. The PCS and FEC sublayer between
 them is soft RTL, is algorithmically demanding, changes with every new standard, and
 has far fewer credible suppliers. That combination — soft, hard, and
 changing — is the profile of a good product for a small house, and it is the
 reason this book's prior-art survey chose it. The specific opening at the time of
 writing is IEEE 802.3dj's concatenated FEC, where the outer RS-KP4 is well
 understood and the inner code and its interleaving are new.

The code appendix contains 260,596 lines of an
 open-source Ethernet family, of which 29,336 lines in 89 files
 are the BASE-R PCS itself — the 64b/66b encoder and decoder, the scrambler,
 the block synchroniser and the gearbox. Reading those files against the
 derivation above is the fastest way to see how a standard's prose becomes
 RTL.
