절: Y3.4 Flow control, buffering and the numbers a customer checks
글:
Y3.4 Flow control, buffering and the numbers a customer checks

[Table 413. Buffer needed to stop a sender in time, 100 m of copper]
Rate (Gbit/s) | One-way propagation (µs) | Round trip (µs) | Bandwidth–delay product (kB) | Max-size frames in flight
1 | 0.5 | 1 | 0.1221 | 1
10 | 0.5 | 1 | 1.221 | 1
25 | 0.5 | 1 | 3.052 | 3
100 | 0.5 | 1 | 12.21 | 9

This is the buffer a receiver must have after it decides to send a PAUSE frame, because frames already in flight will arrive regardless. Add the PAUSE frame's own transmission and the partner's reaction time and the requirement grows further. The bandwidth–delay product appears for the third time in this book, in its third guise; it is the same formula that sized the credit buffer and the PCIe completion buffer.

Problem. A customer reports frame loss under burst traffic although your MAC reports no errors and the link is not saturated on average. Where do you look?
Solution. ‘Not saturated on average’ is the clue: averages hide bursts, and Ethernet traffic is bursty at every timescale. The sequence is: read the drop counters and find out which stage dropped — a MAC that cannot say whether a frame was dropped at the PHY interface, in the receive FIFO, or by the filter is much harder to defend, so this instrumentation is worth building. Then check the receive FIFO's depth against the consumer's worst-case stall, not its average service rate; if the consumer is a bus master, the stall is the interconnect's worst-case arbitration latency from Part X11, which is usually far longer than anyone estimated. Then check whether flow control is enabled at both ends, since PAUSE is negotiated and frequently disabled by default. Finally, check the clock-rate mismatch: two ends nominally at the same rate differ by up to 200 ppm, so a receiver without rate adaptation slowly falls behind and drops a frame every few seconds — a distinctive signature worth recognising, because the loss rate is remarkably constant.

Problem. Why does a MAC need an idle-insertion and idle-deletion mechanism at all, given that both ends are specified at the same rate?
Solution. Because ‘the same rate’ means the same nominal rate within a tolerance, typically ±100 ppm each, so the two can differ by 200 ppm — one part in five thousand. Over a continuous stream that is one extra or missing byte every 5000, which accumulates without bound. The mechanism uses the inter-packet gap as elastic: if the local clock is slower, delete an idle byte from the gap; if faster, insert one. The gap can be shortened to a floor (five bytes in the 10 Gbit/s specifications, from twelve) which is what limits how much rate difference can be absorbed. The consequence for a design is that the IPG a MAC sees on receive is not the IPG the far end transmitted, so any logic that assumes twelve bytes is wrong, and any logic that uses IPG timing to infer anything about the far end is wrong twice. This elasticity, and its floor, is also why the FEC and PCS layers above must tolerate the alignment markers that periodically consume the same budget.

장: Y4. A Verification Agent That Runs While You Sleep
절: Y4. A Verification Agent That Runs While You Sleep — 들어가며
글:
Y4. A Verification Agent That Runs While You Sleep

A one-person design house has one engineer and twenty-four hours in a
 day, and the engineer needs some of them. The only way the arithmetic works is for
 verification to run unattended overnight and to leave behind something better than a
 log file. This part documents such a system, which lives in this repository under
 edu/agent/ and which is exercised by
 tests/test_verif_agent.py. It is deliberately small — roughly the
 size one person can maintain — and it is deliberately suspicious of
 itself.

[그림] Figure 52. One iteration of the loop. The first box is the one most regression systems lack, and it is the reason the rest can be believed.

장: Y4. A Verification Agent That Runs While You Sleep
절: Y4.1 The design, and the two failures it is built around
글:
Y4.1 The design, and the two failures it is built around

An unattended regression can fail in two directions, and the second is
 far more dangerous than the first. It can report a failure that is not there, which
 wastes a morning. Or it can report success while checking nothing, which wastes a
 tape-out. The loop is structured so that the second is caught by construction.

[Table 414. What each stage is for, and what would go wrong without it]
Stage | What it does | Without it
Self-check | Corrupts one golden value and asserts that the comparison notices | A comparison that silently stopped comparing reports green forever. This is the failure mode this whole repository is organised against
Regression | Runs the DUT and the golden model on the same stimulus and compares every output | —
Distinct-output count | Counts how many different values the golden model produced | A stimulus that drives one constant passes trivially. The loop treats fewer than two distinct outputs as a failure, not a pass
Shrink | Re-runs the single failing stimulus on its own | A 4000-transaction failure report that nobody can debug
Repair search | Generates single-edit candidates from a rule library and tests each | The engineer starts every morning from a raw failure
Three gates | Original seed, an unused seed, and the self-check | An edit that special-cases the failing input passes. The overfitting gate is the reason this can be left running unattended

The overfitting gate deserves its own sentence,
 because automated repair without it is actively harmful. A search that accepts any
 edit making the failing test pass will, given a large enough rule library, eventually
 find one that hard-codes the answer. Such an edit is worse than the original bug: the
 bug was visible and the patch is not. The rule here is that a candidate must pass a
 seed that was never used during the search, which is the same
 train/test separation that any honest empirical claim requires. This book's
 Part X8 makes the same point about a bug-find-rate curve, and
 Part X1 about a range justified by simulation: a number validated on the data
 that produced it is not validated.

장: Y4. A Verification Agent That Runs While You Sleep
절: Y4.2 The blocks under test, measured now
글:
Y4.2 The blocks under test, measured now

[Table 415. The agent's blocks, run at build time against their golden models]
Block | Golden model | Stimuli | Mismatches | Distinct outputs | Checker bites? | Wall time
crc32_8 | Python's zlib.crc32 | 1,500 | 0 | 1,499 | yes | 0.0491 s
crc32_stream | — | 52 | 0 | 51 | yes | 0.0556 s
enc8b10b | — | 3,000 | 0 | 488 | yes | 0.0529 s
gf_mul | the repository's gf.py | 1,500 | 0 | 808 | yes | 0.0429 s
regfile | — | 1,500 | 0 | 169 | yes | 0.0635 s
rs_syn_step | the repository's gf.py | 1,500 | 0 | 796 | yes | 0.0458 s

Run by this chapter as the book is rendered, with Icarus Verilog. The ‘distinct outputs’ column is the one that makes the ‘mismatches’ column mean something; a zero in the fourth column beside a one in the fifth would be a false green.

Why the CRC block's golden model is
 zlib and not a hand-written CRC. If the reference and the design are
 written by the same person from the same understanding, they share that person's
 misunderstandings, and the comparison certifies the misunderstanding rather than
 detecting it. This is not hypothetical: reflected versus non-reflected CRC, initial
 value, and final XOR are four independent conventions and a hand-written reference
 gets at least one of them wrong about as often as the RTL does. An independent
 reference is worth more than a more accurate one. The same argument is why a
 modelling team is organisationally separate from the design team — the
 independence is the product.

장: Y4. A Verification Agent That Runs While You Sleep
절: Y4.3 Repair, measured on injected faults
글:
Y4.3 Repair, measured on injected faults

The claim that the agent repairs Verilog is only worth making with
 numbers behind it. The following table injects known faults into the GF multiplier and
 reports what the search did, computed while this page was rendered.

[Table 416. Injected faults and what the repair search did, run at build time]
Injected fault | Mismatches before | Candidates tried | Rule that repaired it | Rejected for overfitting | Search time
overflow bit read one position low | 393 / 400 | 7 of 7 | MSB 인덱스 M-2 / M-1 | 0 | 10.2 s
accumulate with OR instead of XOR | 384 / 400 | 3 of 7 | OR / XOR | 0 | 0.104 s
reduction shift in the wrong direction | 390 / 400 | 5 of 7 | 우시프트 / 좌시프트 | 0 | 0.141 s

The search is exhaustive over single edits from the rule library, so a ‘not repaired’ result means the fault is outside the library — which is information, not a failure. The candidate counts are small because the rule library is deliberately narrow; a library that edits anything would find something for every fault and most of it would be wrong.

What this system is not. It is not a bug finder
 for logic it has no golden model of, and it is not a substitute for a verification
 plan. The rule library covers the small syntactic faults that a tired engineer
 introduces at two in the morning — an inverted comparison, a shift the wrong
 way, an index off by one — and nothing else. A missing state in a state machine,
 a protocol rule that was never implemented, or a specification misread will all pass
 the repair search untouched, because there is no single-token edit that fixes them.
 The value is not that it repairs everything; it is that it removes the trivial
 failures from the morning's queue, with a patch and a minimal reproducer attached
 to each of the rest.

장: Y4. A Verification Agent That Runs While You Sleep
절: Y4.4 Running it for twenty-four hours
글:
Y4.4 Running it for twenty-four hours

The launcher follows this repository's rule for background work, which
 exists because the obvious way does not work: a process started with a bare
 & from inside an agent session is reaped when that session's process
 exits, and the evidence for that is a night in which nothing ran and a message the
 next morning saying it had.

```
edu/agent/run.sh — the launcher
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 24시간 회귀 에이전트를 **부모가 죽어도 사는** 방식으로 띄운다.
#
# CLAUDE.md 의 백그라운드 규칙 그대로다: setsid + nohup + disown, 그리고
# stdin/stdout/stderr 를 전부 리다이렉트한다. claude -p 가 응답 직후 끝나도
# 이 프로세스는 남는다.
#
# 사용: bash run.sh [--적용] [시간]
#
# 확인은 `ps -p $!` 가 아니라 `pgrep -af agent.py` 로 한다 -- setsid 가 fork 하므로
# $! 는 이미 끝난 래퍼다. 셸 변수명에 한글을 쓰지 않는다 (bash 는 받지 않는다).
set -u

HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
LOGDIR="${SE_AGENT_LOG:-/home/user/SE/logs}"
mkdir -p "$LOGDIR"
LOG="$LOGDIR/verif_agent.log"

APPLY=""
HOURS="24"
for a in "$@"; do
 case "$a" in
 --적용|--apply) APPLY="--적용" ;;
 *) HOURS="$a" ;;
 esac
done

setsid nohup python3 "$HERE/agent.py" --시간 "$HOURS" ${APPLY:+$APPLY} \
 > "$LOG" 2>&1 /dev/null; then
 echo "살아 있다:"
 pgrep -af "agent.py"
 echo "로그: $LOG"
 sleep 2
 echo "--- 로그 첫 줄 ---"
 head -3 "$LOG"
else
 echo "띄우지 못했다. 로그:"
 cat "$LOG"
 exit 1
fi
```

[Table 417. The three things that make an unattended launch survive]
Element | What it detaches from | What happens without it
setsid | The parent's session and process group | The process dies with the session that started it
nohup | SIGHUP | The process dies when the terminal closes
disown | The shell's job table | The shell may still signal it on exit
Do not put non-ASCII text in a pgrep -f
 pattern. The pattern is matched against /proc/<pid>/cmdline,
 whose bytes may not decode in the current locale; a pattern containing characters that
 cannot be decoded matches nothing, and a match of nothing reads as
 ‘finished’. A job that is running is then reported as done, or started a
 second time. Wait on a PID with kill -0, or match an ASCII-only
 fragment of the command line.

Worked example 64. What a night actually buys

Given. The loop measured above runs roughly 900–2000 regression rounds per minute on this container for these small combinational blocks, each round a fresh seed.

Method. Extrapolate to eight hours and compare with what a person can supervise. Then note the limit, which is not the compute.

Rounds per hour (order of magnitude) | 10 5
Rounds in an eight-hour night | ≈10 6
Distinct seeds consumed | one per block per round
Engineer-hours consumed | 0
What limits the value | the golden models and the stimulus, not the machine

How this is got wrong. By reading the round count as coverage. A million rounds of the same random distribution explore the same region a thousand times. Part X8's coupon-collector arithmetic says where the return flattens, and the answer is far below a million for any of these blocks. The honest use of an overnight run is not volume but variety: rotate the constraint sets, inject faults deliberately to measure whether the suite still bites, and re-run the previous night's minimal reproducers as a growing regression. A loop that only turns the seed is a loop that stops learning after the first hour.

Problem. You arrive in the morning to nine failures, all in one block, all with the same minimal reproducer shape. What do you do first?
Solution. Deduplicate before debugging. Nine reports with one shape are one bug, and the first task is to confirm that by checking whether a single edit makes all nine reproducers pass — which the repair search has already attempted and logged. If it found an edit and the overfitting gate rejected it, that rejection is the most informative line in the whole night's ledger: it says a plausible local fix exists and is wrong, which usually means the bug is one level up from where it manifests. If the search found nothing, read the minimal reproducer and ask which of the four X8 categories it belongs to before opening the RTL. The failure the agent cannot repair is the one worth your morning; the ones it repaired are worth only a review of the patch.

Problem. Your manager asks whether the agent could write the RTL as well as fix it. What is the honest answer?
Solution. The honest answer distinguishes two things this chapter has kept separate. Search over a small edit space with a strong oracle is reliable, and that is what this agent does: the golden model is the oracle, the edit space is a dozen rules, and the three gates bound the false-accept rate. Generation without an oracle is not, because nothing is checking the result except a human reading it, and the failure mode is code that looks right. The useful framing for a design house is therefore: let generation propose and let the oracle dispose, and invest in the oracle. A team with an excellent golden model and a mediocre generator will out-ship a team with the reverse, because the first can accept help from any source and the second cannot tell good help from bad. That is also why the modelling role — the one this book is written for — becomes more valuable as generation improves, not less.

장: Y5. The Commercial Mechanics of Selling an IP Block
절: Y5. The Commercial Mechanics of Selling an IP Block — 들어가며
글:
Y5. The Commercial Mechanics of Selling an IP Block

A design house that cannot price, license and support its work does not
 have a business, it has a hobby with good documentation. This part gives the
 arithmetic of the commercial side with the same seriousness as the technical parts,
 because the failure modes are just as specific and rather less discussed.

장: Y5. The Commercial Mechanics of Selling an IP Block
절: Y5.1 The three revenue models and when each applies
글:
Y5.1 The three revenue models and when each applies

[Table 418. How semiconductor IP is actually sold]
Model | Customer pays | Suits | Risk to you | Risk to them
Licence + royalty | A licence fee, then a per-unit royalty | High volume, standard function | Royalty depends on their success and their honesty — audit rights matter | Ongoing cost; they will try to convert it to a buyout
Paid-up / perpetual licence | One fee, unlimited units | Customers who cannot tolerate per-unit accounting | You capture none of their upside | Large up-front commitment
Services / NRE | Engineering time | Where a one-person house should start | No leverage — you are paid once for each hour | Low; they own the result
Subscription | Annual fee for access and updates | Rapidly changing standards | Churn | Dependence on your survival
Open core + support | Support and customisation | Building reputation from nothing | Hard to monetise | Very low

Worked example 65. When a royalty beats a buyout, from the customer's side

Given. A block licensed at $150 000 plus $0.20 per unit, or $600 000 paid up. The customer's forecast is 1 million units over three years, but forecasts in this market are routinely out by 3× in both directions.

Method. Compute the break-even volume, then compute what each party's exposure is above and below it. The break-even is arithmetic; the interesting part is the asymmetry around it.

Break-even volume | 2,250,000
Royalty model cost at 1M units | 3.5000×10 5  USD
Buyout cost | 600,000 USD
Royalty cost at 0.3M units (forecast ÷ 3) | 2.1000×10 5  USD
Royalty cost at 3M units | 7.5000×10 5  USD
Your revenue at 3M units under buyout | 600,000 USD
Your revenue at 3M units under royalty | 7.5000×10 5  USD

How this is got wrong. By negotiating the break-even and not the distribution. Both parties can compute 2.25 million units; what decides the deal is who is more confident and who can bear the downside. A one-person house with no cash reserve should prefer the larger up-front fee even at a worse expected value, because surviving to the next contract dominates expected value when a single bad quarter ends the business. The standard compromise is a royalty with a cap and a floor, which bounds both parties' exposure and is easier to agree than either extreme.

장: Y5. The Commercial Mechanics of Selling an IP Block
절: Y5.2 What a customer actually receives
글:
Y5.2 What a customer actually receives

[Table 419. The delivery package, item by item]
Item | Form | Why it is not optional
RTL | Encrypted or plain SystemVerilog | The product — but the smallest part of the package
Testbench and tests | UVM or equivalent, runnable | The customer must be able to re-verify after editing ; without it your block becomes untouchable and therefore unusable
Reference model | C or C++, bit-accurate | Their system model needs it; also it is what makes your claims checkable
Synthesis scripts and constraints | SDC plus a script | Timing closure in their flow is where integrations fail
Lint and CDC waivers | Files with justifications | Their sign-off will run these tools; unexplained violations stop the project
IP-XACT / integration metadata | XML | Automated integration; increasingly a purchase requirement
Register map | Generated from one source | Hand-maintained duplicates diverge, and the divergence is discovered by software at the worst time
Documentation | Datasheet, integration guide, release notes | Support cost is inversely proportional to documentation quality
Known-issue list | A document | Omitting it does not remove the issues, it removes your credibility when they are found

The known-issue list is the item that distinguishes a
 professional supplier, and it is counter-intuitive to first-time vendors. Every
 block has limitations: a configuration that was never verified, a corner that fails a
 lint rule for a defensible reason, a performance figure that holds only above a
 certain clock ratio. A customer who finds these themselves concludes you did not know;
 a customer who reads them in your release notes concludes you did. The second
 customer calls you when they have a problem instead of calling your competitor.
 Write the list, keep it honest, and put dates and workarounds beside each
 entry.

절: Y5.3 Support: the cost nobody budgets
글:
Y5.3 Support: the cost nobody budgets

[Table 420. Support load against customer count, at 1.5 engineer-hours per query]
Customers | Queries per customer per year | Queries per year | Engineer-hours | % of a person-year (1800 h) | Working weeks
1 | 40 | 40 | 60 | 3.33 | 1.5
3 | 30 | 90 | 135 | 7.5 | 3.38
5 | 25 | 125 | 187.5 | 10.4 | 4.69
10 | 20 | 200 | 300 | 16.7 | 7.5
20 | 18 | 360 | 540 | 30 | 13.5

Queries per customer fall with experience because the documentation improves and the frequent questions get answered in it. At twenty customers support is a full-time job, which for a one-person house means either hiring, raising prices to slow growth, or investing hard in documentation and self-service — and the third is the only one available immediately.

Worked example 66. Pricing that accounts for support

Given. You expect 8 customers over three years for a block that took 44 weeks to build. Target: recover the build and support and earn a living. Your cost of living plus overhead is $120 000 a year.

Method. Total the engineering, add the support from the table above, and divide. Then compare with what the market will bear, because the two are independent numbers and the smaller one wins.

Build effort | 44 weeks
Support over 3 years at 8 customers | 19.8 weeks
Total effort | 63.8 weeks
Cost at $120k/year | 1.4723×10 5  USD
Break-even price per customer | 18404 USD
With a 40 % margin | 30673 USD
If only 3 customers materialise | 65929 USD

How this is got wrong. By pricing from cost and ignoring the market. The last row is the real risk: with three customers instead of eight, the price that covers cost is more than double, and there is no reason a customer will pay it. The standard mitigations are to start with services revenue, which is paid whether or not the block sells; to sell the first block below cost to a reference customer in exchange for a public reference, which is worth more than the margin; and to build blocks whose adjacent variants share most of the effort, so the second customer in a family costs a fraction of the first.

장: Y5. The Commercial Mechanics of Selling an IP Block
절: Y5.4 Legal and quality items that bite a small vendor
글:
Y5.4 Legal and quality items that bite a small vendor

[Table 421. Contractual terms and what each one means in practice]
Term | What the customer wants | What you should watch
Indemnification | You cover patent claims against the block | Cap it at fees received. Uncapped indemnity can exceed the company's value; it is the single most dangerous clause for a small vendor
Warranty | The block conforms to the specification | Define the specification precisely and tie the warranty to it, not to ‘fitness for purpose’
Escrow | Source held by a third party in case you disappear | Reasonable; budget the fee and keep the deposit current
Acceptance criteria | A defined test they run | Insist the criteria be written and runnable before delivery. Undefined acceptance is an unbounded obligation
Exclusivity | Nobody else gets the block | Price it as the lost market, and time-limit it
Support term | Years of updates | Define what an update is; a new standard revision is a new product

Provenance of the source you ship is a hard
 requirement, not a formality. If any part of your block derives from code with a
 copyleft licence, or from a previous employer's work, or from a reference design with
 redistribution limits, a customer's legal review will find it — they scan for
 this — and the deal ends there. Keep a per-file record of origin, do not paste
 from sources you cannot name, and be able to produce that record on request. The
 code appendix of this book is an illustration of the standard: every file
 reproduced in it is named with its repository and its line count, and a reader can
 trace any line back to its source.

Problem. A prospective customer asks for a three-month free evaluation with full source. How do you respond?
Solution. Not with a flat refusal, and not with the source. The request is reasonable in intent — they cannot buy what they cannot assess — and unreasonable in form, because full source for three months is the product. The standard structures, in increasing order of what you give away: an evaluation package of documentation, the datasheet, the register map and simulation results, which costs you nothing and answers most questions; an encrypted or obfuscated netlist or FPGA bitstream they can integrate and measure but not read, which answers the performance question; and a paid evaluation licence whose fee is credited against the full licence if they proceed, which aligns both parties and filters out tyre-kickers at no cost to a serious buyer. The paid evaluation is the one to propose; a customer who will not pay a small fee to evaluate is very unlikely to pay a large one to license.

Problem. Your block has been shipping for a year when a customer reports a bug that affects every unit they have built. What do you do, in order?
Solution. Reproduce it before saying anything about cause. Ask for the configuration, the stimulus and the failing condition, and reproduce it in your own environment; a report is a hypothesis. Then determine the blast radius — which configurations, which versions, which other customers — because the answer determines whether this is one email or a notification to everyone. Then notify affected customers before they find it, with what is known, what is not, and when the next update will come; a vendor who reports their own bug keeps the account, and one who is caught concealing it does not. Then fix, with a regression test that would have caught it, and say in the release notes what that test is. Finally, ask why the verification plan missed it and fix the plan, not just the code — Part X8's mutation argument applies directly: if the suite did not catch this, inject it and find out what else of the same shape it would miss.

장: Y6. From a Paper to a Block, and Back to a Paper
절: Y6. From a Paper to a Block, and Back to a Paper — 들어가며
글:
Y6. From a Paper to a Block, and Back to a Paper

Research papers are the cheapest source of architecture a design house
 has, and the most dangerous, because a paper's incentives are not a product's
 incentives. A paper must be novel; a product must be robust. A paper reports the
 configuration that worked; a product must survive the ones that did not. This part is
 a procedure for extracting value from the literature without inheriting its
 optimism — and, in its second half, for publishing without committing the same
 offence.

장: Y6. From a Paper to a Block, and Back to a Paper
절: Y6.1 Reading a hardware paper in the order that matters
글:
Y6.1 Reading a hardware paper in the order that matters

[Table 422. What to read, in order, and what you are looking for]
Read | You are asking | Stop if
The results table | What was actually measured, in what units, against what baseline | The baseline is the authors' own strawman rather than a published comparable
The methodology section | Simulated, synthesised, or fabricated? At what node? Post-layout or post-synthesis? | Post-synthesis numbers compared against someone else's post-layout numbers — a 20–40 % difference presented as a contribution
The assumptions | What is held fixed, and is it fixed in your application? | The gain depends on a parameter your customer sets differently
The limitations paragraph | What do the authors admit? | There is not one
The related work | Who else did this, and how does this compare? | It is a list of citations rather than a comparison
The algorithm | Can you implement it from the text alone? | Only now — reading the algorithm first is how a fortnight disappears

The recurring pattern in hardware papers is the
 unstated operating point. A result is reported at the configuration where the
 proposed technique wins, and the sweep that shows where it loses is absent. This is
 not usually dishonesty; it is page limits and the reviewing process. But it means
 the first thing to do with a promising technique is to reproduce the sweep the
 paper did not print, in your own model, and find the crossover. If the crossover
 is on the wrong side of your customer's operating point, the technique is a
 publication and not a product — and you have learned that in a week rather than
 a quarter. This repository's own record contains the mirror image of this mistake: a
 headline figure of ‘1/59 the area’ taken from the most favourable corner
 of a sweep, with the loss condition present elsewhere in the same document.

Worked example 67. Reproducing the missing sweep: a worked reading

Given. A paper claims an unrolled architecture removes a timing bottleneck and reports a 59× area advantage over the standard-cell baseline at one operating point.

Method. Identify the parameter the advantage depends on, sweep it, and find where the sign changes. Here the parameter is the number of taps that must be unrolled, which grows with channel loss; area grows as 2n.

Claimed advantage at the reported point | 59×
Unrolled taps at that point | 2
Area factor at n =2 | 4
Unrolled taps at a realistic 30 dB channel | 5
Area factor at n =5 | 32
Advantage rescaled | 7.38×
Taps at which the advantage disappears | 7.88

How this is got wrong. By quoting the headline and moving on. The arithmetic above takes ten minutes and changes the conclusion from ‘adopt’ to ‘adopt for short channels only’, which is a completely different product decision. The general procedure is: find the exponential, and find where it eats the constant. Almost every architecture paper contains exactly one such exponential, and the paper's operating point is chosen just below where it bites.

장: Y6. From a Paper to a Block, and Back to a Paper
절: Y6.2 The prior-art search, done so that it means something
글:
Y6.2 The prior-art search, done so that it means something

This book's repository enforces a rule that a prior-art note must be
 committed before the code for a topic. The rule exists because the same failure
 occurred five times: choose a topic, build, measure, write, and only then discover the
 work already existed. The procedure below is what the rule requires.

[Table 423. A prior-art note that is worth the time it takes]
Section | Content | The failure it prevents
Closest prior work | arXiv or DOI, year, and one sentence on what it did | ‘I could not find anything’, which is not a finding
How we differ | One paragraph, specific, falsifiable | A difference that evaporates under a reviewer's first question
Queries run | The literal search strings, at least three, with the databases | An unrepeatable search
Where you have not looked | Named: patents, a paywalled venue, a language, an industry body's documents | Treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence
Confidence of each citation | Full text, abstract, listing, or snippet | Citing something you have not read as though you had
Possibilities not yet eliminated | A list | A false sense of completion

The confidence marker is the mechanically enforceable
 part and therefore the part worth automating. This repository requires every
 citation in a paper to carry, on the document's face, whether the author read the full
 text, the abstract, a listing entry, or only a search snippet; a gate checks the
 document against a ledger of citations and fails the build if they disagree. What the
 gate cannot check is whether the marker is honest, and the repository's notes
 say so explicitly. That is the correct division: the machine forces the claim to be
 stated, and a human is accountable for its truth. A process that pretends the
 machine can verify reading is worse than one that admits it cannot, because it invites
 everyone to stop looking.

Problem. You find a patent that appears to cover the architecture you were about to build. What are the possible responses, and which are realistic for a one-person house?
Solution. Six responses exist and only some are realistic. Design around: read the claims, not the abstract — the claims are the legal scope and are usually much narrower than the description — and find an element of the independent claim you can avoid. This is the normal answer and it is realistic. Check the status: the patent may have lapsed for unpaid maintenance fees, may never have been granted in your customers' jurisdictions, or may expire before your product ships; all are cheap to check and all are common. License it: realistic only if the holder licenses, which large semiconductor holders often do not to small parties. Challenge validity: not realistic — the cost exceeds a small house's annual revenue. Ignore it: not an option; wilful infringement carries enhanced damages, and your customer's legal review will find it anyway. Change topic: often the correct answer, and the reason the prior-art search comes first. The meta-point is that the patent is information, not a verdict, and reading the claims carefully is a skill worth acquiring because it converts a project-ending discovery into a design constraint about half the time.

장: Y6. From a Paper to a Block, and Back to a Paper
절: Y6.3 Measuring so that the number survives a reviewer
글:
Y6.3 Measuring so that the number survives a reviewer

The four rules below are this repository's response to four specific
 measurements that were reported and were wrong. They are stated as a checklist because
 each failure looked, at the time, like a result.

[Table 424. Four checks before a number is said aloud]
Check | What went wrong without it | How to do it
Did you measure the quantity you defined? | A tool reported the longest path in the whole netlist; the quantity wanted was the longest path around a loop . Different number, same units | Isolate the quantity — cut the loop, build the combinational equivalent, and measure that
Is the operating point healthy? | A residual analysis was run at a point where the bit error rate was 0.49 — the link was not working, so every derived number was noise | Sweep first, find a working point, then measure. Report the point
Is there an independent cross-check? | A reconstruction double-counted a term; the error was invisible until the same quantity was computed a second way | Closed form, a second estimator, or a hand calculation — and print the difference
Have you killed the trivial explanations? | ‘Seven gates, zero mismatch’ — because at that operating point the equalizer taps were near zero and the loop was doing nothing | Write the list of boring reasons the number could look good, then measure each one away

If you cannot do all four, say which one you could
 not do. A number with a stated gap is usable by a reader, who can weigh it. A
 number presented as complete when it is not is a claim the reader cannot calibrate,
 and when it turns out to be wrong it costs more than the information was ever worth.
 This applies with full force inside a company: the colleague reading your slide has no
 way to know which checks you ran unless you say.

Problem. Your simulation shows a 3× improvement. What do you do before telling anyone?
Solution. Assume it is a bug, because at that magnitude it usually is, and spend an hour trying to prove it. Check the baseline actually runs: the commonest cause of a large speed-up is a baseline that is mis-configured, unoptimised, or silently failing, and comparing against a broken baseline is the strawman failure from Y6.1 committed against yourself. Check the units and the normalisation — per operation, per cycle, per joule and per second are four different claims. Check that both sides did the same work: a fast path that skips a case the baseline handles is not faster. Compute the improvement a second way, from first principles, and see whether 3× is even plausible given what changed; if the change removed 20 % of the operations, a 3× speed-up needs an explanation beyond the operation count. Only then look for the mechanism, and when you report it, report the mechanism rather than the multiplier — a number with an explanation survives scrutiny and a number without one does not.

Problem. Should a one-person design house publish at all?
Solution. Yes, and for reasons that are commercial rather than academic. A publication is evidence a customer can check before trusting a supplier they have never heard of, which is the central problem of a new house. It is defensive prior art: published material cannot later be patented against you, which is cheap insurance compared with a patent of your own. It forces the four checks above, because a reviewer will ask, and work that survives review is work you can quote in a datasheet. And it brings the people — collaborators, customers and the occasional acquirer read the literature of their field. The cost is real: a paper is several weeks, and a rejection is several more. The pragmatic compromise many small houses take is an arXiv preprint plus a workshop or industry conference talk, which captures most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost of a top-tier submission, and which is perfectly compatible with holding back the implementation details that are actually the product.

장: Y7. Debug and Bring-Up, With the Arithmetic
절: Y7. Debug and Bring-Up, With the Arithmetic — 들어가며
글:
Y7. Debug and Bring-Up, With the Arithmetic

Bring-up is the phase in which the difference between engineers is
 largest, and most of that difference is method rather than knowledge. The method is
 binary search over hypotheses, executed with discipline, and it can be made
 quantitative: each observation should halve the space of possible causes, and an
 observation that does not is a waste of an afternoon.

장: Y7. Debug and Bring-Up, With the Arithmetic
절: Y7.1 Debugging as information gain
글:
Y7.1 Debugging as information gain

Why the right measurement is the one that splits the space evenly

 | Step | Justification
1 | Let there be N plausible causes, each with prior probability p i . | The hypothesis space after reading the symptom.
2 | A test partitions the space: outcome A is consistent with a subset, outcome B with the rest. | Any observation does this, well or badly.
3 | The information gained is the entropy reduction, maximised when the two subsets have equal probability mass. | Not equal count — equal probability. Splitting off one unlikely cause teaches almost nothing.
4 | k ideal tests reduce N equiprobable causes to N /2 k . | So twenty causes need about five tests, not twenty.
5 | A test whose outcome you can predict has zero information. | If you are confident what will happen, do not run it. This single rule eliminates most wasted bring-up time.

[Table 425. Tests needed under binary search versus one-at-a-time elimination]
Plausible causes | Ideal tests (log 2 ) | One-at-a-time, worst case | One-at-a-time, average | Ideal as % of worst case
4 | 2 | 4 | 2 | 50
8 | 3 | 8 | 4 | 37.5
16 | 4 | 16 | 8 | 25
32 | 5 | 32 | 16 | 15.6
64 | 6 | 64 | 32 | 9.38

A bring-up with 32 plausible causes is five good measurements or thirty-two bad ones. The whole skill is in choosing tests that split the space rather than tests that confirm a favourite hypothesis.

The favourite-hypothesis trap has a specific
 signature. An engineer who believes the problem is in module X runs tests that
 would be consistent with X, gets results consistent with X, and becomes more
 confident — while every one of those tests was also consistent with Y and Z.
 The discipline that prevents it is to write down what each outcome would rule
 out before running the test. If the answer is ‘nothing, either way’,
 the test is confirmation and not evidence. This is the same rule as the verification
 one in Part X8: a test that no broken implementation would fail is not a
 test.

장: Y7. Debug and Bring-Up, With the Arithmetic
절: Y7.2 The bring-up sequence, in dependency order
글:
Y7.2 The bring-up sequence, in dependency order

[Table 426. Bring up in this order, because each step depends on the previous]
Step | Check | If it fails
1. Power | Every rail at the right voltage, in the right sequence, with the ripple in spec | Nothing above this means anything. Sequence violations can damage parts
2. Clocks | Every clock present, at the right frequency, with acceptable jitter | Measure at the die if possible; a clock present at the oscillator is not a clock present at the block
3. Reset | Asserted long enough, released cleanly and synchronously | The most common silent failure — a block that half-resets produces a state that no simulation ever visited
4. Register access | Read an ID register; write and read back a scratch register | If this fails, everything above is suspect; if it works, the bus, clock, reset and power are all proven at once
5. Static configuration | Program the block; read back every register | Read-back mismatch localises to the register file immediately
6. Loopback | Internal loopback first, then external | Separates the block from the channel — the single most valuable feature to design in
7. One transaction | One packet, one frame, one transfer | Debuggable; a stream is not
8. Line rate | Continuous traffic | Reveals everything the single transaction hid: buffering, back pressure, rate adaptation, alignment
9. Corner conditions | Temperature, voltage, rate extremes | Where the margin problems live

Step 4 is worth more than its position suggests.
 A readable identification register with a known constant value proves, in one
 transaction, that the supply is up, the clock is running, the reset released, the bus
 is connected, the address decode is right and the endianness matches. There is no
 other single test with that much power, and providing one costs a design a dozen
 gates. An IP block without an ID register and a scratch register is harder to bring
 up by a factor that is hard to overstate, and their absence is a reasonable reason
 for a customer to choose a competitor.

Worked example 68. Why internal loopback pays for itself in one bring-up

Given. A SerDes-attached block fails to pass traffic. Without loopback there are, say, 24 plausible causes spanning the transmitter, the channel, the connector, the far end and the receiver. Internal loopback splits them into 'inside the chip' and 'outside'.

Method. Apply the information argument: count the tests needed with and without the feature, at roughly two hours per test including setup.

Plausible causes | 24
Ideal tests without loopback | 5
Causes remaining after a loopback result | 12
Ideal tests after loopback | 5
Hours saved if each test costs 2 h | 0
But: tests without loopback are not even splits | this is the real saving
Realistic sequence without loopback | 10–15 tests, several requiring board rework
Realistic sequence with loopback | 4–6 tests, none requiring rework

How this is got wrong. By counting only the ideal test count, which barely changes. The value of loopback is not that it reduces log2N by one; it is that without it, no available test splits the space evenly — every measurement is at one end of the chain and rules out little. A feature that creates an even split where none existed is worth far more than its effect on the count suggests. The same argument justifies per-stage error counters, snapshot registers and a pattern generator: each one manufactures a clean partition of the hypothesis space.

장: Y7. Debug and Bring-Up, With the Arithmetic
절: Y7.3 Reading a symptom
글:
Y7.3 Reading a symptom

[Table 427. Symptom to first hypothesis]
Symptom | Most likely class | The distinguishing test
Works at low rate, fails at high rate | Timing or bandwidth | Vary the rate and find the exact threshold; a sharp threshold means timing, a gradual one means buffering
Fails after a fixed time, always the same | A counter wrapping, or a buffer filling | Compute what wraps in that time at that rate — the arithmetic usually names the register
Fails randomly, low rate of failure | Metastability, marginal timing, or a rare data pattern | Vary temperature and voltage: timing moves, a data pattern does not
Works in simulation, fails in silicon | Something not modelled | Reset, clock, power, X-propagation, or an unmodelled analogue behaviour. List what the simulation did not contain
Fails only with a specific partner | Interoperability | Capture the link and compare against the specification, not against your other partner
First transaction after idle fails | A power or clock state exit | Disable the low-power state and see if it disappears
Corrupt data with a regular period | Rate mismatch or an alignment marker | Compute the period in symbols and compare with the marker interval

Problem. A link passes traffic for exactly 71 minutes and then drops a frame, reliably. What wraps in 71 minutes?
Solution. Do the arithmetic rather than guessing. At 1 Gbit/s and 8 bits per byte a byte counter increments 125 million times a second; 71 minutes is about 4260 s, giving roughly 5.3×1011 bytes — close to 239. At a 156.25 MHz clock, 4260 s is about 6.7×1011 cycles, near 239.3. So look for a counter of about 39 or 40 bits — a 40-bit statistics counter, or a timestamp. The technique generalises: convert the failure period into counts of every periodic event in the system and see which lands on a power of two. It also works for suspiciously round numbers in other bases: 71 minutes is not obviously special, which is exactly why the conversion is necessary. A failure at 49.7 days would be a 32-bit millisecond counter and is recognisable on sight; the same reasoning found it.

Problem. Silicon fails a case that simulation passes. Where do you look first, and what does that tell you about your verification plan?
Solution. Look at the list of things the simulation did not model, because that is where the answer is by definition. The usual entries: reset — simulation often starts from an initialised state that silicon never has, so an uninitialised register that simulation reads as a known value reads as garbage in silicon; X-propagation — a simulator's optimistic X handling can let an unknown resolve to a definite value through a multiplexer, hiding exactly this class of bug, which is why X-pessimistic or four-state gate-level simulation exists; clock and power sequencing, rarely modelled at all; analogue behaviour, from supply droop to the settling of an off-chip device; and real timing, since RTL simulation is untimed. What this says about the plan is concrete: each of these has a known mitigation — randomised reset values, X-pessimistic simulation, gate-level simulation with back-annotated timing, and a modelled power sequence — and the plan should name which ones it uses and which it consciously declines. A plan that does not mention them has not declined them; it has forgotten them, and the difference shows up here.

장: Y8. The One-Person Path from Model to Product
절: Y8. The One-Person Path from Model to Product — 들어가며
글:
Y8. The One-Person Path from Model to Product

The three-team structure of a large company — design, modelling,
 verification — exists because independence catches bugs. A single engineer
 cannot have organisational independence, so it has to be manufactured by process: the
 golden model is written before the RTL, from the specification rather than from the
 design, and it is never modified to agree with the RTL. This part is the procedure,
 with the realistic schedule and the places it goes wrong.

[그림] Figure 53. The solo flow. The dashed line is the one that matters: the golden model is the reference for every stage below it, which is what replaces organisational independence.

장: Y8. The One-Person Path from Model to Product
절: Y8.1 The rule that replaces a second engineer
글:
Y8.1 The rule that replaces a second engineer

[Table 428. How to be your own independent checker]
Rule | Why | What breaks without it
Write the model before the RTL | The model then encodes your reading of the specification, not your design | The model inherits the design's misunderstanding and certifies it
Never edit the model to match the RTL | A disagreement is information; resolving it by editing destroys the information | The commonest single failure of solo verification — and it feels productive while you do it
Resolve every disagreement by returning to the specification | One of the two is wrong and the text says which | You pick the one that is less work to change
Use a third source where one exists | zlib, a reference implementation, a vendor model, published vectors | Two of your own artefacts agreeing proves only that you are consistent
Write the test before the fix | Otherwise the fix is unverified and may be wrong | Regressions reappear
Record why each parameter has its value | You will not remember in six months, and a customer will ask | Undocumented constants become unchangeable

‘I will fix the model later’ is the
 moment a solo project loses its verification. When the RTL and the model disagree
 and the deadline is close, editing the model makes the test pass in minutes and
 investigating takes hours. Every such edit removes one independent check permanently,
 and they are not recoverable later because nobody remembers which ones were principled.
 The practical defence is mechanical: keep the model in a separate commit history
 and require a written reason in the commit message for any change to it after the RTL
 exists. The friction is the point.

장: Y8. The One-Person Path from Model to Product
절: Y8.2 A realistic schedule, with the failure points marked
글:
Y8.2 A realistic schedule, with the failure points marked

[Table 429. A 39-week single-engineer plan for a medium protocol block]
Stage | Weeks | Cumulative | Where it goes wrong
Specification study and requirements | 3 | 3 | Under-reading the standard; the parameters you assume are the ones that fail interoperability
Golden model in C++ or Python | 3 | 6 | Modelling what you intend to build rather than what the spec says
Architecture study and word lengths | 2 | 8 | Choosing uniform word lengths — Part X1's sweep exists for this
RTL, first pass | 5 | 13 | Writing before the architecture is settled
Testbench and checkers | 4 | 17 | Checkers that cannot fail; run mutation testing here
Random and directed regression | 5 | 22 | Believing a flat find rate; Part X8's recovery test
Lint, CDC, synthesis | 2 | 24 | Discovering a CDC problem that needs an architecture change
Timing closure at target | 2 | 26 | Finding that the target was never achievable — check in week 2, not week 24
FPGA prototype and bring-up | 4 | 30 | No loopback or ID register — Part Y7
Documentation and packaging | 3 | 33 | Leaving it to the end, when the details are forgotten
Buffer for the unforeseen | 6 | 39 | Omitting it

The buffer is 15 % of the total and it is the row most often deleted by someone who wants the number smaller. A plan without a buffer is not an optimistic plan, it is a plan that has already failed, because the unforeseen is the only certainty in the list.

Worked example 69. What the schedule implies about what you can build

Given. 39 weeks for one block, a working year of 46 weeks, and a need to spend some of it selling and supporting.

Method. Compute how many blocks a single engineer can produce and what that means for the product strategy.

Weeks per block | 39
Working weeks per year | 46
Weeks available for sales and support | 7
Blocks per year | 1.18
Blocks in three years, ignoring support growth | 3.54
With support at 20 % from year two | 3.07
Implication | a family of related blocks, not unrelated ones

How this is got wrong. By planning a catalogue. At roughly one block a year, a catalogue of unrelated blocks takes a decade and each one is supported alone. The strategy that fits the arithmetic is a family: one architecture parameterised across a range — the same FEC core at three code rates, the same MAC at three line rates — where the second member costs perhaps a quarter of the first and shares its verification environment, its documentation structure and its support material. Choose the first block for the family it opens, not for its own merits.

장: Y8. The One-Person Path from Model to Product
절: Y8.3 What to build first
글:
Y8.3 What to build first

[Table 430. Criteria for a first block, weighted for a house with no reputation]
Criterion | Why it matters more than it looks | Good sign
A specification you can obtain | A block you cannot legally read the standard for cannot be built | Open standard, or a membership you can afford
A checkable golden model | Without an independent reference, solo verification is much weaker | Published test vectors, or an open reference implementation
Soft, not hard | A hard macro needs analogue skills and foundry access | The block is RTL from end to end
Changing standard | Incumbents' blocks go stale; a new revision resets the field | A draft is in ballot now
Few credible suppliers | You can win | Searching finds two vendors, not twenty
Adjacent to a family | Second and third members are cheap | The same core serves several rates or profiles
A customer you can name | Speculative IP is how houses die | Someone has said they would evaluate it

Applying these criteria is what selected this book's
 own subject. The PCS and FEC sublayer of a high-speed Ethernet link scores on
 every row: the sublayer is soft RTL between two hard boundaries; Reed–Solomon
 has an independent reference in any number of open implementations and a golden model
 that can be verified by its algebraic properties rather than by sample values; the
 802.3dj revision is in progress, which resets the incumbents; the supplier list is
 short; and the family extends naturally across code rates and generations. The row
 that is not yet satisfied is the last one, and this book says so rather than
 quietly omitting it — a named first customer is the thing that converts the
 other six rows from an argument into a business.

Problem. You have 39 weeks and no income. What is the order of operations that keeps you solvent?
Solution. Invert the order the technical plan suggests. Sell services first: contract verification, modelling or integration work pays weekly and, crucially, puts you in front of the customers who will later buy the block — the conversations are the market research. Build the golden model and the architecture study in the gaps, because they are the parts that need thinking rather than long uninterrupted stretches, and because they are what you show a prospective customer to prove you understand the problem. Do the RTL and verification in a funded block — ideally funded by a customer who wants the first instance and will accept that you retain the rights, which is a negotiation worth having explicitly and early. Do not build speculatively for 39 weeks on savings: the failure mode is not that the block is bad, it is that you run out of runway three weeks before the first sale, and at that point the asset is worth nothing to you and a great deal to whoever buys it from the liquidator.

장: Y9. Standards, Compliance and Interoperability
절: Y9. Standards, Compliance and Interoperability — 들어가며
글:
Y9. Standards, Compliance and Interoperability

A protocol block is worth what it can be shown to interoperate with.
 That showing is a separate activity from verification, with its own vocabulary, its
 own costs and its own failure modes, and it is the part of the work that first-time
 vendors most consistently under-budget. This part lays it out.

장: Y9. Standards, Compliance and Interoperability
절: Y9.1 Three different things called ‘testing’
글:
Y9.1 Three different things called ‘testing’

[Table 431. What each activity proves and what it does not]
Activity | Question answered | Who runs it | What it misses
Verification | Does the block do what I specified? | You | Whether your reading of the standard is right
Conformance | Does the block do what the standard says? | You, or a test house, against a published test suite | Whether real partners interoperate — conformant implementations can still fail together
Interoperability | Does it work with this specific partner? | A plugfest, or a lab with partner equipment | Partners not present; the next revision
Certification | Will the body let me use the logo? | An accredited laboratory | Everything above — it is a process outcome, not a technical one

Two conformant implementations can fail to
 interoperate, and the reason is structural rather than anyone's fault. Standards
 contain optional features, permitted ranges and ambiguous sentences. If your block
 implements an option and the partner does not, both conform and neither works with the
 other unless the negotiation that selects it is itself implemented correctly on both
 sides — and negotiation code is under-tested everywhere, because testing it
 requires a partner that behaves differently from you. The practical consequence is
 that the negotiation and fallback paths deserve more verification effort than the
 steady-state datapath, which is the opposite of where effort naturally goes.
 In every protocol in this book, the bugs found at plugfests are concentrated in link
 training, capability exchange and error recovery.

장: Y9. Standards, Compliance and Interoperability
절: Y9.2 The cost of a standard, itemised
글:
Y9.2 The cost of a standard, itemised

[Table 432. What conformance costs before any revenue arrives]
Item | Order of magnitude | Note
The specification document | $0–$5,000 per document | Some are free (IETF); most industry standards are not
Body membership | $5,000–$50,000+ per year | Often required to obtain drafts, to attend, or to use the name
Test suite or test equipment | $10,000–$200,000+ | Protocol analysers and compliance fixtures; rentable
Plugfest attendance | $2,000–$10,000 per event plus travel | The highest-value line in this table per dollar
Accredited laboratory testing | $10,000–$100,000 per campaign | Where a logo is required
Engineering time to fix what it finds | 4–12 weeks | The line that is always omitted from the budget

Ranges, not quotations — the actual figures depend on the body and the year, and this repository has not obtained current price lists. The purpose of the table is to prevent the commonest planning error, which is budgeting zero for all six rows.

Worked example 70. Whether to certify at all

Given. A block that could be sold with or without a logo. Certification costs $60 000 and eight weeks. Without it you expect 4 customers over three years at $80 000; with it you expect 7, and you can charge $95 000 because the logo removes a risk from the buyer's evaluation.

Method. Compute both revenues net of cost and time. Then note the factor the arithmetic does not contain.

Revenue without certification | 320,000 USD
Revenue with certification | 665,000 USD
Certification cost | 60,000 USD
Eight weeks of engineering at $120k/yr | 18462 USD
Net with certification | 5.8654×10 5  USD
Net without | 320,000 USD
Difference | 2.6654×10 5  USD

How this is got wrong. By treating the customer counts as data. They are forecasts, and the forecast with certification is the one you have least evidence for, since it is the counterfactual. The robust way to use this calculation is not to trust its output but to find the break-even customer count and ask whether it is plausible: here certification pays if it brings even one additional customer at the higher price. Framed that way the decision is usually easy, and the arithmetic has done its job by converting an argument about strategy into a question about one number.

장: Y9. Standards, Compliance and Interoperability
절: Y9.3 Getting value from a plugfest
글:
Y9.3 Getting value from a plugfest

[Table 433. Before, during and after]
Phase | Do | Do not
Weeks before | Test against every partner implementation you can obtain, including open-source ones; exercise every negotiation path | Arrive to discover a problem you could have found at home
Bring | Two of everything, a logic analyser or protocol analyser, a way to rebuild and reload on site, and a colleague if possible | Rely on borrowing; the other vendors are busy
Instrument | Counters, snapshot registers, and a way to capture the first failing exchange | Debug by re-running and watching
Record | Every partner, every configuration, every result — including the ones that worked | Remember it afterwards; you will not
When something fails | Determine which side deviates from the text before discussing it | Assert that the partner is wrong — roughly half the time it is you
After | Turn every failure into a regression test; publish an interoperability list | Fix the symptom and move on

The interoperability list is a sales document as much
 as an engineering one. ‘Tested against these seven implementations, at these
 configurations, on these dates’ answers the question a buyer cannot otherwise
 answer about a supplier they do not know, and it answers it with something checkable.
 It also has a defensive function: when a customer reports an interoperability failure
 with an eighth partner, the list makes it immediately clear that this is new
 territory rather than a regression, which changes the conversation entirely. Keep
 it current and date every row; a list without dates is read as a list of claims
 rather than of tests.

Problem. A partner at a plugfest insists your implementation is wrong. You believe theirs is. How do you proceed?
Solution. Stop arguing and go to the text, together. Find the clause, read it aloud, and establish what each implementation does at that point in the exchange with a capture rather than with an assertion. Three outcomes follow and all three are useful. The text is clear and you are wrong: fix it, and you have discovered a real bug cheaply. The text is clear and they are wrong: show them, courteously, and consider whether to interoperate with their behaviour anyway — if they ship in volume, your customers will meet them, and a conformant block that fails against a popular partner is a commercial problem whoever is right. The text is ambiguous: this is the most valuable outcome, because it means everyone has the problem. Raise it with the working group; a clarification with your name on it is reputation, and it is one of the few ways a small house becomes visible to the people who buy. In all three cases the conduct matters more than the verdict: plugfests are small worlds and the engineer across the table is a future customer, partner or employer.

Problem. Why should a soft-IP vendor care about compliance at all, when the customer's chip is what gets certified?
Solution. Because the customer's certification failure becomes your problem regardless of whose name is on the certificate. Practically, three things follow. Your block must be testable in their chip: the compliance tests require modes — loopback, pattern generation, error injection, counter read-out — that must exist in the RTL and be reachable from their software, and adding them late is expensive. You must supply the evidence they will be asked for: which clauses your block implements, which options, which are the customer's responsibility. And you should have run what you can run yourself, because a block that has never seen a compliance suite will fail one, and it is far cheaper to fail it in your lab than in theirs. A vendor who arrives with a clause-by-clause implementation statement and their own test results is selling a lower-risk product, and that is precisely what the premium in protocol IP is paid for.

Sub-block | Stimulus that must be in the set | Why
Syndrome | Zero errors; 1 error; exactly t =15; t +1; all-zero codeword; all-ones | Zero errors must not pass as success — rs.측정() refuses to report a pass from a zero-error trial

Worked example 71. What the agent can check that a human review cannot

Given. RS(544,514) over GF(2^10), t=15. The decoder must correct every pattern of up to 15 symbol errors and must not silently miscorrect beyond.

Method. Count the patterns. Then note which of the two properties is checkable by sampling and which is not.

Error positions of weight 15 | C(544,15) ≈ 10 29
Magnitudes per position | 1,023
Total patterns | astronomically many
What sampling establishes | a bound on the failure rate, not correctness
What the algebra guarantees | all patterns of weight ≤ t , by the code's minimum distance
So the RTL must be checked against | the model, not the space
And the model against | the algebra — which tests/test_rs.py does by property, not by sample

How this is got wrong. By trying to verify the RTL directly against the specification's guarantee. The guarantee is over a space nobody can enumerate; what is checkable is agreement with a model whose own correctness rests on properties that are checkable. This two-level structure is why the golden model must be verified by properties rather than by vectors — and it is exactly what this repository's test_rs.py does when it breaks the syndrome computation and asserts the measurement notices.

절: Z10.3 The three unconfirmed constants, and the plan around them
