Z10.3 The three unconfirmed constants, and the plan around them

[Table 436. What is not known, and what it blocks]
Unknown | Fixed by | Blocks | Work that proceeds anyway
Field polynomial | IEEE 802.3 Clause 91 | Interoperability — not correctness | Everything. It is a parameter; the RTL takes it as one
First consecutive root fcr | Same clause | Interoperability | Same — a parameter
Symbol bit order | Same clause | The byte/symbol packing at the boundary | The core; only the top-level packer depends on it

Parameterising is not a substitute for reading the
 clause, and the plan should not pretend otherwise. A parameterised decoder is
 correct for whatever parameters it is given and interoperable with nothing until the
 parameters are right. What parameterising buys is that the unknown stays
 visible — a hard-coded constant dissolves into an assumption nobody
 questions, and Part Y15's scorecard would quietly lose its most important row.
 The first item in the plan remains: obtain the document. Everything else is
 work that can proceed in parallel, and none of it is work that can substitute.

Problem. Sixteen weeks of RTL and the specification is still unobtainable. Do you build it anyway?
Solution. Build the parts that are parameter-independent and stop before the parts that are not, and be explicit with yourself about which is which. The field arithmetic, the Berlekamp–Massey iteration, the Chien search structure and the Forney computation are all generic — they are correct for any primitive polynomial and any first root, and building them is not speculative. The top-level packing, the interoperability claim and the datasheet are parameter-dependent and should not be written. What you must not do is pick a plausible value and proceed as though it were confirmed, because that converts a known unknown into an unknown one, and the failure surfaces at a plugfest in front of the people you most want to impress. The strategic answer, though, is to reconsider the product. Part Z5's scorecard weights specification availability at 3 precisely so that this situation is visible before sixteen weeks are spent, and its winner — a post-quantum core whose standard, reference implementation and test vectors are all public — exists because that row was weighted honestly. A block you cannot obtain the specification for is not a cheaper project; it is a different one.

장: Z11. Writing the AXI Wrapper a Customer Will Accept
절: Z11. Writing the AXI Wrapper a Customer Will Accept — 들어가며
글:
Z11. Writing the AXI Wrapper a Customer Will Accept

Almost every block a design house sells is bought as an AXI
 peripheral, and almost every integration complaint is about the wrapper rather than
 the core. This part is the wrapper — what it must do, what it must not do, and
 the specific mistakes that cost a week at the customer's end.

[그림] Figure 54. The separation that makes a core sellable more than once.

장: Z11. Writing the AXI Wrapper a Customer Will Accept
절: Z11.1 Keep the protocol out of the core
글:
Z11.1 Keep the protocol out of the core

Why the boundary pays for itself three times

 | Step | Justification
1 | A core that consumes and produces values, with a simple ready/valid or an enable, has no protocol in it. | It can be tested against the golden model directly — Part Z1's arrangement.
2 | The wrapper translates AXI into that. | And it is the same wrapper for every core you build.
3 | First payment: verification. The core is verified against the model; the wrapper is verified against the protocol. | Two small problems instead of one large one, and the protocol half is reusable.
4 | Second payment: the customer. Some want AXI-Stream, some AXI4, some a bare FIFO, some APB for configuration only. | A core with the protocol baked in has to be rewritten for each.
5 | Third payment: the standard changes and the core does not. | AMBA revisions, a move to CHI, a customer's proprietary fabric — all wrapper work.
6 | The cost is one extra level of hierarchy and a handful of registers. | Which Part X37's skid-buffer argument says you wanted anyway , because registering the boundary is what keeps your timing independent of their floorplan.

[Table 437. What belongs on each side of the line]
Belongs in the wrapper | Belongs in the core
AXI channels and their handshakes | The algorithm
Burst handling, ID management, ordering | Word lengths and pipelining
The register file (generated — Part Z4) | Nothing about registers — it takes parameters and strobes
Clock domain crossing, if the customer's is different | One clock; no assumptions about its rate
Error responses (SLVERR, DECERR) | An error flag , not a bus code
Back pressure and buffering | A stall input it honours — nothing more
Low-power and isolation (Part X43) | A clock enable

장: Z11. Writing the AXI Wrapper a Customer Will Accept
절: Z11.2 The wrapper mistakes that cost a week
글:
Z11.2 The wrapper mistakes that cost a week

[Table 438. Eight wrapper defects, what each looks like, and the fix]
Mistake | Symptom | Fix
s_ready depends combinationally on s_valid | Deadlock or oscillation when the partner does the same | Register one side; a skid buffer costs two entries and one cycle
No skid buffer, both directions registered | Throughput halves and functional tests still pass | Part X37's table — measure transfers per cycle, not correctness
Read and write share an internal queue | Deadlock in the customer's system, never in yours | Part X11 — keep the AXI channels independent all the way in
Bursts allowed to cross a 4 kB boundary | Protocol violation the interconnect may not check | Split in the wrapper; it is a comparison and an adder
WSTRB ignored | Neighbouring bytes corrupted on a narrow write | Honour it, or declare the register file 32-bit-only in the guide
Write response returned before the write is visible | A driver's read-after-write returns stale data | Define and document the visibility point
Reset not synchronised per domain | One boot in a thousand (Part X42) | Two flops per domain; the constraint shipped with the block
Register map hand-written into the wrapper | Diverges from the header and the datasheet | Generate it — Part Z4

Six of the eight pass a functional test. They are found at integration, at line rate, or in the customer's system — which is why the release gate of Part Z3 checks throughput and why the testbench must apply randomised back pressure rather than accepting everything.

Worked example 72. Proving the wrapper does not halve your throughput

Given. An AXI-Stream wrapper around a core that accepts one word per cycle. The customer will measure sustained throughput with back pressure applied at random.

Method. State the bound, measure it, and put the measurement in the datasheet — the same three steps the agent's throughput check performs.

Ideal | 1 word/cycle
With random back pressure at 50 % | 0.5 word/cycle — expected
With a missing skid buffer | 0.25 — and every value is still correct
What a value-only regression says | pass
What the throughput check says | cycles > bound → red
Where the bound comes from | measured on the clean block over several seeds
This repository's example | crc32_stream: 2.18 clean vs 3.16 broken cycles/byte, bound 2.6

How this is got wrong. By declaring a bound from the architecture rather than from a measurement. The architectural ideal is one word per cycle and no real testbench achieves it, so a bound set from the ideal never fires and a bound set by guessing is either useless or a false alarm. Measure the clean block on several seeds, check the spread is small, and set the bound just above it — which in this repository's case caught a mutation that a value-only suite had missed.

장: Z11. Writing the AXI Wrapper a Customer Will Accept
절: Z11.3 What ships with the wrapper
글:
Z11.3 What ships with the wrapper

[Table 439. The wrapper's own deliverables]
Item | Why the customer needs it
The SDC constraints for the boundary | Your timing claim is meaningless without them — Part X14
CDC constraints, if the block crosses domains | Their tool will flag the crossing and stop; the waiver must come from you
Protocol assertions (SVA) on the AXI interfaces | They can bind them in their environment and see your block behaving
A bus functional model or a trivial testbench | So they can run it in ten minutes, which is when they decide
The register map in IP-XACT | Automated integration
A reference integration: your block plus a stub master | Removes the whole class of ‘it does not work’ reports where the wiring was wrong

The reference integration is the item with the best
 return and the one most often left out. It is an hour's work: your block, a
 minimal master that writes the registers and streams some data, and a script that runs
 it. What it removes is the first two days of every customer's evaluation, during
 which they are wiring your block up for the first time and every problem looks like
 your problem. A customer who runs your reference in ten minutes and sees traffic
 move has formed an opinion about your competence before reading the
 datasheet, and that opinion is expensive to change later in either
 direction.

Problem. The customer's interconnect is CHI, not AXI. How much work is that?
Solution. Ask first whether it has to be, because the answer is often no. Most CHI systems provide AXI bridges for peripherals, and a block that does not need coherence has no reason to speak CHI — so the first move is to establish whether the block is a coherent agent or a device behind a bridge, and for a datapath accelerator it is almost always the latter. If it genuinely must be a coherent agent, the work is substantial and is not a wrapper change: CHI is a coherence protocol with a snoop interface, ordering rules and a state machine, and Part X28's verification argument applies — the state space is the kind that needs formal methods, and the effort is comparable to the core itself. For a one-person house that is a reason to decline or to scope it as a separate project, not a line item in a wrapper quote. The middle case worth naming: some blocks need only IO-coherence, where the block's accesses snoop the host caches but nothing snoops the block. That is an interconnect feature, not a block feature, and it costs you nothing — which is worth knowing so you do not quote for work the customer's fabric already does.

장: Z12. Writing the Documents
절: Z12. Writing the Documents — 들어가며
글:
Z12. Writing the Documents

Documentation is where a one-person house is at its biggest
 disadvantage and, unusually, where it can be at its best: a document written by the
 person who made the decisions is better than one written by a technical writer
 three months later. This part is the structure, the rules, and what this repository's
 own documents look like.

장: Z12. Writing the Documents
절: Z12.1 Three documents, three readers
글:
Z12.1 Three documents, three readers

[Table 440. Who reads each one, and what they are deciding]
Document | Reader | The decision they are making | Fails when
Datasheet | An evaluator, before buying | Does this block do what we need, at the rate we need? | Numbers without conditions; claims without evidence
Integration guide | An engineer, after buying | How do I wire this in without calling them? | It documents the block and not the integration
Known issues | Both | Can I trust this supplier? | It is absent, or it says ‘none’

The known-issue list is read as a character reference
 and should be written as one. An evaluator has seen datasheets before and knows
 every block has limitations; what varies is whether the supplier says so. A list with
 eight dated entries, each with impact, workaround and status, says that someone has
 thought about the failure modes and is willing to be held to them. An absent list says
 either that nobody looked or that somebody decided not to tell you, and the evaluator
 cannot tell which — so they assume the worse one. This is the cheapest
 credibility available to a supplier nobody has heard of, and it costs an
 afternoon.

장: Z12. Writing the Documents
절: Z12.2 The rules that make the numbers usable
글:
Z12.2 The rules that make the numbers usable

[Table 441. Six rules, each with the version that fails it]
Rule | Good | Bad | Why
Every number carries its conditions | ‘2.18 cycles/byte, random back pressure, seeds 1/7/99’ | ‘1 byte per cycle’ | A number without conditions cannot be reproduced or disputed
Name the tool, the library and the version | ‘208 cells, yosys 0.33, open library’ | ‘~2 kGE’ | Part Y14 — the honest smaller claim beats the unattributed larger one
Say what was not measured | ‘Area in your process: not measured. Scripts included’ | Silence | Silence is read as a claim
Separate measured from derived | ‘measured 2.18; bound set at 2.6’ | ‘2.6 cycles/byte’ | A bound and a measurement are different facts
Give the reproduction command | bash edu/house/release.sh crc32_stream | — | This is what turns claims into evidence
Date everything | ‘2026-09-19, v1.0’ | undated | An undated known-issue list is a list of excuses

All six are about the reader's ability to check you, which is the only thing that distinguishes a datasheet from marketing. A vendor who makes checking easy is making a bet that the numbers hold, and evaluators read that bet correctly.

[Table 442. This repository's own documents, counted at build time]
File | Reader | Lines | Table cells | Measured-value mentions | Links to the issue list
DATASHEET.md | evaluator | 72 | 100 | 3 | yes
INTEGRATION.md | integrator | 62 | 0 | 0 | —
KNOWN_ISSUES.md | both | 27 | 80 | 0 | yes

Counted by reading the files as this page rendered. The measured-value column is the one to watch: a datasheet whose count is zero is a list of intentions.

장: Z12. Writing the Documents
절: Z12.3 The datasheet, section by section
글:
Z12.3 The datasheet, section by section

[Table 443. What each section must answer]
Section | The question | The commonest omission
1. What it is | Does this solve my problem? | Naming the standard but not the profile or the options
2. Interface | Can I connect it? | The handshake rules — which side may depend on which
3. Performance | Is it fast enough? | The conditions the number was measured under
4. Area and frequency | Does it fit? | Either silence, or an FPGA number presented as an ASIC one
5. Verification | Can I trust it? | Evidence that the tests bite — the mutation score
6. Configuration | Can I tune it? | Parameters listed without their legal ranges or their interactions
7. Known issues | What will bite me? | The whole section
8. Deliverables | What do I get? | Whether the testbench and scripts are included

Worked example 73. How long the documents take if written weekly

Given. A 39-week block. Documentation written at the end, versus twenty minutes at the end of each week.

Method. Compare the totals, and then the quality, which is the part that does not appear in the total.

Written at the end | 1–2 weeks solid
Written weekly | 13 hours total
Ratio | about 3× cheaper
And the quality difference | weekly notes record why ; end-of-project notes record what
What is lost by waiting | the reason a constant has its value, the corner that forced a structure, the thing that nearly went wrong
Who needs the why | the customer's integrator, and you in a year

How this is got wrong. By treating documentation as transcription. It is not — it is the record of decisions, and decisions are only recoverable while they are fresh. The three-times cost difference is real and is the smaller of the two effects; the larger one is that a document written at the end cannot contain the information that makes it worth reading. Part Z2 puts this in the Friday slot for exactly this reason, and it is the slot that disappears first.

Problem. Your block has 40 configuration parameters. How do you document them without writing 40 pages?
Solution. Generate the list and write prose only about the interactions, because the list is mechanical and the interactions are not. Generated: name, type, legal range, default, and what it affects — from the same source that produces the RTL parameters, exactly as Part Z4's register map is generated. That is a table nobody writes and nobody can get out of sync. Written by hand: the three or four combinations that matter — which parameters must move together, which ones are ignored when another is set, which ones change the area or the latency and by roughly how much. And a short list of the two or three configurations you have actually verified and synthesised, named, with their numbers. That last item is the honest core of it: 40 independent parameters is 240 configurations and you have verified a handful, so say which handful and state the covering argument for the rest (Part X19's pairwise criterion is the standard one). A customer choosing an unverified combination should know that is what they are doing, and a supplier who tells them is worth more than one who implies all 240 were tested.

장: Z13. Week One
절: Z13. Week One — 들어가며
글:
Z13. Week One

This book is long and the first Monday is short. This part is what to
 do in the first five days if the aim is a two-member team producing sellable IP, in
 an order that leaves something working at the end of each one. Everything it names
 exists in this repository and can be copied.

장: Z13. Week One
절: Z13.1 The five days
글:
Z13.1 The five days

[Table 444. Week one]
Day | Goal | What you do | Why this and not something else
Monday | Get the flow running | Install iverilog, verilator, yosys, Python. Clone this repository. Run bash edu/house/release.sh gf_mul and watch it pass. | You now have a working gate on somebody else's block , which is the fastest way to see what one looks like
Tuesday | Make it your block | Copy edu/agent/blocks/gf_mul . Replace the RTL with the smallest thing you actually want to build. Write block.py 's 자극() against a golden model you did not write. | The golden model must be independent — a library, a reference implementation, the standard's vectors
Wednesday | Make the checks bite | Run mutscore.py . Read every escape. Fix the stimulus until the score is above 90 % with every remaining escape judged in writing. | This is the day that teaches the most , and it is the day this repository's register file went from 58 % to 100 % and surfaced two real bugs
Thursday | Declare a bound | Measure the clean block's cycles over several seeds. Declare 성능한계() just above the spread. Break the block so it is only slower and confirm the gate catches it. | A value-only suite cannot see a block getting slower
Friday | Write the three documents and run the gate | Datasheet, integration guide, known issues — short, with the numbers you measured this week and their conditions. Then release.sh and read what it says. | It will say you cannot sell it yet, and it will say exactly why

No architecture, no algorithm, no big block. The week builds the apparatus; the apparatus is what makes every later week cheap. A week spent the other way round produces a nicer block and no way to know whether it works.

The instinct is to start with the interesting
 block. It is the reason to be doing this at all, and it is the wrong first week:
 a large block with no gate is a large block you cannot make claims about, and the
 gate is far easier to build against something trivial. The 30-line GF multiplier
 in this repository exists for exactly that reason — it is small enough that
 every part of the apparatus can be seen working, and the apparatus transfers
 unchanged to a block a hundred times larger.

장: Z13. Week One
절: Z13.2 What each day leaves behind
글:
Z13.2 What each day leaves behind

[Table 445. The artefacts, and what each proves]
After | You have | You can say
Monday | A green gate on a known-good block | ‘my flow works’ — which you could not say before
Tuesday | Your RTL compared against an independent model | ‘it agrees with X on n cases’
Wednesday | A mutation score with judged escapes | ‘the suite catches k  % of injected defects, and here are the ones it does not and why’
Thursday | A measured throughput bound that fires | ‘it sustains x , and the gate proves it has not regressed’
Friday | Three documents and a gate report | ‘here is what is done, here is what is not’

Worked example 74. What the first week costs and what it saves

Given. Five days building apparatus instead of five days building the block.

Method. Count what the apparatus does over the following months, using this book's own measurements.

Cost | 5 days
Nightly regression thereafter | free
Bugs the mutation score surfaced here in one afternoon | 2
Where those bugs would otherwise have been found | the customer's driver
Cost of a bug found by a customer (Part X8) | 10 3 –10 4 × a specification-stage fix
Break-even | the first real bug
Additional return | every block after this one starts on Tuesday

How this is got wrong. By counting the week as lost time. It is the only week whose output is reusable without modification across every block the house will ever build, and the ratio in the fifth row means it pays for itself the first time the gate catches something. The honest caution is that it does not feel like progress, which is why it is worth deciding in advance to spend it.

장: Z13. Week One
절: Z13.3 Where to go next in this book
글:
Z13.3 Where to go next in this book

[Table 446. Reading order after week one]
If you are | Read | Because
Choosing what to build | Part Z5, then Part Y6 | Scorecard first, then the prior-art discipline that stops you rebuilding something
Writing the golden model | Parts X1 and Y11 | Fixed point is most of the work and independence is the whole point
Choosing an architecture | Parts X2, X6, X13 | Timing budget, memory-versus-arithmetic, the roofline
Stuck on verification | Parts X8, X33, Z6 | Coverage arithmetic, where formal helps, what the agent cannot do
Getting it to close timing | Parts X2, X14, X34 | The budget, the physical consequences, what synthesis can and cannot fix
Preparing to sell | Parts Z3, Z4, Y5, Z12 | The bar, the pack, the commercial terms, the documents
Talking to a customer | Parts Y5, Y9, Z8 | Scoping, compliance, money
Scaling past a toy | Part Z9 | What breaks and what replaces it

Problem. You have read this book and you have a day job. Is any of this possible part-time?
Solution. The apparatus is, and the block is not — and separating the two is the useful answer rather than a discouraging one. The apparatus is compatible with part-time work because the agent runs when you are not there: an hour in the evening spent strengthening the oracle is repaid by a night of unattended checking, which is the one part of this arrangement that does not scale with your hours. Week one is five evenings rather than five days. What is not compatible is the customer side: evaluations, plugfests, support response times and the conversations of Part Z5 all happen during business hours and cannot be deferred, and Part Z8's arithmetic says the customer side is what decides whether the business exists. So the honest part-time plan is to build the apparatus and one small, complete, publishable block — which is a portfolio (Part Y13) and an asset and a genuine thing to point at — and to treat the transition to selling as a separate decision that needs the day job to end. Conflating the two is how people spend two years part-time and arrive with neither.

장: Z14. The C++ Model Layer — One Source, Two Destinations
절: Z14. The C++ Model Layer — One Source, Two Destinations — 들어가며
글:
Z14. The C++ Model Layer — One Source, Two Destinations

Ask a working design house where its models live and you rarely hear
 “SystemVerilog.” You hear C or C++. The RTL is what you sell; the C++ is
 what tells you the RTL is right, and increasingly it is also what generates
 the RTL. This part builds that layer for real. Every file named here is in this
 repository, compiles with g++, and is exercised while this page
 renders.

장: Z14. The C++ Model Layer — One Source, Two Destinations
절: Z14.1 Why the model is C++ and not Python
글:
Z14.1 Why the model is C++ and not Python

Earlier parts of this book used Python golden models (zlib
 for CRC-32, gf.py for the Galois field). That was right for those blocks:
 the model existed already, independently, which is the property that makes a golden
 model worth having. It stops being right the moment the model has to do two jobs:

[Table 447. What the model layer has to do, and what language can do it]
Job | Python | C++ | Why
Be the verification reference | yes | yes | Both express the algorithm exactly.
Run billions of vectors | no | yes | Measured below: 144 M evaluations/s in C++. CPython is ~1000× slower.
Be the HLS input | no | yes | Every HLS tool in industry takes C, C++ or SystemC. None takes Python.
Be bit-accurate to the RTL | awkward | yes | Python ints are arbitrary precision. Overflow and truncation must be simulated by hand; in C++ the fixed-width types do it.

The third row is the one that changes the architecture of the whole
 flow. If the model is also the HLS input, then the model and the RTL cannot
 disagree, because there is only one description:

[그림] One source, two destinations

```
edu/model/fir.h 

The conventional flow has three descriptions — a Python model, a
 C++ HLS source and hand-written RTL — and therefore three chances to disagree.
 When they disagree, nobody knows which is right, because each was written from the
 spec by a different person on a different day. The structure above removes two of the
 three.

장: Z14. The C++ Model Layer — One Source, Two Destinations
절: Z14.2 The shared header, and why it has no vendor types

장: Z14. The C++ Model Layer — One Source, Two Destinations
절: Z14.3 Proving three architectures equal — by exhaustion
글:
Z14.3 Proving three architectures equal — by exhaustion

fir.h contains the same filter written three ways: the
 textbook form, a width-narrowed form, and a symmetry-folded form that uses two
 multipliers instead of four. They have to compute the same function. Most projects
 establish that by running a few thousand random vectors and declaring victory. Here
 the input space is four 8-bit samples, so it has exactly 4,294,967,296 points — and that is
 small enough to check all of them.

[Table 448. Exhaustive equivalence, measured]
Quantity | Value | What it means
Input space | 4,294,967,296 | 256 4 — every possible input
Wall time | 29.7 s | g++ -O2, one core
Rate | 144,419,484/s | Each point evaluates all three variants
Disagreements | 0 | Not “none found” — none exist
Distinct outputs | 256 | All 256 output codes occur, so the check is not degenerate

That last row is the gate this repository puts on every measurement. A
 comparison that only ever sees one output value has proved nothing, however many
 vectors it ran. equiv.cpp counts distinct outputs and exits non-zero if
 there are fewer than two — the same rule the RTL harness applies in
 Part Z1.

The word “proof” is used carefully. This is exhaustive over
 the stated input space, which is the combinational function of four samples.
 It says nothing about the sequential wrapper, the reset behaviour, or the handshake.
 Those need different arguments — and in Part Z15 one of them costs us a
 bug.

장: Z14. The C++ Model Layer — One Source, Two Destinations
절: Z14.4 What verification time actually looks like
글:
Z14.4 What verification time actually looks like

“C++ simulates a thousand times faster than RTL” is repeated
 everywhere and is almost never measured by the person repeating it. Measuring it on
 this design produces a more useful answer than the folklore.

[Table 449. Vectors per second, same algorithm, same machine]
Path | Vectors/s | Relative | What is included
C++, compute only | 144,419,484 | 1,616× | The arithmetic, nothing else ( equiv.cpp )
C++, formatted to a file | 5,110,455 | 57× | Same arithmetic plus printf of five integers
RTL, iverilog + vvp | 89,345 | 1× | Event-driven simulation of the synthesisable design

Worked example 75. Where the speed advantage goes

Given. C++ computes at 144,419,484/s but emits formatted vectors at only 5,110,455/s.

Method. Divide. The ratio is the cost of text formatting relative to the algorithm itself.

Numbers. 28×. Formatting five integers as decimal text costs about 28 times more than computing the filter output.

The practical rule: a C++ reference that talks to the RTL through a text file throws away almost all of its speed advantage. Use the file for the few thousand vectors the RTL will actually run, and keep the billion-vector sweeps entirely inside C++.

How this is got wrong. The obvious reading is “file I/O is slow.” It was measured and it is not: writing 200,000 vectors to a file ran at 5,110,455/s and discarding them to /dev/null ran at 5,398,353/s — a 5 % difference. The cost is printf's decimal conversion, not the disk. Replacing text with a binary buffer, or comparing in memory and never serialising at all, recovers the other 96 %.

So the honest version of the folklore is: the algorithm is about
 1,600× faster in C++, and a badly plumbed harness will give you 57×. Both
 are worth having; they buy different things. The 57× path is how you drive the
 RTL. The 1,600× path is how you settle the algorithm before any RTL exists
 — and that is where the schedule is actually won, because a bug found in the
 C++ costs minutes and the same bug found in a gate-level regression costs
 days.

장: Z14. The C++ Model Layer — One Source, Two Destinations
절: Z14.5 Order of work, and what it saves
글:
Z14.5 Order of work, and what it saves

[Table 450. Where each class of defect should die]
Defect class | Cheapest place to catch it | Cost if it escapes to RTL
Algorithm wrong (wrong formula, wrong rounding) | C++, exhaustive or bulk | Days — the RTL is right and the spec is wrong, which is the slowest kind of debug
Overflow / width | C++ with fixed-width types | Weeks — appears as “fails occasionally”
Handshake, reset, backpressure | RTL only | Cannot be found in C++; budget RTL time for exactly this
Timing / area | Synthesis and P&R only | Cannot be found in simulation at all

The two lower rows are why HLS does not remove the need for RTL
 verification. It removes the top two rows, which are most of the defects by count, and
 leaves the bottom two, which are most of the defects by difficulty.
 Part Z15 hits one of the third-row defects within ten minutes of first running the
 generated RTL.

장: Z15. HLS — What It Costs, and How to Make It Win
절: Z15. HLS — What It Costs, and How to Make It Win — 들어가며
글:
Z15. HLS — What It Costs, and How to Make It Win

High-level synthesis has two well-known drawbacks. The first is that it
 does not always compile what you give it. The second is quality of results: the
 generated RTL can use noticeably more of the device than RTL a person would have
 written. Both are real, and both are measured in this part on a filter that exists in
 this repository.

But “generated RTL is worse than hand RTL” is not a law. It is what
 happens when the C++ is written as if it were software. If you understand the
 specification, the architecture you actually want, and what the HLS tool does with what
 you wrote, the generated RTL can beat hand-written RTL — and below it does, by
 1.38× in clock frequency. The rest of this part is how.

장: Z15. HLS — What It Costs, and How to Make It Win
절: Z15.1 Drawback one: what the tool refuses
글:
Z15.1 Drawback one: what the tool refuses

Before any quality question there is a compile question. These are
 one-variable controls run against PandA Bambu 2024.10 in this container: each row
 changes exactly one thing from the row above, so the cause is not inferred.

[Table 451. What Bambu accepts and refuses — one-variable controls]
Control | What changed | Result
1 | Pure C, 8-tap FIR | rc=0, Verilog produced, 101.0 MHz
2 | Control 1 plus one line : #pragma HLS PIPELINE II=1 | rc=11 — Loop pipelining pragma not supported
3 | C++ templates, no pragmas | rc=0, Verilog produced
4a | ap_uint only | rc=0, Verilog, 119–147 MHz
4b | hls::stream only | rc=1 — crash in FixStructsPassedByValue
5 | ap_fixed complex 8×8 Cholesky | rc=124 — 40-minute timeout in the front end

Control 2 is the important one: the same file, one line added, a
 hard failure. The blocker is not C++ and not the algorithm — it is the
 pragma dialect. Every vendor has its own, and pragmas are exactly the part of
 an HLS source that does not port. Control 4a is the pleasant surprise: Xilinx's
 arbitrary-precision integer type compiles fine on a tool that has nothing to do with
 Xilinx, because it is ordinary C++ templates. Control 4b is the unpleasant one,
 and it has no workaround.

The design rule that falls out of this table, and the one
 edu/model/ipmodel.h follows: put the algorithm in portable C++ and keep
 every tool-specific thing out of it. No pragmas in the header, no vendor stream
 types, no heavy template arithmetic. Then the same header compiles under
 g++ as the golden model and under the HLS tool as the design, and
 retargeting to a different HLS tool is a build-script change rather than a
 rewrite.

장: Z15. HLS — What It Costs, and How to Make It Win
절: Z15.2 Drawback two: quality of results, measured
글:
Z15.2 Drawback two: quality of results, measured

The filter is four taps, 8-bit samples, constant symmetric coefficients.
 Written naturally in C++ — int parameters, int
 accumulator, the way anybody would write it — and handed to Bambu, it produces
 this:

[Table 452. The same algorithm, the same tool, only the C types differ]
HLS source | Port width | Cells | SB_LUT4 | SB_CARRY
int fir_top(int,int,int,int) | 32 bit | 1,218 | 890 | 199
signed char fir_top_tuned(signed char×4) | 8 bit | 338 | 228 | 97

Worked example 76. Where a 4-tap filter's 890 LUTs came from

Given. A 4-tap FIR with constant coefficients needs, by hand, about 200 LUT4 on this device. The naive HLS version used 890.

Method. Compare the two rows above. The algorithm is identical — the same header, the same arithmetic, verified bit-identical. Only the C parameter types differ.

Numbers. 3.60× reduction (1,218 cells to 338) from changing int to signed char in the function signature. Nothing else changed.

This is the single largest QoR lever in HLS and it costs one line. It is also the first thing to check when generated RTL comes back four times too big.

How this is got wrong. The tempting explanation is “HLS tools are bloated.” It is not that. C's integer promotion rules widen char and short operands to int before arithmetic, so a C++ source that says int is requesting a 32-bit datapath and 32-bit ports. The tool built what the source asked for. A person writing Verilog types [7:0] and cannot make this mistake — which is most of why naive HLS loses to hand RTL.

장: Z15. HLS — What It Costs, and How to Make It Win
절: Z15.3 Making the comparison honest
글:
Z15.3 Making the comparison honest

Three things had to be fixed before any number in the next table meant
 anything. Each of them, left unfixed, produces a confident and wrong result.

[Table 453. Three ways this comparison was wrong before it was right]
Problem | Symptom | Fix
The two designs computed different functions | None — area numbers looked fine and meant nothing | Verify both against the same C++ golden vectors first. Every design in the next table passes 400 vectors with 0 mismatches.
Reset polarity differed | The generated RTL never asserted done ; 400/400 “failed” | Bambu defaults to active-low reset; the hand RTL used active-high. --reset-level=high --reset-type=sync .
Frequency was measured on the wrong path | Adding pipeline registers made Fmax fall (324 MHz → 74 MHz), and the hand RTL reported no frequency at all | nextpnr reports register-to-register paths only. Wrap every design in an identical registered timing shell ( fir_shell.v ) so the path being measured is the datapath.

The third deserves emphasis because it is the kind of error that
 survives review. The numbers before the fix were not noise — they were stable
 across seeds and they were monotonic in the wrong direction. A stable, reproducible,
 completely meaningless measurement is the most dangerous kind, because every instinct
 says to trust it. What made it visible was not a tool warning; it was noticing that
 more registers cannot make a design slower, and refusing to write the number
 down until that contradiction was explained.

글:
Z15.4 The sweep — where HLS loses and where it wins

[Table 454. Area, frequency and latency — all verified against the same C++ golden model (0 mismatches in 400 vectors each)]
Design | LC | Fmax (MHz) | Latency (cyc) | Fmax vs hand pipe | Area vs hand pipe
Hand combinational | 252 | 47.2 | 1 | 0.61× | 0.98×
Hand 3-stage pipeline | 256 | 76.9 | 3 | 1.00× | 1.00×
HLS @ 10ns | 299 | 57.2 | 2 | 0.74× | 1.17×
HLS @ 6ns | 307 | 72.7 | 4 | 0.95× | 1.20×
HLS @ 3ns | 386 | 105.9 | 9 | 1.38× | 1.51×
HLS @ 2ns | 460 | 92.3 | 12 | 1.20× | 1.80×
HLS @ 1ns | 544 | 82.6 | 18 | 1.08× | 2.12×

Frequency is the mean of three placer seeds; the spread was under
 7 % on every row, so the differences below are larger than the noise. Device is
 iCE40 HX8K, nextpnr-ice40 --freq 300 --placer heap.

Worked example 77. Does the generated RTL beat the hand-written RTL?

Given. Hand-written 3-stage pipeline: 256 LC at 76.9 MHz, latency 3. Best HLS point (HLS clock=3ns): 386 LC at 105.9 MHz, latency 9.

Method. Compare each axis separately. There is no single QoR number; area, frequency and latency trade against each other.

Numbers. Frequency: 1.38× better. Area: 1.51× worse. Latency: 3.0× worse.

So the answer is: yes on frequency, no on area and latency, and only at one point in the sweep. Anyone quoting the 1.38× without the 1.51× area and 3× latency is selling, not measuring.

How this is got wrong. Two trivial explanations had to be killed. First, that the hand RTL was a straw man: the comparison is against a hand-written pipelined design, not the single-cycle one, precisely so the answer is not rigged. Second, that tightening the constraint always helps: it does not. At 2 ns and 1 ns the generated design is both larger and slower than at 3 ns. The knee is at 3 ns and you only find it by sweeping.

장: Z15. HLS — What It Costs, and How to Make It Win
절: Z15.5 The method — how to get better QoR than hand RTL
글:
Z15.5 The method — how to get better QoR than hand RTL

The 1.38× did not come from the tool being clever. It came from
 four things, in this order. Each is a thing you do, not a thing the tool does.

Why the generated RTL could win at all

 | Step | Justification
1 | Write the interface at the true width, not the C default. | Measured above: 3.60× area from this alone. Until this is done, nothing else matters — the design is four times too big and every later measurement is taken on the wrong design.
2 | Express the architecture you want, not just the arithmetic you want. | The folded form computes h0(x0+x3)+h1(x1+x2): two multipliers instead of four. The tool will not discover the symmetry; you state it, and equiv.cpp proves you stated it correctly.
3 | Let the tool re-schedule, and sweep the constraint. | One number, --clock-period , produced five different microarchitectures with latencies 2, 4, 9, 12 and 18 cycles. In hand RTL each of those is a redesign; here each is a rebuild.
4 | Pick the knee from the sweep rather than the tightest point. | The best frequency is at 3 ns, not at 1 ns. Constraining harder past the knee adds registers that the fabric cannot exploit, so area rises and frequency falls.

Step three is where the structural advantage lives, and it is worth
 being precise about what it is. The tool is not out-scheduling a human. A human given
 a week could hand-pipeline this filter to 3 ns and would probably land smaller
 than 386 LC. The advantage is that the sweep above cost four rebuilds and no
 design work, so five architectures were evaluated instead of one. Hand RTL usually
 gets pipelined once, for one target, because re-pipelining is expensive and risky; it
 then stays that way when the target moves. The generated design is re-derived from the
 specification every time.

That is the real claim, and it is narrower and more useful than “HLS beats
 hand RTL.” Hand RTL beats HLS at a point you have already designed for. HLS
 beats hand RTL at a point you have not. In a one-person design house, where nobody
 has a week to re-pipeline a block because a customer moved the clock from 75 to
 100 MHz, the second case is the one that keeps happening.

장: Z15. HLS — What It Costs, and How to Make It Win
절: Z15.6 Where this result stops being true
글:
Z15.6 Where this result stops being true

Stating the conditions under which a measurement flips is not a
 disclaimer; it is part of the measurement. This one flips under any of these:

[Table 455. Invalidation conditions for Z15.4]
Condition | Why the result changes
A different fabric | iCE40 has no DSP blocks usable here, so constant multiplies became LUT shift-adds. On a device with hard multipliers the area picture changes completely.
Wider data or more taps | At 4 taps the hand design is small enough for one person to hold in mind. The argument for HLS gets stronger with size, but this table does not prove that — it was not measured here.
A hand design with more than 3 stages | The comparison is against a 3-stage hand pipeline. A 6-stage hand pipeline would likely beat the 3 ns HLS point on both axes. What it would cost in engineer-days is not in the table.
A different HLS tool | Bambu's scheduler is not Vitis HLS's. The pragma dialect result in Z15.1 guarantees the sources are not portable unchanged.

The last row is the one to plan around commercially. An IP built on one
 HLS tool's pragmas is tied to that tool. An IP built the way
 edu/model/ipmodel.h is built — portable C++, tool-specific settings
 on the command line — is not, and that portability is worth more than the few
 percent a vendor pragma might buy.

장: Z16. Before Any Code — System, Spec, Schematic
절: Z16. Before Any Code — System, Spec, Schematic — 들어가며
글:
Z16. Before Any Code — System, Spec, Schematic

Everything so far in this volume started from a piece of RTL or a piece
 of C++. That is the wrong end. In a real design house the code is the fifth
 thing you produce, and by the time you type it most of the decisions that matter are
 already made. This part walks the four things that come first, for the same 4-tap
 equaliser the previous parts built: where it sits in a system, what it is responsible
 for, what its specification says, and what it looks like as a drawing — all the
 way down to transistors.

Nothing here assumes prior hardware knowledge. If you have written C++ and never
 seen a schematic, this part and the two after it are written for you.

장: Z16. Before Any Code — System, Spec, Schematic
절: Z16.1 What problem this IP exists to solve
글:
Z16.1 What problem this IP exists to solve

A serial link sends bits down a copper trace. At 10 Gb/s a bit is
 100 picoseconds wide, and a 30 cm PCB trace behaves like a low-pass filter:
 high frequencies are attenuated more than low ones. The consequence has a name —
 inter-symbol interference (ISI). Energy from bit n is still arriving when
 bit n+1 is being sampled, so the receiver's decision about one bit depends on
 the bits around it.

[그림] Figure 55. What the channel does. The transmitted waveform (top) is clean. The received
 waveform is smeared across bit boundaries — drawn as ‘unknown’
 because at the sampling instant its value depends on neighbouring bits, not just the
 current one. Recovering the top row from the middle row is the equaliser's job.

An equaliser undoes that smearing. A feed-forward equaliser
 (FFE) does it with a filter whose response approximates the inverse of the channel:
 take the last few samples, scale each by a coefficient, add them up. That sum is the
 filter this book has been building. Four taps, 8-bit samples, coefficients
 {−18, 111, 111, −18} in Q1.7 — a mild high-frequency boost, which is
 exactly the shape that undoes a mild low-pass channel.

Worked example 78. Why those coefficients have that shape

Given. The coefficients are {−18, 111, 111, −18} in Q1.7, i.e. {−0.141, 0.867, 0.867, −0.141}.

Method. Sum them to get the DC (zero-frequency) gain. Alternate their signs and sum to get the Nyquist (highest-frequency) gain.

Numbers. DC gain = (−18+111+111−18)/128 = 186/128 = 1.453. Nyquist gain = (−18−111+111+18)/128 = 0/128 = exactly zero. The filter passes DC at 1.45× and has a perfect null at the highest representable frequency.

This is the difference between a teaching example and a product. The structure, widths, saturation, handshake and verification in this book are all real. The coefficient values are placeholders, and the book says so rather than letting the reader assume otherwise.

How this is got wrong. That is a low-pass response — and not a mild one: a null at Nyquist is what a smoothing filter does, the opposite of what an equaliser is supposed to do. The negative outer taps make it look like a boost, but the adjacent equal centre taps dominate and their sum 111−111 cancels exactly at Nyquist. Treat this filter as what it is — a worked example with realistic structure, arithmetic and saturation behaviour — not as a coefficient set anyone should ship. Real FFE coefficients are adapted at run time by an LMS loop against the measured channel, and the sign pattern is typically the other way round.

장: Z16. Before Any Code — System, Spec, Schematic
절: Z16.2 Where it sits — the whole receive chain
글:
Z16.2 Where it sits — the whole receive chain

The filter is one box in a chain. Knowing the boxes on either side is
 not background reading; it is what determines your interface, your latency budget and
 your clock.

[그림] Figure 56. The 10 Gb/s receive chain. Our IP is the fourth box. Everything before it
 is analogue or mixed-signal; everything after it is ordinary synchronous digital
 logic. The boundary sits at the ADC — which is exactly why the IP's input is an
 8-bit two's-complement sample and not a voltage.

[Table 456. Each neighbour, and what it forces on our design]
Block | What it does | What it forces on us
CTLE | Continuous-time linear equaliser: an analogue filter that boosts high frequencies before sampling. | It removes the bulk of the ISI, so our digital FFE only has to clean up the residue — which is why 4 taps is enough and 40 is not needed.
VGA / AGC | Variable-gain amplifier with automatic gain control: scales the signal so it fills the ADC's input range. | It guarantees our input occupies most of the 8-bit range. If AGC is broken our input is tiny and the filter output is mostly quantisation noise — a failure that looks like our bug.
ADC | Analogue-to-digital converter: turns a voltage into an 8-bit number, once per unit interval. | Defines our input format. 8-bit, two's complement, Q1.7, one sample per clock. Everything about our widths comes from this box.
DFE | Decision-feedback equaliser: subtracts the known ISI contribution of already-decided bits. Contains a feedback loop. | It sits immediately after us and its loop must close in one unit interval. Our latency is in series with nothing critical, but our throughput must be one sample per clock or the DFE starves.
Slicer | A comparator: decides 0 or 1 from the equalised sample. | It consumes our 8-bit output and only really needs the sign plus a few bits of margin — which is why saturating (rather than wrapping) matters so much: a wrap flips the sign and the slicer decides exactly wrong.
CDR | Clock and data recovery: extracts the sampling clock from the data. | It provides our clock. Our design must be fully synchronous to it and must tolerate its reset sequencing.
PCS / MAC | Protocol layers: alignment, 64b/66b coding, FEC, framing, CRC. | Far enough away not to constrain us directly, but they set the overall latency budget the whole chain is measured against.

장: Z16. Before Any Code — System, Spec, Schematic
절: Z16.3 “Front end” and “back end” mean two different things
글:
Z16.3 “Front end” and “back end” mean two different things

This trips up every newcomer, because the same two words name two
 unrelated axes and practitioners switch between them without warning.

[Table 457. Two meanings of front-end / back-end]
Axis | Front end | Back end | Where our IP is
Signal chain (where in the data path) | Analogue and mixed-signal: CTLE, VGA, ADC, CDR. Deals in volts and picoseconds. | Digital: PCS, MAC, bus, software. Deals in bits and packets. | First block of the digital back end — immediately after the ADC.
Design flow (where in the schedule) | RTL design, verification, synthesis-for-estimate. Produces a netlist. This is where this book lives. | Floorplan, place and route, clock tree, timing closure, DRC/LVS, GDSII tape-out. | Parts Z14–Z15 are flow front-end. synth.sh 's nextpnr step is the smallest possible taste of flow back-end.

So “our IP is in the back end” and “we are doing
 front-end work” are both true at once, and mean different things. When someone
 says it, ask which axis.

장: Z16. Before Any Code — System, Spec, Schematic
절: Z16.4 The specification, written before the code
글:
Z16.4 The specification, written before the code

A specification is not a description of what you built. It is the
 contract you write first, and then check what you built against. Here is the real one
 for this block. Every row is a number a customer can hold you to, and every row was
 measured in Parts Z14–Z15 — the spec came first and the measurements
 came back to fill it in.

[Table 458. IP specification: 4-tap feed-forward equaliser]
Item | Value | How it is verified
Function | y[n] = sat 8 ( (Σ h[i]·x[n−i]) >> 7 ) | Exhaustive C++ equivalence over all 2 32 inputs (Z14.3)
Input | 4 × 8-bit signed, Q1.7, one sample per clock | Testbench drives all corner combinations plus random
Output | 1 × 8-bit signed, Q1.7, saturating | Saturation exercised by corner vectors; all 256 output codes seen
Coefficients | Compile-time constants, symmetric | Symmetry asserted at build; folding verified bit-exact against unfolded
Throughput | 1 sample/clock, no back-pressure | Cycle count checked in the harness, not just values
Latency | 1 clock (combinational variant) / 3 clocks (pipelined) | Measured start-to-done in simulation
Clock | Single clock, synchronous, rising edge | Lint (no latches, no multiple drivers) plus synthesis
Reset | Synchronous, active high | Explicitly stated because the HLS tool defaults to active low — see Z15.3
Area | 252 LC (hand) / 386 LC (HLS @3ns) on iCE40 HX8K | yosys + nextpnr, three placer seeds
F max | 76.9 MHz (hand, 3-stage) / 106.0 MHz (HLS @3ns) | nextpnr with a registered timing shell
Deliverables | RTL, C++ model, testbench, vectors, synthesis script, datasheet, integration guide, known issues | edu/house/release.sh gates all of them

Two rows are worth pausing on. The reset polarity row exists
 because getting it wrong cost a debugging session in Part Z15 — a
 specification that does not pin down polarity, edge and synchronicity has not specified
 the reset at all. And throughput is a separate row from latency because a
 value-only regression cannot see a block getting slower; Part Z1 caught a mutant
 that broke throughput while keeping every output value correct.

장: Z16. Before Any Code — System, Spec, Schematic
절: Z16.5 What else you must own to ship this
글:
Z16.5 What else you must own to ship this

A 4-tap filter is not a product. A customer who buys “an
 equaliser” expects a block they can drop into a chip, and that means a
 surprising amount of surrounding machinery. For a one-person design house the
 question is not whether you need these — you do — but which you write,
 which you take from an open collection, and which you decline to support.

[Table 459. Supporting IP, and the one-person make/buy call]
What | Why it is needed | Call
Register file / CSR block | Coefficients, bypass, status, ID. No customer accepts a block with no software interface. | Make. Generated from one description — edu/house/regmap.py emits RTL, C header, docs and IP-XACT from a single source.
APB or AXI-Lite bridge | How the CSRs are reached from the SoC. | Make (APB is ~100 lines and fully specified) or take an open one. AXI-Lite is bigger; buy or adapt.
Clock-domain crossing / FIFO | The CSR bus and the data path are usually on different clocks. | Buy or adopt. CDC is the single most common source of bugs that pass simulation and fail silicon. Do not hand-roll a synchroniser.
Reset synchroniser | An asynchronous reset release violates recovery/removal timing on every flop it reaches. | Make , from the standard two-flop pattern, and lint for it.
PLL / CDR | Provides the clock. | Decline. This is analogue IP. A one-person digital house does not build a CDR; you specify the clock you need and document it.
SerDes PHY | Serialiser, driver, receiver front end. | Decline. Same reason, larger.
DFT / scan insertion | Manufacturing test. Without it the chip cannot be screened. | Defer to the integrator , but write RTL that is scan-friendly: no gated clocks you invented, no latches, no async logic.
Lint and CDC rule decks | Customers run them and send you the report. | Make. verilator --lint-only -Wall is free and catches most of it; ship the clean report as a deliverable.
Documentation set | Datasheet, integration guide, known issues. | Make. This is the cheapest thing you can do to look like a real vendor, and the thing most one-person efforts skip.

The honest summary of that table: the filter is perhaps 15 % of the
 work of selling the filter. Parts Y and Z4 build the other 85 %.

장: Z16. Before Any Code — System, Spec, Schematic
절: Z16.6 The five levels of drawing
글:
Z16.6 The five levels of drawing

“Schematic” is not one thing. The same design is drawn at
 five levels of detail and each answers a different question. Knowing which level you
 are being shown is half of reading a drawing.

[Table 460. Levels of representation, from system to silicon]
Level | What a box is | What a line is | Question it answers | Where in this book
System | A whole function (ADC, MAC) | A stream of data | Does the architecture close? | Z16.2, above
Block / RTL | A module with ports | A named bus of bits | What are the interfaces and widths? | Z16.7
Datapath | An adder, a multiplier, a register | A bundle of wires | Where does the critical path run? | Z17.4
Gate | A NAND, a flip-flop | One wire carrying one bit | How many gates deep is it? | Z17.3
Transistor | One MOSFET | One node | Why does a gate behave as it does? | Z17.1–Z17.2

장: Z16. Before Any Code — System, Spec, Schematic
절: Z16.7 Our IP at block level
글:
Z16.7 Our IP at block level

This is the drawing that belongs at the top of the datasheet. Boxes are
 modules, lines are buses, and the widths are on the lines because a width mismatch is
 the most common integration failure there is.

[그림] Figure 57. The equaliser at block level. Reading left to right: samples enter and are held
 in a 4-deep shift register; symmetric pairs are added (9 bits, because adding two
 8-bit numbers needs 9); each sum is multiplied by one constant coefficient (17 bits);
 the result is shifted right by 7 to return to Q1.7 and saturated back to 8 bits. Every
 width change on this diagram is a place where a bug can hide silently.

Why every width on that diagram is what it is

 | Step | Justification
1 | The input is 8 bits because the ADC produces 8 bits. | The interface is set by the neighbour, not by us.
2 | The fold adders are 9 bits, not 8. | Adding two n -bit signed numbers can need n +1 bits: 127+127 = 254, which does not fit in 8-bit signed. Truncating here would be wrong only for large inputs — a bug that passes random testing.
3 | The multiply result is 17 bits. | 9-bit operand times 8-bit coefficient gives up to 17 bits. The accumulator is declared 18 in the C++ model, and the maximum magnitude is 127×(18+111+111+18) = 32,766, which fits in 17 bits signed with room to spare — so the 18-bit saturation in the model never actually fires.
4 | The shift is by 7, not 8. | Both sample and coefficient are Q1.7, so their product is Q2.14. Returning to Q1.7 means discarding 7 fractional bits.
5 | The output saturates to 8 bits rather than wrapping. | The next block is a slicer that decides sign. A wrap turns a large positive into a large negative and the slicer decides exactly wrong; a saturate is wrong in magnitude but right in sign.

That last derivation is the whole argument for drawing before coding. It
 took five steps and no Verilog, and it fixed every width in the design. Written the
 other way round — code first, widths discovered during debug — each of
 those five steps becomes a regression failure somebody has to chase.

장: Z17. From One Transistor to Our Datapath
절: Z17. From One Transistor to Our Datapath — 들어가며
글:
Z17. From One Transistor to Our Datapath

This part builds the equaliser upward from a single transistor. Nothing
 is assumed. If you know that a computer is made of transistors and nothing more
 specific than that, start here; by the end you will be able to read the gate-level
 schematic of the adder inside the filter and say why it is shaped the way it is.

The reason this matters to someone writing RTL or HLS is not nostalgia. Every
 decision the previous parts made — why saturation costs more than truncation,
 why a 9-bit adder is not an 8-bit adder, why the critical path runs where it does,
 why you register a signal before it leaves the chip — is a fact about these
 drawings. You can write RTL without them and you will write slower RTL.

장: Z17. From One Transistor to Our Datapath
절: Z17.1 The switch
글:
Z17.1 The switch

A MOSFET is a voltage-controlled switch with three terminals that matter:
 gate, source and drain. Current flows between source and drain
 when the gate says so. There are two flavours and they are opposites:

[Table 461. The two switches]
Type | Turns on when its gate is | Good at passing | Where it goes
NMOS | high (1) | a strong 0 | between the output and ground
PMOS | low (0) | a strong 1 | between the output and VDD

The third column is the one people skip and then get wrong. An NMOS can
 pull a node down to 0 V cleanly but cannot pull it all the way up to VDD —
 it stops roughly a threshold voltage short. A PMOS is the mirror image. So neither type
 alone can build a good logic gate, and that is why every static CMOS gate
 contains both: PMOS above to pull up, NMOS below to pull down. The circuit family is
 called complementary MOS for exactly this reason.

장: Z17. From One Transistor to Our Datapath
절: Z17.2 The inverter, and why CMOS won
글:
Z17.2 The inverter, and why CMOS won

[그림] Figure 58. The CMOS inverter: one PMOS pull-up, one NMOS
 pull-down, gates tied together. This is the smallest complete CMOS gate and the
 template for every other one. The red bar at the top is the supply (VDD); the striped
 symbol at the bottom is ground (0 V).

Why this circuit inverts, and why it costs no static power

 | Step | Justification
1 | Input A = 0. The PMOS gate sees 0, so the PMOS is on . The NMOS gate sees 0, so the NMOS is off . | From the table above: PMOS turns on with a low gate, NMOS with a high gate.
2 | With only the PMOS on, the output node is connected to VDD and disconnected from ground. Y is pulled up to 1. | The only conducting path from Y goes to the supply.
3 | Input A = 1. Now the PMOS is off and the NMOS is on, so Y is connected to ground and disconnected from VDD. Y is pulled down to 0. | The mirror image of the previous step.
4 | In both steady states exactly one of the two devices conducts, so there is no path from VDD to ground . | A path from supply to ground would be a short circuit drawing continuous current.
5 | Therefore a CMOS gate that is not switching draws (almost) no current. | This is the property that let CMOS displace every earlier logic family. Power is consumed charging and discharging capacitance when the output changes , which is why dynamic power is proportional to activity and frequency.
6 | The word ‘almost’ is doing real work at modern nodes. | Sub-threshold leakage and gate leakage mean an idle gate does draw a small current, and below roughly 28 nm leakage becomes a first-order design problem. Part X43 covers what is done about it.

장: Z17. From One Transistor to Our Datapath
절: Z17.3 NAND: pull-up and pull-down are duals
글:
Z17.3 NAND: pull-up and pull-down are duals

Now the gate that everything is actually built from. The rule that
 generates every static CMOS gate is a single sentence: build the pull-down network
 from NMOS so that it conducts exactly when the output should be 0, then build the
 pull-up network as its dual.

[그림] Figure 59. A 2-input CMOS NAND. The two NMOS are in
 series : current only reaches ground when A and B are both 1, which is exactly
 when NAND's output should be 0. The two PMOS are in parallel : a path to VDD
 exists when A is 0 or B is 0. Series means AND; parallel means OR.

[Table 462. Reading the NAND schematic as a truth table]
A | B | Pull-down (series NMOS) | Pull-up (parallel PMOS) | Y
0 | 0 | both off → open | both on → conducts | 1
0 | 1 | top off → open | left on → conducts | 1
1 | 0 | bottom off → open | right on → conducts | 1
1 | 1 | both on → conducts | both off → open | 0

Why the pull-up is the dual of the pull-down, always

 | Step | Justification
1 | The output must be driven to exactly one value in every input combination. | If neither network conducts the output floats (high-impedance, value undefined); if both conduct you have a short from VDD to ground.
2 | So the pull-up must conduct exactly when the pull-down does not — the two conditions are logical complements. | That is what ‘exactly one’ means.
3 | The pull-down for NAND conducts when (A AND B). | Series transistors both have to be on, and NMOS is on for a 1.
4 | Its complement is NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B), by De Morgan's law. | De Morgan converts a negated conjunction into a disjunction of negations.
5 | PMOS is on for a 0, so a PMOS whose gate is A implements (NOT A). An OR of two conditions is a parallel connection. | Either path alone is enough to conduct.
6 | Hence: series NMOS below, parallel PMOS above. Swap series and parallel and you get NOR instead. | NOR's pull-down is parallel (output 0 when A OR B) and its pull-up is series.

Two consequences worth carrying into RTL. First, NAND and NOR are
 the cheap gates — four transistors each. AND and OR are more
 expensive, because CMOS naturally produces an inversion and a non-inverting gate is a
 NAND followed by an inverter: six transistors. This is why synthesis tools cheerfully
 rewrite your logic into seas of NANDs, and why the classic identity
 AND(a,b) = NOT(NAND(a,b)) is worth recognising in a netlist.

Second, series transistors are slow. A 4-input NAND has four NMOS in series
 and its pull-down is roughly four times weaker than an inverter's. That is why wide
 gates get decomposed into trees, and why a 17-bit ripple adder is not simply
 ‘a bit slower’ than an 8-bit one.

장: Z17. From One Transistor to Our Datapath
절: Z17.4 Pull-up resistors — a different thing with a similar name
글:
Z17.4 Pull-up resistors — a different thing with a similar name

The phrase “pull-up” is used for two different circuits and
 conflating them causes real design errors.

[그림] Figure 60. Two things called “pull-up”. Left: a real resistor on a
 board, holding an open-drain line high until some device pulls it low. Right: 
 a PMOS pull-up network inside a CMOS gate. Only the left one is a resistor; the
 right one is the transistor network of Z17.2.

[Table 463. Resistor pull-up versus transistor pull-up]
 | Pull-up resistor (board level) | PMOS pull-up (inside a gate)
What it is | A physical resistor, typically 1–10 kΩ | A transistor network, the dual of the pull-down
Where | On the PCB or inside an I/O pad | Inside every static CMOS gate
Why | The line has no active driver for the high state — open-drain or open-collector outputs can only pull down | Every state is actively driven
Static current | Yes — whenever the line is held low, current flows through the resistor to ground | No — exactly one network conducts
Speed | Slow rising edge: RC charging of the bus capacitance. This is why I²C is limited to 100 kHz/400 kHz/1 MHz modes | Fast: the PMOS actively charges the node
Typical use | I²C SDA/SCL, shared interrupt lines, reset lines, strapping pins, unused inputs | All ordinary logic
Relevance to our IP | None inside the block. It appears at the chip boundary and in the CSR bus pads | Every gate the filter synthesises into

Worked example 79. Sizing a pull-up resistor, and why the choice is a squeeze

Given. An I²C bus at 3.3 V with 200 pF of bus capacitance. The standard requires the low level to stay below 0.4 V while a device sinks at most 3 mA, and the rise time to be under 300 ns for 400 kHz fast mode.

Method. The lower bound comes from current: R must be large enough that (VDD−VOL)/R does not exceed the sink current. The upper bound comes from speed: the RC rise to the input threshold must fit in the rise-time budget, which for 0 → 0.7 VDD takes about 1.2 RC.

Numbers. Lower bound: R ≥ (3.3−0.4)/3 mA = 967 Ω. Upper bound: R ≤ 300 ns/(1.2×200 pF) = 1250 Ω. So R must sit between roughly 1.0 and 1.25 kΩ — a narrow window.

Note what dominates: capacitance. Halving C doubles the upper bound. On a board, capacitance is trace length and the number of devices, so the electrical problem is really a layout problem.

How this is got wrong. The window being this narrow is the finding, not an arithmetic slip. The usual reflex is to grab the familiar 4.7 kΩ part, which violates the upper bound by nearly 4× and produces a bus that works on the bench at low speed and fails at 400 kHz with long traces. If the window closes entirely, the fix is not a different resistor — it is less bus capacitance, or an active terminator.

장: Z17. From One Transistor to Our Datapath
절: Z17.5 The clock, and why anything is clocked at all
글:
Z17.5 The clock, and why anything is clocked at all

Combinational logic has no memory: outputs follow inputs after a delay.
 To build anything that accumulates, you need an element that holds. The
 universal one is the edge-triggered D flip-flop: it samples its D input at the
 rising edge of the clock and holds that value on Q until the next rising edge.

[그림] Figure 61. A D flip-flop. Q takes the value D had at the rising edge and holds it for the
 whole cycle. Note that Q changes only at rising edges, never in between — that
 is the entire point.

The clock is not there to make things go. It is there to make things
 agree on when. Combinational paths through different amounts of logic finish
 at different times; without a clock, a downstream block cannot know whether what it is
 looking at is the final answer or a value still settling. The clock defines an instant
 at which everything is required to have settled, and the design's job is to make that
 true.

[Table 464. The two timing constraints, and what violating each looks like]
Constraint | What it requires | Fix if violated | Symptom
Setup | Data must arrive at the flop at least t su before the edge. Limits the longest path. | Shorten the logic, add a pipeline stage, or slow the clock. | Works at low frequency, fails above some clock rate. Reproducible.
Hold | Data must remain stable at least t h after the edge. Limits the shortest path. | Add delay (buffers). Slowing the clock does not help. | Fails at every frequency. Usually a silicon respin — which is why hold violations are feared more than setup.

That asymmetry is worth memorising: a setup failure is a performance
 bug, a hold failure is a functional bug. It is also why Part Z15's measurement
 needed a registered timing shell — a path that starts or ends outside the chip
 has no flop at one end, so neither constraint is defined and the tool has nothing to
 report.

장: Z17. From One Transistor to Our Datapath
절: Z17.6 Our adder, at gate level
글:
Z17.6 Our adder, at gate level

Now put it together. The filter's first operation is
 a0 = x0 + x3 on 8-bit signed values producing 9 bits. An adder is built
 from full adders, and a full adder is built from the gates above.

[그림] Figure 62. One full adder: sum = a XOR b XOR cin, cout = (a AND b) OR (cin AND (a XOR b)).
 Five gates. The 9-bit fold adder in the filter is nine of these chained, with each
 cout feeding the next cin — a ripple-carry adder.

Worked example 80. Why the carry chain sets the critical path

Given. A ripple-carry adder of N bits. Each full adder's carry output takes about 2 gate delays (one AND, one OR) after its carry input is valid.

Method. The last bit's carry cannot be computed until every earlier carry has rippled through. Count gate delays along that chain.

Numbers. Roughly 2N gate delays for N bits: 18 for the 9-bit fold adder, 34 for a 17-bit accumulator. The sum bits themselves add only one more XOR after their carry arrives.

This is also why fast-adder architectures exist — carry-lookahead, carry-select, prefix adders — trading area for a logarithmic rather than linear carry depth. On an FPGA you usually get the vendor's carry chain and the question does not arise; in an ASIC the synthesiser picks from a library of adder architectures based on your timing constraint.

How this is got wrong. The tempting conclusion is that our filter's critical path is the adder. It is not, and assuming so sends you optimising the wrong thing. The measured designs in Z15 use iCE40's dedicated carry chain (SB_CARRY), which is far faster than generic gates — the hand design used 48 of them. On this fabric the multiply-by-constant shift-add network, not the ripple, dominates. Count gates to understand the structure; measure the tool output to know the number.

장: Z17. From One Transistor to Our Datapath
절: Z17.7 Why saturation costs more than wrapping
글:
Z17.7 Why saturation costs more than wrapping

Part Z16 justified saturation on system grounds: a wrap flips the
 sign and the slicer decides exactly wrong. Here is what it costs, in gates.

[Table 465. Truncate versus saturate, at gate level]
Operation | What the hardware does | Cost
Truncate (wrap) to 8 bits | Discard the upper bits. Route 8 wires, ignore the rest. | Zero gates. It is a renaming of wires.
Saturate to 8 bits | Detect whether the value exceeds the 8-bit range, and if so substitute the limit. Needs two comparisons and an 8-bit 2-to-1 multiplexer. | Two comparators plus a mux — tens of gates, and it sits after the adder, so it adds directly to the critical path.

This explains a result in Part Z15 that looked backwards at first.
 Narrowing the accumulator from 32 bits to 18 should have shrunk the design,
 but the narrowed variant came out larger in Bambu's estimate — because the
 narrowing was implemented with sat() at every accumulation step, and each
 of those saturations bought comparators that the plain 32-bit accumulation did not
 need. The width saving was real and the saturation cost was larger.

The lesson generalises: narrowing a datapath is only free if you narrow it
 somewhere the value provably cannot overflow. In the final tuned design the
 accumulator is wide enough that no intermediate saturation is needed at all —
 Z16.7 derived the bound, 32,766, which fits in 17 bits — and saturation happens
 exactly once, at the output, where the specification demands it.

장: Z17. From One Transistor to Our Datapath
절: Z17.8 The whole stack, one page
글:
Z17.8 The whole stack, one page

[Table 466. Every level, and what our filter looks like there]
Level | Our filter at this level | Who works here
System | One box in the receive chain, between ADC and DFE | Architect; the spec of Z16.4 is written here
RTL / HLS | 40 lines of Verilog, or 12 lines of C++ plus a build command | You, in Parts Z14–Z15
Netlist | 338–1218 cells depending on how the C++ was typed | Synthesis ( yosys ); you read its report
Gate | SB_LUT4 ×228, SB_CARRY ×97 — NANDs and carry chains in a specific arrangement | The tool; you influence it through coding style and constraints
Transistor | Each LUT4 is a small memory plus a mux tree; each is CMOS pull-up/pull-down as in Z17.2 | The FPGA vendor, or in an ASIC the standard-cell library team
Silicon | Configuration bits in an iCE40, or diffused transistors in a mask set | The foundry

The practical point of having walked down this stack is that the levels
 are not independent. A choice at the top — “saturate rather than
 wrap” — became comparators and a mux at the gate level, which became area
 and delay in the measurements of Part Z15, which fed back into the specification
 in Z16.4. An engineer who can only see one level cannot follow that chain, and will
 make the choice at the top without knowing what it costs at the bottom.

장: Z18. SystemVerilog for the C++ Programmer
절: Z18. SystemVerilog for the C++ Programmer — 들어가며
글:
Z18. SystemVerilog for the C++ Programmer

SystemVerilog looks enough like C to be dangerous. The braces are
 begin/end, the types are unfamiliar, and about a third of
 the constructs mean something that has no software equivalent at all. This part is a
 complete tour, written for somebody who knows C++ and has never seen a hardware
 description language. It covers the synthesisable language in full, then the
 verification subset, and says at every point which of the two you are in.

The single most important idea, before any syntax: you are not writing
 instructions that execute. You are describing hardware that exists. Every
 always block in a design is a piece of circuitry that is powered on all
 the time, simultaneously with every other block. Sequence exists only inside a single
 block, and even there it is often a fiction the synthesiser unrolls into wires.

장: Z18. SystemVerilog for the C++ Programmer

절: Z18.3 Types: the four-state trap
글:
Z18.3 Types: the four-state trap

C++ has bool. SystemVerilog has a bit that can hold four
 values, and the two extra ones are the most useful debugging tool in the
 language.

[Table 468. The four values a logic bit can take]
Value | Means | Where it comes from | Why you want it
0 | low | driven low | —
1 | high | driven high | —
x | unknown | uninitialised register, two drivers fighting, reading before reset | It propagates. An x in a sum makes the sum x , so a missing reset shows up as garbage rather than as a plausible zero.
z | high impedance (not driven) | a tri-state driver that is off, an unconnected input | Models buses where several drivers share a wire.

[Table 469. The types, and which to use]
Type | States | Use it for | C++ analogue
logic | 4 | Almost everything. One bit, or logic [7:0] for a vector. | Closest to bool / uint8_t , but 4-state
wire | 4 | Legacy. A net that must be continuously driven. logic covers it in SystemVerilog. | —
reg | 4 | Legacy Verilog name for a procedural variable. It does not mean ‘register’ — this misnaming has confused people for thirty years. Use logic . | —
bit | 2 | Testbench code where you want C semantics and speed. | bool
int | 2 | Loop counters, testbench arithmetic. 32-bit signed. | int32_t
byte , shortint , longint | 2 | 8/16/64-bit signed testbench integers. | int8_t , int16_t , int64_t
integer | 4 | Legacy 32-bit 4-state. | —
real | — | Floating point, testbench only. | double
string | — | Testbench messages. | std::string

```
// ── 벡터와 부호 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
logic [7:0] u; // 8비트 **부호 없음** (기본값)
logic signed [7:0] a; // 8비트 부호 있음 -- `signed` 를 빼면 조용히 틀린다

// [7:0] 과 [0:7] 은 다르다. [7:0] 이 관례다 (왼쪽이 MSB).
// C++ 배열과 달리 **비트 번호를 내가 정한다** -- [15:8] 도 legal 하다.

// 부호를 빠뜨리면 어떻게 되나 -- 실제로 물리는 자리다
logic [7:0] p = 8'hFF; // 255 로 읽힌다
logic signed [7:0] q = 8'hFF; // -1 로 읽힌다
// p > 0 은 참, q > 0 은 거짓. **같은 비트, 다른 답.**

// ── 리터럴 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// '
8'd10 // 8비트 십진 10
8'hFF // 8비트 16진
8'b1010_1010 // 밑줄은 자리 구분용. 무시된다 (C++14 의 ' 와 같다)
8'sd10 // 8비트 **부호있는** 십진
'0 // 폭을 문맥에서 가져오는 전부-0. `'1` 은 전부-1 (0001 아님!)
8'bx // 전부 unknown -- 리셋 전 상태를 흉내낼 때

// ── 구조체와 배열 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
typedef struct packed { // packed = **비트가 연속**이다. 합성된다
 logic valid; // [16]
 logic [7:0] data; // [15:8]
 logic [7:0] tag; // [7:0]
} beat_t; // 통째로 17비트 벡터처럼 쓸 수 있다

typedef struct { // unpacked = 그냥 묶음. **합성 안 된다**
 int count;
 string name;
} stat_t; // 테스트벤치용

logic [7:0] mem [0:255]; // unpacked 배열 = 메모리. `[개수]` 가 **뒤**에 온다
logic [3:0][7:0] lanes; // packed 배열 = 32비트를 4x8 로 본 것
beat_t queue [$]; // 동적 큐 (테스트벤치). C++ 의 `std::deque`
```

Worked example 81. Why signed is the most expensive missing keyword in the language

Given. The filter adds two 8-bit samples: a0 = x0 + x3, where both may be negative. Written as logic [7:0] x0 without signed.

Method. Work out what the comparison and the shift do under unsigned interpretation.

Numbers. x0 = −1 is stored as 8'hFF. Unsigned, that reads as 255. Adding −1 and −1 should give −2; unsigned it gives 510, and the right shift that follows brings in zeros from the top instead of sign bits, so the result is a large positive number instead of a small negative one.

The rule in SystemVerilog: an expression is unsigned if any operand is unsigned. One unsigned literal in a long signed expression silently converts the whole thing. When in doubt, wrap in $signed().

How this is got wrong. Nothing warns you. The bit patterns are identical — only the interpretation differs, and the interpretation lives in a keyword you forgot to type. The design simulates, synthesises, and is wrong for exactly the half of the input space where the sample is negative. Random testing finds it; directed testing with positive-only stimulus does not. This is why edu/model/fir4_hand.v writes $signed({x0[7], x0}) explicitly rather than relying on declarations being right.

장: Z18. SystemVerilog for the C++ Programmer
절: Z18.4 The two assignments, and when to use which
글:
Z18.4 The two assignments, and when to use which

This is the rule that separates working RTL from RTL that simulates and
 then fails in hardware. C++ has one assignment; SystemVerilog has two and they mean
 different things about time.

[Table 470. Blocking versus non-blocking]
 | = blocking | b -> c, 한 edge 에 한 칸. **맞다.**

always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
 b = a; // b 가 **즉시** a 가 된다
 c = b; // 그래서 c 도 **같은 edge 에** a 가 되어 버린다
end
// 결과: b 와 c 가 둘 다 a. 시프트 레지스터가 아니라 그냥 팬아웃이다.
// 더 나쁜 것: 다른 always 블록이 b 를 읽고 있으면, 그 블록이 이 블록보다
// 먼저 도느냐 나중에 도느냐에 따라 **옛 b 를 보거나 새 b 를 본다.**
// 시뮬레이터가 순서를 정하고, 그 순서는 명세에 없다 -- 그것이 경주다.

// ── 조합 논리에는 = 를 쓴다 ───────────────────────────────────────
always_comb begin
 sum = a + b; // 중간값
 outv = sum + c; // **방금 계산한** sum 을 쓴다 -- 그래서 blocking
end
// non-blocking in
 always_ff, blocking in always_comb, never both in one
 block, and never assign the same signal from two blocks. Every lint tool checks
 it. The generated RTL in Part Z15 obeys it because the HLS tool cannot make this
 mistake — which is one genuine, if unglamorous, advantage of generating RTL.
