절: Z19. The C++ Used for Hardware, Keyword by Keyword — 들어가며
글:
Z19. The C++ Used for Hardware, Keyword by Keyword

The model layer in edu/model/ is about 250 lines of C++,
 and almost every line uses a keyword that means something slightly different when the
 output is a circuit rather than a program. This part goes through them. It assumes you
 can write C++ and explains what each construct costs in hardware, which is
 the part no C++ book covers.

장: Z19. The C++ Used for Hardware, Keyword by Keyword
절: Z19.1 inline — and why it matters more here
글:
Z19.1 inline — and why it matters more here

```
static inline int32_t asr(int32_t v, int n) {
 return (v > n) : (v >> n);
}
```

[Table 475. What inline actually does]
Belief | Reality
“It tells the compiler to inline the function.” | It is a hint , and modern compilers ignore it for inlining decisions. -O2 inlines small functions whether or not you write it.
“It is about speed.” | Its actual required meaning is a linkage rule: it permits the same function to be defined in multiple translation units without a duplicate-symbol error. That is why it is mandatory for a function body in a header.
“In HLS it makes things faster.” | In HLS it changes what hardware is built . An inlined function is flattened into the caller's datapath; a non-inlined one may become a separate module that is shared between call sites, with arbitration logic.

That last row is the hardware-specific part. If four call sites share
 one non-inlined multiply-accumulate, the tool builds one instance and a state machine
 that takes turns — small and slow. Inline them and you get four instances in
 parallel — large and fast. In C++ this is a performance micro-decision; in HLS
 it is an architecture decision.

In edu/model/ everything is static inline in
 headers because the same header is compiled by g++ (where the linkage
 rule is what matters) and by bambu (where full flattening into one
 datapath is what we want). static here means internal linkage — the
 function is private to each translation unit — and combined with
 inline it is the conventional way to put a small helper in a header.

장: Z19. The C++ Used for Hardware, Keyword by Keyword
절: Z19.2 The five meanings of static
글:
Z19.2 The five meanings of static

C++ reused one keyword for several unrelated jobs. Three of them appear
 in the model code, and one of them is a bug waiting to happen in HLS.

[Table 476. static , by position]
Where it appears | What it means | Hardware consequence
On a function at namespace scope static inline int32_t asr(...) | Internal linkage: not visible to other translation units. | None — a linker concept.
On a variable at namespace scope static const int32_t TH[4] = {...} | Internal linkage, plus (with const ) a compile-time-known value. | Large. Constant coefficients let the tool replace multipliers with shift-adds. See Z19.4.
On a local variable inside a function static int count = 0; | One instance, shared by all calls, persisting between them. | Becomes state. In HLS this infers a register or a RAM that survives across invocations — usually not what you meant, and it silently makes a pure function impure.
On a class member | Shared by all objects. | Not used in synthesisable code.
In an anonymous namespace (the modern alternative) | Same as internal linkage for names. | None.

The third row is the trap. A C++ programmer writes
 static inside a function to keep a counter cheaply. In HLS that counter
 becomes a register whose value carries between calls, so the generated block is no
 longer a function of its inputs — and the golden-model comparison that passed in
 C++ can fail in RTL, or worse, pass in both while the block is unusable because two
 instances would interfere. In synthesisable C++, a function-local
 static is almost always a mistake.

장: Z19. The C++ Used for Hardware, Keyword by Keyword
절: Z19.4 Why const on the coefficients is worth hundreds of gates
글:
Z19.4 Why const on the coefficients is worth hundreds of gates

Worked example 82. Constant multiply versus variable multiply

Given. The filter computes a1 * 111. In one version 111 is a static const; in the other it arrives as a function parameter.

Method. A constant multiply can be expanded into shifts and adds at compile time. 111 = 64+32+8+4+2+1, so it is a sum of six shifted copies — or, better, 111 = 128−16−1, which is three terms.

Numbers. Constant: about 2 adders and 1 subtractor of 9–17 bits — roughly 40–50 LUT4 on iCE40. Variable: a full 9×8 array multiplier, roughly 150–200 LUT4, or a hard DSP block where one exists.

The design consequence for a sellable IP: if customers need programmable coefficients, you pay for real multipliers and you must say so in the datasheet. If the coefficients are fixed at build time, you can offer a block a quarter the size. These are two different products, and the difference is one const.

How this is got wrong. The trivial explanation to kill is “the tool is smart.” It is not being smart; it is being given different information. Make the coefficient a parameter and the same tool produces the big version, because it now must handle every possible coefficient value. The measured evidence is in Z15: the tuned design used 97 SB_CARRY and zero hard multipliers, because every multiply had a compile-time-constant operand.

장: Z1. The Two-Member IP Team: You and the Agent
절: Z1. The Two-Member IP Team: You and the Agent — 들어가며

Z1. The Two-Member IP Team: You and the Agent

This volume is written for a specific arrangement: one engineer and
 one automated verification agent, producing IP that is good enough to sell. That is a
 smaller team than any company would assign to the job, and it can work — but
 only if the division of labour is decided deliberately rather than by what happens to
 be convenient. This part sets it out, and every claim about the agent in it is
 measured by running the agent while this page is rendered.

[그림] Figure 63. The division of labour. Everything on the right is mechanically checkable; everything on the left needs a judgement.

장: Z1. The Two-Member IP Team: You and the Agent
절: Z1.1 The rule that decides who does what
글:
Z1.1 The rule that decides who does what

Why the boundary falls where it does

 | Step | Justification
1 | The agent can only act where there is an oracle — something that says right or wrong without a human. | A golden model, a standard's test vectors, a compiler, a timing report.
2 | Where an oracle exists, the agent's work is search plus check , and search with a good oracle is reliable and improves with compute. | This is the regression, the shrink, the repair attempt and the mutation score.
3 | Where no oracle exists, any output must be read by a human, and the failure mode is work that looks right. | Which is the expensive kind of failure , because it is found late.
4 | So: the agent owns everything downstream of a model; you own the model and everything upstream of it. | Reading the specification, deciding what the block should do, deciding which side of a disagreement is wrong — none of these has an oracle.
5 | The corollary is where to invest: make the oracle better and the agent gets better for free. | A stronger golden model, a wider stimulus, a throughput bound, a lint rule — each one extends the region the agent can work in, permanently.

[Table 479. Task by task, and why]
Task | Who | Because
Read the standard, resolve ambiguities | You | No oracle; and the ambiguities are what you will be asked about
Write the bit-accurate golden model | You | It is the oracle. Writing it is how you find out what the specification actually says
Choose the architecture, the word lengths, the parallelism | You | Judgement against cost; Parts X1–X2 give the arithmetic
Write the RTL | You | For now. The agent repairs small defects; it does not architect
Run the regression on every seed, all night | Agent | Pure search against an oracle
Reduce a failure to one stimulus | Agent | Mechanical, and it is the difference between a debuggable and an undebuggable report
Attempt a single-edit repair | Agent | Bounded search; three gates bound the false-accept rate
Measure the mutation score | Agent | The number that says whether the suite bites — and the escapes say where the stimulus is thin
Measure throughput against a stated bound | Agent | A value-only regression cannot see a block getting slower
Decide whether an escape is an equivalent mutant | You | A machine cannot decide behavioural equivalence in general
Decide which side of a disagreement is wrong | You | Only the specification settles it, and only you have read it
Talk to the customer, price the work, scope it | You | Part Y5

The temptation to let the agent write the model is
 the one thing that destroys the arrangement. If the model and the RTL come from
 the same process, they share its misunderstandings and their agreement proves nothing
 — this is the independence argument of Part Y11, and it does not change
 because one of the two authors is a machine. The agent may write stimulus, may
 write checkers derived from the model, and may repair RTL; it must not be the
 source of the reference. Your reading of the specification is the asset the
 business is built on, and it is the one part that cannot be delegated.

An escape is a finding, not a defect in the score: it is either an equivalent mutant or a place the stimulus does not reach, and both need a human to say which. Every block reads 100 % with zero unjudged escapes, which is the state the release gate of Part Z3 requires — a column that is constant because the bar was met, not because the measurement is stuck. 장: Z1. The Two-Member IP Team: You and the Agent
절: Z1.3 A worked morning: what the escapes actually told us
글:
Z1.3 A worked morning: what the escapes actually told us

The mutation score is not a grade; it is a pointer. The following
 happened while this book's own register-file block was being built, and it is the
 clearest illustration in the book of why the number is worth measuring.

[Table 482. From a score to two real bugs]
Step | What happened | What it cost
Regression written, all green | 400 APB accesses, no mismatch | —
Mutation score run: 58.3 % | Five escapes, all pointing at the same place | 20 minutes
Escapes read | r | hw_set → r ^ hw_set not caught — because hw_set was tied to zero, and 0 behaves identically under both | The W1C and RC paths had never executed
Testbench fixed to pulse the hardware inputs | Plus a directed sequence: set three bits, read, clear one, check the other two survive | an hour
Regression re-run: two failures | Both were real generator bugs — an ID register that could not hold a constant, and an RC register cleared during the APB setup phase because penable was missing from the read term | —
Fixed, re-scored | 100 % (13 of 13) | Two bugs that would otherwise have been found by a customer's driver

Note what the green regression was worth before the
 mutation score ran. It was not wrong — those 400 accesses really did match
 — and it was nearly worthless, because the stimulus never reached the logic that
 was broken. This is the difference between ‘the tests pass’ and
 ‘the tests would fail if the design were wrong’, and only the second
 is evidence. For a one-person house it is also the only affordable substitute for a
 verification team's scepticism: you cannot review your own work with fresh eyes, and
 the mutation score does not need fresh eyes.

Problem. You are one person. How much of the day should go to verification?
Solution. More than feels reasonable, and the arithmetic from Part Y1's effort table says roughly how much: verification and everything downstream of RTL is about three quarters of the work in a sellable block. But the useful answer for a day rather than a project is a shape, not a fraction. Verification infrastructure is built once and runs forever, so it belongs early and its cost is amortised; the agent runs it while you sleep, so the marginal cost of running verification is zero and only the marginal cost of improving it is real. That changes the allocation: spend your hours on the golden model, the stimulus and the checkers — the things that decide what the agent can catch — and almost none on running or triaging, which the agent does. A practical daily target is that every session leaves the oracle stronger than it found it: one more property checked, one more corner in the stimulus, one more bound measured. That compounds, and it is the only thing in a one-person house that does.

Z20. The Free Toolchain, Command by Command

Every number in Parts Z14–Z19 was produced by tools that
 cost nothing and install from a package manager. A one-person design house can take a
 block from C++ to a placed-and-routed netlist with a timing number without a single
 licence. This part is how, command by command, with the real output each one
 produces.

[Table 483. The toolchain, as measured in this container]
Tool | Version here | Job | Licence
Verilator | 5.020 | Lint, and fast C++-based simulation | LGPL-3 / Artistic-2
Icarus Verilog | 12.0 | Event-driven simulation of the full language | GPL-2
Yosys | 0.33 | Synthesis: RTL → gate netlist | ISC
nextpnr-ice40 | 0.6 | Place and route, static timing | ISC
PandA Bambu | 2024.10 | High-level synthesis: C/C++ → RTL | GPL-3
GCC | g++ -O2 | Compiles the golden model | GPL-3

Two things are missing from that list and it is worth being honest about
 them. There is no free sign-off static timing analyser for ASICs (OpenSTA
 exists but was not available here), and there is no free formal equivalence
 checker. For FPGA work the gap does not bite; for an ASIC tape-out it does, and
 Part Y13 covers what that means commercially.

장: Z20. The Free Toolchain, Command by Command
절: Z20.1 Step one: lint, because it is the cheapest
글:
Z20.1 Step one: lint, because it is the cheapest

```
verilator --lint-only -Wall --top-module fir4_hand edu/model/fir4_hand.v
```

[Table 484. What the flags do]
Flag | Meaning | Why
--lint-only | Parse and check; do not build a simulator. | Runs in well under a second. This is the whole point.
-Wall | Enable all the style and width warnings. | The default set is too quiet. -Wall is what industry actually turns on.
--top-module | Name the top of the hierarchy. | Without it, a file with several modules gives confusing 'no top' errors.

The warnings that matter most, and what each is telling you:

[Table 485. Verilator warnings you will actually see]
Warning | Means | Take it seriously?
WIDTHEXPAND / WIDTHTRUNC | An assignment or operation changes bit width implicitly. | Yes, always. This is the class of bug Z16.7 spent five derivation steps preventing. Every silent truncation lives here.
UNUSEDSIGNAL | A signal is declared or driven and never read. | Usually. Either it is dead logic (remove it) or you forgot to connect something. Suppress deliberately with a comment when a port is genuinely reserved.
LATCH | Combinational block does not assign in all paths. | Yes. Almost never intended. See Z18.5.
MULTIDRIVEN | Two blocks drive one signal. | Yes. This is a hard bug: x in simulation, contention in silicon.
BLKSEQ / COMBDLY | Blocking assignment in sequential logic, or vice versa. | Yes. The race of Z18.4.
DECLFILENAME | Module name does not match file name. | Cosmetic, but fix it — every build system assumes the convention.
GENUNNAMED | Unnamed generate block. | Fix it. Hierarchical names shift when loop bounds change.
SYNCASYNCNET | A net is used as both sync and async reset. | Investigate. Usually a real reset-architecture problem.

Worked example 83. Reading a lint report on generated code

Given. Running the command above on Bambu's generated fir_top.v returns 19 warnings: 7 WIDTHEXPAND, 6 UNUSEDSIGNAL, 3 WIDTHTRUNC, 1 UNUSEDPARAM, 1 SYNCASYNCNET, 1 DECLFILENAME.

Method. Separate warnings that indicate a defect from warnings that indicate a generator's house style.

Numbers. Effectively all 19 are style, not defects. Generated RTL uses parameterised width-adapter modules, so WIDTHEXPAND and UNUSEDSIGNAL appear wherever a generic module is instantiated narrower than its maximum.

The same reasoning applies to hand-written RTL with a different conclusion: there, a clean -Wall report is achievable and should be a release gate. edu/model/fir4_hand.v is clean.

How this is got wrong. The wrong conclusion is “lint is useless on generated code.” The right one is that you must lint the generator's output once, triage it, and then watch for new warning types. A WIDTHTRUNC that was not there yesterday is a real signal; the same six UNUSEDSIGNAL every build is noise. Counting warnings by type — which is what synth.sh prints — makes the difference visible.

장: Z20. The Free Toolchain, Command by Command
절: Z20.3 Step three: synthesise with Yosys
글:
Z20.3 Step three: synthesise with Yosys

```
yosys -p "read_verilog -sv edu/model/fir4_hand.v; \
 hierarchy -check -top fir4_hand; \
 proc; opt; fsm; opt; memory; opt; techmap; opt; \
 stat"
```

[Table 486. The Yosys script, pass by pass]
Pass | What it does
read_verilog -sv | Parse. -sv enables SystemVerilog; without it always_ff is a syntax error.
hierarchy -check -top M | Resolve the module tree from M downward. -check makes a missing module an error rather than a black box — without it, a typo in a module name silently synthesises to nothing.
proc | Convert always blocks into multiplexers and registers. This is where <= becomes a flip-flop.
opt | Constant folding, dead-code removal, simplification. Run it between every other pass; it is cheap.
fsm | Detect state machines and re-encode them.
memory | Turn array accesses into RAM primitives.
techmap | Map to generic gates ( $_AND_ , $_XOR_ , …).
stat | Print the cell count. Do not pass -q to yosys — it swallows this output, which was measured here the hard way.

The real output for the hand-written filter:

```
=== fir4_hand ===

 Number of wires: 268
 Number of wire bits: 1681
 Number of public wires: 14
 Number of public wire bits: 97
 Number of cells: 780
 $_AND_ 340
 $_MUX_ 15
 $_NOT_ 10
 $_OR_ 142
 $_SDFF_PP0_ 9
 $_XOR_ 264
```

Reading that report without guessing

 | Step | Justification
1 | $_SDFF_PP0_ × 9 — nine synchronous flip-flops, positive edge, positive reset, reset-to-0. | The design has exactly nine state bits: done_port (1) plus return_port (8). The number matching the count you expected is the first thing to check — a surprise here means inferred state you did not intend.
2 | $_XOR_ × 264 dominates the combinational logic. | XOR is the sum output of a full adder (Z17.6). Two 9-bit adds plus a 17-bit add plus the constant-multiply shift-add network accounts for it.
3 | $_AND_ × 340 and $_OR_ × 142 are the carry logic. | cout = (a AND b) OR (cin AND (a XOR b)) — two ANDs and an OR per bit.
4 | $_MUX_ × 15 is the saturation. | Two comparisons selecting between three 8-bit values. This is the gate-level price of saturating rather than wrapping, as Z17.7 predicted.
5 | But 780 generic cells is not the area of the design. | These are technology-independent gates. The device has 4-input lookup tables and a dedicated carry chain, so the mapping in the next step collapses this dramatically — 780 generic cells became 257 iCE40 cells. Never quote generic cell counts as area.

Now the numbers mean something physical. SB_LUT4 is a

절: Z20.5 Step five: place, route, and get a real frequency
글:
Z20.5 Step five: place, route, and get a real frequency

```
nextpnr-ice40 --hx8k --package ct256 --json fir4_hand.json \
 --pcf-allow-unconstrained --placer heap --freq 300 --seed 1
```

[Table 487. The flags that change the answer]
Flag | Meaning | Why it matters
--hx8k --package ct256 | Device and package. | Pin count is a real constraint. Measured here: up5k/sg48 has 39 I/O and refused to place a design needing 43, with Unable to find a placement location . That is not a quality problem with the design.
--pcf-allow-unconstrained | Allow pins with no physical assignment. | Needed when you are measuring a block rather than building a board.
--placer heap | Analytic placer. | Better and more repeatable than the default SA placer.
--freq 300 | Target frequency in MHz. | Without this the target defaults to 12 MHz and the tool stops optimising the moment it passes — the reported Fmax then reflects routing luck, not the design.
--seed N | Placement random seed. | Run three and report the spread. A single seed is a sample of one.

```
Info: ICESTORM_LC: 211/ 7680 2%
Info: Max frequency for clock 'clock$SB_IO_IN_$glb_clk': 455.79 MHz (PASS at 12.00 MHz)
```

Worked example 84. Why that 455.79 MHz was not usable and 47 MHz was

Given. Placing the hand-written filter directly gives 455.79 MHz. Wrapping it in a registered timing shell and re-placing gives 47.4 MHz. Same design.

Method. Ask which paths the tool is measuring in each case.

Numbers. Without the shell the design has 9 flops, all at the output. The only register-to-register paths are trivial, and the real datapath runs from an input pin to those flops — unconstrained, therefore unreported. With the shell, every path starts and ends at a flop, so the 47.4 MHz is the actual combinational depth of the filter.

The general rule: a frequency number is meaningless unless you can say which two registers the path runs between. Ask that question of every Fmax anyone quotes you, including your own.

How this is got wrong. The 455.79 MHz figure is stable across seeds and looks entirely credible. A reproducible measurement of the wrong path is the most dangerous kind, because every instinct says to trust it. What exposed it was a contradiction, not a tool warning: adding pipeline registers made the reported frequency fall, and more registers cannot make a design slower.

[Table 488. Two things the script does that look fussy and are not]
Choice | What went wrong without it
Tool output goes to a file , then is filtered — never piped straight into head . | head closes the pipe, the tool dies of SIGPIPE, and the exit code comes back 141 . A lint that passed and a lint that crashed became indistinguishable. Measured here.
Cell counts are extracted from inside the stat block, not by grepping the whole log. | Yosys prints Generating RTLIL representation for module \SB_LUT4 while loading its cell library. A naive grep SB_LUT4 counts those lines as if they were cells.

Both are the same failure in different clothes: a measurement
 harness that reports a plausible number when it has actually failed. That is the
 defect this whole book is organised against, and it turns out to be just as easy to
 build into a twelve-line shell script as into a verification environment.

장: Z21. Building Protocol IP When You Cannot Get the Spec
절: Z21. Building Protocol IP When You Cannot Get the Spec — 들어가며
글:
Z21. Building Protocol IP When You Cannot Get the Spec

Every previous part of this volume built a block whose definition was
 ours to choose. A protocol block is different: its correctness is defined by a
 document somebody else wrote, and for the protocols a design house most wants to sell
 into — MIPI CSI-2, PCIe, Ethernet — that document is expensive,
 membership-gated, or both.

This part is about what to do then. It is not a workaround chapter. The discipline
 it describes — separate what you can prove from what you have assumed, and
 publish the boundary — is the same discipline you need with the spec in
 hand, because having the document does not mean you implemented it correctly.

장: Z21. Building Protocol IP When You Cannot Get the Spec
절: Z21.1 The honest starting position
글:
Z21.1 The honest starting position

The container this book is built in has no outbound network: a
 CONNECT to ieee802.org returns 403. So the normative tables
 for 8b/10b and the MIPI packet-header ECC were not available while the blocks in
 Parts Z22 and Z23 were written. That is stated first, because everything
 else in those parts has to be read against it.

There are exactly three things you can do in that position, and only the third is
 defensible:

[Table 489. Three responses to a missing specification]
Response | What it produces | Verdict
Write the constants from memory and ship | A block that looks finished and is wrong in ways nobody will notice until integration. | No. This part demonstrates concretely why — three sets of remembered constants were wrong, and one was not even a valid code.
Refuse to build anything | Nothing. The structure, the verification harness and the microarchitecture are all independent of the exact table values. | No. It throws away the 90 % of the work that does not depend on the document.
Build it, prove everything provable, and publish the boundary | A block that is correct by construction on every property you can state, with a written list of what remains unverified and how to close it. | Yes. This is what Parts Z22–Z23 do.

장: Z21. Building Protocol IP When You Cannot Get the Spec
절: Z21.2 What “provable without the document” means
글:
Z21.2 What “provable without the document” means

A protocol constant is not arbitrary. It was chosen to make the code
 satisfy properties — and those properties are usually stated in the open
 literature even when the tables are not. That gives you a check with real teeth:
 assert the properties the constants exist to provide, and test them
 exhaustively.

[Table 490. The two blocks, and what each property buys]
Block | Property asserted | What a wrong constant would do
8b/10b | Bijective within each running disparity | Two data bytes encode to the same codeword → the link cannot decode at all.
 | Running disparity stays in {−1, +1} | DC wander on an AC-coupled link → the receiver's slicer drifts off centre.
 | No more than 5 identical bits in a row, across codeword boundaries | The CDR loses lock. This is the property that caught two of the three defects below.
 | The comma pattern never occurs in data | The receiver aligns to a false byte boundary and every subsequent byte is garbage.
24+6 ECC | All 29 single-error syndromes distinct and non-zero | Two different single-bit errors look identical → the decoder ‘corrects’ the wrong bit.
 | No double-error syndrome equals a single-error syndrome | A 2-bit error is silently ‘fixed’ into a 3-bit error. Worse than no ECC.

Every one of those is checkable by enumeration on a laptop in under a
 second, and every one of them failed at least once during this work.

기억하고 있던 CSI-2 ECC 마스크 | 신드롬 30 개 중 서로 다른 것이 27 개. 단일오류 정정 부호조차 아니었다. | 쓰기 전에 신드롬 distinctness 를 셌다. 그래서 **안 실었다**
ecc24_dec 의 전체패리티 | 다시 부호화해 여섯째 비트를 비교했더니 신드롬 자신의 패리티가 섞였다. 신드롬 무게가 홀수인 단일오류 90/180 이 이중오류로 오인됐다. | 전수 단일오류 확인이 절반 실패
tb.v 의 자극 | valid 가 0 인 구간을 아예 안 밟아, code_valid 를 가짜로 띄우는 변이가 통과했다. | 변이 점수 71.4 % 의 탈출 하나. 놀림 사이클을 관찰하게 고쳐 100 % 가 됐다

Worked example 85. The defect that would have shipped

Given. The MIPI CSI-2 packet-header ECC parity masks, written from memory, were about to go into both the C++ model and the RTL.

Method. Before writing any code with them, count the syndromes: each of the 24 data bits and 6 parity bits must produce a distinct, non-zero syndrome, or the code cannot even correct single errors.

Numbers. 27 distinct syndromes out of the 30 required, and 96 pairs where a double-bit error is indistinguishable from a single-bit error.

The check that caught it is four lines of Python and it ran before any Verilog existed. The cost of not running it would have been discovered at a customer's integration bench, months later, as ‘your ECC sometimes makes things worse’.

How this is got wrong. The tempting reading is “close enough, it is mostly right.” It is not mostly right — it is not a single-error-correcting code at all. Three of the 24 data bits share a syndrome with another bit, so roughly one single-bit header error in ten would be ‘corrected’ by flipping the wrong bit, turning a recoverable error into a corrupted packet length. A block like this passes a random-data regression perfectly, because random data contains no bit errors.

장: Z21. Building Protocol IP When You Cannot Get the Spec
절: Z21.4 The pattern in the three 8b/10b defects
글:
Z21.4 The pattern in the three 8b/10b defects

Three separate defects in the encoder all had the same root, and it was
 not a typo. It was a compression rule that was really an unstated hypothesis.

How a good idea became three bugs

 | Step | Justification
1 | The 8b/10b tables have two columns — one per running disparity. Writing both invites a typo in one column only. | A typo in one column is invisible to any check that only exercises the other.
2 | Observation: most second-column entries are the bitwise complement of the first, and entries with zero disparity appear in both columns unchanged. | True for the majority of entries, which is what made it convincing.
3 | So: store one column, derive the other. Half the table, half the typo surface. | This reasoning is correct as far as it goes, and the comment in the first draft said exactly this.
4 | But ‘zero disparity implies one codeword’ is a hypothesis, not a fact. | A 4-bit code with two ones and two zeros has disparity zero — and so does its complement. Both are legal on disparity grounds, so disparity alone cannot pick one.
5 | What picks between them is run length , not disparity. | D.x.3 is 1100 after one six-bit prefix and 0011 after another, because 001111 followed by 1100 puts six ones in a row and breaks the CDR.
6 | The compression therefore collapsed nine genuinely-distinct table entries into one each, and the property check found it: 1082 run-length violations and 2048 false commas. | Then, after fixing the 4-bit tables, 556 violations remained — the same hypothesis was also wrong for exactly one 5b/6b entry, D.07 ( 111000 / 000111 ).

The lesson generalises past 8b/10b: every scheme for not writing
 something down twice encodes an assumption about why the two copies agree. When
 that assumption is right, the scheme removes a whole class of error — the
 register-map generator of Part Z4 and the single-C++-source flow of
 Part Z14 both work exactly this way. When it is wrong, it replaces typos with a
 systematic error, which is much harder to see, because every instance is
 wrong in the same plausible way.

The difference between the two cases is not cleverness. It is whether you checked.

장: Z21. Building Protocol IP When You Cannot Get the Spec
절: Z21.5 The provenance ledger
글:
Z21.5 The provenance ledger

The repository already requires this for paper citations
 (Gate G022): every claim carries how well it was verified. Protocol constants get
 the same treatment, because they are the same kind of claim.

[Table 492. Confirmation level for every constant in edu/proto]
Constant | Level | What that means here
8b/10b 5b/6b and 3b/4b tables | property-proven, not source-verified | All four defining properties hold exhaustively over all 528 codewords and every codeword pair. The normative tables were not available for comparison.
8b/10b well-known codewords (K.28.5, D21.5, D10.2, …) | corroborated | Seven widely-quoted codewords match exactly. Weak evidence — the same memory produced both — but it is independent of the property proof.
K.28.x selection (K.23.7 etc. omitted) | scoped out, deliberately | Only K.28.x is implemented. Stated in the datasheet rather than left for a customer to discover.
24+6 ECC parity masks | constructed, explicitly not MIPI | A valid SEC-DED built from first principles and proven exhaustively. It is not byte-compatible with CSI-2 and the header of ecc24.h says so in the first paragraph.
Ethernet FCS CRC-32 (Part Z1) | independently verified | Checked against Python's zlib.crc32 , an implementation written by somebody else from the standard. This is the strongest level available and it is available only because a free reference implementation exists.

Notice how much the last row differs from the rest. Ethernet's CRC-32
 is fully pinned down not because the Ethernet standard is easier to read, but because
 somebody shipped a free, widely-used implementation of it. When you are
 choosing which protocol block to build first as a one-person house, the existence of
 an independent reference implementation is worth more than the clarity of the
 specification — it is the difference between “proven” and
 “argued”.

절: Z21.6 What to write in the datasheet
글:
Z21.6 What to write in the datasheet

All of the above is worthless if it stays in a commit message. The
 boundary between proven and assumed belongs on the page the customer reads, phrased

```
## 확인 수준 (Verification status)

이 블록은 다음을 **전수로** 확인했다:
 * 코드워드 528 개가 RD 마다 서로 다르다 (전단사)

 * 같은 비트가 5 개를 넘게 이어지지 않는다 -- **코드워드 이음 전부에서**
 * 콤마 무늬가 데이터 흐름에 나타나지 않는다

이 블록은 다음을 **확인하지 못했다**:

 -> 상호운용 시험 전에 그 표로 대조할 것. 구조는 그대로 쓸 수 있고

 * K.23.7 · K.27.7 · K.29.7 · K.30.7 (일부러 뺐다)

```

A customer who reads that knows exactly what they are buying and what
 work remains. A customer who reads “IEEE 802.3 compliant” on a block that
 was never compared to IEEE 802.3 finds out later, and tells other people.

There is a commercial argument here too, and it is not the obvious one. Publishing
 the boundary does not make the block look weaker — it makes it look
 measured, and it is the only version of the claim that survives contact with
 a reviewer. Every vendor says “compliant”. Almost none says which of their
 properties were checked by enumeration and which by reading.

장: Z22. 8b/10b — One Block, Two Markets
절: Z22. 8b/10b — One Block, Two Markets — 들어가며
글:
Z22. 8b/10b — One Block, Two Markets

Of everything a one-person design house could build first, an 8b/10b
 encoder is unusually well chosen, for a reason that has nothing to do with the
 technology: the same block sells into PCIe and into Ethernet. PCIe Gen1 and
 Gen2 use it as the physical-layer line code; so does 1000BASE-X, the gigabit Ethernet
 PCS. So do SATA, DisplayPort, Fibre Channel and USB 3 Gen1. One verification
 effort, one datasheet, several customers who do not compete with each other.

장: Z22. 8b/10b — One Block, Two Markets
절: Z22.1 Where it sits
글:
Z22.1 Where it sits

[그림] Figure 64. The transmit chain (top) and receive chain (bottom). Our encoder is the last
 digital stage before serialisation. The two blocks that depend on it most are drawn
 on the receive side: the CDR needs the transitions 8b/10b guarantees, and comma
 alignment works only because the comma pattern cannot occur in data.

Read that diagram as a list of obligations rather than a picture. The
 CDR cannot recover a clock from a long run of identical bits, so the code must bound
 run length. The AC coupling capacitors in the channel cannot pass DC, so the code must
 bound the imbalance between ones and zeros. The deserialiser has no idea where a byte
 starts, so the code must provide a pattern that means ‘here’ and cannot be
 forged by data. Each of those is one of the four properties Part Z21 proved.

장: Z22. 8b/10b — One Block, Two Markets
절: Z22.2 What the code does, in one worked byte
글:
Z22.2 What the code does, in one worked byte

Encoding 0x00 with running disparity −1

 | Step | Justification
1 | Split the byte into low 5 bits and high 3 bits: 0x00 → x = 0, y = 0. This is written D0.0. | The code is built from a 5b/6b stage and a 3b/4b stage. The naming D x . y is universal in the literature.
2 | Look up x = 0 in the 5b/6b table for RD = −1: 100111 . | Four ones and two zeros, so its disparity is +2.
3 | Running disparity was −1; adding +2 gives +1. | This is why the table for RD = −1 holds the codeword with positive disparity: it pulls the imbalance back toward zero.
4 | Now look up y = 0 in the 3b/4b table, using the updated disparity RD = +1: 0100 . | One one and three zeros, disparity −2. The 3b/4b stage sees the disparity after the 6-bit stage, not the disparity the byte started with — a detail that is easy to get wrong and that the property check catches immediately.
5 | RD becomes +1 − 2 = −1, and the codeword is 100111   0100 . | Back where we started, which is exactly what bounded running disparity means.
6 | Check the result: 1001110100 has five ones and five zeros, and its longest run is two. | Verified against the published value for D0.0 as one of the seven corroboration vectors.

[그림] Figure 65. Why the code exists, drawn. An all-zero byte sent raw (top, shown held) offers
 the receiver's clock-recovery loop no transitions at all. The same byte encoded
 (middle) carries five transitions in ten bits. The encoder's job is to make every
 byte look like the middle trace.

장: Z22. 8b/10b — One Block, Two Markets
절: Z22.3 The four properties, proven
글:
Z22.3 The four properties, proven

Part Z21 explained why these are the right things to check. Here
 is what they came back as, over all 528 codewords and every ordered pair of codewords
 that can actually follow one another:

[Table 493. Exhaustive property check, edu/proto/proto_check.cpp]
Property | Why the code needs it | Result
P1 — bijective within each disparity | Otherwise two bytes share a codeword and the link cannot decode. | 0 collisions
P2 — running disparity stays in {−1, +1} | DC balance on an AC-coupled channel. | 0 excursions
P3 — at most 5 identical bits in a row | The CDR needs transitions to hold lock. | longest run 5 , violations 0
P4 — comma never appears in data | Byte alignment depends on the comma being unforgeable. | 0 occurrences
Not degenerate | A check that only ever sees a few values proves nothing. | 456 distinct codewords of 1024

The third row is worth dwelling on, because it is the one that cannot
 be checked by looking at a codeword. A run of six can straddle a boundary: each
 codeword is individually fine and the pair is not. That is why the checker enumerates
 pairs, filtered by which disparity each one can follow — and it is why
 the two table-compression defects of Part Z21 were invisible until it ran.

Worked example 86. Why the longest run is exactly 5 and not 4

Given. P3 reports a longest run of 5, and that is a pass rather than a failure.

Method. Ask what produces the run of 5 and whether it is avoidable.

Numbers. The comma itself. K.28.5 is 0011111010 — five ones in a row, by construction. Any code that also bounded data runs at 5 without exception would have no pattern left that data cannot produce.

This is the general shape of the run-length/alignment trade. The comma must be distinguishable from data, so it must do something data cannot. Making the bound tighter for data is what buys the comma its distinctiveness.

How this is got wrong. The tempting reading of ‘longest run = 5’ is that the design only just passes and a small change might push it to 6. The opposite is true: the 5 is designed in, it occurs only in K codes, and the data codewords are strictly better behaved. Reporting the maximum without saying where it comes from would leave a reader with the wrong impression of the margin.

장: Z22. 8b/10b — One Block, Two Markets
절: Z22.4 The circuit
글:
Z22.4 The circuit

The encoder is almost entirely combinational. There is exactly one bit
 of state in the whole block.

[그림] Figure 66. The datapath. Two table lookups (which synthesise to multiplexers), two
 popcount-and-compare blocks to update the disparity, and one flip-flop holding it.
 The 3b/4b stage is selected by rd_mid — the disparity after 
 the 6-bit stage — which is the sequencing the worked example in Z22.2 walked
 through.

Why the running disparity register is one bit wide

 | Step | Justification
1 | Running disparity is conventionally described as a signed accumulator. | That is how the literature explains it, and it invites an implementation with a width and a saturation question.
2 | But P2 proves it only ever takes the values −1 and +1. | Every codeword has disparity −2, 0 or +2, and the table selection always moves it back toward zero.
3 | Two possible values need exactly one bit: 0 means −1, 1 means +1. | The accumulator, its width, and its saturation logic all disappear.
4 | So the entire sequential state of an 8b/10b encoder is one flip-flop. | Measured: the synthesised block has 13 flip-flops — code 10 + rd 1 + code_valid 1 + err 1. Exactly one of them is the protocol state.
5 | Knowing an invariant is what bought that. | The proof did not just check the design; it simplified it. This is the usual return on proving a property rather than assuming it.

장: Z22. 8b/10b — One Block, Two Markets
절: Z22.5 The one-bit-state rule, in code

장: Z22. 8b/10b — One Block, Two Markets
절: Z22.6 Verification
글:
Z22.6 Verification

[Table 494. What was run against the encoder]
Check | Result | What it establishes
Exhaustive property proof (C++) | P1–P4 all pass, 528 codewords | The code is internally consistent and does what 8b/10b exists to do.
Published codeword spot-check | 7 of 7 match | Weak but independent corroboration that these are the tables.
RTL vs C++ golden, streamed | 3000 vectors, 0 wrong, 520 distinct outputs | The hand-written Verilog agrees with the independently written C++, including the disparity carried between codewords .
Self-check (corrupt one golden value) | 통과 | The comparison can actually fail. Without this the row above means nothing.
Mutation score | 16/16 = 100 %, 5 judged equivalent | The tests bite . This is a different question from ‘do the tests pass’.

The stream matters more than the count. The golden generator threads
 running disparity from one vector to the next, so the expected value on line 2000
 depends on every line before it. A single disagreement anywhere makes everything after
 it wrong — the regression cannot quietly pass with a broken state machine, which
 is the failure mode a per-codeword test would have.

Worked example 87. What the mutation score found that 3000 passing vectors did not

Given. The regression passed 3000 streamed vectors with 0 mismatches. Mutation scoring then reported 71.4 % with six escapes.

Method. Look at each surviving mutant and ask why the tests cannot see it.

Numbers. Five were provably equivalent — OR replaced by XOR in a condition whose terms are mutually exclusive, verified over all 32×2 = 64 inputs with zero differences. The sixth was real: code_valid <= valid & ~bad_k mutated to | survived.

The fix was to observe code_valid during a deliberate idle beat after each transaction, which took four lines and moved the score to 100 %. This is the same lesson as the throughput mutant in Part Z1: a regression measures what you told it to look at, and mutation scoring is how you find out what you forgot.

How this is got wrong. The real one is not a subtle bug — the mutant asserts code_valid on every idle cycle, which would break any downstream consumer immediately. It survived because the testbench never looked at an idle cycle. The stimulus drove a transaction every beat, so the entire idle path was unexercised. No amount of additional random data would have found it.

장: Z22. 8b/10b — One Block, Two Markets
절: Z22.7 What it costs
글:
Z22.7 What it costs

[Table 495. Synthesis and place-and-route, iCE40 HX8K]
Measure | Value | Note
Cells (standalone) | 91 | yosys synth_ice40
SB_LUT4 | 74 | The two table multiplexers dominate
SB_CARRY | 4 | The popcount adders
Flip-flops | 13 | code 10 + rd 1 + code_valid 1 + err 1
ICESTORM_LC (with timing shell) | 106 | Includes the shell's input registers
F max | 86.3 / 84.9 / 86.3 MHz | Three placer seeds; spread under 2 %
Verilator -Wall | 0 warnings | Clean, not suppressed

74 LUTs and 13 flip-flops for a block that sits in the datapath of
 every PCIe Gen2 lane in the world. But the frequency is the number that decides what
 this block is actually good for, and it is worth doing that arithmetic rather than
 assuming.

Worked example 88. Is this fast enough to sell?

Given. The encoder reaches 84.9 MHz on iCE40 HX8K at one byte per clock. 1000BASE-X carries 1 Gb/s of payload; PCIe Gen2 runs 5 GT/s per lane and 8b/10b passes 8 payload bits per 10 transmitted.

Method. Convert each protocol's payload rate into the byte rate the encoder must accept, then compare.

Numbers. 1000BASE-X needs 1 Gb/s ÷ 8 = 125 Mbyte/s. PCIe Gen2 needs 5 GT/s × 8/10 ÷ 8 = 500 Mbyte/s per lane. At one byte per clock this block delivers 84.9 Mbyte/s — 68 % of gigabit Ethernet and 17 % of one PCIe Gen2 lane. It meets neither.

The fix is architectural, not a matter of squeezing the timing. Encoding two bytes per clock gives 170 Mbyte/s, which clears 1000BASE-X with margin; the two encoders are independent except that the second must take the first's updated disparity, so the disparity path becomes the critical path. PCIe Gen2 needs six bytes per clock at this frequency, which on this fabric is not the right answer — that part belongs on a faster process.

How this is got wrong. The tempting sentence to write was ‘comfortably past gigabit Ethernet’ — it was in the first draft of this page, and it was wrong by a factor of 1.5. 84.9 MHz sounds fast, and a block being small and clean invites the assumption that it is also fast enough. Neither area nor cleanliness implies throughput; only the arithmetic does. The same draft also multiplied 84.88 by 8 and got 686 instead of 679.

So the honest positioning is: on this FPGA, at one byte per clock, the
 block is a demonstration rather than a shippable PHY. Widened to two bytes per clock
 it is a plausible 1000BASE-X part. PCIe Gen2 is a different process, not a different
 day of optimisation. A datasheet that says that is more useful than one that quotes
 84.9 MHz and leaves the division to the reader.

장: Z23. The Packet Header ECC — Why Headers Get More Than Payloads
절: Z23. The Packet Header ECC — Why Headers Get More Than Payloads — 들어가며
글:
Z23. The Packet Header ECC — Why Headers Get More Than Payloads

A MIPI CSI-2 short packet is four bytes: one Data Identifier, two Word
 Count, one ECC. A long packet adds a payload and a 16-bit CRC at the end. So the
 header gets an error-correcting code and the payload gets a merely
 error-detecting one, and the header's code costs a quarter of the header's own
 size.

That asymmetry looks wasteful until you ask what each failure costs. This part
 builds the header code, proves it, and puts it on silicon.

장: Z23. The Packet Header ECC — Why Headers Get More Than Payloads
절: Z23.1 Why the header is worth more protection
글:
Z23.1 Why the header is worth more protection

[그림] Figure 67. The camera path. The receiver must read Word Count out of the header to know
 where the payload ends — and therefore where the next packet begins.

Why a 1-bit header error is not a 1-bit problem

 | Step | Justification
1 | The header's Word Count says how many payload bytes follow. | The receiver has no other way to find the packet boundary; CSI-2 packets are not self-delimiting.
2 | A single bit flipped in Word Count changes that length — by 1, or by 32768 if it lands in the top bit. | Binary weighting means the damage is not proportional to the number of bits flipped.
3 | The receiver then looks for the next packet header at the wrong offset. | It reads payload bytes as a header, whose ECC will not check, whose Word Count is garbage.
4 | The error does not stop. Every subsequent packet in the frame is misaligned. | One bit has cost an entire video frame, and possibly re-synchronisation time beyond it.
5 | Whereas a single bit flipped in the payload corrupts one pixel. | The CRC flags the packet as bad; the frame is imperfect but its structure survives. An ISP can interpolate one pixel.
6 | Therefore: correct the header, merely detect on the payload. | The cost asymmetry is thousands to one, so the protection asymmetry is justified. This is the same reasoning that puts ECC on DRAM address lines before data lines.

장: Z23. The Packet Header ECC — Why Headers Get More Than Payloads
절: Z23.2 What SEC-DED means, precisely
글:
Z23.2 What SEC-DED means, precisely

[Table 497. Three codes, three guarantees]
Code | 1-bit error | 2-bit error | Cost for 24 data bits
Parity (1 bit) | detected | missed | 1 bit
Hamming SEC (5 bits) | corrected | miscorrected — silently turned into a 3-bit error | 5 bits
Extended Hamming SEC-DED (6 bits) | corrected | detected, not corrected | 6 bits

The middle row is the trap, and it is why the sixth bit is not
 optional. A plain Hamming code always produces a syndrome that names some bit, so
 given a 2-bit error it confidently flips a third one. You end up worse off than with
 no ECC at all. The extra overall-parity bit is what lets the decoder say “I do
 not know” — the same distinction this repository insists on everywhere
 else, here implemented in six wires.

Worked example 89. How one extra bit buys double-error detection

Given. 5 Hamming parity bits give each of the 30 bit positions a distinct 5-bit syndrome. Add a 6th bit that is the parity of the entire codeword.

Method. Work out what each error class does to the syndrome and to the overall parity, separately.

Numbers. A single error flips an odd number of bits, so overall parity becomes 1, and the syndrome is non-zero and names the bit. A double error flips an even number, so overall parity returns to 0, while the syndrome (the XOR of two distinct non-zero syndromes) is still non-zero. So syndrome non-zero with parity 0 is a signature no single error can produce.

That bug is instructive because it is conservative: it never corrupts data, it just declines to fix things it could have fixed. In the field it would look like an unexplained doubling of the dropped-frame rate, with no corrupted output to point at — the kind of defect that gets blamed on the cable for a year.

How this is got wrong. The decoder must compute overall parity directly from the received codeword, not by re-encoding the received data and comparing the 6th bit. Re-encoding folds the syndrome's own parity into the comparison: the result is 1 XOR parity(syndrome), which is 0 for every data bit whose syndrome has odd weight. Measured — the first version of ecc24_dec did exactly this and reported 90 of 180 single errors as double errors, i.e. refused to correct half of the correctable ones.

장: Z23. The Packet Header ECC — Why Headers Get More Than Payloads
절: Z23.3 Constructing the code
글:
Z23.3 Constructing the code

Part Z21 explained why the remembered MIPI parity masks were
 discarded: counted before use, they produced 27 distinct syndromes out of the 30 required. So the code here is built from first
 principles instead, and is not byte-compatible with CSI-2. The construction is
 four lines:

```
# 24 데이터 비트에 신드롬을 배정한다.
# 무게 1 짜리 패턴은 **패리티 비트 자신의 오류**가 쓰므로 데이터에 주면 안 된다.
cand = [s for s in range(1, 32) if bin(s).count('1') >= 2] # 26 개
syn = cand[:24] # 24 개만 쓴다

# 패리티 i 의 마스크 = 신드롬의 i 번째 비트가 1 인 데이터 비트들
masks = [[b for b in range(24) if (syn[b] >> i) & 1] for i in range(5)]
```

Why the syndromes must have weight ≥ 2

 | Step | Justification
1 | Each parity bit can itself be corrupted in transit. | The ECC field travels over the same lanes as the data.
2 | If parity bit i flips, the recomputed syndrome is 2 i — a weight-1 pattern. | Only that one parity check disagrees.
3 | So the five weight-1 patterns are already spoken for, and no data bit may be assigned one. | Otherwise a flipped parity bit and a flipped data bit look identical, and the decoder corrupts good data trying to fix a parity bit that nothing depends on.
4 | Of the 31 non-zero 5-bit patterns, 26 have weight ≥ 2, and we need 24. | It fits, with two spare. Had we needed 27 data bits, 5 parity bits would not have been enough.
5 | Verified rather than argued: all 29 syndromes distinct, none zero, no double-error syndrome colliding with a single-error syndrome. | 29/29, 0 인 것 없음

장: Z23. The Packet Header ECC — Why Headers Get More Than Payloads
절: Z23.4 Proven exhaustively
글:
Z23.4 Proven exhaustively

[Table 498. edu/proto/ecc_check.cpp]
Case | Enumerated | Result
No error | 6 representative data values | all report ECC_OK, data unchanged
Single error | 180 (30 bit positions × 6 data values) | 0 wrong — every one corrected
Double error | 2610 (all C(30,2) pairs × 6 data values) | 2610 detected, 0 miscorrections
Not degenerate | 20,000 random headers | 64 of 64 possible ECC values seen

Six representative data values rather than all 224, because
 the code is linear: the syndrome of a corrupted codeword depends only on the
 error pattern, not on the data underneath it. That is a property worth stating rather
 than assuming, so the six values span all-zeros, all-ones and four irregular patterns,
 and they all agree — which is the evidence that linearity holds in the
 implementation and not merely in the theory.

The stimulus mix in that table is the part most easily got wrong. A

Z2. The Daily and Weekly Loop

A two-member team has an unusual property: one member works when the
 other does not. That makes the shape of the day the main scheduling decision, and
 getting it right is worth more than working longer.

[그림] Figure 68. One day.

장: Z2. The Daily and Weekly Loop
절: Z2.1 The day
글:
Z2.1 The day

[Table 501. Four slots, and what each is for]
When | You do | Why then | What it must not become
Morning | Read the night's ledger. Triage: real failure, equivalent mutant, infrastructure noise. Apply or reject the proposed patches. | The information is freshest and the decisions unblock the rest of the day | Debugging. Triage decides what to debug; the debugging happens midday
Midday | The work that needs an unbroken stretch: the golden model, architecture, RTL, the hard bug from triage. | It is the only slot long enough | Email, or fiddling with the flow
Afternoon | Strengthen the oracle: one more property, one more corner in the stimulus, one measured bound, one lint rule. | This is what decides what the agent can catch tonight | Optional. It is the compounding part and it is always the first thing sacrificed
Evening | Launch the run and stop. Check it is alive, not that it is finished. | The agent has the night | Watching it. If you are watching, the ledger is not good enough

```
The evening command, and the morning one
# 저녁 -- 밤새 돌린다 (setsid/nohup/disown; 확인은 pgrep)
bash edu/agent/run.sh 12

# 아침 -- 무엇이 있었나
bash edu/agent/status.sh
python3 edu/agent/mutscore.py # 주 1회면 충분하다

# 밤새 빨간불이 났다면: 최소 사례와 제안된 편집이 원장에 있다
grep '빨간불' edu/agent/ledger/regress.jsonl | tail -5
```

The failure mode of this loop is that the afternoon
 slot disappears. It is the only slot with no immediate consequence — skip it
 and tonight's run still happens, this week's deliverable still moves — so it is
 the one that gets spent on whatever is urgent. Three weeks later the agent is finding
 nothing, not because the design is clean but because the oracle stopped growing while
 the design kept growing. The measurable symptom is a flat mutation score against a
 rising line count, and it is worth plotting: if the design grew 30 % and the
 mutant count did not, the suite is covering a smaller fraction of it than it
 was.

장: Z2. The Daily and Weekly Loop
절: Z2.2 The week
글:
Z2.2 The week

[Table 502. The week]
When | What | Why
Monday | Plan against the deliverable list; pick this week's one thing | A week with two goals finishes neither
Tuesday–Thursday | The daily loop | —
Friday morning | Mutation score across every block; read every escape | Weekly is the right cadence — daily is noise, monthly is too late to act on
Friday afternoon | Documentation for what changed this week | Written now it takes twenty minutes; written at release it takes days and is wrong
Friday, last thing | Tag, and run the full gate from a clean checkout | A green working directory is not a green repository — the commit may be missing a file

The Friday items are the ones that make a release possible without a release scramble. Both are cheap weekly and expensive in a batch, which is the general shape of everything in this chapter.

Worked example 90. What a night is actually worth

Given. The agent runs 12 hours. Each block's regression takes about 0.02 s of simulation per 600 stimuli, and a full mutation pass over five blocks takes about a minute.

Method. Count what the night can cover, then note what limits it — which is not the machine.

Regression rounds per hour (order) | 10 5
Distinct seeds consumed in 12 hours | ≈10 6
Mutation passes possible in one night | hundreds
Engineer-hours consumed | 0
What actually limits the value | the stimulus distribution and the golden model
Marginal value of the 500th mutation pass | zero
Marginal value of one new checker | large and permanent

How this is got wrong. By measuring the night in rounds. A million rounds of the same distribution explore the same region a thousand times — Part X8's coupon-collector arithmetic says the return flattens far below that. The honest use of the night is variety, not volume: rotate the constraint sets, replay every previous minimal reproducer as a growing regression, and run the mutation pass. A loop that only turns the seed stops learning within the first hour and then keeps the machine warm until morning.

장: Z2. The Daily and Weekly Loop
절: Z2.3 Triage: what to do with each thing in the ledger
글:
Z2.3 Triage: what to do with each thing in the ledger

[Table 503. The morning decision table]
Ledger says | You do | Time
초록 on every block | Nothing. Read the mutation trend instead | 1 min
자해검사 failed | Stop. The night's results mean nothing. Fix the harness first | Highest priority — a broken checker is worse than a broken design
자극이 DUT 를 안 건드렸다 | The stimulus degenerated — a constraint is over-tight or a parameter is wrong | 10 min
빨간불 -- 수리 적용됨 | Read the patch. It passed three gates; it still has to be right for the right reason | 5 min per patch
빨간불 -- 수리 후보 있음 (적용 안 함) | The agent found an edit and was not allowed to apply it. Decide | 5 min
빨간불 -- 수리 실패 | This is the real work. The minimal reproducer is in the ledger; it is outside the repair library, which usually means it is structural | The morning's budget goes here
적용했다가 되돌림 | The edit passed the first seeds and failed after application — look at why, it is usually an interacting change | 15 min
An escape in the mutation report | Equivalent mutant, or a hole in the stimulus. Write down which, and the reason | 5 min each, weekly

Record the verdict on every escape, permanently.
 An escape you have judged to be an equivalent mutant will reappear in every run
 forever, and re-deciding it each week is both wasted time and an invitation to stop
 reading the list. Keep a file of judged escapes with the reason — ‘extra
 loop iteration reads an out-of-range bit, which is x, so the branch is
 never taken’ — and have the report mark them as known. What must not
 happen is suppressing them silently: a suppressed escape whose reasoning was
 wrong is a permanent blind spot, and the file is the thing that lets a reviewer, or
 you in six months, check the reasoning.

Problem. The agent applied a patch overnight and the regression is green. Do you trust it?
Solution. Trust the evidence and check the reason, which are different things. The evidence is strong: the edit passed the original seed, passed a seed never used during the search (the overfitting gate), and passed the self-check confirming the comparison still bites. That rules out the classic automated-repair failure of special-casing the failing input. What it does not establish is that the edit is the change a human would have made. An edit that makes the symptom go away by tightening a condition can be correct on every stimulus the suite has and wrong in a case the suite does not reach — and if the suite reached that case, the bug would have been caught before the patch. So: read the diff, and ask what the original defect was. If you can state the defect in one sentence, keep the patch. If you cannot, the patch is masking something and the right response is to extend the stimulus until the failure is understood. Five minutes per patch, and it is the five minutes that keeps the arrangement honest.

장: Z3. The Quality Bar: What ‘Sellable’ Means as Numbers
절: Z3. The Quality Bar: What ‘Sellable’ Means as Numbers — 들어가며

Z3. The Quality Bar: What ‘Sellable’ Means as Numbers

‘Industry level’ is not a feeling. A customer's technical
 evaluation is a list of questions with numerical answers, and a block either has them
 or does not. This part is that list, with the acceptance criterion for each and the
 command that produces it. A block that passes every row is sellable; one that
 passes most of them is a prototype.

장: Z3. The Quality Bar: What ‘Sellable’ Means as Numbers
절: Z3.1 The gate list
글:
Z3.1 The gate list

[Table 504. The gates a sellable block passes]
Gate | What it asserts | How it is measured | Why
Functional agreement | Zero mismatches against an independent golden model, on many seeds | agent: 잰다() 틀림 == 0 , ≥ 20 seeds | Non-negotiable
The checker bites | Corrupting a golden value makes the comparison fail | 자해검사() == True every run | Without it the row above is meaningless
Stimulus is non-degenerate | The golden model produced many distinct outputs | 서로다른출력 ≥ 2 , in practice > 20 | A constant stimulus passes any design
Mutation score | Injected defects are caught | mutscore.py ≥ 90 %, every escape judged in writing | The number a knowledgeable buyer asks for
Throughput | Cycles per unit of work within a stated bound | 성능한계() declared and met | A value-only suite cannot see a block getting slower
Code and toggle coverage | Every line and every bit exercised | Verilator or a coverage-capable simulator | Weakest of the metrics; necessary, not sufficient
Lint clean | No inferred latches, no width mismatches, no incomplete sensitivity | verilator --lint-only -Wall , zero warnings or a written waiver | The customer will run this and judge you by it
Synthesises | To a gate netlist, with reported area and frequency | yosys plus a timing run, scripts shipped | An unsynthesisable block is not a product
CDC analysed | Every crossing identified, structured and constrained | A CDC tool, or a documented manual analysis with the constraints | The commonest integration failure
Reset verified | Random initialisation, many seeds; de-assertion synchronised per domain | Regression with randomised initial state | The commonest silicon failure
Register map generated | RTL, header, docs and IP-XACT from one source | house/regmap.py --전부 | Hand-maintained copies diverge
Documentation | Datasheet, integration guide, known issues, release notes | They exist and match the code | Support cost is inversely proportional to this
Reproducibility | A clean checkout reproduces every number | scripts/precheck.sh from HEAD, not the working directory | A missing file passes locally and fails for the customer

Nine of the thirteen are runnable by the agent, unattended. The four that are not — judging escapes, CDC analysis, documentation, and deciding what the block should do — are the ones this volume says belong to you.

The bar is not ‘no known bugs’; it is
 ‘here is the evidence, and here is what is not covered’. Every real IP
 block ships with limitations, and Part Y5 argues that naming them is what
 distinguishes a professional supplier. The gate list above is what converts that from
 a posture into a document: each row either passes, or fails with a stated reason and a
 workaround. A customer can evaluate that. They cannot evaluate an
 assurance.

절: Z3.2 Running the whole bar in one command

Z3.2 Running the whole bar in one command

A gate that requires remembering to run it is a gate that will be
 skipped in the week it matters. The repository's own discipline applies: one command,
 from a clean checkout, that runs everything and refuses to report green on anything it
 could not check.

```
edu/house/release.sh — the release gate
bash edu/house/release.sh 

 1. 깨끗한 판을 꺼낸다 -- 작업 디렉터리를 안 본다
 2. 자해검사 -- 비교가 무는가
 3. 회귀 (씨앗 20개) -- 값과 순서
 4. 성능 -- 선언된 한계 안인가

 7. 합성 (yosys) -- 면적과 셀 수

**못 잰 것을 초록이라고 하지 않는다.** 도구가 없으면 '없어서 못 쟀다' 로 낸다.
```

Worked example 91. What the gate costs to run

Given. Five blocks, the regression at 20 seeds each, a mutation pass, lint and synthesis.

Method. Estimate from the measured per-step times in this book's own runs.

Regression, 600 stimuli | 0.03 s per seed per block
20 seeds × 5 blocks | 3 s
Self-check | 0.15 s
Mutation pass, 5 blocks | ≈60 s
Lint | seconds
Synthesis | seconds to minutes per block
Whole gate | a few minutes
How often it should run | every push, and nightly

How this is got wrong. By assuming the gate is expensive and running it at release. At a few minutes it is cheap enough to run on every push, and a gate that runs on every push finds the regression on the commit that caused it rather than three weeks later. The expensive parts — a full mutation pass over a large block, a long synthesis — belong in the nightly run, which costs nothing at all because nobody is waiting.

절: Z3.3 What the numbers should look like
글:
Z3.3 What the numbers should look like

[Table 505. Acceptance thresholds: internal and at release]
Metric | Internal (keep working) | Release | Note
Mismatches | 0 | 0 | Any non-zero is a stop
Self-check | passes | passes | A failure invalidates the run
Distinct outputs | > 20 | > 20 | Low means the stimulus degenerated
Mutation score | ≥ 90 % | ≥ 95 % | Escapes all judged and recorded
Escapes unjudged | 0 | 0 | An unjudged escape is an unexamined hole
Lint warnings | 0 | 0 | Or a written waiver per warning
Coverage (line) | > 95 % | > 99 % | Unreached lines explained
Throughput margin | > 10 % | > 20 % | Against the declared bound
Documented registers | 100 % | 100 % | Generated, not typed
Known issues listed | yes | yes | Absence is not a clean sheet

Two columns because they serve different purposes. The internal column is what you refuse to go home below; the release column is what a customer's evaluation will find. Setting the internal bar lower than the release bar is how a release becomes a scramble.

Problem. A customer's technical evaluation asks for your verification plan. What do you send?
Solution. Not a narrative. Send four things, and their existence is most of the answer. The gate list of Z3.1 with each row's current value — this is a table of facts and it is what they are actually trying to establish. The mutation report, escapes included, because it is the one artefact that demonstrates the suite bites rather than merely runs, and very few suppliers have one; including the escapes with their judgements is more convincing than a higher score without them. The known-issue list, dated, with workarounds. And the command they can run themselves on the delivered package to reproduce every number. The fourth is the one that converts the first three from claims into evidence, and it is the reason the release gate must run from a clean checkout rather than from your working directory — if it only works on your machine, they will find that out, and it will cost more than the bug it hides.

The map validates itself, and that is most of the

장: Z4. The Deliverable Pack, Built and Gated
절: Z4.4 Three generator bugs the gate found
글:
Z4.4 Three generator bugs the gate found

The register-map generator was written from Part Y10's argument
 and looked correct. The agent and the gate found three defects in it, none of which
 any amount of reading would have found, and each is instructive about a different
 failure mode.

[Table 509. What was found, and by which gate]
Bug | Found by | Why reading would not have found it
An ID register could not hold a constant. Every RO field was wired to a hardware input, so a vendor code read as zero | The regression, against an independent model | The generator was internally consistent — it did exactly what its author intended, and the intention was incomplete
A read-clear register cleared during the APB setup phase. rd was psel & ~pwrite , missing penable | The regression, after the stimulus was extended | It reads as correct; the defect is in the protocol's two-phase timing, which only a running comparison exposes
A software-set field had an unused hardware port. W1S defaulted to hardware-driven, which is wrong for the common case | verilator -Wall (UNUSEDSIGNAL) | An unused port is harmless functionally and is a question the integrator has to ask you

And the mutation score found the stimulus hole that
 hid the second one. Before it ran, the register-file regression was green on 400
 accesses and scored 58.3 %. Five escapes all pointed at the same place: the
 hardware-side inputs were tied to zero, so the W1C and RC paths had never executed.
 Driving them turned up two real failures within minutes. The green regression was
 not wrong — those 400 accesses did match — and it was nearly
 worthless. That distinction is the whole argument for measuring whether a suite
 bites rather than whether it passes.

Problem. You have one week before a customer evaluation. What do you build first?
Solution. Not more features. Build, in this order, the things the evaluation will actually test. First the gate, because everything else is easier to trust once one command produces the numbers; a day. Then the mutation score, because it is the single artefact that distinguishes you from a supplier who says ‘we tested it thoroughly’, and because it will find the stimulus holes you do not know about; half a day plus whatever it turns up. Then the known-issue list, which costs an afternoon and is read as competence rather than as weakness. Then the integration guide, written as if for someone you will never speak to. Only then the datasheet, because by that point every number in it exists and is reproducible — which means writing it takes an hour instead of a day and none of it is invented. A week spent this way produces a smaller block that can be bought; a week spent on features produces a larger one that cannot.

Scores are judgements, and stating them as numbers is what makes them arguable. A reader who disagrees can change one cell and see whether the ranking moves — which is the point of a scorecard and the reason it beats a paragraph of reasoning.

On these weights the winner is
 ML-KEM (Kyber) NTT 코어, and the reason is worth reading off the table rather than taking on
 trust: it is the only candidate that scores 3 on all four of specification
 availability, independent golden model, soft RTL, and a changing standard with few

 demanding block into a market whose incumbents built their portfolios around RSA and
 ECC. And Part X6's entire FFT analysis transfers to the NTT — same
 radix choices, same twiddle symmetries, same memory-versus-multiplier trade, with
 modular arithmetic replacing complex arithmetic. A team that has built an FFT has most

Every candidate scores zero on ‘a customer you
 can name’, and that is the real finding. The scorecard ranks technical and
